Luciano Carlos Cunha

A Journey Through Animal Ethics: From Basic to Advanced

The complete text of the 12 volumes, in plain HTML

About this file

This file gathers the complete text of Luciano Carlos Cunha’s collection, in English translation: 12 volumes, 186 chapters, 1,219 author’s notes and 1,198 references, about 270,000 words (22 hours of reading). There are no menus, scripts or study layers: only the text, with the notes at the end of each chapter and the references at the end of each volume. It was made for readers who prefer a single document, want to read offline or want to turn it into an e-book.

How to use it

  • Save: press Ctrl+S (⌘S on a Mac) and choose “Web page, HTML only”. The file works offline; only the images in the text are loaded from the site.
  • Make an e-book: open the saved file in Calibre (free) and convert it to EPUB or to your reader’s format. The volume and chapter titles become the e-book’s table of contents.
  • Print or save as PDF: press Ctrl+P; each volume starts on a new page.
  • Read on the site: the full version, with interactive notes and sources, simplified versions, lessons, quizzes and tools, is at questaodeetica.biblioverse.org/en/. The original PDFs, in Portuguese, are at senciencia.org.

Volume I

Discussing Speciesism

This book offers a critical analysis of the arguments most commonly advanced in an attempt to defend the view that nonhuman animals either should not receive moral consideration or should receive it to a lesser degree than humans.

Original text by Luciano Carlos Cunha, translated into English · ISBN 978-65-01-30510-3 · 1st edition, January 2025.

1. An Overview of the Debate on the Moral Consideration of Animals

1.1. Views according to which nonhuman animals do not matter in themselves

According to some views, the good of nonhuman animals does not matter in itself. On these views, the reasons against harming them and for helping them have nothing to do with the possible harm or benefit the animals themselves would experience, but rather with the indirect impact those attitudes would have on other things (which, by contrast, are seen as important in themselves), such as human interests1 and environmentalist goals2, like conserving species or ecosystems.

One example is the claim that what is wrong with causing suffering and death to a nonhuman animal has nothing to do with the harm to the animal, but rather with the risk that it might serve as practice for later harming humans, or with the idea that whoever attacks the animal would be wounding humanity in themselves through brutalization3.

Another example along these lines is the claim that the problem with consuming animals lies not in the harm done to the animals, but in the risk to human health or in its possible negative impact on the environment.

1.2. Views that give consideration to animals, but to a lesser degree

Positions of a second type agree that the good of nonhuman animals matters directly, but hold that it matters less than the good of humans4. They recognize that the possibility that nonhuman animals will be harmed if we adopt a certain course of action is already, in itself, a reason to try to avoid that course of action. However, they maintain that these reasons are weaker than they would be if humans were at risk of suffering an equivalent harm (or even a lesser harm, according to some positions in this group).

In short, these views give moral consideration to nonhuman animals, but they build hierarchies with humans at the top. This does not mean, however, that such positions will necessarily favor animal exploitation or oppose helping animals. Everything will depend on the weight each variant of this type of position gives to the good of animals compared with the conflicting human interest.

This group includes both positions that give very little consideration to animals and positions that consider them to a greater degree. An example of the former would be asking, "why worry about nonhuman animals while there are still so many humans in need of help?" The latter, on the other hand, might even oppose animal exploitation out of concern for the animals themselves, and might also recognize that we have direct reasons to help them, even when what threatens them is not human practices (as when they are victims of natural processes such as hunger, thirst, disease, natural disasters, and so on). What all these positions have in common, however, is that they would hold that these reasons are weaker than they would be if humans were at risk of suffering an equivalent harm (or even a lesser harm, according to some positions).

Sometimes other positions build similar hierarchies, based not on the species of individuals but on their cognitive capacities5. According to these views, equivalent harms (or even harms of lesser magnitude) matter more if they are suffered by more cognitively complex beings6. An example of this type of view is the claim that equivalent harms matter more if they are suffered by adult humans than by children, or by mammals than by fish.

1.3. Views that give equal consideration to all sentient beings

Finally, other positions defend equal consideration for all sentient beings, that is, for all beings capable of having positive and negative experiences. These positions hold that harms and benefits of similar magnitude should be given the same weight, regardless of the individuals' species, physical characteristics, capacities, the degree of relationship they have with us, and so on.

According to these positions, the harm caused to animals is sufficient to make animal exploitation unjust, regardless of any other indirect harms it may cause to humans or to the environment. However, as we have seen, this could also be recognized by some positions that give some consideration to animals, though less than that given to humans. What is distinctive about positions that defend equal consideration is that they would maintain that animal exploitation is just as unjust as it would be if humans were being exploited, suffering harms of similar magnitude.

The same holds for the harms animals suffer not as a result of human practices, but as a result of natural processes (such as disease, hunger, thirst, natural disasters, and so on). For example, the situation of wild animals is already very bad as a result of natural processes themselves. Again, we have seen that some positions that give some consideration to animals, though less than that given to humans, could recognize that in these cases too the harm to the animals already gives us direct reasons to try to help them. But positions that defend equal consideration would go further: they would say that we should give as much importance to trying to improve the situation of these animals as we would if human victims were suffering harms of similar magnitude.

In short, positions that defend equal consideration argue that nonhuman animals are discriminated against not only when they receive no consideration at all, but also when they receive lesser consideration. We will see more about this below:

1.4. Speciesism and anthropocentrism

The use of nonhuman animals as resources is widely accepted and practiced. However, doing the same to humans is widely considered unacceptable. For example, if humans were being bred and killed to be turned into food, it would hardly be said that the reasons for not eating them have to do with concern for our own health or for the environment. Instead, it would be recognized that the injustice the victims suffer is reason enough. But because the actual victims are nonhuman animals, the discourse is the opposite: concern for the animals is placed last (when it appears at all), behind concern for human interests and environmentalist goals;

Anthropocentric attitudes are not limited to exploitation. For example, as we have seen, wild animals constantly suffer and die prematurely as a result of hunger, thirst, disease, and natural disasters7. The common view is that there are reasons to help them only if doing so is necessary to achieve environmentalist goals8 (preserving endangered species, ecosystems, biodiversity, ecological balance, and so on) or anthropocentric ones (for example, preventing them from transmitting diseases to humans). Beyond that, what is usually advocated is "letting nature take its course." The suffering and mortality of animals living in the wild could in many cases be prevented, but given the predominance of this kind of mindset, people usually choose not to help them. By contrast, when humans are victims of the same natural processes, the common view is that we should help them, out of concern for their own good and not for indirect reasons.

These two kinds of situations show that most people rely on a moral double standard, depending on whether or not the victims belong to the human species. Since the 1970s, several authors9 have accused this double standard of committing a form of discrimination analogous to racism: speciesism10. Discrimination can be defined as unfavorable treatment that is unjust11. Speciesism, then, is discrimination against those who do not belong to a certain species (or species). Anthropocentrism is therefore a form of speciesism: it is the unjust unfavorable treatment of those who do not belong to the human species.

2. Is Species What Matters?

2.1. A double standard

Enormous numbers of nonhuman animals suffer and are killed as a result of their exploitation for the most diverse purposes. Moreover, nonhuman animals rarely receive the help they need when they are affected by natural processes such as hunger, thirst, disease, natural disasters, and so on. All of this is widely accepted and rarely questioned. However, if similar attitudes were held toward humans, they would be widely considered unacceptable. Is it possible to justify this moral double standard?

2.2. Do humans matter more simply because they are human?

It is sometimes argued that the reason only humans should receive moral consideration (or should receive it to a greater degree) is the very fact that they belong to the human species12.

The central problem with this argument is that it does not explain why belonging to the human species would be relevant to questions of moral consideration. What is at issue is precisely what it is about humans that would justify disadvantaging nonhuman animals. Saying that "humans are human" does not provide that answer. That is, the argument assumes in advance what it sets out to prove, committing the fallacy known as begging the question13. This fallacy consists in trying to show that the conclusion of an argument is true while already starting from the assumption that it is true and using it as one of the premises.

For example, imagine someone said that only frogs should be respected. We would certainly want to know why. If the person replied, "well, it's simply because frogs are frogs," we would immediately see that this "explanation" explains nothing at all. Yet the same applies to humans.

2.3. Should each of us favor members of our own species?

Another attempt to justify anthropocentrism consists in claiming that only humans should receive moral consideration (or should receive it to a greater degree), not because they belong to the human species, but because they belong to the same species we belong to14.

Unlike the claim that there is something special about humans simply because they are human, what this attempt claims is that there is something special about the fact that whoever is making a decision belongs to the same species as those who will be affected by it. According to this position, because we belong to the human species, we should favor humans, but if we belonged to, say, the species Sus scrofa domesticus, we should favor pigs. Proponents of this position say they do not need to explain what is special about humans, because they do not claim that "everyone should favor humans," but rather that "everyone should favor members of their own species."

The central problem with this attempt is that it does not explain why whether those affected by a decision belong to the same species as the decision-maker would be relevant to questions of moral consideration. Instead of offering that explanation, this attempt assumes in advance that the species one belongs to is what matters (and that is precisely what is at issue in the debate about speciesism). Therefore, this defense also commits the fallacy of begging the question.

To draw an analogy, imagine a racist claimed that he did not need to explain what is special about the members of his race, because what he is saying is "let each person favor members of their own race" (and not that everyone should favor members of his race). We could still challenge him by asking: "and what is the relevance of race to determining how much consideration we should give someone?" And, clearly, simply saying "let each person favor members of their own race" does not provide that explanation. Yet the same happens when someone says "let each person favor members of their own species."

Of course, there are other attempts to justify anthropocentrism, discussed elsewhere. Our conclusion here, however, is more specific: these two attempts, because they beg the question, fail to justify it.

3. Could Metaphysical Characteristics Justify Speciesism?

3.1. The appeal to metaphysical characteristics

It is sometimes argued that only humans should receive moral consideration (or should receive it to a greater degree) because humans are allegedly the only beings that possess one of the following characteristics15:

(a) They were created in the image and likeness of a creator; (b) They have a special relationship with that creator; (c) They have an immortal soul; (d) They have dignity; (e) They belong to a higher ontological category.

The ideas of dignity and of a higher ontological category are generally used in a quite specific sense by the proponents of these positions. What they usually mean is that humans have a special value that implies they should be the only ones respected (or should be respected to a greater degree), and that the reasons we have to respect them have nothing to do with the possibility of harming or benefiting them, but rather with their possessing this special value.

3.2. Problems with the appeal to metaphysical characteristics

There are three main problems with all of these attempts to defend anthropocentrism16.

The first is that it is impossible to prove whether or not anyone meets these criteria. It is not only that it is impossible to verify empirically whether someone meets them: there also seems to be no way of showing in any other manner that humans satisfy these criteria and nonhuman animals do not.

The second problem is that none of these defenses explains why possessing any of those characteristics would be relevant to questions of moral consideration. They simply assume in advance that they are relevant.

The third problem is that there are reasons to think that whether or not one possesses these characteristics is irrelevant to questions of moral consideration. What is at stake in questions of moral consideration is the possibility that our decisions will harm or benefit those affected by them. So what seems relevant to knowing whom to give moral consideration to is knowing who can be harmed or benefited. Possessing those characteristics does not determine who can be harmed and benefited. What determines that is sentience (that is, being capable of having positive and/or negative experiences).

Author’s notes

  1. Examples are the positions defended by Harrison (1989) and Reichmann (2000). ↩
  2. For a detailed analysis of the problems with these attempts to justify anthropocentrism, see Horta (2007, p. 429-464). ↩

4. Could the Possession of Capacities or Relationships Justify Speciesism?

4.1. The appeal to capacities

It is sometimes argued that only humans matter (or matter to a greater degree) because they possess certain capacities17, such as reason; language; freedom; a sense of right and wrong; a sense of justice; autonomy; culture, and so on. These capacities enable humans to do things such as: make mutual agreements; understand the notion of rights; respect the rights of others; claim their rights, and so on.

Proponents of this view commonly claim things like: "animals cannot have rights because they have no duties"; "animals cannot have rights because they are incapable of fighting for their rights"; "animals do not suffer injustice because they do not understand what justice is," "only cognitively sophisticated beings should be respected," and so on.

4.2. The appeal to relationships

At other times it is said that only humans matter (or matter to a greater degree) not because they possess certain capacities, but because they have certain relationships with one another18, such as relationships of affection, mutual solidarity, political relationships, and power relationships. An example of an appeal to political relationships is the claim that we are justified in giving lesser consideration to nonhuman animals (or even in disregarding them completely) because they do not contribute their labor to our society19. An example of an appeal to a power relationship, in turn, is the claim that we are justified in doing whatever we please with nonhuman animals simply because we have the power to do so20.

4.3. Problems common to all these arguments

A first problem, common to all these arguments, is that many humans do not possess these capacities or relationships21. For example: babies, children up to a certain age, and humans who are victims of certain diseases or accidents that prevent the exercise of those capacities or relationships. If the lack of these capacities or relationships in these humans does not justify treating them worse (much less justify disregarding them completely), then neither could it justify treating nonhuman animals worse (much less justify the suffering and deaths to which they are routinely subjected).

The second problem is that none of these arguments explains why possessing those capacities or relationships would be relevant to questions of moral consideration. This is simply assumed in advance. Yet that is exactly what these arguments would need to explain, since it is not obvious (indeed, as we have seen, it is widely rejected when humans are affected by our decisions).

The third problem is that there are reasons to think that whether or not one possesses these capacities or relationships is completely irrelevant to questions of moral consideration22. What is at stake in questions of moral consideration is the possibility that our decisions will harm or benefit those affected by them. So what seems relevant to knowing whom to give moral consideration to is knowing who can be harmed or benefited. Possessing those capacities or relationships does not determine who can be harmed and benefited. What determines that is sentience (that is, the capacity to have positive and negative experiences).

Author’s notes

  1. Examples are the positions defended by Francis; Norman (1978); Mccloskey (1979); Frey (1980); Leahy (1991); Carruthers (1992) and Ferry (2009 [1992]). ↩
  2. Examples are the positions defended by Narveson (1977, 1987); Becker (1983); Midgley (1983); Callicott (1989); Næss (1989); Mosterín (1998); Petrinovich (1999) and Goldman (2001). ↩
  3. See, for example, the position defended by Goldman (2001, p. 61) ↩
  4. Examples can be found in Narveson (1977) and Petrinovich (1999). ↩
  5. For this criticism in detail, see Ehnert (2002) and Horta (2014). ↩
  6. For this criticism in detail, see Horta (2018a) and Cunha (2021, p. 57-61). ↩

5. Could Humans' Supposed Potential Justify Speciesism?

5.1. The appeal to potential

It is sometimes argued that only humans should be respected (or should be respected to a greater degree) because all humans (and only humans) allegedly have the potential to develop certain capacities or relationships, even though many humans do not in fact have them23. The capacities most often cited are complex cognitive capacities, and the relationships most often cited are relationships of mutual solidarity, political relationships, or power relationships.

What is meant by potential is the following. Babies do not yet possess, for example, complex cognitive capacities, but they may one day come to have them as adults. Elderly people with a degenerative mental illness no longer possess those capacities, but they once had them. They are therefore potential bearers of those capacities and relationships, even if not actual bearers.

Nonhuman animals, on the other hand, allegedly lack this potential, and therefore, according to this view, it would be justified to do certain things to them that would never be right if done to humans, such as using them for food, clothing, as test subjects, and so on, and also not helping them when they are victims of disease, hunger, thirst, and so on.

5.2. Problems with the appeal to potential

Let us look at some problems with this argument24:

A first problem is that there are humans who do not even have the potential to develop those capacities or relationships. For example, there are humans with an incurable congenital condition that will prevent them throughout their entire lives from exercising those capacities and relationships. According to the appeal to potential, it would be right to do to them all the terrible things that are done to nonhuman animals.

In response to this, proponents of the appeal to potential sometimes argue that, in the case of these humans, we have to take into account the possibility of a scientific breakthrough or even a miracle25. However, one could reply that it would then be arbitrary not to take the same possibilities into account in the case of nonhuman animals.

A second problem is that the appeal in question does not explain why possessing (actually or potentially) those capacities or relationships would be relevant to whether someone should receive moral consideration or to determining how much consideration they should receive. This is simply assumed by the argument, without any explanation.

The third (and main) problem is that the reasons we have, for example, not to cause suffering to a child seem to exist simply because suffering is something bad, and not because the child may in the future come to develop those capacities and relationships. For example, if we know that a child has a terminal illness and will die before developing those capacities and relationships, it seems we still have every reason to respect her as much as any other human being. If so, then it makes no sense to say that we do not have to respect nonhuman animals (or that they should be respected to a lesser degree) because they lack the potential for those capacities or relationships.

Author’s notes

  1. See, for example, the positions of Devine (1978); Mccloskey (1979); Leahy (1991) and Wetlesen (1999). ↩
  2. For other criticisms of the appeal to potential, see Singer (2022 [1979], p. 163; 1991, p. 60). ↩
  3. See, for example, McCloskey (1979, p. 42) and Paton (1984, p. 33). ↩

6. Is What Matters Belonging to the Same Species as Those Who Have Certain Capacities?

6.1. The appeal to the group

It is often argued that what makes it right to exploit nonhuman animals and not to help them when they are victims of disease, hunger, thirst, and so on, while at the same time making it wrong to do the same to humans, is the fact that humans possess certain capacities (for example, complex cognitive capacities) or certain relationships (of mutual solidarity, political relationships, power relationships, and so on).

One reply to this argument points out that it is simply false that all humans possess these capacities or relationships26. For example, children up to a certain age and victims of certain diseases or accidents that affect mental capacities do not possess them. However, this does not seem to justify treating them worse (much less justify doing to them what is normally done to nonhuman animals). Quite the contrary: the lack of these capacities and relationships is seen as a reason to give them even greater care, since it makes them more vulnerable. But if so, then the lack of these capacities and relationships in nonhuman animals could not justify treating them worse (much less justify the terrible things done to them): on the contrary, it is a reason for them to receive even greater protection.

Some authors, however, think this reply does not work. In defense of anthropocentrism, they put forward what is known as the appeal to the group. The appeal to the group consists in saying that only humans matter (or matter to a greater degree) because all humans belong to a species whose normal members possess those capacities or relationships, regardless of the fact that many humans do not possess them (or do not even have the potential for them)27.

Below we will look at some problems with this argument28:

6.2. Problems with the appeal to the group

The first problem is that the appeal to the group commits the fallacy known as begging the question (it assumes what it sets out to prove). For example, imagine we ask: "Why do only humans matter?" and the answer is: "Because they possess a series of capacities or relationships." But imagine that, in response, we ask: "And what about the humans who do not possess them?" and the answer is "They matter equally, because they are human."

This reveals that the argument, although it sets out to explain why the species criterion is relevant to questions of moral consideration, already assumes in advance that belonging to the same species as the individuals who possess those capacities or relationships is what matters for questions of moral consideration. One could equally say, for example, that what matters is belonging to the same biological kingdom (rather than species) as the individuals who possess those capacities or relationships.

The second problem is that the argument does not explain why possessing those capacities or relationships would be relevant to whether someone should receive moral consideration or to how much consideration they should receive. This, too, is simply assumed in advance.

The third problem is that there are reasons to think that whether or not one possesses these capacities or relationships is irrelevant to questions of moral consideration. What is at stake in questions of moral consideration is the possibility that our decisions will harm or benefit those affected by them. So what seems relevant to knowing whom to give moral consideration to is knowing who can be harmed or benefited. Possessing those capacities or relationships does not determine who can be harmed and benefited. What determines that is sentience (that is, being capable of having positive and negative experiences). Moreover, possessing those capacities or relationships does not determine the degree of harms and benefits either. Therefore, it is also not relevant to determining the degree of consideration someone should receive.

The fourth problem with the appeal to the group is that it is arbitrary, since it would include within the sphere of moral consideration the humans who lack the characteristics cited to exclude nonhuman animals, and would exclude even those nonhuman animals who had those characteristics. For example, suppose we ask: "Why don't nonhuman animals matter?" and the answer is: "Because they do not possess a series of capacities or relationships." Imagine that we then ask: "And what if some nonhuman animal possesses those capacities or relationships?" and the answer is: "Even so, it does not matter, because it is not human." In short, the argument is highly biased.

6.3. The appeal to a combination of the species criterion and the capacities/relationships criterion

It is sometimes said that, for an individual to matter, they need to meet only one of these two criteria: either belonging to the human species or possessing certain capacities or relationships. This would avoid the fourth problem of the appeal to the group (since, in that case, if a nonhuman animal had any of those capacities or relationships, it would receive full moral consideration).

However, this combination still faces four similar problems:

The first problem is that it still begs the question. It aims to explain the relevance of the species criterion but, instead, assumes in advance that this criterion is relevant.

The second problem is that it still does not explain why possessing those capacities or relationships would be relevant to questions of moral consideration.

The third problem is that there are good reasons to think that possessing those capacities or relationships is relevant neither to knowing whom we should give consideration to nor to how much consideration we should give, since such capacities or relationships determine neither who can be harmed or benefited nor the degree of harm or benefit one would be subject to.

The fourth problem is that, although it avoids being biased in the way the previous argument is, it remains biased, only in a different way: it requires nonhuman animals to have some of those capacities or relationships in order to receive moral consideration, but does not require the same of members of the human species.

Author’s notes

  1. For this criticism in detail, see Ehnert (2002) and Horta (2014). ↩
  2. See, for example, Scruton (1996, p. 54-5); Campbell (2001, p. 164) and Machan (2002, p. 11). ↩
  3. For more detailed criticisms, see Clark (1977, p. 135); Singer (1991, p. 61-2) and Rollin (1998, p. 418). ↩

7. If Species Are Not a Social Construct, Is Speciesism Justified?

7.1. The appeal to the distinction between the biological and the socially constructed

Nonhuman animals are exploited for the most diverse purposes. They are used for food, clothing, as test subjects, for entertainment and leisure, and as workers or tools. This use kills literally trillions of animals every year, usually after a life full of suffering. Animals living in the wild are also constantly victims of disease, hunger, thirst, natural disasters, and so on. In many of these cases, it would be possible to prevent their suffering and deaths. However, the standard view is that it is wrong to help them. It is commonly said that we should let nature take its course, even if the outcome is terrible for the animals.

In both kinds of situations, if the victims were human, such attitudes would be widely condemned. In fact, more than that: such attitudes would be considered monstrous, heinous. This moral double standard based on the victim's species has been accused of committing a form of discrimination analogous to racism and sexism: speciesism29

However, there are people who disagree with this comparison. For example, it is sometimes said that using the species criterion for questions of moral consideration is not unjust because it is a criterion that refers to biological characteristics30. According to this argument, racism and sexism, on the other hand, would be unjust because the very ideas of race and gender are allegedly social constructs. Let us look at some problems with this argument.

7.2. Problems with the appeal to biological distinctions

A first problem is that it does not explain why a criterion's being based on biological characteristics or on a social construct would be relevant to whether it is just

or unjust. This is simply assumed by the argument, without any explanation.

A second problem is that there are examples of criteria referring to biological characteristics that are clearly unjust. Imagine, for example, a system of slavery based on individuals' height. If the fact that this criterion is based on a biological characteristic cannot make it just, then the fact that the species criterion is based on a biological characteristic cannot make it just either.

Indeed, it seems that a criterion's being based on a biological characteristic cannot even make it less unjust than it would be if it were based on a social construct. This is because the injustice of a criterion depends on its treating individuals in a biased way, and not on whether the criterion it uses refers to social constructs or to biological traits.

Racism and sexism are unjust because they disadvantage individuals of certain groups in a biased way. If it were shown, for example, that races and genders are not social constructs, racism and sexism would remain just as unjust as they would be if races and genders are social constructs. Yet the same is true in the case of speciesism. The fact that the concept of species refers to biological characteristics does not make speciesism just, nor does it even make it less unjust than other forms of discrimination, such as racism and sexism.

Author’s notes

  1. On the definition of speciesism, see Horta (2022 [2010]); Horta; Albersmeier (2020) and Albersmeier (2021). ↩
  2. A similar argument is given by Cohen in a debate with Regan. See Cohen; Regan (2001, p. 61-2). For a criticism of this argument, see Cunha (2021, p. 46; 2022a, p. 39). ↩

8. If Speciesism Is Natural, Is Speciesism Justified?

8.1. The appeal to nature

It is often argued that what makes it just to give moral consideration only to humans (or to give greater moral consideration to humans) is that this is a natural attitude for us. For example, in an attempt to justify eating animals, people commonly say "that's just how nature is: animals kill and eat members of other species"; "humans are at the top of the food chain"; "humans are naturally hunters," and so on.

Animal advocates sometimes respond by denying that eating animals is natural for humans. However, this response does not address (and instead assumes) the main problem with the argument: the assumption that, if an attitude is natural, it is justified.

Therefore, below we will look at some problems with the appeal to what is natural31.

8.2. Problems with the appeal to nature

The first problem is that the argument does not explain why the fact that a behavior is natural would make it just. This is simply assumed, without any explanation. But that is exactly what the argument would have to explain.

The second problem is that the expression "natural behavior" is used in a wide variety of senses. However, in whatever sense it is being used, the fact that a behavior is natural does not seem to make it just. Below we will look at some examples of what is commonly meant when it is claimed that eating meat is natural for humans. However, the same problems arise for any other appeal to what is natural.

Sometimes what is meant by "eating meat is natural for humans" is that it is possible for the human body to consume meat. However, if the mere fact that a behavior is possible made it just, any possible behavior would be just. For example, it is also possible for the human body to consume human flesh, but this does not seem to

justify such an act. In the same way, the mere fact that it is possible for the human body to consume the flesh of other animals does not imply that it is just to do so.

At other times, what is meant when it is claimed that a behavior is natural is that there is an instinctive inclination toward that behavior, as if it were something "written in our genes." However, once again, this does not seem sufficient to justify a behavior. Imagine, for example, that humans had an instinctive inclination to be biased in their judgments and to abuse the most vulnerable. The fact that there is an instinctive tendency does not make such behaviors just. It may be that, if we had such a tendency, most of us would consider such behaviors just. But the fact that, under such conditions, we would consider such behaviors just does not show that they are in fact just.

Another very common claim is that eating animals is justified because, in nature, animals eat one another. The idea behind this argument is that, if animals in nature do a certain thing, then we should do the same.

However, there are two problems here. The first is that there are animals that do not eat other animals. Since the argument aims to justify eating animals, it is biased, to say the least, to choose to imitate precisely the animals that eat other animals, and not those that do not, without giving any further reason for this choice.

The second problem is that there are animals in nature that steal, rape, kill, and eat members of their own species, including the offspring of rivals or even their own offspring. No one argues that it is right for humans to do the same just because other animals also do it. The appeal to what animals do arises almost exclusively in attempts to justify eating animals. Moreover, animals in nature also do not have hospital systems, cell phones, computers, schools, libraries, clothes, cars, and so on. It is arbitrary, to say the least, to want to imitate animals in nature only when they eat other animals, and not in everything else.

At other times, what is argued is that killing animals for food is right because humans are at the top of the food chain. It is often pointed out that, in nature, larger animals kill and eat smaller ones, and that this is what makes it right for humans to kill other animals for food. However, nothing forces humans to eat other animals. So this is no different from saying that we are justified in doing something just because we have the power to do it (and we have already seen above the problems with this view, when we discussed the definition of natural behavior as synonymous with possible behavior). For example, imagine there were a species more powerful than humans, and that its members bred humans to eat. These beings would be at the top of the food chain, but that does not seem to make their behavior just.

Finally, sometimes what is meant when a behavior is said to be natural is simply that it is right. But if so, when someone says "this behavior is right because it is natural," the claim is empty, because what is being said is that "this behavior is right because it is right," without giving any reason to think it is right.

All of this leads us to the following conclusion: there seems to be no correlation whatsoever between what is natural and what is justifiable.

Author’s notes

  1. For a detailed criticism of the appeal to nature, see Mill (1904) and Rachels; Rachels (2012, p. 44-8, 54-8). ↩

9. Does the Fact That Speciesist Practices Are Traditions Show That We Should Respect Them?

9.1. A double standard depending on the victims' species

Animals are exploited for the most diverse purposes, which means that they usually have a life full of suffering, in addition to being killed. Moreover, when they are victims of natural processes such as hunger, thirst, disease, and natural disasters, the standard view is that we should let nature take its course, without helping them. However, such attitudes would never be considered acceptable if the victims were human. In fact, if the victims were human, such attitudes would be considered monstrous. Many people believe there is nothing wrong with this double standard of treatment based on the victims' species. But is it possible to justify this disparity?

9.2. The appeal to tradition

It is sometimes argued that common attitudes toward nonhuman animals are justified because they are traditional, that is, they have been cultivated for a long time, passed down from generation to generation. For example, the use of nonhuman animals for the most diverse purposes is traditional in a wide variety of cultures. Appeals to respect for traditions and cultures are very common. However, this does not make them free of problems. Below we will look at some of these problems32.

9.3. The appeal to tradition could not justify anthropocentrism

The first problem is that the argument has the opposite implication from the one it intends. The argument aims to explain why exploiting nonhuman animals is just, whereas doing the same to humans would not be. However, if the fact that a practice is traditional made it just, then it would equally have to be said that racism, sexism, and even human slavery are just practices, since they are traditional practices.

9.4. Not every tradition is just

The second problem is that the argument does not explain why the fact that a practice is traditional would make it just. There are countless examples of practices that were (and some still are) deeply traditional in many societies and are also highly unjust and even heinous: human slavery, human sacrifice, burning people accused of witchcraft, throwing people to the lions, female genital mutilation, crucifixion, impalement, marriages between adults and children, and so on.

9.5. Discussing the defenses of the claim that traditions should be respected

The third problem is that there seem to be only two ways of defending the claim that we should respect traditions, but neither would support the claim that we should respect traditions that create victims, as speciesist practices do. Let us see:

9.5.1. The defense that traditions are good because they benefit individuals

One way to defend the claim that we should respect traditions is to point to the benefit they bring to individuals. For example, one could point to the benefits that animal exploitation provides to humans.

However, if the benefit a tradition brings to certain individuals is a reason in its favor, then it would be arbitrary not to count the harms it causes to other individuals as a reason against it. And in the case of speciesist practices and of other traditions that create victims (such as those listed above), the harm they cause to the victims is vastly greater than the benefit they produce. In the case of speciesist practices, there is the further aggravating factor that the number of victims is enormously greater than the number of beneficiaries.

Moreover, such practices would never be considered just by their proponents if they did not know whether they would be among those who benefit from them or among those harmed by them. This is a sign that not even they themselves believe that the benefit these practices produce could justify the harm they cause.

Therefore, if what matters is the way individuals are affected, then we have strong reasons to abolish such traditions.

9.5.2. The defense that traditions are good in themselves

Another way to defend the claim that we should respect traditions is to argue that they have value in themselves, regardless of whether or not they benefit individuals. There are two problems with this defense. Let us look at each separately:

The difficulty of grounding the existence of this value

The first problem is managing to show that traditions really are good in themselves. For example, another possibility is that they have only instrumental value (that is, that their value depends solely on how they affect individuals). Yet another possibility is that they are bad in themselves. So, given these other possibilities, whoever holds that they are good in themselves would have to present an argument for this thesis, rather than simply assuming it as if it were obvious. A further difficulty for this position is that the attempt to establish that traditions have intrinsic value cannot appeal to the benefits they provide to certain individuals (since that would be showing their instrumental value, and showing that something has instrumental value is obviously not showing that it has intrinsic value).

A defender of traditions might say that their intuitions tell them that traditions are good in themselves. However, other people do not share this intuition, so the defender of traditions would have to explain with some other argument why it is their intuitions that are correct. Moreover, our intuitions may simply be the result of our prejudices.

The defender of traditions might point out that it has not been proven that traditions lack this value either. However, the burden of proof lies with the defender of traditions, since it is they who assert the existence of a value that cannot be verified (all the more so since these are practices that cause enormous amounts of suffering and death).

Even if this value existed, it would not follow that these traditions are justified

The second problem is the following. Let us assume, for the sake of argument, that it had been proven that traditions have intrinsic value. This would still be insufficient to establish that traditions that create victims are justified. To establish that conclusion, it would also have to be shown that the supposed value of traditions is more important than the victims' basic interests, such as not suffering and not dying. If, as we have seen, it is already difficult to establish that traditions have intrinsic value, it is even more difficult to establish that this value is so important that it justifies causing suffering and death in its name.

9.6. Conclusion

Everything discussed here seems to show that the fact that a practice is traditional does not show that it is just. Therefore, the fact that animal exploitation is traditional does not show that it is just either. In fact, it is quite possible that animal exploitation is also a highly unjust or even heinous practice, and that the very fact that it is traditional is one of the factors that keep this from being noticed, just as happened with human slavery, for example.

Author’s notes

  1. For a detailed criticism of attempts to justify speciesism through an appeal to tradition, see Cunha (2021, p. 49-56). For a general criticism of the appeal to tradition, see Rachels e Rachels (2012, ch. 2). ↩

10. If Ethics Is a Human Activity, Is It Just to Disregard Animals?

10.1. The appeal to ethics as a human activity

One of the arguments sometimes used to deny moral consideration to animals points out that ethics is a human activity and that, therefore, only humans should receive moral consideration. Below we will look at three criticisms of this argument.

10.2. Is every human capable of moral agency?

The first criticism points out that it is false that ethics is a human activity. Humans who reflect on ethics do not do so because they are human, but because they are rational. For example, if there are rational beings on other planets, they will very likely not be human, but they will quite probably be able to reflect on how they should act. And, more importantly: there are humans who lack the capacity to think about ethics, such as babies, children up to a certain age, and victims of certain accidents or diseases that affect cognitive capacities. So ethics is an activity of beings who have certain developed cognitive capacities, not of humans in general.

10.3. Do the beneficiaries of a practice need to be capable of engaging in it?

The second criticism points out that, from the fact that an activity is carried out by a group of beings, it does not follow that the beneficiaries of that activity must also be capable of carrying it out. For example, to practice medicine, one needs to be a doctor, but it makes no sense to say that, because of this, only doctors should receive medical treatment. To teach music, one needs to know about music, but it makes no sense to say that only those who already know something about music should take music lessons.

Therefore, from the fact that ethics is an activity of beings who possess certain cognitive capacities, it does not follow that the beneficiaries of their decisions must be only beings who possess those same capacities. This is already widely accepted in the human case. Otherwise, children up to a certain age and humans with certain cognitive impairments would be used in the same way nonhuman animals are used (as food, to make clothing, as test subjects, and so on). However, if the fact that these humans lack those capacities cannot justify doing to them what is commonly done to nonhuman animals, then the fact that nonhuman animals lack such capacities could not justify what is commonly done to them either33.

Therefore, the argument in question confuses what is relevant to knowing who can be held responsible (the capacity to reflect on what one should do) with what is relevant to knowing who needs consideration (the capacity to be harmed/benefited)34.

10.4. Circularity

Finally, the third criticism points out that the argument is in fact circular. The argument aims to explain the relevance of belonging to the human species for knowing who should be considered. It claims that nonhuman animals should be excluded from the sphere of moral consideration because they are not capable of acting ethically. However, the argument includes within the sphere of moral consideration the humans who lack this capacity (at least, that is what seems to be suggested when someone says that ethics is a human activity, since one could say instead, for example, that it is an activity of rational beings, which does not include all humans).

In other words, the argument aims to explain a morally relevant difference between humans and nonhumans, but, on realizing that there are humans who do not meet the criterion it proposes, it includes them within the sphere of moral consideration because they belong to the same species as those who can reason about ethics. In short, the argument is circular because it claims to explain the relevance of the species criterion but in fact already assumes that criterion in advance.

In short, this argument is no different from the appeal to capacities and the appeal to the group, only presented in other words. It therefore has exactly the same problems.

Author’s notes

  1. For a development of this argument, see Ehnert (2002) and Horta (2014). ↩
  2. For a discussion of what is relevant to questions of moral consideration, see Horta (2018a) and Cunha (2021, p. 57-61). ↩

11. If Ethics Is an Invention, Is It Just to Disadvantage Animals?

11.1. The claim that ethics is an invention

It is sometimes claimed that ethics is an invention. What is meant by this is that it is not something that has always existed in the universe, since rational agents must exist in order to reflect on what they should do. Ethics as an activity, therefore, seems to have arisen with the appearance of rational beings. From this observation it is sometimes said that, since ethics is an invention, all criteria in ethics are equally arbitrary, and that we therefore have no good reason to reject speciesism.

11.2. If an activity is an invention, is it necessarily arbitrary?

The main problem with this argument is that it presupposes that, if an activity is an invention, then the criteria for studying the subject of that activity are all equally arbitrary. Yet every human activity is, in the sense the argument points to, also an invention. Before the first scientists appeared, there was no activity of science. Before the first mathematicians appeared, there was no activity of mathematics. And so on. But this does not imply that things in science and mathematics are therefore arbitrary and that all views are equally plausible.

The same happens in ethics, however. For example, there are moral positions based on relevant criteria and others based on criteria that are irrelevant to what is at stake35. For example, suppose we want to know whether or not someone can be held responsible for what they choose. In that case, what seems relevant is whether or not that someone is capable of reflecting on how they should decide. Now suppose we want to know to whom we should give moral consideration (that is, whom we should avoid harming and seek to benefit). In that case, what seems relevant is knowing who can be harmed or benefited (since that is why someone needs consideration). However, it is sometimes argued that nonhuman animals should not be considered because they do not understand the notion of ethics. In that case, what is being done is confusing what is relevant for someone to be held responsible with what is relevant for someone to be considered.

Moreover, there are positions that are arbitrary and others that are not. For example, the principle of equal consideration36 is not arbitrary. According to this principle, avoiding greater harms is more important than avoiding lesser harms, regardless of the race, gender, species, capacities, and so on of whoever would suffer those harms. The aim is precisely not to be biased with respect to anyone. There are, on the other hand, completely arbitrary positions, which hold, for example, that only harms to humans should be avoided, or that we should give greater importance to avoiding harms to humans even when the harm to the nonhuman animal is of the same magnitude (or even when the nonhuman animal would suffer a greater harm, according to some views). That being so, it is false that in ethics all views are equally arbitrary. In fact, what we saw above shows that some views are arbitrary and others are not.

Finally, there are also positions that are partial and others that are impartial. There are positions we would consider just if we did not know what position we would occupy among those affected by them. These positions pass the impartiality test. On the other hand, there are other positions that are defended only because those who defend them know they will not be harmed by them. Speciesism is an example. If we did not know what species we belonged to, we would consider it completely unjust to privilege humans37. This position, therefore, does not pass the impartiality test.

All of this seems to show that it is false that, if ethics is a human activity, then all positions in ethics are equally arbitrary.

Author’s notes

  1. For a discussion of what is relevant to questions of moral consideration, see Horta (2018a) and Cunha (2021, p. 57-61). ↩
  2. The best-known formulation of this principle can be found in Singer (2002[1979], p. 29-35). However, it is a principle that appears in every ethical theory that is not arbitrary. On this, see Cunha (2022b). ↩
  3. On this, see Rowlands (1998, 2009 [1998]). ↩

12. If Ethics Was Invented for Self-Protection, Is It Just to Disadvantage Animals?

12.1. The appeal to self-interest

It is sometimes claimed that humans invent ethics to protect themselves. According to this view, people condemn things like murder not because they genuinely care about others, but because they are afraid others will do the same thing to them. This view is sometimes used to argue that, if the basis of ethics is self-interest, then there is no reason to consider nonhuman animals, since they have no power to threaten us38.

12.2. Could the appeal to self-interest justify speciesism?

A first problem with this argument is that it could not justify the view that it is right to commit atrocities against nonhuman animals and wrong to do the same to humans. After all, there are also humans who have no power at all to threaten other humans. Babies, children up to a certain age, and victims of certain diseases and accidents that cause physical or mental disability are good examples. If what the argument claims were correct, then it would be right to commit every kind of atrocity against them, and not only against nonhuman animals39.

12.3. Is the claim about ethics and self-interest correct?

The second problem is that what the argument claims about the facts is false, namely, that people respect only those they fear. Of course, there are people who respect only those who have the power to threaten them. But, fortunately, many other people are not like that. Many people respect highly vulnerable individuals who have no power at all to pose a threat to them. What the argument claims may be true of the argument's proponents. It is possible that they, indeed, respect only those who have the power to threaten them. However, this is certainly false if it refers to humanity in general. In fact, this mistake is very common: when someone says "that's what humanity is like," they are sometimes actually making a hasty generalization from the observation that they themselves are like that.

12.4. The appeal to the origin of ethics

Suppose, however, that the argument is about the origin of ethics, and not about how people apply it today. For example, one could say that the first ethical systems in history arose out of self-interest, on the part of individuals seeking mutual protection. On this basis, someone might then argue that, for this reason, we have no reasons to consider those who cannot threaten us.

Here, again, there are two problems. The first problem is that, once again, the factual claim the argument makes is probably false. Observations of the behavior of nonhuman animals seem to suggest that ethics arises from altruistic behaviors that are probably a genetic inheritance40, much older than any self-interested ethical system.

However, there is an even bigger problem with the argument. Suppose ethics had arisen out of self-interest. This does not imply that this conception of ethics is correct. For example, the first astronomers had certain convictions about astronomy, but this does not mean they were necessarily right. Over time, in fact, many of the things they thought were proven wrong. The same applies to ethics.

The argument in question confuses describing how the activity of ethics arose with justifying a particular conception in ethics. Even if egoism were a good explanation of the origin of the activity of ethics (and, as we have seen, not even that seems to be the case), this would be no reason at all to think that egoism is justified. To think otherwise is to make the mistake of thinking that descriptions of the way people act, or of what motivations they have, could ground questions that are normative (that concern what is just or unjust, what we should or should not do, and so on). This would be the equivalent of trying to prove that a mathematical calculation is correct by pointing out that this was the way the calculation was done thousands of years ago.

13. Attempts to Justify Speciesism That Appeal to Authorities

13.1. A moral double standard

The good of nonhuman animals is generally not given much importance. For example, around the world, nonhuman animals are exploited for the most varied purposes. In the vast majority of cases this involves killing them, after subjecting them to a life full of intense suffering. Another example: when wild animals are victims of natural processes such as hunger, thirst, disease, and natural disasters, the standard view is that we should not help them: "we should let nature take its course."

In both cases, however, if the victims were human, the standard attitude would be the opposite. This shows that most people apply a double standard, depending on the species of those affected by their decisions. This standard is anthropocentric: if they are human, they are respected and helped; if they are nonhuman animals, they are not.

There have been various attempts to justify this anthropocentric moral standard. In this text, we will discuss one in particular: the claim that this standard is justified because some moral authority approves of it.

13.2. The appeal to authorities

Below we will give examples involving attempts to defend eating animals. However, it is important to remember that everything said here applies equally to the appeal to moral authorities in an attempt to defend any other practice or attitude.

It is often claimed that eating animals is justified because some moral authority allegedly approved of it. For example, it is often pointed out that the Bible approves of eating animals, and that Jesus ate fish. At other times, appeal is made to other kinds of moral authority (not necessarily authorities tied to a religion). In short, the pattern of these arguments is the following: "a certain moral authority approved of a certain practice; therefore, the practice in question is justified."

13.3. How not to respond

Some people sometimes try to counter this kind of argument by denying that the authority in question approved of eating animals. However, this way of responding does not address the main problem with the argument (in fact, it also assumes it), which is the very appeal to authorities in debates about ethical questions. Let us see:

13.4. The Euthyphro dilemma

Plato, 399 years before Christ, had already noticed the problems with this kind of argument (so appeals to moral authorities were probably already quite common at that time). The main problem is illustrated by Plato in the dialogue titled Euthyphro41, which is why it became known as the Euthyphro Dilemma.

Basically, the dilemma consists in asking the following: "Does an authority approve of a certain practice because the practice in question is right, or does it become right because it was approved by the authority?" This reveals a serious problem with appeals to moral authorities, whatever answer one gives to this dilemma. Let us see:

13.5. The possible answers to the dilemma do not support the appeal to authority

Suppose someone says it is the second case (the practice becomes right because it was approved by the authority). If so, then the authority in question approves of the practice not because the practice has good reasons in its favor, since anything the authority randomly chose to approve would be right. If so, then we are not really dealing with a moral authority, but with someone who arbitrarily chooses what to approve.

Of course, if someone considers a certain person, book, or deity a moral authority, they will say that the authority in question is an authority because it has a great deal of moral knowledge, and so approves of certain things because it knows they are right (and not that they become right because they were approved by the authority). So it seems that the only way to claim that

we are dealing with an authority is to defend the first option: "the authority approves of a certain practice because it knows the practice is right."

But then this implies that it is not the authority's will that makes the practice right: the authority merely knows of some reason that makes the practice right. But if so, in order to assess whether the practice really is right, or whether the authority in question was mistaken, we need to know what that reason is.

13.6. It doesn't matter who said it: what matters is assessing the reasons

In short, the point is this: pointing out that a certain authority approves of a practice is not enough to justify it. We have to know what reasons that authority would have put forward in trying to show that the practice is right. And if we come to discover what those reasons are, we have to assess those reasons on their own merits.

That is, the argument presented will be sound or not regardless of who presented it. If the argument is good, it is good, whether it was put forward by an authority or by anyone else. On the other hand, if the argument is bad, it remains bad, even if it was put forward by an authority.

That is why, if our goal is really to discover which practices are justifiable, we will reject appeals to moral authorities entirely. We will assess the soundness of arguments regardless of who put them forward. This shows, then, that the fact that certain authorities approved of speciesist practices is not enough to show that such practices are justified.

14. The Appeal to Differentiated Degrees of Moral Status

14.1. The Magnitude Thesis

The principle of equal consideration prescribes that we not be biased when considering the good of the individuals affected by our decisions. Equal consideration has the following implication:

  • Magnitude Thesis (MT): The strength of the reasons to avoid harming and to benefit someone depends on the magnitude of the harms and benefits, not on the species of those affected. The greater the harm/benefit, the stronger these reasons.

Thus, according to the MT, we have reason to prioritize avoiding harm to, or benefiting, nonhuman animals whenever doing so would mean avoiding a greater harm or providing a greater benefit than prioritizing humans would.

14.2. The appeal to degrees of moral status

The MT is sometimes rejected by appealing to the idea of special status:

  • Special Status Thesis (ST): Some individuals have a special status that entitles them to be prioritized even when they would be less harmed if they were not.

According to the ST, it is as if certain individuals held a trump card. This trump is usually called dignity. In this respect, we can distinguish two types of ST:

Total ST: If A has the special status and B does not, A has priority, no matter how much more B would be harmed if not prioritized.

Threshold ST: If A has the special status and B does not, A has priority, unless the harm to B is above a certain threshold*.

*The many variants of this position set this threshold at different points.

Whether we are talking about total ST or threshold ST, both reject the MT, since they hold that there are at least some circumstances in which we should prioritize the individuals who would be less harmed if they were not prioritized.

The beings granted special status under the ST vary. Most commonly, it is held that they are the members of the human species42. At other times, however, it is held that they are not all humans, but only those who have the capacity to make autonomous decisions43 (roughly, normal adult humans).

Is it just to assign differentiated degrees of moral status? We will discuss this below.

14.3. Is it just to assign differentiated degrees of moral status?

To assess whether assigning differentiated degrees of moral status is just, we need to know how to assess whether a decision is just. On this point, a widely accepted view is that a decision is just if it is impartial, in the sense of not being biased. But how do we know whether a decision is impartial? A widely used method consists in imagining whether we would approve of it if we did not know what position we would occupy among those affected by it.

A method of this kind was first proposed by John Harsanyi44 in 1955, and a very similar method was later used extensively in John Rawls's 1971 work A Theory of Justice45, influencing many later works.

The method consists in imagining rational and self-interested agents who aim to maximize their own well-being but have not yet been born into the world in which they will live. This is the so-called original position. In it, these agents must decide which moral and political principles will govern that future world. However, they must decide behind a veil of ignorance, where they do not know what characteristics they will have after they are born. They will not know their race; gender; nationality; whether they will be born into rich or poor families; whether they will be born healthy or with some disease; what talents or difficulties they will have, and so on. In short, behind the veil of ignorance we can know nothing about factors that depend on good or bad luck.

The basic idea is that whatever rational, self-interested agents would consider just/unjust under such conditions would in fact be just/unjust.

It is sometimes argued that the veil of ignorance thought experiment does not apply to our decisions that affect nonhuman animals or that affect humans who lack a sense of justice (such as babies, children up to a certain age, and adults who are victims of certain diseases or accidents that impair cognitive capacities). Rawls himself thought so. He believed that it only makes sense to protect with principles of justice those beings who have a sense of justice46 (since this is necessary for deciding on the basis of the veil of ignorance). However, this reasoning would only make sense if, for someone to be treated unjustly, it were also necessary for that someone to have a sense of justice. Yet the following example suggests that beings who lack a sense of justice can also be treated unjustly. Let us see:

Imagine that a baby girl was born with a disease that will prevent her throughout her entire life from developing a sense of justice. Imagine that, because of this, she receives less food than the other babies in a nursery. The fact that she does not now have (and never will have) a sense of justice does not make the treatment she received any less unjust. It is unjust simply because her well-being is given less weight on the basis of an arbitrary factor, which is the result of the natural lottery and which does not lessen the harm she suffers from receiving less food. Of course, for someone to be held responsible for committing an injustice, they need to have a sense of justice. But this example seems to show that one does not need to have a sense of justice in order to suffer an injustice. If so, then the alleged lack of a sense of justice in nonhuman animals cannot justify our failing to apply the veil of ignorance method to our decisions that affect them.

Another objection to applying the veil of ignorance to our decisions that affect nonhuman animals was raised by Peter Carruthers. He argued that, if the agents are reasoning on the basis of the veil of ignorance, then they can presume they will be human after the veil is lifted, since animals are not capable of this47. However, as

Donald VanDeVeer48 and Richard Ryder49 observed, the agents in the original position also know that they are capable of understanding and arguing about very complex moral and political principles, but this does not mean that in the original position they can presume they would retain this very high level of rationality after the veil was lifted, since, if they could, they would be tempted to favor the most rational individuals in a biased way. Thus, if in the original position the agents cannot assume they will be highly rational after the veil is lifted, then it makes no sense to maintain that they can know what species they would belong to or that they would have complex cognitive capacities.

Mark Rowlands50 observed that one of the aims of the veil of ignorance is to rule out undeserved advantages and disadvantages that are the result of the natural lottery, such as the characteristics one is born with. That is exactly why the veil of ignorance excludes knowledge of the natural properties one would have. However, membership in a species, like all other natural properties, is an undeserved result of the natural lottery, and therefore the benefits and harms that result from it are also undeserved. That is why, Rowlands concludes, knowledge of what species we will belong to must be excluded in the original position. For exactly the same reason, knowledge that we are capable of autonomy must be excluded in the original position. True justice must take into account all those who may be affected by our decisions, and not only humans or only beings who also have a sense of justice.

So let us apply the veil of ignorance method to the claim that all members of the human species (or only humans capable of autonomy) should have a higher status. To test whether these positions pass the impartiality test, we have to ask:

(1) Would we consider it just to give a higher status to humans if we knew we could be born as members of any other species?

(2) Would we consider it just to give a higher status to beings capable of autonomy if we knew we could be born without this capacity?

Remember that behind the veil of ignorance we have to decide on the assumption that we have an equal probability of being assigned to be any of the individuals in the future world. That being so, it seems that rational, self-interested agents would certainly reject such higher statuses, given the possibility of discovering, after the veil was lifted, that they are not human or that they are humans incapable of autonomy. And the greater this possibility, the more vehemently they would seem to reject them.

In the real world, this possibility would be enormous, given that the number of nonhuman animals is astronomically greater than the number of humans. The human population is around 8 billion individuals. According to some estimates, at any given time there are somewhere between 1 and 10 quintillion sentient nonhuman animals51 on the planet. This difference in size is so astronomical that it is hard to picture. An example, however, will help. If we draw an analogy with the span of one year, the human population would represent at most 0.25 seconds of the year. The entire rest of the year would be nonhuman animals.

Thus, after the veil was lifted, we would very likely discover that we had been assigned to be born as nonhuman animals. The odds of being human would be, at best, 1 in 125 million (and the odds of being humans who will one day develop autonomy would be even smaller).

This suggests that the idea of a higher moral status for members of the human species or for bearers of autonomy is grounded:

(1) In self-interest (since we know that, in the real world, we are not nonhuman animals or humans incapable of autonomy)

(2) In the mistaken belief that we ourselves could not be disadvantaged by it (each of us, because of disease or accident, may come to lose autonomy).

All of this seems to show that a privileged status for humans or for beings capable of autonomy is defended only because its defenders belong to the privileged group. From an impartial point of view, we would consider such things extremely unjust. Perhaps we would even consider them the height of arbitrariness. If so, then the idea of differentiated moral status is itself completely unjust52.
