15. Attempts to Justify Speciesism That Appeal to Metaethics

15.1. When metaethical claims are disguised normative claims

In debates about ethical questions, the claim almost always comes up that in ethics there is no objective right and wrong. Unlike normative claims such as "act x is right/wrong," this claim is metaethical, that is, it is a claim about ethics (and not about which actions are right/wrong).

This text will argue the following:

  • In many of the cases in which this claim is made (perhaps the vast majority), what is actually sought with it is to ground a normative claim (namely, that the position one is defending in ethics is justified).
  • However, metaethical claims are incapable of doing any such thing.

This comes up in the debate over any ethical question. As an example, we will look at this discussion in the context of the debate about the moral consideration of nonhuman animals, explained below.

15.2. A moral double standard depending on the victims' species

Consider two situations involving nonhuman animals:

(1) Enormous numbers of nonhuman animals are exploited for the most diverse purposes: for consumption, in experiments, for clothing, entertainment, as workers and tools, and so on. This use usually involves killing them, as well as their having a life full of excruciating suffering, from beginning to end. Most people, however, seem to see nothing wrong with this. Yet if the victims were human, this would be seen as monstrous, to say the least.

(2) Wild animals, regardless of whether they are harmed by human practices, are also greatly harmed by natural processes, such as hunger, thirst, disease, natural disasters, accidents, hostile weather events, and so on. These conditions are the norm in nature, and have been since long before the human species appeared. In many cases it would be possible to prevent and minimize the suffering and deaths resulting from these events without thereby bringing about worse consequences in the long term. But the standard view is that, even so, what we should do is "let nature take its course." Yet, once again, if the victims were human, the standard attitude would be the opposite: it would be that we should help them.

These examples show that most people hold opposite attitudes depending on whether or not the victims belong to the human species.

15.3. When does the claim that there is no right/wrong in ethics come up?

Attempts are sometimes made to justify this double standard by claiming that there is no right and wrong in ethics: "in ethics, everything is relative," people say.

This claim usually does not come up at the beginning of a debate. On the contrary: people normally start by trying to show that there is some good reason to give full respect only to humans. It is only when they realize that none of the arguments they offer really justifies what they intend that they jump to the claim that there is no right and wrong in ethics.

But if they really believe there is no right and wrong in ethics, why were they trying until then to show that the position they defend is correct? This attitude is similar to that of someone who accepts the rules of the game while winning but, on seeing that they are about to lose, says they do not accept those rules.

So it seems that what actually happens is that these people realize they have not found any good justification for what they defend, but refuse to admit that they have "lost," and so start claiming that there is no right and wrong.

15.4. Could metaethical claims justify positions in ethics?

Debates usually begin on the ground of ethics itself, where reasons are offered for accepting or rejecting a given practice. Some people, when they see that they have no good reasons to defend what they defend, jump to the domain of metaethics, claiming that there is no right and wrong.

The question we should ask, then, is: can claims about metaethics ground conclusions about ethics (that is, conclusions about what to do in practice)? Below are some reasons to think this is not possible.

For the morality of each practice, there seem to be only three logical possibilities:

(1) Either we ought to do it; (2) Or we ought not to do it; (3) Or it makes no difference whether we do it or not.

These categories are usually expressed, respectively, by the terms required, forbidden, and permissible. For simplicity, I have included in the permissible category both acts that make no difference whether one does them or not and acts classified in some theories as praiseworthy but not required (also called supererogatory acts).

Whatever category someone claims a given practice falls into, it seems they are making that claim in objective terms (that is, they seem to be saying that whoever disagrees with placing it in the category in question is wrong). In other words, moral judgments seem to be objective by nature. Let us look at an example:

Sometimes, when someone says "there is no right and wrong in ethics" and intends thereby to justify a certain practice, what they seem to mean is that the practice in question should be permissible (that is, that it should be neither required nor forbidden). In other words, the person seems to mean that whoever wants to do it is justified, and that whoever does not want to is also justified.

But then they are claiming that there is an objective right and wrong regarding this practice. After all, they are claiming that the right thing is to consider it permissible, and that both those who think it should be forbidden and those who think it should be required are wrong. The same would apply if they were claiming that the practice in question should be required or forbidden. In any case, saying that "there is no right and wrong in ethics" adds nothing toward grounding the position being defended. On the contrary, it counts against it. Let us look at an example:

Suppose someone says: "practice X should be permissible." As we have seen, this seems to imply that the person is claiming that whoever thinks practice X should be forbidden or required is wrong. Suppose they add: "there is no right and wrong in ethics." What does this imply? Well, it implies that those who contradict what they are saying (that is, those who say practice X should be forbidden, and those who say it should be required) are not wrong (and it also implies that they themselves are not right in claiming that the practice should be permissible).

But that is not what these people usually mean. What they usually mean is that they themselves are right to make the judgment they make, and that whoever disagrees is wrong. But once they realize there is no good reason to defend what they defend, they claim there is no right and wrong in ethics. Yet, as we have seen, if that were so, then they could not say that those who disagree with them are wrong.

Important: we also add no reason in favor of what we are defending if we say "there is right and wrong in ethics," since this does not show that what we are defending is correct. In short, what counts are the reasons that can be put forward for and against a given practice (and, as we have seen, both saying that there is no right/wrong in ethics and saying that there is seem to add nothing to those reasons). That is why, it seems, claims about metaethics can serve as a basis neither for accepting nor for rejecting positions in ethics.

That being so, both asserting "there is no right and wrong in ethics" and asserting "there is right and wrong in ethics" offer no reason for (or against) speciesism. Therefore, appeals to metaethics are incapable of justifying speciesism.

Volume II

Considering Sentient Beings

This book presents the main arguments that ground full moral consideration for all sentient beings, that is, for all beings capable of suffering and enjoyment. It also examines the main objections to this proposal, as well as its practical implications, and investigates what criteria we could use to determine which beings are sentient.

Original text by Luciano Carlos Cunha, translated into English · ISBN 978-65-01-30511-0.

1. What Is Relevant to Knowing to Whom We Owe Consideration?

1.1. A double standard

Nonhuman animals are exploited and killed by humans every day for the most diverse purposes. They are used for food, clothing, as test subjects, for entertainment, leisure, and as workers or tools. These practices cause suffering and death to a gigantic number of nonhuman animals and are widely accepted. However, if the victims were human, such practices would be considered monstrous.

In addition to being victims of human practices, nonhuman animals are also greatly harmed by natural processes such as malnutrition, hunger, and thirst, disease, physical injuries, psychological stress, hostile weather events, natural disasters, and interspecific, intraspecific, and sexual conflicts. This is the typical situation of most animals living in the wild. The standard view is that we should not help them: we should let nature take its course. But, once again, if the victims were human, the standard view would be the opposite, namely, that resources should be devoted to helping them.

These attitudes reveal that a large proportion of people apply a double standard, depending on the species of those affected by their decisions. If they are nonhuman animals, they receive no help and are tortured and killed. If they are human, they receive full moral consideration. This is, therefore, an anthropocentric speciesist moral standard.

1.2. Attempts to justify anthropocentric speciesism

There are various attempts to justify this moral double standard. Among the reasons most often given in an attempt to justify the view that either only the good of humans matters or it matters to a greater degree are:

(1) The very fact that they belong to the human species.

(2) The fact that they belong to the same species we belong to. (3) Metaphysical claims, such as that humans were created in the image and likeness of a creator; have a special relationship with that creator; have an immortal soul; have dignity; belong to a higher ontological category, and so on.

(4) The claim that humans possess (or have the potential for) capacities such as reason, language, freedom, moral agency, a sense of justice, autonomy, culture, the capacity to make mutual agreements, to respect rights, to claim rights, and so on.

(5) The claim that humans have (or have the potential to have) various kinds of relationships, such as relationships of affection, mutual solidarity, political relationships, and power relationships.

(6) The fact that all humans belong to the same species as those who possess those capacities or relationships (even though not all humans actually possess them).

(7) The claim that the idea of species is not a mere social construct (it is based on biological characteristics).

(8) The claim that disregarding nonhuman animals is a natural attitude.

(9) The fact that animal exploitation is traditional and part of the culture of many peoples.

However, it makes sense to ask what relevance these things have to knowing whom we should respect. In asking this question, we can see that all defenses of anthropocentrism simply assume that the criterion they adopt is relevant to knowing to whom we should give moral consideration, without offering any explanation of why it would be relevant.

This applies to all attempts to justify anthropocentrism, whether those based on the criterion of membership in a certain species, on the possession of certain metaphysical characteristics, or on the possession of certain capacities or relationships, as well as those based on the fact that a distinction rests on a biological characteristic or that a behavior is natural or traditional.

Moreover, there are reasons to think that none of these criteria is relevant to knowing to whom to give moral consideration. This is pointed out by the argument from relevance, described below.

1.3. The argument from relevance

The argument from relevance1 starts from the trivial premise that, for a criterion to be justified, it must be based on a distinction relevant to the question it aims to answer. For example, what is relevant to evaluating a candidate for a medical team at a hospital is their medical skills, their level of knowledge in the field, whether they are punctual, whether they treat patients well, and so on. To evaluate who should be seen in a hospital emergency room, on the other hand, what matters is knowing who is injured, who is seriously ill, who is at risk of dying, and so on.

Switching the criteria would mean applying criteria that are relevant in one context to another in which they are not. This would happen, for example, if it were required that, to be accepted onto a medical team, one would have to be ill and that, to be seen by a doctor, one would also have to be a doctor. Of course, the absurd attitude described in this example would hardly occur in real life. However, the argument from relevance points out that the anthropocentric moral standard commits a very similar confusion. Let us see:

The argument from relevance holds that none of the defenses of anthropocentrism adopts criteria relevant to determining who should receive moral consideration. This is so because what is at stake in questions of moral consideration is how our acts and omissions could positively or negatively affect whoever is affected by them. To give moral consideration to someone is to act so as to avoid harming them and to seek to benefit them. If so, then the appropriate criterion for knowing to whom to give moral consideration is knowing who can be harmed and benefited.

The species to which someone belongs; whether or not they were created in the image and likeness of a deity; whether or not they have an immortal soul; whether or not they have certain capacities and certain relationships; whether or not they have the potential for such capacities or relationships; whether or not a behavior is natural or traditional, and so on: none of this determines who can be harmed or

benefited. Therefore, these cannot be relevant characteristics for knowing to whom to give moral consideration, the argument from relevance concludes.

On the other hand, being capable of having positive and negative experiences (that is, being capable of enjoying and suffering) determines whether someone can be harmed and benefited. That is why proponents of the argument from relevance hold that sentience (that is, the capacity to have experiences) is the appropriate criterion for moral consideration.

1.4. What is relevant for consideration and what is relevant for responsibility

Traditionally, criteria that are relevant to determining whom it would make sense to hold responsible have been applied to determine who should receive moral consideration. For example, it is commonly argued that, for us to have obligations toward someone, that someone must also be capable of recognizing obligations2; that for someone to receive the protection of principles of justice, they must have a sense of justice3; that to have rights, one must be capable of understanding the notion of rights4, and so on.

These claims have been widely used in an attempt to justify all the terrible things that are done to nonhuman animals. However, possessing these capacities may be relevant to knowing whom to hold responsible, but not to knowing whom to consider morally. This is already recognized in the case of babies, children, humans with cognitive disabilities, and so on. Recognizing this, however, implies recognizing that every sentient being, regardless of species, should receive moral consideration.

The disregard that nonhuman animals typically receive arises, at least in part, from the belief that, for us to owe moral consideration to someone, that someone must also be capable of acting morally. However, as the argument from relevance points out, this is a confusion analogous to thinking that, for someone to be seen by a doctor, that someone must also be a doctor.

2. What Is the Argument from Species Overlap?

The argument from species overlap, despite having a rather strange and complicated name, is an easy argument to understand. Moreover, it is one of the main arguments in defense of respect for nonhuman animals. It arises as a response to attempts to justify disregard for nonhuman animals that appeal to capacities or relationships. All of this will be explained in detail below.

It is often argued that what makes practices that cause suffering and death to nonhuman animals right, and also what makes it right not to give them the help they need, is the fact that nonhuman animals lack certain capacities or certain relationships.

For example, it is commonly said that nonhuman animals do not deserve the respect humans deserve because they lack complex cognitive capacities. At other times, it is said that it is right not to help animals because they are in no position to help us (that is, we have no relationships of mutual solidarity with them), or because they do not contribute to our society (that is, we have no political relationships with them). At yet other times, it is said that what makes it right to torture and kill animals is the simple fact that we have the power to do so and they have no power to defend themselves, being completely vulnerable.

The argument from species overlap5 begins by observing that, whatever capacity or relationship is chosen as the criterion for excluding nonhuman animals from the sphere of moral consideration (or for giving them lesser consideration), there will always be humans who do not possess it and who would therefore also be disadvantaged by such criteria.

This is the case, for example, of babies, children up to a certain age, and victims of certain diseases or accidents that prevent the development or exercise of those capacities and relationships. Such humans do not possess the complex cognitive capacities that adult humans typically possess. Also, unfortunately, many of them are not in relationships of mutual solidarity (on the contrary, they have been abandoned), and they are also in no position

to contribute to society. Moreover, they exercise power over no one (on the contrary, like nonhuman animals, they are completely vulnerable).

The argument from species overlap then observes that, if the lack of those capacities or relationships in these humans cannot justify treating them worse than normal adult humans - much less doing to them what is typically done to nonhuman animals - then the lack of those capacities or relationships in nonhuman animals could not justify treating them worse than normal adult humans either, much less justify the typical disregard they receive.

Moreover, the lack of those capacities and relationships in those humans is normally seen as a reason to give them even greater care, since it increases their vulnerability. Thus, the lack of those capacities and relationships in nonhuman animals is also a reason to give them greater care, and not a reason to treat them worse or to disregard them.

Other examples can be found in Singer (2002 [1979], p. 85); Ehnert (2002); Miller (2002) and Wilson (2005). ↩

3. What Is Sentience and Why Does It Matter?

If what is relevant to knowing to whom to give moral consideration is knowing who can be harmed and benefited, then it is important to investigate what makes someone capable of being harmed and benefited. That is where the importance of sentience6 lies.

The term "sentience" is used in the animal ethics debate as a synonym for consciousness. It refers to any and every experience someone could have, starting with the simplest. It also refers to any other mental state someone could have, such as desires, intentions, memories, and so on. It is what makes there be someone, an individual inhabiting a body, and not merely a living, empty body. It is what separates, on the one hand, a human, a dog, a fish, and a bee7 and, on the other, a shoe, a plant, a bacterium, and a fungus. Thus, sentience determines who can be harmed or benefited because it is sentience, in the first place, that determines when there is someone and not merely something.

Moreover, another feature of sentience, essential for there to be the possibility of harm and benefit, is that experiences have what is called valence8 - that is, they can be experienced as positive or negative. This is also what makes sentient beings prefer to be in a certain condition rather than another (that is, it is what gives them desires and preferences).

For this reason, there are two basic ways in which a sentient being is harmed: by the presence of what is negative for them (as happens when they suffer, for example) and by the absence of what is positive for them (as happens when they die or are in some other way prevented from enjoying something that would benefit them).

Similarly, there are two basic ways in which a sentient being is benefited: by the presence of what is positive for them (as happens when they feel pleasure, for example) and by the prevention of what is negative for them (as happens when suffering is relieved, for example).

That is why nonhuman animals need consideration. It is not because they belong to the animal kingdom, or because they are alive in a biological sense (as plants are, for example). It is because they are someone and because they are capable of being harmed or benefited.

Therefore, to know which beings to consider, it is important to know which ones are sentient. How can we investigate this? We will address this topic next.

4. Which Beings Are Sentient?

4.1. Why is it important to know which beings are sentient?

It is important to know which beings are sentient because sentience is what makes a being capable of being harmed and benefited. This is so because it is sentience (that is, the capacity to have experiences) that makes that being someone rather than something, and because experiences can be experienced as positive or negative (that is, they have valence9).

There are three main types of criteria for investigating which beings are sentient: physiological, behavioral, and evolutionary10. We will look at each of them below.

4.2. The presence of a centralized nervous system

The main physiological criterion is the presence of a nervous system with a centralizing organ (such as a brain or ganglia, for example). Information reaches the organism through the nervous system, but it is the processing of that information, which takes place in the centralizing organ, that provides the conditions for consciousness to arise11.

This means that organisms that lack a nervous system (such as bacteria, protozoa, fungi, plants, and animals of the phylum Porifera, such as sponges) or that have a nervous system but no centralizing organ (such as animals of the phylum Cnidaria, such as jellyfish, and of the phylum Echinodermata, such as sea cucumbers) lack the structures necessary for consciousness to arise12.

4.3. Other physiological indicators

This first type of criterion (the presence of a centralized nervous system) is the main one, with the following criteria being additional indicators that a being is sentient. That being so, it is possible for an organism to be sentient without meeting these other additional criteria.

However, it does not seem possible for an organism to be sentient by meeting the additional criteria without having a physical structure that meets the first criterion, since in that case there would be no way for the organism to process the information received by the nervous system and create the conditions for consciousness to arise.

Other additional physiological criteria are the presence in the organism of substances that act as painkillers13 and the presence of nociceptors14 (which detect harmful or potentially harmful stimuli and send this kind of information to the brain).

4.4. Behavior

The second type of additional criterion is behavioral15. If a being has a centralized nervous system, the way it behaves can be an additional reason to think it is sentient.

For example, if an animal's behavior changes in response to stimuli under various kinds of conditions, it is probably avoiding stimuli that generate negative experiences and seeking stimuli that generate positive experiences.

That being so, to investigate whether the way a being behaves is additional evidence that it is sentient, what matters is not investigating how it behaves in specific situations, but how it behaves in general.

4.5. Evolutionary advantage

The third type of additional criterion is evolutionary advantage. The traits most likely to be passed on are those that are most efficient at transmitting genetic information. The parts of the body responsible for creating the conditions for consciousness to arise require a considerable investment of energy on the part of the organism. For example, in humans up to 20% of the energy consumed is spent keeping the brain active16. For this reason, the traits responsible for creating the conditions for consciousness to arise probably prevailed because they provided an advantage in terms of transmitting genetic information (since, if that were not the case, other traits that use much less energy would most likely have prevailed).

Thus, there is an evolutionary advantage for animals in being conscious, since, because they can move around in their environment, they are able to flee harmful stimuli and seek positive ones. This contributes indirectly to their survival, which in turn increases the likelihood that they will pass on their genetic information.

This is not the case, for example, with plants, since they cannot move. In their case, maintaining the structures necessary for consciousness to arise would involve a considerable expenditure of energy and would not result in any evolutionary advantage.

4.6. What is the minimum degree of centralization?

There is still no consensus on the minimum degree of centralization a nervous system must have (in terms of the number of neurons and the interaction among them) in order to provide the conditions for consciousness to arise.

It is known, however, that it need not be a brain like that of humans, nor like that of mammals, nor even like that of vertebrates17. For example, cephalopods meet all the criteria for sentience and are invertebrates18. There is also a series of studies suggesting that many kinds of insects, crustaceans, and other arthropods

are very probably sentient19. For this reason, it is a mistake to think that the sentience criterion excludes invertebrates from moral consideration.

4.7. The possibility of non-organic sentience

It is also possible that a being need not even be organic to be sentient. If sentience appears whenever a physical structure is organized in such a way that it performs certain functions, and this is independent of the material that makes up that physical structure, then it is possible that non-organic sentient beings20 will come to exist in the future (for example, in digital media).

This may sound strange at first. However, there is a thought experiment that can help us understand this possibility. Imagine that we undergo surgery that involves replacing some of our organic neurons with neurons made of some non-organic material. If, after the surgery, the new neurons continue to perform the same functions, and the experiences associated with them remain present, this would be a reason to think that sentience is possible in non-organic beings. For example, if we kept periodically replacing the rest of our current neurons with non-organic neurons until all of them had been replaced, and the experiences did not fade away, this would be a strong indication that non-organic sentience is possible.

So far, every sentient being belongs to the animal kingdom. But this may change in the future.

5. Why Equal Consideration?

5.1. Hierarchical views

A very common view is that we should give some consideration to nonhuman animals, but that we should give greater consideration to humans.

Another view, sometimes defended, is that beings with greater cognitive capacities should receive greater consideration than beings with lesser cognitive capacities (whether they are human or nonhuman). According to this view, normal adult humans should receive greater consideration than nonhuman animals, children, and humans with cognitive impairments. For the same reason, according to this view, animals such as mammals should receive greater consideration than, for example, fish or insects.

In short, these views build hierarchies of moral status.

5.2. The principle of equal consideration

There is, however, a principle, called the principle of equal consideration21, which suggests that the very idea of a hierarchy of moral status is biased. According to the principle of equal consideration, all morally considerable beings have the same moral standing. The principle of equal consideration is explained in more detail below.

The idea of equal consideration is already built into the argument from relevance. If we have reasons to give moral consideration to someone because that someone can be harmed and benefited, then the strength of those reasons depends on the magnitude of the harms and benefits at stake — and not on the species, race, or gender to which they belong, their capacities, the relationships they have with others, and so on. In short, in an unbiased approach, harms and benefits of similar magnitude receive the same weight, and greater harms and benefits receive greater weight than lesser harms and benefits. This is what it means to give equal consideration to those affected by a decision.

This suggests, then, that not only is there no justification for excluding nonhuman animals from the sphere of moral consideration: there is also no justification for giving them lesser consideration22. That is why speciesism23 is analogous to racism: both violate this principle and are therefore forms of discrimination24.

Note that the principle of equal consideration is compatible with (in fact, requires) prioritizing this or that individual depending on the circumstances. This is because the principle prescribes that greater harms receive greater weight. However, the principle requires that this be done in an unbiased way.

For example, if in a certain situation I prioritize A because he is more seriously injured, then if in another situation it is B who is more seriously injured, I should prioritize B. I would be discriminating against B if, in this second situation, I chose not to prioritize him because of his race, gender, species, and so on.

In short, according to the principle of equal consideration, although the good of each affected individual receives the same weight, the magnitude of the harms and benefits to which they would be subject may differ (and, therefore, the reasons for prioritizing this or that individual may vary).

5.3. Violations of the principle of equal consideration

The principle of equal consideration is routinely violated in practices that affect nonhuman animals. For example, if the experiments that are widely accepted when performed on nonhuman animals25 were performed on humans, subjecting them to a similar harm (suffering of similar magnitude and harming them through death to the same extent, for example), they would be widely repudiated. This is an example of a case in which harms of similar magnitude receive different weight depending on whether the victim is human or nonhuman.

There are, moreover, more blatant violations of the principle of equal consideration, which occur not when similar harms receive different weight, but when lesser harms receive greater weight than greater harms. These violations are extremely common. The very use of animals for food production is an example. If humans stop eating animals, they do not suffer a great harm. They just have to eat plant-based food. But if humans choose to eat them, the animals, in addition to usually living a life full of suffering, also lose their lives26.

5.4. Speciesism is not limited to exploitation

As we have seen, animal exploitation is one form of violation of the principle of equal consideration. However, nonhuman animals are also disadvantaged in a biased way even in situations in which they are not exploited. An example is the claim that nonhuman animals, when they are victims of natural processes27 such as disease, thirst, hunger, and natural disasters, should be left to their fate, but that humans in similar situations should be rescued.

5.5. Speciesism is not limited to total disregard

One of the main implications of the principle of equal consideration is that an individual is discriminated against (that is, receives unjust unfavorable treatment) not only when their good is completely disregarded, but also when, for unjust reasons, their good receives less weight compared with the good of other individuals. That is why giving lesser consideration to the good of nonhuman animals is also unjustly disadvantaging them, even if some consideration is given to their good.

5.6. Speciesism is not limited to anthropocentric speciesism

There are also non-anthropocentric forms of speciesism, which rank the degree of moral consideration given to different nonhuman animals. For example, animals

such as dogs and cats generally receive greater consideration than fish, chickens, pigs, and cows. It is also common for animals considered more intelligent to receive greater consideration than animals considered less intelligent; for large animals to receive greater consideration than very small ones, such as insects; and so on. As should be clear by now, all of this violates the principle of equal consideration.

In what we have seen above, we focused mainly on examining anthropocentrism. There were three reasons for this. The first is that anthropocentrism is by far the most prevalent of all forms of speciesism. The second is that humans are usually placed at the top of the hierarchy. Even the animals favored by non-anthropocentric forms of speciesism typically receive far less consideration than humans do, and things are done to them that would never be considered acceptable if done to humans. Finally, the third reason is that what explains why anthropocentrism is unjustifiable (violating the principle of equal consideration) implies that any other form of speciesism is unjustifiable.

In fact, the principle of equal consideration explains the moral irrelevance of the species criterion in general, regardless of whether hierarchies are drawn among members of different species. For example, it is sometimes said that using animals in experiments is right as long as it benefits other animals of the same species. To see the problem with this argument, consider that in the past human victims were used in experiments aimed at benefiting other humans. The fact that the victims and the beneficiaries belong to the same species does not seem to make such practices justifiable. They equally violate the principle of equal consideration by assigning different weight to the good of the affected individuals.

5.7. Other little-noticed forms of discrimination

Another important implication of the principle of equal consideration is that it rejects hierarchies of moral standing based not only on race, gender, and species, but also on size, degrees of cognitive capacity, and the type of substrate that makes up the sentient being's body (that is, whether or not it is organic).

For example, if non-organic sentient beings come to exist in the future (for example, in digital media), according to the principle of equal consideration the good of these beings should receive the same weight as the good of organic sentient beings28. In short, according to the principle of equal consideration, all sentient beings count equally29.

  8. On this, see Tomasik (2015b). ↩
  9. For a criticism of the idea of hierarchies of moral status, see Horta (2017b). ↩

6. Could Questions of Desert Justify Speciesism?

6.1. The principle of equal consideration

The principle of equal consideration30 holds that harms and benefits of similar magnitude should receive equal weight. According to this principle, assigning different weight to harms and benefits of similar magnitude depending on the race, gender, or species of those affected by our decisions is unjustifiable, since in that case one is considering the good of each individual affected by one's decision in a biased way. The principle of equal consideration therefore implies that we are unjust toward nonhuman animals not only when we disregard them entirely, but also when we assign less weight to their good compared with the good of humans.

6.2. Questions of desert

It could be objected that the greater harm should not always receive greater weight. For example, if someone deserves31 the harm they suffer, it seems justified to prioritize helping other individuals who do not deserve the harm they suffer, even if they are suffering to a lesser extent. In light of this, one might think the following: if the factor of desert can justify an exception to the principle of equal consideration, why couldn't the species to which those affected by the decision belong?

6.3. The idea of desert depends on equal consideration

One possible reply would be to say that the idea of desert is not an exception to the principle of equal consideration: on the contrary, it depends on it in order to make sense. This is so because a non-arbitrary criterion for knowing when someone deserves a harm is whether that someone has previously violated the principle of equal consideration. For example, imagine that individuals A and B are injured, but that A is more seriously injured. Suppose, however, that A was injured while trying to murder B, who is innocent. Imagine that the reason A tried to kill B is the color of B's skin.

In this case, it seems justified to prioritize helping B, even though B is less injured than A, because A did something to deserve the harm he suffers. And the reason it makes sense to say that A deserves the harm he suffers is that his act first violated the principle of equal consideration by using race as a criterion for moral consideration. Race is irrelevant as a criterion for moral consideration because it determines neither who can be harmed and benefited nor the magnitude of the harms and/or benefits. However, the same can be said of the criteria of species, degree of intelligence, size, and so on.

6.4. Two dimensions of roles in morality

There are two dimensions of "roles" in morality: there are the individuals who will decide how to act and the individuals who will be affected by their decisions. It only makes sense to hold someone responsible for their decisions if that someone has cognitive capacities developed enough to understand what they are doing. On the other hand, for someone to be affected by a decision, it is enough that they can be harmed and benefited.

The criterion of desert refers to individuals who can be held responsible (even though it has implications for the appropriate way to treat these individuals when they are in the position of being affected by other people's decisions). It is because someone who can be held responsible behaved in a certain way that it makes sense to say they did something to deserve a harm or a benefit. There is nothing analogous in the case of the species to which someone belongs, since being born a member of this or that species is not a matter of merit or demerit.

Author’s notes

  1. For a more detailed explanation of this principle, see Singer (2002 [1979], ch. 3) and Cunha (2021, p. 61-6) ↩
  2. For a discussion of the relevance of the notion of desert in ethics, see Feinberg (1970) and Sher (1987). ↩

7. Is the Rejection of Speciesism Compatible with Only One View of Ethics?

7.1. To reject speciesism, is it necessary to subscribe to a specific ethical theory?

A common mistake is to think that, to reject speciesism, one must accept a specific view of ethics, such as utilitarianism. Thus, opponents of respect for nonhuman animals sometimes try to argue against utilitarianism with the aim of concluding that speciesism is justified.

7.2. The rejection of speciesism is compatible with various views of ethics

However, to recognize that the defenses of speciesism have problems, it is not necessary to assume a specific theory of ethics. Moreover, the principle of equal consideration is compatible with any unbiased view of ethics32. This is because it is a formal principle. That is, it does not itself prescribe what the right action is (that is done by the various substantive normative principles of each ethical theory). What the principle of equal consideration says is that, whatever substantive principle we adopt to determine what the right action is, there is no justification for being biased in its application.

As we will see below, utilitarianism certainly must give equal consideration to all sentient beings and, therefore, must reject speciesism. However, the moral consideration of all sentient beings and the rejection of speciesism have been defended from the most varied theories of normative ethics33. Below, we will look at an example with three different ethical theories.

7.3. An example with three different ethical theories

Imagine that we have rescued two animals, and that there are two ways in which we can house them. In the first, one of the animals will be in a much better condition than the other, although both will be in a positive condition. In the second, the first animal will not be as well off as it would be in the first option, but the second will be better off than it would be in the first option.

These options are laid out in the following table, where S1 and S2 are the possible situations for individuals A and B, and the numbers represent their levels of well-being.

SituationIndividual AIndividual BAggregate totalMinimum levelInequality
S1+20+10+30+10-10
S2+14+15+29+14-1

Now let us take as an example three views of ethics that accept equal consideration but have different goals: utilitarianism, maximin, and egalitarianism.

Utilitarians would say that S1 is better, since their goal is to maximize the aggregate total. Proponents of maximin, on the other hand, would say that S2 is better, since their goal is for the minimum level of well-being to be as high as possible. Egalitarians, in turn, would also agree that S2 is better, but because the level of inequality in it is lower.

So in what sense do all these views of ethics accept equal consideration? In the following sense: if the individuals switched places, these views would maintain the same decision. The following table illustrates this switch:

SituationIndividual AIndividual BAggregate totalMinimum LevelInequality
S1+10+20+30+10-10
S2+15+14+29+14-1

In this case, utilitarians would still maintain that we should choose S1, and proponents of maximin and egalitarians would still maintain that we should choose S2.

If someone refuses to defend the same decision when the individuals switch places (for example, because they are speciesist and always want to prioritize A or B), then they will no longer achieve the goal that the ethical theory in question aims to achieve. Thus, any unbiased view of ethics gives equal consideration to all sentient beings. Therefore, it is false that, to reject speciesism, one must assume a specific ethical theory.

That any plausible ethical theory must reject speciesism (and, consequently, advocate the abolition of speciesist practices, such as animal exploitation) is something that is increasingly being recognized. For example, on October 4, 2022, the Montreal Declaration on Animal Exploitation was signed. More than 500 specialists in ethics and political philosophy from more than 40 countries signed it, declaring the following:

"...We rarely agree with one another. We do agree, however, on the need for a profound transformation in our relationships with other animals. We condemn practices that involve treating animals as objects or commodities."

We can cite, for example: utilitarianism (SINGER, 2002 [1979]; MATHENY, 2006); rights theories (REGAN, 1983; FRANCIONE, 2000); egalitarianism (GOMPERTZ, 1997[1824]; FARIA, 2014; HORTA, 2016), prioritarianism (HOLTUG, 2007); sufficientarianism (CRISP, 2003); suffering-focused ethics (VINDING, 2020); negative consequentialism (PEARCE, 2017); ethics of care (ADAMS; DONOVAN, 1996); the capabilities approach (NUSSBAUM, 2006); virtue ethics (ROLLIN, 1981; DOMBROWSKI 1985; NOBIS 2002; HURSTHOUSE 2006; ABBATE 2014); Kantianism (FRANKLIN, 2005; KORSGAARD, 2005); neo-Kantianism (PLUHAR, 1995) and Rawlsian contractualism (VANDEVEER, 1979; ROWLANDS, 1998). For a summary of how several of these theories approach the question, see Ética Animal (2015f) and Cunha (2022b). ↩

8. If We Reject Speciesism, How Will We Decide Questions of Priority?

In the vast majority of situations, we will be unable to avoid harming every individual, nor will we be able to help everyone in need. Given this, someone might think that, if we give equal consideration to all sentient beings, we will have no guide for deciding: if everyone counts equally, how will we decide on priority34? Wouldn't it be necessary to build hierarchies of moral status? For example, if someone assigns a higher status to humans, or to the most intelligent beings, they will have a criterion for deciding in cases of conflict.

However, equal consideration is fully compatible with priority criteria. The difference, compared with hierarchical views, is the following. In views that build hierarchies of moral status, priority always goes to members of the privileged group. The priority criteria that could be adopted by views that accept equal consideration, by contrast, are interchangeable (that is, anyone could come to occupy the position that deserves priority). Consider, for example, the criterion "priority goes to whoever is worst off." This criterion is interchangeable because priority would go to anyone who was in the worst situation, regardless of their species, size, age, gender, capacities, and so on.

There are various priority criteria compatible with the principle of equal consideration. Below is a list of four examples (although there may be many others35):

(1) Severity: the worse the individual's situation, the higher their priority. (2) Number: the greater the number of individuals in a bad situation, the higher the priority. (3) Benefit: the greater the size of the benefit that can be provided to those in a bad situation, the higher the priority. (4) Long-term impact: The greater the positive impact that one or more individuals would have from then on if they are helped, the higher their priority.

Sometimes two or more criteria point in the same direction, and at other times they conflict with one another. Deciding questions of priority is not an easy task. There are many possible ways of establishing which criterion weighs more and whether that weight is fixed or variable. However, what we have seen above is enough to show that equal consideration is compatible with priority criteria. Therefore, it is false that, in order to decide questions of priority, we have to subscribe to a view that builds hierarchies of moral status.

Author’s notes

  1. On how each theory of normative ethics that accepts the principle of equal consideration approaches questions concerning priority criteria, see Cunha (2022b). On applications of priority criteria to cause selection, see Cunha (2023). ↩
  2. On how to decide priority taking levels of inequality into account, see Faria (2014). ↩

9. But Aren't Humans Capable of Suffering to a Greater Degree?

It is sometimes argued that prioritizing humans is consistent with equal consideration. The reason for this would be that, because of their more sophisticated cognitive capacities, humans would suffer more intensely. For example, they are capable of suffering from anticipating and remembering negative events.

It is true that greater cognitive capacity sometimes entails greater suffering. For example, only someone who understands that they will be killed a week from now is capable of suffering in anticipation. Only someone who remembers violence they suffered a few decades ago is capable of suffering through recollection. However, in many other cases it is lesser cognitive capacity that entails greater suffering. For example, nonhuman animals and young children typically suffer more when given an injection or medication precisely because they do not understand that they are being helped by it. Moreover, beings with greater cognitive capacities can also have their present suffering relieved by remembering or anticipating positive events, something impossible for beings who lack this capacity36.

Moreover, lesser cognitive capacity usually comes with greater vulnerability. That is why babies or adults with a cognitive impairment need much more care than normal adults do.

Of course, there may be cases in which someone has greater cognitive capacity and also greater vulnerability. For example, someone with the mental faculties of a normal adult human who is quadriplegic is more vulnerable than a young child. However, if, in addition to being quadriplegic, they also had reduced cognitive capacities, they would be even more vulnerable. In other words, even though a lower degree of cognitive capacity does not by itself determine someone's level of vulnerability, it always contributes to increasing it.

Therefore, greater cognitive capacity does not always entail greater harm. In fact, given the relationship between lesser cognitive capacity and vulnerability, in most cases exactly the opposite is true.

Author’s notes

  1. See Rollin (1989, p. 144). ↩

10. What Would We Decide Under Conditions of Impartiality?

10.1. The impartiality test

How can we know whether a decision is just or unjust? A widely accepted view is that, for a decision to be just, it must be impartial. What is meant by impartiality is not remaining neutral and making no decision at all. What is meant is making an unbiased decision.

But how can we know when a decision has been made impartially? A widely used method consists in imagining what we would decide if we did not know what position we would occupy among those affected by it. In that case, we must sincerely imagine ourselves in the place of each of those affected by the decision. Another similar method consists in imagining what we would decide if we had to live the lives of each of those affected by our decision.

A method centered on impartiality was used extensively in John Rawls's A Theory of Justice37 and influenced many later works. The method consists in imagining self-interested agents who already exist as rational beings but have not yet been born into the world in which they will live. This is the so-called original position. In it, they must decide which moral and political principles will govern that future world. However, they must decide behind a veil of ignorance, where they do not know what characteristics they will have after they are born. They will not know their race, gender, nationality, whether they will be born into rich or poor families, whether they will be born healthy or with some disease, what talents or difficulties they will have, and so on. The idea is that, under conditions of impartiality, discrimination based on these factors would not be tolerated, since rational, self-interested agents must decide bearing in mind that they have an equal probability of being born as any of the individuals in the future world.

10.2. Does the impartiality test apply to our decisions that affect animals?

Rawls believed that the veil of ignorance thought experiment did not apply to our decisions that affect nonhuman animals38. This is because he believed that, for someone to be protected by principles of justice, they must have a sense of justice (since this is necessary for deciding in the original position).

However, this reasoning would only make sense if, for someone to be treated unjustly, they needed to have a sense of justice. But consider the following example. Imagine that a baby receives less food than the other babies in a nursery because of the color of its skin. Imagine also that this baby was born with a disease that affects its cognitive capacities in such a way that it will be prevented throughout its entire life from developing a sense of justice. The fact that the baby does not have (and can never come to develop) a sense of justice does not make the treatment it received any less unjust. The injustice occurred because its well-being was given less weight on the basis of an arbitrary factor (skin color), and this is unjust regardless of whether or not the victim has a sense of justice, and whether or not it has the potential to develop one.

Of course, for someone to be held responsible for committing an injustice, they need to have a sense of justice. But one does not need to have a sense of justice to be the victim of an injustice. Thus, the lack of a sense of justice in animals does not make the disregard they typically receive any less unjust.

Peter Carruthers is another author who has argued that we have no reasons to avoid harming animals39. He argued that, if the agents are reasoning on the basis of the veil of ignorance, then they can presume they will be human, since animals are not capable of this. One reply to this is to observe, as Donald VanDeVeer40 did, that the agents in the original position also know that they are capable of understanding and arguing about very complex moral and political principles, but this does not mean that in the original position they can presume they would retain this very high level of rationality, since, if they could, they would be tempted to favor the most rational individuals in a biased way. But if behind the veil they cannot assume they will be highly rational, then it also does not seem to make sense to maintain that they can know what species they would belong to.

Mark Rowlands41 observed that one of the aims of the veil of ignorance is to rule out undeserved advantages and disadvantages that are the result of luck, such as the natural characteristics one is born with. According to Rawls himself, this is why the veil of ignorance excludes knowledge of the natural properties one would have. However, Rowlands observes, membership in a species, like all other natural properties, is an undeserved result of the natural lottery, and therefore the benefits and harms that result from it are also undeserved. For this reason, Rowlands argues, knowledge of what species we will belong to must be excluded in the original position.

10.3. Impartially considering our decisions that affect animals

If we apply the impartiality test to our decisions that affect nonhuman animals, we have to imagine what we would decide if we did not know whether we would be born as humans or as nonhuman animals. Below are some examples of applying this test in various contexts.

10.3.1. Animal exploitation

It seems that, under such conditions, we would certainly consider animal exploitation highly unjust. None of us would consider it just to be forced to die and to go through all the suffering it causes so that other individuals could enjoy the benefits that result from it. This seems to suggest that those who consider animal exploitation just do so only because they know they will not be its victims. But if so, then it is not just, since it does not pass the impartiality test.

10.3.2. Speciesism

It is not only animal exploitation that would be considered unjust under conditions of impartiality, but speciesism in general, even when it does not involve exploitation. For example, suppose we had to decide whether or not it is just to give greater consideration to humans, but without knowing whether we would be born as humans or as nonhuman animals. Under

such conditions, it seems we would see giving greater consideration to humans as highly arbitrary.

That is, it seems that speciesism does not pass the impartiality test, and that it is defended only because humans know they will not be its victims and will reap its benefits. If impartiality is an essential component of justice, then speciesism is unjust. This seems to show that nonhuman animals are treated unjustly not only when they are exploited, but also, for example, in situations where they do not receive the help they need and in the little importance given to the animal cause. We will look at some of this below.

10.3.3. Wild animal suffering

Animals living in the wild are harmed on a daily basis by factors such as hunger, thirst, disease, natural disasters, hostile weather conditions, physical injuries, conflicts, and so on.42 Moreover, extremely high rates of premature mortality result from the predominant reproductive strategy, which consists in having thousands or even millions of offspring per brood (in stable populations, on average only two per brood survive)43.

Since this kind of situation occurs independently of human action (it was already this way long before the human species appeared), the standard view is that we should "let nature take its course" and not help them. However, it seems that, under conditions of impartiality, we would argue for exactly the opposite, namely, that resources should be devoted to preventing/minimizing this gigantic amount of suffering and death.

10.3.4. The importance of the animal cause

A question commonly put to animal advocates is: "why worry about animals while there are humans in need of help?" A common view is that, even if animals are usually in a much worse situation, even if the total number of nonhuman victims is enormously greater, and even if there is a much larger number of people already investing in helping humans, we should nonetheless prioritize humans.

However, we would never say this if we did not know the species of the victims in each case. Moreover, remember that, behind the veil of ignorance, we have an equal chance of being born as any of the sentient beings existing in the world. According to some estimates, there are around 1 to 10 quintillion nonhuman animals in the world at any given time44. There are 8 billion humans. This difference in size is so gigantic that an analogy is needed to grasp it. If we draw an analogy with the span of one year, the human population would represent at most 0.25 seconds of the year. All the rest would be nonhuman animals. This means that, once the veil was lifted, you would probably discover that you are a nonhuman animal. This shows that, under conditions of impartiality, we would condemn the current neglect of the animal cause. On the contrary, we would argue for giving it a high priority45.

10.3.5. The importance of the future

The impartiality method also makes it possible to assess what we owe to future generations of sentient beings. For example, we can imagine that, behind the veil of ignorance, we also will not know in what era we will live. If we do this, we will realize that the probability of being born in exactly the era in which we actually exist is minimal (given that we have an equal chance of being born in any other era of the future). It seems that, under such conditions, we would argue that what we should do is adopt strategies that have a high probability of ensuring that the history of the world from now on is not full of suffering46.

Usually, people (including animal advocates), when they reflect on how they should decide, take into account only the impact of their decisions on beings who already exist now, or who will exist in the near future. Topics related to the distant future have been largely neglected. However, just as the rise of factory farming made it possible to cause suffering and death to a gigantic number of animals, new technologies may emerge with the potential to cause suffering

many orders of magnitude greater from then on. For this reason, from an impartial perspective, we will conclude that we should give great importance to preventing suffering in the future.

10.4. Conclusion

These were just a few examples of applying the impartiality method to our decisions that affect nonhuman animals. However, it is important to remember that it is a method that allows us to think through and assess questions we had never encountered before, and even to detect questions that we had not previously realized were questions of justice. It is therefore a very wide-ranging tool.

11. Testing Whether an Attitude Is Speciesist

An attitude is speciesist if it is unjust toward sentient beings who do not belong to a certain species (or species) — as, for example, when it is unjust toward those who are not human — or who do belong to a certain species (or species) — as, for example, when it is unjust toward animals classified as members of invasive species.

There are several ways to test whether an attitude is unjust. One is to check whether it violates the principle of equal consideration. Another is to check whether it passes the impartiality test.

Testing whether or not an attitude is speciesist may be simpler than we imagine. There are some questions47 we can always ask to test whether we are being unjust toward nonhuman animals.

For example, we can ask whether we would consider the attitude in question just:

(1) If we did not know the species of those who would be harmed and those who would be benefited by it;

(2) If we did not know what species we belong to;

(3) If its victims were human, suffering harms of the same magnitude;

(4) If the roles were reversed (for example, if the beneficiaries were nonhuman animals and those harmed were humans);

(5) If we had to bear the harms it causes in order to obtain the benefits it provides;

(6) If we had to bear the harms it causes so that other individuals could obtain the benefits it provides.

If we asked these questions sincerely, it seems we would reach the following conclusions:

(1) Animal exploitation would be widely considered unjust, or even heinous.

(2) It also seems that we would reject giving differentiated degrees of moral consideration depending on the species a sentient being belongs to or on its capacities. That is, we would reject speciesism.

(3) It seems that we would consider unjust not only practices that involve actively harming nonhuman animals, but also the failure to help them when they are victims of natural processes48 such as hunger, thirst, disease, natural disasters, and so on (which is what commonly happens to wild animals).

All of this seems to indicate not only that there is no justification for what is done to nonhuman animals, but also that we should do something to try to change this situation.

Author’s notes

  1. These questions are an application of the impartiality method. On this method, see Ética Animal (2015g, 2015h, 2016f) and Rowlands (2009[1998]). ↩
  2. For an analysis of this question, see Cunha (2022a). ↩

12. How Much Importance Should We Give to the Situation of Animals?

Anyone who advocates for animals has very likely come across this objection: "why worry about nonhuman animals while there are still so many humans in need of help?"

Animal advocates usually reply that helping animals does not prevent anyone from helping humans. This is true, but it does not touch the main problem with the objection, which is that it assumes that the good of humans is more important. This assumption is highly questionable, for several reasons. One is that it seems it would be widely rejected if we were under conditions of impartiality49 (that is, if we were under conditions that prevented us from being biased). Let us see why:

A common view is that, even if nonhuman animals are usually in a much worse situation than humans, even if the total number of nonhuman victims is enormously greater than that of human victims, and even if there is a much larger number of people already investing in helping humans, we should nonetheless prioritize helping humans.

However, we would never say this if we did not know the species of the victims in each case. Much less would we say the same thing if the roles were reversed. Imagine, for example, that humans were in a worse situation than nonhuman animals, that there were a larger number of human victims, and that there were a larger number of people already investing in helping nonhuman animals. In this scenario, the claim that we should nonetheless prioritize helping nonhuman animals would be seen as absurd.

The reverse is not seen as absurd only because of the predominance of speciesism, which is itself a violation of impartiality. Indeed, if we were under conditions of impartiality, given the number of victims, the severity of their situation, and the degree to which they are neglected, we would conclude that the animal cause should receive a very high priority50.

Author’s notes

  1. On impartiality, see Ética Animal (2015g, 2015h, 2016f). ↩
  2. For an analysis of this question, see Cunha (2021, p. 193-223; 2023). ↩

13. Uncertainty About Sentience and the Benefit of the Doubt

13.1. Moral consideration and uncertainty about whether a being is sentient

It is sometimes argued that, with regard to nonhuman animals (or at least some of them), we are justified in denying them moral consideration because there is no proof that they are sentient.

Animal advocates usually respond to this objection by pointing out that there is a growing body of scientific evidence establishing sentience in a large proportion of nonhuman animals, to the point that this is now the default position among scientists. This is expressed in declarations issued by the scientific community. For example, the Cambridge Declaration of July 7, 2012, attests that all mammals and birds, as well as invertebrates such as cephalopods, possess the neurological substrates that create the conditions for the emergence of consciousness51. In turn, the New York Declaration of April 19, 2024, attests that the empirical evidence indicates at least a realistic possibility of consciousness in all vertebrates and in many invertebrates (at a minimum, cephalopod mollusks, decapod crustaceans, and insects)52.

However, not even this entire body of scientific evidence will satisfy the skeptic. In this text we will first discuss the objection raised by skeptics. It will be argued that, as far as ethics is concerned, the burden of proof lies with the skeptic. That is, it is not the animals that possess a centralized nervous system who have to prove that they are sentient: it is the skeptic who has to prove that they are not (until then, we should give them the benefit of the doubt).

Next, we will discuss the position that moral consideration should be assigned in degrees: according to this position, the greater the degree of uncertainty about whether a being is sentient, the less it should count in our moral deliberations. Some arguments for rejecting this position will then be offered.

13.2. The skeptical objection

Consider the claim that we cannot be certain whether nonhuman animals are sentient for the simple reason that the only case in which anyone can be certain of this is their own sentience, since it is the only one they can experience directly. This is known as the Problem of Other Minds53.

One possible response would be to agree that the only case in which each individual can prove sentience with absolute certainty is their own, but to maintain that we nevertheless have good reasons to believe that there are other individuals who are sentient. The first kind of reason is behavior. For example, if I step on a shard of glass, I pull my foot away because I am feeling pain. So if other individuals pull away every time they step on a shard of glass, that is a reason to suppose they are doing so because they too are feeling pain. The second kind of reason is physiology. If I know that I can have experiences because I have a nervous system with a brain, and I know that it is the processing that takes place in the brain that creates the conditions for consciousness to arise54, then that is a reason to suppose that any other being with a nervous system that has a centralizing organ (a brain or ganglia) carrying out this kind of processing is also sentient. This is known as the Argument from Analogy.

However, this response will not satisfy the skeptic. He will say that it is a hasty generalization from a single case. Law (2003, p. 102-3) gives the following example: if I open a thousand cherries and find a pit in the middle of each one, I am still not justified in concluding that every cherry necessarily has a pit in the middle, and I would be even less justified in concluding such a thing if I had opened only one cherry. In the same way, the author concludes, generalizing from one's own case that other individuals who have brains and nervous systems and behave similarly are also sentient is like concluding that all cherries have pits from observing a single cherry. Thus, the skeptic concludes, we have no reason to think that there are other minds besides our own (since all the scientific evidence of sentience rests on the Argument from Analogy).

At this point one might ask who bears the burden of proof. The skeptic says that we have no reason to think there are other minds besides our own. However, the skeptic does not

offer any reason for thinking that there are none either. Who bears the burden of proof here? In epistemic terms, this is debatable. In ethical terms, however, the burden of proof certainly lies with the skeptic. This will be explained in more detail below.

13.3. The principle of the benefit of the doubt

If the fact that the only case in which we can prove there is sentience is our own were a good reason to deny moral consideration to nonhuman animals, it would equally be a reason to deny it to all humans, since we cannot verify through direct experience that they are sentient either.

There is a principle that grounds the view that, even if we are not certain that other beings with centralized nervous systems are sentient, we should nevertheless give them moral consideration: the Principle of the Benefit of the Doubt55 (also known as the Precautionary Principle). The principle prescribes that, where there is reasonable doubt about whether or not a being is sentient, we should treat it on the assumption that it is sentient, because the probability of harm is then lower.

The reasoning behind this principle is as follows: if the being in question is sentient and we treat it as if it were not, the harm we cause will probably be greater than the harm that would occur if we treat it as if it were sentient and it actually is not. In short, the principle prescribes erring on the side of caution.

If the principle of the benefit of the doubt is reasonable, then pointing out that each of us can only be certain of our own sentience is not a good reason to deny moral consideration to anyone.

13.4. Degrees of consideration according to the degree of confidence about sentience?

There is a position holding that the degree of moral consideration we should give someone ought to depend on the degree of confidence we have about whether or not the being in question is sentient: if we are certain that it is, the individual counts as 1; if we are not, we multiply by less than

1 according to the degree of confidence we have about whether or not it is sentient56.

On the basis of this position it could be argued that, since the degree of confidence in the sentience of, for example, humans or vertebrates in general is much greater than in the case of various kinds of invertebrates, we should give less consideration to the latter.

There are at least four responses to this objection, which will be addressed below.

13.4.1. Rejecting the degree-of-confidence criterion

The first response is to reject assigning differentiated degrees of moral consideration on the basis of our degree of confidence about whether or not the being in question is sentient. For example, one alternative would be to propose a minimum threshold of reasonable evidence and to maintain that everyone above that threshold would count as 1, without hierarchies, regardless of how close to or far from the threshold they are. Thus, proponents of a hierarchy based on degree of confidence would need to defend it, not simply postulate it, given that other possibilities exist.

Moreover, in many cases our low confidence regarding the sentience of certain kinds of animals stems from the scarcity of research on their sentience, or from biases on our part in assessing the data from the available research, and not from their clearly failing to meet the criteria for sentience57. Thus, against the degree-of-confidence criterion, it could be argued that in a matter as serious as moral consideration, what we should do is establish safeguards against our lack of information and against our likely biased judgment, rather than use these limitations as a criterion.

13.4.2. Arguing that the degree of confidence is high

The second way of responding would be to argue that the existing evidence for the sentience of invertebrates58 such as decapod crustaceans59 and insects60 is sufficiently

strong, and so it makes no sense to say that such animals should count as much less than 1 even if we accepted the degree-of-confidence criterion.

Of course, it may be that in the case of other animals, such as gastropods and bivalves, the available evidence is not as strong. But, again, this is not because they clearly fail to meet the criteria for sentience, but rather because it is not known exactly what the minimum number of neurons and of interactions among them is for sentience to exist61.

13.4.3. Pointing out that counting for less is not enough to justify exploitation

The third way of responding points out that, even if such animals counted as less than 1, it does not follow that exploiting them is justifiable or that we are justified in failing to help them. It is one thing to be able to establish that certain individuals should count for less. It is another to be able to establish that we are justified in exploiting, or in failing to help, the individuals who should count for less. An additional argument establishing this second conclusion would have to be put forward, since it does not necessarily follow from the first. For example, the probability that they are sentient may be high enough that we should protect them from being exploited and help them when they are in need.

13.4.4. The number of individuals can offset the smaller weight given to each

The fourth response is to observe that, even if each of these animals counted as much less than 1, the number of them who suffer and are killed is so enormous that we should still prioritize protecting them.

For example, suppose that each human counted 1,000 times more than each invertebrate. This would mean that, for us to invest the same amount of resources in helping invertebrates as we should invest in helping humans, there would have to be 1,000 times more invertebrates than humans in equally bad situations. Since in the real world the number of invertebrates who suffer and die is vastly greater than that (whether

by being exploited or in the wild), the balance would tip toward prioritizing protecting them even if it were postulated that each human counts many times more. However much smaller the weight assigned to each invertebrate, there would always be a number of invertebrate victims above which the balance would tip toward prioritizing them.

The only way to avoid this conclusion would be to set up a trump-like barrier that would forbid prioritizing invertebrates no matter how many more of them were harmed62. However, this move is ad hoc, because an additional argument would have to be put forward to ground this trump, since it does not follow from the claim that an individual's moral weight should be multiplied by our degree of confidence about whether it is sentient (on the contrary, in this case it aims to limit the implications of the degree-of-confidence criterion).

In this other text you can read an argument against the establishment of trumps or any other kinds of hierarchies of moral status.

13.5. Conclusion

In this text we have seen that there are good reasons to apply the principle of the benefit of the doubt and that, therefore, at least in ethical terms, the burden of proof lies with those who are skeptical about the sentience of beings that possess a centralized nervous system, whether with a brain or with ganglia. This also shows that, although a great deal of scientific evidence supports sentience in many kinds of animals, in ethical terms such proof is not necessary for us to owe them moral consideration: reasonable doubt is enough.

We also examined the position that the degree of moral consideration should depend on the degree of confidence we have about whether or not the being in question is sentient. We saw that it is possible to question the validity of the degree-of-confidence criterion, and we also saw that, even if we adopted this criterion, it would still not follow that we would be justified in exploiting the animals in whose sentience our degree of confidence is lower, nor that we would be justified in investing little in helping them. In fact, given their numbers, we should still prioritize helping them.
