Volume III

Animals and the Harm of Death

This book presents the main arguments in the debate on the harm of death for nonhuman animals. It investigates what the conditions are for death to be a harm and also what criteria we should use to assess the magnitude of the harm of death.

Original text by Luciano Carlos Cunha, translated into English · ISBN 978-65-01-35507-8 · 1st edition, February 2025.

1. What Does the Harm of Death Consist Of?

1.1. Introduction

The subject of this book is the harm of death and its magnitude. In general terms, it investigates what conditions must be met for individuals to be harmed by death and how to assess how much they are harmed. In specific terms, it addresses these questions with regard to the death of nonhuman animals.

Some people claim that only humans are harmed by death. We will discuss this position in chapter 2. In this chapter we will discuss the position that death never harms anyone, whether human or nonhuman. After that, in this same chapter, we will see what the idea that death is a harm is grounded on.

Before we begin, it is important to understand exactly what each of these views holds. The view that death is a harm does not claim that it is always better to stay alive than to die. This view claims only that, under certain conditions, if someone dies, they are harmed. This is compatible with recognizing that there are certain situations in which dying is less bad than staying alive (for example, if all that awaits the individual if they stay alive is excruciating suffering). On the other hand, the view that death is not a harm is not the view that it is sometimes better to die than to stay alive. Rather, it is the view that death never harms anyone. We will discuss both views below

1.2. The view that death is not a harm

The philosopher Epicurus (341-270 BC) argued that death is not a harm on the basis of the following argument: when the individual exists, death does not exist; and when death arrives, the individual ceases to exist — therefore, the two will never meet1. What Epicurus meant by this is that death is not a harm because, unlike suffering, it is not a negative experience2. Epicurus defended this view with the aim of making people lose their fear of dying, and this view is often mentioned with the same aim.

If Epicurus's view is correct, there really is no reason to fear dying, because then death harms no one. However, if Epicurus is correct, there are two other implications that often go unnoticed3. The first is that dying sooner would be no worse than dying later. In fact, according to this view dying is not bad at all, whenever it occurs (what is bad is only any suffering there may be at the moment of death). Thus, according to this view there is no reason to avoid death, since it is not considered a harm. The second implication is that all the reasons against killing would come either from concern about the victim suffering at the moment of death or from respect for individuals other than the one who died (for example, the grief they would feel at the loss of the deceased). According to this view, as long as the victim is killed without being caused pain, nothing bad would be done to the victim.

Below we will look at some reasons for rejecting Epicurus's view of death. From these reasons we will be able to understand what the idea that death is a harm is grounded on.

1.3. Death as a harm by preventing what is positive

Underlying the Epicurean conception that death is not a harm is the idea that the only possible form of harm is negative experiences. This is why Epicurus did not consider death a harm: if it is the cessation of experiences, it is obviously not experienced and therefore cannot be a negative experience, as suffering is.

The view opposed to the Epicurean view is that one can be harmed both by the presence of what is negative and by the absence of what is positive, and that death is a harm because it prevents what is positive4. According to this view, death is not experienced as an evil (as suffering is), but it is a harm because it prevents the enjoyment of what would be good5.

One argument in favor of this view is that, if someone is harmed by the presence of negative experiences because these are bad in themselves, then, analogously, someone is harmed by the absence of positive experiences because these are good in themselves.

According to this view, to know whether it is better to stay alive or better to die, we have to try to imagine what the life the individual would have if they stayed alive would be like (whether it would be more positive or more negative, and in what proportion) and assess whether this would be better or worse than dying. Thus, this account of the harm of death is compatible with claiming that, depending on how negative the life awaiting someone would be, staying alive could be even worse than dying. Therefore, this conception does not claim that dying is always a harm. Rather, it explains what the harm of death consists of and, on that basis, offers a criterion for knowing under what conditions death is a harm.

1.4. The magnitude of the harm of death and the moment at which it occurs

Contrary to the Epicurean view, it is also possible to explain why it makes a difference, in terms of the magnitude of the harm, whether death occurs sooner or later.

Suppose we have only two possibilities: (1) either to be born to live 15 very happy years and then die painlessly; (2) or to be born to live 70 equally happy years and then die painlessly. Suppose also that the amount of suffering experienced in 1 or 2 is the same (no extra suffering would be added in 2; only positive experiences would be added) and that whether we live life 1 or life 2 would be decided by lottery.

If the Epicurean conception of death were correct, it would make no difference whether we were drawn to live 1 or 2, since in both cases death is painless and the amount of suffering experienced is the same. But clearly, if we are drawn to live life 1 we have been unlucky, and if we are drawn to live life 2 we have been lucky, and the reason is simply that in life 2 the amount of positive experiences is greater.

1.5. Conclusion

Above we saw some reasons for rejecting the Epicurean view of death and maintaining that death is indeed a harm. Moreover, it is important to remember that, even if the Epicurean conception of the harm of death were correct, it would not provide grounds for the claim that only humans are harmed by death. According to the Epicurean view, no one is harmed by death. In the next section we will discuss some views holding that only humans are harmed by death.

2. Discussing the Claim That Animals Are Not Harmed by Death

2.1. Views that deny that animals are harmed by death

A common position is that there is nothing wrong with consuming animals, as long as they have had minimally meaningful lives and have been killed painlessly. This position is often defended by claiming that nonhuman animals are not harmed by death. Below, we will discuss this claim.

2.2. To be harmed by death, must one understand what death is?

It is sometimes claimed that nonhuman animals are not harmed by death because they allegedly do not understand what death is. However, we can ask: "why, for someone to be harmed by death, must they understand what death is?". Below we will examine two attempted explanations.

The first claims that it is because understanding what death is is necessary for fearing death. According to this view, death itself would not be a harm: instead, the harm is the fear of dying itself.

One problem with this explanation is that it only makes sense to fear dying if death is a harm. But if it is not the fear of dying that makes death a harm (such fear arises from the recognition that death is already a harm), then for someone to be harmed by death it is not necessary for them to fear dying.

A second attempted explanation recognizes that death is a harm because it deprives the individual of continuing to enjoy their life. However, it claims that, for someone to be harmed by an event that deprives them of something, they must value that something. Yet this view maintains that for someone to value something, they must understand the misfortune that losing it would be. That is why it maintains that, for someone to value the continuation of their life, they need to understand what it is to be dead6.

One way to reject this conception is to deny that, for someone to be harmed by being unable to experience something, they must understand the misfortune of losing it. For example, a baby is certainly harmed if prevented from nursing, even if it does not understand the harm it will suffer if this happens. Since nursing produces a positive experience for the baby, it makes sense to say that the baby values nursing.

In the same way, it makes sense to claim that nonhuman animals value the positive experiences they have in their lives, and that they are harmed by death because it prevents them from having these experiences, even if they do not understand the misfortune that death would bring them. In short, there is a difference between "suffering a loss" and "being aware of the loss one would suffer"7.

2.3. For death to be a harm, must it frustrate a future-oriented desire?

Another argument sometimes put forward to try to establish that nonhuman animals (or at least many of them) are not harmed by death is the claim that, for someone to be harmed by death, death must prevent the fulfillment of some future-oriented desire8. For example, if someone plans to travel next month and dies today, they are harmed because they never get to carry out what they planned.

According to this view, some nonhuman animals are harmed by death (those capable of having future-oriented desires, such as the pig who hides food to eat later), but this would not be the case for many other animals, nor for many humans (for example, children up to a certain age), because they would not be capable of having future-oriented desires.

One possible criticism of this view is that it wrongly assumes that a condition that is sufficient for someone to be harmed by death is also a necessary condition for it. For example, it could be said that an individual is harmed when they fail to fulfill a future-oriented desire not because of having the desire, but because of not enjoying the object of their desire. This suggests that the harm would lie in the absence of the enjoyment of that object, regardless of whether or not the individual had formed the desire to enjoy it in the future.

For example, imagine that two small children are going to be taken to a playground tomorrow and will have a great time, but that only one of the two is already able to understand the notion of "tomorrow" and form the desire to go to the playground tomorrow. If both die today, it seems that both are harmed by not getting to have fun at the playground, and not only the one who had formed a desire to go to the playground tomorrow. Indeed, if the child who is unable to plan for the future were going to have more fun than the one able to plan for the future, it seems that she would be more harmed by not getting to go to the playground than the other. This suggests that being capable of having future-oriented desires is not necessary for someone to be harmed by death, nor does it determine how much someone is harmed by death9.

2.4. When are sentient beings harmed by death (and when are they not)?

A widely accepted position is that death is a harm because it prevents the positive things the individual would enjoy if they stayed alive10. Among authors who accept this account of the harm of death, there is disagreement about what the positive things are that death would prevent. In this sense it is possible to distinguish at least four accounts of why death is a harm:

(1) Because it prevents the positive experiences someone would have if they stayed alive11;

(2) Because it prevents the fulfillment of any and every desire the individual has12 (and not only those directed toward the future);

(3) Because it prevents the fulfillment not of the desires the individual actually has, but of the desires they would have if they were fully rational and had the relevant information13;

(4) Because it prevents the individual from experiencing objective goods (for example, in addition to pleasure, also the development of capacities, certain kinds of relationships, etc.)14.

These accounts are not mutually exclusive. For example, it could be said that an individual is harmed by death because they are deprived of enjoying positive experiences and also because it frustrates their desires and prevents them from experiencing objective goods.

Moreover, accounts 2, 3, and 4 usually incorporate the first account15, so that the deprivation of positive experiences is a sufficient condition for death to be a harm.

In general terms, these accounts converge on the following conclusion: death is a harm when, comparing being dead with the life that would await the individual if they did not die (in terms of the proportion between positive and negative events), it would be better for that individual to stay alive.

If this is correct, then every sentient being with the possibility of a minimally meaningful life ahead of them is harmed by death, regardless of what species they belong to and of the degree of their cognitive capacities.

3. Objections to the Account of the Harm of Death as the Prevention of What Is Positive

3.1. The epistemological problem

One objection to the account of the harm of death as the prevention of what is positive is the so-called epistemological problem16: we cannot be certain whether the life someone would have ahead of them would be predominantly positive or negative, and so we can never know whether it is better to stay alive or better to die.

One response to this objection is to point out that, although we cannot be certain about these things, we can still make estimates in terms of the probability of what would happen. These estimates could be made on the basis of the individual's age, state of health, habits, the species to which they belong, the context in which they live, etc.17

3.2. The temporal asymmetry objection

Another objection to the account of the harm of death as the prevention of what is positive is based on the temporal asymmetry argument: we think we are harmed by death, but not that we are harmed by not having been born earlier18. According to this objection, if death were a harm because it prevents what is positive, we should be equally concerned about not having been born earlier, since that prevented us from experiencing many positive things.

One response to this objection is to maintain that, although in the logical sense it is possible to be born earlier, such a thing is not possible in real life. Our future existence, on the other hand, can be prolonged19. This, therefore, explains why it is rational to be concerned with avoiding death but not rational to be concerned with not having been born earlier. If we could make someone be born earlier and this increased their total of positive experiences, this would be just as desirable as delaying the arrival of death. For example, if we lived on a planet that will explode in six decades, but it were still possible for its inhabitants to have meaningful lives until then,

it would be better to be born as early as possible, because in that case it is the moment of birth, and not that of death, that can be changed20.

3.3. The objection from potential beings

Another objection to the account of the harm of death as the prevention of what is positive claims that it implies that potential beings (that is, beings who could have existed but never came to exist) are also harmed by not having existed (provided the life that would have awaited them was worth living). Since this seems absurd, the objection concludes, the account of the harm of death as the prevention of what is positive is inadequate.

One possible response to this objection is to maintain that the statement “individual x was harmed by being prevented from enjoying what is positive” only makes sense with regard to already existing sentient beings, because only in that case do we have individuals (rather than various future possibilities of individuals). For example, if Luciano dies, then Luciano was harmed by not enjoying the positive things he would have experienced if he had stayed alive. On the other hand, if we do not yet have an individual, but countless possibilities of future individuals, it makes no sense to say that this or that possibility was harmed by not coming to exist. For example, suppose that, if a couple conceives a child this month, individual A will be born nine months from now, but that, if they wait until next month, another individual, B, will be born. It makes no sense to claim that, if they decide to wait until next month, they have harmed A, since individual A does not exist (has never existed and never will exist; A is only a possibility) – and vice versa with regard to B, should they decide not to wait until next month.

One objection to this response is to point out that, if no one is harmed by not coming to exist, then we have no reason to prefer a world in which sentient beings continue to be born to have positive lives over a world in which no more sentient beings are born. One response to this objection is to point out that we could still have reasons to prefer a world in which sentient beings continue to be born to have positive lives, but that these reasons would be impersonal. That is, they would not be reasons derived from the concern to avoid harming this or that future possibility of a sentient being, but rather reasons derived from the general goal of achieving the best outcome.

4. Are Those Incapable of Intellectual Pleasures Only Slightly Harmed by Death?

It is sometimes argued that the more cognitively sophisticated experiences are, the more valuable they are, and that, for this reason, someone is harmed to a greater degree if they cannot experience them21. This view is sometimes used to argue that, since nonhuman animals are not capable of the intellectual pleasures of which normal adult humans are capable, death would not deprive them of anything very valuable. According to this view, although nonhuman animals are harmed by death, it would be a small harm to them, and therefore there would be nothing very wrong with killing them or with failing to save their lives.

The first problem with this argument is that the claim that intellectual pleasures are necessarily more valuable is questionable. For example, it could be said that a nonarbitrary way of determining the value of a pleasure is in terms of its intensity and its duration, rather than assuming in advance that certain kinds of pleasures are necessarily more valuable than others.

In this sense, being close to someone one is very fond of (a nonintellectual experience) and playing a game of chess (an intellectual experience) may be equally valuable experiences for whoever has them, as long as they produce the same amount of satisfaction and last the same length of time. On the other hand, the conception according to which intellectual experiences are more valuable would have to say that, in this case, playing chess has more value, even if it produces the same satisfaction (and even if it produces less satisfaction!), which seems biased.

The second (and main) problem is that, even if intellectual pleasures were more valuable, this does not imply that nonintellectual pleasures are not valuable, or that they are of little value. Therefore, claiming that intellectual pleasures are more valuable cannot ground the conclusion that nonhuman animals are only slightly harmed by death. Their nonintellectual experiences can be, just as in the human case, extremely rewarding, and for this reason they can be harmed by death to a high degree by being prevented from enjoying them.

5. How Can We Assess How Much Someone Is Harmed by Death?

5.1. The magnitude of the harm of death: future and past aspects

In chapter 2 we discussed what the conditions are for death to be a harm. We will now discuss a distinct but related question: how can we assess how much someone would be harmed if they died?

Let us begin with an example. Imagine that someone has just been born and has two possible futures ahead: either they live 10 years, or they live 80 years. Imagine that both lives would be very positive. It seems worse to die at 10 than to die at 80. There are at least two ways of explaining why. Both will be presented below.

5.1.1. The future-focused explanation

If we die at 10, the amount of positive things that we would still have to experience and that will not happen is greater than if we die at 80. If death is a harm because it prevents the enjoyment of what is positive, then the more enjoyment is prevented, the greater the harm of death.

5.1.2. The past-focused explanation

If we die at 10, we have enjoyed less so far. According to this explanation, the assessment of the magnitude of the harm of death would be guided by the principle “the less someone has enjoyed, the more they are harmed if they are prevented from enjoying more.”

5.1.3. When the explanations converge and when they diverge

The two explanations will converge when whoever has enjoyed less would also have more ahead of them to enjoy. Comparing a 10-year-old child and an 80-year-old, the child seems to be more harmed if she dies, both because she would have more to live and because she has lived less. However, if the child has lived 10 years so far but would only have another 10 ahead, and the elderly person is now 70 but could still live another 15, the appeal to the future would say that the elderly person is more harmed if he dies, whereas the appeal to the past would say that it is the child.

How should we establish the appropriate relation between future factors and past factors in measuring the magnitude of the harm of death? We will return to this question in section 5.4. First, however, we will discuss in more detail how to compute the magnitude of the harm of death separately for each of the factors (future and past).

5.2. Factors in assessing the magnitude of the harm of death: time and quality of life

For the sake of simplicity, in the previous section we relied only on time: how much longer someone would have to live and how long they have lived so far. However, length of life (past, future, or both) does not seem to be all that matters in assessing the seriousness of the harm of death. Quality of life also matters. This can be illustrated by the following example.

5.2.1. Adding the quality-of-life factor with regard to the future

Suppose that A and B have lived the same amount of time so far, and that A would have 20 years ahead and B would have 5. Taking only future time into account, A loses more if he dies now (20 years). However, imagine that, of those 20 years, 16 would be spent in extreme torment. Thus, as far as lifetime with a minimum quality is concerned, A has only 4 years ahead. Suppose that B's remaining 5 years would all be of satisfactory quality. Thus, if we add the factor of quality of future life, it is B who would have more enjoyment ahead, not A.

5.2.2. Adding the quality-of-life factor with regard to the past

The same holds for the past. Imagine that C and D would have 30 equally satisfactory years ahead of them. Imagine also that C has lived 50 years so far, and that D has lived 30. At first glance it seems that D is more harmed if she dies, since she has lived less. But suppose that the 30 years D lived were satisfactory, and that C spent 25 of his 50 years in constant suffering. Thus, taking into account the quality of past life, it is C who has enjoyed less (25 years, compared to D's 30 years).

Of course, in real life years of life (whether future or past) are not entirely good or entirely bad. In real life, each year has good moments and bad moments (and the intensity of the good and bad moments also varies). Below we will see a way of measuring this more precisely.

5.2.3. Measurement based on quality-adjusted life years (QALYs)

One way of assessing the magnitude of the harm of death is to measure it in QALYs (Quality-Adjusted Life Years), which involves multiplying time by quality of life22. This kind of assessment can be applied both to future factors and to past factors23. By multiplying time by quality of life, we can then say that someone has already enjoyed an amount “x” of QALYs and would have an amount “x” of QALYs ahead of them to enjoy. The fewer past QALYs someone has already enjoyed, the more they are harmed if they die; the more future QALYs they would have to enjoy, the more they are harmed if they die24.

5.3. Why past factors should also be taken into account

If death is a harm because of the positive things it prevents one from experiencing, then the greater the value someone would be deprived of by death, the greater the magnitude of the harm of death. One might think this would imply taking only future QALYs into account when assessing the magnitude of the harm of death. However, it could be argued that past factors also influence the size of the future loss. For example, it could be said that the fewer QALYs someone has enjoyed so far, the more valuable to that person are the QALYs they still have left.

One way of explaining the importance of considering past QALYs is to imagine the moments of enjoyment in a life as a cake. Imagine that A was given 20 slices of cake, and that B was given 100. Suppose that A has so far eaten 10 slices (because he started eating later), and that B has already eaten 80 (because she started eating earlier). Now imagine that both lose the slices they have left. Who was harmed more? It seems it was A, since he has eaten only 10 slices so far, even though all he had left was just 10 slices.

Individual B, in turn, seems to have been harmed less, since she has already eaten much more, even though she still had 20 slices left to eat.

5.4. Establishing the relation between future and past factors

How should we establish the relation between future and past factors in order to measure the magnitude of the harm of death? There are many possible ways of establishing this relation. One example is the following formula25: g(T) – g(P), where T is the total well-being of the individual's life if they lived to the maximum of their life expectancy, P is the well-being the individual has lived so far, and g is a strictly increasing and strictly concave function. It is strictly increasing because the more well-being an individual has had so far, the greater the value of the total well-being, and it is concave to represent the idea that the less well-being someone has had so far, the greater the harm of not having an additional unit of well-being.

5.5. QALYs and comparisons between the harm of death for humans and nonhumans

The QALY theory could in no way serve to argue that humans are always more harmed by death than nonhuman animals.

If we took only future factors into account, perhaps this would be so in many cases, given that humans have a longer life expectancy than animals of many other species. But even if we took only future factors into account, sharks, whales, and turtles of various species would normally have more ahead of them to enjoy (since their typical lifespan is much longer). Moreover, even if the average life expectancy of members of the human species is greater than that of members of various other species, there would still be situations in which, comparing two individuals, it is the human who would have fewer QALYs ahead. This would happen if we were comparing, for example, an 80-year-old human and a 5-year-old pig.

Moreover, we have seen that there are strong reasons to take past QALYs into account as well. It is crucially because of this factor that the QALY theory leads us to conclude that nonhuman animals are generally quite unfortunate with the lives they have had, since,

besides dying, in the overwhelming majority of cases, very prematurely, they typically live lives that contain nothing but suffering from beginning to end (both under exploitation and in the wild).

5.6. How important is the question of the magnitude of the harm of death?

It is not uncommon to believe that, for us to have to revise our attitudes toward the death of nonhuman animals, it is crucial to show that they are as harmed by death as humans are. According to this belief, if it is shown that, for some reason, humans are more harmed by death than nonhuman animals, then killing nonhuman animals and failing to save their lives is justified.

This common belief is mistaken for a very simple reason: showing that A is more harmed by death than B does not show that B is only slightly harmed by death. Although assessing the magnitude of the harm of death is important in certain situations (for example, in questions of prioritizing whom to save), it is not essential for recognizing that we should change our attitudes toward killing and failing to save nonhuman animals. For that, it is enough to recognize that animals are greatly harmed by death. We will discuss this point in more detail in chapters 9, 10, and 11.

In the next chapter we will discuss some objections to measuring the magnitude of the harm of death on the basis of QALYs.

6. Objections to Assessing the Magnitude of the Harm of Death on the Basis of QALYs

6.1. The objection from absurd implications

In the previous chapter we saw an approach that assesses the magnitude of the harm of death solely on the basis of how much someone has already enjoyed and/or would still have to enjoy, estimating this in terms of QALYs (Quality-Adjusted Life Years).

One objection to this approach claims that it leads to absurd conclusions. Among these conclusions are: (1) that in certain cases a nonhuman animal would be more harmed by death than a human; (2) that in most cases children would be more harmed by death than adults; (3) that the moment at which someone would be most harmed by death is the very first instant at which the fetus becomes sentient (since it has not yet enjoyed anything and would still have everything ahead of it to enjoy) and, therefore, already-sentient fetuses would be more harmed by death than those already born26.

Before we look at the main response to this objection, it is important to note that measuring the magnitude of the harm of death on the basis of QALYs does not imply that each and every already-sentient fetus is more harmed by death than each and every individual already born. Depending on how many more positive future QALYs (and/or how many more negative past QALYs) the already-born individual had, they could be more harmed by death than the already-sentient fetus. The same would hold for the comparison between the harm of death for adults and children, and between humans and nonhuman animals. This is in fact a virtue of assessing the magnitude of the harm of death on the basis of QALYs: it takes into account the complexities of each case, avoiding generalizations of the type "this or that kind of being is always more harmed by death".

However, the proponent of the objection could insist that, in most cases, assessing the magnitude of the harm of death on the basis of QALYs would have those allegedly absurd implications. That being so, the main response to this objection is to point out the following: saying that an implication is absurd is not offering any reason to show that it is in fact

absurd. An explanation of why they would be absurd must be provided. Below we will discuss some attempts to do so.

6.2. Discussing the appeal to intuitions

One way of arguing that those implications are absurd is to point out that they are counterintuitive, in the sense of contradicting the beliefs we hold before reflecting on the matter. According to this approach, if a conclusion we reach through reflection contradicts our prior beliefs, there must be something wrong with the conclusion.

There is an obvious problem with this approach: it would only make sense if our prior beliefs were always correct. But if that were so, it would make no sense to reflect on anything, since the purpose of reflection is precisely to investigate which of our prior beliefs hold up after examination. If prior beliefs are to be the criterion for assessing reflection, then why reflect? It is one thing to say that, if an approach has a strange implication, we should test the approach further. It is another to say that the conclusions we draw after reflecting are wrong if they contradict our prior beliefs.

Another possibility is to agree that a conclusion's being counterintuitive does not show that it is wrong, but to maintain that the burden of proof lies with whoever goes against the intuition. This may make sense with regard to basic beliefs that we all hold. For example, if someone claims that the Earth is shaped like a guitar, the burden of proof certainly lies with that person. However, in ethical matters intuitions vary greatly from person to person. Consider the intuitions we are discussing regarding the magnitude of the harm of death. Many people have exactly the opposite intuitions. The way the proponents of the objection put it suggests that everyone has those intuitions, but this is not true. Therefore, even if we assumed that the burden of proof lies with whoever challenges the intuition, we still would not know who bears the burden of proof, since intuition varies widely.

It is also possible to question the idea that the burden of proof lies with whoever goes against intuitions. One can argue for exactly the opposite, that is, that if an approach fits our initial beliefs, that is a reason to be suspicious of it, since we may believe it simply because it spares us the discomfort of questioning our initial beliefs27. Reliance on intuitions in ethics would only make sense if we had some special kind of "sensor" that automatically revealed to us, without any reflection, what is right and wrong in ethics. There seems to be no reason to think that anything of the sort exists. On the contrary, our intuitions (that is, the beliefs we hold before reflecting) are probably the result of ideas we have cultivated all our lives and that our society also cultivates, which may very well be prejudices.

Moreover, many intuitions may be the result of biases due to the way the brain operates28. One example is the bias known as an availability cascade, which occurs when a collective belief gains more and more acceptance through its increasing repetition in public discourse, even if it is not plausible. This is one more reason to be suspicious of our intuitions. One does not show that an idea is plausible merely by pointing out that it seems plausible (which is what the appeal to intuitions does).

It is also interesting to note that some proponents of the objection we are discussing defend other positions that sound highly counterintuitive to many people, such as veganism29 and intervention in nature to help wild animals when they are victims of natural processes30 (two positions that I, in fact, also defend31). Quite possibly these authors did not always hold these positions, and it was reflection that made them change (just as happened in my case). But if in this case prior beliefs were abandoned in the light of reflection, why should prior beliefs about the harm of death function as a kind of authority over reflection?

6.3. Defending the QALY criterion

We will now look at a reason to think that the burden of proof, in the case of the magnitude of the harm of death, lies with whoever contradicts the conclusions of measurement based on QALYs. The reason is that measuring the magnitude of the harm of death in terms of QALYs follows directly from the account of what the harm of death consists of: if death is a harm because it prevents the positive things the individual would experience if they stayed alive,

then the more they would have to experience and/or the less they have experienced so far, the greater this harm.

If someone claims that the conclusions following from this assessment are wrong because they contradict certain intuitions, then they need to put forward a principle showing that these intuitions are correct (rather than simply assuming in advance that they are correct).

One attempt to do so is the Time-Relative Interest Account (abbreviated here as TRIA), which we will discuss in more detail in chapters 7 and 9. It holds that the magnitude of the harm of death should be measured by multiplying the value someone would be deprived of by death (as is done in the QALY approach) by the degree of psychological connectedness that person would maintain over time32. According to this approach, already-sentient fetuses, nonhuman animals, and human children have weaker psychological connectedness and would therefore be much less harmed by death.

However, in this approach the psychological connectedness criterion is not independently grounded: it is postulated because it would ground those intuitions and, on the other hand, those intuitions are defended as correct because they agree with the psychological connectedness criterion33. If so, the reasoning is clearly circular34.

Moreover, since the aim of the TRIA is to ground intuitions, it is worth noting that it has implications that are even more counterintuitive to most people than the implications of the QALY-centered approach. For example, according to the TRIA, young children would hardly be harmed by death at all35.

Regardless of which approach is more intuitive or counterintuitive, it is important to take seriously the possibility that our intuitions are wrong before setting out to defend them at all costs. It is possible that the death of nonhuman animals, human children, and already-sentient fetuses (of whatever species) is something much more serious than is normally recognized.

Obviously, this does not mean that every approach that has counterintuitive implications is necessarily correct. It means only that, to show that an approach is mistaken, it is not enough to show that it has counterintuitive implications.

Of course, this also does not show that there cannot be other criteria for measuring the magnitude of the harm of death besides QALYs. It does show, however, that until such criteria are independently grounded, we have reason to rely on QALYs alone.

7. Do Animals Have Weaker Psychological Connectedness?

It is sometimes argued that, for someone to be greatly harmed by death, they must maintain strong psychological connectedness with their future36. By psychological connectedness is meant the degree to which memories, character traits, beliefs, desires, intentions, etc., are retained.

Proponents of this view claim that nonhuman animals (or at least many of them), because they have less cognitive complexity, have very weak psychological connectedness and are therefore hardly harmed by death at all: "it is almost as if the future they lose in dying were someone else's future37". This idea is sometimes used to argue that there would be nothing very wrong with killing them or failing to save their lives.

One possible criticism of this view is to question the claim that, for someone to be seriously harmed by death, it is necessary to maintain strong psychological connectedness with their future. We will return to this criticism in chapter 9.

In this chapter we will look at another possible kind of criticism of this position: questioning the claim that beings with lesser cognitive capacities have little psychological connectedness with their future38. Below we will look at an example that illustrates this criticism39.

Suppose that A at instant T1 has 10 mental contents and at instant T2 also has 10, retaining 9 of those already present at T1 and replacing a single content. B also had 10 mental contents at T1, and at T2 retained all 10, but gained another 90.

IndividualMental contents at T1Mental contents at T2Contents in commonNew contentsProportion retained
A1010 (9+1)9190%
B10100 (10+90)109010%

If the degree of psychological connectedness is measured by the number of mental contents in common, B has greater psychological connectedness (10 contents in common, compared to A's 9).

On the other hand, if the degree of psychological connectedness depends instead on the proportion of mental contents in common, it is A who has greater psychological connectedness (A retained 90% of its mental contents, while B retained only 10%), even though B's mind is more complex.

On this basis it could be said that, if what the concept of psychological connectedness aims to express is how psychologically similar someone is from one instant to another, then the appropriate way to measure it is in terms of the proportion of mental contents in common, not their number.

If so, then less cognitively sophisticated beings do not necessarily have little psychological connectedness with their future selves. On the contrary: since the proportion of the mental contents of less cognitively complex beings varies less, they may be psychologically connected to their futures much more strongly than cognitively more complex beings are.

Thus, even if the degree of psychological connectedness is relevant to the magnitude of the harm of death, this does not imply that nonhuman animals or humans with lesser cognitive capacities are only slightly harmed by death — quite the contrary. Moreover, as we have seen, it is also possible to question the thesis that the degree of psychological connectedness is relevant to the magnitude of the harm of death. We will look at this criticism in chapter 9.

8. Discussing the Claim That Animals Are Replaceable

It is sometimes argued that there is nothing wrong with killing nonhuman animals, as long as they have led a meaningful life up to that point, are killed painlessly, and are replaced by others who would be born to take their place and lead equally positive lives (and so the cycle would continue). This argument is sometimes used to defend the use of animals for consumption. It is commonly said that consuming animals benefits them, since "otherwise they would not be born". Let us call this position the replaceability defense.

One way of responding to this position is to point out that animals raised for consumption live lives full of extreme suffering and are killed in brutal ways, and other animals replace them by being born to live in that same hell. It would therefore be ridiculous to say that they were benefited by being born in such a context. However, the proponent of replaceability could say that their proposal is precisely to reform the system of animal exploitation so that those ideal conditions occur in practice and the animals live good lives. Of course, it is doubtful that this would be possible in practice. Regardless of that, however, it is also possible to challenge the idea that animals are replaceable even under the ideal conditions the argument assumes. That is what we will see in this chapter.

Let us begin by asking why anyone would think that animals are replaceable. One of the reasons is the belief that animals are not harmed by death. But, again, we can ask: why would anyone think that? In this chapter we will examine one of the explanations most often given by proponents of replaceability: the identity-based explanation (in chapter 9 we will discuss another explanation that is sometimes given: the explanation based on prudential reasons).

The identity-based explanation claims that what makes someone the same individual over time is their psychological connectedness40. On this basis it is argued that beings who lack a temporal sense of self (that is, who have no memories and cannot imagine themselves in the future) are replaceable41. The reason for this would be that, if a being lacking a temporal sense of self is not the same individual over time, then it makes no difference whether we

keep that body alive or kill it and bring another into being: either way, the individual who exists now is annihilated (the only difference will be whether the new individual is born in this same body or in another).

A first possible criticism of this argument is to point out that, even if it made sense, it could only justify replacing beings who have no psychological connectedness at all, and this is not the case for the vast majority of animals (if it is the case for any).

A second criticism is directed at the very idea that an individual's identity is determined by their psychological connectedness. The criticism suggests that this idea confuses two senses of the term "the same"42. It makes sense to claim that someone who has lost their memories "is no longer the same" qualitatively, that is, in the sense of being psychologically very different from what they were before. However, this does not mean that it is a numerically different individual who occupies that body and that the previous individual was annihilated. It is not another consciousness experiencing the world: it is the same individual, who simply does not remember. If so, then psychological connectedness does not determine an individual's numerical identity.

Let us look at an example to illustrate this point43. Imagine that Ana has all of her psychological connectedness copied into a new body. When the new body starts functioning, a new individual comes into being: AnaB. This new individual, because she has Ana's psychological connectedness, believes she is Ana, and remembers everything Ana has experienced up to that moment as if she herself had experienced it.

Imagine also that AnaB is physically identical to Ana and has all of her mannerisms. When AnaB walks down the street, people think she is Ana. Remember, however, that the original Ana did not die. Both Ana and AnaB are alive. If psychological connectedness determined individual identity, Ana and AnaB would be the same individual. But it seems clear that they are two distinct individuals, even though they have the same psychological connectedness, because they are two distinct consciousnesses: what one experiences, the other does not; the decisions of one affect only the movement of her own body and not the body of the other, etc. This suggests that it is not psychological connectedness that determines an individual's identity.

Let us look at a second example. Imagine that, as in Ana's case above, you will have all of your psychological connectedness copied into a new body, which has not yet started functioning. As in the previous example, the person who will be in the new body will remember all of your experiences and will think they are you. However, something unexpected happened. When copying your psychological connectedness into the new body, they accidentally erased your psychological connectedness from your brain. Now the new individual is alive, in the other body, remembering that they are you and thinking that they are you. You are also alive, not remembering who you are. The question is: where are you, in the new body or in the old one?

It seems clear that you are in the body you were already in, which no longer has the psychological connectedness it had, because it is you, your consciousness, who will be there experiencing everything that body experiences from then on, even if you remember nothing of your past. The other person in the new body remembers being you and thinks they are you, but they are mistaken, because they are a different consciousness, despite having the same psychological connectedness. Thus, this example also suggests that an individual's identity is not determined by their psychological connectedness.

If what these examples suggest is correct, then one of the main defenses of the idea that certain animals are replaceable (the identity-based explanation) has serious problems.

  3. On this distinction, see Noonan and Curtis (2018). ↩

9. Are Nonhuman Animals Only Slightly Harmed by Death?

9.1. The appeal to psychological connectedness

It is sometimes argued that nonhuman animals (or at least many of them) are only slightly harmed by death because they allegedly lack strong psychological connectedness with their future. What is meant by psychological connectedness is the degree to which memories, character traits, beliefs, desires, intentions, etc., are retained.

However, we can ask: why, for someone to be greatly harmed by death, would they need strong psychological connectedness with their future? One explanation holds that it is because psychological connectedness determines someone's identity (that is, it is what makes someone the same individual over time). We have already seen the problems with this explanation in chapter 8. In this chapter we will discuss another explanation that is sometimes offered. This explanation claims that psychological connectedness is relevant to determining the strength of an individual's prudential reasons, even if it is not relevant to determining their identity44.

9.2. The appeal to prudential reasons

What is meant by prudential reasons? They are the reasons someone has to avoid negative events and to pursue positive events that could happen to themselves. According to the position we are going to discuss, the strength of the reasons someone has to avoid or pursue a given event that would happen to them in the future would be determined by multiplying how good or bad that event is by the psychological connectedness they would maintain with their "future self"45.

According to this approach, for this reason, if nonhuman animals have little psychological connectedness, they are not greatly harmed by death, even if it deprives them of having very satisfying experiences.

We saw in chapter 7 that one way of questioning this argument is to deny that nonhuman animals have little psychological connectedness with their future. In this chapter, however, we will address another kind of criticism: we will look at two counterexamples that challenge the idea that psychological connectedness matters for the strength of prudential reasons46.

9.3. Does the strength of reasons to avoid negative events depend on psychological connectedness?

The first counterexample concerns the strength of reasons to avoid negative events.

The case of the greater evil

Imagine that Ana finds out that it is impossible to avoid Alzheimer's disease at the end of her life and that, after a year, the disease will have destroyed all psychological connectedness with who she is now. In addition, she also finds out that she will suffer from a second condition, which will cause her a great deal of pain. However, it is possible to choose when the second condition will occur: either after Alzheimer's has made her lose all her psychological connectedness, or before she has the disease, while she still retains strong psychological connectedness with who she is now. There is, however, one difference: if she chooses to have the second condition occur after she has completely lost psychological connectedness, the pain will be much more severe.

It seems that, from Ana's own point of view, it is preferable to choose to have the pain occur while she still has strong psychological connectedness with herself now, simply because the pain will be less. If the degree of psychological connectedness were relevant to determining the strength of the reasons someone has to try to avoid a negative event that would happen to them in the future, we would have to say that it is preferable for Ana to go through the much more intense pain, by choosing to have it occur after the total loss of psychological connectedness. If this is not the case, then it seems that the strength of prudential reasons to avoid a negative event does not depend on the degree of psychological connectedness.

9.4. Does the strength of reasons to pursue positive events depend on psychological connectedness?

The second counterexample aims to show the same thing, but with regard to the strength of prudential reasons to pursue positive events (and, consequently, to avoid death).

The case of the greater good

Imagine that Bia is still a five-year-old child and wishes to see the pyramids of Egypt. Imagine, however, that if she travels now, while she has strong psychological connectedness with who she is now, the trip will be pleasant, but that it will be much more pleasant if she travels when she is an adult. When she is an adult, however, she will have extremely weak psychological connectedness with who she is now (her memories, character traits, beliefs, desires, intentions, etc., will have changed a great deal).

It seems that Bia has prudential reasons to prefer to take the trip when she is an adult, simply because the trip will be much more pleasant. If this is correct, then psychological connectedness is not relevant to determining the strength of the prudential reasons someone has to pursue positive events either.

This suggests that an individual who has weaker psychological connectedness (or even one who retains no psychological connectedness at all) is not necessarily only slightly harmed by death, since missing out on the positive events that death would prevent is not, for that reason, only slightly harmful to them. Therefore, an appeal to psychological connectedness does not seem able to show that nonhuman animals are only slightly harmed by death.

9.5. Discussing responses to the examples

For the sake of simplicity, let us call the multiplicative approach the one holding that the strength of prudential reasons to pursue/avoid a given event should be determined by multiplying how good/bad the event would be by the degree of psychological connectedness someone would maintain between the present time and the moment at which the event would occur.

Dossena (2024b, p. 86-7) responds to the Case of the Greater Evil by arguing that, contrary to what it may seem, the multiplicative approach would not imply choosing to go through the more severe pain. According to the author, this would be so because such an approach would also take into account the future interests someone would have, provided that some degree of prudential unity relations (in this case, some degree of psychological connectedness) is maintained between the present moment and the future moment at which the interest will be frustrated, even if these prudential unity relations are weak. Below we will look at three problems with this response.

The first problem is that in the Case of the Greater Evil the stronger pain will occur after the disease has made the individual lose psychological connectedness with who they are now completely. Thus, in this case the condition suggested by the author ("provided there is some degree of prudential unity relations") is not met. But if the individual still has reasons to prefer to avoid having the pain occur in this condition simply because the pain will be more intense, then the degree of psychological connectedness is not relevant to the strength of prudential reasons (since in this case the degree of psychological connectedness is equal to zero).

The second problem is that both the Case of the Greater Evil and the Case of the Greater Good acknowledge that the multiplicative approach would take into account all the positive and negative events that would happen to the individual from then on (and would therefore take into account their future interests). However, it is important to remember, such an approach prescribes multiplying how good or bad the event would be by the degree of psychological connectedness the individual maintains between the present moment and the moment at which the event would occur, in order to determine the strength of prudential reasons. And it is in this sense that such an approach would have to say that we have very weak prudential reasons, whether to pursue a very good event or to avoid a very bad one, if such events are to occur at a moment when we no longer maintain strong psychological connectedness with who we are now. In the Case of the Greater Evil, where the individual retains no psychological connectedness with the present moment, such an approach would have to say that the individual has no reason at all to avoid the stronger pain.

The third problem is that if, as the author acknowledges, we have reasons to avoid the greater pain even if at the moment it would occur we would have little (or even no) psychological connectedness with who we are now, then the response the author offers to the Case of the Greater Evil, instead of showing that the degree of psychological connectedness matters for the strength of prudential reasons, emphasizes exactly the opposite (which is exactly what the Case of the Greater Evil aims to emphasize): that what matters for the strength of prudential reasons is how good or bad the event would be, and not the degree of psychological connectedness we would maintain between the present moment and the moment at which the event would occur.

The author acknowledges that his response is incompatible with the idea that the strength of prudential reasons is a function of the value/disvalue of the future event and the strength of prudential unity relations (in this case, the degree of psychological connectedness)47. As a solution, he suggests recognizing that any negative or positive future event already provides significant prudential reasons, but that, if the degree of psychological connectedness between the present and that future is lower, these reasons would carry somewhat less weight48.

The problem with this way out is that, if these reasons carried less weight, then we should not conclude that it is better to avoid the greater evil, since it would occur after we had lost all psychological connectedness. The lesser evil, by contrast, would occur while we still have strong psychological connectedness, and, according to the solution offered by the author, we would have to say that the reasons to avoid it would be stronger than those to avoid the greater evil.

Moreover, the response offered by the author does not explain the importance of the degree of psychological connectedness for the strength of prudential reasons. In fact, what the response suggests is that, if we maintain that the degree of psychological connectedness is much less relevant to the strength of prudential reasons, then we will not reach the conclusion that it is rational to choose to go through a much greater pain. But this is not to show that the degree of psychological connectedness is relevant to the strength of these reasons, not even to a lesser degree49.

Dossena (2024a, 2024b) has made a very honest and thorough analysis both of the position defended here and of the position that the counterexamples I offered aim to criticize. However, as I understand it, the responses offered by the author come much closer to the position defended here than they rescue the degree-of-psychological-connectedness criterion. If so, then it seems that the thesis still stands that individuals (including nonhuman animals) can be seriously harmed by death because of factors that have to do solely with what they would miss out on enjoying if they died, regardless of the degree of psychological connectedness they would maintain over time.

10. The Claim That Having Little Time Left Makes Death a Small Harm

10.1. The claim that it is not wrong to kill animals who have little time ahead of them

One position sometimes defended is that animals who would have little lifetime ahead of them would be only slightly harmed by death. Having little lifetime ahead is something that could occur: (1) either when the characteristic lifespan of the animal's species is short; (2) or when it is long, but the animal is near the end of that lifespan. According to this position, under these conditions there would be nothing wrong with killing them.

There are at least two ways of questioning this position. The first is to question the thesis that, if someone has little lifetime ahead of them, they are only slightly harmed by death. The second is to argue that someone's being only slightly harmed by death is not enough to justify killing them. We will look at each of these challenges separately below.

10.2. Various ways of calculating the magnitude of the harm of death

Let us first examine the claim that having little lifetime ahead makes death a small harm. Underlying this claim is the idea that the seriousness of the harm of death should be measured solely on the basis of the time remaining to be lived.

However, as we saw in chapter 5, another crucial factor in measuring the magnitude of the harm of death50 is how positive or negative the life would be (the life remaining to be lived and/or the life lived so far, as we will detail later on). We saw that in the literature on the magnitude of the harm of death, one form of measurement that relates the two factors (multiplying time by quality of life at each instant) is QALYs (Quality-Adjusted Life Years)51. In this sense, we say that an individual would have an amount X of QALYs ahead and has already enjoyed an amount X of QALYs so far. Taking this into account, it is possible that A has more lifetime ahead than B, but that it is B who has more QALYs ahead, given that the expected level of B's future well-being is higher.

However, since we are assessing only the claim that having little lifetime ahead makes death a slight harm, for the sake of simplicity we will assume that the individuals being compared will have the same amount of well-being ahead, and that this well-being will be positive to the point that death is a harm.

To assess the claim that having little lifetime ahead makes death a trivial harm, it is important to note that there are various ways of measuring how serious the harm of death is, taking into account the moment at which it occurs. Some of them follow.

The first two take into account either only the future or only the past:

(1) Future only. The greater the amount of time remaining, the greater the harm of death.

(2) Past only. The less someone has lived so far, the greater the harm of death.

There are other forms that take into account both the future and the past. However, there are many ways of establishing the relation between these two factors in measuring the magnitude of the harm of death. Two examples follow:

(3) Percentage. The smaller the percentage of life expectancy that the time lived so far represents, the greater the harm of death. For example, imagine that an animal belongs to a species whose typical lifespan is one year, and it dies at one month of age. It has thus lived 8.3% of what it could have lived. According to the formula in question, the harm of its death is 91.7% (100% being the maximum harm, which is when someone dies as soon as they begin to exist as a sentient being).

(4) Priority. This consists in measuring the magnitude of the harm of death on the assumption that the less someone has lived so far, the more value an additional instant of life has52. Thus, suppose that A and B would have 40 years of life ahead of them, but that A has lived 20 years so far and B has lived only 10. According to this way of measuring, although A and B have the same lifetime ahead, that time would be more valuable for B because he has lived less up to

now. This way of measuring will give different results from the one based on percentage. For example, suppose that A has a lifespan of 20 years and has already lived 10 years, and that B has a lifespan of 10 years and has already lived 5 years. According to the Percentage formula, the magnitude of the harm of death is the same for both, since both have lived 50% of the total. According to the Priority formula, by contrast, it would be taken into account both that the time remaining for A is greater and that the time lived so far by B has been less.

As we saw in chapter 5, one formula for measuring the magnitude of the harm of death according to this conception would be the following53: g(T) – g(P), where T is the total well-being of the individual's life if they lived to the maximum of their life expectancy, P is the well-being the individual has lived so far, and g is a strictly increasing and strictly concave function. It is strictly increasing because the more well-being an individual has had so far, the more value the total well-being has. And it is concave to represent the idea that the less well-being someone has had so far, the greater the harm of not having an additional unit of well-being.

Below we will see how each of these forms of measurement would have to assess the magnitude of the harm of death.

10.3. Assessing the magnitude of the harm of death according to four formulas

(1) According to the Future only formula, the harm of death for individuals who have little lifetime left ahead would be smaller (compared to individuals who have more time left), whether they are individuals whose lifespan is short or individuals whose lifespan is long and who are at the end of that lifespan. For example, suppose that an animal has a lifespan of 1 year and has lived 1 month so far, and that a human (whose average life expectancy is 73 years) has lived 72 years and 1 month so far. According to this

way of measuring, the magnitude of the harm of death is the same for both, since what they have left is 11 months.

An important observation regarding this formula is that it does not necessarily imply that individuals who have less time ahead are only slightly harmed by death. It implies only that they are less harmed than individuals who have more time left. This is so because the point at which a line could be drawn to establish how much remaining time it takes for death to become a serious harm is variable. For example, if what we have left is one month of positive life, we would probably already say that we have lost something significant. And certainly, if it were a year, we would say that we have lost something very significant. Thus, even this formula would still not imply that animals who have little time ahead are only slightly harmed by death.

For example, suppose that a human is born with a disease and we know that the most they will be able to live is a few years (and that until then their life can be satisfactory). We would not say that this human is only slightly harmed by a premature death merely because their life expectancy is short. Quite the contrary: it seems that they are harmed to a high degree if they cannot experience the little time they still have left.

(2) According to the Past only formula, how much someone has ahead does not matter: all that matters is how much that someone has lived so far. According to this formula, all nonhuman animals (regardless of the length of their lifespans and of how much they have left to live) are as harmed by death as humans who died at the same age would be.

(3) According to the Percentage formula, neither the length of the lifespan nor the amount of time remaining to be enjoyed matters directly: all that matters directly is how much the time lived so far represents as a percentage of the total expectancy. For example, according to this formula a nonhuman animal who is killed at 15% of their lifespan is as harmed by death as a human killed at 15% of their lifespan would be, whatever the length of the typical lifespan of each species.

(4) According to the Priority formula, the time remaining to be lived would have to be weighed against what has been lived so far. For example, let us again compare an animal with a life expectancy of 1 year who has lived 1 month so far with a human (whose average life expectancy is 73 years) who has lived 72 years and 1 month so far. According to the Priority formula, in this case the nonhuman animal would be harmed by death to a greater degree than the human, since, although both have the same lifetime ahead, the nonhuman animal has lived much less so far. Of course, according to this formula the magnitude of the harm of death would vary greatly, depending on how much the remaining time and the time lived so far varied for the individuals being compared. However, according to this formula, in most cases the harm of death for nonhuman animals is greater than according to the Future Only formula.

10.4. Conclusion regarding the harm of death and the moment at which it occurs

Of all four formulas we have seen, the one that takes into account only future time is the one least favorable to recognizing that death greatly harms animals who have little lifetime ahead. However, as we have seen, even this formula would have to recognize that they are as harmed by death as humans with the same lifetime ahead would be.

We also saw that there are at least three other formulas, and that all of them generally imply recognizing a greater harm of death than the formula that takes into account only the future. This is because all these other formulas take past factors into account (exclusively or in addition). As we saw in section 5.3, the importance of taking past factors into account can be explained by the following analogy: if I have already eaten five slices of a cake, missing out on one more harms me less than it would if I had eaten only one.

10.5. What if the passage of time is different for animals of different species?

It is possible that members of different species have a different perception of the passage of time. According to one theory, smaller animals would have brains that process information more quickly, making their “internal clock” that marks the perception of the passage of time run faster, such that what seems to us a week would be experienced by such an animal as the equivalent of months or years54.

Let us call this theory the Different Time Theory (DTT), since it holds that the passage of time is perceived at different speeds by animals of different species. In contrast, let us call the theory holding that this perception is the same, regardless of species, the Equal Time Theory (ETT).

It could be said that, if the DTT is correct, animals who have a short lifespan would in fact have already enjoyed much more time so far, and that we would have to take this into account when assessing the magnitude of the harm of death. This is true, but it does not necessarily imply that the formulas that take the past into account would have to maintain that such animals are only slightly harmed by death. Below we will see how each of the four formulas above would have to assess this question if the DTT is correct.

  • The Future Only formula would have to maintain that the harm of death for these animals, if the DTT is correct, would be greater than if the ETT is correct, since they would then have more time of enjoyment ahead (how much greater would depend on how much faster their internal clock marking the perception of the passage of time is).
  • According to the Past Only formula, the harm of death for these animals would be smaller than if the subjective passage of time were the same, but this would not imply that the harm of death would necessarily be small.
  • According to the Proportion formula, there would be no change at all in the magnitude of the harm of death, since for this formula what matters is how much the moment of death represents as a proportion of the total lifespan, not the length of the lifespan.
  • According to the Priority formula, while the fact that they have experienced more subjective time so far would contribute to decreasing the magnitude of the harm of death, the fact that they have a greater amount of subjective time ahead would contribute to increasing the harm of death.

In short, whether it is the DTT or the ETT that is correct, there seems to be no basis for claiming that death harms sentient beings only slightly, even those who have little lifetime ahead.

10.6. If someone has little lifetime ahead, does that justify killing them?

In the previous sections we saw that it is possible to question the claim that, because someone has little lifetime ahead, they are only slightly harmed by death. However, let us assume for the sake of argument that, under such conditions, an individual is only slightly harmed by death. This does not seem enough to justify killing them. For example, even if a human has only a few months, or just a few more days (or even a single day) of positive life ahead, it is normally considered unacceptable to kill them, even while recognizing that, in this case, the magnitude of the harm of death for them would be much smaller than if they had years of life ahead.

Those who hold that it is right to kill a nonhuman animal who has little lifetime ahead would then have to hold that it is right to kill any human who has the same lifetime ahead. One alternative is for them to accept that a human's having little lifetime left is no justification for killing them. But then this implies accepting that a nonhuman animal's having little lifetime ahead is no justification for killing them either.

The only way to deny these implications would be to demonstrate that humans should have a special status that would protect them under these conditions, one that would be absent in the case of nonhuman animals. However, as we will discuss in detail in chapter 12, there seems to be no justification for assigning differentiated moral statuses. If this is correct, then the implications above remain the same, whether those affected by the decision are human or nonhuman animals.

  2. For an application of this theory to the harm of death for nonhuman animals, see Horta (2010) and Cunha (2021, p. 2022, p. 71-73) ↩

  4. This formula for the harm of death was developed by Ribeiro (2024) from a formula suggested by Holtug and Adler (2019) for comparisons of harms in general (and not only the harm of death) in prioritarian theory. Prioritarianism is the theory of normative ethics according to which the worse an individual's level of well-being, the more value an additional unit of improvement in their well-being has. The prioritarian principle is different from the principle of diminishing marginal utility, according to which an additional unit of a resource generates more well-being the smaller the amount of that resource someone has. According to the prioritarian principle, by contrast, an additional unit of well-being has more value the lower the level of well-being of whoever would receive that additional unit. Parfit (1995, p. 105) sums up the difference this way: “just as resources have diminishing marginal utility, utility has diminishing marginal value”. On prioritarianism, see Parfit (1995) and Holtug (2007). ↩
