11. What If Humans Were More Harmed by Death?

11.1. Common views about killing and about saving lives

The following two positions are commonly defended:

  • (1) That it is right to kill nonhuman animals (for example, for consumption, in experiments, or for various other purposes).
  • (2) That we should not use resources to save the lives of nonhuman animals (for example, when they are victims of diseases or of disasters).

In this chapter these positions will be referred to as the "two common positions".

These positions are often defended by claiming that nonhuman animals are less harmed by death than humans are. In previous chapters it was argued that humans are not necessarily more harmed by death than nonhuman animals. In this chapter, however, it will be argued that, even if they were, this would still be insufficient to ground those two positions.

11.2. If one being is more harmed by death than another, what are the implications?

Suppose that A is more harmed by dying than B. What does this imply? It implies only that we have stronger direct reasons55 against killing and for saving the life of A. It does not imply that there are no direct reasons against killing and for saving the life of B. Nor does it even imply that these reasons are weak in B's case. They may in fact be extremely strong, only slightly less strong than the reasons against killing and for saving the life of A.

Thus, what would have to be shown to justify the two common positions is not that nonhuman animals are less harmed by death than humans are, but rather that nonhuman animals are hardly harmed by death at all. In chapters 4, 5, 8, 9, and

10 it was argued that every sentient being can be harmed by death to a high degree. This is enough for there to be strong direct reasons against killing them and for saving their lives in situations where they would be greatly harmed by death.

11.3. Does someone's being more harmed by death already justify killing others to save them?

One might think that, if A is more harmed by death than B, this would justify killing B if doing so saved A's life. However, if we look at examples involving humans, it becomes evident that this, by itself, is insufficient to justify such an act. Let us see:

The degrees to which different humans are harmed by death are also highly variable. Some have already enjoyed life a great deal; others have lived very little. Some have lived a meaningful life so far; others have lived predominantly in suffering. Some have the prospect of a meaningful life ahead; for others, all that awaits them if they stay alive is extreme suffering. Some would still have a lot to live; others would have little time ahead. In short, the harm of death also varies greatly in the case of different humans. However, this does not seem enough to justify killing a human just because doing so would save another human who would be more harmed by death. If that were so, it would be right to kill elderly people or older adults every time doing so made it possible to save the lives of younger humans.

One might think that what was said above only makes sense on ethical views based on inviolable rights, according to which it is always wrong to kill one individual to save another (or others). However, those who hold that it is right to violate rights if this is necessary to achieve the best consequences can also agree that the mere fact that A is more harmed by death than B is still insufficient to justify killing B to save A. This is explained in more detail below.

If what one seeks is the best consequences, and death is a harm, it would have to be shown that there is no less harmful way of saving A's life than killing B. It would also have to be shown that authorizing the killing of some to save others in the context in question produces the best consequences in the long run, taking into account how this act influences other people's future decisions. Of course, someone who seeks the best consequences would also take into account, in deciding, the fact that one individual is more harmed by death than another. However, it is not the only thing they need to take into account if their goal is to achieve the best consequences. Therefore, they would also have to recognize that the finding that one individual is more harmed by death than another is, by itself, insufficient to justify killing one to save another.

Thus, if the fact that B is less harmed by death than A is insufficient to justify killing B even if doing so saves A's life, it would be all the less sufficient to justify killing B for entirely unnecessary purposes, such as consuming them.

This does not necessarily mean that it is always wrong to kill, or that it is always wrong to fail to save a life. It means only that the fact that A is more harmed by death than B is insufficient to establish that it is right to kill B or that we have no obligation to save B's life.

11.4. Reasons to save lives, the harm of death, and the number of victims

Let us imagine for the sake of argument that it were proven that humans are more harmed by death than nonhuman animals. Would this imply that we must necessarily prioritize problems whose victims are human? No, because an important factor has not yet been considered: the number of individuals we could save. The relation between the number of individuals and the harm per individual will be explained below.

Let us grant for the sake of argument that each human were harmed by death 100 times more than each nonhuman animal. This is really granting a great deal. But even this would still be insufficient to conclude that we always have stronger reasons to save humans. For example, if the choice were between saving one human or saving 101 nonhuman animals, in that case the balance would already tip toward saving the nonhuman animals.

However much more someone said humans are harmed by death, there would always be a number of nonhuman animals beyond which we would have to prioritize saving nonhuman animals. That being so, even if nonhuman animals were less harmed by death than humans, this too would be insufficient to ground the conclusion that we should invest more resources in saving human lives.

It could be objected that we should save those who are more harmed by death, no matter how many more individuals we could save otherwise. However, this idea is far from obvious. Therefore, it would need to be justified, not merely assumed. Pointing out that postulating it would imply the conclusion one prefers is not showing that it is correct. Thus, until proven otherwise, we have reason to think that the number of victims we could save also matters, and, as we have seen, this factor can sometimes tip the balance toward saving those who would be less harmed by death.

11.5. Conclusions

It is often assumed that, if humans are more harmed by death than nonhuman animals, then it is right to kill nonhuman animals, and that we should not use resources to save the lives of nonhuman animals.

However, we have seen that, even if humans were more harmed by death than nonhuman animals, this would not imply that there are no reasons against killing and for saving the lives of nonhuman animals, nor that these reasons are weak.

Moreover, as we have seen, even if nonhuman animals were less harmed by death than humans, depending on the number of nonhuman animals we could save with a given amount of resources, there could still be reasons to prioritize saving them.

Important: in this chapter we assumed solely for the sake of argument that humans would be more harmed by death than nonhuman animals. The aim was only to show that, even if this were the case, it would not have the implications that are normally supposed. However, as argued in previous chapters, there seems to be no basis for grounding the claim that humans are necessarily more harmed by death than nonhuman animals56. If so, then the reasons against killing and for saving the lives of nonhuman animals in situations where they would be harmed by death are even stronger than those described in this chapter.

  1. There could be indirect reasons for us to prefer to save B, even if B were less harmed by death than A. For example, this would be the case if saving B ensured that we would save the lives of other individuals, and this would not happen (or would happen to a lesser degree) if we chose to save A. ↩

12. Differentiated Moral Status, the Harm of Death, and the Wrongness of Killing

12.1. The harm of death and the wrongness of killing

Compare these two claims:

Claim 1: "There are stronger reasons against killing and for saving the lives of humans because they are more harmed by death than nonhuman animals".

Claim 2: "There are stronger reasons against killing and for saving the lives of humans even if they are less harmed by death than nonhuman animals".

We discussed claim 1 in previous chapters. In this chapter we will discuss claim 2.

12.2. Reasons against killing and for saving lives: direct and indirect

With regard to reasons against killing and for saving lives, there are direct and indirect reasons:

Direct: these relate to the individual who would die.

Indirect: these relate to the impact that someone's death would have on other individuals.

An example of a direct reason would be the harm the individual would suffer if they died. An example of an indirect reason would be the sense of loss other individuals would feel, or the possibility that the individual would benefit others if they stayed alive.

12.3. The debate on direct reasons: the magnitude thesis versus the status thesis

In the debate on the strength of reasons against killing and for saving lives, there is a discussion about whether only direct reasons should count, or whether indirect reasons should count as well, and, if so, whether or not they should have the same weight as direct reasons.

In this chapter we will not go into these discussions. Instead, we will address the discussion of which factors the strength of direct reasons against killing and for saving lives should depend on.

On one side, the Magnitude Thesis (MT) holds that it should depend solely on the magnitude of the harm of death. That is, according to this position, the more someone is harmed by death, the stronger the direct reasons against killing them and for saving their life.

On the other side, the Status Thesis (ST) holds that we can have stronger direct reasons against killing and for saving the life of someone, even if they are less harmed by death, if that someone has a special status.

In the following sections, we will look at some implications of these two theses.

12.4. Direct reasons against killing as dependent on the harm of death

According to the MT, given two individuals A and B, we have stronger direct reasons against killing and for saving the life of whichever one is more harmed by death, whoever that may be.

This does not mean that, according to the MT, there are no direct reasons against killing and for saving the life of the one who is less harmed by death. In fact, according to the MT these reasons can also be extremely strong (this depends on how much the individual would be harmed by death). It means only that, according to the MT, the reasons against killing and for saving the one who would be more harmed by death are even stronger.

Consider, then, two implications of the MT:

Implication 1: Comparing a human who has the cognitive capacities of a normal adult and a human who lacks these capacities (such as babies, children, already-sentient fetuses, or adults who are victims of certain diseases or accidents that prevent them from having such capacities), if the human who lacks these capacities is more harmed by death than the human who has these capacities, we have stronger direct reasons against killing and for saving the life of the human who lacks these capacities.

Implication 2: Comparing a nonhuman animal and a human, if the nonhuman animal is more harmed by death than the human, we have stronger direct reasons against killing and for saving the life of the nonhuman animal.

12.5. An example of an approach centered on privileged moral status

Some people believe that the direct reasons against killing and for saving the lives of normal adult humans are stronger, even when they are less harmed by death. This view is commonly defended by claiming that normal adult humans have a special status (usually called dignity).

One example is the Two-Tiered Account (in the original, Two-Tiered Account), proposed by Jeff McMahan, which we will abbreviate here as TTA57. This approach draws a distinction between the wrongness of killing beings who are capable of autonomy and those who are not.

The TTA defends the following four theses58:

(1) According to the TTA, the wrongness of killing beings incapable of autonomy (whether nonhuman or human) depends on how much they are harmed by death. Therefore, the wrongness of killing these beings varies in degree.

(2) According to the TTA, the wrongness of killing autonomous agents does not depend on how much they are harmed by death, but rather on respect for their dignity. This implies the so-called Equal Wrongness Thesis. According to this thesis, these individuals have dignity because they are capable of making autonomous decisions. This capacity also varies in degree, but, according to the Equal Wrongness Thesis, dignity is a trump and admits of no degrees: all who have dignity have it equally. According to the TTA, the wrongness of killing autonomous agents does not vary in degree, because it is grounded in respect for their autonomous will not to die.

(3) According to the full variant of the TTA, the wrongness of killing an autonomous agent is always greater than the wrongness of killing a being incapable of autonomy, no matter how much more the latter is harmed by death. According to the threshold variant of the TTA, by contrast, the trump of

dignity applies only up to a certain point: depending on how much more the being incapable of autonomy is harmed by death, the wrongness of killing that being is greater.

(4) According to the TTA, it is right to kill beings incapable of autonomy if this is the only way to save one or more autonomous agents (or to save a sufficiently large number of beings incapable of autonomy), but it is not right to do the same to autonomous agents. Here, again, depending on the variant of the TTA, the trump of the dignity of autonomous agents applies fully or only up to a certain point. According to the threshold variant, there would be a number beyond which the possibility of saving many other individuals (whether autonomous agents or not) would make it right to kill autonomous agents to save them.

Are these theses plausible? We will discuss this in sections 12.7, 12.8, and 12.9. First we will discuss whether these theses could justify the current view of animals and of the practices that affect them. We will look at this next, in section 12.6.

12.6. Would the two-tiered account justify the common view of animals?

A common mistake is to think that, if it is more wrong to kill or fail to save humans, then there is nothing wrong with killing or failing to save nonhuman animals. This is mistaken, because act A's being more wrong than act B does not show that act B is not wrong (in fact, it may still be extremely wrong, only slightly less wrong than A).

Thus, contrary to what one might initially think, the TTA could not justify animal experimentation, much less the consumption of animals or other forms of animal exploitation. Note that thesis number 4 of the TTA holds that killing beings incapable of autonomy is justified only if this is the only way to save other individuals. The consumption of animals, obviously, is not about saving lives, since we can meet our nutritional needs with plant foods. As for animal experimentation, a large part of it is not carried out with the aim of discovering medicines, and even with regard to the part that is, there is no way to show that the same benefits could not have been obtained without using animals (indeed, it might be that not using animals would be more efficient for obtaining them).

As for saving lives, the TTA holds only that it is even more wrong not to save the lives of normal adult humans. But it can still recognize that it is very wrong not to save the lives of nonhuman animals (including the lives of animals who live in the wild and are victims of natural processes). McMahan himself, the creator of the TTA, advocates intervening in nature to help animals in the wild who are victims of natural processes59.

Important: nothing said above means that it is more wrong to kill and fail to save humans. It means only that, even if it were, this would not justify the common practices of killing nonhuman animals and of neglecting to save their lives.

Below we will discuss some problems with the TTA.

12.7. How much should we trust intuitions?

As we have seen, the TTA holds that (always or generally, depending on the variant) it is more wrong to kill autonomous agents, even when they are less harmed by death. However, it is up to the proponents of the TTA to explain why, since they are making an exception to the general principle that the seriousness of the wrongness of killing depends on how much the victim would be harmed by death. This, by itself, does not show that the TTA is wrong, but it does show that the burden of proof lies with its proponents to justify the exception they want to make.

In response, proponents of the TTA argue that it is because autonomous agents have the trump of dignity, which would exist because of their autonomy. But why would the capacity for autonomy generate a trump? And why would autonomy specifically generate this trump and not, say, sentience or any other characteristic60? All of this is simply postulated by the TTA.

The reason for postulating these things, according to proponents of the TTA, is that doing so would allegedly ground certain intuitions61: that the wrongness of killing nonhuman animals and humans incapable of autonomy varies in degree but that the wrongness of killing normal adult humans does not vary in degree; that the wrongness of killing autonomous agents is greater than the wrongness of killing beings incapable of autonomy; that it is right to kill beings incapable of autonomy in circumstances in which killing autonomous agents would not be, etc. It is then argued that these

intuitions can be grounded by postulating that autonomous agents have the trump of dignity and that dignity, in turn, would arise from their very capacity for autonomy62.

However, this postulate is not independently grounded. What grounds it is simply the fact that it agrees with those intuitions. Those intuitions, in turn, are considered correct because they agree with this postulate. But then the TTA is clearly circular: the postulate comes into play to ground those intuitions, and the postulate itself is grounded in those intuitions.

Besides the evident circularity, we must take seriously the possibility that these intuitions are biased. We will see more about this below.

12.8. How can intuitions be tested?

McMahan, a proponent of the TTA, claims that coherence among various beliefs increases our reasons for thinking that each of the beliefs is justified: they reinforce one another through their mutual support63. One problem with this is that any intuitions that do not contradict one another can reinforce one another and still be arbitrary, biased, or stem from morally irrelevant factors, false factual beliefs, etc.

To avoid this problem, McMahan holds that justified intuitions are those that survive a filtering process that would eliminate intuitions that are: (1) the obvious product of self-interest, (2) implausible metaphysical bases, or (3) factual errors64.

He also acknowledges that, for a principle to support one or more intuitions, it must have independent credibility (rather than being accepted only because it would ground the intuitions)65. The aim, according to the author, is to transcend our subjective points of view and achieve the greatest possible degree of objectivity and impartiality66.

These seem to be good criteria for testing intuitions. However, it seems that the TTA does not pass this filtering test. To begin with, it seems that the TTA would be vehemently rejected from an impartial perspective. We will look at this below.

12.9. Does the two-tiered account pass the impartiality test?

How can we know whether a decision is impartial? A widely used method consists in imagining whether we would consider it fair if we did not know which position we would occupy among those affected by it. A method of this kind was first proposed by John Harsanyi67 in 1955, and a very similar method was later used extensively in John Rawls's 1971 work A Theory of Justice68, influencing many other later works.

The method consists in imagining rational and self-interested agents who aim to maximize their own well-being but have not yet been born into the world in which they will live. This is the so-called original position. In it, these agents must decide which moral and political principles will be in force in that future world. However, they must decide behind a veil of ignorance, where they do not know what characteristics they will have after they are born. They will not know their race; gender; nationality; whether they will be born into rich or poor families; whether they will be born healthy or with some disease; what talents or difficulties they will have, etc. All of this will be decided by lottery, and behind the veil of ignorance we can know nothing about factors that depend on good or bad luck. Thus, the agents have equal probabilities of being born as any of the individuals in the future world. The basic idea is that whatever rational and self-interested agents would consider just/unjust under such conditions would in fact be just/unjust.

It is sometimes argued that this method applies only to those of our decisions that affect beings who have a sense of justice. According to this view, the method does not apply to our decisions that affect nonhuman animals and humans incapable of understanding such a method (such as babies, children, and adults with some cognitive impairment).

However, this reasoning would only make sense if, for someone to be treated unjustly, it were also necessary to have a sense of justice. But consider, for example, the case of a human child born with a cognitive limitation that will prevent her throughout her life from

developing a sense of justice. Imagine that this child is treated worse than others because of the color of her skin, because of her cognitive limitations, or because of any other factor that is the result of the natural lottery. The fact that this child does not have a sense of justice (and can never come to develop one) does not make the treatment she received any less unjust. It is true that it only makes sense to hold someone responsible for committing an injustice if that someone has a sense of justice (this is why it makes no sense to hold babies responsible, for example). However, it is not necessary to have a sense of justice in order to be the victim of an injustice.

If so, then nonhuman animals' lack of a sense of justice is not a good reason to exclude them from the protection of principles of justice, since they too can be victims of injustice. For this reason, true impartiality requires that, behind the veil of ignorance, knowledge of the species to which one belongs also be excluded, since this too is a result of the natural lottery69.

Taking this into account, one way of testing whether the TTA passes the impartiality test is to imagine whether rational and self-interested agents would consider it fair if there were a possibility that they might be born as beings who will not develop autonomy.

Let us recall that, according to the TTA, (sometimes or always, depending on the variant) the reasons against killing beings incapable of autonomy are weaker, even when they are more harmed by death. That being so, it seems that the greater the probability that rational and self-interested agents (that is, agents who aim to maximize their own well-being) would be drawn to be born as beings incapable of autonomy once the veil is lifted, the more strongly they would reject the TTA.

In the real world this possibility would be enormous, given that the number of nonhuman animals is astronomically greater than the number of humans. The human population stands at around 8 billion individuals. According to some estimates, at any given moment there would be at least 1 to 10 quintillion sentient nonhuman animals in the world70. This difference in size is so astronomical that it is hard to visualize. However,

an analogy will help us understand it: if we make an analogy with the span of a year, the human population would represent at most 0.25 seconds of the year.

This strongly suggests that the intuition that beings capable of autonomy should have a special status would not pass the impartiality test. Moreover, it suggests that this intuition is grounded: (1) in self-interest (since we know that, in the real world, we are capable of autonomy) and (2) in the belief that we ourselves could not be disadvantaged by this intuition (which is a factual error, since each of us may come to lose autonomy if a disease or accident affects our cognitive capacities).

Therefore, if we should seek impartiality and reject intuitions that are the result of self-interest and factual errors, as McMahan proposes, it seems that there are good reasons to reject the intuition that beings capable of autonomy should have a special status.

12.10. Conclusions

If what has been argued above is correct, it seems that there is no way to justify the idea that certain individuals should have a privileged moral status. If so, then the strength of direct reasons against killing and for saving lives should be determined solely on the basis of the magnitude of the harm of death.

13. Further Reflections: Death, Annihilation, Rational Decision, and Probabilities

13.1. The imprecision of the terms "death" and "life"

The word "death" is used in at least two different senses:

1. Biological death: As indicating that the body has irreversibly ceased to perform certain functions.

2. Annihilation of the individual: As a synonym for the impossibility of having experiences again (the individual ceases to exist for good).

In what follows, the term "death" will be used in the first sense, and the term "annihilation" will be used in the second sense.

The word "life" is also used rather imprecisely. For example, when people ask: "is there life after death?", they are not talking about biological life without any experience (such as a mere living body, with no one living that life). What they want to know is whether there is sentience after death. That is, they want to know whether biological death annihilates the individual, or whether the individual goes on having experiences (or at least retains the potential to have experiences again at some point). Thus, when the word "life" appears below, we are always talking about psychological (and not merely biological) life, that is, we are talking about sentience.

13.2. The harm of death and beliefs about whether or not death coincides with annihilation

As we saw in chapters 1 and 2, in the literature on the harm of death the most widely accepted position is that it is a deprivation harm. That is, death is a harm (when it is one) because it deprives the individual of the positive things they would experience if they stayed alive. In light of this, someone might think that, in that case, those who believe there is life after death have no reason to think that death is a harm (and perhaps, by implication, not even any reason to avoid death, whether their own or that of others). However, this is not so, as explained below.

In assessing this question, it is necessary to compare two possible courses of action available to us (going on living or dying) with states that could occur after death and that do not depend on our decision (annihilation occurring or there being life after death). However, it is also necessary to take into account that, if there is life after death, it may be better or worse than the current life, and better or worse than annihilation. These possibilities will be explored below71.

13.3. Decision possibilities and their relation to the assessment of post-death scenarios

For the sake of simplicity, in what follows the same degree of probability will be assigned to each of the possible post-death scenarios.

13.3.1. If the current life is better than annihilation

Let us first address a scenario in which the current life is (and would continue to be) better than annihilation.

Consider the possible courses of action (available to the agent):

A: Go on living B: Die

Consider the possible post-death scenarios (which do not depend on the agent's decision):

1: Annihilation 2: Life after death 2.1: Better than the current one 2.2: Worse than the current one but still better than annihilation 2.3: Worse than the current one and worse than annihilation

We have the following possibilities:

If 1...If 2.1...If 2.2...If 2.3....
A1A2.1A2.2A2.3
B1B2.1B2.2B2.3

Let us now relate the possible post-death scenarios and assess in each of them what the best course of action would be. The symbol ">" means "better than".

If death brings annihilation, it is better to go on living (A1 > B1).

If death brings a life better than the current one, it is better to die (B2.1 > A2.1).

If death brings a life worse than the current one, but still better than annihilation, it is better to go on living (A2.2 > B2.2).

If death brings a life worse than the current one and worse than annihilation, it is better to go on living (A2.3 > B2.3).

In short, if the current life is (and would continue to be) better than annihilation, then it is better to live. This is because, if death is annihilation, death is a harm, and, if it is not, the life after death could be worse than the current life (and perhaps even worse than annihilation). Of course, such a life could also be better than the current one, but the risk to be run would be very great. Therefore, the precautionary principle would prescribe protecting the current life.

13.3.2. If the current life is worse than annihilation

Let us now address a scenario in which the current life is (and would continue to be) worse than annihilation.

Consider the possible courses of action (available to the agent):

C: Go on living D: Die

Consider the possible post-death scenarios (which do not depend on the agent's decision):

3: Annihilation 4: Life after death 4.1: Worse than the current one 4.2: Better than the current one but still worse than annihilation 4.3: Better than the current one and better than annihilation

We have the following possibilities:

If 3...If 4.1...If 4.2...If 4.3....
C3C4.1C4.2C4.3
D3D4.1D4.2D4.3

Let us now relate the possible post-death scenarios and assess in each of them what the best course of action would be. Again, the symbol ">" means "better than".

If death brings annihilation, it is better to die (D3 > C3).

If death brings a life worse than the current one, it is better to live (C4.1 > D4.1).

If death brings a life better than the current one, but not better than annihilation, it is still better to die (D4.2 > C4.2).

If death brings a life better than the current one and better than annihilation, it is better to die (D4.3 > C4.3).

In short, if the current life is (and would continue to be) worse than annihilation, we have reason to prefer to cut it short, because, although there is a risk that the subsequent life, if annihilation does not occur, will be even worse than the current one, cutting the current life short is, in this case, also the only opportunity someone has of trying to improve their current state, even at some risk. For example, in this scenario not only annihilation would represent an improvement over the current life, but even a life worse than annihilation yet still better than the current one.

13.4. Further complications

A series of further complications regarding the question above arise because we also have no idea, should death not coincide with annihilation, how long the subsequent life would last, nor whether or not the moment of death influences the amount of pleasure/suffering that would be experienced afterward.

Taking this into account, there are three possibilities regarding what the individual would experience:

(1) A finite and fixed amount of pleasure/displeasure (which would not change, whenever death occurred).

(2) A finite amount of pleasure/displeasure, but how long it would last (and hence the total amount) would depend on when death occurred.

(3) An infinite amount of pleasure/displeasure.

In the first option it makes no difference at all to consider post-death scenarios. All decisions about whether it is better to stay alive or to die will depend solely on what we expect would happen in the current life. In the second option, by contrast, it does make a difference to consider the possible post-death scenarios (as we did in the previous section). In the third, there is the further complication of how to deal with the idea of pleasure/suffering for an infinite time, which for reasons of space we will not address here.

13.5. Conclusion

It might seem at first glance that, if we take into account various possible post-death scenarios and also our uncertainty about which of them might occur, our assessment of the reasons for protecting or cutting short a life would have to change radically compared with the assessment we would make if we were certain that annihilation would occur. However, as we have seen, although recognizing these possibilities and our high degree of uncertainty introduces a series of complications, if we take into account the risks and their relation to how good or bad the current life is, it seems that our conclusions would not be very different from the assessment we would make if we were certain that annihilation would occur.

Volume IV

The Debate on Animal Exploitation

This book describes the typical situation of animals exploited by humans and also analyzes the arguments of the opposing positions in the debate over whether or not there is any justification for animal exploitation.

Original text by Luciano Carlos Cunha, translated into English · ISBN 978-65-01-40062-4 · 1st edition, March 2025.

1. How Do the Animals Exploited by Humans Live and Die?

1.1. Animal exploitation

Nonhuman animals are exploited and killed by humans every day for a wide variety of purposes. They are used as food, for clothing, as test subjects, for entertainment and leisure, and as workers or tools. The form of exploitation that kills by far the most animals is their use as food. Counting vertebrates alone, it is estimated that at least 2 trillion are killed worldwide every year for consumption. That already means that on average, in a single day, around 5.5 billion vertebrates are killed. To get a sense of how large this number is, we need only recall that there are around 8 billion humans in the world. However, the overwhelming majority of the animals humans exploit are invertebrates1. The following table presents some statistics on the kinds of animals killed in each form of exploitation for consumption.

Type of exploitation for consumption Animals killed worldwide per year
Mammals and birdsAround 80 billion2.
Farmed fish3Between 51 and 167 billion.
Fish caught in the wild at sea4Between 787 billion and 2.3 trillion.
Aquatic animals used as feed for farmed fishBetween 462 billion and 1.1 trillion5.
Farmed decapod crustaceans6Between 255 and 604 billion.
Silkworms used in silk productionBetween 420 billion and 1 trillion7.
Insects killed for consumptionBetween 2 and 3.2 trillion8.
Cochineal insects used to produce carmine dye9Between 4.6 and 21 trillion.
Shrimp caught in the wild at sea10Around 25 trillion.

Adding up these numbers suggests that somewhere between 34 and 54 trillion animals are killed every year worldwide. This means that, for consumption alone, between 93 and 147 billion nonhuman animals are killed per day. In other words, for consumption alone, the number of animals killed per day is between 11 and 18 times the human population.

1.2. The general situation of animals raised for consumption

Below, as an example of the typical life of exploited animals, we will illustrate the situation of animals raised for consumption. However, it is important to bear in mind that the situation of animals exploited for other purposes is quite similar11.

Animals raised for consumption, besides losing their lives, usually endure intense suffering from the moment they are born until the moment they are killed12. Because of the demand for animal products, factory farms are organized to raise as many animals as possible in the smallest possible space and at the lowest possible cost. Most of the animals have no room at all to move. Many cannot even turn around. They live on concrete floors or wire mesh, constantly standing in their own excrement, which causes them various diseases and injuries. We will look at all this in more detail below.

1.3. The situation of hens, broiler chickens, and chicks

Laying hens live crammed into overcrowded cages, each in a space the size of a sheet of paper13. They spend their whole lives standing on the wire floors of their cages. In some cases their feet become caught in the wire mesh, and when they are pulled out to be sent to the slaughterhouse, their legs often break and part of them is torn off.

Chickens raised for meat, in turn, have been genetically selected to grow extremely fast14. Their legs cannot support their weight, which causes them injuries and pain. Many of them cannot even stand.

The male chicks of laying hens, for their part, are not raised to be eaten, since they would not grow as fast as the birds selected for that purpose. They are thrown into a machine where they are ground up alive, or into a garbage bin where they die of suffocation or are crushed by the other chicks thrown on top of them.

1.4. Diseases affecting animals exploited for consumption

Given the overcrowded conditions on farms, diseases can spread quickly, giving rise to epidemics. This happens in the farming of both land and aquatic animals. When it does, animals are commonly culled en masse, including healthy ones, even when they could be treated (because it is cheaper to kill them and breed others to replace them). In the case of land animals, this is usually done by burying the animals alive and covering them with quicklime, or else by boiling them alive15.

Diseases can also be found at very high concentrations in aquatic animals farmed for consumption (although they also occur to a high degree among those living in the wild). As with land animals, the fact that aquatic animal farms are overcrowded makes it much easier for diseases to spread. Overcrowding, poor water and environmental quality, and how stressed or weak the animals are, are among the many factors that impair their immune systems, making them more susceptible to disease16. In addition, the chemicals present in the tanks can irritate their skin and mucous membranes, leaving them highly susceptible to germs, much as when they suffer from wounds17. Crustaceans are also massively affected by diseases that cause, among other things, blindness and severe deformities, and some of these diseases can wipe out entire populations in a matter of days18.

1.5. The situation of sows

Many of the sows exploited for breeding spend four months confined in tiny metal crates with slatted floors. They cannot even turn around, and can lie down or stand up only with great difficulty19. Their muscles and joints are severely damaged, and they literally go mad from never being able to move and from the boredom of never being able to engage in any activity. The piglets are weaned from three weeks of age. At that point the sows are impregnated again, and the cycle starts over until they are three years old, when they are killed.

1.6. The situation of cows and calves

Cows, like all female mammals, produce milk only after giving birth. That is why they are kept continually pregnant, usually through artificial insemination. Producers do not want the calves to drink the milk, since that would reduce profits. So mothers and babies are separated shortly after birth, which is terribly traumatic for both of them; they cry and bellow for days. Cows are usually milked for 10 months after being separated from their babies. Then they are impregnated again, and the cycle is repeated until they are completely worn out, at which point they are killed.

Calves used to produce veal often live in tiny crates in which they cannot even turn around. It is common for their heads to be restrained so that they cannot exercise their muscles, to make their flesh as tender as possible. For this reason they are fed low-nutrient formulas, which leave them so weak that many cannot even walk when they are sent to be killed20.

1.7. Procedures involving mutilation

Many mammals are branded with hot irons and have pieces of their bodies cut off, such as parts of their ears and tails. Steers and bulls have their horns sawn off or burned with caustic substances. Hens have their beaks cut off with hot blades.

Baby piglets have their teeth pulled out and their tails cut off. All of this is done without painkillers or anesthesia, since these would raise costs without increasing productivity.

1.8. Vulnerability to the decisions of workers

The animals are completely at the mercy of whatever the workers decide to do. For example, if a worker is stressed, is angry at some animal, or is simply sadistic and wants to have some cruel fun, there is nothing that really stops him from torturing the animals however he pleases and as much as he wants. The animals are completely vulnerable in his hands.

Gail Eisnitz's book Slaughterhouse: The Shocking Story of Greed, Neglect, and Inhumane Treatment Inside the U.S. Meat Industry (Abatedouro: a história chocante de ganância, negligência e tratamento desumano na indústria de carne dos EUA, in the author's own Portuguese rendering) contains a series of testimonies from slaughterhouse workers describing what they do to the animals. The following testimony is one example:

"You're going to kill the hog anyway, but that's not enough. It has to suffer... you don't just kill it, you go in hard, push hard, blow the windpipe, make it drown in its own blood. Split its nose. A live hog would be running around the pit. It would just be looking up at me. I'd stick it. And then I'd take my knife and – eerk! [imitating the hog's squeal] while it just sits there doing nothing, I'd cut its eye out! And the only thing the hog can do is scream in pain. One time I took my knife – it's sharp enough – and I sliced off the end of a hog's nose, just like a piece of bologna. The hog went crazy for a few seconds, and then it just sat there looking kind of stupid. So I took a handful of salt brine and ground it into its nose. Now that hog really went nuts, rubbing its nose all over the place. I still had a bunch of salt left on my hand – I was wearing a rubber glove – and I stuck the salt right up the hog's ass. The poor hog didn't know whether to shit or go blind. But I wasn't the only guy doing this kind of stuff. One guy I work with chases hogs into the scalding tank21" .

1.9. Transport to the slaughterhouse

During transport to the slaughterhouse, the animals are loaded onto trucks using prods, hammers, and electric shock sticks. Birds are hoisted up as if they were objects. They are usually grabbed by the legs and thrown into crates, which often breaks their

legs and other bones22. Overcrowding on the trucks is even worse than on the farms. In addition, the animals are exposed to extreme heat or cold and are given no food or water during the entire journey, since doing so would not be profitable. Many animals die before reaching their destination, which shows how much they suffered on the way23.

1.10. How animals are killed in slaughterhouses

The animals are killed in ways that cause excruciating suffering. When they arrive at the slaughterhouse, they are struck with poles to make them move along the corridors. Sometimes they are given electric shocks with prods, and they are also kicked and punched. When they cannot walk, they are dragged with hooks driven into various parts of their bodies, which sometimes tear those parts apart. In addition, they can see and hear other animals being killed and smell those animals' blood. After being stunned, they are shackled by the legs and hoisted off the ground upside down, which sometimes breaks their legs.

Because slaughter lines have to move quickly, this process is carried out at high speed, so it is common for the animals not to be properly stunned and to be fully conscious when their throats are cut. Moreover, the cut often fails to kill them, and so they are dismembered, sliced up, and skinned or scalded while still fully conscious24. This fate awaits all animals used for food, regardless of whether they were raised on factory farms or on so-called "free-range" farms.

1.11. How animals are killed in fishing

Fishing is one of the forms of exploitation that kills the most animals25. Besides losing their lives, the animals suffer intensely, whether on aquatic animal farms or in open-sea fishing. In hook fishing, the hook pierces the mouth or other parts of the body and, as the fish is dragged out of the water, the whole weight of the animal's body is concentrated on the pierced area. As a result, the hook pierces ever more deeply and tears ever more of the

part of the body in which it is lodged26. Animals caught with nets also suffer intensely, for a number of reasons detailed below.

The most common ways in which caught animals die are27: their internal organs bursting from decompression; suffocation; having their bodies cut open while still conscious; being crushed under the weight of the other animals piled on top of them or trapped in the nets; blows to the head; electrocution; hypothermia; carbon dioxide poisoning; or a shot to the head. Others are cooked alive or even eaten alive28.

1.12. The exploitation of insects

The exploitation of insects harms an enormous number of animals. The space allotted to insects on farms is even smaller, in proportion to their size, than that given to other animals29. Before they are removed from confinement, the common practice is to deprive them of food for 12 to 24 hours and to lower the oxygen concentration. They are then kept alive and chilled to temperatures close to 0ºC. Typical methods of killing them are: freezing; immersion in water hotter than 80ºC; microwaving; infrared tunnel ovens; and grinding30.

1.13. The exploitation of decapod crustaceans

Examples of decapod crustaceans are crabs, swimming crabs, lobsters, crayfish, and shrimp. These animals are among those most exploited by humans. For example, around 25 trillion shrimp are killed every year for consumption31. In 2021 an official UK government report prepared by a team of expert scientists reviewed more than 300 studies and concluded clearly that decapod crustaceans are sentient32. Below we will look at the procedures to which these animals are typically subjected when they are exploited.

Capture and holding

Decapod crustaceans destined for the food industry are either captured in the wild or "harvested" on farms. Capture methods vary depending on the species and on the number of animals caught, but all of them seriously harm the animals through changes in barometric pressure, physical trauma, injuries, crushing, exhaustion, and death33.

Once on deck, wild-caught decapods are exposed to air, light, temperature fluctuations, noise, handling, and also high stocking densities, since they are confined very close to one another. This results in restricted behavior, wounds, infections, aggression, and even mutilation and death by suffocation34. Holding usually lasts several days after capture35.

Despite their hard shells, they are fragile animals. For example, their limbs can be injured or torn off when they are removed from nets or taken out of pots36. In addition, the speed at which they are brought from the sea to the boat can cause a rapid change in pressure and temperature, causing them intense suffering37.

Once out of the sea they are exposed to air, and since they are animals that breathe underwater by means of gills, this makes it hard for them to take in oxygen. Exposure to air can cause stress and vulnerability to disease, and can even be fatal through suffocation. During storage on board, these animals are kept out of water for long periods of time38.

Mutilations

Mutilations is a term used to describe procedures that destroy, remove, or damage limbs or other parts of the body39. The mutilations described below are

common practices in the industry that exploits crabs, lobsters, and shrimp, and they are almost always carried out without any anesthesia or painkiller40.

Eye mutilation (eyestalk ablation)

Eyestalk ablation (eyestalk ablation) consists in the removal or destruction of one or both eyestalks, which are the stalks that support the eyes of shrimp. It is performed on female breeding shrimp in order to increase total egg production and the percentage of females in a given population that will take part in reproduction (since the eyestalk contains glands that regulate the ovaries)41. It is routinely practiced in almost all marine shrimp maturation or breeding facilities in the world, both research and commercial42.

The procedure involves pulling off or crushing the eyestalk, cutting it with a blade and squeezing out its contents, and then cauterizing or tying off the stalk.

The techniques used vary43. For example, one technique consists in pinching the eyestalk, usually half to two-thirds of the way down from the eye, as shown in the following image.

Image credit: Kannan et al. (2015).

Another technique involves making a cut in the eye with a blade or scissors and then crushing the eyestalk between the thumb and index fingernail until the contents of the eye have been removed, as shown in the following image.

Image credit: Kungvankij et al. (1989 [1986]).

Cauterization is done with an electrocautery device, a hot wire, or forceps44. Ligation, in turn, is done by tying the eyestalk tightly with surgical thread45.

All of these procedures are normally performed without anesthesia46. Studies have shown that shrimp display pain-related behaviors during and after eyestalk ablation, such as tail flicking, rubbing the affected area, and recoiling47. There are also studies showing that such behaviors are reduced after an anesthetic cream is applied to the affected area, which further confirms that the procedure is painful48.

Besides the intense pain and the obvious damage to the eyes and the resulting loss of vision, studies show that the practice impairs their physiological, metabolic, hormonal, and immune systems49, as well as their sensory perception50 and their ability to swim and to move around51. All of this results in higher mortality rates52.

Rowe (2018) cites eyestalk ablation as an example of a practice that would be considered a violation of even the most basic animal welfare standards if it were done to vertebrates, but that is nonetheless routinely practiced on invertebrates53.

Claw removal (declawing)

Declawing (declawing) is the manual amputation of one or both claws of a decapod crustacean. It is most commonly performed on crabs, both farmed and wild-caught. The procedure leaves the animal with impaired feeding and lowers its survival rates54.

Since crabs can naturally shed their own claws in response to stress or danger (which is called autotomy), it is commonly believed that declawing is not painful. This is mistaken, however, since research shows a greater stress response and higher mortality in crabs declawed by humans than in those that underwent autotomy55.

Declawed crabs display behaviors that indicate awareness of the resulting wounds (such as trembling and touching or guarding the wounds with their remaining legs)56. These behaviors are not observed in autotomy, which indicates that the crabs are feeling pain as a result of having their claws removed57.

Returning declawed crabs to the sea

Removing a crab's claws and then returning it to the sea is regarded as a sustainable source of food, since a claw can be torn off for sale and the crab put back into the water, where it is presumed that another claw will grow back58.

However, besides the painful wounds caused by declawing59, the practice also seriously impairs the crab's quality of life after it returns to the sea, since it reduces its ability to feed and to access food sources (which also hinders the regrowth of the claw60), as well as its ability to defend itself against predators61 and to compete for important resources (such as territory, shelter, or mates62). Consequently, the practice also lowers their survival rates63.

Claw nicking

The stressful and cramped conditions in which these animals are kept increase the likelihood of conflict and cannibalism64. Disabling their claws minimizes the risk of harm to other animals and to the workers who handle them. The claw-nicking process (claw nickling) involves fracturing the apodemes65 and cutting the tendons in the dactyls66 of the claws in order to stop them from working. It is performed on animals such as crabs and lobsters, at the time they are being prepared for transport.

The process is extremely harmful to the animals. Since parts of the claw are fractured and cut, they are left with an open wound – besides the pain, the wounds and the damage to internal tissues result in blood loss and an increased risk of infection67. Crabs whose claws had been nicked showed mortality rates of 83%68, whereas crabs that had not been nicked showed a mortality rate of 16.7%69. Moreover,

since the claws are essential to these animals' movement70, the procedure also reduces their ability to feed, to groom themselves, to defend themselves, and even to move71.

Claw banding

Another typical procedure during holding is claw banding (claw banding). The procedure significantly restricts these animals' basic behavior and movements and, if applied over the long term, is associated with muscle atrophy, inhibited feeding, and stress72, besides also reducing the animal's ability to feed, to groom itself, to move, and to defend itself73.

V-notching

Tail notching (also called V-notching, or V-notching) is meant to identify egg-bearing lobsters so that they can be returned to the sea and go on reproducing74. The purpose of the notch is to allow quick and easy identification should they be inadvertently caught again75.

The notch is made by removing a small triangular piece of the tail fan76. Besides the procedure itself being painful, it harms the lobsters through handling, blood loss, risk of infection, and long-term effects such as reduced locomotion and reduced perception of the presence of predators77.

Holding and storage

At some stage of their lives, decapod crustaceans destined for the food industry (whether farmed or caught in the wild) are stored for some period

of time: (1) before, during, or after transport, (2) before being killed, or (3) while on display at points of sale, restaurants, or markets78.

Regardless of its duration (which can reach several months), storage has many negative impacts on the animals because of the risk of poor water quality, inadequate or fluctuating temperatures, restricted behavior, high population density, handling, and mutilations79. Depending on the species and on how long they are stored, they will be kept in water (in tanks with or without recirculation), in air (with varying levels of humidity), or directly on ice80.

Transport

Transport can last several days, subjecting these animals to conditions such as poor water quality, inadequate temperatures, lack of shelter, proximity to other animals, handling, and vehicle vibration and noise81. Besides causing suffering, these factors result in extremely high levels of mortality, whether during transport82 or upon arrival at the destination83.

Being transported out of water and exposed to air, light, and other conditions also seriously harms these animals, since they are aquatic84. Even when they are transported in tanks of water, it is hard to maintain water quality and the correct temperature on long journeys. During transport, the animals at the bottom of the tank are more likely to lose limbs or to be crushed to death by those above them85.

The animals are often starved, since withholding food reduces the amount of waste that builds up during the journey. They are also transported and stored very close to many other animals, sometimes of different species, with very little space. Crustaceans tend to be solitary and territorial, so being close to other animals is

extremely stressful for them. Hunger and dehydration combined with high population densities lead to aggressive behavior and cannibalism86.

Stunning

Stunning is the procedure that would supposedly render the animal completely insensible to pain before it is killed87. At present, electrical stunning is the only method for which research confirms a total loss of central nervous system activity and of responsiveness to sensory stimulation88. Even this method, if it is to stun quickly (within one second), must be carried out with specialized equipment and in accordance with species-specific criteria. However, other methods are used throughout the industry, such as chilling, chemical anesthetics, and CO2 gassing, all of which produce intense agony89.

How they are killed

Decapod crustaceans destined for the food industry are killed in a variety of ways. The most common method is boiling them alive, either by dropping them into boiling water or by gradually raising the water temperature to boiling point90. Live boiling results in severe and prolonged suffering and agony before death, as shown by the animals' vigorous struggling, thrashing, and attempts to escape91.

Other methods include dismemberment, chilling, exposure to high-salt solutions, CO2 gassing, and the use of fresh water to kill animals of marine species, all of which result in intense and prolonged agony92.

Mechanical killing, in turn, whether by "spiking" or by "splitting," carries an extremely high risk of severe suffering because of the precision required, which is hard to

achieve in animals with non-centralized nervous systems93. To avoid pain and agony, all the nerve centers would have to be destroyed simultaneously, which makes mechanical killing incredibly difficult to carry out without causing intense suffering, even for an expert94.

Online sales of decapod crustaceans

Crabs and lobsters are sold online, with the animal delivered alive to the consumer to be stored and killed at home95. The animals may spend hours or days in transit, trapped in boxes, sometimes crammed together in groups, which puts them at risk of injury, suffocation, and death96. Fractures and other fatal injuries are also common, since their bodies are extremely fragile97. Being aquatic animals, they are unable to take in enough oxygen from the air. So if they are denied water, they risk a slow and agonizing death by suffocation before they are even delivered98.

Once delivered, they may be kept, handled, and killed in whatever way the consumer sees fit99. It is extremely difficult to create a storage environment that meets their health and welfare needs, since this involves factors such as the right water quality, temperature, salinity, and light100. Many consumers store crabs and lobsters in the refrigerator or freezer before killing and cooking them, which causes them intense suffering101. Common ways of killing them are chopping them into pieces or boiling them alive while they are fully conscious102. If, as we have seen, it is already extremely difficult for a trained professional to kill them without causing them intense suffering and agony, there is no way an untrained consumer can do so without causing extreme suffering.

1.14. Opposite attitudes, depending on the species of the victims

Despite the immense amount of death and suffering it causes every day, animal exploitation is considered perfectly acceptable by most people. In fact, most people, even without thinking about it, demand that it take place, through their consumption of animal products. Yet if something similar were done to members of the human species, the vast majority of people would consider it not only unjustifiable but also heinous and monstrous. By contrast, the decision whether or not to collaborate with animal exploitation is often seen as a matter of personal preference, of the same kind as choosing what color clothes to wear or what music to listen to, or as something that only animal lovers should care about, rather than as a matter of justice (something that would be widely recognized if the victims were human).

1.15. Can this double standard be justified?

If people hold such disparate attitudes depending on the species to which the victims belong, then they need to explain why it would be right to do such things to nonhuman animals and at the same time wrong to do the same to humans. In fact, many people believe this is so obvious that it needs no explanation. But if that is so, then it should be quite easy to justify this disparity. There is, however, a strong reason to think that it cannot be justified, and the reason is this: whatever explains why it is wrong to do these things to humans automatically implies that it is wrong to do them to any other being capable of suffering and enjoyment. A brief explanation of this follows.

The reason it is unjust to do the same to humans is not that humans belong to the same species we do, or that they possess a range of complex cognitive capacities, a set of relationships with one another, and so on. The reason is much simpler: suffering and dying in those ways seriously harms the victims. However, to be seriously harmed by those situations, one does not need to have complex cognitive capacities or to stand in certain relationships (as the case of babies, for example, attests). Nor does one need to belong to the human species: it is undeniable that the animals subjected to that terrible situation are enormously harmed. To say that their suffering and their deaths do not matter because they do not belong to the human species is analogous to saying that the suffering and deaths of certain humans do not matter because of their race or gender. That is, it would be a case of speciesism. For this reason, there seems to be no way to justify this moral double standard based on the species of the victims. We will look at this in more detail in the next chapter.
