2. Why Is Animal Exploitation Unjust?

Consider the following claims:

(1) "There is nothing wrong with animal exploitation, since the animals are being raised for that purpose."

(2) "Eating animals is right because it is natural: it is the food chain."

(3) "Animal exploitation must continue; otherwise many traditions would be lost."

(4) "It is essential that animal exploitation continue, since many people make their living from it."

(5) "The problem with animal exploitation is its environmental impact; so there is nothing wrong with it if it is practiced in an ecologically sustainable way."

(6) "The problem is industrial animal exploitation; there is nothing wrong if the animals are hunted or fished directly."

(7) "The problem is suffering. There is nothing wrong if the animals are raised and killed painlessly."

(8) "The problem is not animal exploitation but capitalism. So there is nothing wrong with animal exploitation if it takes place within other economic models."

Now imagine that the same justifications were offered for raising humans in order to eat their flesh, make clothing from their skin, use them as test subjects, have them pull carts, or kill them in rituals.

None of these justifications would be considered acceptable. In fact, all of them would be considered repugnant. However, as we will see in detail below, all the reasons that make it unjust to do such things to humans automatically imply that it is unjust to do the same things to nonhuman animals. Below, two arguments supporting the claim that animal exploitation is unjust are presented in more detail.

2.1. It is unjust because it violates the principle of equal consideration

The principle of equal consideration prescribes that similar levels of harm and benefit be given the same weight, and that greater levels of harm and benefit be given more weight than lesser harms and benefits. This is so because, if what gives us reasons to avoid harms is their very negative character, and what gives us reasons to pursue benefits is their very positive character, then the more negative or positive they are, the stronger those reasons are. Giving different weight to similar levels of harm or benefit, or giving less weight to greater harms or benefits, is acting in a way that is biased with respect to the individuals affected. Below we will see why animal exploitation violates the principle of equal consideration by weighing the harms and benefits to those affected in a biased way.

Consider, for example, the use of animals for consumption. If humans consume animals, the animals lose their lives and, in addition, usually have to live a life full of suffering. On the other hand, if humans stop consuming animals, all they have to do is eat a plant-based diet. This is not even a harm, but even if it were, it would certainly be a much smaller harm than the harm the animals would endure as a result of being consumed. Anyone who has any doubt need only ask themselves which of the two situations they would rather be in: that of the animal who would be killed, or that of a human who would have to eat a plant-based diet. This shows that animal exploitation for consumption gives less weight to greater harms and therefore violates the principle of equal consideration.

It might be objected that there are certain cases of animal exploitation in which the harms to humans would not be smaller than the harms to the exploited animals. This would be the case, for example, when killing an animal would save a human life (that is, the harms would be equivalent). It might even be said that if, in the case at hand, the human would lose more by dying than the animal, or if killing the animal would save many other individuals, then killing the animal would be in keeping with the principle of equal consideration, since it would amount to preferring the lesser harm.

However, this is not enough to show that such a practice does not violate the principle of equal consideration. What would have to be shown is that, in a situation involving similar harms, it would be acceptable to kill humans. For example, suppose someone pointed out that a particular human would be less harmed by dying than other individuals, or that killing him would save the lives of several other individuals. If this is insufficient to justify killing him, then what is consistent with the principle of equal consideration is to conclude that it is also insufficient to justify killing nonhuman animals. Thus, even practices of animal exploitation that do not involve giving more weight to lesser harms may still violate the principle of equal consideration by giving different weight to harms of similar magnitude, depending on whether the victim in the situation would be human or nonhuman.

This does not mean that there can be no justification for making exceptions to the principle of equal consideration. It means only that the burden of proof lies with whoever advocates making the exception: they must present a well-grounded principle that justifies it. What would such a principle have to look like? One example would be to hold that if, for some reason, an individual deserves the harm they suffer, then there is justification for giving their harm less weight. For example, imagine that a normal adult human (and therefore morally accountable) tries to torture a child purely for fun but, being clumsy, falls out of the window and is hurt even worse than the child. Suppose we are the team arriving on the scene to provide help. In this case it seems we still have reasons to give priority to helping the child, even if she is less badly hurt, simply because here it makes sense to say that the torturer deserves the harm he suffered (and perhaps, for that reason, we should not even help him). This, then, would be a case in which the factor of desert justifies giving priority to the lesser harm.

However, none of this shows that there is justification for making exceptions to the principle of equal consideration on the basis of species, race, gender, brain complexity, and so on. Note that in the case we saw above, the exception to the principle of equal consideration was justified because someone morally responsible had first violated the principle of equal consideration. The species someone belongs to, their race, their gender, or their brain complexity have nothing to do with desert: they are all undeserved outcomes of the natural lottery. For this reason, there is no justification for giving less weight to the good of nonhuman animals by pointing out that they are not human or that they lack the cognitive capacities typical of humans.

Accordingly, one way of showing that animal exploitation is unjust and ought to be abolished is to show that it violates the principle of equal consideration, since it gives each individual's good a different weight on the basis of arbitrary factors, such as the species to which they belong (a factor that, like race and gender, is an outcome of the natural lottery).

2.2. It is unjust because it fails the impartiality test

Another way of supporting the same conclusion – namely, that animal exploitation is unjust – but by a different route, is to point out that it violates impartiality. We will see more about this below.

First of all, it is important not to confuse impartiality with neutrality. Impartiality is not avoiding making a decision and remaining neutral. Rather, it is making a decision that is not biased with respect to those affected. So not every practice that involves favoring or disfavoring certain individuals violates impartiality: the favoring or disfavoring has to be biased.

But how can we know whether a practice passes the impartiality test or is biased? There are several questions we can ask to find out. For example, we can ask whether we would consider the practice in question fair in the following circumstances.

(1) If we did not know which position we would occupy among those affected by it.

(2) If we knew that we would be the ones harmed by it.

(3) If the roles were reversed (for example, if the animals were the beneficiaries and we were the ones harmed).

(4) If we had to bear the harms it causes in order to obtain the benefits it provides.

(5) If we had to bear the harms it causes so that other individuals could obtain the benefits it provides.

If we sincerely ask ourselves these questions, we will realize that animal exploitation is defended only because its proponents know they will not be its victims. If that is so, then it is biased, since it clearly fails the impartiality test.

2.3. Conclusion

If what we have seen above is correct, then animal exploitation is not only unjust: it is as unjust as it would be if human victims were subjected to harms of similar magnitude. Yet if humans were subjected to harms of similar magnitude, such practices would be considered not merely unjust but a paradigmatic example of abominable and monstrous conduct. If so, then it seems there is no alternative but to judge animal exploitation in the same way. Most likely it is not generally perceived as such a serious problem simply because we are certain that we will not be its victims. This shows, once again, that it is a blatant violation of the principles of equal consideration and impartiality.

This also means that animal exploitation does not cease to be unjust, nor does it become less unjust, if it is carried out in an ecologically sustainable way, if it takes the form of small-scale hunting or fishing, if the animals are killed without suffering, or if it takes place within economic models other than capitalism. The problem is, first and foremost, animal exploitation itself, and not the form or context in which it occurs. For these reasons, the goal must be to abolish animal exploitation.

3. What Is Veganism?

Animals are exploited because there is demand for animal products and services. Every time people pay for such products and services, they cause more animals to be born to suffer all the horrors we saw in chapter 1.

One way of combating this is by adopting a vegan way of life. If, as we saw in chapter 2, animal exploitation is unjust, then in fact we ought to be vegan. Veganism consists in trying to avoid harming animals as far as possible. It is not the same as not consuming animal products, whatever the motive. Vegans, obviously, eat without animal products. However, there are several differences between veganism and not eating animal products for reasons unrelated to consideration for animals (such as concern for one's own health, for other humans, or for the environment). The first difference is that veganism means rejecting animal exploitation in all its spheres, not only in food. The second is that veganism involves rejecting animal exploitation even when it does not harm humans or is carried out in an ecologically sustainable way.

It is sometimes said that if veganism is founded on respect for all sentient beings (that is, all beings capable of having positive and negative experiences), then veganism is obviously also for humans, since they too are sentient beings. However, it is nonhuman animals who are bred to be killed and used as food, clothing, test subjects, tools, and so on. Humans suffer from various forms of discrimination, but nonhuman animals are usually treated much worse than humans are. The things routinely done to nonhuman animals, and widely accepted, would be considered monstrous and heinous if done to humans. That is why there needs to be a term for the position that emphasizes that it is also unjust to exploit those who do not belong to the human species, and that term is veganism.

It is true that the word veganism is sometimes used to mean avoiding animal products, whatever the motive. The problem with this is that there would then no longer be a word to identify the position that avoids harming animals out of respect for the animals themselves. Imagine, then, that a new word were coined to identify this position (exactly as happened with the word veganism). Over time, just as happened with the word veganism, some people might begin to use this word to refer to the act of avoiding animal products whatever the motive (and so on for each new term coined to replace the previous ones). The result is that there would never be a term to identify the position that avoids harming animals out of respect for the animals themselves, since every time such a term was coined, its meaning would be distorted so as to weaken the focus on respect for animals.

That is why the attempt to change the meaning of the term veganism may well be deliberate: by claiming that veganism need not be for the animals, and that it can be for humans or for the environment, one conceals the fact that animal exploitation is unjust even if it harms neither humans nor the environment.

For these reasons, veganism, besides being a way of trying to avoid causing harm to animals, can also be a way of exposing the injustice that nonhuman animals suffer. This happens when people explain why they are vegan, explaining that animal exploitation is the result of discrimination against those who do not belong to the human species and that, because of this discrimination, terrible things are done to nonhuman animals every day that would never be considered acceptable if they were done to humans.

4. What About Plants?

A very common argument put forward in defense of consuming animals claims that whatever could make it wrong to consume animals implies that it would also be wrong to consume plants, and so it makes no difference whether we consume one or the other. Let us call this argument the plant objection. It comes in two variants, discussed separately below.

4.1. The "plants are alive too" variant

The first variant of the plant objection says that it makes no difference whether we consume animals or plants, since in both cases we will be causing deaths.

This objection is often answered by pointing out that if one's goal is to kill the smallest number of living organisms, then one should give up consuming animals, since a large share of the plants grown in the world is used to fatten the animals that will be killed103. There are two problems with this reply. The first is that the defender of consuming animals could respond that if we ate only aquatic animals caught in the wild at sea, we would kill even fewer organisms, since no crops are used to fatten these animals. The second problem is that the reply does not address the assumption, present in the objection, that if death is a harm for animals, it is also a harm for plants. As we will see below, this assumption is mistaken.

The reason death is a harm is not that it stops biological life from continuing, but that it prevents the individual from going on to enjoy the positive things they would experience if they stayed alive. This shows that death harms only sentient beings, since only in their case is there someone inhabiting that body (an individual, a consciousness) whom death would deprive of enjoying something positive. Living beings that lack consciousness are living bodies. There is no one living those lives. So there is no one there to be harmed by death.

It might be objected that each and every life, even with no possibility whatsoever of sentience, is always valuable. However, the following thought experiment suggests that for a life to be valuable, there must be the possibility of experiences occurring in that life.

Imagine that someone assures us that they can give us an afterlife if we pay a good sum every month until the end of our lives, and guarantees that the future life will be valuable for us. Suppose, however, that after paying our whole lives, we discover that we will be reborn as living organisms, but with no possibility whatsoever of sentience. If in that case we have been cheated, it is because a merely biological life, with no possibility of experiences at all, is not valuable104.

Thus, the reasons against killing animals do not imply that there are reasons against killing plants; quite the opposite. Therefore, the first variant of the plant objection fails.

4.2. The "plants are sentient too" variant

The second variant of the plant objection maintains that plants are sentient, and that we are therefore justified in consuming animals since, whatever we choose to consume, we will be killing sentient beings (who would therefore be harmed by death). This variant has two problems, which we will discuss below.

The lesser problem

The lesser problem is that, most of the time, the claim that plants are sentient rests on the mistaken idea that behavioral evidence is a sufficient indicator of sentience. For example, in support of the view that plants are sentient, it is often mentioned that they display a range of behaviors. For instance, some plants close up when touched, such as the sensitive plant and carnivorous plants. In addition, plants perform countless functions related to absorbing nutrients from the soil, carrying out photosynthesis, and so on.

The problem with this is that the presence of behavior does not, by itself, show that there is sentience. There can be quite complex behaviors that are nonetheless merely physicochemical stimulus-response reactions, with no one internally experiencing what is happening. Even in the case of animals, behavior is not, by itself, sufficient evidence of sentience. This is because of reflex arcs, explained below.

When information from an external stimulus reaches a nervous system, it travels along two pathways. One of them, the shorter, goes straight to the muscles, producing the reaction that is a reflex (hence the name reflex arc)105. The other, longer pathway goes to the brain, where the information is processed and the conditions for experience to take place are created. For example, when we touch a hot plate with our hand, we pull the hand away instantly, but only a few microseconds later do we feel anything. A muscle can keep displaying the reflex even if the sensory part has been cut off (for example, by means of local anesthesia)106. Some kinds of nervous systems operate solely with the reflex-arc part. This is the case of animals that have nervous systems but no centralizing organ (no brain, no ganglia), such as cnidarians (jellyfish, for example) and echinoderms (such as starfish and sea cucumbers). These animals may even display quite complex behaviors, but solely through reflexes, without anyone there experiencing anything. In the case of plants, there is not even a nervous system. So it is very likely that their behaviors, of whatever kind, are merely the result of physicochemical reactions.

Thus, the main criterion for assessing whether a being is sentient is the presence of a centralized nervous system (a brain or ganglia, for example), since it is the processing of information that takes place in the centralizing organ that provides the conditions for consciousness to arise107. If an organism has such a structure, the way it behaves can be a good additional indicator that it is sentient, but only if the best explanation of its overall behavior is to assume that it is avoiding negative experiences and seeking positive ones. For this reason, the behavioral evidence useful for determining whether or not a being is sentient is not evidence about behavior in specific situations, but the way it behaves in general. In the case

of plants, besides the fact that they do not even have a nervous system (let alone a centralizing organ), it seems that the best way to explain their behaviors is not by assuming that they are sentient. We will see more about this below.

The traits most likely to prevail over generations are those that give an advantage in terms of passing on genetic information. For example, if a given trait helps an animal survive, it increases the likelihood that the animal will also reproduce and thus pass that trait on. If sentience gave its bearers no advantage at all, it would most likely not have been passed on, since it requires a considerable expenditure of energy. For example, in humans, around 20% of the organism's energy is spent maintaining the structures associated with the brain108. Thus, sentience probably prevailed because it gave its bearers some survival advantage. Otherwise its bearers would probably have perished without leaving descendants.

The evident advantage is that sentience is associated with the motivation for behavior: a sentient being tends to avoid negative experiences and seek positive ones. Since animals can move about in their environment, this capacity increases their chances of survival and, consequently, of passing on their genetic information. This is not the case for plants, however, since they cannot move. In their case, sentience would involve a considerable expenditure of energy with no advantage at all. Therefore, it is very unlikely that such a trait would have prevailed in plants or fungi, for example109.

Thus, to maintain that plants are sentient, it would have to be shown that: (1) having a nervous system with a centralizing organ, or a structure performing a similar function, is not necessary for sentience; (2) behavioral evidence is sufficient for sentience; and (3) traits that involve a considerable expenditure of energy and give their bearers no apparent evolutionary advantage can nonetheless prevail over generations. This is, at the very least, very hard to demonstrate.

This does not mean that it is impossible to meet these conditions. It does mean, however, that the burden of proof lies with those who claim that plants are sentient. For example, regarding the first

condition, it would have to be explained by what other mechanism sentience could arise that would make the nervous system unnecessary. It would also have to be explained, then, what the role of the nervous system would be, and so on.

One of the factors that sometimes leads people to believe that plants are sentient is that there are many studies of plants and fungi that use terms such as "learning," "memory," "communication," "experience," and so on. In most of these studies, these terms are used to refer solely to behavior, without claiming that sentience is present. In ordinary language, however, these terms are associated with sentience; that is, they are used in a way that indicates there is someone there learning, memorizing, communicating, experiencing, and so on. So it is possible for a given study of plants or fungi to use these terms in a sense that does not imply sentience, and for someone who reads the study not very carefully to think that it is a study demonstrating sentience in plants or fungi.

The greater problem

The greater problem with the argument is this: even if it had been shown that plants are sentient, the practical implication that would follow is the opposite of what the argument's proponents conclude. Recall that the claim that plants are sentient is usually brought up in an attempt to justify consuming animals. However, if plants were sentient (or were morally considerable for some other reason), what would follow is not that we are justified in consuming both animals and plants, but rather that we ought to be ethical botanical fruitarians.

This stance is characterized by consuming only what detaches from a plant. Besides everything usually called fruit (such as bananas, oranges, apples, strawberries, and so on), this includes nuts, seeds, grains, legumes, and vegetables such as tomatoes, pumpkins, zucchini, bell peppers, eggplant, and so on.

Note that the implication that we should practice fruitarianism would hold whether one maintains that plants are sentient or that plants should be morally considered because they are alive. That is why, whichever variant of the plant objection we are talking about, it fails to justify consuming animals.

Usually, when people realize that the plant objection implies fruitarianism, they immediately stop defending it. This reveals that they had no real concern for plants: it was just an excuse to keep consuming animals. Regardless of this, however, the important point to note from the above analysis is this: whether it is raised hypocritically (as is usually the case) or out of a serious concern for plants (as is rarely the case), the plant objection fails to justify consuming animals.

5. The Objection That Consuming Animals Is Natural

One of the most common objections to veganism is the claim that eating meat is natural. It is also common for animal advocates to respond by denying that consuming animals is natural for humans. Below we will see that both the objection and this response suffer from the same problem: they assume that if a behavior is natural, it is justified. There are different things someone might mean when they claim that eating meat is natural. We will discuss each of them below.

5.1. The appeal to possibility

Sometimes what is meant is that it is possible for the human organism to consume meat. However, if the mere fact that a behavior is possible made it justifiable, any possible behavior would be justifiable. For example, it is also possible for the human organism to consume human flesh, but this does not seem to justify raising humans to kill and eat. Likewise, the mere fact that it is possible for the human organism to consume the flesh of other animals does not imply that there is any justification for doing so.

5.2. The appeal to instinct

At other times, what is meant by "eating meat is natural" is that there is an instinctive inclination to do so. A first problem with this is that many people have no such inclination. But even if everyone had it, we could still ask why having an instinctive inclination to do something would show that it is justifiable. Imagine, for example, that humans had an instinctive inclination to rape children. If we all had this instinctive tendency, perhaps most of us would see nothing wrong with such behavior. But the fact that, under such conditions, we would consider such behavior justifiable does not show that it really is justifiable. Indeed, the very fact that there was an instinctive inclination toward it might be what kept people from seeing how unjustifiable the act is. To justify an act is to show that there are good reasons in its favor. Showing that a behavior is what we would do if we did not reflect on it is obviously not offering a good reason in its favor.

5.3. The appeal to what animals do

Another very common claim is that consuming animals is justified because, in nature, animals eat one another. The idea behind this argument is that if animals in nature do a certain thing, then we are justified in doing the same.

The first problem with this is that there are animals who do not eat other animals. Since the argument aims to justify consuming animals, it is at the very least biased to choose to imitate precisely the animals who eat other animals, rather than those who do not, without giving any further reason for that choice.

The second problem is that there are animals in nature who steal, rape, kill, and eat members of their own species, including the young of rivals or even their own young. No one argues that it is right for humans to do the same just because other animals do it too. The appeal to what animals do comes up almost exclusively in attempts to justify consuming animals. Moreover, animals in nature do not have hospital systems, cell phones, computers, schools, libraries, clothes, cars, and so on either. It is at the very least arbitrary to want to imitate animals in nature only when they consume other animals, and not in everything else.

5.4. The appeal to the food chain

At other times, consuming animals is defended on the basis of the claim that humans are at the top of the food chain. It is often pointed out that, in nature, larger or more powerful animals kill and eat smaller or more vulnerable ones, and that this is what makes it right for humans to kill other animals for food.

However, nothing compels humans to consume other animals. So this is no different from saying that we are justified in doing something just because we have the power to do it (and we have already seen the problems with this view above, in section 5.1). For example, imagine that there were a species more powerful than humans, and that its members bred humans for food. Or imagine that a group of human cannibals kidnapped other humans to kill and eat them. These beings would be at the top of the food chain, but that does not seem to make their behavior just (especially if they had no need whatsoever to do it).

Sometimes what is meant when the food chain is mentioned is that, if animals are not consumed, there will be overpopulation in those species and, because of scarcity, the result will be even more suffering and death than if they were killed for consumption. There are at least two problems with this claim. The first is that there are in fact only so many animals of these species because humans breed them for consumption. So consuming these animals does not control their populations; quite the opposite. The second is that, even if killing and consuming the animals helped control their populations (for example, in the case of animals hunted or fished in the wild), this would still be insufficient to justify the act. For example, killing and eating humans would also help control the human population, but that does not seem sufficient to justify doing such a thing. Furthermore, if the goal is to control animal populations, there is the option of sterilizing them. There is no way to justify an act that causes harm if other options are available that would cause less harm, since that would amount to defending a harm that is wholly unnecessary for achieving the intended goal. In addition, there are studies showing that sterilization is more effective at controlling wild animal populations than killing them110. Therefore, a concern with population control could not justify consuming animals.

5.5. Conclusion

We have seen that there are several things someone might mean when they claim that "eating meat is natural." However, we have also seen that, in whatever sense the expression is being used, the fact that a behavior is natural gives us no reason at all to think that it is justifiable. This does not mean that there cannot be behaviors that are natural (in one of the senses above) and that are also justifiable. It means only that, if they are justifiable, this will be for some other reason, not because they are natural. In addition, we have also seen that eating animals is not one of those behaviors, whether or not it is natural.

6. The Claim That Consuming Animals Puts an End to Their Suffering

6.1. Is consuming animals right because it puts an end to their suffering?

It is sometimes argued that we should consume animals out of concern for the animals themselves, on the grounds that, since the life awaiting them would be full of suffering, consuming them is doing them a favor, because it spares them that fate.

According to this position, this would apply both to animals raised to be consumed (since, as we saw in chapter 1, they are usually raised in conditions highly detrimental to their well-being111) and to those fished or hunted in the wild (since the vast majority of animals born in the wild also have lives full of suffering).

In the wild this happens mainly because the vast majority of animal species have enormous broods, with thousands or even millions of offspring depending on the species (something common in amphibians, reptiles, fish, crustaceans, and invertebrates in general), which always results in extremely low survival rates. For example, a single clutch of the common frog contains around 25,000 offspring112; that of octopuses, hundreds of thousands113; those of salmon, cod, and tuna, millions114; and that of the ocean sunfish reaches 300 million115. Land invertebrates can also lay hundreds, thousands, or even millions of eggs at a time116. In periods of roughly stable population, the rate of premature mortality can be measured from brood size: if the population has remained roughly constant over a few generations, then on average only one offspring per adult has survived (that is, two per brood, and fewer than that if there are adults who reproduce more than once in their lifetime). All the rest are generally born only to experience intense suffering and die very prematurely, often without ever having had a single positive experience117.

For these reasons, according to the position we are going to discuss, consuming animals, whether those

raised for this purpose or those captured directly in the wild, benefits them precisely by causing their deaths.

6.2. Does the fact that consuming them would end their suffering justify consuming them?

Let us begin by examining the claim that consuming animals raised for consumption benefits them because it frees them from a life full of suffering. The fact is this: if we have reasons to end their lives because those lives are full of suffering, then this gives us even stronger reasons to prevent them from being born into that situation in the first place. By consuming them, we encourage such production, causing new animals to be born into that situation. Thus, pointing out that the death of someone living a life full of suffering frees them from that suffering does not imply that raising animals for consumption is justified. Quite the contrary: it is a strong reason against animal exploitation.

In response, it might be objected that, in the case of animals born in the wild, ceasing to consume them does not prevent new ones from being born, and since we are in no position to choose to keep them from being born, the best we can do is to kill them (and fishing and hunting would contribute to this, for example). However, it is false that we are in no position to try to keep them from being born. For example, programs could be carried out to ensure that fewer of them are born. One example would be the administration of contraceptives and sterilization, something that is already often done118. Another example would be researching which kinds of vegetation, soil, or other components of the environment contribute to fewer births in species that maximize the number of offspring119. Another option would be researching which animals, if present, contribute indirectly to a lower total balance of suffering. For example, large herbivores such as elephants consume a great deal of vegetation that, if it were available, would contribute to more reproduction in those animal species whose vast majority are born only to suffer and die prematurely120. Thus, protecting large herbivores could

greatly reduce the total number of animals who would be born only to suffer and die prematurely121. In short, there are many things that could be done to reduce the number of animals who would be born in the wild to have lives full of suffering. Moreover, these other measures, because they attack the root of the problem, would most likely be more effective at reducing such populations than hunting or fishing.

One possible objection would be to point out that everything suggested concerns things that could be done to prevent new animals from being born to have lives full of suffering, but that, as regards those already born, consuming them benefits them because it causes them to die, freeing them from lives full of suffering.

A first problem with this objection is that, if the concern really is for the good of the animals (as the objection claims), then for animals already born in factory farming what would be advocated is, for example, direct-action activism to rescue them (since, unlike consuming them, this neither kills them nor causes new beings to be born into that system). As for animals already born in the wild, we could study how to modify the environment so that their lives are positive. This is something that could be done, for example, through studies in the field of welfare biology122. Thus, whether we are talking about animals bred to be exploited or about animals in the wild, pointing out that their lives are negative is not enough to justify killing them, since death is a benefit only if there is no other way to improve the life in question.

Furthermore, the main reason why the vast majority of animals in the wild have lives full of suffering is that they die very prematurely. If they manage to live longer, their chances of positive experiences usually increase. This is because the factors that cause them suffering usually also cause their deaths. So, by eliminating a source of suffering for an animal, we both increase the likelihood that it will have positive experiences and probably increase its lifespan123.

6.3. Conclusion

Whether with respect to animals raised to be consumed or animals captured in the wild, there are other ways of trying to help them that would not involve killing them. This alone already weakens the claim that consuming them is justified because it puts an end to lives full of suffering. In addition, these other options, unlike consuming them, would prevent other animals from being born to have lives full of suffering (or, at the very least, would not have the effect of causing more animals to be born to such a fate).

This shows that the claim that we should consume them because doing so would free them from lives full of suffering is probably just an excuse to keep consuming them, and not the real reason their consumption is defended. That is, what is claimed is concern for the animals themselves, but the real concern is probably simply one's own benefit.

7. Is Raising Animals for Consumption Justified Because It Brings Them into Existence?

7.1. Does consuming animals benefit them by bringing them into existence?

Consuming animals, although it causes their deaths, causes others to be born into the same system to replace them. It is sometimes argued that this makes consuming animals right since it would allegedly benefit them by bringing them into being. This argument has come to be known as the replaceability defense124.

7.2. The argument does not apply to the vast majority of cases

A first problem with this argument is that, as we saw in chapter 1, an enormous number of the animals raised for consumption live lives that are, quite literally, hell. This is the case for animals born into factory farming, for example. So they are in no way benefited by being born into such conditions. Quite the opposite.

However, the proponent of replaceability could say that their proposal is precisely to reform the system of animal exploitation so that the animals lead positive lives. Of course, it is doubtful that this would be possible in practice, given the high demand for animal products. Regardless of that, however, it is possible to challenge the very idea that animals are replaceable. That is what we will see next.

7.3. Does conferring a benefit entitle one to inflict a harm?

The second problem with the replaceability defense is that, even if consuming animals caused them to be born to have positive lives, this does not necessarily imply that it is right to kill them. If it did, it would also be right for parents to kill their children, as long as they had given them positive lives and had other children to replace them.

If animals were not harmed by death, it might make sense to say that it is fine to kill them, as long as they had a positive life and were replaced. However, animals

are harmed by death because it prevents them from enjoying the positive experiences they would have if they stayed alive.

Of course, there are cases in which animals, if they stayed alive, would experience nothing but suffering. In those cases, dying is less bad than staying alive. However, this cannot be the case for the animals the replaceability defense refers to, since the argument tries to justify consuming animals by claiming that the practice would bring into being animals who would have positive lives. Under those conditions, however, such animals would be harmed by death, since it would prevent the continuation of a positive life.

In short, there may be reasons to cause animals to be born to have positive lives (for example, if one's goal is for the world to contain as many sentient beings with positive lives as possible). However, once animals are already leading positive lives, there are strong reasons against killing them, since they are harmed by death. Therefore, the fact that consuming animals could, under ideal conditions, cause certain animals to be born to have positive lives is not sufficient to justify consuming animals.

At this point the following question might be raised: if the harm of death lies in preventing the positive experiences someone would have, what difference is there between killing a being who already exists and failing to produce a new being, since in both cases someone is prevented from enjoying what is positive? The answer is that, in the case of sentient beings who already exist and lead positive lives, there are individuals who would be harmed by death. By contrast, in the case of failing to produce new beings, there is no one who would be harmed: all there is are countless possibilities of future individuals. To make this clearer, consider the following example.

Imagine that if a woman decides to become pregnant this month, individual A will be born nine months later, but if she decides to wait until next month, individual B will be born, from a different egg, and so on for the following months. Whether she decides to become pregnant now, next month, or at any other time, there will be many possible future individuals who will never come to be. But this is not the equivalent of killing someone who already exists, since in this case what there are are possibilities of future individuals, not individuals. If it were equivalent, then everyone who did not have as many children with positive lives as possible would have to be convicted of serial homicide. This strongly suggests that killing already existing sentient beings is a graver wrong than failing to produce new sentient beings with meaningful lives.

This does not mean that we must necessarily reject the goal of bringing about the greatest possible number of sentient beings with positive lives in the world over time. It means only that this goal does not seem to justify killing already existing sentient beings.

7.4. The objection that some animals are hardly harmed by death

It is sometimes argued that some animals (namely, those who allegedly do not retain strong psychological connectedness over time) would not be harmed by death and would therefore be replaceable. Below we will discuss two attempts to support this claim: the appeal to identity and the appeal to prudential reasons125.

7.4.1. The appeal to identity

According to a certain theory, what makes someone the same individual over time is their psychological connectedness126. According to this theory, a being who has no temporal sense of self (that is, who retains no memories and does not imagine itself in the future) is not the same individual over time: at each instant one individual is annihilated and another arises to replace it in the same body. Someone who accepts this theory might then say that, in the case of such a being, it makes no difference whether we keep that body alive or kill it and bring another into being127, since either way the individual who exists now is annihilated (the only difference being whether the new individual will be born in that same body or in another).

One way of criticizing the theory of personal identity based on psychological connectedness is to accuse it of confusing two senses of the term "the same": the qualitative sense and the numerical sense128. It makes sense to say that someone who has lost their memories "is no longer the

same" qualitatively (that is, in the sense of being very different psychologically from what they were before). This does not mean, however, that it is numerically another individual occupying that body and that the previous individual has been annihilated. It may very well be numerically the same individual, despite not remembering anything that has happened to them until then. If this is possible, then psychological connectedness does not determine the numerical identity of individuals (since, if it did, a total loss of memories would necessarily give rise to another, numerically distinct individual).

If psychological connectedness determined the numerical identity of individuals, then if we copied the psychological connectedness of someone who already exists into another brain, both would be numerically the same individual. Of course, in such a situation, both would think they are the same individual. But this does not mean that they really are the same individual. The most obvious reason to think they are two numerically distinct individuals is that what one experiences the other does not experience, and one's decisions affect their own body and not the other's body. In short, they are two distinct consciousnesses (that is, two distinct subjective points of view), despite having the same psychological connectedness. So if in this case we have two numerically distinct individuals with the same psychological connectedness, then psychological connectedness does not determine an individual's numerical identity.

Accordingly, if the theory of identity based on psychological connectedness is not correct, neither is the replaceability defense based on it.

One possible objection would be to agree that psychological connectedness does not determine numerical identity, but to argue that the reasons for avoiding death depend on qualitative identity, not numerical identity. On this view, what matters is keeping the psychological connections in existence, not their bearers. Consider, however, the following example. Imagine that a scientist promises that, as long as you pay a good sum, you will have an afterlife, and that it will be a very pleasant life. You gather your savings and pay the sum. The scientist then explains how the procedure will work: your psychological connectedness (memories, character traits, etc.) will be copied into another brain, in another body, and the being who lives in that body will remember being you and will think it is you, and will live the happy life you paid to have. Indignant, you protest: "But I (pointing to yourself) want to live the life I paid to have! This guy is another individual, even though he has my psychological connectedness!" The scientist replies: "I agree that this guy is another individual numerically, but he is the same as you qualitatively, since he has your psychological connectedness, and that is what matters." The point this example aims to show is this: if it makes sense for you to feel indignant about what the scientist did to you, then the reasons for avoiding death do not depend on qualitative identity, but on numerical identity. But if, as we saw earlier, psychological connectedness does not determine numerical identity, then the replaceability defense that appeals to psychological connectedness does not succeed.

7.4.2. The appeal to prudential reasons

Another attempt to argue that animals with little psychological connectedness are replaceable agrees that psychological connectedness is not relevant to determining an individual's identity, but holds that it is relevant to determining the strength of an individual's prudential reasons129.

Prudential reasons are the reasons someone has to try to avoid negative events and to seek positive events that could happen to them. According to the view we are discussing, the strength of these reasons should be determined by multiplying how good or bad the event would be by the psychological connectedness the individual would maintain between the present moment and their "future self"130.

On this view, beings with little psychological connectedness are not greatly harmed by death, even if it deprives them of very satisfying experiences (because the value of those experiences would then have to be multiplied by a very low number, corresponding to their psychological connectedness).

Consider, however, the following example. Imagine that Bia is still a five-year-old child and wants to see the pyramids of Egypt. Suppose, however, that if she travels now, while she has strong psychological connectedness with who she is now, the trip will be enjoyable, but it will be far more enjoyable if she travels when she is an adult. When she is an adult, however, she will have extremely weak psychological connectedness with who she is now (her memories, character traits, beliefs, desires, and intentions will have changed a great deal).

It seems that Bia has prudential reasons to prefer to make the trip when she is an adult, simply because the trip will be far more enjoyable for her. If this is correct, then psychological connectedness is not relevant to determining the strength of the prudential reasons someone has to seek positive events and, consequently, to avoid death.

This suggests that an individual who has little (or even no) psychological connectedness with their future is not necessarily harmed only slightly by death, since missing out on the positive events that death would prevent is not, for that reason, only slightly harmful to them. Therefore, an appeal to psychological connectedness does not seem able to show that nonhuman animals who, allegedly, have little psychological connectedness are only slightly harmed by death.

7.5. The objection that consuming animals could increase the total positive balance

Some authors131 have argued that if consuming animals caused them to be born to have positive lives, then, since each animal would be replaced by another after being killed, over time there would be many more animals being born and leading satisfying lives than if animal exploitation were abolished (since fewer animals would then probably be born). For this reason, they have advocated reforming animal exploitation so that animals lead meaningful lives, rather than abolishing animal exploitation.

One way of criticizing this position is, as we saw in section 7.3, to argue that the wrong of killing a being who already exists is not offset by the benefit of producing a new being who would lead a meaningful life. However, another way of criticizing it is to argue that, even taking into account only the goal of maximizing the total balance of well-being, if we take into account all the consequences (and not only the direct consequences of consumption), advocating the abolition of animal use seems far more likely to achieve that goal than an ideal that reinforces the idea that nonhuman animals are resources for humans.

The abolition of the use of animals as resources, by spreading the ideal of consideration for sentient beings, could motivate people to try to minimize the suffering and deaths that

animals endure as a result of natural processes132 (which, contrary to what one might initially think, affect an enormously greater number of animals than the number of animals who are victims of exploitation). It could also motivate people to try to minimize risks of future suffering, which, should they materialize, could be so astronomical that they would make the suffering that exists today (adding together the suffering resulting from human practices and that resulting from natural processes) a "grain of sand" by comparison.

The defense of consuming animals, on the other hand, reinforces speciesism133 and the idea that nonhuman animals are mere resources, making it quite likely to contribute to their suffering also being neglected, whether its origin is anthropogenic or natural. Thus, if one's goal is to achieve the best consequences over time, one will have to prohibit replacement134.

7.6. Conclusion

We have seen that there are good reasons to think that animals are, in fact, greatly harmed by death, all the more so under the ideal conditions the replaceability defense assumes, in which they would lead positive lives. In addition, we have seen that the wrong of killing a sentient being who has a positive life does not seem to be offset by the creation of new beings who would lead positive lives.

Finally, we have seen that, even if we did not take the harm of death into account and our goal were only to maximize the total balance of well-being, replacement would probably contribute to producing a highly negative balance of well-being over time. On the other hand, as we have seen, advocating the abolition of animal use, by promoting consideration for all sentient beings and the resulting concern with all the problems that could affect them, would be a very promising way of maximizing the total balance of well-being over time. If this is correct, then we have strong reasons to reject replacement.

8. Does It Matter What We Would Do on a Desert Island or in a Burning House?

Scenarios involving catastrophic situations are often brought up in order to justify consuming animals. For example, it is sometimes said that, since most of us would consider it right to kill an animal if that were necessary to survive on a desert island, consuming animals is justified. At other times it is said that, since most of us would choose to save a relative rather than a nonhuman animal from a burning house, consuming animals is justified. In the view of these arguments' proponents, this would show that the criterion of species is not unjust in the way the criteria of race and gender are.

The first problem with these arguments is that they assume that what most of us would do is necessarily right. But there is no necessary connection between the one and the other. We may simply be acting wrongly. So the fact that we would act in a certain way in certain contexts does not show that acting that way is justified. Ethics is about grounding what we ought to do. It is not about what we would do. To think that what we would do grounds what we ought to do is to make an unjustified leap from a description of people's attitudes to a conclusion about which attitudes are justified. The second problem is that, even if the appeal to what most people would do were plausible, it would not support what these arguments' proponents intend (namely, that it is right to kill and eat nonhuman animals but not right to kill and eat humans), since in catastrophic situations most people would also save themselves or their loved ones rather than save other humans.

The third, and main, problem is that, whatever the right action in catastrophic situations may be, it makes no sense to extrapolate it to other, very different situations. For example, suppose someone said that if we are justified in giving priority to saving a loved one over a stranger in a burning house, or in eating human flesh if we are starving on a desert island, then we are justified in enslaving human strangers in order to eat their flesh. Faced with such a claim, it is very easy to see that the two kinds of situation are very different, and that one does not justify the other. For the same reason, what we would do on a desert island or in a burning house cannot justify the exploitation of nonhuman animals. The truth is this: we are not on a desert island or in a burning house.

9. Is It Necessary to Consume Animal Products?

It is sometimes argued that consuming animal products is necessary for maintaining good health and that, therefore, consuming animals is justified.

However, consuming animal products is not necessary for maintaining good health. This is attested by many organizations of nutrition experts around the world. Examples are the positions of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics135, the National Health Service of United Kingdom136, the Dietitians Association of Australia137, Dietitians of Canada138, the Irish Nutrition and Dietetic Institute139, the Asociación Española de Dietistas y Nutricionistas140, the Sociedad Argentina de Nutrición141, Portugal's Programa Nacional para a Promoção da Alimentação Saudável142, the Italian Society of Human Nutrition143 and Nordic Co-operation144, which includes Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, and Sweden. These are not vegan organizations (in fact, they publish other studies on animal-based diets). What leads them to take this position is simply the weight of the evidence.

For example, the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics concluded that a well-planned vegan diet is healthy and nutritionally adequate (and may even help prevent and treat certain diseases) at every stage of life145, including pregnancy, breastfeeding, childhood, adolescence, and old age, as well as for athletes146. This is because what we need are the nutrients that foods contain, not specific foods147. Moreover, even if it were necessary to consume animal products, we should still research how to make this unnecessary, just as, if it were necessary to kill other humans in order to survive, the right thing to do would be to research how to make that unnecessary.
