10. Is Veganism Only for the Rich?

Veganism is the practice of avoiding harming nonhuman animals. Where food is concerned, adopting veganism means not consuming animal products.

It is sometimes argued that veganism is feasible only for those who have a lot of money, on the grounds that vegan products are more expensive.

The first problem with this argument is that, even if this were the case, there would still be reasons to call for more and more people to become vegan, since the increase in demand would bring prices down.

The second problem with the argument is that living as a vegan is not more expensive than living as a non-vegan. Vegetables, greens, fruits, and grains are usually cheaper than animal-based food.

Of course, there are certain processed vegan products that are more expensive than certain equivalent animal products (largely because of low demand). However, it is not necessary to consume such products. And even if someone chooses to do so, since they have stopped buying many kinds of animal products, their total spending is likely to be even lower than it would be with animal products.

11. If the World Went Vegan, Would There Be an Excess of Domesticated Animals?

Animal exploitation is sometimes defended on the grounds that, if the world went vegan, it would be overrun by domesticated animals, since humans would no longer kill them.

A first problem with this argument is that, even if this were the case, such a world might still contain less suffering than one with animal exploitation.

Moreover, if the world went vegan, it would be because people in general had consideration for animals. In such a scenario, people would probably try to research harmless ways of controlling domesticated animal populations (for example, through contraception and sterilization, something that is often already done in the case of wild animals).

The second (and main) problem with this argument is that exactly the opposite of what it supposes would happen: in a vegan world there would be far fewer domesticated animals than there are now.

In fact, there are only so many domesticated animals in the world because of animal exploitation. The demand for animal products is so great that it requires an enormous number of animals to be bred to meet it, and that is why, as we saw in chapter 1, they live confined in tiny spaces.

Thus, as more and more people became vegan, gradually fewer animals would be born into such conditions.

12. Would Veganism Ruin the Economy and Cost Jobs?

12.1. The objection that veganism would ruin the economy

The animal exploitation industry is big business. It moves a great deal of money around the world. On this basis it is sometimes argued that if many people became vegan, the economy would collapse, and that for this reason we should not be vegan.

The first problem with this argument is that, even if large-scale veganism ruined the economy, it would still result in a world with less suffering and death than there would be in a world where animal exploitation continued.

The second problem is that it is false that large-scale veganism would ruin the economy. As the demand for animal products decreased, the demand for vegan products would increase.

12.2. The objection that those who work in animal exploitation would lose their jobs

It is sometimes claimed that large-scale veganism would cause the people who work in animal exploitation to lose their jobs and that, for this reason, animal exploitation is justified.

There are two fundamental problems with this argument. One concerns the conception of ethics the argument assumes. The other concerns what it assumes about the facts. Below we will look at each of them separately.

The first problem is that, even if what the argument claims were to happen, losing a job, although it is something quite bad, is nowhere near comparable to what exploited animals suffer. Anyone who has any doubt need only imagine which of the two situations they would rather be in.

If humans were bred and killed to be eaten, to make clothing, or to be used as test subjects, it would sound ridiculous to say that we should not end such practices just because doing so would cause the workers in that system to lose their jobs. The reason attitudes are so disparate depending on whether we are talking about the exploitation of nonhuman animals or of humans is simply that respect for humans is already taken seriously to a far greater degree than respect for nonhuman animals.

Thus, the ethical problem with the argument is that it assumes a biased conception that gives more weight to the lesser harm, just because the greater harm would fall on nonhuman animals. It is therefore a speciesist conception. Such a conception would never be accepted if we did not know who would be benefited and who would be harmed. For example, imagine you had to say which of these two things is more important: (1) avoiding losing one's job, or (2) avoiding going through extreme torment for an entire lifetime and being killed brutally. No one in their right mind would say that avoiding losing one's job is more important. This shows that the conception of ethics assumed by the argument fails the impartiality test. It is therefore a biased conception and, for that reason, an unjust one.

The second problem concerns what the argument assumes about the facts. The argument assumes that the more people became vegan, the fewer jobs there would be. However, this forgets that, as the demand for vegan products increased, job opportunities would increase accordingly, whether in companies focused exclusively on vegan products or in companies that sell products from animal exploitation but also deal in vegan products. Therefore, there is no necessary connection between an increase in the number of vegans and an overall decrease in job opportunities.

13. But Does Veganism Really Have a Practical Impact?

In the world we live in, it is almost impossible to eliminate our contribution to animal exploitation entirely, since almost all products and services involve animal exploitation to some degree.

In addition, the techniques used to plant and harvest crops and to transport plant goods also kill small animals accidentally (and even intentionally, as in the extermination of animals that eat the crops).

These observations are an important reminder that we should try to do something to reduce the deaths that the production of plant foods also causes to animals. However, they are not a good reason to reject veganism, since the fact that we cannot avoid all harm does not justify our failing to avoid as much as we can.

The aim is to avoid harming as many animals as possible, even if we cannot avoid harming all of them. Even if veganism enabled us to prevent the death of just a single animal, it would still be worth it. Moreover, in reality, the practice of veganism prevents a large number of animals from being born only to suffer and be killed. We will see this in more detail below.

Some people have the impression that veganism has no practical impact because they notice that, despite the increase in the number of vegans in recent decades, there has also been an increase in the number of animals exploited. However, this does not show that veganism has no practical impact. What we need to do to assess the practical impact of veganism is not to compare the number of animals exploited today with the number exploited in past decades, but to imagine what the world would be like today if every person who is vegan were not. Remember that, if the number of vegans were smaller, the number of animals killed today would be even greater than it already is. Below we will look at some estimates of the practical impact of veganism.

For the sake of argument, let us assume that 2 trillion vertebrates are killed for consumption each year (the actual number is probably higher148). Given that the human population is approximately 8 billion people, this amounts to an average of 250 vertebrate animals killed per person per year. Given the average human life expectancy (75 years), practicing veganism would mean that each person would prevent, over their lifetime, at least 18,000 vertebrates from being born to meet this fate.

The calculation above concerns only vertebrates. If we include invertebrates, we find that the number of animals killed in animal exploitation each year is far greater: between 34 and 54 trillion individuals149. This amounts to an average of 4,250 to 6,750 animals killed per person per year. Given an average human life expectancy of 75 years, each vegan would prevent, over their lifetime, somewhere between 318,000 and 506,000 animals from being born to meet this fate.

Thus, veganism certainly has a practical impact. And, as we have seen, this impact is not small.

Author’s notes

  1. For statistics on the exploitation of aquatic vertebrates, see Fishcount (2019). For statistics on the exploitation of land vertebrates, see Our world in data (2018) and Sanders (2018). ↩
  2. For statistics on the exploitation of land invertebrates, see Schukraft (2019) and Rowe (2020a, 2020b, 2021). For statistics on the exploitation of aquatic invertebrates, see Waldhorn; Altric (2023); Fishcount (2019). ↩

14. But Doesn't Veganism Cause Even More Deaths Than Consuming Animals?

It is sometimes argued that, contrary to what might seem at first glance, veganism causes even more deaths than consuming animals. According to this claim, this would be because of the animal deaths caused as a side effect of agriculture, such as the accidental deaths of small animals during harvesting and the transport of plant foods, and even intentional deaths, as in the use of pesticides during planting150.

The reply usually offered to this objection points out that the greater the number of vegans, the fewer crops would be required, since a large share of the grain produced in the world is used to fatten the animals humans exploit for consumption.

However, a proponent of the objection could point out that if everyone consumed only aquatic animals caught in the wild at sea, there would be no need to grow crops at all, and this, all told, would allegedly result in fewer deaths than a vegan world.

One possible reply here is to question whether, all told, doing so would result in fewer deaths than there would be in a vegan world. Regardless of that, however, there is another possible reply, which points to the importance of taking into account all the consequences, and not just some of them. This reply will be explored in more detail below.

It could be pointed out that the objection takes into account only the direct consequences of each form of consumption, neglecting the influence of the worldview passed on through each kind of attitude. To defend consuming animals is to reinforce the view that they are resources at our disposal. To defend veganism, on the other hand, reinforces the view that animals are beings we ought to be concerned about.

It is only in a world where animals receive moral consideration that there will be people concerned with minimizing the indirect deaths resulting from agriculture and with trying to improve the situation of animals in general. Defending the consumption of animals definitely does not help make such a world possible (on the contrary, it hinders it). Therefore, these two

kinds of attitudes have very different consequences in the long term, because of the ideal they reinforce.

The consequences of the influence that worldviews exert are much greater than the direct consequences of each person's consumption, since they extend over many generations. The consequences of consumption last until the moment the person dies. The consequences of the worldview they promote, by contrast, continue long after they die.

For this reason, the indirect positive impact of a vegan way of life, that of reinforcing consideration for animals, is even greater than the direct positive impact of preventing more animals from being born to suffer and die. Of course, these positive indirect consequences exist only if one emphasizes that one does not consume animal products out of respect for animals (not consuming animal products for anthropocentric or environmentalist reasons does not have the same positive indirect effect of reinforcing moral consideration for animals).

Therefore, even if it were true that practicing veganism killed more animals because of the indirect harm caused by planting, harvesting, and transport (and, incidentally, there is no evidence that this number of deaths is greater than the deaths resulting from animal exploitation), still, if we take into account the consequences of the worldview each practice helps pass on, it is more likely that advocating veganism would still have better overall consequences over time.

Author’s notes

  1. For an example of this objection, see McWillians (2014). For a reply, see Cunha (2023b). ↩

15. Does Concern for Species Justify Consuming Animals?

15.1. The claim that consumption preserves domesticated species

Consuming animals is sometimes defended on the grounds that these animals would not exist if they had not been bred to be consumed. This argument was discussed in chapter 7. In this chapter we will discuss a similar attempt, but one that appeals not to the supposed benefit to the exploited individual of having been born, but to a concern with preserving the species to which the exploited individuals belong.

This attempt points out that several of the species of typically exploited animals (such as chickens, cattle, pigs, etc.) exist only because of their domestication, and that the purpose of this domestication was to breed them to be consumed. Therefore, the argument concludes, it is essential that the consumption of animals continue; otherwise these species would no longer exist.

This argument has problems both with respect to the ethical principles it assumes and with respect to what it claims about the facts. Below we will look at each of these problems separately.

15.2. Do species matter in themselves?

Note that the argument in question does not advocate preserving these species because doing so would be good for the members of the species itself or of other species (for example, for humans). On the contrary: what is claimed is a concern for the species themselves. So the first problem with the argument is that it assumes (without explanation) that species matter in themselves. That is, it assumes that preserving species has something positive about it, even if it benefits no sentient being, and even if it only harms sentient beings. It is not impossible that species matter in themselves. But this is a highly controversial idea, and an argument would have to be offered in its defense. The argument we are discussing does not do this. Instead, it simply assumes that this is so, and that is that.

What is more, there are reasons against the idea that species matter in themselves. Species are nonsentient entities. What is more, they are abstract entities: they are categorizations of living beings according to a certain criterion (for example, being able to interbreed and produce fertile offspring151). There is no one who is the species. So there is no one there who would be benefited by continuing to exist or harmed by ceasing to exist.

The members of these species, on the other hand, being sentient, are indeed someone, and they can be harmed and benefited because they are capable of having negative and positive experiences. The consumption of animals brings them negative experiences and deprives them of positive experiences (since they are killed). Therefore, if the consumption of animals harms the members of these species, and species cannot be harmed, we have here a strong reason against such consumption.

One way of trying to get around this criticism is to claim that it depends on assuming that, for an entity to matter in itself, it must be capable of being harmed and benefited. Someone who rejects this view could say that species, although they cannot be harmed or benefited, have impersonal intrinsic value, in the sense that the world becomes worse if they disappear, even if no one is harmed by it (not even the species themselves).

This is a possible way out, but it would still have to be shown that this kind of value really exists and that species are bearers of this kind of value152. However, we do not need to enter into that discussion in order to discuss this defense of consuming animals, since it faces a greater problem, which would remain even if it were shown that species have intrinsic value. This problem will be discussed below.

15.3. Do species matter more than sentient beings?

Suppose it were shown that species matter in themselves. This does not necessarily imply that it would be justified to harm sentient beings, even if doing so were

necessary to preserve the species. For a simple reason: showing that something matters in itself is not showing that it matters more than something else.

So what the argument would have to demonstrate is two things:

(1) That species matter in themselves;

(2) That they matter so much more than the good of sentient beings that it would be justified, if necessary to preserve them, to cause extreme suffering and death to an enormous number of sentient beings.

As we have seen, if demonstrating the first claim is already a difficult task, demonstrating the second is even more so. In fact, regarding the second, we can give reasons for thinking exactly the opposite: even if species mattered in themselves, there would still be reasons to give priority to sentient beings in cases of conflict. The reason is the same one we have already seen, which will be recapitulated in more detail below:

Only sentient beings are someone, and therefore only sentient beings can be harmed or benefited. Sentient beings are capable of negative and positive experiences. So they are harmed if they suffer, since suffering is a negative experience. They are also harmed by death, since it prevents them from enjoying positive experiences. These are particularly serious harms that no nonsentient entity is capable of suffering. Here we have reasons to give priority to the good of sentient beings, even if it had been shown that species (or any other nonsentient entity) matter in themselves.

The argument has yet a third problem, concerning what it claims about the facts. We will discuss this problem below.

15.4. If the consumption of animals were abolished, would these species disappear?

Suppose it had been shown that species matter in themselves, and that they matter so much more than the good of sentient beings that it would be justified to harm an enormous number of sentient beings enormously if this were necessary to preserve them. Even so, the argument we are discussing would still not succeed, since the claim it makes about the facts is false.

The argument assumes that, because certain species of animals used for consumption arose through domestication aimed at using them for consumption, such consumption must continue so that these species do not disappear. But this is simply false: if the consumption of these animals were abolished, nothing would prevent them from continuing to reproduce. Therefore, these species would continue to exist even in the absence of such consumption.

Finally, it is curious that this argument is sometimes offered by the same people who argue that we should not abolish the consumption of animals because doing so would supposedly lead to overpopulation in these species, since one claim contradicts the other. The claim that in the absence of animal consumption there would be overpopulation in these species is also false, since, as we saw in chapter 11, there are only so many animals of these species because they are mass-bred for consumption. In short, both the claim that in the absence of animal consumption there would be overpopulation of these species and the claim that consuming them is necessary for these species to endure are false.

15.5. Conclusion

We have seen that the argument claiming that the consumption of animals is justified because it would supposedly be essential for the continuation of these species has three central problems:

(1) It assumes that species matter in themselves.

(2) It assumes that species matter more (in fact, much more) than the good of the sentient beings who are members of these species.

(3) It assumes that these species would disappear if the consumption of animals were abolished.

We have seen that the first assumption is highly controversial; that there are strong reasons to reject the second; and that the third is simply false (which would make the argument a bad one even if the other two assumptions had been proven). Therefore, there is no way for this argument to be sound.

Author’s notes

  1. Among specialists, the most widely accepted definition of the biological concept of species is the one proposed by Mayr (1977): two individuals belong to the same species if they are able to interbreed and produce fertile offspring. ↩
  2. For examples of different defenses of the claim that nonsentient entities have intrinsic value, see Callicott (1989, ch. 8 and 9); Eckersley (1992, p. 46, 47); Hettinger (1994, p. 14); Hurka (2006); Leopold (1949, p. 224- 225); Regan (1981); Rolston (1988, p. 68, 73, 184-186, 223-25; 1999, p. 260, 261); Sagoff (1974, p. 228); Wenz (1998, p. 295). For a detailed critique of each of these defenses, see Cunha (2018, section 6.5.). For a general critique, see Singer (2002 [1993], ch.10), ↩

16. The Claim That the Struggle for Animals Should Be Put Off Until Later

It is often said that if it is already hard to get people to accept giving consideration to humans, it will be even harder to get them to accept giving consideration to nonhuman animals. On this basis, it is sometimes argued that we should fight for humans and leave the defense of nonhuman animals to future generations.

One way of responding to this suggestion is to point out that if it is hard to get people to accept giving consideration to animals, then postponing their defense is a terrible strategy. Usually, the sooner an idea begins to be defended, the sooner it begins to have practical consequences. For example, imagine that speciesism had been widely questioned since antiquity. Things would most likely be different for animals today. Indeed, one of the main reasons some people resist giving up speciesism is the very fact that they have never come across the arguments against speciesism, since the equal consideration of all sentient beings is not yet a widely held idea. So there is no reason to put off speaking up for animals. Indeed, there is not a minute to lose.

Moreover, the suggestion in question assumes that it is not possible for someone to accept equal consideration for animals while there are still other people who do not accept equal consideration for humans. This is false. An ever greater number of people are rejecting speciesism. The fact that there are racist, sexist, and speciesist people does not prevent other people from accepting equality for all sentient beings.

Each individual person makes a considerable difference to the animals affected by their decisions. So even if it were impossible to convince a majority, it would still be worth trying to convince as many people as we could. Furthermore, there is nothing to prove that most people would not accept the arguments against speciesism, since most people are not yet familiar with these arguments.

Thus, the suggestion that it is pointless to fight for animals as long as there is disrespect toward humans is suspect, to say the least. Although it is presented as a suggestion for improving the situation of animals, its real aim may be to block the struggle for animals.

For example, imagine it were suggested that we abandon the defense of women and children until all adult men are respected, on the claim that this is the best way to achieve respect for women and children. In that case we would have every reason to suspect that, contrary to what is claimed, what the proponents of the suggestion really think is that women and children are worth less.

In the same way, the suggestion we are discussing may be a disguised speciesist suggestion. While an avowed speciesist would say "humans should come first because they are superior," a disguised speciesist would say "the best way to help nonhuman animals is to put humans first." Yet both are proposing exactly the same thing.

17. Aren't Animals Already Protected by the Law?

A common belief is that animals already have rights guaranteed by law, and that animal exploitation happens because the laws are systematically violated. However, that is not how things are. Animal exploitation is legal. It takes place within legal systems that legitimize it and ensure that it can continue to exist, protecting humans' interest in using animals as resources.

It is important to remember that we live in speciesist societies, and legal systems generally reflect the prevailing thinking in societies. Thus, the legal status in which animals are placed protects the interest in using animals as resources, since it prevents them from having rights, given that they are considered things, items of people's property. We will see this in more detail below.

Rights are guarantees that protect their holders153 (for example, they protect their physical integrity, their life, their liberty, and so on). Rights can be legal or moral. Moral rights are independent of whether or not they are recognized by law. Legal rights, by contrast, are protections guaranteed by legal systems.

Whatever the legal system in force in a country, in terms of legal status there is usually a clear distinction between two categories: persons and objects. Only persons can be holders of legal rights. Objects are items of people's property and, as such, cannot have rights. Persons even have the right to exploit their items of property.

The legal status of nonhuman animals is usually that of items of property154. In practice, this means that as long as they remain in this category, they cannot have legal rights, and so no truly meaningful protection of their interests will be possible (given that their owners would still have the right to exploit them).

That is why, despite the existence of animal welfare laws, in practice they do not prevent animals from being exploited and living a veritable hell155.

A common objection to recognizing rights for nonhuman animals is the claim that, to have rights, one must understand the notion of rights, since this would be necessary in order to respect the rights of others and to claim one's own. However, if it makes sense to recognize rights for humans who lack these capacities (such as children and adults with cognitive impairments), then it makes no sense to say that nonhuman animals cannot have rights because they lack these capacities.

There are, therefore, reasons to advocate changing the legal status of animals, removing them from the category of things and granting them the status of holders of legal rights156. However, this is unlikely to happen as long as most people consume animal products, the demand for which entails the existence of an entire system of animal exploitation to meet it. For this reason it is necessary, alongside the call for a change in the legal status of animals, also to seek to get more and more people to stop using animals.

However, to achieve such a change in behavior, it is necessary to change the way people see animals. That is why it is extremely necessary, both to get more people to stop using animals and to change the legal status of animals, to spread the arguments supporting equal consideration for all sentient beings.

  1. On the definition of a right, see Wenar (2021). ↩
  2. See Tannenbaum (1995); Francione (1995); McCartney-Smith (1998); Bryant (2008) and Maddux (2012). ↩
  3. For an analysis of this question, see Francione (1995). ↩
  4. On this, see Feinberg (1974); Finsen (1997); Teubner (2006); Lourenço (2008); da Silva (2020) and Ataíde Júnior (2025). ↩

18. The Claim That Animal Advocates Are Imposing Their Lifestyle

An objection frequently raised against guaranteeing legal rights for animals is the claim that this would be imposing on people, since it would force them to respect animals (for example, exploiting animals would then be prohibited).

According to this objection, animal advocates have the right to present arguments in defense of their position, but each person should have the right to choose whether or not to accept them of their own free will, without a law forcing them to.

This argument has two fundamental problems, which we will discuss below.

The first problem is that it is speciesist, since its proponents accept legal rights for humans. So much so that the argument maintains that those who want to exploit animals should have their right to do so guaranteed.

Moreover, this argument would be widely repudiated if the victims were human. Imagine, for example, someone arguing that people should be free to accept or not accept the rule against murdering humans, without a law forcing them to, since that would be imposing on people. Likewise, such an argument would be strongly repudiated if we did not know whether we would be born as humans or as nonhuman animals. Therefore, this argument also fails the impartiality test.

The second problem is that the argument is self-refuting, since it maintains that there should be a legal right protecting individuals against impositions, and at the same time maintains that there should be a legal right to impose on nonhuman animals, including causing them extreme suffering and death. Thus, despite what they say, the proponents of this objection are not against impositions. Quite the contrary: what they are defending is a supposed right to impose extreme things on nonhuman animals. But obviously it makes no sense to defend something like this by claiming that imposing on others is wrong. For this reason, the argument is self-refuting.

Sometimes this argument takes a more extreme form, claiming that the mere fact of arguing against animal exploitation is already wrong, since it would be "imposing a lifestyle on others."

Besides having the same problems as the previous argument, this argument is an extreme example of arbitrariness. On the one hand, the mere fact of presenting arguments in favor of animals is considered an unjustified imposition. On the other, literally imposing a life of extreme suffering, and death as well, on an enormous number of individuals is not even considered an imposition, because its victims are nonhuman animals.

Needless to say, if the same accusation were made regarding practices whose victims are human, it would immediately be seen how dishonest it is. It is only because of the overwhelming prevalence of speciesism that accusations of this kind arise when the victims are nonhuman animals.

The fact that there are people who call themselves vegan and adhere to this point of view, saying things like "I'm vegan, but anyone who wants to exploit animals should have their right to do so guaranteed, because no one should impose anything on anyone," is a sign of how present speciesism is even within the so-called vegan movement. If the victims were human, it would immediately be seen how contradictory it is to maintain, at the same time, that we have no right to impose anything on anyone and that anyone who wants to impose something on someone should have their right to do so guaranteed. Under the mask of tolerance, what they are in fact defending is that it is wrong to oppose those who want to exploit animals, and that it is right to impose suffering and death on nonhuman animals.

In short, although these people do not consume animals, they hold a view about animals that is exactly the same as the view of those who consume animals and think it is right to do so: they believe there is a right to cause suffering and death to animals. The only difference is that they choose not to consume them. But that is exactly how those who consume animals and think it is right think (since they do not maintain that there is an obligation to consume animals; they maintain only that it is permissible to do so). In short, this shows that, unfortunately, not everyone who is vegan has rejected speciesism.

19. The Exploitation of Insects and Why We Should Oppose It

19.1. Are insects sentient?

There is a growing body of evidence of sentience in insects. Some examples of this evidence are given below. Since this is a class with an enormous diversity of species, a good number of them have not yet been studied with respect to their sentience. So the evidence below concerns studies carried out on a few species. However, we can generalize this evidence (at least in terms of the benefit of the doubt) to evolutionarily related species. This is because it is not that insects of other species were studied and failed to meet the criteria for sentience: what has happened is that they have hardly been studied at all.

Generalizing the conclusions reached for studied species to related species is already standard practice in recognizing sentience in other kinds of animals. For example, with respect to vertebrates, cephalopods, and crustaceans, the laws that mention their sentience are based on generalizations from the evidence obtained in intensively studied species to other related species157. So there is no reason to proceed differently with respect to insects. This means we have reasons to treat all insects as sentient until proven otherwise.

Let us look, then, at some evidence of sentience in insects.

  • Insect behavior is flexible, displaying decision-making in changing circumstances, adaptive behavior, cognitive generalization, and also learning that integrates different kinds of information158.
  • They have centralized nervous systems with distinct brains. Among the regions of their brains is the protocerebrum, which includes the so-called mushroom bodies, containing between one hundred thousand and one million neurons159.
  • Local field potentials (that is, electrical activity) with a response between 20Hz and 30Hz have been recorded in their brains160.
  • The connectome of some insects (that is, the map of their neural connections) is comparable to the fiber-tract networks found in primates, displaying so-called small-world organization (which consists of high connectivity between neighboring regions combined with shortcut connections to distant regions)161.
  • Insects' mushroom bodies receive and integrate distinct multisensory information, enabling them to learn from previous experiences, remember them, and integrate information162, and they are thus a specialized center for processing spatial information and organizing movement163.

This evidence seems more than sufficient for us, at the very least, to give insects the benefit of the doubt.

19.2. The exploitation of insects

The use of insects has grown enormously in recent years. Besides the exploitation of cochineal insects to produce dye, of silkworms to produce silk, and of bees to produce honey and other products, insects are increasingly being used directly for human consumption, often disguised as flours or burgers, and also to manufacture feed for other animals that humans also exploit164.

Below are some figures on the annual deaths of insects in exploitation165.

  • Cochineal insects killed in the production of carmine dye: between 4.6 and 21 trillion166.
  • Insects killed for consumption: between 2 and 3.2 trillion167.
  • Silkworms killed for silk production: between 420 billion and 1 trillion168.
  • There are no data on the number of bees killed for honey production, but the population of bees kept for honey production is between 1.4 and 4.8 trillion individuals at any given time169.

19.3. How insects are harmed in exploitation

The use of insects raises the number of animals killed to enormous levels. Since these animals are so much smaller, a vastly greater number of individuals is needed to produce the equivalent amount of meat or other product.

Moreover, they probably suffer a great deal throughout the whole process. The space allotted to insects on farms is even smaller, in proportion to their size, than that given to other animals170. Before they are removed from confinement, the common practice is to deprive them of food for 12 to 24 hours and to lower the oxygen concentration. They are then kept alive and chilled to temperatures close to 0ºC. Typical methods of killing them are: freezing, immersion in water hotter than 80ºC, microwaving, infrared tunnel ovens, and grinding171.

19.4. Reasons to oppose the exploitation of insects

The first obvious reason to oppose the exploitation of insects is that it causes suffering and death to an enormous number of sentient beings. In addition, the exploitation of insects is unjust for the same reasons that the exploitation of any other sentient being is unjust. Below we will recapitulate three of these reasons.

First, like every practice in which there are exploiters and exploited, it violates the principle of equal consideration172 because it is biased in how it assigns weight to each individual's good.

Second, like every speciesist practice, it determines who will be benefited and who will be harmed on the basis of the species to which they belong. Species, like race and gender, is also a morally irrelevant property, since, besides being an outcome of the natural lottery (and therefore not resulting from merit or demerit), it does not determine whether someone can be harmed or benefited, nor the magnitude of the harms and benefits.

Third, it would never be approved if we did not know whether we would be born as humans or as insects. This shows that those who defend this practice do so only because they know they will not be its victims. If so, then it fails the impartiality test173.

19.5. Responding to some objections

19.5.1. Are insects barely capable of suffering?

The exploitation of insects is sometimes defended on the grounds that animals with less complex brains are barely capable of suffering174.

There are at least two ways of responding to this objection.

The first is to point out that, even if they were barely capable of suffering, they would still be seriously harmed by their exploitation, since they would still suffer and lose their lives. So even if they were barely capable of suffering, this seems insufficient to justify their exploitation.

The second is to deny that lower brain complexity implies that the individual is barely capable of suffering. The capacity to experience suffering and pleasure is a trait that prevailed in evolutionary history probably because it is directly connected to the motivation for behavior175. That is, sentient beings avoid the stimuli that make them suffer and seek the stimuli that give them pleasure. This behavior, by increasing their chances of survival, also increases their chances of reproducing and passing this trait on. The point is this: the greater the cognitive capacities, the greater the diversity of

motivations for behavior and learning. So it is possible that beings with greater cognitive capacities can survive and pass on their genes even if they do not have very intense experiences of suffering and pleasure. On the other hand, the lower an animal's cognitive capacities, the more its motivation to act one way or another will be tied solely to the intensity of pain and pleasure176.

This means that animals with lower cognitive capacities may quite possibly suffer even more intensely since, if this were not so, these species would most likely not have succeeded in passing on their genes and would no longer exist. Ryder (2002, p. 64) emphasizes this point: "Their experiences may be more simple than ours, but are they less intense? Perhaps a caterpillar's primitive pain when squashed is greater than our more sophisticated sufferings177".

19.5.2. Are insects only slightly harmed by death?

It is sometimes argued that the more cognitively sophisticated experiences are, the more valuable they are, and that, for this reason, someone is harmed to a greater degree if they cannot experience them178. Someone might want to appeal to this view to claim that nothing very bad is done to insects if they are killed, since they would not be capable of the intellectual pleasures humans are capable of.

However, what would have to be shown in order to maintain that beings with lower cognitive capacities are only slightly harmed by death is not that intellectual pleasures are more valuable, but that non-intellectual pleasures have almost no value. Yet when we think of all the non-intellectual pleasures we enjoy (being near those we love, going for walks, eating, having sex, swimming, and so on), it seems this could hardly be the case.

19.5.3. What if insects counted for less?

Let us suppose, for the sake of argument, that each insect should count for less than other sentient beings in our decisions. What would the implications be?

One might think that one implication is that the exploitation of insects would be justified. However, there is no such implication. It is one thing to be able to establish that certain individuals should count for less. It is another to be able to establish that we are justified in exploiting and killing the individuals who should count for less. An additional argument establishing this second conclusion would have to be put forward, since it does not necessarily follow from the first.

One might also think that if insects count for less, then we are justified in attaching little importance to trying to change their situation. But, again, there is no such implication. On the contrary: the number of them who suffer and are killed is so enormous that we should still keep protecting them as one of our priorities even if they counted for less179. For example, suppose each human counted 1000 times more than each insect. This would mean that, for us to invest the same amount of resources in helping insects as we should invest in helping humans, there would have to be 1000 times more insects than humans in equally bad situations. Since in the real world the number of exploited insects is vastly greater than that, the balance would still tip toward giving priority to protecting them, even if each of them counted for much less.

19.6. What is the important conclusion to draw on this question?

If every sentient being matters, then the exploitation of insects (like that of decapods) is one of the most important problems there are, given the vast number of victims. This number is so large that this conclusion would hold even if there were justification for giving less weight to the good of each insect. Moreover, it is important to note that nothing we have seen shows that there is justification for giving less weight to the good of insects. If that is so, then the importance we should give to this problem is even greater180.

20. The Debate on Animal Experimentation

20.1. Introduction

This chapter first examines the main arguments used in defense of animal experimentation and points out the problems with those arguments. It then presents some of the main arguments against animal experimentation.

20.2. The arguments from necessity and efficacy

The argument from necessity

One of the arguments most frequently employed by defenders of animal experimentation is that it is indispensable for scientific research. For example, Beauchamp (1999, p. 472) argued that granting nonhuman animals the right to life is something that should not be done because it could have negative effects on scientific research.

One way to respond to this argument is to point out that there is a whole range of research procedures that do not use nonhuman animals, such as inanimate and computer models, cell and tissue cultures, epidemiological studies, research on microorganisms, and so on.181. Therefore, animal experimentation would not be indispensable for research to continue.

It could be objected that there may be no substitute method for the use of animals in certain contexts. However, this does not necessarily imply that using animals is justifiable in such contexts. For example, imagine that in certain contexts the only way to carry out a piece of research were to kidnap and kill humans. That would still be insufficient to justify adopting such a method. This is because the mere fact that a certain means is the only way to achieve a certain end does not necessarily imply that there is justification for using that means. This holds whether one adopts a deontological perspective in ethics (where, for example, individuals would have the right not to be used as mere

resources, regardless of the consequences) or a consequentialist perspective (since, according to consequentialism, it would have to be shown that adopting the means in question produces the best consequences, taking into account everyone who would be affected, and not only in this case in isolation, but also taking into account the future ramifications of the consequences, including the way such an act would influence the future decisions of other agents). This does not mean that it is impossible to justify the use of a harmful means in certain circumstances. It means only that pointing out that a certain means is the only way to achieve a certain end is insufficient to establish that we are justified in using that means. Much more would have to be demonstrated.

The argument from efficacy

One of the frequent objections to methods that do not use animals in experiments is the claim that, at least in some cases, using animals would be more efficient. This objection therefore assumes that efficacy is the fundamental criterion for choosing among the various research methods.

Are we in a position to compare efficacy?

One way to respond to this objection is to deny that we are in a position to compare the efficacy of methods that use animals and methods that do not, since not enough work has been done on the latter, given that funding for research that does not use animals is minimal182.

Thus, even if the currently existing methods that do not use animals were not as efficient as those that use animals for the same purposes, there would be no basis for concluding that, if a similar amount of resources were devoted to both kinds of methods, the methods that do not use animals could not be as efficient as (or even more efficient than) the methods that use animals.

Moreover, the companies involved in research that uses animals invest a great deal of resources in promoting the idea that animal testing is necessary. These resources are

several orders of magnitude greater than the amount of resources devoted to developing methods that do not use animals183. Thus, paradoxically, a large amount of resources that could be used to develop methods that do not use animals is used instead to spread the idea that the use of methods harmful to animals is necessary, on the basis of the claim that there are no other methods for the same purposes.

Does being more effective automatically justify a practice?

Another way to respond to the appeal to efficacy is to point out that, if the fact that a method is the most effective automatically justified using that method, then this would be a reason to prefer testing directly on humans instead of testing on nonhuman animals, since doing so would avoid problems in the results due to the difficulties of extrapolating data between different species184. That is, the appeal to efficacy cannot justify experimentation on nonhuman animals185. However, even though testing on humans is more effective, most of us (including many scientists who experiment on animals) would consider it unacceptable, for moral reasons, to do so. This seems to show that such scientists do not in fact accept the criterion they claim to accept.

In short, there are two main reasons why the appeal to efficacy does not justify the use of animals. The first is that the very idea that, because a method is the most effective way of achieving a certain goal, adopting it is automatically justified is highly questionable. The second is that, even if that idea were correct, it would imply testing directly on humans, since that would be more effective than using animals.

20.3. Would giving greater weight to humans justify animal experimentation?

A moral double standard

Defenses of animal experimentation reflect a moral double standard, one that considers the use of nonhuman animals in experiments acceptable (a use that is

often defended on the grounds that it would be more efficient than methods that do not use animals) while at the same time considering the use of humans under the same conditions unacceptable, even though it would be more efficient than methods that use nonhuman animals186.

In other words, it is held that experiments on nonhuman animals are acceptable (even imperative) despite the harms such experiments cause, and that the same procedures are unacceptable in the case of human beings precisely because of the harms they cause. It is, therefore, a moral double standard based on the species of the victim.

The claim that the good of nonhuman animals does not matter

One way to try to justify this double standard would be to maintain that the good of nonhuman animals does not count to any degree. However, it would have to be explained why the good of animals does not matter, rather than simply assuming it from the outset187.

Even the guidelines that endorse the use of animals usually maintain that the good of nonhuman animals matters to some degree, however minimal. For example, the Declaration of Helsinki, despite completely disregarding several important interests of animals (such as not being used as resources, not suffering at all, not being killed, and so on), upholds the need to protect animal welfare, in the sense of minimizing their suffering while they are being used as resources188.

It is therefore contradictory for defenders of animal experimentation to claim that the good of nonhuman animals does not count to any degree and also to claim that such experiments are justified because they allegedly comply with animal welfare guidelines.

The claim that human interests should always weigh more

Another way to try to defend the double standard is to claim that, although the interests of animals matter to some degree, human interests would always matter more, whatever they may be. One problem with this view, however, is that it would imply that a trivial interest of a human (such as avoiding a light pinch on the arm) would carry more weight than the interest of a nonhuman animal (or even of billions of nonhuman animals) in not suffering the worst possible torture for years. This would be the height of arbitrariness, to say the least. As we saw in chapter 2, it is a blatant violation of the principles of equal consideration and impartiality.

Moreover, the guidelines regulating animal experimentation do not seem to accept this view, for by maintaining that some interests of nonhuman animals matter (however minimally), they are holding that the interests of nonhuman animals outweigh at least some human interests (since respecting these interests of animals costs humans at least some effort, however minimal, that could have been devoted to other purposes).

The claim that similar human interests should count more

Faced with the implication above, someone might then argue that it is not that all human interests are more important than all the interests of nonhuman animals, but only that the relevant interests of humans weigh more than similar interests of nonhuman animals.

A first problem with this position is that, if the interests of nonhuman animals are given some weight, even if much less, when we add up the interests of a large number of nonhuman animals, this already amounts to a significant weight. Therefore, the claim that nonhuman animals should receive some consideration, but less, implies accepting that there is a certain number of animals above which their interest in not being used as resources outweighs the human interest in using them.

That is, even giving greater weight to human interests, animal experimentation could not be considered acceptable once it exceeded a certain limit in terms of the number of animals used. And in practice that limit is routinely exceeded189.

Moreover, a second (and main) problem with this position is that, as we saw in chapter 2, there seems to be no justification for giving different weight to similar levels of harms and benefits depending on the species of those affected. If so, then it is unjustifiable to give less weight to harms that befall nonhuman animals than to similar harms to humans.

20.4. Kantianism for humans and utilitarianism for nonhumans?

Another way to argue that the double standard is consistent is to maintain that we should adopt a pluralist approach: Kantian principles for human beings and utilitarian principles for nonhuman animals190.

Kantian principles would prohibit using human beings as mere means. Utilitarian principles (which, according to this view, should be applied only to nonhuman animals), on the other hand, could accept such use when doing so is the most efficient way of maximizing utility (understood as the total aggregate balance of well-being).

There are two fundamental problems with this position, which will be spelled out below.

The first problem is that, even if the double standard in question were acceptable, the use of animals would be justified only under the conditions in which utilitarianism approved of it. However, utilitarianism would certainly take into account the sum of the interests of animals (giving equal weight to similar interests of humans). Since the number of animals used in experiments is estimated at more than 100 million individuals per year191, their aggregate interests would carry an enormous weight, one that would outweigh the aggregate interests of humans in using them192.

The second problem is that the position in question offers no reason for adopting this double standard: instead, it simply assumes that it is justified. In any other context, adopting Kantianism in some cases and utilitarianism in others would be considered a paradigmatic example of incoherence. For it to be accepted in this case, a justification would have to be presented, rather than simply assuming it as though it were obvious.

Sometimes an attempt is made to justify adopting this double standard by claiming that humans have autonomy, and that this would give rise to a protection against being used as resources193. However, there are two problems with this move, detailed below.

The first problem is that an enormous number of humans do not have autonomy. If someone is human but not yet an adult, or is already an adult but lacks the cognitive capacities typical of an adult human, then they do not have autonomy. Therefore, according to this position, children and people with some cognitive impairment should be used in experiments in the way animals are currently used.

The second problem is that this move does not explain why it would be the capacity for autonomy that gives rise to protection against being used as a resource, and not some other characteristic (such as, for example, sentience). One might reply that autonomy gives rise to this protection because autonomous agents are harmed when their autonomous will is thwarted and, for that reason, must be objects of respect. However, sentient beings in general, whether or not they have an autonomous will, are also harmed when they are used in experiments, especially if they suffer and/or are killed. Therefore, it is completely arbitrary to say that the reason autonomous agents should not be used in experiments is that they would be harmed by it, and then to say that beings incapable of autonomy should be used in experiments despite being harmed by it.

20.5. Questioning the assignment of greater weight to human interests

In the two previous sections we saw that, even if greater weight were assigned to human interests, this would still be insufficient to justify animal experimentation. Now we will look at the central critique of the very idea that human interests should count more.

If we have reasons to give moral consideration to someone because that someone can be harmed and benefited, then it follows that the strength of the reasons for avoiding a harm and for pursuing a benefit depends on the magnitude of the harm and of the benefit, and not on the species of the one who bears it. This becomes clearer with the principle of equal consideration, which we examined in detail in chapter 2 and which will be briefly recapitulated below.

The principle of equal consideration194 is a safeguard ensuring that individuals are not unfairly favored or disfavored in the consideration of the harms and benefits they might receive. The principle prescribes that harms and benefits of similar magnitude must be given the same weight.

For example, suppose someone claims that the suffering of individual A matters to a certain extent, but that the equivalent suffering of individual B, who likewise has done nothing to deserve it, matters less. In that case, this person is violating the principle of equal consideration by unfairly disfavoring individual B.

In the example above, the principle was violated because similar harms were given different weight. There is, however, another, even more extreme way of violating the principle of equal consideration: when lesser harms are given greater weight than greater harms.

For example, suppose someone holds that relieving A's mild pain is more important than relieving B's intense pain. Suppose that neither of them did anything to deserve the pains they suffer. In that case, B is being unfairly disfavored in an even more blatant way, since the harm B suffers is given less weight not only than similar harms to A, but even than lesser harms to A.

The vast majority of experiments using animals are violations of the principle of equal consideration of this more blatant kind, which gives less weight to the greater harm, and those that are not still violate the principle by giving different weight to similar harms.

For example, the vast majority of experiments on animals aim to satisfy minor human interests, such as obtaining new cosmetics or new cleaning products, by sacrificing greater interests of nonhuman animals, such as their interests in not suffering and not dying. It could be objected that there is research using animals that aims to fulfill important human interests, such as curing diseases or developing vaccines. However, as stated above, the fact that one of the interests at stake is an important interest is not enough to show that the principle of equal consideration is not being violated. In the case of animal experimentation, it is violated when the similar interests of nonhuman animals (such as their interests in not suffering and not dying) are given less weight. If the roles were reversed (that is, if the proposal were to kill humans to secure equally important interests of nonhuman animals), the practice would be considered unacceptable. This shows that animal experimentation is grounded in a biased principle, one that determines who will be the victims and who will be the beneficiaries on the basis of the species to which they belong, and not on any even minimally impartial criterion.

20.6. What is really the ethical problem with animal experimentation?

The following argument, attributed to the philosopher Charles R. Magel, is often used by animal advocates against animal experimentation:

"Ask the vivisectionists why they experiment on animals, and they will answer: ‘Because animals are like us.’ Ask the vivisectionists why it is morally 'OK' to experiment on animals, and they will answer: ‘Because animals are not like us.’ Animal experimentation rests on a logical contradiction195".

Below we will see some reasons to think that this is not a good argument. This does not mean that animal experimentation is justified, since, as we saw above, there are several other good arguments against it. What we intend to show here is that the ethical problem

with animal experimentation does not lie in committing a logical contradiction, but rather in treating differently cases that are similar in their morally relevant properties.

Let us begin by observing that what the argument claims about animal experimentation could equally be said of cell cultures, computer models, or any other method that substitutes for the use of animals. For example:

"Ask animal advocates why they are in favor of testing on cell cultures, and they will answer: ‘Because cells are like sentient beings.’ Ask animal advocates why it is morally 'OK' to experiment on cells, and they will answer: ‘Because cells are not like sentient beings.’ The defense of methods that substitute for the use of animals rests on a logical contradiction".

The mistake in both arguments is the failure to distinguish between physiological similarities and similarities in morally relevant properties. Two beings can be similar in one sense but not in the other.

If we reformulate the two arguments, this time taking that distinction into account, we can see that the problem with animal experimentation does not lie in committing a logical contradiction, but rather in assuming that nonhuman animals differ from humans in their morally relevant properties. Let us see:

"Ask the vivisectionists why they experiment on animals, and they will answer: ‘Because animals are like us physiologically.’ Ask the vivisectionists why it is morally 'OK' to experiment on animals, and they will answer: ‘Because animals are not like us in their morally relevant properties’".

Now we can see that there is no logical contradiction. This does not mean that animal experimentation is justified. On the contrary. Both claims made by proponents of animal experimentation are probably false. For example, several authors have pointed out that physiological differences between species make the animal model scientifically inadequate196. However, the bigger problem lies with the claim that animals are not like humans in their morally relevant properties (and this problem would remain even if there were no problem at all with the claim that animals are like humans physiologically). This point will be explained in more detail below.

The reason humans need moral consideration is not that they belong to the human species, or that they possess a certain set of capacities, a certain set of relationships with one another, and so on. They need moral consideration simply because they can be harmed and benefited. However, this shows that every sentient being is similar in what is relevant for receiving moral consideration, since every sentient being can be harmed and benefited (given that sentience is what makes someone capable of experiencing suffering and pleasure, for example).

Now consider the same adaptation of the second argument:

"Ask animal advocates why they are in favor of testing on cell cultures, and they will answer: ‘Because cells are physiologically like sentient beings.’ Ask animal advocates why it is morally 'OK' to experiment on cells, and they will answer: ‘Because cells are not like sentient beings in their morally relevant properties".

Now we can see that the animal advocates' position does not commit a logical contradiction either and, more importantly, that it rests on true premises. Substitute methods are probably much more similar to the organisms of the beneficiaries (whatever species those beneficiaries may belong to) than the animal model is. But, more importantly, these substitute methods are not similar to sentient beings in their morally relevant properties since, not being sentient, they cannot be harmed or benefited.

Animal advocates' frequent use of the argument attributed to Magel stems from the mistaken belief that, for an argument to be bad, it must commit a contradiction. An argument's containing contradictory premises is one way in which an argument can be bad. However, an argument can be bad without its premises contradicting one another. For example, one or more premises may be false. As we have seen, this is certainly the case with the premise that claims that sentient animals are not similar to humans in what is relevant for someone to be owed moral consideration.

20.7. Conclusion

If the arguments presented above are sound, then two important conclusions follow:

(1) Given what we saw in section 20.5, there is no justification for giving less weight to the good of nonhuman animals.

(2) Given what we saw in sections 20.2, 20.3, and 20.4, even if there were such a justification, it would not imply that animal experimentation is justified.

Therefore, there are good reasons to reject animal experimentation. This does not mean, obviously, that scientific research should be halted. It means only that there seems to be no justification for carrying it out by means of animal experimentation.

Volume V

Differences Between Environmentalism and Consideration for Animals

This book presents a comparison of the differences between consideration for animals and environmentalism, both with regard to their foundations and goals and with regard to the practical conflict that results from these theoretical differences.

Original text by Luciano Carlos Cunha, translated into English · ISBN 978-65-01-42971-7 · 1st edition, April 2025.

1. Respect for animals and environmentalism: complementary or opposed?

1.1. Basic differences in foundations

Animal advocacy is often seen as a form of environmentalism. It is also not uncommon for animal advocacy and environmentalism to be seen as complementary perspectives, though different ones. Below we will see why both beliefs are mistaken. Consideration for animals and environmentalism are grounded in diametrically opposed ideals, which very often generate conflicting prescriptions in practice1.

To understand this divergence, it is essential to define what we mean by environmentalism, since the term is used in several different senses. For example, there are positions holding that the value of the environment lies in its being an important resource for humans2 or for sentient beings in general3 (that is, for all beings capable of suffering and enjoyment). These positions are sometimes called environmentalist. By contrast, there are positions holding that at least some aspects of the environment (such as ecosystems or species) have intrinsic value (that is, that they have value regardless of whether or not they benefit sentient beings). These positions are also called environmentalist.

In the first type of position, the center of moral concern is not the environment (which is seen as a resource, a means, whether for humans or for sentient beings in general, depending on the position). For this reason, throughout this work we will use the term environmentalist positions only for those of the second type, since in these the center of moral concern is the environment itself (or at least certain aspects of it). It is these positions that are often confused with consideration for animals. Below we will see why consideration for animals and environmentalism start from diametrically opposed foundations.

Environmentalist positions advocate preserving the environment not because animals need it as a resource. On the contrary: in most environmentalist positions it is animals that are seen as mere resources for preserving nonsentient entities such as

species and ecosystems. For this reason, these positions will advocate keeping the environment in a certain configuration, even if what is best for the animals living there would be to keep it in another.

Consideration for animals, by contrast, is grounded in respect for them as sentient individuals, capable of having positive and negative experiences. The aim is to avoid harming them and to seek to benefit them, and the environment is seen as a resource for them. It is a proposal to extend to nonhuman animals what is already accepted for humans: respecting individuals, preventing them from suffering, preventing them from dying. In environmentalist positions, by contrast, what is valued intrinsically are certain nonsentient entities.

Thus, the key concepts for understanding the differences in foundations between consideration for animals and environmentalism are the concepts of intrinsic value and instrumental value. The main divergence is this: what animal advocacy values intrinsically (the good of animals), environmentalism values only instrumentally (in order to preserve species or ecosystems); on the other hand, what environmentalism values intrinsically (certain aspects of the environment), consideration for animals values only instrumentally (as a resource for sentient beings).

1.2. Variants of environmentalism

1.2.1. Regarding which entities have intrinsic value

Environmentalist positions differ from one another in several respects4. One of these concerns which nonsentient entities are valued intrinsically. In this regard, environmentalist positions are usually classified as either holist or biocentrist5.

In holism6, what is valued intrinsically are wholes such as ecosystems or species. It is important not to confuse this with valuing the inhabitants of ecosystems and the members of species. What is valued in holism are ecosystems or species as nonsentient entities. This means that, according to these approaches, as long as the ecosystem or the species does not go extinct (or does not have its properties that environmentalism considers valuable altered), there is no problem at all with killing a large number of animals (since according to these positions individuals have no intrinsic value, but only value as components of ecosystems and/or specimens of species). Biocentrism7, by contrast, values intrinsically each individual living organism (each animal, each fungus, each plant, and so on). In this sense, the main difference is between environmentalist approaches centered on valuing wholes and those centered on valuing each organism.

1.2.2. Regarding what gives them value

The various environmentalist positions also diverge regarding what makes an entity acquire intrinsic value. These characteristics are also usually used to measure the degree of that value. Commonly used criteria include8: degree of rarity; of complexity; of biodiversity; of ecological balance; the time it took to form; the degree to which it exhibits certain aesthetic properties; the degree to which it represents certain ideals; not having originated from human practices; the degree to which it has not been altered by humans; the degree to which it contains only animals and plants of species native to the area; and so on.

These criteria are used by both holist and biocentrist approaches. For example, one commonly used criterion is the degree to which the entity in question has not been altered by humans (the less altered, the more value is assigned). This criterion is used both by some holist approaches9 (to say which ecosystems and/or species have intrinsic value and how great that value is) and by some biocentrist approaches10 (to say which animals, plants, or fungi have intrinsic value and how great that value is).

Despite all these differences, what makes all these positions examples of environmentalism is that they value some kind of nonsentient entity intrinsically.

1.3. Animal ethics and environmental ethics

The difference between consideration for animals and environmentalism is also reflected in the distinction between animal ethics and environmental ethics. As we have seen, the moral consideration of nonhuman animals is grounded in the criterion of sentience. Issues affecting sentient beings are what is discussed in the field of animal ethics. Environmentalist positions, on the other hand, are characterized by valuing certain nonsentient entities intrinsically (such as species, ecosystems, plants, and so on). Issues affecting nonsentient entities are what is discussed in environmental ethics, a field in which environmentalist positions predominate.

1.4. Environmentalist practices that involve exterminating animals

The theoretical divergence between environmentalism and consideration for animals has many practical implications. Below are some examples of conflicting attitudes on the part of environmentalists and animal advocates. This practical conflict arises precisely because these perspectives have opposing theoretical foundations.

First, it is not uncommon for environmentalists to advocate practices that involve causing suffering and/or death to animals. For example, as long as it is done sustainably, the consumption of animals is encouraged by many prominent environmental organizations11, despite all the suffering and death it causes.

Animal experimentation is also frequently promoted by environmental groups12, which results in an enormous number of animals being forced to suffer intensely and to die in experiments meant to test how polluting certain chemicals are in the environment13. There are even environmental organizations that support animal experimentation when the effect of the chemical is already known14, and that oppose the application and development of methods that substitute for the use of animals15.

Many of the leading proponents of environmentalism are advocates of hunting16. They argue that it is a way of connecting with a way of life in its natural state, of controlling populations, and of maintaining ecological balance. Some hold that hunting is something sacred17. Others go so far as to argue that hunting is not only permissible but an obligation18.

In addition, environmentalist population control programs typically involve killing animals, completely ruling out the option of sterilizing them. For example, all around the world there are environmentalist programs to exterminate animals belonging to species classified as invasive19.

These attitudes are often met with surprise. However, they should come as no surprise at all since, as we have seen, environmentalism and respect for animals start from diametrically opposed foundations. It is hardly surprising that, with such divergent foundations, the attitudes prescribed by each position conflict enormously.
