2. The divergence concerns ends, not only means

2.1. Different goals

All around the world there are environmentalist programs to exterminate wild animals in the name of preserving ideals such as biodiversity and ecological balance20. These programs enjoy wide acceptance, including among people who care about animals. One of the reasons this happens is the prevalence of a mistaken idea about what the goals of environmentalism are. According to this idea, environmentalists kill a good number of animals now only because this is the only way to ensure that, from then on, there will not be an even greater amount of suffering and death for animals. According to this view, animal advocacy and environmentalism share the same goal (achieving the best world for animals), but disagree about the means of achieving it.

However, what environmentalism aims at in killing animals is not a better world for animals. The fundamental divergence between these two perspectives concerns ends, not means. In views centered on respect for animals, what is valued intrinsically is the good of sentient individuals, that is, of beings capable of suffering and enjoyment. In these views the environment is valued as a resource for these beings. In the vast majority of environmentalist positions, exactly the opposite occurs: what is valued intrinsically are certain nonsentient entities, such as species (and not their members) and ecosystems (and not their inhabitants). Environmentalism holds that these entities have intrinsic value. This means that environmentalism does not aim to preserve the environment as a resource for animals. On the contrary, in most environmentalist positions it is animals that are seen as mere specimens of species and as mere resources for maintaining ecosystems21.

It is precisely for this reason that, as we saw in chapter 1, environmentalists generally support the consumption of animals, animal experimentation, hunting, and animal exploitation in general. In doing so, they are not being inconsistent with the environmentalist ideal. Quite the contrary: it is the environmentalist ideal itself that does not value the good of animals intrinsically. Environmentalists who advocate killing animals are merely putting this ideal into practice.

2.2. What "considering individuals" and "considering wholes" mean

If it is so evident that consideration for animals and environmentalism have opposing goals, why is the idea that they share the same goal but disagree about the means of achieving it so prevalent? At least part of this confusion is due to a mistaken interpretation of the following statement: "animal advocacy is centered on consideration for individuals, while environmentalism is usually centered on consideration for wholes". We will see more about this below.

This statement is sometimes interpreted as meaning that, if the only way to save many individuals is to kill a minority, then animal advocacy would oppose such an action and environmentalism would approve of it. That is, "consideration for individuals" is interpreted as "prioritizing one individual (or a minority) over many", and "consideration for wholes" is interpreted as "prioritizing the majority".

This is mistaken for two reasons. First, because among the various perspectives centered on consideration for animals as individuals, there is disagreement about the right action in cases where the only way to save a majority is to kill a minority. There are both perspectives holding that in such cases killing the minority is justified and perspectives holding that it is not22. Second, it is mistaken because, as we have seen, environmentalism is not centered on consideration for individuals, whether a minority or a majority. Considering wholes, in environmentalism, does not mean considering the sum of individuals. Below is a more detailed explanation of what it means to consider individuals and to consider wholes in each of these positions.

What it really means to say that consideration for animals is centered on consideration for individuals is that actions will be judged right or wrong depending on how they affect sentient beings (that is, individuals, those capable of having positive and negative experiences). Whether, in cases of dilemmas, a position of this kind will prioritize the majority or the minority is a separate question. There are many variants of sentience-centered positions23.

In turn, what it really means to say that environmentalism is generally centered on consideration for wholes (such as ecosystems and species) is not that it prioritizes a majority of individuals or the sum of individuals, but rather that actions will be judged right or wrong depending on how they affect these nonsentient wholes (which environmentalism values intrinsically, and not as a resource for sentient beings). For example, environmentalism will hold that, as long as an action does not threaten the stability of an ecosystem and/or does not put a species at risk of extinction (or does not in some other way alter certain properties of these ecosystems or species considered valuable), there is nothing wrong with that action, even if its result is, from then on, a worse world for sentient beings (with more suffering, more premature deaths, and so on).

One piece of evidence that this is not consideration for the majority or for the sum of individuals is that, according to these positions, as long as the species does not go extinct, there is no problem at all with killing as many individuals as one wishes. In fact, the smaller the population of a species, the harder environmentalist perspectives will work to preserve it – not because they value the minority of individuals, but because in that case the risk of extinction of the species (which, for its part, is valued intrinsically) is greater. That is, in these positions individuals are valued only as resources for maintaining the existence of species or ecosystems.

All of this shows that the fundamental divergence between consideration for animals and environmentalism concerns what is being aimed at. That is, it is not that they share the same goal and disagree about the means of achieving it: they have completely divergent goals.

Once we are clear on this point, we can move on to the next question: depending on the situation, could one and the same means help achieve both goals? If so, how often would this happen? We will discuss this in the next chapter.

3. Despite their differences, do animal advocacy and environmentalism converge in practice?

One might think that, despite their opposing goals, in practice animal advocacy and environmentalism always go hand in hand. For example, it is sometimes said that, since animals need the environment as a resource, and environmentalism aims to preserve the environment, animal advocates should support environmentalist measures. According to this view, the conflict is only in theory, not in practice. One problem with this view is that it fails to see that it is possible to preserve the environment in very different configurations, and that the configuration environmentalism aims at is not the best one (or even a minimally good one) for animals.

For example, suppose that modifying the natural configuration of a certain ecosystem would reduce the suffering and the number of deaths of animals from then on over time. If our concern is with the good of animals, we will support that modification. The configurations valued by environmentalism, by contrast, vary according to each environmentalist school of thought24, but none of them is centered on concern for the good of animals. For example, configurations commonly valued by environmentalist perspectives are: the one the ecosystem exhibited before the first human intervention; the one that contains only animals and plants of native species; the one that contains the rarest species; the one with the greatest degree of aesthetic properties; the one with the greatest degree of biodiversity; and so on.25 Environmentalists will advocate keeping ecosystems in these configurations even if this increases the suffering and deaths of animals over time.

For example, when evaluating which type of vegetation it is best to have in a given ecosystem, a sentience-based ethics would be guided by a criterion such as "which of them results in the least amount of suffering and premature death for the animals affected over time?". An environmentalist position, by contrast, would be guided by criteria such as "which of them is the native vegetation?", "which is rarer?", or "which increases biodiversity?", and so on, regardless of whether this is better or worse for the animals living there.

It is possible that in several cases the two will coincide. However, this will not be so in many other cases. For this reason, if our goal is the good of animals, we should not be

guided by environmentalist criteria, but rather by criteria that indicate directly how well or badly off the animals will be26. This could be informed by the field of welfare biology. Welfare biology is a proposed field of research that would study animals in their ecosystems from the standpoint of what could affect them positively or negatively as sentient individuals who have a well-being27. We will see more details about welfare biology in chapter 6.

4. The divergence does not lie in a focus on the short or the long term

Consider below two different types of interventions affecting animals in the wild28 and two common but mistaken beliefs about both.

(1) There are environmentalist programs that involve killing large numbers of wild animals in the name of preserving biodiversity and ecological balance29. A common view is that these interventions harm some animals now in order to prevent even greater harm to many animals in the long term.

(2) By contrast, there are proposals for helping wild animals that are focused on concern for the good of the animals themselves, and not on environmentalist goals30. A common view is that these proposals benefit some animals now while neglecting the risk that this will further increase suffering and death in the long term.

According to these two common beliefs, both perspectives share the same goal (benefiting animals), and the difference between them would be that one takes into account the long-term impact of actions and the other does not. We will see why both beliefs are mistaken if we look at which criteria animal advocates and environmentalists would use to evaluate how good or bad the complete history of the world would be31. In this way, we will avoid any confusion that might arise about what each of these perspectives aims at in the short and the long term.

Animal advocates will evaluate how good or bad the complete history of the world is on the basis of how sentient beings are positively or negatively affected. Environmentalist perspectives, by contrast, will evaluate it according to the degree to which ecosystems exhibit characteristics such as complexity, diversity, rarity, and aesthetic properties, how well they represent certain ideals, whether or not they contain only members of native species,

how little they have been transformed by humans, and so on.32 In environmentalism these characteristics are valued intrinsically (and not instrumentally, to secure the good of animals).

This means that environmentalism would say that, if a complete history of the world exhibits ecosystems in those configurations to a greater degree, then it is better, even if it is much worse for animals (for example, even if it contains much more suffering and premature death, fewer positive lives, and so on).

Accordingly, the goal of environmentalist practices of exterminating wild animals is not to prevent more suffering and premature death from occurring from then on. The goal is to ensure that ecosystems exhibit those properties, even if this increases the amount of suffering and death from then on.

On the other hand, in programs to help wild animals that are motivated by concern for the animals themselves, what is aimed at is precisely to ensure that, from then on, the best history of the world for the animals affected comes about. Therefore, the belief that the proposal to help wild animals helps some animals now and neglects the long-term impact of such actions is also mistaken.

In short, programs to help wild animals that are motivated by concern for the good of the animals themselves aim at exactly what common sense mistakenly believes environmentalism aims at: that there be less suffering and premature death from then on. This mistaken belief about what each of these perspectives aims at is one of the factors that lead many people to reject the proposal to help animals and to accept environmentalist measures.

5. Do ecological balance and biodiversity coincide with what is best for animals?

As we saw in chapter 4, many environmentalist programs are carried out in the name of preserving ecological balance and biodiversity. We also saw that several of these programs involve exterminating animals. In this chapter we will address another belief that contributes to animal advocates' acceptance of programs of this kind: the belief that ecological balance and biodiversity coincide with what is best for animals.

This belief is also one of the factors that contribute to environmentalism often being confused with consideration for animals. In short, there are people who believe that ecological balance and biodiversity coincide with what is best for animals; these people notice that one of the goals of environmentalism is to preserve ecological balance and biodiversity; and so these people conclude that environmentalism aims at what is best for animals.

The belief that ecological balance and biodiversity coincide with what is best for animals is mistaken. As explained below, a situation can have a high degree of biodiversity or ecological balance and yet be extremely bad for animals.

The notion of ecological balance concerns a certain stability relative to a state taken as a reference point33. This concept is generally used with respect to variation in

population size, but it could be used with respect to any other factor (for example, the water level of a river). The notion of biodiversity, on the other hand, concerns the variety of species. Neither of these notions is based on what is best for sentient beings (nor does either have any direct relation to it). In other words, there are situations that are balanced and in which there is a high degree of biodiversity that can be terribly bad for animals34. We will see an example of this below.

Animals of most species have enormous numbers of offspring. Depending on the species, there are thousands or even millions of young (something common in amphibians, reptiles, fish, and invertebrates in general). In periods of approximate population stability (and therefore in balanced situations according to the definition above), it is possible to measure the rate of premature mortality from the size of the brood: if a population has remained approximately constant for several generations, then on average only one offspring per adult has survived (that is, two per brood). All the rest of the young (thousands, millions) had a short existence, usually full of suffering35. This is a balanced situation, but in it suffering and premature death are maximized. Situations in which there is biodiversity also usually show this same result.

It could be objected that, if there were less balance or less biodiversity, then suffering and premature death would be even greater. However, there is not necessarily such a correlation. Everything will depend on how a greater or lesser degree of balance or biodiversity affects other factors that directly influence the well-being of sentient beings. For example, it will depend on whether they result in a larger number of births in species most of whose members have lives full of suffering, or in species whose members have a better chance of having positive lives. It will also depend on how they affect factors such as the availability of food and shelter and the amount of disease and conflict among animals. There is no direct correlation between higher levels of ecological balance or biodiversity and the prevalence of positive lives over negative ones, or of long lives over short ones.

In short: ecological balance and biodiversity could only coincidentally result in something better for animals, and they often result in highly negative situations for them. Therefore, if the goal is to achieve the best state of affairs for animals, we should not center our analysis on the degree of biodiversity or balance, but rather investigate directly how animals are positively or negatively affected. This is something that could be done by the field of welfare biology36, which we will look at in more detail in the next chapter.

Author’s notes

  1. Contrary to common belief, the notion of ecological balance is not used technically in ecology. The closest technical term would be stability. However, this term also lacks a precise definition and, for that reason, has also been abandoned among specialists. Grimm and Wissel (1997), reviewing the academic literature in ecology, found 163 distinct definitions (many of them mutually contradictory) of the term stability. Lévêque (2003, p. 224-6) points out that attempts to define it have concluded that it is too complex to be defined precisely (since it is a cluster of many other concepts) and needs to be broken down into smaller concepts, such as resilience (the capacity of an ecosystem to return to its original structure after a disturbance); elasticity (the speed of that return); amplitude (the maximum range of disturbance that still allows a return to the original state); resistance or persistence (the capacity of an ecosystem to remain constant or to show a response to environmental variations); and irreversibility (when an ecosystem cannot return to a previous state through natural processes). These concepts are a modern version of the notion of ecological balance. However, the author's conclusion is that none of these concepts can be defined precisely enough to be truly operational either. One of the reasons for this is that any point in time corresponding to a state in which an ecosystem finds itself can be taken as the reference point, and any period of time can be taken as the frequency for new measurements aimed at determining whether or not the ecosystem is stable. This implies that, depending on the point taken as the reference and on the frequency of measurement, one and the same result may or may not be considered balanced/stable, which is arbitrary. Grimm and Wissel (1997, p. 323-4) concluded that the term stability is the haziest in all of ecology, so ambiguous as to be useless, and that it could be replaced by “remains essentially unchanged,” “returns to the reference state after a disturbance,” and “the persistence over time of an ecological system,” depending on what one wants to express with the term. Moreover, the stability imagined by common sense has never been a reality in nature. On these points, see Grimm;Wissel (1997) and Lévêque (2003, p. 202-44). ↩

6. Animal advocacy and environmentalism: the divergence is ethical, not scientific

Environmentalists need to draw on knowledge from ecology and other related sciences to achieve their goals. Because of this, there is an idea that, in order to use the existing knowledge in these fields and to obtain new knowledge in them, one must adopt an environmentalist stance. According to this view, programs aimed at helping wild animals, if their goal is to secure the good of the animals themselves37 (and not, indirectly, an environmentalist goal), could not be scientifically informed.

This idea is mistaken. Ecology deals with categories such as species and ecosystems, but this does not imply that, in order to obtain knowledge in ecology or to use existing knowledge, it is necessary to incorporate a perspective that values entities such as species or ecosystems intrinsically, rather than sentient individuals. Scientific, descriptive knowledge is one thing; the normative goals that guide the use of that knowledge and the search for new knowledge are another38.

It is not only interventions with environmentalist goals that can be well informed scientifically. To think so is to confuse ecology with environmentalism. Ecology is the science that describes how interactions take place in ecosystems. Environmentalism, on the other hand, is the normative view holding that what has intrinsic value are nonsentient entities such as species and ecosystems, and not sentient beings. Scientific knowledge is descriptive and, as such, can be used by the most varied normative positions to achieve different goals. Environmentalism is only one of these positions.

Knowledge from ecology and related fields is predominantly used to achieve anthropocentric and environmentalist goals. However, it could equally be used in an attempt to achieve the goal of reducing the suffering and deaths of animals. Indeed, much more knowledge in these fields would be sought if animals received moral consideration, since there would then be an interest in finding out how animals are positively or negatively affected by what happens in ecosystems (something that does not happen – or happens to a much lesser extent – if the good of animals is not valued

intrinsically). This is one of the reasons why the creation of the field of welfare biology39 is being proposed. We will see more about this field below.

Welfare biology focuses on investigating how animals in their ecosystems are positively and negatively affected as sentient beings who have a well-being. It is therefore different from conservation biology40, which studies animals as components of ecosystems or specimens of species. It is also different from compassionate conservation41, which studies animals from the standpoint of conservation while avoiding harming them in that pursuit. Finally, it is also different from conservation welfare42, which investigates how to promote the well-being of animals when conservation measures are implemented. Knowledge from these other fields can be useful to welfare biology (and vice versa), but the focus of each of these fields is different. What essentially distinguishes welfare biology from all these other fields is that it studies the way animals are positively or negatively affected as sentient beings who have a well-being, regardless of whether or not this serves conservation purposes.

Welfare biology would bring together knowledge from several other disciplines, such as ecology, animal welfare science, zoology, ethology, and veterinary science. It is a crossdisciplinary field of research, which is something different from interdisciplinary and transdisciplinary fields. This will be explained in more detail below.

With regard to their disciplinarity, types of research are usually classified as43: (1) intradisciplinary (when research is carried out within a single discipline); (2) multidisciplinary (when several disciplines offer different perspectives on a problem); (3) interdisciplinary (when knowledge and methods from several disciplines are integrated and synthesized); (4) transdisciplinary (when a framework is created that goes beyond the various disciplines involved); and (5) crossdisciplinary (when one or more disciplines are viewed from the perspective of another). Welfare biology is crossdisciplinary because each discipline involved would be conducted with a focus on

investigating how animals are positively or negatively affected as sentient beings who have a well-being.

Everything we have seen above clearly indicates that the normative perspective that intrinsically values the good of animals as sentient beings (and, consequently, the goal of preventing and minimizing their suffering and premature deaths) can be as scientifically well informed as any other normative perspective.

7. Why is respect for animals confused with environmentalism?

We saw in the previous chapters that consideration for animals and environmentalism have divergent goals that often conflict in practice. We also saw that, despite this, these perspectives are often confused with each other. In this chapter we will look at a summary of the various factors that contribute to this confusion.

(1) Most people are unaware of the foundations on which environmentalism rests and of what the goals of this position really are. This happens simply because they do not usually read what is proposed by the position they sympathize with. For example, most people are unaware that prominent representatives of various schools of environmentalism, such as holism44, deep ecology45, and social ecology46, frequently take a stand against the moral consideration of nonhuman animals47. They are also unaware that animal exploitation is typically defended by many of the leading environmentalist authors48 and by several of the leading environmental organizations49. In doing so, these environmentalist authors and organizations are not being inconsistent with the principles they uphold. Quite the contrary: they take a stand against consideration for animals because the environmentalist principles they uphold do not value the good of animals intrinsically.

In addition, there are other environmentalist positions that do not necessarily imply disregard for animals or a speciesist stance, but several of whose representatives have defended anthropocentric speciesist stances, as is the case with biocentrism50 and ecofeminism51. However, many people, because they do not read what the proponents of a position actually argue, tend to assume that these are necessarily positions that give full moral consideration to all sentient beings.

(2) Environmentalists tend to frame the question in terms of "preserving or destroying the environment", which hides the fact that it is possible to preserve it in several different configurations. For example, we can aim to preserve the environment in the configuration that most benefits sentient beings (and, as we saw in chapter 3, this will not necessarily coincide with the configurations environmentalism aims at).

Framing things in terms of the false dichotomy "preserve or destroy", besides hiding the fact that it is possible to preserve the environment in the most varied configurations, can mistakenly suggest that, if we do not share environmentalist values, then we do not care about the effects of human practices on the environment. This is simply false. We can reject environmentalist values and care just as much about these issues because we are concerned with the impact on sentient beings.

(3) The mistaken belief that biodiversity and ecological balance necessarily coincide with the best situation for animals. As we saw in chapter 5, these concepts refer, respectively, to the variety of species and to an ecosystem's remaining within a range of variation that still allows it to return to an earlier point taken as a reference52. We also saw that none of these concepts indicates the levels of well-being of animals. In other words, it is possible for a situation to contain a high degree of biodiversity and balance and to have a highly negative balance for animals (and it is also possible for it to be worse for animals than another situation that contains less biodiversity or balance).

However, since environmentalist measures are often carried out in the name of biodiversity and ecological balance, and in common sense many people associate these concepts with a better situation for animals, this is one of the factors that can lead people to confuse environmentalism with consideration for animals.

(4) The confusion between ecology and environmentalism. As we saw in chapter 6, ecology is the science that describes how interactions take place in ecosystems. Environmentalism, on the other hand, is the normative position holding that certain nonsentient entities have intrinsic value. There is

a difference between descriptive knowledge and the normative goals that guide the application of existing knowledge and the search for new knowledge. To seek new knowledge in ecology (and to use existing knowledge), it is not necessary to adopt environmentalism as a normative stance. Such knowledge could be used with the goal of benefiting the animals themselves.

Since it is also possible to use knowledge from ecology to benefit animals, and since environmentalism is confused with ecology, this sometimes also contributes to the confusion between animal advocacy and environmentalism.

(5) Environmentalist interventions sometimes benefit some animals. This can suggest that environmentalism values the good of animals intrinsically. However, in these cases animals are helped by environmentalist programs only because doing so is a means to achieving other goals, such as preserving certain species or keeping the ecosystem in a certain configuration. The proof that the goal of environmentalism is not the good of animals is that, when animals are members of species that are not at risk of extinction, environmentalists usually see nothing wrong with killing them, and when they are members of species classified as invasive, environmentalists carry out extermination programs53.

Of course, there are many people who, in addition to being environmentalists, are also in favor of the moral consideration of nonhuman animals. These people therefore hold a hybrid position, one that combines environmentalist principles with sentience-centered principles. The fact that there are people who, in addition to being environmentalists, also consider animals can help get environmentalists to promote interventions that benefit animals and not to promote those that harm animals. However, this does not mean that environmentalism as such considers animals, for the reasons already seen. What happens in these cases is that these people are combining another idea (consideration for animals) with environmentalism.

(6) Often, when environmentalism carries out programs to exterminate animals, the public mistakenly understands that this is the only way to ensure that, from then on,

there will not be even more suffering and premature death of animals. In short, the public mistakenly understands that both animal advocacy and environmentalism have as their goal the best world for animals, but that they disagree about the means of achieving that result. As we saw in detail in chapter 2, the goal of environmentalism is not the good of animals.

One point that contributes to this confusion is that, as we saw in section 2.2, the statement that "animal advocacy focuses on the individual and environmentalism focuses on the whole" is often mistakenly understood to mean that animal advocates prioritize the good of one individual over a majority, and that environmentalism prioritizes the majority of sentient beings over a minority. According to this interpretation, environmentalist programs kill animals only because this is necessary to save an even greater number of animals. This interpretation is mistaken, since what the statement means is that animal advocacy is centered on consideration for individuals, sentient beings, and that environmentalism values intrinsically nonsentient wholes such as species and ecosystems (and not the members of species or the inhabitants of ecosystems). Environmentalist programs that kill animals do not aim to save sentient beings, whether the majority or the minority. In environmentalism, the center of moral consideration is nonsentient entities.

(7) When environmentalists carry out killings of animals belonging to species classified as invasive54, the public sometimes understands that these are animals that are invading some place (which does not justify the killing, but makes it easier for the public to accept it). However, the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) defines an invasive species as "an alien species that becomes established in a natural or semi-natural ecosystem or habitat, is an agent of change, and threatens native biological diversity"55. That is, the term refers to the origin of the species, and not to the origin of its members. Therefore, an animal of an invasive species may have been born in the place where it lives. This is usually the case, since the introduction of the species into a place outside its natural range was usually done many generations ago. We will discuss this question in more detail in chapter 8.

(8) Environmentalists use terms that contribute to the animals that will be killed being seen as villains (for example, they are usually called pests or threats). In addition, they usually highlight the harms that the animals to be killed cause to other animals of the species that environmentalists value56. This can suggest that the environmentalist goal is to reduce the total rate of suffering and death. However, environmentalist rhetoric does not mention the harms caused by animals of the species environmentalists value, nor the harms suffered by the animals who will be the targets of the killing. If the concern were with the good of animals, harms of equal magnitude would be given equal weight, regardless of whether they are suffered or caused by members of a rare or abundant, native or invasive species, and so on. This is definitely not what happens in environmentalist interventions.

These are some of the main factors underlying the confusion between consideration for animals and environmentalism. This confusion often leads animal advocates to approve of environmentalist practices that are extremely harmful to animals, precisely because they think the goal of such practices is to benefit animals.

8. What do environmentalist extermination programs aim at?

It is not uncommon for environmentalist programs around the world to carry out mass exterminations of animals of species classified as invasive57. These programs are often supported by the public because of the belief that their goal is to ensure that, from then on, something even worse does not happen to animals. We saw in previous chapters that this is not what such programs aim at, since reducing suffering and death is not one of the goals of environmentalism. In this chapter we will investigate what such programs really aim at.

The Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) defines an invasive species as "an alien species that becomes established in a natural or semi-natural ecosystem or habitat, is an agent of change, and threatens native biological diversity"58. Note that this definition is about the origin of the species, and not about the origin of its members. This means that an animal of an invasive species may have been born in the place where it lives (as we will see later, this is usually the case). Below we will look at an example of a case that illustrates what can be considered a threat to native biological diversity according to this definition (since this is one of the key factors for classifying a species as invasive).

The case of the program to exterminate ruddy ducks in southern Europe59 offers a good example to illustrate what environmentalism aims at with programs of this kind. The white-headed duck (Oxyura leucocephala) is a species native to Europe and is considered endangered. The ruddy duck (Oxyura jamaicensis), on the other hand, was introduced into Europe by humans in the 1950s and is not at risk of extinction. The only characteristic that distinguishes the members of these species is the color of the feathers on their heads. In this case, what motivated the killing policies was the fact that, over the years, Oxyura jamaicensis interbred with Oxyura leucocephala, and in the hybrid offspring the head-feather color of the species of American origin prevailed, rather than the color of the native species.

This was considered a threat to biodiversity because hybridization was seen as contributing to the extinction of the native species. However, what was classified as a threat to biodiversity and as a contribution to extinction in this case was simply the fact that the color of the native species did not prevail in the offspring (and not, as might be understood at first glance, deaths of members of the native species). A program was then carried out to kill all the ducks of the species Oxyura jamaicensis and also all the hybrid ducks.

It is therefore very clear that the program was not aimed at reducing the suffering and deaths of animals. In fact, the program greatly increased suffering and the number of deaths. What, then, is the goal environmentalists sought to achieve with this extermination program? In this case, they could not appeal to a concern for ecological balance, since the ecological function of the European, American, or hybrid ducks is exactly the same. Nor does this practice seem to make sense from the standpoint of biodiversity, since with only the European ducks there are fewer species than if the American and hybrid ducks are also present.

This point shows that the goal was to ensure that only the members of the species valued by environmentalism would be present in the area (for example, native species60, or those that exhibit characteristics admired by environmentalists61). The aim of the killing, in this case, was to prevent hybridization and keep the native species "pure". In the environmentalist view, this is a goal so important that it justifies killing an enormous number of sentient beings.

Goals like this would be widely considered heinous if they were applied in the human case. For example, the Nazi extermination programs based on the ideal of racial purity are widely cited as a paradigmatic example of a heinous practice. In fact, the vast majority of environmentalists themselves strongly reject applying their measures to human beings, upholding them only when the victims would be nonhuman animals62. This shows that, in the vast majority of cases, environmentalists combine the environmentalist principle

with an anthropocentric principle, giving greater weight to the latter, so as not to have to accept for humans the implications of the environmentalist principles they uphold.

This strongly suggests that environmentalist practices involving the extermination of animals do not pass the impartiality test, since the people who approve of them do so only because they know they will not be their victims. Since impartiality is one of the central requirements of justice, this shows that there is no way such practices can be just.

9. Is environmentalism anthropocentric?

In the previous chapters we saw the differences between environmentalism and consideration for animals. We also investigated some factors that can lead people to confuse one position with the other. In this chapter we will investigate a related question: is environmentalism anthropocentric?

As we will see below, environmentalism by itself is not anthropocentric. What happens is that most proponents of environmentalism combine it with anthropocentrism and give greater weight to the latter. This does not mean, however, that if environmentalist principles are not combined with anthropocentrism, the result for animals will be positive. Quite the contrary. All of this will be explained in detail below.

Environmentalist positions tend to present themselves as the opposite of anthropocentrism. However, proponents of environmentalism who approve of slaughtering nonhuman animals to achieve their goals typically condemn doing the same to humans63. This disparity is curious, to say the least, since the human species is the greatest of all threats to environmentalist goals: it is overpopulated, it would have to be classified as an invasive species in most of the places where it is found, and it is an enormous threat to ecological balance, to the preservation of ecosystems, to biodiversity, and so on.

This indicates that those who maintain this disparity are subordinating their environmentalist position to anthropocentric speciesism. That is, these people, even though they accept environmentalist goals, believe that the good of humans is more important than these goals, unlike the good of nonhuman animals. This is a blatantly anthropocentric speciesist attitude, since it places the good of humans above environmentalist goals and the good of nonhuman animals below them. Nevertheless, it is the predominant position among proponents of environmentalism64.

A rare few environmentalists argue that environmentalist extermination programs should also be applied to humans. For example, Pentti Linkola, in addition to defending

the consumption of nonhuman animals, also advocated breeding humans for consumption65 and praised the Holocaust perpetrated by the Nazis for contributing to the maintenance of ecological balance66. Linkola was one of the few environmentalists who applied the principles of environmentalism without subordinating them to anthropocentric principles.

Linkola's view, however, is widely considered repugnant by the vast majority of people, including the vast majority of environmentalists. Yet the problem with Linkola's position is easy to see because it harms not only nonhuman animals but also humans. Since the victims of other environmentalists' positions are only nonhuman animals, the predominance of anthropocentric speciesism keeps most people from seeing that there is exactly the same problem with environmentalism in general: placing nonsentient entities above the good of sentient beings.

The point is this: the central reason for rejecting a position like Linkola's also implies rejecting environmentalist practices of killing nonhuman animals. The reason is this: sentient beings, human and nonhuman, are harmed if they suffer and also by death, since death prevents them from having positive experiences. No nonsentient entity is capable of suffering or of being prevented from enjoying positive experiences. These harms are particularly serious (which is why we try so hard to avoid them in our own case). This reason explains why the good of humans should be placed above environmentalist goals, but it implies at the same time that there are exactly the same reasons to place the good of nonhuman animals above environmentalist goals.

This means that there are good reasons to reject not only positions like Linkola's (which are purely environmentalist and advocate exterminating both nonhuman animals and humans to achieve environmentalist goals) but also the positions of the vast majority of other environmentalists (who subordinate their environmentalist position to anthropocentric principles and advocate exterminating only nonhuman animals to achieve environmentalist goals). The central reason, as we have seen, is that there are reasons to prioritize sentient beings over nonsentient entities.

10. Questioning environmentalist assumptions

Many people take it as obvious that environmentalist programs to exterminate animals are justified. As we saw in previous chapters, in the case of many of these people this is due to the mistaken belief that such programs aim to reduce the suffering and deaths of animals from then on. However, there are also people who know that the goal of such programs is not to benefit animals and who nevertheless take it as obvious that such programs are justified. In this chapter we will discuss the theses implicitly assumed by this second group of people.

10.1. Do nonsentient entities have intrinsic value?

The first is the thesis that nonsentient entities have intrinsic value (that is, that they have value entirely independently of how they affect sentient beings). This by itself is already highly controversial. First, because we can explain what these entities are (ecosystems, species, biodiversity, ecological balance, and so on) without necessarily having to say that they are something good in themselves. This shows that being good in itself is not a necessary characteristic of these things. Compare this, for example, with describing suffering and happiness. In that case it is impossible to explain what these things are without citing, as their central characteristics, their being, respectively, negative and positive in themselves.

Second, the alleged value of those nonsentient entities is not something we can verify by direct experience. Let us compare this again with the claim that suffering is bad in itself and that happiness is good in itself. Imagine that there were beings from other planets capable of experiencing suffering and happiness but who had never yet experienced them (until then all their experiences had been neutral). Suppose that these beings are therefore unsure which is negative and which is positive, suffering or happiness. In that case, to find out the answer, all they need to do is to become acquainted with (that is, to experience) each of them67. By contrast, there is nothing equivalent with regard to nonsentient entities. Species, ecosystems, biodiversity, ecological balance: none of these has the property of being experienced as positive in itself once someone becomes acquainted with it.

What we have seen above does not show that the entities valued in environmentalism necessarily lack intrinsic value. It does show, however, that the burden of proof lies with those who claim that they have such value.

10.2. Do nonsentient entities have more value than sentient beings?

Those who approve of environmentalist programs to exterminate animals implicitly assume not only that the nonsentient entities these programs aim to protect have intrinsic value. They must also implicitly assume one of the following theses:

(A) Either that these entities are the only thing that has intrinsic value (that is, that the good of sentient beings does not matter in itself);

(B) Or that, even if the good of sentient beings matters in itself, the value of these nonsentient entities is so much greater that it justifies causing suffering and death to a gigantic number of sentient beings.

As we have seen, if the thesis that nonsentient entities have intrinsic value is already quite difficult to prove, these additional theses are even more so. In fact, in the case of these additional theses, there are strong reasons for us to reject both. Let us see:

The main reason for rejecting thesis A is that, if the beings who can literally be harmed and benefited do not matter in themselves, it is hard to explain why any other kind of entity would matter in itself. As for thesis B, there are reasons to think exactly the opposite of what it claims. That is, we have reasons to prioritize sentient beings over nonsentient entities. The main reason is that only sentient beings are someone, and only sentient beings are capable of experiencing suffering and of having death prevent them from continuing to have experiences. These are particularly serious harms (we need only remember how hard we ourselves try to avoid our own suffering and death) that no nonsentient entity can undergo. Thus, even if it had been proven that nonsentient entities have intrinsic value, there would still be reasons to prioritize sentient beings, at least on occasions when sentient beings would be at risk of suffering and/or dying.

It is for this reason that, in order to know that environmentalist practices involving the extermination of animals are unjustifiable, it is completely unnecessary to enter into the debate about whether the entities valued in environmentalism have intrinsic value. This is because, as we have seen, even if it had been shown that they really do have this value, there would still be reasons for us to prioritize protecting sentient beings from suffering and death.

10.3. What if nonsentient entities do have intrinsic value?

If it had been proven that the entities valued in environmentalism have intrinsic value, some interests of sentient beings would have to be limited in order to preserve those entities. However, as we have seen, this would not justify violating the basic interests of sentient beings, such as not suffering and not dying. This is already accepted by most environmentalists with regard to humans. They hold that certain human interests (such as recreational, aesthetic, and economic interests) should be limited in order to achieve environmentalist goals, but not that causing suffering and death to humans is justified. Thus, in the same way, if it had been shown that the nonsentient entities valued in environmentalism really do have intrinsic value, this would justify limiting only nonbasic interests of nonhuman animals in order to preserve those entities.

Moreover, it is important to note that nothing said above shows that we should therefore embrace this hybrid position that values both sentient beings and certain nonsentient entities, giving priority to the basic interests of sentient beings. What was said above is that this is the position that would follow if it had been proven that the nonsentient entities valued in environmentalism really do have intrinsic value. But until such proof emerges, we have reasons to adopt an ethics based exclusively on consideration for sentient beings.

10.4. Questioning environmentalist criteria for assigning value

It is also possible to question at least some of the criteria that environmentalism uses to determine whether or not an entity has intrinsic value, and to what degree. Below we will look at three examples.

One of the goals of environmentalism is to keep, in each place, animals of native species with the characteristics they exhibited before the first human intervention. We saw in chapter 8 that the reason a program to exterminate ruddy ducks was carried out in Europe is that the American ducks were interbreeding with the native ducks and the head-feather color of the non-native species was prevailing in the offspring. But then we could question several things: "why would it be valuable to keep native species the way they were before the first human intervention?"; "why would native species have more value than non-native species?"; "why would hybridization make a species lose value?"; "why not simply let the mixing happen?", and so on.

It could also be pointed out that environmentalism (at least in many of its forms) suffers from an anti-human bias, since what is usually aimed at is to have a species or ecosystem remain in (or return to) the state it was in before the first human intervention. It is curious, to say the least, that environmentalists hold that humans are part of nature, yet at the same time hold that human intervention in ecosystems makes them cease to be natural (or makes them less natural).

One could also ask: "if certain nonsentient entities have intrinsic value, would a world with no sentient beings at all, but containing these entities, really have value?".

In short, there are many ways of questioning the criteria environmentalism uses for assigning value. In fact, most people simply accept environmentalist criteria because they are usually presented as obvious, in no need of justification. But once we think clearly about these criteria, we see that they are highly controversial, to say the least. The tendency most people have not to reflect on whether the foundations of the views they adopt really make sense is one of the factors that explains the widespread adherence to environmentalism. Another factor, as we have seen, is the lack of clarity about what environmentalism really aims at.

10.5. Conclusion

Many people take it as obvious that environmentalist programs are justified, even when they involve exterminating sentient beings. As we have seen, for some people this is because they mistakenly believe that the goal of such programs is to prevent something even worse from happening to sentient beings. However, other people are clear that this is not the goal of such programs, but they nevertheless take it as obvious that such programs are justified.

But then these people are assuming that it is obvious not only that the nonsentient entities valued in environmentalism have intrinsic value, but also that this value is so much greater than the value of the good of sentient beings that it justifies causing them suffering and death. We saw that the first thesis is already highly controversial and that, in fact, there are many ways of questioning the criteria for assigning value adopted by environmentalism. Moreover, we saw that even if it had been shown that the nonsentient entities valued in environmentalism really do have this value, we would still have strong reasons to prioritize protecting sentient beings from suffering and death.

All of this leads us to conclude clearly that environmentalist practices that cause suffering and/or death to sentient beings are completely unjustifiable. In addition, what we have seen also gives us reasons, until proven otherwise, to adopt an ethics centered solely on sentience.

11. Why are animal advocates reluctant to acknowledge the divergence?

In the previous chapters we saw that many people who care about animals accept environmentalist programs because they mistakenly think the goal of environmentalism is to benefit animals. That is, environmentalism is often confused with animal advocacy. In chapter 7 we investigated several possible explanations for why this confusion exists and is so prevalent. In this chapter we will investigate something related, but different. We will investigate some possible reasons why, even after understanding the (theoretical and practical) opposition between consideration for animals and environmentalism, many animal advocates are reluctant to acknowledge this divergence and continue to act as if it did not exist.

11.1. The fear of going against environmentalism

One of the main factors behind animal advocates' reluctance to acknowledge the divergence is the belief that, if someone criticizes environmentalism, then that person is arguing that we should not care about the effects of human practices on the environment, and that it is therefore fine to pollute, deplete natural resources, increase environmental degradation, set fires, and so on. This is one of the main reasons why any criticism of environmentalism tends to be viewed with suspicion at first.

As we saw in chapter 1, this is a confusion that exists because the word environmentalism is used in several different senses. Sometimes it is used to refer to the view that advocates concern for the environment as a resource for sentient beings. At other times it is used to refer to the view holding that certain nonsentient entities have intrinsic value (and not as a resource for sentient beings). As made explicit in chapter 1, it is in this second sense that we have used the term in this work, since it is this view that is confused with consideration for animals. Rejecting environmentalism in this second sense does not imply saying that we should not care about issues affecting the environment. We can care just as much, but because we are concerned with the way sentient beings will be affected.

However, most people do not see this point, and so the fear that rejecting environmentalism implies not caring about the way our actions affect the environment is one of the factors underlying animal advocates' reluctance to acknowledge the divergence between environmentalism and consideration for animals.

Moreover, this terminological confusion is sometimes exploited deliberately. For example, suppose that someone dishonest wants to distort sentience-centered ethics and falsely claims that, because it rejects environmentalism, it implies not caring about the way we affect the environment. As we have seen, this claim is false. However, when a false statement is repeated countless times, the number of people who may come to believe it can be surprisingly large.

There is a bias related to this phenomenon, the availability cascade, which occurs when an idea gains more and more acceptance the more it is repeated in public discourse, even if it is implausible. This happens mainly because most people do not check whether the information they receive is true and also because of the bandwagon effect (the habit of adopting certain behaviors or beliefs just because many other people do the same). Another related effect is the illusory truth effect: when we hear a piece of false information repeated many times, we commonly come to believe that it is true even if we know it is not.

These biases seem to explain much not only of the fear of going against environmentalism, but also of the mass adherence to environmentalism itself

11.2. The difficulty of revising beliefs and practices

Most animal advocates have believed for years that environmentalism and animal advocacy go hand in hand. This association goes beyond beliefs: it also involves practices. Many of these activists have supported environmentalist programs, actively participated in environmental campaigns, donated to environmental organizations, and so on. There are several biases that incline us to be reluctant to abandon the beliefs and practices we hold. This reluctance is greater the longer we have held these beliefs and practices. Thus, this may be another of the factors that explain animal advocates' reluctance to acknowledge the divergences between animal advocacy and environmentalism.

There are a great many biases that can incline us in this direction. These biases can make someone insist that environmentalism and animal advocacy do not conflict, even when presented with all the evidence that they do. Examples of biases of this sort are belief perseverance (the tendency to cling to the beliefs we already hold in the face of contrary evidence) and anchoring bias (the tendency to rely heavily on the first piece of information we receive about a subject).

Moreover, discovering that environmentalism and animal advocacy diverge can produce cognitive dissonance, that is, a discomfort that arises from holding beliefs that conflict with one another. One way of dealing with this dissonance is to assess which of the beliefs we should reject and then act accordingly. However, the conflict is usually "resolved" by discrediting or avoiding the information that would reveal the inconsistency.

There are also biases that can make someone act as if there were no divergence even after acknowledging that there is one (simply because they acted for a long time believing there was none). One example is the continued influence effect, which occurs when a mistaken belief continues to influence memory and reasoning even though it has already been corrected and we agree with the correction.

Moreover, certain biases can incline people to think that whoever points out the divergence is ill-intentioned, not because there is any evidence of this, but simply because that person is asking them to revise their beliefs and attitudes. One example is the hostile attribution bias, which inclines us to see an interlocutor who questions our beliefs not as someone who wants to inform us of something, but as someone who has a hidden malicious intent

Finally, there are certain biases that influence resistance to change depending on how much someone has already invested in practice in what would have to be changed. One example is commitment bias (the tendency to remain committed to our past behaviors, especially when they were displayed publicly).

11.3. Conclusion

We have seen that there are at least two factors underlying animal advocates' reluctance to acknowledge the divergences between animal advocacy and environmentalism. One of them is the mistaken belief that, if we reject environmentalism, we will not care about the impact of our practices on the environment. The other is the set of biases that produce a tendency to be reluctant to revise beliefs, attitudes, and practices, especially if they have been held for a long time.

Animal advocates, when they advocate the abolition of animal exploitation, rightly point out that we all need to overcome these biases and do what is just. However, what we have seen above shows that animal advocates, like anyone else, are not immune to being strongly influenced by the same biases when it comes to revising other beliefs, attitudes, and practices. Therefore, if our goal is really to benefit animals, we must also strive to abandon the idea that animal advocacy and environmentalism do not conflict, since the practical consequences of this idea have led many people, including animal advocates, to approve of practices that seriously harm an enormous number of animals.

Volume VI

To Whom Do We Owe Moral Consideration?

This book presents the grounds for choosing sentience as the criterion for moral consideration, as well as the criticisms that have been made of this criterion and the responses that have been offered to these criticisms.

Original text by Luciano Carlos Cunha, translated into English · ISBN 978-65-01-44289-1 · 1st edition, April 2025.

1. What is relevant for knowing to whom we owe consideration?

1.1. A double standard

Nonhuman animals are exploited and killed by humans every day for the most diverse purposes. They are used for food, clothing, as test models, for entertainment, leisure, and as workers or tools. These practices cause suffering and death to a gigantic number of nonhuman animals and are widely accepted. However, if the victims were human, such practices would be considered monstrous.

In addition to being victims of human practices, animals are also severely harmed by natural processes such as malnutrition, hunger, and thirst, disease, physical injuries, psychological stress, harsh weather events, natural disasters, and interspecific, intraspecific, and sexual conflicts. This is the typical situation of most animals living in the wild. The standard view is that we should not help them: instead, we should let nature take its course. But, again, if the victims were human, the standard view would be the opposite (that is, that resources should be devoted to helping them).

These attitudes reveal that a large share of people apply a double standard, depending on the species of those affected by their decisions. If they are nonhuman animals, they receive no help and are tortured and killed. If they are human, they receive full moral consideration. It is, therefore, an anthropocentric speciesist standard of morality. Speciesist because harms and benefits of similar magnitude are given different importance depending on the species of those affected. Anthropocentric because it disfavors those who do not belong to the human species.

1.2. Attempts to justify anthropocentric speciesism

There are several attempts to justify this moral double standard1. Among the reasons most often given in an attempt to justify that either only the good of humans matters, or that it matters to a greater degree, are:

(1) The very fact that they belong to the human species.

(2) The fact that they belong to the same species we belong to.

(3) Metaphysical claims, such as that humans were created in the image and likeness of a creator; have a special relationship with that creator; have an immortal soul; have dignity; belong to a higher ontological category; and so on.

(4) The claim that humans have (or have the potential for) capacities such as reason, language, freedom, moral agency, a sense of justice, autonomy, culture, the capacity to make mutual agreements, to respect rights, to claim rights, and so on.

(5) The claim that humans have (or have the potential to have) various kinds of relationships, such as affective relationships, relationships of mutual solidarity, and political and power relationships.

(6) The fact that all humans belong to the same species as those who have those capacities or relationships (even though not all humans actually have them).

(7) The claim that the idea of species is not a mere social construct (it is based on biological characteristics).

(8) The claim that disregarding nonhuman animals is a natural attitude.

(9) The fact that animal exploitation is traditional and part of the culture of many peoples.

With regard to all these attempts, it makes sense to ask what relevance these things have for knowing whom we should consider morally. This applies to all those attempts to justify anthropocentrism, whether they are based on the criterion of membership in a certain species, on the possession of certain metaphysical characteristics, or on the possession of certain capacities or relationships, and also to those based on the fact that a distinction rests on a biological characteristic or on the fact that a behavior is natural or traditional.

Thus, this is a first problem with these attempts: they would have to explain why the criteria they use would be relevant to questions of moral consideration, rather than simply assuming them as though they were obvious. Moreover, there is an even more serious problem: there are reasons to think that none of these criteria is relevant for knowing to whom to give moral consideration. This is pointed out by the argument from relevance, presented below.

1.3. The argument from relevance

The argument from relevance2 starts from the trivial premise that, for a criterion to be justified, it must be based on a distinction relevant to the question it seeks to answer. For example, what is relevant for evaluating a candidate for a medical team at a hospital is their medical skills, whether they are punctual, whether they treat patients well, and so on. For evaluating who should be seen in a hospital emergency room, on the other hand, what matters is knowing who is injured, who is seriously ill, who is at risk of dying, and so on.

Swapping the criteria would mean applying criteria that are relevant in one context to another in which they are not. For example, this would happen if it were required that, to be accepted to work on a medical team, someone would have to be ill, and that, to be seen by a doctor, someone would also have to be a doctor. Of course, the absurd attitude described in this example would hardly occur in real life. However, the argument from relevance points out that the anthropocentric standard of morality commits a very similar confusion. This will be explained in more detail below.

The argument from relevance holds that none of the defenses of anthropocentrism adopts relevant criteria for determining who should receive moral consideration. This would be so because what is at stake in questions of moral consideration is knowing how our acts and omissions could positively or negatively affect whoever is affected by them. To give moral consideration to someone is to act so as to avoid harming them and to seek to benefit them. If so, then the appropriate criterion for knowing to whom to give moral consideration is knowing who can be harmed and benefited.

The species to which someone belongs; whether or not they were created in the image and likeness of a deity; whether or not they have an immortal soul; whether or not they have certain capacities and certain relationships; whether or not they have the potential for such capacities or relationships; knowing whether or not a behavior is

natural or traditional, and so on: none of this determines who can be harmed or benefited. Therefore, these cannot be relevant characteristics for knowing to whom to give moral consideration.

On the other hand, being capable of having positive and negative experiences (that is, being capable of enjoyment and of suffering) determines whether someone can be harmed and benefited. It is for this reason that proponents of the argument from relevance hold that sentience is the appropriate criterion for moral consideration. In the following sections we will see what sentience is and how it is connected to the capacity to be harmed and benefited.

1.4. What is relevant for considering and what is relevant for holding responsible

Traditionally, criteria that are relevant for determining whom it would make sense to hold responsible have been applied to determine who should receive moral consideration. For example, it is commonly argued that, for us to have obligations toward someone, that someone must also be capable of recognizing obligations3; that, for someone to be protected by the principles of justice, they must have a sense of justice4; that, to have rights, one must be capable of understanding the notion of rights5; and so on. These claims have been widely used in an attempt to justify all the suffering and death caused to nonhuman animals. However, possessing these capacities may be relevant for knowing whom to hold responsible, but not for knowing whom to consider morally. This is already recognized in the case of babies, children, humans with cognitive disabilities, and so on. It is widely recognized that these humans are morally considerable even though they are not morally accountable. However, recognizing this implies recognizing that every sentient being, regardless of the species to which it belongs and of the capacities it has, should receive moral consideration.

The disregard that nonhuman animals typically receive occurs, at least in part, because of the belief that, for us to owe moral consideration to someone, that someone must also be capable of acting morally. However, as

the argument from relevance points out, this is a confusion analogous to thinking that, for someone to be seen by a doctor, that someone must also be a doctor.

1.5. The criterion of sentience

If what is relevant for knowing to whom to give moral consideration is knowing who can be harmed and benefited, then it is important to investigate what makes someone capable of being harmed and benefited. This is where the importance of sentience for ethics lies6.

The term "sentience" is used in the animal ethics debate as a synonym for consciousness in its broadest and most basic sense. It refers to each and every experience someone could have, starting with the simplest. It is what makes there be someone, an individual inhabiting a body, and not merely a living but "empty" body. It is what separates, on one side, a human, a dog, a fish, a crustacean, and a bee7 and, on the other, a shoe, a plant, a bacterium, and a fungus. Thus, sentience determines who can be harmed or benefited because it is sentience, in the first place, that determines when there is someone in a body, and not merely something.

In addition, another characteristic of sentience, one directly connected to the capacity for harm and benefit, is that experiences have what is called valence8 - that is, they can be experienced as positive or negative. For example, if I step on a nail, I have a negative experience; if I listen to a piece of music I really like, I have a positive experience.

For this reason, there are two basic ways in which a sentient being is harmed: by the presence of what is negative for them (as happens when they suffer, for example) and by the absence of what is positive for them (as happens when they die or are in some other way prevented from enjoying something that would benefit them).

Similarly, there are two basic ways in which a sentient being is benefited: by the presence of what is positive for them (as happens when they feel pleasure, for example) and by the prevention of what is negative for them (as happens when suffering is relieved, for example).

It is for this reason that nonhuman animals need moral consideration. It is not because they belong to the animal kingdom, or because they are alive in a biological sense (as plants are, for example). It is simply because, being sentient, they can be harmed and benefited.

However, the criterion of sentience, like any other criterion, is also criticized. In the remaining chapters we will examine these criticisms as well as several other recurring questions related to sentience-centered ethics.
