2. Is the criterion of sentience anthropocentric at bottom?

Proponents of anthropocentrism choose a typically human characteristic (for example, a certain way of reasoning) and assign moral standing to nonhuman animals according to their degree of similarity to humans in that characteristic. Defenders of the criterion of sentience are sometimes accused of doing the same9: they notice that sentience is a characteristic of humans, and choose to consider only beings that are sentient (excluding plants, fungi, and bacteria, for example). The objection concludes that, in both cases, only those who have similarities to humans receive consideration (all that changes, in each case, is the characteristic chosen as the standard of similarity).

The main response to this criticism points to two things.

First, there is a difference between using a way of reasoning and using sentience as the criterion for moral consideration: as we saw in chapter 1, the former does not determine who can be harmed and/or benefited, and the latter does.

Second, it is not that proponents of the criterion of sentience first postulate that humans matter and then look, among the animals they also intend to consider, for some similarity to humans. They are not arguing: “we should consider sentient beings because they resemble humans,” but exactly the opposite: “we should consider humans because they are sentient.” The criterion of sentience would continue to indicate which beings can be harmed and benefited (and, therefore, which should receive moral consideration) even if humans were not sentient. Thus, it is false that the criterion of sentience is, at bottom, anthropocentric.

Author’s notes

  1. For an example of this accusation, see Regan (1981, p. 20, 21). ↩

3. Does the criterion of sentience discriminate against those who do not belong to the animal kingdom?

The criterion of sentience prescribes that we give moral consideration to all beings that have the capacity to have experiences, such as suffering and pleasure. The criterion of sentience is sometimes accused of committing a kingdom-based discrimination, by including members of the animal kingdom in the sphere of moral consideration and excluding members of other kingdoms, such as plants and fungi.

However, proponents of the criterion of sentience do not claim that we should consider sentient beings because sentience is a characteristic of the animal kingdom. Instead, they hold that we should consider a large share of animals because they are sentient and, therefore, can be harmed and benefited.

Although every sentient being found to date belongs to the animal kingdom, there are members of the animal kingdom that, because they have no nervous system, or not even a minimally organized one, are very probably not sentient10 (such as sponges and jellyfish, for example). Proponents of the criterion of sentience do not advocate considering these animals since, according to the criterion of sentience, there is no possibility of their being harmed and/or benefited (whatever we do will make no difference to them, since there is no one there for whom things could go better or worse; there is only a living body).

If it were someday discovered that, for example, a certain plant or fungus is sentient, then the criterion of sentience would include it in the sphere of moral consideration, giving it equal consideration. However, to date there is no evidence of anything like this. In the future, if sentient robots, sentient machines, sentient beings in digital media, or any other form of nonorganic sentience come to exist, the criterion of sentience would include them in the sphere of moral consideration, giving them equal consideration (since they could be harmed and/or benefited)11.

Therefore, the accusation of “kingdomism” does not hold up. The criterion of sentience is different from the criterion "belonging to the animal kingdom".

Author’s notes

  1. On this, see Ética Animal (2015e). ↩
  2. On why we should take the possibility of nonorganic sentience seriously, see Tomasik (2015b). ↩

4. According to the criterion of sentience, is suffering the only problem?

Sentience is the capacity to have experiences. It is what distinguishes individuals from things: sentient beings are someone; nonsentient things are something. That is, sentient beings are not mere living bodies: they are individuals who can be positively or negatively affected. In the case of sentient beings, there is someone "inhabiting" those bodies.

To give moral consideration to someone is to avoid harming them and to seek to benefit them. The criterion of sentience holds that we should give moral consideration to all beings capable of having experiences (that is, to all sentient beings).

It is sometimes said that, if the criterion of sentience were correct, then all moral questions would be solved by the use of analgesia and anesthesia. Given that there are ways for someone to be harmed without suffering (for example, by death12, even without suffering; or by winning a prize and not being told about it), it is sometimes claimed that there must be something wrong with the criterion of sentience. This objection then concludes that, in order to oppose painless killing and other harms that do not cause suffering, we must reject the criterion of sentience and postulate that biological life has value in itself.

The mistake in this argument is to presuppose that considering sentient beings implies only a concern with avoiding their suffering, which is false. As we saw in chapter 1, a sentient being is harmed by the presence of what is harmful to them and also by the absence of what is beneficial to them. The two examples the objection offers (the harm of death and the harm of someone not being told they have won a prize) are recognized by the criterion of sentience. Indeed, the most obvious way of explaining the harm in these cases is in terms of sentience: they are harms consisting in the absence of (all or some) positive experiences.

To explain the harm of death and the harm someone suffers by not being told they have won a prize, it is necessary to imagine what the individual would experience in each situation (staying alive versus dying, and being told about the prize versus not being told) and to evaluate in which of them they would be better off. Thus the objection, without realizing it, assumes the criterion of sentience.

Therefore, it is false that the criterion of sentience would not recognize the existence of harms that do not involve suffering. Thinking that it would not is perhaps one of the most common misconceptions about the criterion of sentience, and one of the reasons why some people have rejected it. Avoiding suffering is an extremely important part of consideration for sentient beings, but it is not the only concern.

Author’s notes

  1. For an analysis of the harm of death for nonhuman animals, see the third volume of this collection. See also Horta (2007, p. 537-778; 2010c) and Cunha (2022a, p. 61-92) ↩

5. If sentience is what matters, why are there harms that do not affect experiences?

As we have seen, to give moral consideration to someone is to avoid harming them and to seek to benefit them. The criterion of sentience holds that we should give moral consideration to all (and only) beings capable of having experiences. At the basis of the criterion of sentience is the idea that, for there to be harm and benefit, there must be someone who would be harmed or benefited, and what makes a being someone (and not merely something) is the capacity to have experiences. A shoe and a chair are something, because they are not sentient. I, you, a fish, a pig, and a shrimp, for example, are someone, because we are capable of having experiences, which is what gives us a first-person perspective (that is, we are not mere empty bodies: in our case there is someone inhabiting them).

An objection sometimes raised against the criterion of sentience involves pointing out that there are ways of harming someone that do not affect their experiences. Suppose, for example, that someone is raped while unconscious and, on waking up, will never know about the abuse they suffered. Suppose also that this abuse will not cause any later negative experience, nor reduce the amount of positive experiences the victim would have from then on. That is, in this case the abuse did not alter the amount of negative and positive experiences the victim would have. Cases of this kind are sometimes mentioned as an objection to the criterion of sentience.

These cases pose an objection to the view that all forms of harm affect experiences in some way. But are they also an objection to the criterion of sentience? One might think that accepting the criterion of sentience implies having to accept that all forms of harm affect experiences (by producing negative experiences and/or preventing positive experiences). However, although the two are compatible, accepting the former does not necessarily imply accepting the latter. The criterion of sentience says only which beings we should consider: it does not say in what ways these beings can be harmed and benefited. In the example of someone who is raped while unconscious, this is still a harm to a sentient being (if it were, for example, an inanimate object, there would be no harm at all).

Such a harm could be explained, for example, as a failure to respect the preferences of the being in question (their actual preferences or the preferences they would have if they had the relevant information13). A preference is also something that depends on sentience in order to exist.

To better understand this point, it is important to draw the following distinction. One thing is the debate about what the criterion for moral consideration should be, that is, the criterion that says which kinds of entities we should consider morally. The criterion of sentience is a criterion of this kind. Another thing is the debate about the ways in which sentient beings can be harmed and benefited. This second debate takes place among theories of well-being14.

In other words, those who accept the criterion of sentience can recognize that sentient beings are harmed by negative experiences and by being prevented from having positive experiences. However, they need not claim that these are the only ways in which sentient beings can be harmed (although that view is also compatible with it).

In short, pointing to the possibility of harms that would not alter the amount of positive and negative experiences may be an objection to the hedonistic theory of well-being (since this theory claims that, for a sentient being to be benefited/harmed, there must be some change in the amount of positive/negative experiences they would have). However, as we have seen, this does not constitute an objection to the criterion of sentience, since, being a criterion for moral consideration, it need not commit itself to any specific theory of well-being. These are two different debates.

  2. For a brief introduction to the schools of theories of well-being, see Kagan (1998, p. 29-41) and Santos (2017). For a detailed introduction, see Fletcher (2016). ↩

6. Does the criterion of sentience exclude insects?

It is sometimes claimed that the criterion of sentience excludes insects from the sphere of moral consideration15. According to this position, if we should give moral consideration to insects, then we should reject the criterion of sentience and adopt the criterion of biological life in its place.

Someone might put forward this argument because they think that insects are capable of positive experiences (which would come from smelling, hearing, tasting, and so on), but not capable of feeling pain. In that case, however, what is being claimed is that insects are sentient (since they are capable of positive experiences), but not capable of negative experiences. If that were the case, these animals would not be excluded by the criterion of sentience. Sentience concerns each and every experience someone could have, and not only negative ones. Thus, the criterion of sentience also takes into account harms from the deprivation of positive experiences, and not only from the presence of negative experiences.

Although there is doubt in the scientific community about the sentience of some kinds of insects16, any responsible moral theory prescribes giving the benefit of the doubt where there is reasonable doubt. This is because, if these insects are not sentient and we treat them as if they were, the harm to us is smaller than the harm to them would be if they are sentient and we treat them as if they were not. Therefore, we should treat insects as sentient beings until proven otherwise. In short, it is not insects that need to prove that they are sentient. The burden of proof lies with those who doubt that they are.

Moreover, even if only a small percentage of insects were sentient, the number of insects the criterion of sentience would prescribe considering would already be gigantic. According to some estimates, there are around 10 quintillion insects alive at any given moment17. Even if only 0.01% of these insects are sentient, that would still be 100 quadrillion individuals. Furthermore, as we will see below, there are strong reasons to think that the percentage of insects that are sentient is not low.

The objection in question can also be criticized for assuming that insects should be considered even if they were not sentient. This does not explain what is wrong with the criterion of sentience (instead, it assumes from the outset that the criterion is wrong; but that is exactly what the argument was supposed to show). Suppose no insect were sentient. Why would we consider them, if there were no one in those bodies, and whatever happened would make no difference to them? The intuition that insects are worthy of moral consideration seems to come, on the contrary, from the possibility that these animals are sentient. And there is good evidence that at least a large number of them are in fact sentient18. Below we will look at some of this evidence.

Evidence of sentience in insects

The evidence listed below was obtained from studies of insects of certain species. As for insects of other species, however, it is not that they were studied and failed to meet the criteria for sentience: what happens is that they have barely been studied with regard to sentience. Thus, in keeping with the precautionary principle, what we should do is treat all insects as sentient until proven otherwise. This is already standard practice with regard to the sentience of other kinds of animals. For example, the sentience of vertebrates and of invertebrates such as cephalopod mollusks and decapod crustaceans is generalized from studies carried out on animals of certain species to animals of other, related species19.

There is a growing body of evidence on sentience in insects20. One type of evidence is behavioral. The behavior of these animals is flexible, showing decision-making in contexts of changing circumstances, adaptive behavior, and cognitive generalization. Their behavior also shows learning, integrating different types of information21.

There is good physiological evidence as well. Insects have centralized nervous systems with brains. One of the regions of their brains is the protocerebrum. This region includes the

so-called mushroom bodies, which contain between one hundred thousand and one million neurons22. Electrical activity with a response between 20Hz and 30Hz has been recorded in their brains23.

The mushroom bodies of insects receive and integrate various types of multisensory information. This allows them to learn from previous experiences, remember them, and integrate information24. The mushroom bodies are therefore a specialized center for processing spatial information and organizing movement25.

The map of neural connections is called the connectome. The connectome of some insects is comparable to the fiber tract networks found in primates, displaying so-called small-world organization. This organization combines high connectivity between neighboring regions with shortcut connections to distant regions26.

If what this evidence suggests is correct, then these animals are not mere "living bodies": there is someone in these bodies, very probably with the capacity to suffer and to enjoy. Therefore, according to the criterion of sentience, they should receive the same degree of consideration as any other sentient being.

7. Does accepting the criterion of sentience imply assuming that values are subjective?

Sentience-centered ethics holds that, for a situation to be good/bad, better/worse, there must be one or more individuals who are harmed or benefited in that situation. The criterion of sentience holds that the beings for whom things can go better or worse are sentient beings, that is, beings who have a subjectivity, since they are capable of experiences that can be positive or negative, can have their preferences satisfied or frustrated, and so on.

Let us now consider an objection to the criterion of sentience. This objection says that we should reject it because, if we accept that, for a situation to be better or worse, there must exist beings with subjectivity (as is assumed in sentience-centered ethics), then we will be assuming a subjective conception of value (that is, assuming that there is nothing that everyone should recognize as objectively good or bad, regardless of what they prefer).

However, the one does not necessarily imply the other. What every sentience-centered conception of value assumes is that, for there to be value/disvalue in the world, there must exist beings capable of being positively or negatively affected. This is compatible with claiming that there are things that everyone should recognize as good or bad.

For example, it could be said that happiness objectively has intrinsic value and that suffering objectively has intrinsic disvalue. According to this conception, sentient beings merely recognize what has value or disvalue: it is not they who create value or disvalue. It could be said, for example, that it is not sentient beings who "invent" the idea that suffering is bad and that pleasure is good. The value of pleasure and the disvalue of suffering come from their intrinsic characteristics.

Holding that there are things that are objectively good/bad in themselves does not imply having to say that things that are not experiences (such as species, ecosystems, or merely biological life without sentience) have intrinsic value. Holding that there are things that are objectively good or bad in themselves is compatible with claiming that, for there to be value or disvalue, there must be beings for whom things can be positive or negative.

In short, the objection in question confuses two senses of the term "subjective". Something can be subjective in the sense of referring to consciousness. Something can be subjective in the sense that there is no objective truth about it. However, as we have seen, the one does not necessarily imply the other.

8. Are animals with simpler brains less sentient?

8.1. The view that there are degrees of sentience

One view sometimes defended is that animals with simpler brains are less sentient than animals with more complex brains27. For the same reason, this view also holds that there are stages in the life of one and the same individual at which they are less sentient, as in the case of a fetus that is already sentient and in cases of dementia28.

Those who adopt this view usually also hold that, for this reason, it would be justified to rank the moral consideration owed to animals hierarchically: humans at the top, then the other primates, then the other mammals, and so on. This view is also used to argue that we should give greater consideration to adults than to young animals. However, as we will see in the following sections, this view conflates three distinct concepts that are not necessarily related29: sentience, valence, and cognition30.

There are different things someone might mean when claiming that some beings are more sentient than others, depending on how they are using the word sentience. Sometimes this word is used as a synonym for the capacity to have experiences (that is, for there being someone "in there"). At other times, it is used to refer to the capacity not only to have experiences but also to recognize certain experiences as positive and others as negative. For example, if there were a being capable of experiences but who experienced all of them as neutral (that is, neither as positive nor as negative), that being would be sentient according to the first sense of the term, but not according to the second. In what follows we will examine the claim that certain animals are more sentient than others, taking these various possible interpretations into account.

8.2. Sentience

Suppose the word sentience is being used to mean the capacity to have experiences. In this sense, it is the difference between being something and being someone. A shoe is something because it is not capable of experiences; it has no consciousness. There is no point of view of the shoe. What a human, a chicken, a fish, a lobster, and a bee have in common, by contrast, is that they are sentient: there is someone "inside" those bodies; they are conscious.

However, if this is the sense in which the term is being used, it makes no sense to speak of degrees of sentience, because in this sense sentience is a binary matter: either one is sentient or one is not. There are no degrees of how much one is a thing or of how much one is someone. A being with a very simple brain is just as much someone as a being with a very complex brain.

8.3. Valence

What do exist are degrees of valence, which concern how positive or negative experiences are. For example, if I lightly bump my arm against the wall, I will feel mild pain, but if I break a leg, I will feel intense pain. As we have seen, this is one possible interpretation of what someone might mean when claiming that certain beings are more sentient than others. That is, they might mean that some are capable of more intense experiences than others.

However, the fact that there are experiences of different intensities does not necessarily imply that, when we compare the sensations two kinds of beings are feeling, one of them will always have the more intense sensation. For example, suppose that one day a human breaks a leg and a pig suffers a light scratch. In this case, the sensation the human is feeling is more intense. However, suppose that the next day the opposite happens. In that case, the sensation the pig feels is more intense.

Of course, it is quite possible that different beings have experiences of different intensities in response to the same stimulus. Perhaps this is what some people who claim that some beings are more sentient than others mean. However, let us remember that the view we are discussing makes a second claim: that the intensity of a sensation is proportional to the degree of cognition. However, the one does not necessarily follow from the other. That is, it is possible that there are beings who feel more intensely than others in response to the same stimulus, but that it is not the being with the greater cognitive capacity who feels more intensely, but rather the reverse. For example, a slap of the same intensity given to an adult and to a baby will probably hurt the baby much more, and this is so even though adults have a much higher degree of cognition.

Are there animals that feel more intensely than others, in response to the same stimulus, in all situations? It is possible, but most probably in the opposite way from that presupposed by the view we are discussing. For evolutionary reasons, it is quite possible that less complex brains feel more intensely. Below we will see why.

The capacity to have positive and negative experiences is directly linked to the motivation for behavior. That is, the fact that sentient beings experience certain stimuli as positive and others as negative leads them to seek the former and avoid the latter. This capacity also confers advantages in terms of survival. Survival to sexual maturity, in turn, helps increase the chances that they will reproduce and pass this trait on to the next generations.

Because of selective pressure, it is quite possible that experiences are more intense at stages when the animal has not yet developed certain cognitive capacities (for example, when it is still young, or even before it is born or hatches, as long as its nervous system is already formed). This is because at these stages, since the animal has not yet developed its cognitive capacities, the only motivation it would have for its behavior and learning would be to avoid negative experiences and seek positive ones31.

This is especially true in the case of precocial animals, since they need to be quite active in order to break the shell and hatch, and also to have any chance of surviving after hatching32, given that in most oviparous species the young receive no parental care. If these animals did not have the capacity to feel keenly at this age, these species would very probably no longer exist (since probably all of them would have died before sexual maturity, without leaving any offspring). So the fact that these species still exist (together with the fact that these animals already have a formed nervous system at this stage and behave in certain ways) is a reason to suppose that their members are capable of feeling very

keenly. That is, because of selective pressure, it is quite possible that animals with less developed cognitive capacities feel even more intensely. This holds both if we compare adults and young of the same species and if we compare animals of different species.

8.4. Degree of cognition

The degree of cognition, on the other hand, is something else entirely. It concerns how intelligent a given animal is. This does not make one animal more sentient, or less sentient, than another (in the sense of being someone). Beings of little intelligence are just as much someone as highly intelligent beings. We have also seen that their lower intelligence does not make their experiences less intense either. As we saw in the previous paragraph, they may be even more intense. The psychologist Richard Ryder, who coined the term speciesism, emphasizes this point: "Their experiences may be simpler than ours, but are they any less intense? Perhaps the primitive pain a caterpillar feels when it is crushed is greater than our more sophisticated sufferings33"

Of course, there are certain ways of being harmed that depend on one's cognitive capacity. For example, only someone who understands that they are going to die in a few hours is capable of suffering in anticipation of their death. Only beings who remember past negative events can suffer because of them. However, as the case of babies illustrates, there are many other contexts in which it is lesser cognitive capacity that entails greater suffering. In short, there is no necessary correlation between greater cognitive capacity and more intense experience.

8.5. Intelligentism

In the previous section we saw that it is a mistake to infer, from the fact that one being is cognitively more sophisticated than another, that it is therefore capable of feeling more intensely. However, there is another position that is sometimes defended by pointing out that certain animals are cognitively more sophisticated than others. This position holds that

these animals should receive greater moral consideration, even while acknowledging that they are not capable of feeling more intensely.

Basically, what this position holds is that cognitively more sophisticated beings should have a special status. This special status would mean, for example, that when faced with harms of similar magnitude, we should give priority to helping the cognitively more sophisticated individual. Depending on how much higher this status was, some variants of this position would hold that we should give priority to cognitively more sophisticated beings even when the harm they suffer is smaller.

Now, this view is like speciesism, racism, and sexism, except that it uses the degree of cognition as its criterion. It is biased for at least two reasons. First, because it violates the principle of equal consideration by assigning different weight to similar levels of harms and benefits on the basis of a factor that depends on the natural lottery (and therefore implies neither blame nor merit). Second, such a position does not pass the impartiality test, since it would not be approved by rational beings if they did not know what cognitive level they would have after being born. It is, therefore, a form of discrimination that could appropriately be called intelligentism, by analogy with speciesism.

8.6. Conclusion

If what has been argued above is correct, there is no way to justify giving less consideration to cognitively less capable beings. This is so for three reasons. First, we saw that these beings are just as much someone as any other sentient being. Second, we also saw that there are no good reasons to suppose that their lesser cognitive capacity means that they feel less intensely. Finally, third, we saw that there seems to be no justification for assigning a privileged moral status to cognitively more capable beings34.

9. If there is a need for environmental ethics, is the criterion of sentience wrong?

There is an argument holding that, if there is a need to develop an environmental ethics (that is, principles to guide our decisions that affect the environment), and if the questions addressed in environmental ethics make sense (that is, are not absurd questions), then nonsentient entities such as ecosystems or species have value in themselves, and not merely value as a resource for sentient beings35.

However, the need to develop an environmental ethics does not imply that nonsentient entities have intrinsic value. One thing that may make it seem to imply this is that the term environmental ethics is commonly used in two different senses. We will look at this point in more detail below.

The first sense refers to environmentalism, that is, to the position that claims that certain nonsentient entities have value in themselves. The second sense, on the other hand, refers to a certain area of practical ethics that deals with the morality of our actions that affect the environment. Among the central questions addressed in this area, one of the main ones is precisely this: "do nonsentient entities have intrinsic value or merely value as a resource for sentient beings?". This and other related questions certainly make sense. But the fact that a question makes sense does not imply that the answer to it is necessarily affirmative. Below we will look at some examples that illustrate this point.

Questions such as "is there life on Mars?" and "did Brazil win the 2014 soccer World Cup?" make sense. They are not absurd questions. But it does not follow that the right answers are necessarily affirmative. Indeed, the right answer to the second question is "no". It makes sense to ask "do species and ecosystems have intrinsic value?", but this does not guarantee that the appropriate answer is affirmative. It is possible that the appropriate answer is "no".

The same applies to the claim that it is necessary to develop an environmental ethics. It is also necessary to develop an ethics for dealing with income distribution, but this does not imply that income distribution itself has intrinsic value (indeed, the opposite seems true: that this question is important because it affects the good of individuals). Thus, the need for

an environmental ethics does not necessarily imply that nonsentient entities have intrinsic value (it may be that there is a need for an environmental ethics precisely because sentient beings are indirectly affected by the way we affect their environments).

That is, an "environmental ethics" (the area dealing with the morality of our actions that affect the environment) does not necessarily imply an "environmental ethic" (an environmentalist position). The fact that the environmentalist position is sometimes called "environmental ethics" or "genuinely environmental ethics" contributes to this confusion. For example, it is sometimes argued that only environmentalism is truly an "environmental ethic", and that seeing the environment merely as a resource for sentient beings is an "ethic for the management of the environment36". However, using such labels is not offering any argument in favor of environmentalism. Rather, it is assuming from the outset that environmentalism is correct. But that is exactly what is in question. It is, therefore, a circular argument (which is sometimes also used as a dishonest rhetorical strategy).

It is possible that the most appropriate approach to questions of environmental ethics involves rejecting this so-called "genuine environmental ethic" and embracing some form of "environmental management ethic" (for example, keeping or modifying the environment according to what is best for sentient beings). Of course, this does not necessarily guarantee that the environmentalist position is wrong either. The conclusion we should draw here is more specific: the argument from the need for environmental ethics, being circular, does not show that the criterion of sentience is inadequate.

Author’s notes

  1. This argument is offered by Regan (1981, p. 20, 24, 34). For a detailed critique, see Sapontzis (1987). ↩
  2. See, for example, Regan (1981, p. 20). ↩

10. Isn't a World with Less Suffering, but Managed by Humans, Absurd?

One argument sometimes put forward in defense of the environmentalist view and against the sentience criterion is the following37. If how good or bad a situation is should be assessed solely by how it benefits or harms sentient beings, then we will have to say that a world with plastic trees is better if that means sentient beings suffer less and are happier (compared with a world with natural trees in which sentient beings are worse off)38. Proponents of this argument hold that it is absurd to think such a world would be better merely because it would contain less suffering and more happiness, and they conclude that we should therefore reject the sentience criterion.

Something that may make this argument seem appealing at first glance is the use of the term “plastic” rather than “human-made.” When we think of plastic trees, we tend to think of trees that fall far short of a natural tree and that do not benefit sentient beings as much as natural trees do. So when we read “plastic trees,” the last thing we are likely to think of is trees that are better for sentient beings than natural trees.

Thus, the use of the phrase “plastic trees” in the argument may suggest that a human-modified ecosystem could never be better for sentient beings than an unmodified one. The problem, however, is that the argument cannot make that suggestion, since its aim is to show that a natural ecosystem is preferable even if a human-modified ecosystem were much better for sentient beings (so it cannot use as an example a case in which the modification would be worse for sentient beings). To be honest, the argument would have to use the phrase “a human-modified ecosystem that is better for sentient beings” (and not “an ecosystem with plastic trees”).

For example, imagine that in the future we come across an ecosystem that, seen from the outside, is indistinguishable from a natural ecosystem (it contains trees, rivers, mountains, etc.), and that we can tell it was modified by intelligent agents only because it contains

certain measures that cause sentient beings to experience less suffering. If we frame the argument this way, the idea that choosing such a world would be absurd becomes very weak39. Indeed, a world like this is what we seek for ourselves all the time: whenever we use housing, clothing, hospitals, medicines, recreation centers, and almost everything else we do in life. In fact, what most humans seem to find absurd is the opposite (at least when they themselves would be the victims of natural processes). But because of speciesism, the view held regarding nonhuman animals is the reverse: that it is absurd to modify the natural environment so that animals are harmed less. The explanation for this disparity, then, is just one: speciesism, pure and simple.

Another factor that contributes to the rejection of environmental improvement is the difficulty of imagining something human-made that is less bad for animals than a natural ecosystem, given the prevalence of views that equate “human action = worse outcome for nonhuman animals” and “natural = good.” However, most people do not know that in many cases human actions in natural ecosystems benefit animals, nor do they know that natural processes tend to maximize the number of animals born to lives filled with suffering and a very premature, usually violent death40.

So if we rid ourselves of this prejudice and imagine a human-modified ecosystem that is better for sentient beings than a natural ecosystem, what seems implausible is the idea that this ecosystem is worse merely because it has been influenced by human action. It is implausible because it would reveal an unjustified aversion to everything that results from human practices (even when the outcome is beneficial to those affected); an unjustified veneration of everything that results from natural processes (even when the outcome is harmful to those affected); and, in addition, a complete disregard for how nonhuman animals are positively or negatively affected under each possibility.

11. If Sentient Beings Should Be Respected, Does Nature Have Intrinsic Value?

It is sometimes argued that if sentient beings should receive moral consideration, then nature has value in itself, since sentient beings are part of nature. On this view, this would also show that if we deny that nature has intrinsic value, we are at the same time disregarding sentient beings.

This view is sometimes raised as an objection to the proposal to help wild animals that are victims of natural processes41. This proposal involves intervening in natural processes such as hunger, thirst, disease, and natural disasters in order to benefit animals42. The objection then claims that if we hold that it is right to intervene in nature, we must also hold that it is right to intervene in sentient beings, even to harm them, since they are part of nature.

The premise underlying this objection is that if a part of something is morally considerable, then the whole of that something is as well. However, there is no necessary implication from a part being morally considerable to the whole of which it is a part also being so. This is because the reasons for considering the part may not be present in the rest of the group to which it belongs, nor in the whole.

This is exactly what happens in the case of sentient beings: the reason we consider them is that they can be affected positively or negatively (because they are able to experience certain states as positive and/or others as negative). This characteristic is not present in any other part of nature, nor in nature as a whole. Therefore, the fact that there are good reasons to consider sentient beings does not imply that there are good reasons to consider other parts of nature, or nature as a whole.

It is therefore false that, if we hold that it is right to modify nature, we will be authorizing harm to nonhuman animals because they are part of nature. This is safely avoided if we make clear that the prescription is: nonsentient nature should be modified in order to benefit sentient beings.

It is precisely the confusion of thinking that “nature” and “nonhuman animals” are the same thing that gives rise to the (completely mistaken) idea that environmentalist views that advocate preserving nature as a whole necessarily also take nonhuman animals into consideration43. This same confusion in the use of terms also seems to be what leads many people to approve of any and every environmentalist policy, mistakenly believing that they are supporting policies that favor nonhuman animals44.

12. Does the Sentience Criterion Imply Accepting Environmentalist Goals?

Environmentalist positions are generally defended on the grounds that nonsentient entities such as species, ecosystems, and natural processes have value in themselves, entirely independently of how they affect the good of sentient beings45. However, another possible defense of environmentalist goals is to claim that, even if we must consider only sentient beings, environmentalists' interest in achieving their goals (for example, the goal of ensuring that nature takes its course, without interventions to help animals46) must be taken into account and respected, because environmentalists are sentient beings.

In that case, environmentalists would not be claiming that we have direct obligations of respect toward nonsentient natural entities. These obligations would be indirect obligations of respect toward the interests of environmentalists, but respecting their interests would amount to doing the same as we would do if nonsentient entities had intrinsic value.

The central problem with this argument is the assumption that because an interest of a sentient being must be taken into account, we must necessarily satisfy it. The one does not necessarily imply the other, for the following reason: if we must take this interest into account, then it would be arbitrary not to take into account the interests of the sentient beings who would be harmed if this interest were satisfied.

For example, natural processes typically affect animals very negatively47. Malnutrition, hunger, and thirst, disease, physical injuries, psychological stress, harsh weather events, natural disasters, and interspecific, intraspecific, and sexual conflicts are the norm for animals in the wild. Moreover, the predominant reproductive strategy consists in having litters of thousands or even millions of offspring, while the average number of survivors in stable populations is only two offspring per litter48.

Accordingly, satisfying the interest in “letting nature take its course” would entail the suffering and deaths of an enormous number of sentient beings. Whether in terms of the number of beings harmed or in terms of the severity of the harm each affected being would suffer individually, taking into account the interests of everyone involved points toward helping the animals who are victims of natural processes, and not toward satisfying the interest in letting nature take its course.

13. Do Species Have Interests?

The concept of interest often appears in debates about ethical issues. For example, we would say that it is in Maria's interest to avoid suffering, since suffering would harm her. Likewise, we would say that it is in Maria's interest to experience happiness, since happiness would benefit her. In more general terms, we can define the concept of interest as follows49:

It is in A's interest to obtain X if X benefits A.

It is in A's interest to avoid X if X harms A.

The word interest is sometimes used as a synonym for desire. However, the definition above is not necessarily committed to that view. Although satisfying desires may be in someone's interest, the definition above does not imply that, for something to be in someone's interest, that someone must have a corresponding desire. For example, it could be said that if the life a baby would have ahead of it would be meaningful, it is in that baby's interest to go on living, even if it is unable to form a desire to go on living.

Thus, given this broad definition of the term interest, saying that “we should give moral consideration to sentient beings because they have interests” is the same as saying “we should give moral consideration to sentient beings because they can be harmed or benefited.”

However, some authors argue that certain nonsentient entities also have interests. For example, Lawrence Johnson50 argued that species have interests. According to Johnson, there are four reasons for this:

(1) Species carry out complex activities that are not merely the aggregate of the activities of their members;

(2) Species are things with a past, a present, and an orientation toward the future;

(3) Species have unity and self-identity (that is, they are distinguishable from other things); and

(4) Species have a stronger interest in continuing to exist than their members do because, unlike their members, they do not have an inherent mortality.

These claims, especially the last one, could be used to try to justify the programs of killing animals carried out in the name of preserving species and biodiversity as a whole51. However, there are several possible responses to these four claims, which we will now examine52.

One response to the first claim consists in pointing out that it is possible to explain such complex activities without having to assume that they are more than the aggregate of their members' activities. Moreover, it is unclear why carrying out complex activities would be relevant to moral consideration, since it does not determine who can be harmed or benefited.

The second and third claims can be answered by pointing out that having a past, a present, and an orientation toward the future, as well as unity and self-identity, does not seem sufficient for having interests, since political parties and cities also have these characteristics, but that does not mean they have interests. We can speak metaphorically of the interests of the city or of the party, but what we are really talking about are the interests of the citizens and of the party members. The same holds for species. In the case of species of sentient beings, we can speak metaphorically of the interests of the species, but what we are really talking about are the interests of the sentient beings who are its members. This does not mean that species are someone, with a well-being.

As for the fourth claim, one could respond that what is relevant to the existence of an interest in continuing to exist is whether existing is a benefit, and that what is relevant to the strength of this interest is how much someone would be harmed by ceasing to exist. This seems to depend, for example, on how much this someone has lived so far (and how positive or

negative that life has been), and on how much they would have left to live (and how positive or negative that life will be), and not on whether or not their mortality is inherent53.

For this reason, it does not seem to make sense to say that species have a stronger interest in continuing to exist than their members, since species do not even have an interest in continuing to exist. Given that they are incapable of valuing certain states over others (since there is no someone who is the species), it makes no sense to hold that, from the species' point of view, it is better to exist or to cease to exist (since there is no such point of view).

Species are abstract entities. They are categories constructed by humans to group living beings according to certain similarities. There is no someone who is the species, who could literally be harmed by ceasing to exist or benefited by continuing to exist. Those who can be benefited or harmed in these ways are its members, if they are sentient.

14. If Some Nonsentient Entity Had Intrinsic Value, What Would Follow?

Consider the following question: do the nonsentient entities valued by environmentalism (such as ecosystems, species, natural processes, etc.) have value in themselves, or do they have value only as resources for sentient beings? It is often assumed that if they have intrinsic value, then killing nonhuman animals to preserve them is justified, as is prohibiting helping animals in the wild who are victims of natural processes. However, as we will see, this idea is mistaken.

To begin with, the idea that there is value beyond sentience is, to say the least, highly controversial. For example, it would imply that a universe without any sentient beings could still be better or worse, even though there would be no one in that universe for whom things could be better or worse (since in such a universe there would be no one at all). Nevertheless, let us suppose for the sake of argument that the entities valued in environmentalism really did have value in themselves. This would not necessarily imply that harming animals to preserve them, or prohibiting helping wild animals who are victims of natural processes, is therefore justified, since there could be reasons to prioritize sentient beings over nonsentient entities.

The idea that the basic interests of sentient beings should take priority over nonsentient entities is already widely accepted when what is at stake is the good of humans. This is accepted by environmentalists themselves. Environmentalists generally hold that environmentalist goals are more important than certain human interests (such as economic, aesthetic, and recreational interests), but not more important than basic human interests, such as not suffering and not dying. But if speciesism is unjustifiable, then there is also no justification for holding that it is right to kill nonhuman animals or cause them suffering in order to achieve environmentalist goals, or that we should not help them when they are victims of natural processes.

But what if someone claimed that we should sacrifice sentient beings – human and nonhuman – for the sake of environmentalist goals54? This position is not speciesist, but that does not mean it is justified, since there are reasons to prioritize sentient beings. The

main reason is as follows. Unlike nonsentient entities, sentient beings can literally be harmed and benefited, whether through negative experiences (all forms of suffering) or through being deprived of positive experiences (as happens when they die, for example). These are particularly serious harms. Species, ecosystems, natural processes, ecological balance, biodiversity, etc. may be present to a greater or lesser degree; they may exist or disappear; but they cannot experience the horror of excruciating suffering, nor be deprived of good years of positive experiences, because nonsentient entities are not someone.

For these reasons, even if the entities valued in environmentalism had intrinsic value, there would still be strong reasons, in cases of conflict, to prioritize the good of sentient beings. Two main conclusions follow from this. The first is that, even if we ought to accept environmentalist goals, there would still be no justification for causing suffering or death to sentient beings in trying to achieve those goals. The second is that, even if we ought to accept environmentalist goals, this would not be enough to reject the proposal to help animals who live in the wild and are victims of natural processes.

Author’s notes

  1. This has been argued, for example, by Linkola (1979, 2000, 2009). ↩

15. Is Biocentrism Better Because It Includes a Greater Number of Beings?

15.1. Criteria for Moral Consideration of Different Scope

Consider the following criteria for moral consideration:

  • The anthropocentric criterion prescribes giving moral consideration to all members of the human species.
  • The sentience criterion prescribes giving moral consideration to all beings capable of suffering and enjoyment.
  • The biocentric criterion prescribes giving moral consideration to everything that is alive, regardless of whether or not it is sentient55.

It is sometimes claimed that if the sentience criterion is better than the anthropocentric criterion because it includes a greater number of beings in the sphere of moral consideration, then for the same reason the biocentric criterion is better than the sentience criterion, since it includes in the sphere of moral consideration both sentient beings and nonsentient living beings.

15.2. Does the Fact That a Criterion Is Broader Necessarily Make It Better?

One problem with this claim is that it fails to draw the following distinction. What explains why humans should be morally considered (the possibility of being harmed and benefited) implies that every sentient being should be as well. However, what explains why every sentient being should be considered (that is, the possibility of being harmed and benefited) does not imply that every living being should be too.

There is a difference between a criterion being more adequate because it includes beings who would be harmed if they were excluded, and a criterion including beings that cannot be harmed and/or benefited. The number of objects included is not, by itself, relevant.

For example, a theory that gives moral consideration to all living beings and also to tables and chairs includes a greater number of objects in the sphere of moral consideration. But that does not necessarily make it better. Likewise, even if biocentrism includes a greater number of beings, that does not necessarily make it better. What would have to be shown is that nonsentient living beings are harmed if they are not included. One could try to do this by offering other arguments (which we will discuss in the following chapters). For now, however, our conclusion is more specific: the fact that a criterion includes a greater number of beings does not show this.

15.3. Does Biocentrism Really Include All Sentient Beings and All Living Beings?

Furthermore, the claim that biocentrism would include a greater number of beings in the sphere of moral consideration than the sentience criterion is also questionable. The biocentric criterion is sometimes understood as giving moral consideration to all sentient beings and also to all nonsentient living beings. However, it is false that the biocentric criterion would give moral consideration to all sentient beings. This is because the biocentric criterion gives moral consideration only to living beings. For this reason, if nonorganic forms of sentience come to exist in the future (for example, sentient beings in digital media), these beings would be excluded by the biocentric criterion, since, not being organic, they would not be living beings56 (despite being conscious). However, since these beings would also be capable of suffering and enjoyment, they would be included by the sentience criterion. Therefore, it is not true that the biocentric criterion would be an “expansion beyond sentience,” since it would not even give moral consideration to all sentient beings. Moreover, it is possible that in the future nonorganic sentient beings will become very numerous, perhaps far more numerous than biological beings57. Thus, it is also not true that the number of beings included by the biocentric criterion is necessarily greater than the number of beings included by the sentience criterion.

Therefore, it makes sense to claim that the biocentric criterion discriminates against those who are not living beings, since it would exclude from the sphere of moral consideration beings who could in fact be harmed and benefited, since they would be capable of suffering and enjoyment even though they are not organic.

Author’s notes

  1. For examples of proponents of the biocentric criterion, see Goodpaster (1978) and Taylor (1986). ↩
  2. It could be objected that such beings would be alive because they would have a psychological life. However, the terms “psychological life” and “living beings,” although they refer to the same concept (life), refer to very different things. The term living beings refers to beings that maintain homeostasis, are composed of cells, undergo metabolism, are born, grow, age, die, etc. If nonorganic sentience is possible, then it is not necessary to be alive in order to have a psychological existence (that is, an existence as a sentient being). The biocentric criterion prescribes considering all living beings, not all beings capable of having a psychological existence. ↩
  3. On the possibility of sentience in digital media, see Tomasik (2015b). ↩

16. Sentience and Life: What Has Value as an End and What Has Value as a Means?

16.1. If Being Alive Is Necessary for Being Sentient, Does Being Alive Have Intrinsic Value?

It is sometimes argued that, for there to be sentience, the organism must be alive, and that we should therefore give moral consideration to all living beings, sentient or not.

The claim that biological life is necessary for sentience may turn out to be false if nonorganic sentient beings (for example, in digital media) come to exist in the future. This is a possibility accepted by many experts in the philosophy of mind and also by many scientists58. If beings of this kind come to exist, they would be sentient beings, but they would not be alive, since they would lack the essential characteristics that define a living being: maintaining homeostasis, having a life cycle, being composed of cells, undergoing metabolism, etc. Thus, it is possible that in the future there will be sentient beings that are not living beings. However, at least with respect to the sentient beings that have existed so far, biological life seems necessary for sentience.

Regardless of this, however, observing that biological life is necessary for sentience does not serve as a defense of the claim that we should consider nonsentient living beings, since what this observation shows is that biological life has instrumental value for sentience, not value in itself. That is, what the observation in question does is say that biological life is important because it is (at least so far) essential for sentience to exist. But showing that something has value as a means is not showing that it has value in itself.

Of course, this does not show that it is impossible for biological life to have intrinsic value either. It does show, however, that if it does, it will be for some other reason, and not because it has instrumental value for sentience. Obviously, it is not possible to show that something has intrinsic value by pointing out that it has instrumental value. Thus, even though the observation in question offers reasons to keep sentient beings alive, it offers no reasons to keep nonsentient organisms alive.

16.2. Isn't Sentience Just a Means of Sustaining Life?

Now consider the opposite claim. Another argument that tries to show that what has intrinsic value is biological life, and not sentience, points out that sentient beings use the sensation of pain to avoid what would kill them and, through positive sensations, learn which things help them stay alive.

According to this argument, sentience is merely a means of preserving life: positive experiences would have no value in themselves, and negative experiences would not be bad in themselves. On this view, the value of sentience would be merely instrumental to what really has intrinsic value: being alive. The argument then concludes that living beings (sentient or not) should receive direct moral consideration.

The main problem with this argument is that it does not follow from the fact that sentient beings avoid negative experiences and seek to stay alive that they do so because they see biological life as having intrinsic value. The main reason they avoid negative experiences is the very fact that they are negative. Of course, it is possible to avoid something that causes suffering also because we know it would cause our death. But it does not follow from the fact that we aim to stay alive that we see biological life as having value in itself. This will be explained in more detail below.

We normally think that being alive is good because it allows us to have valuable experiences59. Sentient beings seek certain things because they value the experiences those things provide. They do not see these experiences as having value merely instrumental to staying alive. Rather, being alive is good because it makes these experiences possible. If these experiences also help us remain biologically alive or contribute to other things (such as the continuation of the species, for example), this is merely a side effect: by itself, it does not indicate that sentient beings aim at such things as ends.

We normally think that life is worth living when it contains experiences valuable enough for us to consider staying alive better than dying. If we thought that biological life had intrinsic value, we would hold that there is something good about remaining a

living body with no possibility of experiences (nor of ever having them again), and even when we experienced nothing but extreme suffering. However, this does not seem to be the case.

All of this suggests that we have reasons to conclude the opposite of what the objection holds: it is being alive that has value only as a means to having meaningful experiences.

17. Can Nonsentient Living Beings Be Harmed?

Biocentrism is the view that everything that is alive should receive direct moral consideration. Proponents of biocentrism60 agree that it only makes sense to give moral consideration to beings that can be harmed and benefited. However, they disagree that sentience is necessary for there to be a possibility of harm or benefit. Instead, they argue that nonsentient living beings (such as plants and fungi, for example) can also be harmed and/or benefited.

Biocentrists claim that everything that is alive has a good of its own, as evidenced by the fact that it flourishes in some circumstances and perishes in others. For example, according to this view, the fact that a plant grows when watered is a sign that the plant values water. Note that biocentrists are not saying that the plant is sentient and has a preference for being watered (they acknowledge that the plant is not sentient). What they are claiming is that, for there to be valuing, there need not be someone inhabiting that body.

However, from the fact that something flourishes under certain conditions and not under others, it does not follow that it matters to that something whether it is in this or that state, and therefore that it is harmed or benefited by being in certain circumstances rather than others. If the organism in question does not experience certain states as positive and/or others as negative, it is hard to conceive how it could value being in this or that condition. There is no one there to experience anything: it is a living body, but an empty one, inhabited by no one. These are lives that no one lives. Thus, one possible criticism of the biocentric argument is to accuse it of leaping from a metaphorical sense to a literal sense of the term “value”61. We will look at this in more detail below.

The biocentric criterion is sometimes defended by appealing to ordinary language. In ordinary language, we use terms that refer to a supposed well-being of nonsentient entities. For example, the following expressions are often used:

“the plant likes water”; “that was good for the species”; “nature wants ecological balance,” “the fungus wants moisture,” etc.

However, ordinary language can be highly misleading. When we say “the plant ‘likes’ water,” or “the fungus ‘wants’ moisture” (or any of the other examples above), we are using these terms in a metaphorical sense. If we claim that this shows that nonsentient entities have a good of their own, there is then a leap from a metaphorical sense to a literal sense of the terms “likes,” “was good,” and “wants.” It is like saying (metaphorically) “the car wants gasoline,” “that song is sad,” “the sea is angry,” and then concluding (literally) that the car, the song, and the sea have a first-person perspective, with a will and a good of their own.

It is hard to conceive how an organism could value certain states over others without being able to experience certain states as positive and/or others as negative – especially when it is unable to experience any state at all, not even neutral states. This gives us reason to think that the adequate criterion for moral consideration is sentience, and not merely biological life.

18. Does the Behavior of Certain Plants and Fungi Show That They Value Certain Things?

Certain nonsentient living beings exhibit certain behaviors. For example, plants absorb nutrients from the soil, carry out photosynthesis, some close and open in response to touch or light, and so on. There are also studies suggesting that plant growth is affected by sound stimuli, such as speech and music62. There is a common belief that these behaviors show that such organisms are sentient, or else that they have intentionality and a will to remain in this or that state, even if they are not sentient. What follows is an explanation of why this common belief is mistaken.

The presence of behavior does not necessarily imply that there is sentience or valuing. For example, a thermostat reacts to changes in temperature, but this does not imply that the thermostat values being at this or that temperature, or that it has a will to remain in this or that state. It implies only that there is this reaction to a certain stimulus. In fact, there are robots that exhibit behaviors very similar to those of humans. But that by itself does not show that they are beings who value certain states or have a will. The same holds for certain plants that close when touched or grow in response to certain sounds: this does not necessarily imply that the plant likes or wants to be in this or that state. It does not imply that there is necessarily someone there. These behaviors can be explained as the result of physicochemical reactions.

Sometimes the terms used in certain studies of plants or fungi can be ambiguous and mistakenly suggest that plants or fungi are sentient, when that is not in fact what the study shows. For example, certain species of fungi emit electrical signals. In one study, the sequences of these signals were decoded and called a “language”63. When we hear the word language, we normally already assume that there is an individual, a conscious being, who understands the symbols, assigns meaning to them, and uses them to communicate what is going on in their mind. The same study states that “electrical activity is used by fungi to communicate.” This may suggest that the signals are used intentionally by the fungi, that fungi are someone, that they have

consciousness, etc. However, the term “language,” as used in the study, has the same sense as in artificial intelligence: it refers only to something that, although quite complex, may very well occur without being accompanied by any consciousness at all. In this sense, the electrical signals are “used by fungi” in the same sense in which a computer program “uses” input data to perform certain activities. This does not necessarily imply consciousness64.

It could be objected that, just as it is possible to explain such behaviors as the result of physicochemical reactions, it is also possible to explain them on the assumption that there is a will or consciousness in these beings. However, the fact that an explanation is possible does not show that it is necessarily correct. The point here is that such behaviors can be explained without having to assume that these organisms are sentient. This is different from what happens, for example, in the case of invertebrate animals65 such as insects, crustaceans, and arachnids. In their case, it is very difficult to explain their behavior without having to assume that they are sentient. Moreover, these animals, unlike plants or fungi, have a physical structure (a centralized nervous system) that performs the function of processing the information reaching the organism and creating the conditions for consciousness to arise66. In the case of beings that have no nervous system (nor anything performing an analogous function), on the other hand, there are reasons to suppose that their behavior is the result of reflexes. This will be explained in more detail below.

Because they experience certain states as positive and others as negative, sentient beings behave in certain ways (they avoid what would cause them negative experiences and seek what would cause them positive experiences). However, the fact that there is a certain behavior is not sufficient to conclude that an organism is valuing something. Even in the case of sentient beings, it is possible for their sentience to be absent at a given moment (for example, under general anesthesia) while the body still continues to exhibit certain behaviors due to reflexes.

This works this way because of what are known as reflex arcs67. Consider, for example, the tap on the knee with a reflex hammer given during a medical checkup for a driver's license. When the information about the tap reaches the nervous system, it travels along two paths. One, shorter and more direct, goes from the spinal cord to the muscles. The other, longer and more indirect, goes from the spinal cord to the brain, where the information is processed and the conditions for the experience to arise are created. This is why the knee reflex is instantaneous, while the sensation arrives a little later.

There are certain nervous systems that operate in a way similar to reflex arcs, but without the sensation part. For example, there are certain animals, such as jellyfish and sea cucumbers, that have nervous systems but have no brain or any other organ that performs its function68. These animals exhibit reflexes (and sometimes relatively complex behaviors), but this is not an indicator that they have experiences. A similar mechanism appears in certain organisms that have no nervous system, such as carnivorous plants and sensitive plants (mimosa), for example.

Thus, the lack in these organisms of a physical structure that performs the function of creating the conditions for experiences to arise, together with the presence of reflexes, is a strong reason to conclude that the existence of behavior, by itself, is insufficient to conclude that the organism in question is sentient, that it is valuing certain states, or that it is expressing a will.

19. Does Life Without Sentience Have Value?

19.1. Sentience or Life?

If we adopt the biocentric criterion, we will hold that the lives of living beings, sentient or not, are valuable. If, on the other hand, we adopt the sentience criterion, we will say that it is the fact that we can have positive experiences in life that makes it valuable (and not the mere fact that there is biological life). Which of these positions should we adopt? Below are three examples that have been used to defend the sentience criterion.

19.2. The Example of the Total Irreversible Coma

Imagine that you have to choose one of the following two options:

(1) Either die now (with no life at all after death – that is, be annihilated).

(2) Or be placed in a total coma (with no experience at all, not even dreams) that is completely irreversible (that is, with no chance whatsoever of coming out of the coma).

If the mere fact of being alive (without experiences) were something valuable, then we would be benefited by being placed in the total irreversible coma compared with being annihilated now. But from our point of view, it makes no difference whether we are annihilated now or placed in the total irreversible coma: in fact, we are equally annihilated under both options. This suggests that the mere fact of being alive in a biological sense is not valuable in itself.

Obviously, there could be indirect reasons for preferring the coma. Your relatives might want your body kept alive. You might have left a request for your body to be kept alive as long as possible. But these indirect appeals are all appeals to the preferences of sentient beings (those of your relatives, or your own when you were still sentient). Therefore, they do not serve as a defense of biocentrism.

19.3. The Example of the Fraudulent Insurance Company

Sometimes, when people use the word life, what they actually mean is sentience. Because of this ambiguity in the use of the word, it sometimes happens that someone is arguing that it is sentience that has value while believing they are arguing that it is life that has value.

Consider, for example, when people ask: “Is there life after death?” What they really want to know is whether, after death, we go on having experiences (that is, whether we remain sentient). This question is asked for a very simple reason: we value certain experiences and would therefore like to know whether it is possible to go on having them after the death of the body. In this question, what is meant by the word life is not mere biological life, but psychological life, that is, sentience. This can be illustrated by the following example.

Imagine that an insurance company guaranteed that if we paid a monthly premium until we died, we would have a life after death. What's more, the company guarantees that this life would be valuable. Now imagine that you gather all your savings and pay the monthly premium for forty years.

One day, however, you happen to meet the scientist who discovered how to provide a life after death. She tells you that, besides being a scientist, she is also an adherent of the biocentric criterion for moral consideration and believes that all life has value, regardless of whether or not there is sentience. Very curious, you then ask her what this life after death that you spent forty years paying for is like. She answers with a smile: “It is a merely biological life, without any sentience at all. You will never have any experience again, but your body will be kept alive for all eternity. Isn't that wonderful?”

We would certainly be outraged by this answer (especially after paying the monthly premium for forty years). But if we are outraged, it is because we think that such a life has no value. If so, then we do not believe that a merely biological life, with no possibility of experiences at all, has value. What we think has value are the experiences we can have in life. If this is your case, then you accept the sentience criterion, and not the biocentric criterion.

19.4. The Example of Sentience Without Life

Let us look at a third example that also suggests that what has value are experiences, and not biological life.

Suppose you discover, in the future, that you have a terminal illness and that nothing can be done to save your biological body. However, let us imagine that a new technology is available that allows you to gradually replace your biological body with a body made of a nonbiological material. Imagine that this will also apply to your brain, with each biological neuron gradually being replaced by nonbiological neurons. Unlike in the previous example, however, your sentience will not disappear: you will remain just as sentient as you are now, but with a new, nonbiological body69.

In this condition, you would no longer be a living being, since you would no longer have the characteristics that define a living being: maintaining homeostasis, having a life cycle, being composed of cells, undergoing metabolism, etc. The question, however, is this: in this condition, will your existence still have value? It seems that it certainly will, since you will be able to go on doing everything you enjoy and experiencing everything that makes your life valuable now – the only difference will be that your body will not be organic. But then this suggests that what has value is sentience, and not biological life, since in such a condition you would remain sentient, but you would no longer be a living being.

Author’s notes

  1. On the possibility of nonbiological sentience in the future, see Tomasik (2015b). ↩

20. Does Every Living Being Have “Biological Interests”?

A specific case of anthropocentric speciesism consists in not considering certain interests of nonhuman animals because they do not have all the interests that humans have. For example, not taking into account a fish's interest in not suffering because it has no interest in reading a book. Humans have certain specific interests (as a result of their rational capacity), but they share with nonhuman animals certain “interests of sentience,” that is, interests whose existence requires only that the being in question be sentient.

It is sometimes suggested that an analogous discrimination would favor sentient beings over nonsentient living beings70. The argument holds that although sentient beings have certain specific interests (for example, not suffering and having positive experiences), there are interests of sentient beings that concern their biology: eating, sleeping, resting. That is, they concern the basic needs of the biological body.

However, the argument continues, nonsentient living beings also have basic needs. A plant needs to metabolize nutrients from the soil and be watered in order to stay alive. The argument concludes that, just as there are “interests of sentience” that are shared by human and nonhuman animals, there are “biological interests” that are shared by all living beings, sentient or not.

One problem with this argument, however, is that the interest sentient beings have in the satisfaction of their biological needs is merely instrumental to their well-being. The satisfaction of biological needs is not important in itself. It is not these biological needs that make sentient beings have a well-being and, therefore, an interest in satisfying those needs. Sentient beings have a well-being because they are capable of having positive and negative mental states. This point becomes clear when we ask why it is important for us to have our biological needs satisfied. Eating, resting, and sleeping seem to have value precisely because they prevent suffering and provide positive experiences (either directly, or indirectly by preventing death). Since nonsentient living beings are not capable of any experience at all, the

satisfaction of their biological needs would have no value whatsoever for them, given that there is no point of view of theirs: there is no someone inside those bodies.

The following objection could be raised: “the interest in eating, sleeping, and resting is also instrumental to the interest in staying alive, which is a purely biological interest.” However, one can ask “why (and when) is it good to be alive?”. There are some conditions in which being alive is a harm to the one who lives (for example, a life of nothing but extreme suffering). There are also conditions in which being alive is a matter of indifference (for example, a total irreversible vegetative coma, in which there is a living body but no longer an individual). If so, then being alive is not good in itself: it is good depending on what it would be possible to experience in life71. If so, then being alive has value merely instrumental to the fulfillment of interests that depend on sentience in order to exist.

Thus, the fact that sentient beings have certain interests whose satisfaction requires that their biological needs be met indicates neither that nonsentient living beings have the same interests nor that having biological needs is sufficient for having interests.
