21. If Plants Are Morally Considerable, Does It Make No Difference Whether We Eat Animals or Plants?

An alleged respect for all living beings is often invoked not in order to defend nonsentient living beings, but in an attempt to justify excluding nonhuman animals from the sphere of moral consideration. For example, the appeal to a supposed consideration for plants is very commonly used in an attempt to justify consuming animals.

However, this argument would fail to justify what it intends even if all living beings were morally considerable. This is because there would still be a reason to prioritize sentient beings in situations where, whatever we choose, we will necessarily harm either sentient beings or nonsentient living beings.

The reason is that sentient beings, because they can experience suffering and be prevented from enjoying positive experiences (as happens when someone dies, for example), can be harmed in particularly serious ways that no nonsentient being can.

Paul Taylor, one of the leading proponents of biocentrism (the view that all living beings, sentient or not, are morally considerable), agrees with this point72. He acknowledges that any form of suffering is an intrinsically negative occurrence in the life of a sentient being. For this reason, he concludes that, between killing plants and killing sentient animals, it is less wrong to kill plants if the animals would suffer.

One might think that the same view would then have to prescribe that it makes no difference whether we kill the sentient being or the merely living being, as long as the sentient being's death is painless. However, let us recall that Taylor condemns causing a death involving suffering because suffering is negative. But the reverse could be said of pleasure or happiness: they are positive experiences. One way for a sentient being to be harmed is through the presence of negative experiences; but another is through the absence of positive experiences (something that happens when they die73).

If so, then whenever the death of a sentient being prevents the enjoyment of positive experiences, it is worse than the death of a merely living being (even if the death is painless, and even if we had to consider all living beings), since only the sentient being is harmed by being deprived of the positive things it would experience if it went on living. Therefore, even if plants were morally considerable, this would not justify consuming animals.

In fact, as far as diet is concerned, the logical implication for someone who believes that plants are morally considerable is to adopt ethical botanical fruitarianism, a stance characterized by consuming only what falls away from a plant. Usually, when people realize this implication, they immediately stop arguing that plants are morally considerable. This shows that they did not really believe what they were defending. They were merely looking for an excuse to go on consuming animals. However, the important point to note here is that, as we saw above, even if plants were morally considerable, there would still be reasons to prioritize sentient beings – and this is independent of whether those who advocate moral consideration for plants do so sincerely or not.

Volume VII

Ethics and the Situation of Wild Animals

This book describes how natural processes typically affect animals living in the wild, presents the foundations of the proposal to help these animals, and also covers the debate surrounding this proposal.

Original text by Luciano Carlos Cunha, translated into English · ISBN 978-65-01-49140-0 · 1st edition, May 2025.

1. What Should We Do About Animals Living in the Wild?

A common belief is that, as far as animals living in the wild are concerned, we should simply stop harming them and “leave them alone,” and help them only if they are harmed directly or indirectly by human practices. When animals are victims of natural processes such as natural disasters, hunger, thirst, and disease, according to this position we should “let nature take its course.”

This position has been increasingly challenged in recent years1. One possible challenge is to accuse it of anthropocentric speciesism, in the sense of maintaining an arbitrary moral standard depending on whether the victims are human or nonhuman, since when humans are victims of hunger, thirst, disease, and natural disasters, its proponents do not say “let nature take its course.”

Another challenge holds that limiting moral consideration for animals to harms resulting from human practices is incompatible with truly caring about the good of animals. For example, it would be very strange to say, “I care about this person's good, but I would only save her from a fire caused by humans; in a naturally caused fire, I would let her burn to death.” In other words, the argument is that if we truly care about animals (and not about an ideal of supposed “human purity” – not doing harm but letting harm occur), we will hold that they should be helped regardless of whether they are victims of human practices or of natural processes.

At other times, it is acknowledged that we have reasons to prevent animals from being harmed by natural harms, but it is argued that these reasons are weaker than when the harms result from human practices. Here, however, the criticism would be the same: if we truly care about the good of the victims, and not about an ideal of “human purity,” our criterion for determining priority will be based on the magnitude of the harm, not on the origin of the harm. That is, we will prioritize preventing the most serious harms, regardless of whether they result from human practices or from natural processes.

These, in short, are the central arguments of the proposal to help animals who are victims of natural processes. In the rest of this book, we will address the debate surrounding this proposal.

2. How Not to Understand the Issue

2.1. The Idea That It Is Not an Ethical Issue

A common view is that harms resulting from natural disasters, hunger, thirst, disease, and conflicts between animals are not an ethical issue because it makes no sense to hold either natural processes or nonhuman animals morally responsible. According to this view, we should therefore not try to minimize this kind of harm.

There are at least two basic mistakes this view makes, explained separately below.

2.2. Whatever You Think We Should Do, It Is an Ethical Issue

The first mistake lies in the contradiction between the claims “the way natural processes affect wild animals lies outside the scope of ethical evaluation” and “we have a duty not to help wild animals who are victims of natural processes.”

But it goes further: even those who claim that helping animals in this case should be optional are also seeing the issue as an ethical one, since ethics deals not only with what is morally required or forbidden, but also with what is morally permissible but not required. In short, whatever anyone thinks we should do about this situation, it is an ethical issue simply because it concerns whether an action should be required, forbidden, or permitted.

There are questions that are not ethical questions. For example: “Is there life on other planets?”; “What was the identity of Jack the Ripper?”; “Will it rain tomorrow in Florianópolis?”; “When is Luciano Cunha's birthday?”; “What is 2+2?”; “Is there life after death?”; “What is consciousness?” None of these questions is an ethical question, because none of them concerns how we ought to act (even though some of them may have an indirect bearing on our reasons for acting one way or another). The question of what our attitude should be toward the harms animals suffer as a result of natural processes is about how we ought to act. Therefore, it is an ethical question.

2.3. The Question Is Posed to Us, Not to Natural Processes or to Animals

The second mistake is that the fact that natural processes and nonhuman animals cannot be held morally responsible is irrelevant, since the question is not being posed to them, but to us. It is we who must answer what we should do about this issue. The fact that natural processes and animals cannot be held responsible for what they choose does not make us any less responsible.

To illustrate, imagine that the same excuse were offered in a situation involving human victims. For example, imagine that a government could save humans in a flood without sacrificing anything of greater importance in doing so. But let us imagine that the officials said: “We have no obligation to do anything, because the water cannot be held morally responsible.” At the very least, this would be regarded (rightly, in my view) as one of the flimsiest of excuses. However, the fact that the victims are nonhuman animals does not make this same excuse any less flimsy.

3. How Do Natural Processes Typically Affect Wild Animals?

3.1. The Situation of Wild Animals

There are objections to the proposal to help wild animals that deny there is any need to help them. For example, a common belief is that the situation of wild animals is not really all that bad. According to this view, most wild animals live satisfying lives, and the number of animals who are victims of natural processes is much smaller than the number of animals who are victims of exploitation. For this reason, people who hold this view usually argue that we should focus on changing the situation of exploited animals.

The reality, however, is quite different. The typical situation of animals in the wild is also highly negative. Many of the harms they suffer are direct or indirect results of human practices, but, contrary to what is commonly thought, natural processes already harm them to a high degree independently of human actions. They are routinely victims of malnutrition, hunger, and thirst, disease, physical injuries, psychological stress, harsh weather events, natural disasters, and interspecific, intraspecific, and sexual conflicts2. These conditions are the norm in nature, not the exception, and they have been occurring since long before the appearance of the human species (and not because humans caused some “imbalance” or anything of the sort).

One of the factors that contributes most to maximizing the number of animals born to lives filled with suffering is the predominant reproductive strategy. In biology, reproductive strategy is a term that designates the way animals reproduce (for example, by having few or many offspring at a time). It therefore does not mean strategy in the sense of something planned (whether by the animals or by anyone else). It means only that animals reproduce in a certain way.

The predominant reproductive strategy consists in maximizing the number of offspring. Most animal species have enormous broods, with thousands or even millions of offspring depending on the species (something common in amphibians, reptiles, fish, and invertebrates in general). For example, a single clutch of a common frog contains around

25,000 offspring3; that of octopuses, hundreds of thousands4; those of salmon, cod, and tuna, millions5; and that of the ocean sunfish reaches 300 million6. Terrestrial invertebrates can also lay hundreds, thousands, or even millions of eggs at a time7.

This reproductive strategy always results in extremely low survival rates. In periods of approximately constant population, it is possible to measure the rate of premature mortality from the size of the brood. This is because if the population has remained approximately constant over several generations, then on average only one offspring per adult has survived (that is, two per brood, and fewer than that if there are adults who reproduce more than once in their lives). All the rest are generally born only to experience intense suffering and die very prematurely, often without ever having had any positive experience at all8.

This reproductive strategy is normally found in small animal species, which make up the vast majority of animal species. One of the main reasons many people have an unrealistically positive view of life in the wild is that they tend to think of animals who are not representative of typical life in the wild: they think of large animals (who do not follow this reproductive strategy, having few offspring per pregnancy) and of adults (that is, they think of the small minority who escape death before reaching adulthood)9. This is partly because the unrepresentative animals are the ones that generally appear in documentaries and publications on the subject10.

In short, as a result of natural processes, for every animal who manages to survive, thousands or even millions die very young, usually suffering a very painful death. Most animals are born only to experience almost nothing but (or even nothing but) extreme suffering, and many others also suffer significantly, even if not so extremely. What may be surprising at first glance is that the number of animals who meet this fate is so enormous that it makes even the figures of animal exploitation, which are already huge, almost vanish by

comparison11. Trillions of animals are killed in exploitation every year. However, the number of sentient animals in the wild at any given moment is between 1 and 10 quintillion, and the vast majority will reproduce by having thousands or millions of offspring per spawning.

As we have seen, this outcome results from natural processes themselves, independently of the direct or indirect effects of human practices: it was already this way long before the appearance of the human species, even if today all natural effects are already influenced by human action.

3.2. The Objection from Destroyed Eggs

It could be objected that the problem is not as big as it initially seems, since many of the eggs are probably destroyed before they develop into sentient beings. However, there is no evidence that this happens to most eggs. Moreover, the number of eggs is so enormous that, even if most of them were destroyed before developing into sentient beings, it would still result in a huge number of sentient beings born to lives filled with suffering and to premature death. For example, a common cod has on average 2 million eggs per spawning12. Even if only 10% of these eggs developed into sentient beings, there would already be almost 200,000 sentient beings harmed per spawning.

3.3. The Objection That They Hardly Suffer

Another objection holding that the situation is not as serious as it seems claims that these animals, because their cognitive capacities are not yet developed, would not be capable of suffering (or at least would not suffer in very significant ways)13. According to this objection, if this is true, then there is nothing problematic about this situation.

The first problem with this objection is that these animals could still be harmed by death, regardless of suffering. Therefore, the situation would still be serious even if what the objection claims were true.

The second problem is that there are strong reasons to consider what the objection claims to be false. For example, the brain of adult zebrafish has about 10 million neurons14, and that of their young only about 100,00015. Nevertheless, these young respond similarly to adults to the same stimuli that indicate that the adults are sentient16.

Moreover, owing to selective pressure, it is quite possible that animals with less developed cognitive capacities feel even more intensely17. When they are still young, or even before they hatch, since they do not yet have developed cognitive capacities, the only motivation for their behavior and learning is to avoid negative experiences and seek positive ones. This is especially true of precocial animals, since they need to be quite active in order to break the shell and hatch, and also to have any chance of surviving after hatching18, since in oviparous species it is very common for the young to receive no parental care.

3.4. Conclusion

Given what we have seen, there seem to be no reasons to suppose that the number of animals who are victims of natural processes is small, nor that they are less capable of suffering than other animals.

4. The View That It Is Not a Problem Because the Victims Are Nonhuman Animals

4.1. The Disregard for Nonhuman Animals

The situation of animals in the wild is normally seen as a relevant problem only if it indirectly affects human interests or environmentalist goals, such as the preservation of biodiversity or of ecological balance. Underlying this view is the idea that the good of nonhuman animals does not matter in itself.

Below we will see why this view is mistaken. More specifically, we will see: (1) why the good of nonhuman animals matters in itself and (2) why this problem is just as important as it would be if it were humans suffering harms of the same magnitude.

4.2. Why the Good of Nonhuman Animals Matters in Itself

The view we are discussing assumes that the good of nonhuman animals does not matter in itself, but only insofar as it indirectly affects human interests or environmentalist goals (such as preserving species or ecosystems, for example). Such a view therefore assumes that the good of humans matters in itself and/or that the nonsentient entities valued in environmentalism matter in themselves.

One problem for this view is that what really explains why the good of humans matters in itself implies that the good of any other sentient being also matters in itself and, moreover, does not imply that nonsentient entities matter in themselves.

The reason humans are directly morally considerable is simply that they can be harmed and benefited. It is not because they have a set of complex capacities or a set of relationships with one another. So much so that humans who lack such capacities or relationships (such as young children and victims of certain accidents or diseases that affect cognitive capacities) are also directly morally considerable, and just as much as humans who have those capacities and relationships. The purpose of giving moral consideration to someone is to avoid harming and to seek to benefit that someone. Therefore, for someone to be morally considerable, it is necessary and sufficient that they can be harmed and benefited. Therefore, humans are morally considerable not because they are human, nor because they have a set of capacities or relationships, but simply because they can be harmed and benefited.

What makes humans capable of being harmed and benefited is the fact that they are sentient. It is sentience that makes there be someone “inhabiting” a body (as opposed to a merely living, yet empty, body). It is also sentience that makes it possible for an individual to experience certain states as positive and others as negative, because sentience is what makes someone capable of having experiences in the first place.

Accordingly, what really explains why the good of humans matters in itself automatically implies that the good of any other sentient being, whatever species it belongs to, also matters in itself. Moreover, as we have seen, this does not imply that nonsentient entities, such as species and ecosystems, matter in themselves. This shows how mistaken the idea is that the good of nonhuman animals matters only indirectly (whether to human interests or to environmentalist goals).

4.3. Why the Good of Animals Matters as Much as That of Humans

Someone could accept that the good of nonhuman animals matters in itself and still insist that the situation of wild animals is not a very important problem, as it would be if the victims were human. This is because, according to this view, the good of nonhuman animals, although it matters in itself, matters much less than the good of humans. Below we will see why this view is arbitrary.

If we have reasons to give moral consideration to someone because that someone can be harmed and benefited, then this implies that the strength of these reasons must depend on the magnitude of the harms and benefits in question, and not on the species of those who would be affected. That is, any unbiased view will hold that harms and benefits of similar magnitude in different individuals must have the same degree of importance (and that greater harms and benefits must have greater importance than lesser ones).

It could be objected that we sometimes have reasons to prioritize helping those who suffer the lesser harm. This would be the case, for example, if those who suffer the greater harm had done something to deserve that harm. However, this is not the case with nonhuman animals (since, like human babies, they cannot be held morally responsible). Moreover, unlike matters of desert (which depend on choices for which agents can be held responsible), the species to which someone belongs – like their race or gender – is a result of the natural lottery and is therefore beyond individuals' control (and so cannot result in merit or demerit).

Another reason why giving greater weight to the good of humans is a biased attitude is that it does not pass the impartiality test, since it would not be considered fair if we did not know which species we belonged to. This means that those who defend such a position do so only because they know they will be in the group it privileges. This by itself already shows that such a position would not pass the impartiality test. Impartiality is the main characteristic of justice. Therefore, there is no way such a position can be just.

4.4. Conclusion

If the argument above is sound, then the good of nonhuman animals matters in itself, and it matters as much as that of humans. This implies that we should give as much attention to the situation of animals in the wild who are victims of natural processes as we would if the victims were human.

5. Foundations of the Proposal to Help Victims of Natural Processes

5.1. Introduction

In Chapter 1 we briefly saw some of the reasons on which the proposal to help animals in the wild who are victims of natural processes is based. In this chapter, the foundations of this proposal will be explained in more detail.

5.2. The Argument from the Existence of Reasons

The argument from the existence of reasons holds that the explanation of why we should prevent anthropogenic harms implies that we should prevent natural harms. If it is the negative character of harms that generates reasons for us to avoid them in our practices, then we have equal reasons to prevent natural harms (since they are still negative). Harms are negative because of their own characteristics, which do not depend on their origin (therefore, natural harms are negative, not neutral in terms of value).

5.3. The Argument from the Strength of Reasons

The argument from the strength of reasons holds that if it is the negative character of harms that generates reasons for us to prevent them, then the strength of these reasons depends on the magnitude of the harms (and not on their origin). That is, given two harms of equal magnitude, one anthropogenic and the other not, all else being equal (for example, the possibility of preventing both to the same extent), we have direct reasons of equal weight to try to prevent both. And, given two harms of different magnitude, all else being equal, we have reasons to prioritize preventing the greater harm. This implies that the reasons to prevent natural harms will be stronger whenever doing so means preventing a greater magnitude of harm with the same amount of resources.

5.4. Implications of Both Arguments

If the argument from the existence of reasons and the argument from the strength of reasons are sound, we must reject not only the view that we have no reasons to prevent or minimize natural harms, but also the view that these reasons exist but are weaker compared with equivalent anthropogenic harms.

5.5. The Argument from the Weight of the Criterion

Let us suppose, for the sake of argument, that anthropogenic harms should carry greater weight . Even so, this would not imply that minimizing anthropogenic harms would always have priority over minimizing natural harms. That would be the case only if minimizing anthropogenic harms were a trump. If it had greater weight (even much greater), but did not amount to a trump, the priority could be reversed in certain cases. There would have to be a point beyond which, given the possibility of greatly minimizing natural harms at the cost of slightly less minimization of anthropogenic harms, we would have to prioritize minimizing natural harms. Assigning greater weight to anthropogenic harms would also not imply that minimizing natural harms is praiseworthy but not obligatory. These would be somewhat lesser obligations (but not small ones for that reason; they would even take priority depending on the situation).

Important: this supposition was made merely for the sake of argument, in order to show that, even if we gave greater weight to anthropogenic harms, we would still have strong reasons to minimize natural harms. However, given what we have discussed in this section, there do not seem to be good reasons to give greater weight to anthropogenic harms: what matters is the magnitude of harm that could be prevented with a given amount of resources, not the origin of the harm.

6. Is the Proposal to Help Wild Animals Arrogant?

The proposal to help wild animals is sometimes accused of being arrogant because it involves interventions in the natural course of things19. It is commonly said that those who advocate helping wild animals are “playing God.” Does this accusation make sense?

Interventions in the natural course of things are widely accepted and practiced, as long as the goal is anthropocentric or environmentalist. For example, building homes, schools, hospitals, and libraries, agriculture, medicine, and interventions to keep ecosystems in the configurations valued by environmentalism are not accused of arrogance or of “playing God.” Yet they involve massive interventions in the natural course of things.

Indeed, helping animals who are victims of natural processes is widely accepted and practiced, as long as the goal is anthropocentric or environmentalist. One example is vaccinating wild animals in order to prevent the transmission of disease to humans, to animals who live alongside humans, or to animals whom humans intend to exploit directly. Another example is vaccinating wild animals to preserve endangered species.

This suggests that, despite what they say, those who make the accusation of arrogance are not opposed to intervening in nature or in natural processes. Rather, they are opposed to the goal of benefiting nonhuman animals.

Moreover, there is nothing in this objection that actually shows that it is wrong to intervene in the natural course of things. So even if there were someone who rejected any and every intervention in nature (whether to benefit nonhuman animals, to benefit humans, or to achieve environmentalist goals), this would not show that their position is correct.

At other times it is argued that the arrogance lies not in intervening in natural processes, but in the fact that, by choosing to help, we are deciding the fate of those animals. Obviously, however, by deciding not to help we are equally deciding their fate. The difference is that, if we choose not to help, the fate of these animals will be suffering and death.

A similar objection arises when it is said that those who advocate helping animals are arrogant because they are trying to make the world the way they want it to be. But, again, when someone takes a stand against helping, they too are trying to make the world the way they want it to be. In one case, the person wants the world to stay as it is, and in the other, the person wants to change it. But in both cases people are equally trying to make the world the way they want.

  1. See, for example, Baldner (1990, p. 3). ↩

7. Is the Proposal to Help Wild Animals Anthropocentric?

There is an objection to the proposal to help wild animals that accuses it of imposing anthropocentric values on animals (or at least of humanizing them, by assuming that they value things only humans value)20.

A simple response to this objection is to point out that the aim of the proposal to help is to prevent occurrences that would in fact harm animals, such as suffering and premature deaths. It is not only humans who have an interest in avoiding suffering and in enjoying positive lives: these things are in the interest of any sentient being.

Nonhuman animals have no interest in having their suffering and premature deaths maximized so that nature can take its course. Only some humans value that (usually only when they themselves are not the victims, it should be said). Therefore, it is holding that “the right thing is to let nature take its course, even when this results in suffering or death for animals” that would amount to imposing anthropocentric values on animals (or at least humanizing them).

It could be objected that what is meant by the claim that the proposal to help animals is anthropocentric is that it implies that humans decide what will happen to animals in natural ecosystems. However, the appropriate word here would then be anthropogenic (in the sense of a practice carried out by humans), not anthropocentric (since the proposal in question aims to benefit nonhuman animals). Moreover, when our decision has the power to change a situation, we decide what will happen in it, whether we decide to change it or decide to leave it as it is. So those who are against helping wild animals are equally deciding what will happen to animals in natural ecosystems.

Author’s notes

  1. See, for example, Kirkwood and Sainsbury (1996, p. 239). ↩

8. The Less Human Influence in the World, the Better?

It is sometimes argued that the proposal to help wild animals should be rejected because “the less human influence in the world, the better.” This claim can mean at least two different things. We will discuss each of them below.

The Less Human Influence, the Better for Animals?

First, it may mean that the less human influence there is in the world, the better the outcome for animals. But if that is what it means, then the claim is false, since in this case these interventions would be meant to help animals, not to harm them. From the fact that there is an enormous number of human practices that harm animals, it does not follow that every human action will be harmful to animals, or that it will necessarily be worse than letting nature take its course.

The idea that “the less human influence, the better for animals” may arise from a lack of awareness that, as we saw in Chapter 3, natural processes already tend to maximize the number of animals born only to have a life full of suffering and to die prematurely21. It is also possible that it is just an excuse for not worrying about the situation of animals. That is, the apparent concern about making things worse for animals may simply be a disguise for indifference to what happens to them.

The Less Human Influence, the Better, Period?

However, what the objection may mean is the following: the less influence in the world, the better, even if the result of this lesser influence is worse for animals than if there were more human influence.

A first criticism that can be made of this approach is that it would make sense only if it also made sense to think that a world with even more suffering and deaths than it would have with human influence is preferable, if that is the price to be paid for there being less

human influence in the world. No one seems to accept this in their own case. For example, when we are in a hospital emergency room, we want the doctors to help us. Thus, this approach does not pass the impartiality test, since we would not defend it if we did not know who its victims would be.

Moreover, the objection in question simply postulates that human influence is wrong in itself, even when the outcome is positive for animals. But it would have to be explained why this is so, and the objection in question does not do this. From the fact that humans often do bad things, it does not follow that what makes those things bad is that they were done by humans. They are bad because they harm their victims.

Thus, if we adopt a standpoint of genuine concern for the victims, we will not say that “the less human influence, the better.” Instead, we will say that humans should avoid harming them as much as possible and seek to benefit them as much as possible. In short, if we believe that whether a decision is right or wrong depends on whether those affected by it are benefited or harmed, then we will reject the notion that “the less human influence, the better,” since it is possible to exert influence in positive ways, and not only in negative ones.

Author’s notes

  1. For a detailed explanation of why this is so, see Horta (2010). ↩

9. Is the Proposal to Help Wild Animals Welfarist?

Those who reject the proposal to help wild animals sometimes accuse it of being welfarist. The adjective welfarist is used in many senses. For example, in the debate over the morality of animal exploitation, it is used in at least three different senses, explained below.

A first sense refers to the position that there is nothing morally wrong with animal exploitation, as long as the animals' suffering is minimized during their use (even if the use causes death and some suffering).

A second sense refers to the position that accepts that animal exploitation is unjust and should be abolished, but holds that regulating it may lead to its abolition.

Finally, a third sense refers to the position that accepts that animal exploitation is unjust and should be abolished, but holds that regulating it makes animals suffer less, and that this is something that should be done regardless of whether or not it helps abolish it.

There is a debate about whether or not regulations would lead to the abolition of animal exploitation, and about whether they really make animals suffer less. We do not need to enter into this debate for our purpose here, which is to evaluate the claim that the proposal to help wild animals is welfarist.

To avoid confusion (and to see what confusion is involved in the objection we are discussing), we will not call these three positions “welfarist.” Instead, we will use the adjective “regulationist.”

Since regulationist positions are usually called welfarist, people commonly fall into the confusion of thinking that, because a certain position is concerned with the well-being of animals (as is the case with the proposal to help wild animals), it is necessarily regulationist (in one of the three senses above). As explained below, there is no such implication.

The debate over regulationism is a debate either: (1) about the morality of animal exploitation (in the case of the first sense of the term); (2) about whether regulating animal exploitation can help abolish it (in the case of the second sense of the term); or (3) about whether regulating it really reduces animals' suffering (in the third sense of the term).

The position someone holds regarding the morality of minimizing natural harms has no direct implication whatsoever for any of the three debates, since we cannot infer, from the fact that someone cares about the well-being of animals, what position they hold in these three debates.

For example, even those who argue that animal exploitation becomes just if it is regulated so that animals suffer less claim to care (at least to some minimal degree) about the well-being of animals (otherwise, they would not argue that it needs to be regulated so that animals suffer less). But those who advocate the abolition of exploitation also care about the well-being of animals (if the well-being of animals did not matter to these people, they would not advocate abolishing animal exploitation). Likewise, those who argue that regulating animal exploitation helps abolish it and/or reduces animals' suffering are concerned with the well-being of animals, but so are those who disagree with that strategy.

It could be objected that abolitionists care only about the freedom of animals, and not about their well-being. There are two problems with this objection. The first is that if abolitionists really give moral consideration to nonhuman animals, then they must take into account the interests of animals as a whole, and not only their interest in freedom. Since nonhuman animals have an interest in not suffering and in not dying, an abolitionist position that did not take these interests into account would hardly be plausible. The second problem is that even a position focused solely on securing freedom is also a position focused on concern for the well-being of individuals, since if such a position holds that “animals are better off if they are free,” what it is claiming is that freedom is a component (instrumental and/or intrinsic) of their well-being22.

Accordingly, the proposal to minimize natural harms is concerned with the well-being of animals. However, this does not make it a welfarist (that is, regulationist) proposal, since it is not a position that bears on the debate about regulating animal exploitation, in any of the three senses above.

In short, whatever position someone holds in the debates about regulationism (in any of the three senses above), this is no obstacle to accepting the proposal to help wild animals who are victims of natural processes.

Author’s notes

  1. An introduction to theories of well-being can be read here. See also Fletcher (2016) and Santos (2017). ↩

10. Does the Proposal to Help Wild Animals Violate Their Freedom?

It is sometimes argued that the proposal to help wild animals should be rejected because it would allegedly violate the freedom of the animals who would be helped.

The response to this objection consists simply in pointing out that exactly the opposite is the case. This proposal is in fact essential for animals to exercise their freedom, since it would prevent the things that hinder its exercise: extreme suffering and premature death. In short, it is not helping animals that results in animals being unable to exercise their freedom, since they will be dead or in extreme suffering.

It could be objected that there are situations in which we must choose between securing an animal's freedom and ensuring that it is free from suffering or death. This would be the case, for example, if we had to choose between either leaving an animal free in the wild, but subject to all the risks this entails, or removing it from there and placing it in, say, a sanctuary, where it would be cared for and protected but would have access to a much smaller area.

A first important point to note about this objection is that it assesses the degree of freedom by the size of the space available for movement. But there is another way of assessing the degree of freedom: by the extent to which someone is able to fulfill their interests. According to this second way of assessing it, it is possible to have less space and more freedom, and vice versa. For example, if an animal is in the wild, it will have more space than in a sanctuary. But if this also means being injured, diseased, without access to food or water, being attacked, etc., it means not fulfilling even its most basic interests. Likewise, it is possible that in another situation the animal has less space but, because it is cared for and protected, its possibility of fulfilling its interests is much greater. In short, if the degree of freedom depends on the extent to which someone fulfills their interests, this does not necessarily coincide with being in a larger territorial area.

Note that this does not imply that it would therefore be better for animals to be in zoos, precisely because being in a zoo does not coincide with animals being able to fulfill their interests. Sanctuaries are essentially different from zoos. In a sanctuary, the goal is to benefit the animals. In a zoo, the goal is to provide entertainment for humans, disregarding what would be best for the animals.

However, let us suppose for the sake of argument that freedom should be defined solely in terms of the size of the area someone is in. If so, it is not at all clear that what is best for animals would be to be in a larger area, suffer more, and die prematurely.

It could be objected that many animals flee from attempts to rescue them from disaster situations such as fires and floods, or from attempts to vaccinate them, and that this shows that what animals value most is being free from human interference, even if this means suffering more and dying prematurely. However, the appropriate way to assess what someone values most is not by what that someone actually chooses, but by what that someone would choose if they had access to the relevant information23. In the cases in question, the animals very probably flee because they do not know that, in these cases, the humans are there to help them, and above all because they do not know the terrible fate that awaits them in a fire or a flood. If this information were available to them, they would very probably choose to receive help.

Thus, if freedom is defined in terms of the size of the territorial area, then the claim that animals value freedom above everything else is false. This also holds in the human case. For example, given the definition of freedom the objection assumes, if we were dropped in the middle of the Sahara desert we would have more freedom. But no one chooses this for themselves, precisely because they know it would mean suffering and death. This shows that we value being free from suffering and not dying more highly than being in a larger area. And there is no reason to think that the opposite happens in the case of animals, since they too are seriously harmed by suffering and by death.

Some people argue that animals should be left to fend for themselves, “free” in the wild to suffer and die, not because the animals value this, but because they themselves value leaving animals in such conditions. But if so, then the claim that such a position is concerned with respecting animals' interests is merely a rhetorical device, aimed at masking a position that in fact involves a complete disregard

for animals. Those who hold this position often tend to accuse the proposal to help wild animals of being anthropocentric. As should now be clear, it is this position that is anthropocentric.

In fact, this is very common. There are a number of positions that advocate attitudes highly harmful to animals, but present themselves as positions concerned with respecting them. At the same time, those who hold these positions tend to portray genuine proposals to defend and help animals as involving some disrespect for animals. This is a common strategy, for example, among those who exploit animals and in the discourse that tries to justify environmentalist practices of killing animals24. It is therefore to be expected that the same strategy of dishonest rhetoric would emerge among those who are against helping animals living in the wild.

Author’s notes

  1. On this, see Sobel (1994). ↩
  2. The divergences between consideration for animals and environmentalism are the subject of the fifth volume of this collection. For a detailed critical analysis of this rhetoric on the part of environmentalists, see Genovez (2023b). For an example of these killing practices in Brazil, see Conabio (2009). For an example in Europe, see Council of Europe (2016, 2020). For a critique of this kind of practice in Brazil, see Ética Animal (2021b). For a general critique, see Shelton (2004) and Faria (2011, 2012). ↩

11. The Charge of Creating Dependency

There is an objection to the proposal to help wild animals that holds that helping them would make them dependent on human care and would take away their ability to survive.

This objection does not apply to a large part (perhaps most) of the proposal to prevent or minimize natural harms. For example, it does not apply to any program aimed at reducing the number of births (such as sterilization and research into which kinds of elements in the environment result in lower birth rates), nor to the proposal to suspend the environmentalist and anthropocentric interventions that indirectly contribute to natural processes maximizing suffering and deaths.

Even in the case of providing food, water, medicines, vaccines, and treatments, this does not necessarily take away animals' ability to survive. For example, let us imagine that some adult birds who are used to foraging for their food now find themselves in conditions of scarcity. Someone, noticing this situation, constantly provides them with birdseed. This does not make the animals lose the ability they have already acquired, since it does not make them lose their memory. It is not helping, in this case of scarcity, that would result in the animals no longer being able to exercise their ability to forage, since they would die of starvation.

What the objection assumes is that we must choose between the following two options: (1) either the animals have their well-being increased now by receiving help, but have it decreased in the long run by losing the ability to survive; (2) or the animals have their well-being decreased now by not receiving help, but have it increased in the long run by retaining the ability to survive.

However, helping them does not make them lose the ability to survive if they have already acquired it, nor does it prevent them from acquiring it. That is, helping increases their well-being in the short term and increases the possibility of their continuing to have well-being in the long term, without decreasing it. Not helping them decreases their well-being in the short term and very probably decreases it in the long term (or even guarantees that there will be no well-being at all in the long term, since it very probably means their deaths).

Let us suppose that helping animals did make them dependent on human care. It would make sense to hold that, from an anthropocentric point of view, the best thing to do is not to help (helping would create extra work for humans that would not exist if the animals were left to die). But from the point of view of the animals who could be helped, is it really better for them to remain independent, suffer more, and die soon? To defend such a conclusion, one would have to claim that if the animals were aware of everything at stake and had the capacity to deliberate about what is best for themselves, they would prefer to suffer intensely and die just to remain independent. We can see that this is false from the human case itself: those who have the capacity to deliberate about these things prefer to receive help rather than be left to suffer intensely and die25.

Author’s notes

  1. Of course, it could be objected that providing food to certain animals may cause more suffering and deaths than it prevents if it indirectly increases reproduction rates and, consequently, deaths from starvation. However, that is an objection of a different kind, which will be discussed in Chapter 24. ↩

12. The Charge of Paternalism

The proposal to help wild animals is sometimes accused of being paternalistic26, that is, of aiming to benefit the one affected, but against what they prefer27. A paternalistic action occurs, for example, when a child wants to drive a car and we stop them in order to protect them. Hence the name paternalism, since it refers to the action of parents toward their children.

Given this definition of paternalism, however, helping animals in the wild is not paternalistic. It would be only if they preferred not to be helped in situations of starvation, parasitism, disease, accidents, fires, floods, etc. Of course, there are cases in which animals flee from attempts to help them. But this does not show that they prefer not to be helped. They probably flee because they do not understand that someone is there to provide help.

Moreover, the thesis that paternalism is always unjustified can be questioned. If every paternalistic action were wrong, the only appropriate way to raise and care for children would be to do everything they wanted. But it makes sense to accuse of negligence someone who did not stop a child from driving a car, or did not give them first aid just because the child did not want it. If so, then there are paternalistic actions that are justified.

What justifies paternalism in these cases is that the child in question lacks the relevant information about how satisfying the desire in question will affect their well-being as a whole. But that is the condition of nonhuman animals as well. Therefore, even if helping them were paternalistic, it would be of the justified kind.

The Objection That the Satisfaction of Desires Should Sometimes Weigh More

It could be objected that the satisfaction of desires should sometimes weigh more than the content of positive and negative experiences. For example, suppose someone is terminally ill and all that awaits her from now on is intense suffering, but she still has one last desire to satisfy, which is very important to her. Although such a person is harmed in a certain respect if she stays alive (the suffering), she seems to be harmed

to a greater degree if she dies without fulfilling her last desire. It seems wrong to kill such a person to prevent her suffering (since she does not want to die).

However, what such an example suggests is that “there are unjustified paternalistic actions,” not that “all paternalistic actions are unjustified.” There are countless examples suggesting that paternalism is sometimes justified. For example, it is justified in the case of a child who has a lethal disease that is fortunately very easy to treat, and who refuses to take the medicine. So what we need to investigate is whether helping wild animals in nature who are victims of natural harms, if it were a paternalistic action (and, as we saw in the first response, it is not), would be justified or unjustified paternalism.

It could be suggested that the greater someone's degree of autonomy, the more unjustified paternalism is, given that the likelihood of achieving their good is greater if they make decisions for themselves (even if we determine someone's good solely on the basis of the balance between positive and negative experiences).

Even if this is true, it could not be the basis for an objection to the proposal to help animals in the wild. First, because, as we have seen, such action is not paternalistic. And even if it were, almost all nonhuman victims of natural harms have no autonomy of any kind (since they are newborns and juveniles). If the greater the autonomy, the more unjustified paternalism is, then the lesser the autonomy, the more justified paternalism is. This is why we generally consider paternalism more appropriate toward children than toward adults.

It could be objected that paternalism toward children would be justified because it would not really be paternalism, since children are not full rational agents. If so, however, then we must hold the same with respect to nonhuman animals, since they are not full rational agents either. That is, even if there were some nonhuman animal who preferred to remain in a situation in which its suffering would be increased, it would very probably not be in a favorable epistemic position to see what is best for its well-being. Therefore, even if helping it were paternalistic, it would be the justified kind of paternalism.

Author’s notes

  1. This accusation is made by Regan (2004 [1983], p. XXXVI-XXXVIII). ↩
  2. For this definition of paternalism, see Regan (2004 [1983], p. 103-109). ↩

13. The Objection That Suffering Has Instrumental Value

One objection to the proposal to help wild animals holds that we should not minimize suffering because it has instrumental value for the very being who suffers28. For example, pain helps us avoid what would harm us.

However, suffering has instrumental value only in those situations in which the individual is able to use the sensation of suffering to increase their well-being (for example, to avoid harms greater than the suffering they are undergoing at the moment). This is not the case for the vast majority of animals who suffer in the wild because of natural processes. Such animals experience almost nothing but extreme suffering from the moment of birth until death. Rather than helping them promote their well-being, this suffering only harms them. Thus, even if we should not minimize instrumentally useful suffering, there would still be reasons to eliminate useless suffering.

Moreover, there are also reasons to avoid suffering even when it has instrumental value: whenever it is possible to achieve in some other way the positive outcome that would be achieved through suffering. This is precisely why we prefer to receive anesthesia before surgery. Accordingly, even in situations where suffering helped animals achieve something positive, there are reasons to research how to enable them to reach that positive state without having to suffer for it.

Author’s notes

  1. See, for example, Bovenkerk et al. (2003, p. 23) ↩

14. Does the Proposal to Help Animals See Humans as Separate from Nature?

The proposal to help wild animals is sometimes accused of seeing humans as something apart from nature. According to this view, if humans saw themselves as part of nature, they would advocate letting nature take its course, instead of trying to reduce the suffering and deaths of animals that result from natural processes.

One response to this objection points out that it is actually the position opposed to helping wild animals that seems to see humans as separate from nature, since it holds that if humans influence a situation, it ceases to be (or becomes less) natural.

At this point it could be objected that what is unnatural is the product of human actions, not humans themselves. On this conception, humans are part of nature, but an ecosystem that has undergone human interference is no longer natural. However, if a conception regards humans as part of nature, why would the product of human actions not also be a natural outcome? This shows that such a position is arbitrarily using two senses of the terms nature/natural. When it claims “humans are part of nature,” it defines nature as the physical world. When it claims “an ecosystem that has undergone human interference is no longer natural,” it defines natural as whatever is not the result of human practices. So, of course, on this conception the results of human practices will not be considered natural, since this has already been assumed to be true by definition.

It could be objected that, even if humans and the results of their actions are equally natural, it is a fact that the proposal to help wild animals goes against natural processes (such as hunger, thirst, disease, etc.). However, this implies that helping animals is wrong only if it is always wrong to go against natural processes. But there are good reasons to reject this thesis. The main one is the following. Natural processes are not someone. Therefore, they are not harmed if they are thwarted (since there is no one there to be harmed). On the other hand, the victims of these processes certainly are harmed if we allow the natural processes that harm them to take place.

Therefore, for us to have a duty not to thwart such natural processes, it would have to be shown that: (1) we have obligations toward entities that cannot be harmed or benefited; and that (2) these obligations are stronger than those we have toward individuals who can be harmed and benefited. Needless to say, these two theses are very difficult to ground.

In fact, no one accepts these theses for themselves. Someone who accepted them would have to try not to protect themselves from catching diseases, not to get treatment when they fell ill, not to wear clothes, not to live in a house, not to try to escape a natural disaster, not to protect themselves against parasites, and so on. The thesis that it is wrong to go against natural processes is defended only when the victims are nonhuman animals. This shows that such a position is unjust for at least two reasons. The first is that its proponents do not hold it for themselves. This by itself is already completely arbitrary. The second is that its proponents defend it only when nonhuman animals are the victims. This shows that such a position does not pass the impartiality test, since its proponents would not defend it if they did not know which species they belonged to.

15. If Nature Is Not Evil, Is Natural Suffering Neutral?

One objection to the proposal to help wild animals claims that, because the suffering in question is natural, it is neutral in terms of value (that is, it would not be something negative, as suffering caused by humans is), and that there are therefore no reasons to prevent it29.

Sometimes what gives rise to this idea is a confusion between what is relevant for someone to be held responsible and what is relevant for assessing whether a situation is negative. For example, it is sometimes said that “nature is neither good nor evil, it simply is, so we have no reasons to prevent natural suffering.” It is true that the term “nature” refers to a set of ongoing processes and not to a person, and so it makes no sense to hold these processes responsible. However, the fact that the source of the suffering cannot be held responsible does not make the suffering neutral in terms of value. This will be explained in more detail below.

A young child cannot be held responsible, but if she hits someone on the head with a club, the suffering is negative for the victim, and this gives us reasons to help that victim and to prevent it from happening again. The same is true of suffering resulting from natural processes. Nature is not a responsible agent when humans are the victims either. But this does not make such harms neutral, nor does it mean that we cease to have reasons to help these victims or to prevent natural suffering from occurring. This kind of view appears almost exclusively when nonhuman animals are the victims, given the overwhelming predominance of a speciesist view.

What makes suffering negative are its own characteristics. Suffering is the kind of experience whose central characteristic is being negative for the one who experiences it (if it is not experienced as negative, it is not suffering). And suffering is negative entirely independently of whether it originated in human practices or in natural processes. Therefore, it is false that natural suffering is neutral in terms of value. Suffering is a negative event, regardless of its origin.

What generates reasons to prevent suffering is its negative character. If so, then the greater the magnitude of the suffering, the stronger these reasons. We therefore have reasons to prevent natural suffering (since it remains negative for its victims), and these reasons are just as strong as those we have to prevent equivalent anthropogenic suffering.

Author’s notes

  1. For a detailed response to this objection, see Sapontzis (1987, p. 230-1) and Cunha (2022, p. 99-110). ↩

16. If Nature Is Indifferent to the Suffering of Animals, Why Help Them?

Nature is indifferent to the suffering and death of animals. Ecosystems arise, endure, and disappear with complete indifference to the fate of animals. Some people believe this fact shows that we should not help animals who are victims of natural processes. For example, the philosopher J. Baird Callicott holds that the proposal to help animals should be rejected because it involves not accepting that suffering and death are part of life: “it is a view that denies the way things are and always have been”30.

But is it really the case that those who advocate helping animals who are victims of natural harms do not accept that suffering and death are part of life? None of these proponents denies that there are great amounts of suffering and death in life; that this has been so since time immemorial; and that nature is indifferent to suffering and death (whoever's they may be, including humans'). What they hold is that this fact tells us nothing about whether or not we should minimize natural harms. If they denied that suffering and death are part of life, they could not prescribe minimizing natural harms, since they would be denying that such harms exist.

It is possible, however, that what the objection means is that those who advocate helping animals do not accept that suffering and death should be part of life. In that case, the accusation may be true. But it is not an obvious truth that suffering and death should be part of life. For example, we consider it justified to avoid our own suffering and death, even knowing that such things are part of life, that nature is indifferent to this, and that ecosystems arise, endure, and disappear regardless of it.

The objection would have to present some other argument to defend the claim that suffering and death should be part of life, since simply asserting that such things are part of life does not provide that justification, given that the fact that something happens does not imply that it is good, just, desirable, or even acceptable. In other words, the objection makes the mistake of assuming that because something is, it necessarily ought to be. Moreover, if everything that happened were justified, one could not object to anything at all, including intervening in nature to help animals. Therefore, in addition, this argument is self-refuting.

It could be objected that the thesis “if something is part of life, it should not be prevented” should apply only to natural harms. But, again, it would have to be explained why the fact that natural harms occur in life implies that we should not prevent them, while the fact that anthropogenic harms occur in life does not imply the same thing. What this objection does is simply assume this thesis without explaining it. But that is exactly what the objection sets out to explain. The objection says we should not prevent natural harms because they occur in life, but when confronted with the fact that anthropogenic harms also occur in life, the objection says that this case is different, because the harms in question are not natural. But then we can ask again, “Why should we not prevent natural harms?”, and so on ad infinitum. Therefore, the objection commits the fallacy of begging the question.

Accordingly, the fact that natural suffering is part of life does not imply that we should not prevent it.

Author’s notes

  1. See Callicott (1980, p. 333-6) ↩

17. Does Respecting the Nature of Wild Animals Require Leaving Them to Fend for Themselves?

There is a position that holds that each individual should be treated according to what fulfills its nature, and that this nature is determined by the territory to which each individual belongs31. According to this position, the nature of members of the domestic territory is fulfilled by a long life free from suffering, and that of members of the wild territory is fulfilled if they are left to fend for themselves in a hostile environment. This view has been used as an objection to the proposal to help wild animals who live in the wild and are victims of natural processes.

According to this view, what we should do depends on the territory to which each individual belongs (and not on where it happens to be). For example, if a human or a dog gets lost in a forest and is starving to death, this view advocates helping them and then returning them to the domestic territory. On the other hand, if a wild animal is having a positive life in the domestic territory, this position will advocate returning it to the wild territory, even if this makes it have a life full of suffering and a premature death.

One possible criticism of this view consists in pointing out that it chooses in a biased way what counts as the nature of the beings of each territory32. For example, it could be said that our nature, vulnerable to disease, is fulfilled when we do not treat ourselves with remedies of our own making. It could also be said that the nature of wild animals, like that of humans and domesticated animals, is also sentient, and is fulfilled when it is free from suffering. In short, the position in question is completely biased in favor of members of the domestic territory and against members of the wild territory.

It seems no coincidence that the proponents of the view in question all belong to the domestic territory: this view would never be accepted if we did not know which territory we belonged to. If so, then it does not pass the impartiality test, and is therefore unjust.

There is an additional reason to reject this view. When we hear about “fulfilling the nature of each being,” we tend to think of something that benefits the beings in question.

But, as we have seen, what the view we are discussing advocates is fulfilling the nature of wild animals by leaving them to fend for themselves, even if this results in their suffering enormously and dying. Thus, another possible criticism of this view consists in pointing out that it is based on the idea that the right action should be determined entirely independently of what harms or benefits those affected by our decisions. So if how we positively or negatively affect those affected by our decisions is what matters, we must reject the idea that the right thing is to fulfill the nature of each being if doing so will harm them.

In short, we must ask the following: why should we respect someone's nature? If the answer is “because doing so would benefit them,” then it is false that respecting the nature of wild animals requires leaving them to fend for themselves, since this would probably harm them. If, on the other hand, the answer is “just because, even when it would harm them,” then no reason at all is being given to explain why respecting someone's nature would be more important than avoiding harming them.

Author’s notes

  1. See, for example, Everett (2001, p. 65). ↩
  2. For a detailed critique of the territory criterion, see Cunha (2022, p. 110-124). ↩

18. Isn't It Absurd to Intervene in Conflicts Between Animals?

In the wild, animals routinely engage in conflicts with animals of other species33 (as in cases of predation and parasitism) and with animals of the same species34 (as in disputes over food and territory, and also in sexual conflicts35). It is sometimes claimed that the proposal to help wild animals is absurd because it implies intervening in such conflicts36. In this chapter we will discuss the general question of conflicts between animals. The question of parasitism will be discussed in more detail in Chapter 30, and the question of predation in Chapter 31.

There are two variations of this objection. The first says that intervening in these conflicts is wrong because it could result in something even worse than doing nothing. For example, it is commonly pointed out that if we prevent cases of predation, prey animals could reproduce even more, and the result could be even more suffering and more deaths than if nothing were done (for example, through an increase in the number of deaths from starvation due to the increase in the number of births).

One problem with this first variation is that what the proposal to help advocates is researching ways to make the outcome over time better than if nothing were done. Therefore, such a proposal would not say to intervene in cases where doing so would have even worse results than doing nothing. Nor would it say not to plan interventions. Poorly planned interventions could certainly have even worse results than doing nothing. But this does not show that well-planned interventions would have worse results than doing nothing. For example, interventions that directly or indirectly reduced primary productivity (that is, the plants that form the base of the food chain) would tend to reduce the total number of births37 and would therefore escape the objection that the intervention would risk increasing the number of births38.

The second variation of the objection, by contrast, holds that even if doing nothing results in more suffering and deaths over time, the right thing is not to intervene. For example, it is sometimes said that the fact that predators and parasites need to attack other organisms in order to survive makes it wrong to intervene.

We will reject this variation if we reject the idea that an action can be right while having even worse results than other available options. Moreover, it could be pointed out that this variation is speciesist, since when the victims are human, predators and parasites also need to attack in order to survive, yet it is not said that this makes it wrong to rescue the victims.

Large-scale interventions in predation have been widely practiced for many decades39. These interventions aim to protect humans or domesticated animals whom humans intend to exploit. At other times, they aim to achieve environmentalist goals, such as preserving rare species of animals or plants. This suggests that a double standard is commonly adopted: if the intervention has an anthropocentric or environmentalist goal, it is accepted without having to prove that it will have better results; if the intervention is centered on concern for the good of animals, it is rejected even if it has better results. This is the result of the predominance of speciesism.

It is sometimes argued that conflicts between animals do not raise an ethical problem because the animals themselves cannot be held responsible40. But we already saw in Chapter 2 the problems with this kind of view: just as when humans are victims of natural processes, we have reasons to try to help the victims because suffering is negative, and it is negative regardless of whether or not it originated from a responsible agent41.

At other times it is argued that intervening would be taking sides and would therefore violate impartiality. However, this argument confuses neutrality with impartiality. What impartiality requires is not favoring or disfavoring anyone in a biased way. For example, impartiality implies that levels of harm and benefit of similar magnitude in different individuals receive the same weight. This does not imply that, if we do this,

we will conclude that we should not intervene in the situation. For example, if someone has taken into account all the affected animals, whether predators or prey, given equal weight to the good of each, and concluded that the right thing is to intervene because in this way there will be less suffering and fewer premature deaths over time, they are not being biased. On the contrary: they are doing exactly what they would do if they did not know who those affected were (thus meeting the requirement of impartiality). On the other hand, holding that it is right to intervene only if the victims are human is speciesist and therefore violates impartiality.

None of this necessarily means that, given the current state of knowledge, intervening in such conflicts would be the best thing to do to prevent the harms animals suffer in the wild (although it may mean that, as more knowledge about this issue becomes available, preventing such conflicts from occurring might become a promising way of reducing natural harms). It does show, however, that intervening in such conflicts is not wrong in itself.

19. Which Fields Should Answer What to Do About Wild Animals?

Those who advocate helping animals living in the wild are sometimes accused of thinking that a question belongs to the field of ethics when it actually belongs to the field of ecology: “they are making value judgments where such judgments do not belong: they need some basic notions of ecology.” Does this criticism make sense? That is what we will discuss in this chapter.

Describing what happens in natural ecosystems is a task for ecology. However, those who advocate helping wild animals recognize this, and they rely precisely on this knowledge to get an idea of the amount of suffering and death that exists in nature and of how interactions in ecosystems take place, in order then, on the basis of ethical principles, to prescribe what should be done about it. So it makes no sense to suggest that those who advocate helping animals in the wild should study ecology, since that is exactly what they are doing as well. The proposal to create the field of welfare biology42 (which we will look at in more detail in Chapter 27) is a good example of this.

Describing what happens in natural ecosystems is a task for ecology. However, investigating which things have intrinsic value and which have value only as resources is a question for value theory. Establishing which goals we should pursue is a question for the field of ethics. It is these two fields that will provide us with the tools to reflect on whether what we should seek to secure is the good of sentient beings, or whether nonsentient entities such as species and ecosystems have intrinsic value and, if they do, how to weigh this against the good of sentient beings43. This is a debate about what has value and about what we should do. No descriptive science has the answer to these questions. Therefore, those who make the mistake of treating a question from one field as if it belonged to another are those who think that descriptive fields ground what we should value and how we should act.

Moreover, it is not only those who advocate helping animals in the wild who are making moral judgments about what happens in ecosystems. Saying “we should not help

animals living in the wild” is also a moral judgment44. The same happens when someone argues that our goals should be to secure biodiversity and ecological balance, rather than to reduce the suffering of sentient beings. One reason such a position is usually not perceived as involving moral judgments is that it is sometimes advocated by scientists. The discourse of scientists is received by the public as an objective and morally neutral description of the facts. However, as we have seen, it often contains hidden normative and evaluative premises.

Sometimes a moral judgment is intentionally disguised as a description so that it seems neutral, since this increases its chances of being accepted. In this way, listeners unwittingly absorb a whole set of values and rules, thinking that they are simply hearing descriptions, and they reproduce this cycle when they talk about the subject. This is something that sometimes happens even on the part of professionals and students in scientific fields themselves. One reason this happens is that there are often no courses on ethics in scientific degree programs, and so students do not clearly distinguish the descriptive, evaluative, and normative domains. Moreover, in many of these programs environmentalist or anthropocentric values are generally conveyed to students implicitly, and therefore there is no discussion of whether or not they are plausible.

The presence of environmentalist values among life science professionals may give the impression that those who hold that the good of each sentient being matters in itself lack the appropriate scientific knowledge. But this is an illusion, which is due in part to the confusion between the terms “ecology” and “environmentalism”. Environmentalism is the idea that certain nonsentient entities (such as species or ecosystems) should receive direct moral consideration (that is, that they matter in themselves, and not as a means of securing the good of sentient beings), and that they matter more than the good of sentient beings. Ecology, on the other hand, is the science that describes how interactions in ecosystems take place. Animal advocates hold an ethical conception completely different from the one held by environmentalism. However, they do not reject knowledge in ecology (in fact, they depend on such knowledge in order to be able to help wild animals safely).

Science describes the physical world. We need these descriptions in order to try to achieve the goals we pursue. However, since science only describes, it does not tell us which goals to pursue or which things to value. The fields that can tell us something about this are value theory and ethics. Accordingly, ecology would never prescribe that we should value species, ecosystems, biodiversity, or anything else, simply because it only describes how interactions in ecosystems take place – it is not about which things to value or which goals to pursue: it prescribes nothing. People who say they are opposed to helping wild animals and claim that in doing so they are “just applying what ecology dictates” are in fact concealing that they are defending a moral position called environmentalism, and disguising this moral position as a neutral description.

Given the predominance of speciesism, knowledge from fields such as ecology has generally been employed with a view to achieving anthropocentric or environmentalist goals. However, a perspective centered on concern for sentient beings in no way prevents or diminishes knowledge in these fields. The only difference would be that such knowledge would be used to benefit animals, not to harm them. Moreover, concern for animals could even greatly expand such knowledge, since interest in knowing how they are affected as individuals who have a well-being (and not as components of ecosystems and specimens of species) is still largely neglected. We will return to this subject in Chapter 27.
