20. Must Environmentalists Oppose Helping Wild Animals?

20.1. Introduction

Respect for animals and environmentalism have very divergent foundations and goals45. Environmentalists value nonsentient entities, such as species and ecosystems, in themselves. Respect for animals, meanwhile, is grounded in consideration for sentient individuals, capable of suffering and enjoyment46. Because of this divergence, one might think that once someone accepts environmentalist goals, they must disagree with the proposal to help animals living in the wild, since that proposal is centered on concern for the good of individuals.

This view is mistaken for three reasons:

(1) There are some ways of helping wild animals that would also help achieve environmentalist goals.

(2) There are many ways of helping animals in the wild that, although they would not help achieve environmentalist goals, would not conflict with environmentalist goals.

(3) Even with respect to the ways of helping that would conflict with environmentalist goals, there are reasons to defend a priority of preventing the suffering and deaths of sentient beings over those goals (and this holds even if we ought to accept environmentalist goals).

Below we will look at each of these points in detail.

20.2. Ways of Helping Animals That Would Also Achieve Environmentalist Goals

There are programs to help wild animals that could help achieve both the goal of reducing animals' suffering and deaths and environmentalist goals. One example is the vaccination of bees47. From an environmentalist point of view, vaccinating them is good

because it reduces the risk of extinction of bee species. Animal advocates, for their part, have reasons to approve of these programs because vaccination is good for the bees themselves, preventing them from getting sick and dying.

Another example is the protection of large herbivores. Environmentalists have reasons to protect them because several of their species are at risk of extinction. Animal advocates, for their part, have two strong reasons to support this kind of program. The first is that such programs reduce the suffering and deaths of the large herbivores themselves, who are then vaccinated, medicated, and given water, food, shelter, etc.48 The second, and more important, is that these animals consume a large amount of vegetation that, if it were available, would contribute to a greater number of births in those animal species whose vast majority are born only to suffer and die prematurely49. In short, protecting large herbivores can greatly reduce the total number of animals who would be born only to suffer and die prematurely.

Of course, this is a measure that must be investigated in depth, since in each population of large herbivores there could be some other factor that would make their presence increase the suffering of other animals in some other way. However, the aim here is only to show some examples of helping wild animals that both animal advocates and environmentalists could support, albeit for different reasons.

20.3. Ways of Helping Animals That Do Not Conflict with Environmentalist Goals

The proposal to help wild animals and environmentalist goals would perhaps not conflict in the vast majority of cases. For example, the different environmentalist positions on which entities are morally considerable (ecocentrism, biocentrism, and naturocentrism) have no reason to oppose the great majority of programs to help wild animals50. We will look at this in more detail below.

Ecocentrism51 values certain ecosystems (because they are very complex, very rare, formed a long time ago, etc.). Most programs to help

animals living in the wild would neither extinguish these ecosystems nor alter the properties of theirs that ecocentrists value: they would merely mean less suffering and fewer premature deaths for their inhabitants.

Biocentrism52, in turn, values what it calls the “good of its own” of each living organism, sentient or not. That is, what biocentrism aims at is not maximizing the number of living beings, but ensuring that each existing living being can achieve its own good. Biocentrism has to accept even more interventions than proponents of a sentience-centered ethics do, since it must seek to secure the good of sentient beings and, in addition, also protect nonsentient organisms.

Finally, naturocentrism53 values only ecosystems that have not yet been altered (or have been altered very little) by human activities. Given the climate change resulting from human practices, with the exception perhaps of some ecosystems in the depths of the ocean, all ecosystems have already been considerably altered by human practices. Therefore, naturocentrism would have to accept helping animals in all these ecosystems.

Of course, what has been said above does not mean that no environmentalist position whatsoever would ever conflict with the proposal to help wild animals. For example, there could be a variant of naturocentrism according to which ecosystems that have already been transformed by human action would still have value, but would have less value the more human interference had already occurred. According to such a position, we should seek to preserve the value that remains by prohibiting new interventions, or even restore the ecosystem to its state prior to the first human intervention. This variant would therefore oppose programs to help wild animals.

However, the fact that the proposal to help wild animals conflicts with environmentalist goals in certain cases does not mean that we should reject helping animals in those cases, since there may be reasons to prioritize the good of sentient beings over environmentalist goals. This will be explained in more detail in the next section.

20.4. Reasons to Prioritize Sentient Beings over Environmentalist Goals

Attempts are sometimes made to argue against the proposal to help wild animals by claiming that nonsentient entities such as species and ecosystems have value in themselves (and not as a means of securing the good of sentient beings). The idea that there is value beyond sentience is controversial, to say the least. However, let us suppose for the sake of argument that we ought to accept environmentalist goals. This would not imply that we must therefore reject the proposal to help wild animals. This is because, even if it were shown that the entities valued in environmentalism have intrinsic value, this would not show that they are more important than the good of sentient beings, much less that they are the only thing that matters. We will look at these points in more detail below.

If what is relevant for someone to be morally considerable is being capable of being harmed or benefited, then we must give moral consideration to all sentient beings, since sentience is what makes someone capable of being harmed or benefited, as we saw in Chapter 4. For this reason, the environmentalist view that nonsentient entities are morally considerable is already difficult to ground, and even more so the idea that sentient beings are not morally considerable, or that these entities are more important than the good of sentient beings.

For example, even if we accepted environmentalist goals, there would still be reasons, in cases of conflict, to prioritize sentient beings. One of these reasons is that, unlike the entities valued in environmentalism, sentient beings can literally be harmed and benefited, whether through negative experiences (all forms of suffering) or through being deprived of positive experiences (as happens when they die). These forms of harm are particularly serious (just consider how hard we try to avoid them ourselves), and no nonsentient entity is capable of suffering such harms.

When what is at stake is the good of humans, this is already widely accepted, including by environmentalists themselves. They generally hold that environmentalist goals are more important than certain human interests (such as economic and recreational interests), but they do not claim that we should leave humans to suffer and die as a result of natural processes. But if speciesism is unjustifiable, then there is also no justification for holding that we should not help animals who are victims of natural processes.

21. Are We Morally Responsible Only for Human Practices?

21.1. Moral responsibility and the origin of harm

Some people oppose the proposal to help wild animals who are victims of natural processes, claiming that we are morally responsible only for harms that result from human practices54. According to this view, if humanity decides not to allocate any resources to researching ways of reducing the suffering that wild animals endure as a result of natural processes, nothing wrong is done. Below, we will look at some criticisms of this position55.

A first criticism points out that, even if there were no obligation to help these animals, this would not show that it would be wrong to do so (doing so could still be permissible or even praiseworthy). For example, even those who deny that there is such an obligation could still claim that it is a good thing to do, since it could reduce enormous amounts of suffering and premature death. Therefore, denying the obligation to help does not imply that wild animals should not be helped, because denying an obligation is very different from grounding a prohibition.

A second criticism is that, even if we were morally responsible only for human practices, there are many human practices that create the conditions under which natural processes harm animals56. Therefore, even by the criterion the objection adopts, there would be an obligation to help animals in all these cases and to prevent such cases from occurring in the first place (and the number of such cases is not small, as we will see in Chapter 37).

Finally, the third criticism asks: "why would we be morally responsible only for human practices?" For example, another possibility is that we are morally responsible whenever we play a decisive role in influencing how events unfold. Below we will look at an example to illustrate this thesis.

Imagine that two simultaneous situations occur that result in human victims. In the first, a fire breaks out as a result of human practices. In the second, a fire breaks out as a result of a natural phenomenon that has no connection whatsoever with human practices. Imagine that the government has the resources to rescue the victims in both cases (and that using those resources to save them will not compromise anything of greater importance). Suppose, however, that help is denied to the victims in the second case, and that it is claimed that there is nothing wrong with this, since the harms in question were not caused by human practices. If we disagree with this decision, then we reject the thesis that we are morally responsible only for human practices.

Moreover, the idea that the origin of a harm should not determine our moral responsibilities can be grounded in the principle of impartiality. For example, if we knew that we would necessarily be victims of one of the two fires above, but without knowing which one, we would want the people who were in a position to help not to limit themselves to acknowledging responsibility only for harms caused by human practices.

We therefore have good initial reasons to reject the thesis that we are morally responsible only for human practices. Nevertheless, below we will discuss some further attempts to defend this thesis.

21.2. "But we don't cause these harms"

According to a certain view, in order to be morally responsible for a situation, we must have been the cause of that situation57. According to this view, it is wrong to consume animals (since this causes their deaths), but there is nothing wrong if humanity decides not to allocate any resources to helping wild animals who are victims of natural processes (such as hunger, thirst, disease, etc.), since in that case humans did not cause the situation that harms them (it existed long before humanity appeared). However, the following counterexample challenges the idea that, in order to be morally responsible for a decision, we must have caused the situation58.

Imagine that a tree is falling naturally and will fatally strike Maria. Fortunately, Ana is witnessing the scene, and all she needs to do to save Maria's life is to warn her that the tree is about to fall, so that she can get out of the way in time. Imagine, however, that Ana decides not to warn her, and as a result Maria dies. In her defense, Ana says that she was not morally responsible for Maria's death, since she was not the one who caused the tree to fall: "It was the tree that caused her death, not me!" she says. If we think that Ana did something wrong by not warning the victim, then we do not accept that, in order to be morally responsible for a situation, we must have caused that situation.

In the case in question, Ana did not cause the process that ended in death, but her decision was crucial to the death occurring. But the same happens in the case of animals in the wild who are victims of natural processes. In cases where it is possible to help them, the decision whether or not to help is crucial in determining whether or not they will die as a result of natural processes, even if humans did not cause the situation that harms them. If so, then it seems that humanity does something wrong if it does not allocate resources to researching how to help animals living in the wild.

21.3. "But these harms would exist even if we did not exist"

It is sometimes argued that humanity has no obligation to allocate resources to helping animals who are victims of natural processes because such harms would exist even if we had never existed.

However, what seems relevant to whether we are morally responsible for a choice is not what would happen if we did not exist but, given that we do exist, what will happen depending on what we decide59. If an outcome is in our hands, this seems to make us responsible for it.

For example, let us imagine that a doctor in a hospital claims that he has no obligation to treat victims of naturally caused diseases, since these would exist even if humanity did not exist. If we think the doctor is acting wrongly, then we do not accept the idea that we are not morally responsible for natural harms.

21.4. "But we don't intend to produce these harms"

At other times it is argued that humanity has no obligation to allocate resources to helping animals who are victims of natural processes because, in this case, unlike the case of animal exploitation, we do not intend to produce the harm (we may simply intend to do something else entirely and not concern ourselves with it) 60.

The main criticism of this view is that it completely disregards the impact of our decisions on those who will be affected by them in determining whether or not we have an obligation. For example, drivers who exceed the speed limit intend only to get somewhere faster, not to run anyone over. However, this does not mean that they cease to have the obligation not to run anyone over61.

Consider another example. Someone who sees a child drowning in a bathtub and does not rescue her may not intend to kill her (they may simply intend to do something else and not concern themselves with it), but it seems that they do something extremely wrong by not rescuing her62. If so, then it is not necessary for us to intend to produce a harm in order to have an obligation to prevent it.

Thus, the fact that we do not intend to produce the extremely negative situation in which animals in the wild find themselves does not show that humanity does nothing wrong if it decides not to allocate resources to helping them.

21.5. "But we don't have a close relationship with these animals"

It is sometimes argued that humanity has no obligation to allocate resources to helping animals living in the wild because we do not have a close relationship with them.

A first important point to note about this view is that it could not mark a relevant difference with respect to animals who are victims of human practices. For example, we also do not have a close relationship with the animals who are killed in slaughterhouses, but this does not seem to relieve us of the obligation not to harm them, since our decision, made at a distance, affects them directly.

However, the same is true of animals in the wild. In many cases, it is already possible to help them63. In others, it is always possible for humanity to invest resources in researching how to help them64. The decision to do so or to set it aside directly determines their fate, from a distance.

21.6. Isn't choosing whom to help optional?

There are people who acknowledge a duty to help those in need but argue that, since it is impossible to help everyone who needs it, choosing whom to help is morally optional, and therefore humanity has no obligation to allocate resources to helping animals in the wild.

One problem with this view is that it is also impossible to avoid harming everyone, but it does not follow from this that choosing whom to avoid harming is morally optional: we should prioritize avoiding the greater harm.

Analogously, the fact that it is impossible to help everyone should lead us to conclude that we should prioritize the most serious problems (and, above all, those most serious problems that almost no one is concerned about), not that it makes no difference whom we choose to help. Since the situation of animals in the wild is very serious, and very few people are concerned about it, there are strong reasons for humanity to invest resources in researching ways to help them.

21.7. Is the proposal to help wild animals too demanding?

It is sometimes claimed that the proposal to help wild animals is too demanding65 and that, for this reason, no one does anything wrong if they ignore what it proposes.

A first possible criticism of this objection is that, given the gigantic amount of suffering in the world, if a proposal demands a great deal of effort from people to reduce that suffering, this is a virtue of the proposal, not a flaw. Even if the fact that people have to make a great effort to help were a harm, it would still be a far smaller harm than the one the victims would suffer if this demand were not made.

The second criticism, in turn, observes that the proposal to help wild animals is not as demanding as it may seem at first glance. This is because research on how to help animals in the wild and practical programs to help them would be carried out by professionals in the relevant fields, not by ordinary people. The professionals in these fields, in turn, would continue to do their work as usual, with the difference that this time the goal would not be anthropocentric or environmentalist, but centered on concern for the animals themselves. Other people, for their part, could demand that the programs that currently harm wild animals be replaced by programs that help them, and could also spread the word about the importance of this issue, which is not a great demand. Moreover, as we will see in Chapter 37, it is possible to reduce the suffering of wild animals on a large scale merely by avoiding certain practices, and avoiding such practices is not difficult.

21.8. If we are genuinely concerned about the victims, what will we conclude?

We have seen that several reasons are put forward to argue that humanity has no obligation to allocate resources to helping wild animals who are victims of natural processes: "we are not the cause of these harms"; "these harms would exist even if humanity had never existed"; "we do not intend to cause these harms"; "we do not have a close relationship with these animals," etc.

There is a general criticism that can be made of all these views: they all focus on aspects related to the individuals who will make the decision, relegating to the background concern for those individuals whom we could harm or benefit. If we

are truly concerned about the animals affected by our decisions, there are two important implications:

The first is that we will not limit our concern to harms resulting from human practices, since animals are also harmed (to a high degree, as we saw in Chapter 3) by natural processes.

The second is that we will also reject the view that holds that reasons to help animals who are victims of natural processes exist, but are weaker than the reasons to help animals who are victims of human practices. If our concern is truly with the animals, we will determine the strength of the reasons to help them based on how much they would be harmed if they were not helped, not on whether the harm is natural or caused by human practices. This means that we have stronger reasons to prioritize preventing the greater harm, regardless of whether its origin is anthropogenic or natural.

22. Attempts to Argue That Domesticated Animals Have Priority

22.1. The historical debt argument

There is a position which holds that we have a historical debt toward domesticated animals that we do not have toward wild animals, since they are victims of exploitation, which in turn began with domestication66.

This claim is generally invoked in an attempt either to maintain that it is wrong to help wild animals or to deny the duty to help them. However, the claim cannot ground these conclusions, because if the historical debt criterion made sense, at most it would make helping domesticated animals a priority. Such a criterion would not serve to deny the duty to help wild animals (much less to prohibit helping them).

Moreover, even when used only as a criterion of priority, the historical debt criterion is problematic. For example, if priority depends on how serious the victims' situation is, then those victims toward whom we have no historical debt should have priority whenever they would be harmed to a greater degree if they were not prioritized.

Prioritizing domesticated animals could make sense if, because of exploitation and domestication, they were necessarily in a worse condition than wild animals. However, as we saw in Chapter 3, this is false. To think otherwise is to be unaware of what the typical life of animals in the wild is like.

The defender of the historical debt criterion could object that they are not arguing that the criterion is relevant because it indicates which animals are in a worse condition, but rather that it is relevant in itself: "our obligations depend on humanity's past acts, not on how well or badly off the animals we could help are." However, if so, then the historical debt criterion is motivated by personal purity, not by a real concern with improving the condition of individuals who are in a bad situation.

Moreover, the most reasonable explanation of why we would have a historical debt toward domesticated animals implies that we also have a historical debt toward wild animals. The most reasonable way to argue that we have a historical debt toward domesticated animals is the fact that we enjoy benefits that were only possible because of their domestication and exploitation. As a result of these activities, domesticated animals are today in an extremely bad situation.

However, if so, then we have exactly the same debt toward wild animals, given that the vast majority of the benefits we have enjoyed throughout history arose from interventions in nature to favor humans, and the fact that we did not intervene to benefit wild animals resulted in their being enormously harmed by natural processes. We chose to leave wild animals in the domain of those "subjected to the forces of nature": removing them from that category could equally be seen as a historical debt.

22.2. The degree of dependence argument

At other times it is said that wild animals have a certain independence that domesticated animals lack, which would make them less vulnerable: "they can fend for themselves!"67.

Again, even if this claim were true, at most it could ground our giving priority to domesticated animals. It would not serve to deny the obligation to help wild animals, much less to prohibit helping them.

Moreover, someone's having a certain degree of independence indicates that they normally do not need help in certain circumstances, but not in all of them. For example, suppose that a normal adult human (the most commonly cited example of an independent individual) gets lost in the jungle, or is suffering from cancer. The fact that they do not need help in other situations does not imply that they do not need help in this situation.

The same is true of wild animals who have some degree of independence. There are situations (many, as we saw in Chapter 3) in which their independence is of no use whatsoever

in freeing themselves from what harms them. Moreover (as we also saw in Chapter 3), the vast majority of animals who suffer intensely and die prematurely in the wild are young animals and therefore lack the independence the argument presupposes.

The idea that wild animals are independent seems to arise from the fact that, as we saw in Chapter 3, when most people think of animals in the wild, they tend to think of animals who are not representative of typical life in the wild: they think of large, adult animals, who are a tiny minority of the animals in the wild.

Thus, contrary to what the objection assumes, the degree of dependence criterion would give us extra reasons to try to investigate ways of helping wild animals.

23. Would Helping Animals Prevent the Fittest Genes from Prevailing?

23.1. The fittest genes argument

It is sometimes argued that we should not help animals who live in the wild and are victims of natural processes because, if they survive, this would increase the chances of genes that are not the fittest being passed on68. According to this view, we should let nature take its course, because in that way only the best-adapted individuals will survive, resulting in a natural genetic improvement of each species. Below, we will look at three criticisms of this view.

23.2. Do the fittest genes necessarily benefit those who carry them?

The objection in question assumes that, since by letting nature take its course only the fittest organisms will survive and reproduce, this will be a benefit for the members of future generations, who would inherit those genes. However, the traits that are efficient at passing genes on, favored by natural selection, are not necessarily beneficial to those who carry them, nor to their offspring.

For example, a species having the trait of reproducing by maximizing the number of offspring is a sign that it is very well adapted in evolutionary terms, since this greatly increases the probability that the species will endure. Since the broods are gigantic, the probability that at least some individuals will survive and reproduce, ensuring the continuation of the species, is extremely high. However, this trait is not a benefit for the members of the species. On the contrary: to be born a member of a species that reproduces in this way is to have one's chances of survival drastically reduced, since, as we saw in Chapter 3, the overwhelming majority of those born are born only to suffer and die prematurely. For example, in stable populations, in broods with thousands or millions of offspring, on average only two survive69.

Moreover, other traits that are passed on together with this one are often harmful to those who carry them. For example, being born a member of a species that reproduces by maximizing the number of offspring generally also coincides with having a very short natural lifespan. That is, in these species, it is not only the vast majority who fail to survive to adulthood who live short lives, but even those few who survive to old age. In short, what is optimized by natural selection is not what benefits individuals70.

Of course, there may be traits that optimize fitness in terms of maximizing the transmission of genetic information and that also benefit the animals who have them. However, we cannot infer, from the fact that a trait optimizes fitness, that it also benefits those who carry it.

23.3. Does concern about the fittest genes justify not helping animals?

Certainly, when planning aid programs, we must take into account the risk that, by helping animals, the harmful traits they carry will be passed on, harming the animals of future generations. However, recognizing this risk does not imply that the right thing to do is not to help and to let nature take its course.

For example, it could be said that the amount of suffering and death resulting from natural processes is so gigantic that, even if helping animals meant that members of future generations would not have the fittest genes, this would still have a far less negative balance than letting nature take its course.

Moreover, there are various ways of preventing/minimizing the suffering and premature deaths resulting from natural processes that would not prevent the fittest genes from being passed on. This would be the case, for example, of seeking to prevent suffering and premature death through sterilization and through research on which kinds of elements in the environment result in fewer births in species whose members commonly have predominantly negative lives.

23.4. What the objection advocates is considered heinous when it affects humans

When humans are affected by natural processes, no one argues that they should be left to suffer and die so that there can be a natural genetic improvement of the human species. On the contrary, that stance is normally seen as heinous, and what is advocated is exactly the opposite: providing even greater care to these humans, since their vulnerability is greater. If the disease that affects them is serious and hereditary, at most it is suggested that it would be better for them not to reproduce. However, no one argues that they should be left to suffer and die.

If what the objection in question proposes were acceptable, it would not be only the most vulnerable humans who should be left to fend for themselves, but all of us, so that only the fittest humans could pass their genes on. Almost no one accepts this position. That is, most of us consider it more important to minimize suffering and prevent deaths, even if this means that in the future the fittest possible beings will not exist. The standard position when humans are the victims of natural processes is that we should improve humans' living conditions by means other than the brutal ones that result from natural selection. On the other hand, when nonhuman animals are the victims, the standard view is the opposite. But if speciesism is unjustifiable, then this disparity is also unjustified.

24. Couldn't Helping Wild Animals Make Things Even Worse?

24.1. Concern about long-term consequences

One of the main objections to the proposal to prevent/minimize the harms that animals in the wild suffer as a result of natural processes is the concern that, in trying to help, we might inadvertently make the situation even worse71. This concern arises from the observation that ecosystems involve a series of very complex interactions, which makes it difficult to predict what the long-term consequences would be72.

Although this objection involves an important concern, we need to take into account three points suggesting that there is a greater likelihood of achieving better results if this issue is researched in depth than if it is set aside and nature is left to take its course. These points will be explained below.

The first is that it makes no sense to claim, first, that we do not know how long-term consequences will unfold, and then that we know that letting nature take its course has better long-term consequences than trying to help.

The second is that there are various interventions that have been carried out for decades and have benefited many animals, without the negative effects the objection fears73. This is the case with large-scale vaccination of wild animals, which has been carried out for decades for anthropocentric or environmentalist reasons but benefits the vaccinated animals. The knowledge gained from these and similar programs could also be used with the goal of benefiting the animals themselves, and more knowledge could be obtained if there were research focused on the good of the animals themselves.

The third is that it seems clear that the more is invested in studying this issue in depth, the greater the likelihood of knowing how long-term consequences are likely to unfold and, therefore, of achieving the best results. This is, therefore, a reason to reject the idea that "letting nature take its course" would achieve the best

results. For example, we also do not know all the possible long-term repercussions of helping humans. However, no one says that this shows that we should not help these humans and that it is better to let nature take its course.

The objection may be assuming that, if nature is left to take its course, the outcome is predominantly positive for animals. But, as we saw in Chapter 3, this is false. Alternatively, it may be assuming that we are responsible to a greater degree for the consequences of helping than for the consequences of not helping. However, as we saw in Chapter 21, this is arbitrary since, in both cases, the outcomes will turn out one way or another depending on our choice.

24.2. The appeal to ecological balance

It could be objected that there is a reason to think that, if nature is left to take its course, the outcome will probably be better for animals: "nature balances itself." According to this objection, the result of letting nature take its course is ecological balance, and this coincides with what is best for animals. Therefore, according to this objection, if we want what is best for animals, we need only let nature take its course. Below, we will look at the three main problems with this objection.

The first is that whether a situation is considered balanced or not depends on factors that are, to some extent, arbitrary. For example, it will depend on how different the situation is from a previous state taken as a reference point. However, any previous state can be chosen as a reference point and, depending on which state is chosen and how often the measurement is taken, one and the same state may be considered balanced or unbalanced74.

The second is that, in nature, there is no balance of the kind common sense imagines. In nature, populations fluctuate enormously, almost always irregularly75. In fact, entire ecosystems and species arise and go extinct as a result of natural processes, also generally irregularly and at irregular intervals.

It could be objected that this is precisely what is meant by balance: whatever results from natural processes, no matter what it is. But if so, then what is being done is arbitrarily changing the definition of balance in order to make the claim that nature is balanced true. That is, faced with the finding that a claim is false, one changes the definition of the term to make it true. With this maneuver, it is obvious that everything that results from natural processes will be balanced, since the definition of "balanced" has been changed to "everything that results from natural processes." But if that is the definition, then saying "everything that results from natural processes is balanced" is redundant, since it would amount to saying "everything that results from natural processes results from natural processes."

The third, and main, problem is that a situation can be balanced in the sense of being stable and yet be terribly bad for the animals affected. For example, situations like those we saw in Chapter 3, where over generations on average only two young survive per brood (something common in nature), are balanced in this sense, but, given the gigantic size of the broods, they are also a scenario in which suffering and the number of premature deaths are maximized.

It could be objected that, if there were less balance, then the amount of suffering and premature death would be even greater. However, there is not necessarily such a correlation. Everything will depend on how a greater or lesser degree of balance influences other factors that directly affect the good of sentient beings. For example, it will depend on whether it results in a greater number of births in species most of whose members have lives full of suffering or in species whose members have better chances of having positive lives. It will also depend on how it affects factors such as the availability of food and shelter and the amount of disease and conflict among animals. Moreover, since ecosystems tend to reach equilibrium at high levels of plant and animal productivity, disturbances probably tend to reduce, rather than increase, suffering76.

That is, there is no direct correlation between higher levels of ecological balance and a better overall balance for sentient beings. Therefore, if the goal is to achieve the best

state of affairs for animals, we should directly investigate how they are positively or negatively affected, rather than centering the analysis on the degree of balance77.

A few years ago, the creation of a field of research was proposed, welfare biology, which would study how animals are affected in their environments from the standpoint of what is better or worse for them as sentient individuals who have well-being78. This field could inform projects to help animals in the wild. As knowledge in welfare biology increased, the level of safety and efficiency of aid projects would increase.

Therefore, given what we have seen above, the solution to the problem of wild animal suffering is not to let nature take its course, but rather to research ever more deeply the factors that affect the quality of life of animals in their ecosystems, so that ever safer and more efficient aid projects become possible, just as is already done when the victims are human.

25. Objections That Question the Practicality of the Proposal to Help

25.1. The objection that it is not possible to help everyone in need

The number of animals in the wild is gigantic. According to some estimates, there are somewhere between 1 and 10 quintillion sentient individuals in the wild at any given moment79. To get an idea of this number, if we make an analogy with the span of one year and compare it with the human population, the latter would represent at most 0.25 seconds of the year.

It is sometimes argued that it is pointless to help animals in the wild because, given the astronomical number of victims, we will never manage to help them all. However, this objection can easily be answered by pointing out that the impossibility of helping everyone neither prevents nor renders pointless helping in those cases where we can do so. For the animals we could help, our help would make all the difference.

Objections of this kind would never be taken seriously in the human context. Imagine, for example, a doctor refusing to save your life on the grounds that doing so would be pointless because it is impossible to help all the humans who need it. It is only because of the prevalence of speciesism that objections of this kind arise when nonhuman animals are the victims.

25.2. Should we prioritize problems of which we would solve a larger share?

There is another objection to the proposal to help wild animals which says that, even if we manage to help in an enormous number of cases, doing so would not be an efficient way of using our resources since, given the astronomical number of victims, even if we helped many of them, this would still represent a small fraction of the total. According to this objection, we should focus only on exploited animals, since the percentage of the problem we would be able to solve would be greater.

The main problem with this objection is that it makes the mistake of measuring efficiency in the use of resources by percentage, rather than by the actual amount of benefit we could produce. Let us look at an example to illustrate this point.

Let us imagine that with the same amount of resources we could either help 90% of the animals in problem A, or help, to the same extent, 0.1% of the animals in problem B (who are all in a situation as bad as that of the animals in problem A).

If we are guided by proportion, we will choose to help 90% of the animals in problem A. But suppose that problem A involves one trillion animals, and problem B involves one quadrillion. 90% of one trillion is 900 billion. 0.1% of one quadrillion is one trillion. If we choose to solve 0.1% of problem B, we will be helping 100 billion more animals with the same amount of resources.

This reveals how mistaken it is to rely on percentage to measure efficiency in the use of resources. In the example above, if we are guided by percentage, we will fail to help 100 billion animals we could have helped. Therefore, to measure efficiency in the use of the resources we have for helping, what matters is the actual amount of benefit we could produce, not how many similar cases remain to be solved.

Thus, the fact that, even if we helped animals in the wild on a large scale, this could still represent a small percentage of the total number of victims of the problem does not show that doing so would not be an efficient way of using the resources available to us to reduce suffering. What would have to be assessed, among other things, is: (1) how large a benefit we could produce with the same amount of resources by investing in this or that problem; and (2) how neglected each problem is (since this reveals in which problems other people are likely to invest their resources anyway).

Taking these two factors into account, we can see that focusing on preventing wild animal suffering can be a very efficient way of preventing suffering in the world. For example, regarding the first factor, reducing the number of births in animal species that maximize the number of offspring would drastically reduce the number of individuals who would be born to lives full of suffering and a premature death. As we saw in Chapter 3, the reproductive potential of these animals is so gigantic that it exceeds the numbers of animal exploitation by several orders of magnitude. For example, sterilizing a single ocean sunfish would prevent at least 300 million animals from being born to this fate (and more than that if the sunfish in question would reproduce more than once in its lifetime). Carrying out an aid program of this kind does not seem to be more difficult than, for example, managing to shut down a factory farm (in fact, it may be much easier). As for the second factor, the issue of wild animal suffering is highly neglected, even by animal advocates.

All this shows that, far from it being pointless to focus on the issue of wild animal suffering, such a focus has great potential to be an extremely efficient way of preventing or minimizing suffering in the world.

26. What Is Already Being Done to Help Wild Animals?

26.1. Introduction

Some people believe that the proposal to help wild animals, despite having good theoretical foundations, is impracticable. The way to respond to this is simply to show what is already being done to help animals in the wild.

Various things are already being done to help animals in the wild. These aid programs normally have anthropocentric or environmentalist goals. However, the animals benefit too, and this by itself already shows that it is false that there is nothing that can be done to help them. Moreover, the knowledge gained from these programs can be useful in guiding future projects whose goal is to help animals.

Among the ways in which animals are already being helped80, we can highlight vaccination and disease treatment, helping animals in fires and other natural disasters, caring for orphaned animals, rescuing trapped animals and programs to meet animals' basic needs. Below are some examples of these forms of help.

26.2. Vaccination

There are many examples of large-scale vaccination of wild animals. The best known is rabies vaccination, which has taken place in several countries and helped eradicate the disease in large parts of Europe and North America81. Vaccination is carried out by aerial dispersal of baits containing the vaccine82. The use of drones makes it possible to vaccinate 4,000 animals per day83. Similar programs have been implemented around the world, including the vaccination of wild dogs in Africa84 and Asia85, and of wolves in Ethiopia86.

The following examples show the effectiveness of this type of project. Sylvatic plague in prairie dogs has mortality rates close to 100%87, but after a vaccination campaign in South Dakota in 2019, the animals showed a survival rate of 95%88. Anthrax vaccination has proven effective in populations of rhinoceroses, zebras and cheetahs89, and has also been proposed for gorillas90. Wild boars were vaccinated against tuberculosis under natural transmission conditions in 201191. Research at the University of Helsinki found that it is possible to vaccinate thousands of bees simply by vaccinating the queen92. In the United Kingdom there is a Vaccine and Antigen Bank93. Through vaccination, rinderpest became the second disease ever to be completely eradicated (the first was smallpox) and the first among those that affect nonhuman animals94.

26.3. Disease treatment

Probiotics have been used to treat wombats for mange95; fish for various types of infections96; bats for white-nose syndrome (which increased survival rates from 8% to 46%97) and boreal toads for skin diseases (which gave them a survival rate 40% higher than that of other toads98). There is also research on probiotic treatments for snakes99 and bees100. Since the 1940s, insect sterilization has been used to halt the spread of diseases, which benefits both the animals who would be bitten and the insects themselves since, given their population dynamics101, of all those born, few manage to survive102.

26.4. Treating animals in need

Animals have also been helped when they are injured. For example, birds and bats brought to rehabilitation centers with broken wings usually make a full recovery103. Another form of help is the rescue of trapped animals, such as whales trapped in ice104, elephants in mud lakes105 and animals stranded on beaches106. Providing food combined with contraceptives has also had good results107.

There are orphanages for wild animals in South Africa, Kenya and the Republic of the Congo108. Baby turtles have also been helped to reach the water after hatching109. Animals have also been rescued in disasters such as fires110, hurricanes and tsunamis111, volcanic eruptions112 and floods113.

Sometimes animals are also helped through the construction of shelters or nests114, which has benefited bats115, pigeons116, rabbits117 and moths118. The construction of artificial highlands in Kaziranga National Park, in India, cut the number of deaths of large animals in floods by half in two years119.

These are just a few examples of what is already being done to help animals in the wild. However, much more could be done. As we will see in the next chapter, one example would be the establishment of the field of welfare biology120, which would study animals in their ecosystems from the standpoint of what affects them as sentient individuals who have well-being (and not as specimens of species and components of ecosystems).

27. What Else Could Be Done to Help: Establishing Welfare Biology

27.1. What is welfare biology?

The lack of consideration for animals as sentient beings means that wild animals are generally studied only as specimens of species and components of ecosystems. For this reason, there are far fewer data on what affects wild animals as individuals who have well-being.

For this reason, the creation of the field of welfare biology has been proposed, which would study the way animals are affected by their interactions with their environments and with one another, from the standpoint of what is better or worse for them as sentient individuals who have well-being – that is, as beings for whom things can go better or worse121.

As knowledge from welfare biology increases, ever safer and more efficient programs to help animals could be implemented122.

27.2. Welfare biology is a cross-disciplinary field

Research in welfare biology is cross-disciplinary. This is different from interdisciplinary and transdisciplinary research. In terms of their disciplinarity, the different types of research can be classified as follows123. (1) Intradisciplinary research is carried out within a single discipline. (2) Multidisciplinary research involves several disciplines providing different perspectives on a problem. (3) Interdisciplinary research integrates the knowledge and methods of different disciplines, synthesizing their approaches. (4) Transdisciplinary research creates a framework beyond the perspectives of the disciplines involved. (5) Finally, cross-disciplinary research views one or more disciplines from the perspective of another.

Welfare biology would bring together knowledge from several disciplines, such as ecology, animal welfare science, zoology and veterinary science. It is

a cross-disciplinary field of research in the sense that each discipline involved would be conducted from the perspective of welfare biology. That is, all of them would focus on investigating how animals are positively or negatively affected as sentient beings.

27.3. What distinguishes welfare biology from other fields?

Welfare biology is different from conservation biology124, in which animals are studied as specimens of species or components of ecosystems. It is also different from compassionate conservation125, which consists in using methods that do not harm animals when pursuing conservationist goals. Finally, it is also different from conservation welfare126, which investigates how animals' well-being can also be promoted when conservation measures are implemented.

Welfare biology would study what positively or negatively affects animals, regardless of whether or not this knowledge serves conservation. Knowledge from these other fields could be useful to welfare biology and vice versa, but their goals are distinct.

27.4. Which animals would welfare biology study?

Research in welfare biology could be carried out on the situation of any animals. However, far more data are already available in the case of animals living under human control. The way natural processes affect the well-being of animals in the wild is still a widely neglected topic. For this reason, research in welfare biology has reasons to focus on the situation of these animals. However, such research could also include animals who do not live under direct human control and are found in semi-wild, agricultural, suburban and even urban environments (such as pigeons living in cities, for example127).

27.5. Creating the conditions for establishing welfare biology

Some people think that the proposal to help wild animals is not implemented because no one has any idea what to do in practice. This belief is mistaken. As we saw in Chapter 26, various things are already being done to help animals in the wild128. There is also already a good deal of research in welfare biology129, and something is also known about what other kinds of research would be needed. Research programs specializing in welfare biology130 are also beginning to emerge at universities.

Why, then, has welfare biology not yet become a well-established field of research, like other fields? There are several factors. One of them is that it is a relatively recent field compared with other areas. Another factor is that, contrary to that common belief, the main obstacles to establishing welfare biology are not practical but ideological. That is, there is little research on the situation of wild animals simply because that situation is not yet seen as a problem, and also because the prevailing view is that it is wrong to help these animals. In short, the problem is not that there is nothing to be done, but that there is a lack of will to do something.

Thus, for welfare biology to become a well-established field, it is important to combat these ideological obstacles. Below we will look at these obstacles in more detail.

27.6. Ideological obstacles that hinder the development of welfare biology

Speciesism

Because of speciesism, wild animals are normally reduced to components of ecosystems and specimens of species. They are not seen as individuals we should be concerned about. According to this view, when wild animals are victims of natural processes, this gives us no direct reasons to prevent their suffering and deaths: what matters is letting nature take its course, ensuring ecological balance, biodiversity, the conservation of ecosystems, preserving rare species, etc. According to the

prevailing view, we should help wild animals only if doing so is useful for achieving environmentalist or anthropocentric goals.

However, when humans are the victims, the prevailing view is exactly the opposite. The objections raised against the proposal to help wild animals would almost certainly not be raised if the victims were human. Thus, the prevalence of speciesism is one of the main reasons why research in welfare biology is not yet a consolidated field.

The idyllic view of nature

Another obstacle is the idyllic view of nature131, that is, the idea that, if we let nature take its course, the outcome will be predominantly positive for animals. This bias causes the problem of wild animal suffering to be neglected even within animal advocacy, simply because many activists do not know how much wild animals are harmed by natural processes132.

Veneration of what is natural

A third obstacle is the veneration of what is natural. This veneration leads many people to have an idyllic view of nature. But, above all, it also leads many people to oppose reducing the suffering and deaths of wild animals, even when they know that the idyllic view of nature is false. Of course, this veneration of what is natural is normally subordinate to speciesism, since it is not applied when humans are the victims.

The origin-of-harm bias

A fourth obstacle is the idea that we are morally responsible only for harms that originated in human practices. We discussed this view in detail in Chapter 21 and saw that there are good reasons to reject it. Moreover, once again, this view is normally subordinate to speciesism, since it is not accepted when the victims are human.

Several biases operating together

Finally, there are also several biases that incline people to neglect the situation of animals in the wild and even to oppose the proposal to help them. Some examples are status quo bias (the tendency to prefer that things stay as they already are), conservatism bias (insufficiently revising one's beliefs in light of new evidence); the Semmelweis reflex (the tendency to reject new evidence that contradicts a paradigm); anchoring bias (which leads us to rely heavily on the first piece of information we receive about a subject) and the just-world hypothesis (that is, the belief that the bad things that happen in the world are fair).

These biases can lead people to claim that "anything we try to do will only make things worse," or "the public will never accept this proposal," not because they have examined the issue thoroughly and reached this conclusion, but so as not to have to put to the test the belief they already held, that we should not help animals. That is, what is said is "I agree with the proposal, but unfortunately it won't work," but this is a way of disguising disagreement with the proposal (it is a case of a normative objection disguised as a strategic objection).

These are just a few examples of ideological obstacles to the proposal to help wild animals. Challenging these and other ideological obstacles is crucial if the available means are actually to be used to help animals and if more knowledge is to be pursued in this direction.

28. What Technologies Could Be Used to Help Animals in the Wild?

New technologies allow us to observe things that were never possible before, such as identifying insects individually and recognizing them later, and modeling how the various animal populations in a habitat affect one another's presence and numbers. Analysis of the data collected can inform us about the presence of species in an area, their numbers, the way the distribution of different groups of animals changes over time, and the factors that contribute to this, such as the animals' mortality, health and behavior. We will look at some examples below133.

Camera traps are cameras with motion sensors that are installed in the natural habitat. They can take photos periodically or record videos at specific times, providing continuous updates. They can collect information about the location and number of animals, their behaviors and physical condition, helping to monitor the animals' well-being and the factors that affect it, such as rapidly growing populations, the presence of other species, resource limitations in the area and the way the animals use those resources.

Light detection and ranging (LIDAR) technology, also known as 3D laser scanning, produces three-dimensional images of landscapes. It can be deployed on the ground or on an aerial vehicle and produces high-resolution images that show the structure of a habitat in detail, down to the position of leaves on branches. It can detect the abundance and distribution of species populations as well as the physical properties of the habitat that affect those populations. The data can help us understand animals' resource needs and how adequately they are being met.

Thermal imaging134 uses infrared cameras to capture the heat signatures of animals in an area. It can determine the presence of particular kinds of animals and their population numbers, including those of camouflaged animals. One of its greatest uses is detecting physical stress, which may occur because of an injury, disease, fear or some other kind of threat response. It also makes it possible to identify localized injuries.

Acoustic data analysis (of the sounds of animals and of the environments in which they live) provides information about health, interactions between animals and changes in a habitat's conditions. Recordings include infrasonic and ultrasonic sounds, both beyond the range of human hearing. There are microphones that work in water as well as on land and in the air.

Environmental DNA (eDNA)135 is a way of collecting genetic material in natural environments, such as hair, feathers, feces and scales. It requires no interaction with the animals, thus avoiding any negative impact on them. It provides information about an animal's diet, health and age. It can estimate the kinds of animals living in an area and their numbers.

Continuous improvements in data processing power will increase our ability to use data to gain insights into animals' well-being. As awareness of the situation of wild animals grows, the use of these technologies will expand, providing much more practical information on how to help animals.
