  3. For a detailed study, see Ética Animal (2022b). ↩

29. Do Animals Have a Right Not to Be Sterilized?

29.1. The rights violation objection

As we saw in Chapter 3, the maximization of births contributes to a high degree to maximizing the amount of suffering and premature death. Therefore, one of the main focuses of the proposal to prevent natural harms would be to minimize birth rates.

One objection to this proposal points out that it entails advocating sterilization, and that sterilizing someone against their will violates their rights (such as the right to reproduce and the right to bodily integrity). According to this objection, the right course of action is not to minimize birth rates, even if this means more suffering and death over time.

29.2. Three ways of responding to the rights violation objection

There are at least three ways of responding to the rights violation objection.

There are many ways of helping that would not involve sterilization

The first would point out that all the ways of minimizing natural harms that do not involve sterilization would not violate the alleged right not to be sterilized: vaccinating, treating diseases, providing water, food, shelter, rescue in natural disasters, not recreating the conditions for the maximization of births, etc. Thus, even someone who rejected sterilization would have to accept the proposal to help wild animals in all these cases.

The appeal to consequences

The second response is simply to deny that we should respect rights in circumstances in which doing so would result in an even worse situation than if we did not respect them136.

However, in response to this, it could be objected that, to know whether we should respect a rule, what we should do is not assess the consequences of each act, but rather assess whether the

rule would result in the best consequences in most cases if everyone followed it137. According to this position, if a rule passes this test, we should always respect it, even in circumstances where violating it would result in better consequences.

The problem with this, however, is that respecting the alleged right not to be sterilized in most cases would have worse results (and therefore would not be a rule that would result in better consequences if everyone followed it). As we saw in Chapter 3, the vast majority of animals have thousands or even millions of offspring per brood, which always results in extremely low survival rates.

Of course, accepting sterilization in these cases does not necessarily mean having to accept it in the case of animals who have few offspring per brood and invest in parental care, since in these cases there is a greater chance that the young will have a meaningful life (although, depending on the circumstances, perhaps even in these cases sterilization would result in better consequences, given that such animals are often in situations of scarcity or disaster). However, concern with consequences would certainly imply accepting sterilization in the vast majority of cases.

Denying the existence of the right in question

So far our reasoning has centered on assessing consequences. However, it could be objected that consequences do not matter for knowing whether or not we should respect a right. According to this position, if a right exists, we should respect it regardless of what the consequences would be (whether of each act or of its general adoption as a rule)138.

However, even someone who takes a position of this kind need not accept that sterilization violates rights, since they can: (1) either deny that there is a right not to be sterilized (even while acknowledging the existence of other rights); (2) or accept the existence of the right not to be sterilized, but deny that this right exists in each and every situation.

For example, it could be argued that guaranteeing this right may, in certain cases, entail violating other, more fundamental rights. As we have seen, the defense of the

right not to be sterilized is grounded either in the right to reproduce or in the right to bodily integrity. Below we will look at this point first in relation to the right to reproduce, and then in relation to the right to bodily integrity.

29.3. Discussing the defense of the right to reproduce

Suppose a couple knows that, if they conceive a child now, the child will be born only to experience intense suffering. Anyone who holds that there is a moral right to reproduce in each and every case would have to hold that this couple has the right to have the child anyway (and even if it were not just one child, but a large number of them – drawing an analogy here with the reproductive strategy that maximizes the number of offspring).

To argue that, for there to be a right to reproduce, it is sufficient that the parents have an interest in reproducing is to completely disregard the impact of the decision on the well-being of the beings who will be born. Going without reproducing (or even being sterilized) is a far smaller harm than being born into a life that contains nothing but extreme suffering.

It could be objected that, since the offspring do not yet exist, their well-being does not count. The problem with this response is that, unlike when someone decides not to bring about a birth, when someone decides to bring about a birth, those individuals will come into existence.

It could be objected that this reasoning only makes sense if we do not accept that moral rights exist. But this is not true. Someone could, for example, argue that there are other rights (to life, for example), but not the right to reproduce. Or they could accept that there is a moral right to reproduce, but not in this case. They could hold that this right exists only if certain conditions are met (for example, good chances that the lives of the future beings will be at least minimally meaningful). The situation of animals in the wild, at least that of the vast majority of members of species that maximize offspring (which are the vast majority of species), is an extreme in which these conditions are not present139.

29.4. Would sterilization violate a right to bodily integrity?

Whether by surgical intervention or by other methods (for example, offering food containing a sterilizing agent), sterilization is an intervention in someone's body (in the case of nonhuman animals, without their informed consent). On this basis, it could be objected that sterilization violates the right to bodily integrity.

One problem with this objection is that guaranteeing this supposed right to bodily integrity would violate other rights of equal weight or more fundamental ones (for example, the bodily integrity and the lives of third parties). In the case of these reproductions, the bodily integrity and the lives of third parties would be violated (many third parties, thinking here of animals who reproduce by maximizing the number of offspring, who would be born only to suffer and die shortly afterward).

Thus, even if the rights to bodily integrity and to reproduce exist, this would be insufficient to prohibit sterilization (at least in the case of animals whose offspring are born only to suffer intensely), given that the situation of animals in the wild generally does not meet the conditions under which such rights should be guaranteed.

29.5. The human sterilization objection

One objection to the previous conclusion argues that, if it is right to sterilize nonhuman animals because their future offspring cannot have a meaningful life, then it is right to sterilize, against their will, humans who live in poverty.

One problem with this objection is that it fails to distinguish situations in which it is the characteristics of reproduction itself that make it impossible for the lives of future beings to be meaningful from others in which what prevents a meaningful life are social issues. As an example of the first kind of case, we can cite the reproductive strategy that, because of the biology of the animals involved, maximizes the number of offspring far beyond the available resources, or the case in which children will be born with so many diseases and deformities that they will have an existence dominated by intense suffering. Poverty, on the other hand, is an example of the second kind of case.

Thus, for there to be a justification for sterilizing someone (regardless of species) against their will, all three of the following conditions must be met: (1) that, if they reproduce, there is a high probability of giving rise to offspring who would predominantly experience extreme suffering; (2) that there is a high probability of their reproducing; and (3) that there is no other, less harmful and equally efficient way of preventing such reproduction.

29.6. The objection that we should seek other means

The next objection agrees that sterilization is justifiable provided there is no other, less harmful way out. However, it maintains that there is another way out: providing food, resources and basic care to the future offspring.

The problem with this objection is that, given the extremely high number of offspring per reproduction (thousands or even millions per brood), there would have to be an ecosystem of astronomical size with abundant resources, trillions (or quadrillions) of times larger than our planet, for all the offspring to have a minimum of resources available. And even if there were resources available for everyone, and everyone managed to use them, there would still have to be birth control, since, given the gigantic birth rate of these species, resources would quickly become scarce (bearing in mind that the surviving offspring would tend to reproduce, and so on). Thus, at most, this objection can make some sense in the case of animals belonging to species that do not maximize the number of offspring (who are a tiny minority of sentient beings).

Of course, there may be alternatives to sterilization that are just as efficient (or even more efficient) at preventing births. This may be the case with reducing primary productivity, which we will discuss in section 31.18. With less vegetation, the tendency is for this to lead to a decrease in the total birth rate. However, it may be that sterilization causes less harm individually (although reducing primary productivity probably has a better cost/benefit ratio in terms of applicability).

29.7. The animal experimentation objection

Another objection points out that, if it is right to sterilize someone against their will to prevent harm to other sentient beings, then it is right to force someone to serve as a research model. However, in the case of animal experimentation, it is not the animals used who are about to cause harm to other sentient beings, but rather the diseases of which those other beings are victims. In the case of sterilization, by contrast, it is the very bodily activity of those who reproduce that gives rise to millions of deaths. In the case of animal experimentation, it is possible to choose to research other means of curing diseases without using animals. In the case of the suffering and deaths caused by the maximization of animals' reproduction, by contrast, there is no way to reduce them without preventing the reproduction itself. Of course, as we have seen, it may be impossible to prevent this reproduction by other means, such as reducing primary productivity. But whatever means is employed, it is different from the case of animal experimentation.

29.8. Conclusion

The sterilization of domesticated animals is widely accepted by animal advocates. And the reason is precisely the amount of suffering and death caused by reproduction rates. Dogs and cats have on average 4 or 5 offspring per litter. These reproduction rates tend to cause a great deal of suffering and death in the long run, but compared with what happens in the case of animals who have thousands or millions of offspring per brood, these numbers almost vanish. Thus, in the case of the vast majority of wild animals, we have much stronger reasons to justify sterilization.

Let us draw an analogy with the human species. Let us imagine that every time someone reproduced they produced millions of children, and that only two survived while the rest were born only to suffer to the extreme. In that situation we would view sterilization (and even genetic reprogramming) with relief and hope, not with revulsion (rightly so, in my view).

The fact that many people have one kind of attitude toward humans and domesticated animals, and the opposite attitude toward wild animals, may reflect various factors. One of them may be the mistaken belief that animals in the wild normally live well. Another is the idea that the good of wild animals matters very little, and that they matter only as components of ecosystems and specimens of species. As we have seen in other chapters, such attitudes are unjustifiable. The general situation of wild animals comprises the cases in which sterilization programs are most easily justified.

Author’s notes

  1. This reasoning is characteristic of act consequentialist theories. ↩
  2. This reasoning is characteristic of rule consequentialist theories. ↩
  3. This reasoning is characteristic of deontological theories. ↩
  4. This reasoning does not necessarily imply adopting a consequentialist view (although it is compatible with one), since it merely prevents the outcome from being extremely bad (it does not guarantee that it is the best among the available options). ↩

30. The Issue of Parasitism

A common belief is that the proposal to help wild animals would have to prohibit treating cases of parasitism, since it would save a single animal at the cost of the deaths of many, making the resulting situation worse.

However, death is not bad intrinsically, but because of the good it could prevent from being enjoyed. Thus, for the number of deaths to be relevant in determining how bad a situation is, they must be deaths:

(1) Of sentient beings and;

(2) Of sentient beings whose prospects of future life are positive to the point of being preferable to death.

Thus, in cases where the parasites are not sentient and the host is sentient, even if treating the parasitism results in more deaths, the resulting situation is better, since death is not a harm for such parasites.

In the case of parasites that are sentient, it would have to be assessed whether their lives would be at least minimally meaningful. If they are not (and it is not possible to make them so), then death would not represent a greater harm for them than remaining alive. Thus, there could be a justification for treating the victim even if the parasites were sentient, and even if doing so means a greater number of deaths.

Suppose, for the sake of argument, that in a given case the parasites would be more harmed if they died, and that the right decision were therefore not to treat the host. Even so, there could be no objection whatsoever to preventing future cases of parasitism (for example, through sterilization), since refraining from producing new beings is not the equivalent of killing beings who already exist.

Moreover, not treating parasitism would probably result in a greater number of deaths and more suffering. As explained below, this may be so in the short term and is certainly so in the long term.

Even in the short term, not treating the host could result in a greater number of deaths. There are cases in which it is possible to remove the parasites (for example, larvae) alive. And there are cases in which removing the parasites is the only way to enable them to have a longer life. For example, in the case of larvae that will become flies, this will only happen if, at a certain point in their development, they are outside the host's body. Otherwise, they will die there.

However, suppose that treating the host always means a greater number of deaths in the short term (assuming that the parasites are sentient, which is often not the case). Almost all parasites are animals who reproduce by maximizing the number of offspring. If they are sentient, as we saw in Chapter 3, the result of this reproductive strategy is also the maximization of the number of deaths and of suffering for the members of these species themselves. Thus, given that the reproductive potential of these animals is gigantic, not treating the host will result in the parasites continuing to reproduce and to infect new victims (and therefore will result in a greater number of deaths, more suffering, a greater number of lives dominated by suffering, a greater number of extremely short lives, etc.). This gives us reasons not only to treat victims of parasitism who are already infected but, above all, to prevent parasitism in general140.

Therefore, it is false that the proposal to prevent natural harms would prohibit treating cases of parasitism.

Author’s notes

  1. A detailed discussion of the issue of parasitism can be found in Cunha (2022, p. 263-72). ↩

31. The Issue of Predation

31.1. The prevailing view

The prevailing view is that it is wrong to intervene in cases of predation among wild animals. However, a growing number of authors have questioned this view in recent decades141. This chapter examines the main arguments in this debate.

31.2. The idea that predation is not a matter for ethics

It is sometimes argued that predation is not a matter for ethics because predators cannot be held responsible, since they do not understand ethical questions142. However, this fact does not stop predation from being a matter for ethics, because the question of whether we should intervene in predation is not posed to predators, but rather to us, as responsible agents.

It is curious that the claim "predation is not a matter for ethics" is invoked in an attempt to establish that it is morally wrong to intervene in predation, since the one claim contradicts the other. That is, it makes no sense to say "action X is not subject to ethical evaluation" and then to say "it is morally wrong to do action X."

Whenever it is possible to ask whether an action (whether an act or an omission) should be prohibited, required or permitted, it is a matter of ethics. Therefore, the decision about what to do in cases of predation is a matter of ethics.

31.3. The idea that it is wrong to intervene because predators are not to blame

Another similar argument holds that the fact that predators cannot be held responsible makes it wrong to intervene in cases of predation. Underlying this position is the idea that, if someone is not morally responsible for the harm they cause, we should not prevent that harm.

However, the one does not imply the other. For example, it makes no sense to hold responsible a small child who hits another child on the head with a stick; but the victim's suffering is something negative, and that is a reason to prevent such an outcome from taking place. Our moral responsibilities can go beyond redressing the wrongs of other responsible agents (they can involve, for example, making the world a place with less suffering and death)143.

It could be claimed that one difference between the case of predation and the example above is that predators die if they do not prey. However, this is already a different argument, since it appeals to the need to prey in order to survive, not to the fact that the predator cannot be held responsible. We will discuss this other argument in sections 31.10, 31.11 and 31.12.

31.4. The claim that predation is neutral because it results from amoral agents

Another similar argument holds that, because predators cannot be held responsible, the harms they cause are neutral, and that, therefore, there is no reason to prevent them. However, the one does not imply the other. For example, suffering is negative because of its intrinsic characteristics, and these do not depend on whether or not whoever causes it can be held responsible. Therefore, the suffering resulting from predation is negative, not neutral144.

31.5. Absurd because impossible to accomplish

Another argument against intervening in predation points out that we will never manage to end all predation in the world. However, the fact that we cannot end all cases of a problem does not show that we should not act in the cases where we could do so145. Nor can we prevent all the harms that humans suffer, much less all the harms that humans cause to animals, but this does not imply that we should not try to prevent as many as we can. The same applies to predation.

31.6. The accusation of fascism

Another claim holds that intervening in predation is wrong because it would be an act of fascism for not accepting differences (it would be like homophobia and racism). However, this analogy does not work. Someone's race and sexual orientation do not entail the death of other individuals. Predation, by contrast, entails the death (usually with extreme suffering146) of a gigantic number of individuals. Wanting the world to contain less suffering and death is very different from discriminating against someone on account of their race or sexual orientation.

31.7. The accusation of sentimentalism

Another objection holds that intervention in predation is motivated by sentimentalism (compassion for the prey), and that it should therefore be rejected. It is true that someone's having a strong feeling about an issue does not show that the position they defend is necessarily correct. For example, their feeling may be the product of a prejudice; it may violate justice; or their compassion may be selective. However, neither does it show that the position is wrong. It is possible that what someone concludes, motivated by their feelings, is the same as what they would conclude from an impartial perspective, weighing all the arguments for and against a certain action. We will only find out whether or not this is the case if we carry out an impartial analysis of the issue.

31.8. Speciesism and interventions in predation

Another objection holds that intervening in predation is a speciesist attitude. However, this accusation only makes sense in situations in which whoever is deciding: (1) is concerned only with predation on or by members of certain species or; (2) weighs harms arbitrarily according to the species of those involved.

For example, the standard position is that, when humans are the victims of predation, it is always right to intervene regardless of the consequences, and that when nonhuman animals are the victims, it is always wrong to intervene, even if the consequences of not intervening are worse. This is speciesism, pure and simple. Curiously, this is the most common position among those who accuse the proposal to intervene in predation of speciesism.

Intervening in predation is not necessarily speciesist. For example, if someone gives equal weight to each of those affected (whether predators or prey) and claims that the right action (whether intervening or not intervening) is the one that results in the least total harm, they are not being speciesist147. Favoring an individual belonging to a species is not necessarily speciesist (it is speciesist only if the favoring is biased).

31.9. Is intervening in predation partial?

A similar objection holds that intervening in predation means being partial in favor of the prey (whatever species it belongs to). However, this accusation would only make sense if intervening necessarily meant favoring the prey in a biased way. But there is at least one way of defending intervention that could not be accused of favoring the attacked or the attacker in a biased way: the goal of seeking the best outcome, while holding that the good of each sentient being affected has the same weight. According to this view, when not intervening would have worse consequences, we should intervene, regardless of who is the prey and who is the predator. Analogously, this position will advocate not intervening when intervening would have worse consequences. This position is certainly impartial.

31.10. The appeal to the need to prey

Another argument frequently used to claim that it is wrong to intervene in predation involves pointing out that predators die if they do not prey. Below we will look at four problems with this argument.

The first problem is that it is biased: it takes into account only the deaths of predators.

The second is that the argument completely disregards the number of deaths. For example, a predator kills many prey over its lifetime, usually with intense suffering. It could be objected that predation minimizes the total number of deaths, since in the absence of predation the prey would reproduce even more. However, this is not the case with all predation. For example, large herbivores consume a great deal of vegetation, and this drastically reduces the number of insect births. Thus, a decrease in the rate of

predation on large herbivores, precisely by increasing the population of these herbivores, would probably decrease the total number of deaths by decreasing the total number of births. In other words, if the concern is to reduce the number of deaths, then one has to admit that intervening in predation is right when it results in fewer deaths.

The third problem is that intervening in predation does not necessarily entail the death of the predator. There are some plant-based foods that use synthesized nutrients that meet the physiological needs of certain predators, such as cats. Sterilizing or genetically modifying a predator also does not necessarily entail its death148. Regardless of whether or not such practices are right, their existence shows that it is false that intervening in predation necessarily entails the death of the predator.

The fourth problem is that, even if preying were currently necessary for each and every predator, this does not show that it would be wrong to make it unnecessary (for example, through genetic change). What the argument says is that, where there is a need, we should not prevent its fulfillment. However, this does not imply that it is wrong to make that need cease to exist.

31.11. The appeal to lesser harms to the predator

Another possible objection would be to say that the predator is harmed by having to eat plant-based food, or by being sterilized or genetically reprogrammed.

The first possible response to this objection is to deny that some of these actions harm predators. Eating a different food is not necessarily a harm. The same applies to genetic change. Suppose that a genetic change is made in certain predators so that they become herbivores. The animals of the future generation who were born herbivores would lose nothing by the fact that their ancestors were carnivores. Even the animals of the current generation do not seem to lose anything by having their nutritional needs modified. Another example of intervention in predation that causes no harm is preventing predation by carnivorous plants, since they are not sentient.

The second response is to point out that, even if predators are harmed by such actions, the harm to them is much smaller than the harm that will take place if predation is allowed. Thus, the objection is guilty of arbitrariness, since a lesser harm to the predator is treated as a trump over much greater harms to the prey (being eaten alive). On such a view, the harm resulting from intervention, however small, is seen as more serious than the far greater harms that would result from non-intervention.

When humans are at risk of being preyed upon, the standard position is simply that it is right to kill the predators, period. Suppose it were argued, out of concern for the predators of humans, that instead of killing them we should genetically reprogram them, sterilize them, or create a plant-based food that meets their needs. Such a proposal would probably not be accepted, but not out of concern for the predators, rather because resources would be spent on members of other species. However, the judgment is reversed when predation occurs on nonhuman animals: proposals such as sterilization, genetic reprogramming and the creation of plant-based food for predators are rejected out of concern for a possible harm to the predators. This is speciesism.

31.12. The appeal to the right to secure one's survival

It could be argued that the predator has the right to secure its survival, and that we should protect this right, whatever the consequences. Therefore, according to this position, it is always wrong to prevent cases of predation.

Note that this position implies that it is also wrong to defend oneself or other humans from predation. This is something its proponents would hardly accept. But if they do not accept it, they are being speciesist. However, suppose for the sake of argument that someone argues that it is always wrong to prevent a predation from occurring, even if it is on other humans or on oneself. Even in that case, there are other reasons to reject this position, which we will look at below.

The first is that it assumes that we should follow certain rules, whatever the consequences. So anyone who believes that the right action coincides with the one that results in the best consequences could never accept what this view proposes.

The second is that even the perspective which holds that there are rights that must be guaranteed regardless of the consequences does not support this position. This is because, if predators have rights, so do prey, and the position in question is arbitrary in defending only the rights of predators. At this point it could be objected that both predators and prey have the right to try to survive, and that this implies letting each fight with its own strength. One problem with this is that, if guaranteeing rights amounts to the same thing as everyone fighting for themselves, then there is no point whatsoever in claiming that rights exist.

Recognizing a right to survival, by contrast, would imply protecting the interest in living of both the predator and the prey. For example, it would imply research into securing the survival of predators with another kind of food, not non-intervention.

Moreover, the position in question holds that rights must be protected whatever the consequences. So it cannot appeal to the risk of negative consequences of preventing predation. That is, contrary to what may initially seem to be the case, this position would have to advocate always preventing predation, whatever the consequences.

It could be objected that predators, because they have no sense of right and wrong, do not violate rights149. There are two possible responses here. The first is to argue that the violation of a right is characterized by the type of act, and this does not depend on whether or not whoever performed it has a sense of right and wrong. The second is to argue that, even if it is true that predators do not violate rights, this is irrelevant, since the question is whether we, who have a sense of right and wrong, violate a right if we do not intervene in predation.

Another objection would be to argue that there are only negative rights, which imply that agents must refrain from doing certain harmful things, but that there is no right to be rescued150. The first problem with this argument is that, even if there were no right to be rescued, this does not imply that it would be wrong to rescue victims of predation. Rescuing could be permissible and even praiseworthy. The second problem is that, if the reason

for attributing rights to someone is to protect that someone151, it makes no sense to say that rights are limited to negative rights, since threats to someone's good are not limited to the acts of moral agents (they can result from omissions).

Thus, an appeal to rights does not show that it is wrong to intervene in cases of predation.

31.13. Widely accepted interventions in predation

There are a number of interventions in predation that are widely accepted and practiced. For example, to defend oneself, other humans, or the animals who live with us. Another example is interventions in predation motivated by environmentalist reasons, such as the ecology of fear (the reintroduction of predators where they had gone extinct152) and interventions to kill predators if they are threatening a rare species153.

Thus, people seem to consider it wrong to intervene in predation only when it occurs among wild animals and the goal of the intervention is concern for the good of the nonhuman animals themselves (and not anthropocentric or environmentalist goals) – what we will call here the specific arrangement. These people therefore need to explain why intervening in predation would be wrong only in the specific arrangement.

None of the arguments we have discussed so far could explain this difference. For example, in the widely accepted cases of intervention in predation, the predators are also not responsible agents, they also need to prey, and in these cases the intervention also entails one of these things: killing them, genetically modifying them, sterilizing them or changing the way they feed. Is there, then, some other way of justifying that intervening in predation is wrong only in the specific arrangement? Below we will discuss some attempts.

31.14. The appeal to animal behavior

A first attempt to ground the difference points out that animals of social species defend animals of their own species from predation, but not those of other species, and that we should therefore do the same.

There are two problems with this argument. The first is that it is doubtful that animals defend only members of their own species from predation. However, the main problem with the argument is that the fact that a behavior is exhibited by animals does not imply that it is right154. For example, there are animals who kill the young of rivals and even their own young; who kill in power struggles; who steal; who rape, etc. Cannibalism has even been found in more than 1,300 species, in a wide variety of social and ecological contexts155. The fact that animals do such things does not make them right.

31.15. The argument from the ability to avoid the threat

Another argument holds that there is no need to intervene in predation among wild animals because, if their species still exist, it is because they have the ability to escape predation. In the case of human children, on the other hand, we should intervene because they lack this ability, the argument concludes156.

The main error of this argument is that it uses reasoning based on the species in the case of wild animals and reasoning based on individuals in the human case. The fact that a species has not gone extinct shows only that some of its members managed to reproduce before succumbing to predation. It does not even show that these individuals escaped predation until the end of their lives, much less that all members of the species escaped predation. For example, as the argument itself acknowledges, the fact that the human species still exists does not show that all its members have the ability to escape predation.

31.16. Concern about consequences

One of the main arguments against intervening in predation holds that doing so would cause more suffering and death than it prevents because, in the absence of predators, prey animals will undergo

a population explosion, resulting in a greater number of deaths from starvation (and even from predation, given that in many cases they are also predators of smaller animals).

A first problem with this argument is that it, too, could not explain what the difference is between intervening in predation in the specific arrangement and in the widely accepted cases. For example, we also do not know whether preventing predation on humans has better long-term consequences, since, as we will see in detail in Chapters 36 and 37, it is uncertain whether what has better consequences is a larger or a smaller human population.

Moreover, one implication of concern about consequences is that it could not establish that it is always wrong to intervene in predation, since if in a given case it is not intervening that will result in more suffering and death, such a position would have to accept intervening.

It could be claimed that there are no cases of this kind. But there is currently no basis for this claim, since very few studies have been carried out in this direction. Moreover, there are initial reasons to think that there are in fact many such cases. One example is if the predator species targeted for sterilization are also those with the greatest reproductive potential. Another example is the reduction of predation rates on large herbivores, since these animals consume a great deal of vegetation, thereby reducing the primary productivity that is the basis of the food chain (which reduces total birth rates). Thus, a decrease in predation on large herbivores would reduce total suffering and death precisely by increasing the population of large herbivores.

At this point it could be objected that, until there are thorough studies on how consequences unfold in this regard, we should adopt a policy against interventions. This is reasonable, but it does not establish that we should set this issue aside and "let nature take its course" (nor does it establish that it is right to intervene only when the victims are human). On the contrary, it establishes that we should carry out these studies – at least, that is what someone with a serious concern about consequences would do. If this is rejected, then it is an indication that concern about consequences was invoked not as a real concern, but as an excuse to keep holding the belief that intervening in predation is always wrong.

31.17. Existing cases and the prevention of new cases

We saw above that there seems to be no way of establishing that it is always wrong to intervene in predation. However, suppose that any intervention in predation were wrong because of some possible harm to the predator. This would tell us nothing about the morality of preventing new births of predators, since in that case what is at stake are mere possibilities of future sentient beings that would never come to be realized (and not beings who already exist and would be harmed). This will be explained in more detail below.

Most people do not argue that there is a duty to produce new individuals. And even those who argue that there is such a duty acknowledge that killing those who already exist is worse than refraining from producing new individuals. There are good reasons to think this way. When someone who already exists is killed, there is an individual who is harmed. On the other hand, with respect to refraining from producing new births, what there are are possibilities of future individuals that are never realized. For example, let us imagine that, if a couple decides to conceive a child now, an individual will be born nine months from now, but that if they decide to wait until next month, a different individual will be born, and so on for the following months. Realizing one of these possibilities means not realizing several of the others. But this is not the equivalent of killing someone who already exists.

Except in cases where the predator would die before managing to prey for the first time, producing new predators would entail the deaths of prey. Of course, many of the individuals who would be killed by predation probably do not exist yet. But this is different from future possibilities of individuals that are never realized. They would be individuals who would come to exist in the future and would then be killed. On the other hand, preventing the birth of new predators would merely mean not realizing future possibilities of individuals. If, as we saw earlier, killing already existing individuals is worse than refraining from producing new individuals, this implies preventing the birth of new predators (provided, of course, that the consequences are not worse than not doing so).

Let us consider an analogy. When we have scarce resources and many people dying of hunger, different people may disagree about who should have priority in receiving the resources. Giving the resources to some people would mean the deaths of others and vice versa But they would not disagree about whether it would be better for everyone to have resources and for us to eradicate hunger. In the same way, different people concerned about sentient beings, even if they disagree about whether we should favor the prey or the predator in this or that case, could not disagree, out of concern for sentient beings, that a world without predation is better (provided that, in this way, the consequences are not worse than those resulting from a world with predation).

It could be objected that this would mean driving species extinct, and that we should therefore not do it even if the consequences of not doing it are worse for sentient beings in general. In the first place, this would not necessarily mean the extinction of species because, as we have seen, there is the possibility of genetic modification. But even if it did, this would be insufficient to show that it is wrong to do it. It would have to be shown that species have intrinsic value, and that this value is more important than the good of sentient beings. But, as we saw in Chapter 20, there are good reasons to think exactly the opposite.

31.18. The goal of reducing primary productivity

Given what we have seen above, contrary to the prevailing belief, there is nothing inherently wrong with intervening in predation. In fact, there are good reasons to bring it about that predation no longer exists (provided that this does not lead to worse consequences than if there is predation).

However, this does not mean that intervening in predation is necessarily the best way of preventing/minimizing natural harms. Another option (probably more efficient and safer) would be to reduce primary productivity, which is the amount of energy produced by plants through photosynthesis, which serves as the basis for the entire food chain157.

This is not the same as cutting down plants, since in that case others would probably grow in their place. Instead, it would involve covering an area so that plants do not grow there (by paving, covering the lawn with gravel or something else that blocks sunlight), which would reduce the conversion of light into food energy.

One of the most frequent objections to intervention in predation points to the risk that the prey will reproduce even more, so that the intervention will increase the total amount of suffering and

premature death. The proposal to reduce primary productivity easily escapes this objection, since less available energy leads to a smaller total population of animals.

Moreover, there are also interventions in predation that would probably have a positive balance because they indirectly reduce primary productivity. For example, if there are no predators of large herbivores, there will probably be an increase in their populations. These herbivores consume a large amount of pasture, which in turn reduces primary productivity and, consequently, the total population158.

31.19. Conclusion

Everything we have discussed in this chapter shows that the taboo that has arisen around the issue of predation is probably the result of speciesism, since the prevailing position when humans are the victims of predation is exactly the opposite.

Our main conclusions were that: (1) there are good reasons for us to reduce the incidence of predation in the world (provided this does not lead to worse consequences); and that (2) there are certain interventions in predation that would probably have a positive net impact over time because they indirectly reduce primary productivity.

32. Discussing Our Ability to Assess When Life Is or Is Not Worth Living

32.1. The meaningful life argument

As explained in Chapter 3, the vast majority of animals born in the wild experience basically nothing but suffering and die quite prematurely. If so, it makes sense to claim that these animals would be better off had they not been born (and that, therefore, we should prevent births under such conditions).

A possible objection would say that it is possible for a life that seems not worth living from the outside to be satisfying for the one living it, and vice versa. Thus, given the difficulty of establishing a precise point beyond which a life is worth living, the objection concludes that the most prudent decision is to adopt a policy against helping animals in the wild.

Below, several problems with this objection will be pointed out.

32.2. Are we not well placed to assess when a life is worth living?

There are cases in which it is difficult to say whether or not living is worth it. However, there are cases in which such an assessment is very simple. For example, let us imagine that we were offered the chance to be reborn to live a life in which almost all experiences were of extreme suffering. If we were unable to judge that this life is not worth living, we would be unsure whether or not it is worth accepting such an offer.

Almost all the situations in which the proposal to help wild animals needs to make assessments about the value of life are extreme situations like this last one. A large proportion of the animals born in the wild are born only to suffer intensely, without any positive experience at all. If we were offered this kind of life, we would have no doubt: we would reject it completely. And we would do so not because we are human, but because we can understand how bad it would be. Thus, if such an opportunity were given to animals, and if they understood how bad such a life would be, they would certainly reject it too.

It could be objected that someone's life may have been terrible up to a certain point, but that it may be possible to improve it. When there is this possibility of improvement, it makes sense to say that, even if life so far has had a negative balance, it was nonetheless worth being born (given the possibility of a future positive balance), and that, therefore, it is false that, for each animal born in the wild, it would have been better not to have been born.

This is true, but it is not an objection to the proposal to help animals in the wild who are victims of natural processes. On the contrary: it is a reason to try to help them, since the possibility of their coming to have a meaningful life depends on our devoting ourselves to researching how to improve their situation.

Moreover, it is important to note that the goal of improving the living conditions of beings who already exist does not imply rejecting the goal of preventing new births. This is because the greater the number of births, the harder it will probably be to improve the life of each of the individuals born

32.3. Should we not try to assess when a life is worth living?

Even if we did not know how to assess when a life is worth living, any responsible view of ethics would say that we should try to acquire more knowledge about how to do so, since this would increase the likelihood of our benefiting those affected.

32.4. Doesn't the position against helping make assessments about when a life is worth living?

What motivates the objection we are discussing is the fear that we might wrongly judge that a life is not worth living. For example, with sterilization we could reduce the number of sentient beings with meaningful lives, or, in other cases, we could be committing murder while thinking we were practicing euthanasia.

Well, but this shows that the proponents of the objection do make assessments about the value of life, since they believe that intervention to prevent/minimize natural harms could prevent the enjoyment of lives that they judge to be meaningful.

However, we must also take into account the possibility of our judging that a life is worth living when in fact it is not. For example, if we refrain from carrying out a certain sterilization, motivated by the belief that such beings would lead at least minimally meaningful lives, then if our judgment is wrong we are contributing to bringing into existence many beings who would be born into lives full of extreme suffering.

The risk of bringing someone into a life of extreme suffering is much more worrying than the risk of failing to produce a new being who would lead a meaningful life, since only in the case of bringing someone into a life of suffering does there come to exist an individual who is harmed. Given the way natural processes occur, non-intervention would result in the maximization of lives in which extreme suffering predominates from beginning to end.

To argue that "letting nature take its course" results in a greater number of lives worth living is either to have no idea how natural processes occur or to defend the implausible idea that a life containing nothing but extreme suffering is worth living.

33. The Prolonged Agony Argument

33.1. The objection that extending lifespan is worse for animals

Consider the following objection to the proposal to help animals living in the wild. By helping these animals, we are saving them from a given threat of death and therefore prolonging their lives. However, having one's life prolonged is a benefit only when that life is at least minimally meaningful. But, the objection continues, almost all animals born in the wild are born only to experience suffering. Thus, by saving these animals, we would achieve the opposite of the intended effect: we would prolong their agony. Therefore, the objection concludes, what best fulfills the goal of achieving the least bad state of affairs for animals is not to try to help them. Below we will discuss this objection.

33.2. Is prolonging the lives of animals living in the wild always worse for them?

Although they are the vast majority, not all animals in the wild have lives that fail to be even minimally meaningful. We saw in Chapter 3 that the maximization of lives dominated by suffering occurs in the case of species that reproduce by maximizing the number of offspring. In the case of animals who reproduce by having few offspring per litter (for example, large animals such as elephants, zebras, deer, etc.), there is a greater chance that the young will have lives with an acceptable level of well-being. Of course, even these animals will face an environment where food and water may be scarce, and they will be vulnerable to disease, parasitism, predation and other conflicts with animals. However, if we help them (for example, by providing water, food, vaccines and medical treatment), we will help increase the likelihood that their lives will be at least minimally meaningful.

It could be objected that these animals are a very tiny minority of those living in the wild, and that we should therefore intervene only in a very limited number of cases. However, it is important to bear in mind that, regarding animals who reproduce by maximizing offspring, the fact that their lives are full of suffering is due to their being in an environment where the conditions for anyone to survive for long are completely unfavorable. If we intervene by creating conditions in which these animals can survive longer, their chances of having an at least minimally meaningful life would increase159. Prolonging their lives only results in something worse (compared with their dying now) if we do nothing to prevent other forms of suffering to which they will be subject.

Moreover, an important detail is that, for the vast majority of animals in the wild, what causes them suffering generally also causes their death (for example, starvation and disease). Thus, if we save an animal from death, we prolong its existence, but at the same time we ensure that it is no longer suffering from that cause. And, given that the things that make them suffer normally also cause their deaths, if we offer treatment for these ills, we will be prolonging their lives but also eliminating sources of suffering for them, thereby increasing their levels of well-being. The only case in which this does not happen is when an animal suffers from an ailment that makes it suffer but does not cause its death (but such cases are very rare).

One of the reasons why suffering predominates in the lives of animals in the wild is that the vast majority of animals normally die very early. That is, if they have longer lives, the chances that positive experiences will outweigh the suffering in their lives increase. Thus, in the vast majority of cases, preventing the cause of an animal's death is not prolonging its suffering: rather, it is preventing it. So, in the case of the vast majority of animals in the wild (and not only in the case of animals who reproduce by having few offspring), prolonging their lives benefits them.

33.3. Does intervening to help animals in the wild always prolong their lives?

It is also false that all interventions prolong animals' lives: many merely prevent new births. And, given that most of the suffering and premature death in the wild arises from the maximization of reproduction, preventing births would be the central focus of interventions. In this way, even if increasing animals' lifespan prolonged their agony (which, as we have seen, is false), there would still be strong reasons for us to reduce the number of births.

34. The Objection That the Balance of the Situation of Animals in the Wild May Be Positive

34.1. The claim that the overall balance may be positive

It is sometimes argued that the overall balance of the situation of animals in the wild may be positive160. This is because, although the number of animals who die prematurely after lives full of suffering is vastly greater than the number of animals who have lives with a positive balance, the few survivors live for many years, and so the sum of their positive experiences could tip the scales toward the positive.

34.2. If the overall balance is positive, so what?

Suppose the aggregate overall balance were positive. There would still be an astronomical number of animals who individually have lives with negative balances. We would have strong reasons to help these animals. Interestingly, these reasons are equally strong in the case of animals who individually have lives with a positive balance but are facing a negative episode.

Just imagine human victims in their place and everything becomes very clear. The reasons to help humans starving in underdeveloped countries are not weakened just because there are well-off humans in first-world countries. The reasons to help someone who is in terrible suffering are not weakened just because their life may contain, overall, more positive than negative experiences. People think differently in the case of nonhuman animals only because of the prevalence of speciesism.

34.3. Which views could accept helping regardless of the overall balance?

The thesis that, even if the balance (individual or collective) is positive, the reasons for us to help animals are not weakened would be accepted by many views in ethics:

(1) It would be accepted by those who agree that preventing what is negative is more important, at least to some extent, than promoting what is positive.

(2) It would be accepted by those who accept that the happiness of others does not weaken the reasons for us to help those who are badly off, and that the fact that someone is well off at other times does not weaken the reasons to help them when they are badly off.

(3) Even those who believe that all that matters is the overall balance, and who consider promoting what is positive as important as preventing what is negative, would have reasons to prioritize eliminating what is negative. This is so because of the principle of diminishing marginal utility, according to which an extra unit of a resource produces greater increases in well-being the worse off the one who would receive it is. For example, if someone is starving and receives a kilogram of food, this produces a greater increase in their well-being than if we gave it to someone who is already well off. Thus, prioritizing improving the situation of those who are in a negative situation is more efficient for increasing the overall balance.

34.4. Decisions in which the only option is to change the situation as a whole

It could be objected that, unlike scenarios in which it is possible to choose to maintain a situation and merely reduce what is negative in it, there are scenarios in which we can only affect the situation as a whole. Below are some examples.

(1) The decision whether to maintain or destroy an ecosystem. (2) The decision whether or not to create new ecosystems. (3) The decision whether or not to recreate ecosystems that have already gone extinct.

What to do in decisions like these depends on the weight assigned to positive aspects relative to negative aspects. Two people could agree that a situation has a positive balance and still disagree about what should be done about it.

For example, let us imagine that, if we create a new ecosystem, the aggregate overall balance will be positive. However, let us also suppose that an enormous number of individuals with lives full of suffering would be born, though fewer than the number of individuals who would have positive lives. Someone who holds that promoting what is positive is as important as preventing what is negative would say that it is better to create such a situation. However, this is not the only possible position. Another person could agree that such a situation has a positive balance but hold that preventing what is negative is more important than promoting what is positive.

It could be objected that prioritizing preventing what is negative would have absurd implications, such as saying that no amount of what is positive, however great, could compensate for something negative, however small. However, this would be so only if preventing what is negative were considered a trump over promoting what is positive. But that is not the only possibility. Preventing what is negative could carry greater weight without being a trump (depending on how much greater its weight was, the greater the amount of positive aspects would have to be to compensate for a certain amount of negative aspects).

34.5. Conclusion

Even if the aggregate balance of the situation of animals in the wild were positive, this would not weaken the reasons to minimize/prevent its negative aspects, nor would it necessarily be decisive for decisions of the "maintain/eliminate" and "create/not create" type regarding a situation.

In the previous section we saw three examples of situations of this kind:

(1) The decision whether to maintain or destroy an ecosystem. (2) The decision whether or not to create new ecosystems. (3) The decision whether or not to recreate ecosystems that have already gone extinct.

What should the decision depend on in these contexts? The next three chapters address these questions.

35. What Impact Does Veganism Have on the Situation of Wild Animals?

35.1. The idea that preventing natural harms implies rejecting veganism

The main argument in favor of veganism, as far as diet is concerned, is that it reduces the number of animals who are born to suffer and be killed in exploitation. Moreover, it reduces the number of animal deaths that are a side effect of agriculture, since it requires a smaller area of cropland than animal exploitation needs to feed the same number of humans (since the animals who are killed are fattened on plants).

However, it could be objected that the need for a smaller area of cropland would in fact result in greater suffering and more deaths for animals. This would happen because more green areas would be left over, which would increase primary productivity and, consequently, the number of births of animals who maximize the number of offspring. As a result, the amount of suffering and death would be maximized with far greater efficiency than that present in animal exploitation or in the side effects of agriculture.

In short, according to this objection, the large-scale adoption of veganism, despite reducing the number of exploited animals and of animals who are victims of the side effects of agriculture, would increase the total amount of animal suffering and death by indirectly increasing the amount of reproduction in natural territory.

35.2. Does veganism necessarily imply an increase in green areas?

Curiously, the fact that certain forms of raising animals for consumption reduce green areas (for example, raising cattle on open pastures) is normally mentioned as a negative aspect of animal exploitation. However, as should be clear by now, this is perhaps the only respect in which animal exploitation probably prevents more suffering and death than it causes. This does not mean, of course, that animal exploitation is justified. As we will see below, there are other ways of achieving this same positive aspect without the harms that animal exploitation causes.

For example, the connection between veganism and an increase in green areas is not necessary. It could be a very likely result in a world where the vast majority of people hold environmentalist ideals. But let us suppose a future in which consideration for animals was widespread. People would want to pursue the abolition of their exploitation. However, they would also want to prevent their suffering and deaths resulting from natural processes. This shows that the increase in natural territory (and the resulting maximization of suffering and of the number of deaths) is not a necessary implication of veganism: it is an implication only of abstaining from consuming animals out of environmentalist and anthropocentric concerns161.

35.3. Distinguishing first-order and second-order harms

There is another important factor to consider: the way in which each practice influences other agents to act in one way or another. To illustrate this point, it is useful to distinguish between first-order and second-order outcomes.

First-order outcomes are all those direct or indirect effects of a practice that do not depend on the decisions of other agents. The suffering and deaths of animals resulting from their exploitation, or as a side effect of agriculture, or as a result of the increase in green areas, are all direct and indirect first-order effects. Second-order effects, by contrast, would depend on how each action influences other agents to make decisions. Thus, it is possible for a given practice to be less bad with respect to first-order outcomes (adding up direct and indirect outcomes), but to be worse overall because its worse second-order outcomes are much greater.

With this difference in mind, let us suppose for the sake of argument that animal exploitation had turned out to be less bad in terms of the resulting first-order harms (adding up direct and indirect harms). Even so, not consuming animals, provided it is promoted for reasons of consideration for animals (and not for environmentalist or anthropocentric reasons), could contribute to preventing much greater second-order harms, by spreading the ideal of consideration for sentient beings.

If not consuming animals with this kind of motivation were spread on a large scale, there would be no risk of maximizing suffering and death as a result of the increase in natural territory. Since consideration for animals implies preventing/minimizing

natural harms, vegans who were aware of this would want both that animals not be exploited and that they be prevented from being harmed by natural processes (which would imply not expanding natural territory).

The ideal of consideration for sentient beings could help prevent long-term harms not only from natural processes. It could also prevent the development and use of possible future technologies that had the potential to harm a gigantic number of sentient beings162.

Animal exploitation, on the other hand, even if it were less bad in terms of first-order harms, would have a negative impact in terms of second-order harms, since it reinforces the idea that animals are not morally considerable. Therefore, it would not influence people to avoid the harms that animals suffer as a result of exploitation, of other human practices, or of natural processes. It would also increase the probability of a gigantic increase in natural territory, thereby maximizing animal suffering and death extremely efficiently. Moreover, such a worldview would also increase the probability that future technologies will be used in ways that harm sentient beings in general, on a scale far greater than anything done so far.

35.4. Conclusion

Ironically, the potential that the practice of veganism has to bring about improvements for nonhuman animals lies much more in the kind of ideal it could help spread than in the results of the act of not consuming animals. However, this positive potential for animals exists only if not consuming animals is promoted with arguments in favor of the moral consideration of animals (with emphasis on the need to prevent/minimize natural harms). Otherwise, as we have seen, there is a risk that it will result in an increase in natural territory, which would mean the maximization of animal suffering and death. Thus, not consuming animals promoted for anthropocentric and, above all, environmentalist reasons, if adopted on a large scale, runs a high risk of having results even worse than animal exploitation. In this way, the proposal to minimize natural harms supports veganism, provided it is promoted out of consideration for animals.
