36. The Debate on the Destruction of Nature

36.1. The context

Increasing the green areas on the planet (whether through their preservation, restoration or expansion) is almost always seen as something unquestionably positive, above all suspicion. This happens for two reasons: (1) most people hold anthropocentric and environmentalist views, which leads them to attach no importance to the impact each practice has on nonhuman animals. (2) Most people, including those who care about nonhuman animals, do not know that an increase in green areas means an increase in primary productivity and, consequently, in reproduction rates (which indirectly maximizes the amount of animal suffering and premature death).

As we saw in Chapter 3, the vast majority of animals in the wild reproduce by maximizing the number of offspring (in the thousands or even millions per brood depending on the species), and the average survival rate in stable populations is only two per brood. All the rest are normally born to lives full of suffering and a premature death, usually an extremely painful one. In short, the more green areas, the greater the total amount of suffering and premature death.

It could be objected that sentient beings also need green areas as a resource, and that reducing them could therefore harm the quality of life of many sentient beings. This is true, but given the gigantic reproduction rates, the amount of suffering and death caused by an increase in green areas would always be enormously greater than that prevented by such an expansion. In short, an increase in green areas is good from an anthropocentric or environmentalist point of view, but it has a gigantically negative balance if we take into account all the sentient beings affected.

36.2. Arguments in favor of altruistic killing

In this chapter we will discuss what we will call altruistic killing163. According to this position, the best thing we can do to prevent natural harms is to reduce the number of natural ecosystems. This position acknowledges that, in doing so, we will kill and cause suffering to an enormous number of animals. However, it holds that, if we do not do so, the amount of suffering and death that will ensue will be immensely greater.

Defenders of this position acknowledge that the ideal would be to prevent the suffering and premature deaths of animals in the wild without having to cause suffering or death (for example, through a reduction in birth rates, vaccinations, disease treatment and so on). However, they argue that it may take a long time for such solutions to be applied on a large scale, and it may even be that this never happens. For this reason, they argue that altruistic killing is what has the best balance in terms of causing/preventing harm since, even if nonlethal solutions one day come to be applied on a large scale, the time it could take for this to happen would mean the deaths and suffering of many more animals than altruistic killing.

For example, the urbanization of green areas (such as the construction of roads and housing) results in the deaths and suffering of many of the animals living there. However, most of these animals reproduce by maximizing the number of offspring and, consequently, maximize the number of them who are born to experience suffering and die prematurely. Thus, urbanization, despite causing suffering and death, drastically reduces the total balance of suffering and death, whether compared with letting nature take its course or compared with waiting for nonlethal programs to reduce birth rates.

Tomasik (2016a) gives the following example to illustrate the issue. Suppose the world were full of human baby factories. These babies are eaten alive after weeks or months of life, but 1 in every 20 babies manages to live well until 3 years of age. Let us imagine that most people do not want to eliminate these factories and actually like them because, seen from the outside, they are very beautiful and almost no one notices the suffering and deaths that occur there. However, imagine that some people accidentally destroy

these factories while building houses and parking lots. This procedure kills the babies who are there, but prevents many more of them from being born to such a fate. Bearing in mind that the vast majority of humanity is not on your side, and that you have limited resources, you have a choice: (1) either promote economic activities that will destroy one hundred of these baby factories; (2) or close five factories, saving the babies in them, but this means that the other 95 you could have destroyed will continue to operate. The author argues that, if our goal is to reduce suffering and death as much as possible, we should choose 1.

36.3. Arguments against altruistic killing

To assess whether altruistic killing has better results than waiting for nonlethal solutions, it is useful to distinguish between first-order and second-order outcomes164. First-order outcomes are all the outcomes (direct or indirect) of an action that do not depend on how it influences the decisions of other agents. Second-order outcomes depend on how the action influences the decisions of other agents (these decisions, in turn, also have first- and second-order outcomes, and so on).

On this basis it could be argued that altruistic killing, even if it has better first-order outcomes, could have second-order outcomes so negative (because of how it would influence the way humans see the cause of reducing wild animal suffering and consideration for animals in general) that it would be better to wait for nonlethal solutions. There are two main arguments along these lines, explained below.

The first argument is that the cause of reducing wild animal suffering is already widely rejected and, if its proponents advocate killing animals, this rejection will increase even further, especially among animal advocates. In short, advocating altruistic killing may lead people in general never to come to care about the suffering and deaths of wild animals.

The second is that, if altruistic killing is advocated, the public may come to understand that the good of animals does not matter, and this could lead to a further increase in the harms that humans cause to animals.

36.4. Replies from those who defend altruistic killing

Proponents of altruistic killing have offered the following responses to the arguments above:

(1) If altruistic killing is advocated by explaining that it is justified only if every other option would result in even more suffering and death, there is a low risk that this will encourage the public to support other practices that would increase the amount of suffering and death. In fact, it could positively influence the public's decisions, by encouraging people to reason carefully about controversial moral questions, to question the moral relevance of the distinction between acts and omissions, to be concerned about the total amount of suffering and death over time, not to be afraid to question entrenched intuitions (such as the intuition that preserving nature has a positive balance), and so on.

(2) Even if advocating altruistic killing influences humans to increase the harms they cause to animals, the destruction of habitats would prevent far more suffering and death than the sum of all the harms humans cause to animals.

36.5. Rejoinders from those who condemn altruistic killing

In response to the first reply, it could be pointed out that the public normally does not even read what the proponents of a position argue, much less read it with attention to nuance. Therefore, there is a high risk that the cause of reducing wild animal suffering will be rejected even more than it already is if altruistic killing is advocated.

In response to the second reply, it could be said that, so far, the total harm that humans cause to animals is much smaller than the total of natural harms, but that this may change in the future. This would be the case if humans come to restore or expand natural territory on Earth, or if they send life beyond Earth, colonize space and so on165. In that case, humans would create the conditions for natural processes to maximize suffering and death far beyond anything that exists so far.

In short, this response argues that, if altruistic killing contributes to wild animal suffering being even more neglected, and this results in the expansion of nature, then altruistic killing would in the long run have worse results than waiting for nonlethal solutions to wild animal suffering.

36.6. A new reply from the defenders of altruistic killing

In the face of these new arguments, two new responses are available to proponents of altruistic killing.

The first is that all of their opponents' arguments, if sound, would show only that people who aim to prevent natural harms should not advocate altruistic killing, but they would not show that altruistic killing should not be carried out. For example, if it were carried out by people other than the proponents of preventing natural harms, or if it were carried out in secret, there would be no risks in terms of influencing the public's perception of the proposal to reduce natural harms or of the animal cause in general.

The second, more important, is that if the greater risk is that humans will maximize the harms they cause if they come to expand natural territory on Earth or beyond it, then what runs the greatest risk of leading to this is the idea that it is always wrong to destroy natural territory, not altruistic killing. Altruistic killing makes it very clear that expanding natural territory is not a good thing.

36.7. But won't humanity do this anyway?

Those who condemn altruistic killing could argue that, since humanity already automatically tends to expand urbanization, there is no need to advocate altruistic killing and, since advocating it also carries risks, it is better not to advocate it.

However, one could respond that research could be done on which land uses are most likely to have a positive balance for the sentient beings affected166 and,

on that basis, we could encourage these changes and also changes in consumption practices (just as we do in the case of exploited animals). Just to cite one example, Tomasik (2016a) argues that palm oil cultivation probably reduces the total balance of suffering, and that we could therefore encourage its consumption or, at least, oppose campaigns against palm oil cultivation167.

Another response along these lines points out that, if we explain to the public that less habitat means a lower total balance of suffering and death, this may make activists, legislators and the general public less enthusiastic about conservation policies and policies to expand natural territory. Since suspending such policies involves no expenditure of resources and requires no activity at all, it may be easier for the public to accept this proposal than to accept interventions to reduce the suffering of animals in the wild168.

36.8. Who bears the burden of proof?

We saw above that both sides of the debate have arguments grounded in concern about long-term consequences. Given this, a central question is the following: who bears the burden of proof?

On the one hand, it could be suggested that the burden of proof lies with those who advocate lethal solutions to a problem. However, proponents of altruistic killing could respond that they meet this burden of proof by showing that waiting for nonlethal alternatives necessarily means more suffering and death than using lethal alternatives.

We saw that, in response to this, those who oppose altruistic killing argue that, because of the influence it could have on agents' decisions over time, it could mean more suffering and death than waiting for nonlethal solutions. This would be the case if it influences people not to have moral consideration for nonhuman animals and this ends up resulting, for example, in the expansion of natural territory on Earth or beyond it.

On the other hand, however, proponents of altruistic killing could suggest that, in this case, the burden of proof lies with those who condemn altruistic killing, to show that it really

would have these counterproductive implications, since it could be promoted by emphasizing that it is justified only when all other options cause even more suffering and death. As we have seen, those who are against altruistic killing argue that there is a risk that the public will misunderstand the message. But, again, proponents of altruistic killing could respond that the burden of proof lies with their opponents, to show that this risk is greater than the risk that natural harms will be maximized if altruistic killing is not carried out. Moreover, as we have seen, proponents of altruistic killing could point out that it is the view defended by their opponents (that it is always wrong to destroy natural ecosystems) that is more likely to be understood as implying that expanding nature is a good thing.

Finally, proponents of altruistic killing can point out that there are two other factors suggesting that the burden of proof lies with their opponents. One is the fact that we have an inclination to reject violent interventions, and this may lead us to assess the probabilities of consequences in a biased way. The other is the fact that the harms in the case of altruistic killing would occur through action, whereas in the case of waiting for nonlethal solutions they would occur through omission (but would be much greater). Since harms caused by action are more noticeable than those caused by omission, this is a reason to be suspicious of the preference for waiting for nonlethal solutions.

Thus, it seems that the burden of proof lies with the opponents of altruistic killing. However, it is important to stress that the concern that altruistic killing might be counterproductive could also come from a thorough analysis of the risks, and not only from the inclination mentioned above. In any case, in the next chapter we will discuss in detail another way of preventing natural harms on a large scale that could be accepted by both proponents and opponents of altruistic killing: not expanding natural territory.

37. The Debate on the Expansion and Restoration of Nature

37.1. A way of minimizing natural harms that escapes the common objections

Consider the following objections to the proposal of minimizing/preventing natural harms:

(1) Intervening in nature is wrong in itself. (2) If we cannot predict the long-term consequences, it is better not to intervene. (3) We only have a duty not to harm, not a duty to help. (4) Such a proposal is too demanding. (5) It is not acceptable to alter natural territory. (6) There is nothing that can be done on a large scale right now. (7) It is hard to keep such harms from reappearing. (8) Such a proposal requires technology that does not yet exist. (9) Such a proposal requires an enormous amount of resources. (10) All interventions that cause suffering and death should be rejected.

We discussed each of these objections in previous chapters. This chapter will point out a way of minimizing natural harms that escapes all of these objections, even if they were plausible.

Suppose we ought not to intervene in nature to minimize natural harms. Imagine that natural harms no longer existed. Should we intervene in nature to recreate them? It is possible to minimize natural harms on a large scale simply by avoiding certain interventions that help natural processes maximize suffering and death.

Intervention in nature is practiced massively for anthropocentric and environmentalist goals. One type of intervention in particular contributes very efficiently to maximizing natural harms: the expansion of natural territory (such as the expansion of forests), or its recreation where desertification has occurred. Where there is vegetation, there will be many sentient beings reproducing by maximizing the number of offspring, and therefore maximizing suffering and death, given the extremely low survival rate (as we saw in Chapter 3). The result is also an increase in suffering due to other natural harms that are inherent to all natural ecosystems. Of course, some animals in these ecosystems would probably have positive lives. However, given the relationship between birth rates and survival rates, the number of beings who would be born into a life full of suffering and to a premature death would always be vastly greater. Thus, the net balance of expanding/restoring nature is enormously negative.

By avoiding this kind of practice, the reduction in suffering and death would be so great that even if animal exploitation were abolished, the number of individuals who would no longer be born only to experience intense suffering would pale in comparison169. For example, we could avoid creating areas rich in biomass that give rise to harms to many small animals. In their place, environments could be created with components that do not lead to a maximization of the number of births of sentient beings170.

The proposal of avoiding the expansion/recreation of natural territory escapes objections 1 and 2 because it does not require intervening in nature (it only requires avoiding certain interventions). It escapes objection 3 because it involves refraining from harming, not helping. It escapes objection 4 because it is easy to carry out. It escapes objection 5 because it does not require altering natural territory. It escapes objection 6 because it prevents natural harms on a large scale and can be done today. It escapes objection 7 because it permanently prevents the harms resulting from each expansion/restoration. It escapes objection 8 because it does not require technology that does not yet exist. It escapes objection 9 because it costs no resources at all. Finally, it escapes objection 10 because it is the expansion/restoration of natural territory that is an intervention, and it causes a gigantic amount of suffering and death.

Many people who raise those objections to the proposal of helping wild animals also advocate the expansion of natural territory. This is a sign that the concerns involved in those objections are not the real reason they oppose the proposal of helping wild animals, since the expansion of natural territory violates all of those concerns.

The expansion/recreation of the natural environment is usually seen as something with a positive net balance.

However, most people do not know that this practice maximizes the suffering and the number of deaths of animals. Once we are aware of this fact, is it still possible to defend such expansion/recreation? Below we will discuss some attempts.

37.2. Concern for future generations

Could our obligations toward future generations of sentient beings justify expanding/restoring natural territory? There are at least two ways of understanding obligations toward future generations171. The first holds that, if a future generation will exist, we have a duty to ensure conditions for its members to have a satisfying life. However, it holds that there is no obligation to bring that generation into existence. The second would agree that we have an obligation to ensure that the future generation has minimal conditions of well-being. But it will also hold that we have an obligation to bring that future generation into existence.

However, neither position could justify expanding/recreating natural territory. The first does not require producing any new sentient being. The second seeks the existence of the greatest number of sentient beings with predominantly positive lives (and not the greatest number of sentient beings, period). It would never approve of an action that resulted in very few positive lives and an immensely greater number of lives in which suffering predominates. The norm in wild life is for this ratio to be 1 to hundreds, thousands, or millions (and even many millions, depending on the case). So, in fact, concern for future beings weighs very heavily against the expansion/recreation of natural territory.

37.3. Concern for the current generation

It could be objected that expanding/recreating nature may be necessary to ensure the well-being of sentient beings who already exist (or who will come to exist in the future regardless of what we decide).

One problem with this argument is that, given the predominant reproductive strategy (which maximizes the number of offspring), the number of beings who would be born only to suffer would

always be vastly greater than the number of those who are alive now or who would be born to have positive lives and would need the environment as a resource.

It could be objected that the beings of future generations who would be born to have negative lives do not yet exist and therefore do not count. However, if we decide to expand/restore nature, they will come to exist and, therefore, they do count. And in that case it could not be said that we are doing them a favor, since they would be brought into a life of extreme suffering. Moreover, the objection contradicts itself by saying that the good of beings who do not yet exist does not matter, while at the same time saying that it is necessary to expand/recreate natural territory out of concern for the good of beings of future generations who will exist anyway.

37.4. The appeal to environmentalist values

It could be argued that we should expand/restore natural territory because doing so would be better from an environmentalist point of view (for example, it would increase biodiversity and the number of natural ecosystems), even if the result is a world history with a greater amount of suffering and premature death of sentient beings.

This position assumes not only that the nonsentient entities valued in environmentalism have intrinsic value: it also assumes that they are more important than the good of sentient beings. However, we saw in Chapter 20 that: (1) the very idea that there is value beyond sentience is already controversial; and (2) there are reasons to prioritize preventing the suffering and death of sentient beings, even if the entities valued in environmentalism have intrinsic value. Therefore, those arguments will not be repeated here.

37.5. The concern about non-acceptance

Another objection claims that the expansion/recreation of natural territory is so widely accepted and seen as so important that opposing it would carry a serious risk of creating rejection of the proposal to minimize natural harms (and even of consideration for nonhuman animals in general).

Although this risk exists, it has to be weighed against the risk of losing the opportunity to prevent, on a large scale, the emergence of new natural harms, and also against the risk of losing the opportunity to begin questioning ideas that stand in the way of minimizing natural harms and of considering nonhuman animals, and that tend to maximize harms in general.

Discussing the morality of expanding/recreating natural territory is a way of questioning the points that keep people from taking the issue of natural harms seriously (for example, the romanticized view of the lives of animals in the wild and the veneration of what is natural).

Obviously, because it is a controversial topic, it is important to choose to present it to an audience capable of understanding it. But the same holds for any other controversial subject. For example, if someone has never heard of the problem of natural harms, it does not seem a good idea to introduce the subject through the problem of the expansion of natural territory. However, if someone already accepts the goal of helping nonhuman animals in general, there is no reason to hide the fact that the expansion of natural territory would harm them greatly.

37.6. The risk of human extinction

Another concern is that not expanding/restoring natural territory might increase the likelihood of natural catastrophes and climate change, which, in turn, might increase the risk of human extinction. According to this objection, because of this risk, expanding/restoring natural territory would be justified.

There are at least two reasons that could lead someone to think that the risk of the disappearance of the human species would justify expanding/recreating natural territory. We will discuss these reasons separately in the next two sections.

37.7. Concern for humans themselves

The first is concern for humans themselves (of the current generation or of future ones). But if human interests count as a reason in favor of expanding/recreating nature, then the harms to other animals must count as a reason against it. And, given the amount of individual harm and the number of individuals harmed, a nonarbitrary analysis would prescribe not expanding/recreating nature even if humans mattered much more than nonhumans.

37.8. The idea that the human presence has a positive net balance

The second reason is the thought that human extinction would have a negative net balance, taking into account all the sentient beings affected. Of course, humans also cause an enormous amount of harm to sentient beings in general. But, according to this view, even so, the overall net balance of the human presence could be positive, on account of three points:

The first is that humans in the future will probably be the only ones capable of minimizing natural harms. In the absence of humans and of technology to minimize natural harms, natural processes would maximize suffering and death for long ages. That is why it would be important to avoid not only human extinction but also the collapse of civilization.

The second is that, in the absence of humans, the places currently occupied by humans would probably be occupied by animals that reproduce by maximizing their offspring, and therefore the result would be a greater amount of suffering and premature death.

The third is that, as we saw in Chapter 36, human practices that destroy natural ecosystems, despite also causing suffering and death, have a positive net balance. This is because such interventions, precisely because they destroy ecosystems, prevent the birth of an immensely greater number of sentient beings who would have lives full of suffering (even though that is not the goal of such interventions).

Thus, according to this view, if the presence of humanity has a positive net balance, and if not expanding natural territory is a threat to humanity, expanding/recreating natural territory would have a positive net balance in the long run, even if it has a negative net balance in the short run.

We will discuss these points in the next sections.

37.9. The risk that humanity will come to expand suffering

The concerns listed in the previous section are certainly important. However, we must also take into account the possibility that the human presence may come to have a negative net balance in the future, even if it has had a positive net balance so far. This would happen if in the future humanity were to carry out activities that maximize suffering and death far beyond anything that has existed until then. Below we will see two examples of such activities172.

One example would be if in the future humanity manages to develop space colonization. In that case humanity would expand life beyond Earth, probably recreating in many other places the natural processes that result in the maximization of suffering and death. For example, terraforming173 and panspermia174 aim to create, beyond Earth, the conditions for other celestial bodies to become habitable. There are already projects underway in this direction, whether to ensure that humans can live on other planets in the future175 or to maximize the number of living beings throughout the universe176. This would increase enormously the number of sentient beings who are victims of natural processes, to the point of making the suffering of the animals living on Earth a grain of sand in comparison177.

Another example is if in the future it becomes possible to create sentient beings in digital media. This could be useful for simulating universes inside a computer, for example. Such a practice would also have the potential to increase by many orders of magnitude the suffering and death that exist until then178.

These possibilities already show that it is uncertain whether the presence of humans in the world, taking the long term into account, is better or worse. This would depend, among other things, on whether or not the humans of the future will expand nature. In turn, whether or not this will happen depends on whether the humans of the future will be guided by environmentalist and anthropocentric values or by consideration for all sentient beings. Therefore, it seems that the most plausible stance is to leave open whether the human presence over time will have a positive or a negative net balance.

37.10. Is the expansion of nature really necessary to save humanity?

Suppose that the presence of humanity turns out to have a positive net balance and that we should therefore prevent human extinction and the collapse of civilization. This does not necessarily imply expanding natural territory, since there are ways of preventing climate change or reducing its harmful effects without creating new environments such as forests. One example is pursuing energy efficiency and renewable energy179. And even if it were justified to expand/recreate nature in order to avoid disasters or climate change, this would not justify the expansion/recreation of nature for other purposes.

37.11. Conclusion

If the preceding arguments are sound, we should avoid expanding/recreating natural territory as much as possible. As we have seen, the cases in which expansion/recreation could be justified are those in which all the other options would result in something even worse. If such cases exist at all, they are a small fraction of the practices of expanding/recreating natural territory.

Given that avoiding such expansions/recreations requires no expenditure of resources and prevents a gigantic number of sentient beings from being born only to suffer, avoiding the expansion/recreation of natural territory is currently one of the most efficient ways of preventing natural harms (and probably harms in general) on a large scale.

Expanding/recreating nature produces an amount of suffering and death immensely greater even than if a gigantic factory farm were created in the same place, since, as we saw in Chapter 3, natural processes are much more efficient at producing suffering and death than even factory farms.

When we look at a natural territory (for example, a forest), we do not have this impression because, looking from the outside, what we see is a beautiful landscape. This “veneer” keeps us from realizing that the reality for the animals who live there is constant extreme suffering from the beginning to the end of their (short) existences, and that the number of animals who meet this fate continues to be maximized indefinitely by natural processes.

Volume VIII

Effective Activism

This book presents the main criteria for selecting which causes to prioritize and which problems to prioritize within those causes. It also presents criteria for assessing how efficient activism strategies are and applies these criteria to various practical questions.

Original text by Luciano Carlos Cunha, translated into English · ISBN 978-65-01-52404-7 · 1st edition, June 2025.

1. How to Choose Which Causes and Problems to Prioritize and Which Strategies Are Best?

1.1. Introduction

There are many causes in the world, each dealing with important problems. How do we choose which of them to devote ourselves to and which problems to prioritize within those causes?

The following answers are very common:

(1) We should prioritize causes that aim to help humans. (2) Each person should choose the causes and problems they most sympathize with, or that have something to do with their life story. (3) All causes and problems are equally important (so we should divide our dedication equally among each cause and each problem within each cause).

In contrast to all these answers, there is another possibility:

(4) Having the goal of making the world a less bad place in the most efficient way possible, that is, doing the greatest good possible given the resources available to us (money and time spent, for example).

If we adopt this goal, we will need to assess which causes to prioritize, which problems to prioritize within those causes, and which strategies are best for addressing them1. This is because of the following:

  • Different causes deal with problems that affect different numbers of victims, with suffering of different magnitudes and different mortality rates.
  • In addition, different causes are neglected to a greater or lesser degree, which is reflected in the number of activists and the amount of resources available to them.
  • Finally, depending on whether we apply a given resource to this or that problem, and on whether we use this or that strategy to try to solve the problem we have selected, we will do more or less good.

This is one of the most important decisions because, depending on how we decide, we will be more or less efficient at reducing what is bad in the world. Moreover, as we will see in the following chapters, if we do not make a good choice, we even run the risk of unintentionally increasing suffering and death in the world even further.

Below we will look at some criteria that can help us with this kind of decision.

1.2. How serious is the situation?

A first type of criterion for choosing which causes to prioritize and which problems to prioritize within those causes is how serious each situation addressed is (which is sometimes called the scale of harm). Of course, people disagree about which criteria to use to assess how serious a situation is. However, two criteria are widely accepted: the number of victims and how bad the victims’ situation is. For this reason, the examples below use these two criteria, but it is important to remember that there may be others (such as the levels of inequality among the victims, for example).

One difficulty when we have more than one criterion for assessing the seriousness of a situation is that they may point in the same direction sometimes, but in opposite directions at other times. For example, sometimes the problem with the greatest number of victims is also the one in which the victims are in the worst situation. At other times one problem has more victims, but it is another one in which the victims are in a worse situation. When the parameters do not coincide, how should we proceed? There are several possibilities. Below we will look at some of them.

(1) Choosing on the basis of only one of the parameters. However, one criticism of this method is that it seems arbitrary to choose one of the two. If it is the number of victims, why not the seriousness of the victims’ situation, and vice versa?

(2) Establishing a fixed hierarchy between the parameters. However, one difficulty for this method would be to show why one of the parameters, and not the other, would be the most important. Moreover, there are both situations in which it seems preferable to help a much larger number of victims, even if they are not in the worst situation, and situations in which it seems preferable to help victims who are in a much worse situation, even if they are not the majority.

(3) Relying on the total net balance of suffering. This is obtained by adding up the suffering of each victim. For example, if in a certain problem we have victim A with -35 of suffering and victim B with -10, the total aggregate balance is -45. According to this method, the number of victims and how serious each victim’s situation is do not matter in themselves: they matter only indirectly, insofar as they influence the total aggregate balance. However, one criticism of this method is that it could consider more serious a situation that has a much larger number of victims, but in which each one individually suffers a far milder harm.

(4) Giving weight proportional to the seriousness of the situation. This method is also based on the total net balance of suffering, but in it the weight of each individual is proportional to how bad their situation is (the worse it is, the more weight it has). This method largely avoids the problem of the previous method but, in certain cases, it could still consider more serious a situation in which a majority had much smaller harms. However, for this to happen under this method, the size of that majority would have to be much larger than under the previous method.

(5) Establishing absolute priority lines. In this method, a level of well-being is stipulated below which a situation of the individuals is the most serious, no matter how many more individuals above that level other situations involve.

(6) Establishing variable priority lines. This method is similar to the previous one, with the difference that, beyond a certain number of victims who are above the threshold level (for example, N times greater than the number of victims below it) but who are still in a bad situation, the situation of that majority is considered more serious.

These are just a few examples of methods, but there are others. For reasons of space, we will not discuss here which methods are best. These difficulties should not lead us to think that there is no way of assessing which situation is more serious. Even if we cannot achieve precision in these assessments, trying to make them is more likely to bring better results than deciding at random. This is a challenge we will have to face if our goal is to be efficient in the help we can give.

Moreover, even if we did not reach any satisfactory conclusion in situations where the parameters conflict, there are many situations in which the problem with the greatest number of victims is also the problem in which the victims are in the worst situation. The various situations in which nonhuman animals find themselves, whether those exploited by humans2 or those who live in the wild3, are good examples of this today.

1.3. How much of the problem can we try to solve?

Suppose we had reached a conclusion about which problems are most serious. Do we then already have an answer about which situations to prioritize? Not yet, for the following reason: it is possible that nothing can be done to help some of the victims of certain situations. We need to investigate how tractable each problem is (for this reason, this parameter is called tractability). It is illustrated by the following example.

Consider the following three pieces of information:

  • Problem A affects 900,000 victims.
  • Problem B affects 500,000 victims.
  • All the victims of A and B are in equally bad situations.

If we rely only on how serious each situation is, we will prioritize problem A.

However, let us now add the following information:

  • Regarding the 900,000 victims of A, the best we could do with the resources available to us is to help 400,000 of them: there is nothing we can do to help the other 500,000 (unfortunately, they are already doomed).
  • Regarding the 500,000 victims of B, on the other hand, it is possible to help 450,000 of them, providing them with the same amount of benefit we would provide to the 400,000 victims of problem A with the same resources.

Thus, taking into account the part of each situation that can be improved, we have a reason to prioritize problem B because, although A is a worse situation, it is B that presents the worse situation that can be improved.

Important: the tractability of each problem is changeable, since it depends on the technology available at the time. That is, a problem that is not very tractable today may become more tractable in the future, depending on how much we invest in researching how to solve it.

1.4. Choosing the best solutions

1.4.1. The importance of the amount of benefit we could produce

The previous criteria are important for detecting which problems deserve to be the focus of our attention. However, they do not help us find out which solutions would be the most efficient. For that, we have to estimate the amount of benefit that would be produced if we invested a certain amount of resources in this or that problem4. Below is an example that illustrates the importance of this parameter and shows how it relates to the criteria we saw earlier for selecting the most important problems.

Consider the following:

  • Problem A has 100 victims, each with a suffering of -50.
  • Problem B has 90 victims, each with a suffering of -40.

Problem A is more serious, whether by the criterion of the number of victims or by the criterion of the seriousness of each victim’s situation. Imagine also that it is possible to help all the victims of both problems. That is, the problems are equally tractable.

However, imagine that, with the same amount of resources, our only options are:

  • Either moving all the victims of A from -50 to -49 (a very slight relief).
  • Or moving all the victims of B from -40 to -10 (a considerable improvement).

In this case, by prioritizing problem B we would do much more good with the same amount of resources.

1.4.2. Is the amount of benefit always the most important factor?

What we saw above does not mean that the size of the benefit will necessarily always be the decisive factor. For example, depending on the situation, we might prefer to produce a slightly smaller total benefit that was directed to victims who are in a much worse situation, or that helped a much larger number of victims. For example, suppose that, in the example above, the decision were between:

  • Either moving the 100 victims of problem A from -50 to -30. Total benefit = 2,000,
  • Or moving the 90 victims of problem B from -40 to -10. Total benefit = 2,700.

In this case, some people would say that we should choose the first option (since that way the benefit goes to the victims who are in the worst situation, and it goes to a larger number of victims), even though with the second option we would produce a greater benefit (whether in terms of the benefit to each victim or in terms of total benefit, obtained by multiplying the number of victims by the benefit each would receive).

But how do we know when the amount of benefit weighs more and when the seriousness of the situation weighs more? There are several possible ways to proceed. The criteria could be equivalent to some of those we saw in section 1.2. One example would be to seek to maximize benefits, but stipulating that a unit of benefit has more value the more serious the problem it would be directed to (this would be the equivalent of criterion 4 in section 1.2).

1.5. To do the greatest good possible, we need to take the long term into account

Another important thing to consider when assessing the efficiency of each strategy is its impact over time5. Thus, if the goal is to do the greatest good possible, then we have to try to estimate the long-term consequences of each strategy.

For example, when comparing two strategies, it is possible that one produces more benefits initially, but that, taking into account the long-term effects of each, it is the other that will produce a greater total benefit over time. For example, it may be that a certain

strategy helps more animals in the short term, but that its impact gradually diminishes over time, while another, despite helping fewer animals initially, has a “snowball” type of positive impact over time, so that, once the impact of both has ended after a few years, it is the second one that has had the greatest positive impact.

Moreover, it is also possible that a strategy that produces great benefits in the short term has negative ramifications in the long term, and may even have a negative overall net balance. For this reason, it is important to try to estimate the potential long-term effects, even if this is difficult to estimate with precision.

1.6. Treating symptoms or causes?

Impact over time is a factor that strongly suggests we prioritize strategies that attack the causes of a problem, and not just its symptoms. For example, if we compare a strategy that helps many animals if they happen to be caught in a fire with another that prevents fires from occurring, it is probably the second that has the better impact over time.

The predominance of a speciesist mentality is one of the causes of the extremely negative situation in which animals find themselves (whether those who live in the wild or those exploited by humans)6, since it leads people to attach little importance to situations that harm animals. That is why educational efforts to combat speciesism have a great potential for positive impact over time, since they directly attack one of the main causes of the problems that affect animals.

Of course, these are not the only kinds of efforts that would attack the causes. For example, a program investigating which types of elements present in an ecosystem tend to favor a greater or smaller number of births in animal species whose lives are predominantly negative would directly attack another of the main causes of animal suffering7.

1.7. How many people already care about the problem?

The amount of benefit we can produce, curiously, depends on what other people with the power to help are already doing and will probably do, since this determines how neglected each problem is (that is why this parameter is called neglectedness).

All else being equal, the fewer people care about a serious situation, the stronger the reasons for us to support the cause that deals with it. All else being equal because, of course, this factor has to be weighed against other important factors, such as how serious the situation each cause deals with is. And, again, these factors may point in the same direction in certain circumstances (the worst problems being the most neglected), but not in others.

Below we will see two reasons why ascertaining the degree of neglectedness is important for efficiency in helping.

1.7.1. Inefficient distribution of efforts

The first reason is that the degree of neglectedness may reveal that there is an inefficient distribution of efforts. To illustrate this point, consider the following example.

Imagine that problem A is the most serious of all, that problem B is the second most serious, and that both are equally tractable. For this reason, we decide to focus on problem A. However, imagine also that another group of people, reasoning in the same way, also decided to focus on problem A. Imagine that problem A was then solved. However, if we had known that other people would already try to solve it, we could have focused on problem B, which would have increased the chances of both problems being solved (something that did not happen because both groups of people invested in the same problem).

Thus, the more people already involved in trying to solve a given problem, the greater the likelihood that the problem will be minimized (or even solved) without our help.

1.7.2. Diminishing marginal returns

The second reason is that, when a cause is still quite neglected, each additional person makes more of a difference than in causes that already have more supporters. That is, causes (and the specific problems within causes) experience what are called diminishing marginal returns. This concept will be explained in more detail below.

When a cause is very neglected, there are many easy and cheap opportunities to make significant progress. These opportunities are like the fruit hanging from the lowest branches of a tree, which are easier to pick. The first individuals working on a certain cause or problem can identify and exploit these opportunities, and will thus have a great impact. However, as more people come to work on the cause, the cheapest and most impactful opportunities tend to be taken first. Increasingly, what remains are tasks that are harder, more expensive, slower, or that have less impact per unit of effort. Thus, the marginal impact of each new person working on a cause tends to decrease over time (that is, there are diminishing marginal returns).

Let us look at an example. Imagine that a disease is killing a human population but that, fortunately, a vaccine is available. The first volunteers who promote vaccination have an enormous impact, because they can vaccinate the highest-risk groups and contain outbreaks quickly. As more people join the campaign, the groups that are easiest to reach and at highest risk have already been vaccinated, and the new volunteers then need to work with people in places that are harder to reach, who are more resistant to vaccination, and so on. This requires more time, money, and effort for each additional vaccination, which means that the impact of each new volunteer is smaller than that of the first ones. Now compare this case with a problem that is still very neglected, on which almost no one has worked, such as the vaccination of wild animals. In this case, the chances that you will be among the first people to explore the most effective solutions are much greater.

1.7.3. Which problems are the most neglected?

An important point to note about neglectedness is that most people may not even know that the most neglected problems (precisely those on which each of us would have the greatest impact) exist, since the problems reported in the media and addressed by social movements are the ones that many more people are already focusing on.

We will talk about the most neglected problems in Chapter 2 and Chapter 3.

1.8. Conclusion

Above we have seen several criteria that can help us choose which causes and problems to prioritize and which solutions are best.

The difficulties in weighing the different criteria should not make us think that it is impossible to reach any satisfactory conclusion about these problems. For example, as we will see in the next chapter, the animal cause seems to meet the priority criteria very well, as do several problems related to the future. There is greater uncertainty about the best strategies, but even in that regard we can also constantly reassess them8.

As you have surely noticed, the criteria we have seen do not provide a ready-made, simple answer. This is to be expected, since these questions are quite difficult. However, these criteria offer guidance for assessing these questions with the seriousness the subject deserves.

2. How Does the Animal Cause Fare on the Priority Criteria?

2.1. Introduction

Animal advocates are often criticized for fighting for animals while there are still humans in need of help. However, if our goal is a world with less suffering, it makes no sense to neglect nonhuman animals or to give them less importance. If we do so, we will be neglecting, or giving less importance to, most of the suffering that occurs in the world. In that case, we will not be efficient at reducing suffering: on the contrary, we will probably increase it even further. Thus, it is not animal advocates who need to explain themselves. Those who need to explain themselves are those who focus on humans, since most of the suffering in the world is endured by other animals.

Because of the predominance of speciesism, most people, when they choose to support a cause, opt for human causes. However, if we apply in an unbiased way the widely used criteria for determining a cause’s degree of priority, which we saw in Chapter 1, it seems impossible to avoid the conclusion that the animal cause should be one of our top priorities. To illustrate this point, below we will see how the situation of nonhuman animals fares against these criteria.

2.2. Seriousness of each victim’s situation

The vast majority of nonhuman animals are born either into the system of exploitation or in the wild. In both cases, the norm is for them to have lives full of suffering (in many cases without any positive experience) and a very premature death, usually an extremely painful one. Of course, there are humans who have lives full of suffering, die prematurely, and have very painful deaths. However, humans do not usually endure a fate equivalent to that of animals on factory farms or in the wild.

2.3. Number of victims

Counting the deaths of vertebrates and invertebrates, terrestrial and aquatic, animal exploitation kills between 34 and 54 trillion animals annually9. Important: this number refers only to the deaths of animals resulting from their exploitation. It does not include deaths that are an indirect result of human activities or of natural processes.

For comparison, consider that human deaths (adding up all causes, including natural causes) are estimated at 55.3 million annually10. The difference between these numbers is so gigantic that it is hard to visualize. For the sake of argument, let us set aside the number of invertebrates killed and count only the number of fish, birds, and mammals killed annually: “only” about 2 trillion11. This amount alone means that in animal exploitation around 5.5 billion vertebrates are killed per day (compare this number with the world’s human population, which is 8 billion). If we include invertebrates, somewhere between 93 billion and 147 billion animals are killed per day.

In addition, literally astronomical numbers of animals living outside direct human control (such as those who live in the wild) have lives full of suffering and die prematurely because of natural processes themselves. There are no precise statistics on this number of victims, but according to some estimates, at any given moment there are between 1 and 10 quintillion sentient animals in the wild12. The difference in size compared to the human population is so astronomical that, to visualize it clearly, we have to resort to analogies. For example, if we draw an analogy with the span of a year, the human population would be, at most, 0.25 seconds of the year. All the rest (364 days, 23 hours, 59 minutes, and 57.5 seconds) would be the animals in the wild. It is like taking a sheet of A4 paper and making a dot with a ballpoint pen (the dot would be the human population; all the white space would be the population of animals in the wild).

2.4. There are so many victims that even speciesists would have to prioritize the animal cause

These numbers are so gigantic that, even if much greater weight were given to the good of humans, curiously, we would still have to conclude in favor of prioritizing trying to change the situation of nonhuman animals. Let us see why:

Suppose that suffering of the same magnitude mattered 10 times more if the victims were human. This would mean that, for us to invest the same amount of resources in helping nonhuman animals as we would invest in helping humans, there would have to be 10 times more nonhuman animals suffering the equivalent (or else, equal numbers of humans and nonhumans suffering, but with the nonhumans suffering 10 times more).

Now suppose that the annual number of nonhuman animals in a situation of extreme suffering were much smaller than it really is: imagine it were “only” one trillion individuals. Imagine that the annual number of humans enduring suffering equivalent to that endured by nonhuman animals were much greater than it really is: suppose it were the entire human population (that is, 8 billion individuals). If human suffering mattered 10 times more than the equivalent suffering of nonhuman animals, then the suffering of the 8 billion humans would be multiplied by 10 (that is, it would be equivalent to the suffering of 80 billion nonhuman animals). The suffering of each nonhuman animal, in turn, would be multiplied by 1 (that is, 1 trillion). Even making all these concessions, in this case we would still have to invest 12.5 times more resources to help nonhuman animals.

If we take the real numbers into account, the ratio is astronomically greater. As we have seen, the world’s human population is around 8 billion and that of sentient nonhuman animals is 1 to 10 quintillion13. That is, for every human there are somewhere between 126 million and 1.26 billion sentient nonhuman animals. To deny the priority of improving the situation of nonhuman animals, one would have to postulate that human suffering matters at least 126 million times more than the equivalent suffering of nonhuman animals. From an unbiased point of view, there is no justification even for giving slightly greater weight to the good of humans, much less for a discrepancy of this magnitude.

2.5. How many people already care about this issue?

The number of people devoting themselves to each cause and the resources raised are not proportional to the number of victims each cause deals with.

For example, of all donations made in the United States, 97% of the amount raised goes to human causes14. The other 3% goes to environmentalist and animal advocacy causes (and it is not known how much of this 3% goes to the animal cause; it is known only that the popularity of the animal cause is much lower than that of the environmentalist cause).

Even among people who usually donate to the animal cause, on average more than two-thirds of their donations go to human causes15. Moreover, part of the resources allocated to human causes is used to buy products of animal exploitation, which contributes to increasing the number of animals who suffer and die.

Thus, it is not just that other animals receive less help than humans do: in the vast majority of cases they receive no help at all and, moreover, they are used as if they were things, which normally entails their deaths and a life of extreme suffering.

As we saw in Chapter 1, section 1.7, the more neglected a cause is, the more difference each additional person working on it makes. Thus, if our goal is to make the world less bad efficiently, the fact that the animal cause is widely neglected (despite the enormous number of victims and the seriousness of the victims’ situation) is an additional reason for us to prioritize it.

2.6. Tractability and the amount of benefit that could be produced

One might think that there is nothing that can be done to change the situation of nonhuman animals and that, therefore, the fact that they represent an astronomical number of victims says nothing in terms of priority, if there is nothing we can do to help the

majority of them. But there are many things we can do for nonhuman animals, and our decisions affect a large number of them. Below are some examples.

(1) With regard to exploited animals, it is possible to choose not to consume them, thus reducing the demand for animal products and the number of animals who would be born into a life of suffering.

(2) Still with regard to exploited animals, it is possible to invest in the development, cost reduction, and deployment of substitutes for the use of animals, such as cultivated meat.

(3) It is also possible to call for changes in public attitudes and in legislation with the goal of recognizing animals as sentient beings who should be protected by rights16.

(4) There are several ways in which wild animals are already being helped, and much more could be researched in this direction. Studies of this kind could contribute a great deal to increasing efficiency in the use of resources to reduce suffering. For example, studies on the impact of each type of land on the birth rates in the species of those animals who tend to have predominantly negative lives or positive ones could be conducted. This could prevent literally astronomical numbers of animals from being born only to experience extreme suffering.

2.7. Conclusion

If the above analysis is correct, the animal cause meets all the priority criteria very well. The predominance of a speciesist mentality is what keeps it from receiving the importance it deserves.

However, two questions remain: (1) The animal cause deals with several problems. Which ones should be prioritized? (2) Are there other topics that meet the priority criteria just as well (or perhaps even better), which even animal advocates usually fail to notice? We will discuss these questions in the next chapter.

3. Among the Problems Affecting Animals, Which Are the Most Important?

3.1. Introduction

As a result of speciesism, most people have prioritized human problems and, in doing so, have neglected problems that affect an astronomically greater number of victims. We discussed this point in the previous chapter.

We will now see how the same problem (neglect of situations that affect a vastly greater number of victims) also affects animal advocates. Below are four examples.

3.2. Neglect of animals exploited for food

The following data concern a single country and certain kinds of animals, but they represent well what happens in general.

Of all the terrestrial vertebrates exploited in the US17:

  • More than 99.7% are killed in animal agriculture.
  • 0.2% are killed in laboratories
  • 0.07% are killed in the clothing industry
  • 0.03% are killed in shelters.

However, the amount of donations is not proportional to the number of animals affected in each situation. In fact, it is almost inversely proportional.

Of all the donations made to the animal cause in the US18:

  • 66% go to shelters.
  • 32% go to groups with mixed activities.
  • 0.7% go to organizations focused on animals in laboratories.
  • Only 0.8% goes to organizations focused on farmed animals.

3.3. Neglect of the exploitation of aquatic animals and invertebrates

Even when the animals used for consumption are mentioned, the vast majority of the animals used for this purpose are neglected. For example, animal advocates often mention that around 80 billion animals are killed annually for consumption. However, this estimate refers only to the number of deaths of mammals and birds, which leaves out aquatic animals (vertebrates and invertebrates) and terrestrial invertebrates, who are the overwhelming majority of the animals exploited for consumption.

Below are some data on the annual deaths of animals exploited for food. These statistics are given in the short scale, used in Brazil, in which 1 billion corresponds to 10^9, one trillion corresponds to 10^12, and so on.

  • Mammals and birds: about 80 billion19.
  • Fish raised in factory farms: between 51 and 167 billion20.
  • Fish caught directly in the sea: between 787 billion and 2.3 trillion21.
  • Aquatic animals used as feed for the fish that humans raise in factory farms for direct consumption: between 462 billion and 1.1 trillion22.
  • Decapods (shrimp, crabs, and lobsters) raised in factory farms: between 255 and 604 billion23.
  • Silkworms killed for silk production: between 420 billion and 1 trillion24.
  • Insects killed for consumption: between 2 and 3.2 trillion25.
  • There are no data on the number of bees killed for honey production, but the population of bees raised for honey production is between 1.4 and 4.8 trillion individuals at any given moment26.
  • Cochineal insects killed in the production of carmine dye: between 4.6 and 21 trillion27.
  • Shrimp caught directly in the sea and killed: around 25 trillion28.

The sum of these numbers suggests that somewhere between 34 and 54 trillion animals are killed for consumption annually at the global level. This means that the 80 billion usually mentioned by advocates represent only somewhere between 0.1% and 0.2% of the animals killed for consumption. Shrimp, who represent somewhere between 46% and 73% of the animals exploited, are rarely mentioned by advocates and by authors in the field of animal ethics.

This neglect may occur due to various factors. Here are some examples:

  • One of them is the possibility that advocates and authors themselves give less consideration to animals such as insects, crustaceans, and fish. This, in turn, may happen for various reasons, such as, for example, the fact that these animals arouse less empathy in humans, the fact that they are smaller, the fact that they have lesser cognitive capacities, and so on.
  • Another is the bias of scope insensitivity (also called scope neglect or insensitivity to scope). When we compare two very large quantities, this bias keeps us from perceiving the difference in magnitude between them. So it is possible that even someone who gives equal consideration to all sentient beings neglects the problems that affect a vastly greater number of animals simply because they do not realize how much greater that number is.

3.4. Neglect of animals in the wild who are victims of natural processes

The situation of animals in the wild as a result of natural processes is even more neglected. Again, this happens due to various factors. Here are some examples:

  • There is widespread ignorance of the fact that natural processes maximize the number of animals who are born only to suffer intensely and die prematurely.
  • Because of this ignorance, many people mistakenly think that the number of animals suffering in the wild is smaller than the number of exploited animals. Here you can see a comparison of these numbers.
  • There is a prevalent belief that we should limit our attention to the harms that animals suffer as a result of human practices.
  • Another very common belief is that, if we let nature take its course, the result will be predominantly positive for animals.
  • The belief that intervening in natural processes (as long as it is to help animals) is an arrogant attitude is also common.
  • When people think of animals in the wild, they tend to think of animals who are not representative of typical life in the wild29. They tend to think of large animals, such as lions, zebras, gazelles, and elephants, and they think of adults of these species. These animals are a tiny minority of the animals in the wild. The vast majority of animals in the wild are small, and the vast majority of the individuals who are born usually die very young.

As a result of these and other beliefs, animal advocates have neglected a problem whose scale of harm is so gigantic that it makes even the numbers of animal exploitation (which, as we have seen, are already gigantic) nearly vanish in comparison. There are no statistics on the number of annual deaths of animals in the wild resulting from natural processes. But, to get an idea of the difference in proportion, we can compare the sizes of the populations at a given moment.

  • The total population of sentient animals in the wild at a given moment is, according to some estimates, between 1 and 10 quintillion individuals30.
  • Let us compare this, for example, with the world population, at a given moment, of animals raised as stock to be exploited:

o Terrestrial vertebrates: 24 billion31. o Fish: 180 billion32. o Shrimp: 230 billion33.

o The sum of these numbers is 434 billion.

If we draw an analogy with the span of a year, the sum of the populations of exploited animals would represent at most 14 seconds. All the rest of the year (364 days, 23 hours, 59 minutes, and 46 seconds) would be the animals in the wild. This gives us a rough sense of how large the number of animals in the wild is.

3.5. Neglect of the future

The way our decisions influence the history of the world from now on (and, consequently, how they affect the sentient beings who will exist in the future) is a widely neglected question. People in general (including animal advocates) are usually concerned almost exclusively with the problems of the present. When deciding which strategies to adopt to benefit sentient beings, usually only the impact on the sentient beings alive now (or, at most, those who will live in the near future) is taken into account.

This is due in part to the presence of temporal bias, which makes an event receive less importance the further away it is in the future. However, if our goal is to achieve the best for all sentient beings, what will matter to us is the magnitude of the harms, not the time at which they occur. Thus, if this is our goal, when deciding which problems to prioritize and which strategies to adopt, we have to imagine as best we can how the consequences of our choices will affect the future, and choose the course of action that is best over time (and not just best in the present or in the near future)34.

The number of future sentient beings may turn out to be very vast, whether diachronically (because the future may be very long) or synchronically (since the population of sentient beings may come to increase greatly at each moment). Thus, the number of sentient beings we will affect in the long term with these decisions exceeds by many orders of magnitude the sentient beings who exist now or who will exist in the near future. For this reason, this topic is of crucial importance35.

3.6. Conclusion

The four examples above seem sufficient to show that the amount of attention given to each problem has not been proportional to the magnitude of each problem. In fact, it has generally been inversely proportional (that is, the most serious problems have also been the most neglected).

This gives us twofold reasons to focus on these problems. First, simply because they are among the most serious problems. Second, because, since they are highly neglected, this is exactly where we can make the greatest difference.

4. The Use of Anthropocentric and Environmentalist Arguments in the Animal Cause

4.1. The strategy of using anthropocentric or environmentalist arguments

There are many ways of advocating for the moral consideration of all sentient beings. These include not only presenting arguments for rejecting speciesism and other forms of discrimination against sentient beings, but also any other forms of activism that promote this consideration, even if indirectly.

One example of an indirect strategy is to argue against animal exploitation, but with arguments not centered on consideration for animals. Examples include arguing:

  • That animal agriculture has a negative environmental impact.
  • That animal products are harmful to human health.
  • That consuming animals is not natural for humans.
  • That torturing animals is training for torturing humans.
  • That the way animal products are made is disgusting.
  • That animal experimentation poses risks to humans.
  • That animal agriculture is related to human hunger.
  • That a plant-based diet was the original way of eating of certain peoples.

...and so on.

This strategy is based on two premises:

  • The first is the belief that the consequences for animals are the same whether people stop exploiting them out of consideration for them or for other reasons (“for animals, what matters is what you do, not what you think”).
  • The second is the belief that these anthropocentric or environmentalist arguments are more efficient at leading people not to exploit animals because, since people are speciesist, they would be more easily convinced by them.

In this text, we will discuss this strategy36.

4.2. Some problems with the use of anthropocentric and environmentalist arguments

There are at least two ways in which the two premises above can be questioned:

  • It is not only the exploitation of animals that matters. Also mattering are the harms suffered by animals in the wild as a result of natural processes37 and the new forms of suffering that may arise in the future38. As we will see in the next section, anthropocentric and environmentalist arguments, besides not addressing these problems, may increase them.
  • Contrary to what may initially seem to be the case, the different motivations for ceasing to exploit animals do not have the same consequences.

Both points will be explained in more detail in the next section.

4.3. Why different motivations have different consequences

In planning a strategy, we need to take into account all the likely consequences we can estimate, and not just some of them. Thus, we have to take into account not only the direct impact of the use of animal products but also, crucially, the impact of the worldview we strengthen with each strategy.

The influence each person has through their consumption lasts until the end of their life. The effects of the worldview they pass on, by contrast, extend over centuries or millennia, since they affect how other people will decide and how they will influence still other people to decide. The values people adopt guide the way they make all their decisions throughout their lives, and they also determine which values they pass on to other people, including future generations. In short, there is a snowball effect.

With this in view, we have reasons to think that arguments centered on consideration for animals would have a better impact, especially in the long term, since they help increase moral consideration for sentient beings, something no other argument does. In fact, as we will see in the following sections, the use of arguments not centered on consideration for animals could even increase the harms to sentient beings.

4.4. Do indirect arguments make it easier to accept considering sentient beings?

It could be objected that speciesism is often defended not because people believe it is correct, but as an excuse, simply because they like the taste of animal products. Thus, in defense of using anthropocentric or environmentalist arguments, it could be said that, if people stop consuming animals, for whatever reason, it will be easier for them to accept an antispeciesist view later on.

The same would hold for other forms of animal exploitation, such as animal experimentation. According to this view, the people who defend it do not do so because they consider it just, but simply because they do not want to give up the benefits they have obtained from it (for example, having built scientific careers performing experiments on animals).

Therefore, according to this view, getting people, by whatever means, to stop exploiting animals may be more efficient for achieving a world in which sentient beings receive full consideration than advocating for that consideration itself.

This argument is based on an idea that seems correct. However, if the argument succeeds, the conclusion that follows is that we should combine this strategy with advocacy of consideration for sentient beings. Why? Because the argument only indicates that lines of argument not centered on consideration for animals would help with consideration for sentient beings. But that consideration would still be necessary to prevent harms in the long term. Thus, even if the argument were correct, the use of arguments not centered on animals would at most facilitate the expansion of moral consideration for animals. However, if this is so, then it makes sense to think that, to achieve it, it is probably more efficient to spread it directly than to spread other ideas.

Moreover, it is possible that people who defend animal exploitation do so simply because they give very little consideration to nonhuman animals (and not because they consider exploitation wrong and defend it simply to disguise the fact that they do not want to give up consuming animal products). If they considered animals even a little, the enormous amount of suffering and death caused by animal exploitation should already be a minimal motivating reason for them to try to give up, or at least reduce, their consumption of animals. Now, if this does not happen, and if these people would give up consuming animals for anthropocentric or environmentalist reasons, this is a sign that they strongly believe in anthropocentric and environmentalist values. So it is at the very least uncertain whether their stopping consuming animals for anthropocentric or environmentalist reasons would make it easier for them to later accept considering all sentient beings.

4.5. Risks of using arguments not centered on consideration for sentient beings

The risk of implying that animals do not matter

There is also the risk that the use of anthropocentric and environmentalist arguments may delay (or even prevent) consideration for sentient beings. For example, if even when the subject is the exploitation of animals the arguments used to address the issue have nothing to do with the harm to animals, this may help emphasize that the suffering and death of animals is something that does not matter much (or even that does not matter at all). Thus, the use of arguments not centered on consideration for animals may help strengthen the speciesist view, which is precisely the cause of the terrible situation in which animals find themselves.

The risk of strengthening views opposed to consideration for animals

Since anthropocentrism and environmentalism involve values diametrically opposed to consideration for sentient beings, using arguments grounded in these values carries a great risk of making it harder to accept sentience-centered values.

The risk of increasing animal exploitation

Another possible effect of using indirect arguments is to convey the idea that, if animals are being harmed without negatively affecting humans or the environment, then that is fine. This may help encourage the search for more sustainable ways of exploiting animals that may be even worse for them, such as confining them in even smaller spaces, or promoting the consumption of aquatic animals and insects, which would cause a vastly greater number of animals to die, since these animals are much smaller. These practices may even be beneficial for humans or from an environmentalist point of view.

In these cases, the use of arguments not centered on animals may help considerably increase the number of exploited animals, resulting in more animals being killed than even if nothing had been said against animal exploitation.

The risk of increasing the suffering of wild animals

The use of anthropocentric and environmentalist arguments may also contribute to neglect of the suffering of wild animals resulting from natural processes and to a rejection of the proposal to help them39. Besides possibly leading people to approve of forms of animal exploitation that are sustainable or advantageous to humans, it may also lead people to advocate practices such as the expansion of natural territory40, space colonization41, and disregard for possible future nonorganic sentient beings42. All these risks, if realized, would generate much more suffering than animal exploitation43.

4.6. Conclusion

One of the main reasons why there are risks that suffering of astronomical magnitude will be generated in the future is the fact that those who could affect sentient beings positively or negatively do not give them moral consideration. Thus, to reduce such risks, it is essential not to postpone advocating for the moral consideration of all sentient beings.
