5. The Total Approach and the Sufficient Approach

5.1. Introduction

In this chapter we will look at two possible approaches to trying to get more people to accept the goal of pursuing a better world for all sentient beings: the total approach and the sufficient approach. We will see some advantages and disadvantages of each of these approaches, and it will be argued that it is more promising to combine them, at least in most contexts. Several examples will also be presented of particular contexts in which they can be applied and combined, and of how this could be done.

5.2. Ranges of compatibility: open and closed

What we will call the range of compatibility concerns the number of additional ideas that need to be accepted in order to accept a given idea. The more additional ideas are needed, the more closed the range will be, since fewer people accept those additional ideas together. The fewer additional ideas are needed, the more open the range will be, since in that case it is more likely that more people will accept the idea, whatever they think about other questions.

It is important to identify how wide an idea’s range of compatibility is, because if we think an idea has a more closed range when in fact it has a more open one, we will miss the opportunity to get many more people to accept it. This is illustrated by the following example.

Suppose we want to defend idea A, and we believe that, to accept it, one must also accept idea B. We then start defending B in order to get people to accept A. In doing so, we imply to the public that, to accept A, one has to accept B. Imagine that we manage to convince some people to accept A, but that other people do not accept it precisely because they do not accept B. But imagine that we later discover that, to accept A, it was not necessary to accept B. Then we could have convinced many more people to accept A if we had not defended B (or, at least, if we had not implied that, to accept A, it was necessary to accept B).

Thus, if, for people to accept an idea A, it is not necessary for them to agree about other ideas B, C, D, E, and so on, then it is better to emphasize that, whatever they think about these other ideas, they can still accept A.

Emphasizing that, even if there is disagreement about other things, there could still be agreement about what we are proposing has at least two advantages. The first, an obvious one, is that it increases the likelihood that a much larger and more diverse number of people will accept what we are proposing. The second is that it tends to reduce polarization44, since it emphasizes that, despite the many disagreements, there may be some goals in common.

5.3. Examples of views compatible with multiple views in ethics and politics

To accept the following goals, it is not necessary to adopt a specific view, whether in terms of ethical theory or in terms of political orientation:

  • Consideration for all sentient beings.
  • Rejection of speciesism.
  • Abolition of animal exploitation.
  • Veganism
  • Reduction of the suffering of wild animals.
  • Prevention of risks of future suffering.
  • Concern for the long-term future.
  • Consideration for nonorganic sentient beings, should they come to exist in the future.

Thus, instead of defending a specific view in ethics or politics and pointing out that one implication of that view is accepting those goals, we are more likely to get people to accept these goals if we argue that they should be accepted by everyone, regardless of which view in ethics or politics they adopt. Defending specific positions may give the mistaken impression that, to accept the goals in question, it is necessary to accept those specific views (with the result that those who do not accept such views reject these goals).

5.4. The total approach and the sufficient approach

Above we gave examples of goals that can be accepted in their entirety by various positions. At other times, however, depending on what someone thinks about other questions, they will accept a given goal only to a certain extent.

When we argue in favor of an idea, we usually understand the situation in terms of accepting it or rejecting it entirely. However, there is the possibility that someone might accept it partially. Of course, if we defend a given idea, we will think it best that other people accept it fully. However, it can be well worth emphasizing that certain arguments that are sometimes put forward in an attempt to reject the idea we are proposing do not actually imply rejecting it, but rather accepting it partially. By emphasizing this, we increase the chances that even those who disagree with its complete acceptance will still accept it at least to some extent.

In this sense, we can distinguish two approaches:

Total approach: defending what we believe to be the best decision.

Sufficient approach: emphasizing that even those who disagree with our position can accept it partially or accept some of its implications.

Important: these are not mutually exclusive strategies. In fact, at the end of this chapter it will be argued not only that we have better chances of better results if we combine both, but also that it is risky to employ only one of them.

The following table lists several examples of these approaches with regard to various topics:

Topic Total approach Risks involved Sufficient approach
Criterion for moral considerationArguing that the beings we ought to consider are sentient beings, and only sentient beings. Those who think we owe moral consideration to nonsentient entities may think they are justified in disregarding sentient beings.Emphasizing that even those who argue for considering nonsentient entities should recognize that being sentient should be sufficient for being considered, and that there are still reasons to prioritize sentient beings over nonsentient entities, whether these are wholes or living organisms.
Ethical theoryDefending a specific ethical theory that we consider most plausible, and showing that it implies rejecting speciesism.Those who do not accept that specific theory may think they do not need to reject speciesism.Emphasizing that, to accept the arguments for rejecting speciesism, it is not necessary to adopt a specific ethical theory.
Political orientationDefending a specific political orientation, and showing that its ideals are realized only if we reject speciesism.Those of any other political orientation may think they do not need to reject speciesism.Emphasizing that speciesism should be rejected, regardless of which political orientation someone prefers.

However, if the public notices the implication on its own, it will consider us dishonest for hiding it.

5.5. Conclusion: it is important to combine both strategies

As we have seen above, both strategies, if used in isolation, carry risks. The risk of the total strategy is that people will mistakenly understand that, if they do not fully accept a certain view, they have no reason to partially accept what is being proposed. The general risk of the sufficient strategy, in turn, is that it does not discuss questions that are in fact very important and about which people perhaps ought to change their minds.

Thus, the question is about the degree of focus we should have on each strategy, since it seems better to use both. For example, one option is to focus on the total approach and emphasize that even those who do not agree could still partially accept what has been defended. Even if we opt for a greater focus on what is sufficient, this does not mean that arguing in favor of the total goal is not important. For example, a world in which many people are antispeciesist certainly has very different consequences from a world in which many people merely consider nonhuman animals, but to a lesser degree. Thus, the total approach is also very important (at least in many of the contexts listed above).

The decision to focus more on the total or on the sufficient approach depends on knowing what would achieve our goals most efficiently. For example, would they be better achieved if a larger number of people accepted them partially or if a smaller number of people accepted them completely? The answer to this will depend, in the case of each goal: (1) on the number of people who would accept it fully versus the number of people who would accept it partially; and (2) on how much more each person who accepts it fully would do to achieve the goal, compared with those who accept it partially.

Regardless of the answers to these difficult questions, it seems that arguing only in favor of the ideal, without emphasizing what is sufficient, involves high risks. On the other hand, talking only about what is sufficient means not daring to discuss very important controversial questions. Starting to discuss these questions as soon as possible can make a difference in the long term, by making the public less averse to thinking about them.

6. Shifting the Focus in Debates: Why Is Speciesism Rarely Discussed?

6.1. Shifting the focus

It is not uncommon, in debates about practices that harm nonhuman animals, for the defenders of such practices to try to keep the focus of the discussion on aspects that have nothing to do with the harm to animals. Below are some examples.

  • If the subject is the use of animals for consumption, they will approach the topic as if what mattered for knowing whether or not such practices are justifiable were the risks to human health and the environmental impacts. They will then argue that consuming animals can indeed be healthy and sustainable.
  • If the subject is animal experimentation, they will approach the topic as if what mattered for knowing whether such practices are justified were the benefits to humans. They will then argue that animal experimentation can indeed be safe for humans.
  • If the subject is the killing of wild animals motivated by environmentalist ideals, they will treat the question as if what mattered for knowing whether or not such practices are justified were whether or not they help achieve environmentalist goals. They will then argue that such killing is justified because the animals belong to invasive species and pose a threat to native flora and fauna (for example, because they feed on rare plants or interbreed with native animals and produce hybrids, so that the native species is no longer “pure”), and so on.

In none of these cases is it discussed whether, even if such claims are true, these practices might still be unjustifiable because of the harm they cause to animals. Our obligations toward animals and speciesism are rarely discussed topics. It is not that these people go so far as to argue that we should not have consideration for animals, or that this consideration should be very small. The question is simply ignored completely. It is as if it did not exist.

Sometimes this is planned. For example, someone may realize that they have no good arguments to justify speciesist practices, but, since they do not intend to change their position, they shift the focus so that it does not become clear that they have no good arguments.

In other cases, however, such a shift may happen without being premeditated. Some of these people may not even have any idea that the way our decisions affect animals is an ethical question. They may find it so obvious that animals do not deserve respect that it does not even cross their minds that this idea might be mistaken.

Whether or not it is planned, the fact is that in most debates the focus ends up being shifted, and the moral consideration of animals is not discussed. As pointed out below, this result also comes about largely because of the collaboration (again, intentional or not) of the people who say they are there to defend animals.

6.2. Falling into the trap

Animal advocates’ response to the shift of focus is usually, curiously, to accept it and start discussing the other questions raised by those who seek to justify the practices that harm animals. Surprisingly, animal advocates themselves rarely discuss the moral consideration of animals (and the shift of focus often comes from animal advocates themselves!). Below are examples in the three contexts listed above

  • Example 1. Defenders of consuming animals claim that it is justifiable because it can be healthy and sustainable. Animal advocates could simply reply that, even if that is the case, consuming animals would still be unjustifiable, just as killing humans in order to consume them would be unjustifiable even if it were healthy and sustainable.

Animal advocates could ask the following: “why would one act be right because it is healthy and sustainable, while another act would be wrong despite being equally healthy and sustainable?” Defenders of consuming animals would probably answer that it is because in one case the victims are human and in the other they are not. And animal advocates could ask why species would be a morally relevant criterion rather than an arbitrary criterion, as race and gender are, and so the debate would continue.

However, that is not what usually happens. Animal advocates usually focus on contesting the claim that consuming animals can be healthy or sustainable.

  • Example 2. Defenders of animal experimentation claim that it is justified because it can offer benefits to humans. Again, here animal advocates could reply that the fact that a practice offers benefits to members of one group does not automatically justify that practice, especially when the harms to members of other groups are being counted in an arbitrary way (in this case, the harms to animals receive less weight, or receive no weight at all).

An analogy could be drawn with the human case. If a scientist claimed that it is justified to perform experiments on dark-skinned humans because this would benefit light-skinned humans, it would be very clear that pointing this out is insufficient to justify such a practice. One could then ask the following: “why would one practice be right because it produces benefits, despite the harms it causes, while another would be wrong because of the harms it causes, despite producing benefits?”

Again, defenders of experimentation would probably say that the difference is that in one case the victims are human, and in the other they are not. But, again, animal advocates could ask why species would not be an arbitrary criterion like skin color, and so the debate would continue.

But that is not what happens. Animal advocates usually limit themselves to arguing that animal experimentation, due to differences in physiology, is not safe for humans.

  • Example 3. Defenders of the killing of wild animals motivated by environmentalist ideals claim that it is justified because these animals pose a threat to environmentalist ideals. Again, here one could reply that this seems insufficient to justify the killing. After all, there is no species that poses a greater threat to environmentalist ideals than the human species, yet this does not seem to justify killing humans en masse.

So one could ask the following: “why would one killing be right because it protects environmentalist ideals, while another would be wrong despite protecting environmentalist ideals (to a greater degree)?”

Again, defenders of the killing would say that it is because in one case the victims are human and in the other they are not. And, again, one could question the criterion of species, and so the debate could proceed.

But, again, that is not what animal advocates usually do. They choose to argue that killing animals is not good from an environmentalist point of view.

In short, animal advocates could contain the shift of focus and bring the focus back to the discussion of the moral consideration of animals. But that is not what they usually do. They usually “buy into” the shift of focus. The result is that the moral consideration of animals is rarely discussed. Why does this happen? That is what we will discuss in the next section.

6.3. Why do animal advocates accept the shift of focus?

Just as the shift of focus by those who defend practices that harm animals may or may not be planned, the acceptance of the shift by animal advocates may or may not be conscious.

Below are several hypotheses about why animal advocates accept the shift. Of course, these hypotheses are not the only possibilities. And, more importantly, these hypotheses are not mutually exclusive, since the motivation may differ in the case of different people and even in the case of the same person in different situations.

Hypotheses:

1) Distraction.

Animal advocates may not notice that the focus is being shifted. When they do notice (if they notice at all), they are already tangled in the web, discussing other questions, without knowing how to bring the focus of the debate back to the moral consideration of animals.

2) Embarrassment

Animal advocates may notice that the shift of focus is taking place, and disagree with it, but be embarrassed to really defend animals. There is a considerable likelihood that this happens in many cases because of how great an influence social pressure exerts. Since society is highly speciesist, it is quite possible that some people do not defend animals out of fear of being ridiculed (this is compounded if they do not know arguments to defend their position).

3) Agreement

It is also possible that, although they present themselves as animal advocates, some of these people are not in fact advocates, and agree that the harms to animals are not decisive for knowing whether or not the practices in question are justified, and for this reason they accept the shift of focus.

For example, there are many people who call themselves vegan but who do not mean by this that they seek to avoid harming animals as much as possible and that they are against their exploitation, but rather that they do not consume animal products for environmentalist or health reasons, or out of concern for disadvantaged human beings (even though this is not what the term veganism means). Again, the change in the meaning of the concept of veganism may be intentional (to make the public think that these people are there to defend animals) or due to ignorance, because they have no idea what veganism is.

4) The belief that it is not possible to discuss ethics

Another possibility is that some people accept the shift of focus because they believe that it is not possible to discuss ethics. For this reason, they limit themselves to discussing factual claims.

The belief that “in ethics, everything is relative/subjective” and that there are no views that are more or less plausible is quite common. So someone who holds this belief might think: “these people believe it is justified to disregard animals and I disagree, end of story, there is nothing to discuss.”

According to this view, it is not possible to assess whether the goals someone pursues are right or wrong, just or unjust: all that could be done is to investigate whether or not a given action leads to the goal pursued.

Thus, if an animal advocate thinks this way, and realizes that, for the people they are talking to, all that matters is humans or environmentalist goals, they will try to show that consuming animals is not healthy or sustainable, that animal experimentation poses risks to humans, that the killing of wild animals does not achieve environmentalist goals, and so on. In short, the belief is that it is impossible for someone to come to consider animals because it is impossible for someone to change their position regarding goals, values, principles, and so on.

It is surprising that such people think this way. After all, the overwhelming majority of people who are animal advocates today were not always so. For example, the vast majority used to consume animals and at some point in their lives stopped to reflect and concluded that there was no justification for doing so. So it is strange that they believe both that there is nothing to reflect on in this regard and that it is not possible for people to change what they think about it.

Moreover, anyone who knows a little about animal ethics knows that attempts to justify speciesism have been widely discussed at least since the 1970s. When we look at this debate, it becomes very clear how problematic the attempts to justify speciesism are and how solid the arguments in favor of the equal consideration of all sentient beings are. The idea that in ethics all positions are equally plausible sounds reasonable only if we do not take the trouble to look at the arguments offered by each side.

Indeed, if a person has no good argument to defend their position and their opponent has a good argument to defend the opposite position, it is always a good excuse to claim that all positions are equally plausible and that there is no right and wrong.

5) The belief that it is possible to discuss ethics, but impossible to change people

Another possibility is that some animal advocates agree that it is possible to discuss ethics, and that it is even possible to show that speciesism is unjustifiable, but believe that it is impossible for people to change what they think, even when they know they are wrong. According to this view, “some are born good, others are born bad, period.” However, once again, animal advocates should know from their own case that things are not like this.

6) The belief that it is more efficient to limit oneself to discussing the facts

Finally, another possible motivation for animal advocates to accept the shift of focus would be that, although they recognize that there are strong arguments against speciesism and that it is possible to change what people think, they believe that not questioning speciesism (and limiting themselves to discussing the factual claims made by the defenders of speciesist practices) is more efficient for convincing the people they are talking to to stop harming animals.

For example, animal advocates might think that, since they do not have to question the goals and values their opponents adopt, it is easier to get them to change their attitude if they manage to show that the practice in question does not fit with their goals and values.

One problem with this strategy is that very often the goals and values of their opponents will be better achieved by harming animals. For example, it is true that there are many forms of animal consumption that are not healthy and whose ways of exploiting animals are not environmentally sustainable. However, there are various other forms that are (and it is always possible to try to create others that are). Animal experimentation to benefit humans poses risks to humans because of physiological differences. However, animal experimentation to benefit animals of the same species does not pose this risk. Similarly, there are cases in which the most efficient way to secure environmentalist goals is not to harm wild animals (or even to help them). However, at other times the most efficient way to achieve environmentalist goals is to harm animals.

What happens in many cases is that animal advocates insist that it is not possible to exploit animals sustainably, that food of animal origin can never be healthy, and so on. That is, they need to “stretch” the facts to make them fit what they want to defend. But this should not be the path; rather, we should not be afraid to present arguments against speciesism. We will look at something on this below:

When the discussion is limited to the facts, speciesism is never questioned. Speciesism is the reason animals are in the situation they are in. Therefore, it seems impossible to change this situation without questioning speciesism. Moreover, when someone accepts the shift of focus, they are, even if unintentionally, reinforcing the anthropocentric and environmentalist views and emphasizing that animals really do not matter in themselves (and this has a great effect on the public, especially as people notice that animal advocates simply say nothing in favor of animals). So it is not just that accepting the shift of focus may be ineffective at changing the situation of animals: it has a good chance of being counterproductive.

Finally, there is a strategic problem with this view. If we aim to be as efficient as possible at changing people’s behavior in ways that favor animals, then it is better to focus on the audience that shows greater openness to considering animals, since that way it is more likely that their values will come to be aligned with the goal of favoring animals (and we will then achieve a better result by focusing on these people). It seems that many animal advocates have the impression that it is impossible to change people’s behavior in ways that favor animals because they have chosen to focus precisely on the audience most averse to thinking about the moral consideration of animals.

6.4. Conclusion

We have seen in this chapter that, in debates about practices that harm animals, the focus is usually shifted to questions that have nothing to do with the harm to animals. This shift of focus ends up implying that the harm to animals is not decisive (or even important) for knowing whether or not such practices are justifiable.

We have seen that this shift of focus, depending on the case, may or may not be intentional on the part of those who try to justify the practices that harm animals. We have also seen that, likewise, the acceptance of the shift of focus by animal advocates may or may not be deliberate. However, we have seen that, regardless of whether or not it is deliberate, the shift of focus has the same effect: speciesism is not discussed.

There are no good reasons for animal advocates to accept this shift of focus because, as long as speciesism is not widely discussed, there will be no change in the way people see nonhuman animals and, as a consequence, the situation of nonhuman animals will hardly change, since the root of the problem will then never be attacked.

7. Moral Beliefs, Motivation to Act, and the Role of Ethical Reflection

7.1. The case of animal ethics experts who consume animals

This chapter is intended as a brief reflection on the question of moral motivation, based on cases that sometimes come up in the debate on the moral consideration of nonhuman animals.

Animal ethics is the area of applied ethics that studies the morality of our decisions that affect nonhuman animals. It is sometimes argued that the fact that there are animal ethics experts who continue consuming animals is proof that believing that something is right/wrong has no influence whatsoever on changing people’s attitudes.

According to this view, for people to care about changing a practice, it is not enough for them to conclude that it is wrong: something is needed that “touches” them, such as a shocking image or video, a song, an event in their personal lives, reading a moving story, and so on. In short, according to this view, nonrational persuasion is always necessary.

In this text it will be argued that it is hasty to conclude, from the fact that there are animal ethics experts who consume animals, that the belief that something is right/wrong therefore does not create a motivation to act accordingly. As we will see in the following sections, there are at least five other possibilities that may be occurring in the case of these experts.

7.2. Perhaps they do not consider consuming animals wrong

One possibility is that some of these people are experts in animal ethics but, for some reason, do not agree that consuming animals is unjustified. If this is the case, these people are doing exactly what they believe to be right. Of course, this does not mean that they are right to think so. It only means that, if this is what is happening, then pointing to the case of these people does not show that the belief that something is right/wrong does not influence attitudes (quite the contrary: it is their belief that consuming animals is justified that makes them continue to consume animals).

7.3. Perhaps they consider consuming animals only slightly wrong

There are degrees to which people consider an action right or wrong. For example, we normally consider running over a pedestrian a very serious wrong. On the other hand, arriving fifteen minutes late to a meeting is normally considered a minor wrong. That is why we take much more care not to run someone over than to avoid arriving late to a meeting. If this is so, then how much someone thinks a practice is right or wrong has a great deal of influence on how much they will strive to act accordingly.

Thus, it is possible that some of these experts give some moral consideration to nonhuman animals, but much less than that given to humans. Thus, even if they say they consider consuming animals wrong, perhaps they do not consider it a particularly serious wrong. And, once again, the case of these people does not support the thesis that someone’s beliefs about what is right and wrong have no influence on their attitudes. Quite the contrary: if this is what is happening, it shows that their attitude reflects precisely their belief that animal exploitation is not a very serious wrong.

7.4. Perhaps they are not being sincere about what they report

It could be objected that there are people who say they consider the use of animals for consumption extremely wrong, yet do not stop consuming them either. However, this is still not enough to conclude that the belief that a practice is right/wrong does not motivate someone to act accordingly. This is so for two reasons, explained below.

The first is that someone may say they consider consuming animals extremely wrong but not be sincere and, in fact, not consider it all that wrong. The second is that, even if they are being sincere, such a person may display the problem known as weakness of will, which we will address in the next section.

7.5. Perhaps they have a weak will

It could be claimed that there are people who sincerely consider consuming animals an extremely serious wrong and yet do not stop consuming animals. That is, these people display the problem known as weakness of will.

However, although cases of weakness of will show that moral beliefs do not by themselves determine someone’s behavior, they do not show that moral beliefs have no influence on behavior. In the case of these people, the motivation generated by the belief that consuming animals is an extremely serious wrong probably has to compete with other, opposing motivations (for example, social pressure, the pleasure obtained from foods they are already used to, the emotional association between food of animal origin and social events, and so on).

7.6. Perhaps they decide not to do what they feel motivated to do

Yet another possibility is that the moral belief creates a motivation to act accordingly, that there are no other conflicting motivations, but that the person simply decides not to do what they consider right and feel motivated to do. Such cases seem to be rarer. But, again, such cases would show only that moral beliefs do not determine someone’s behavior; they would not show that moral beliefs do not create a motivation to act accordingly.

7.7. Conclusion

The fact that there are animal ethics experts who consume animals is not enough to conclude that someone’s beliefs about what is right/wrong to do do not generate a motivation to act accordingly. As we have seen, there are at least five other possibilities for what is happening in these cases: (1) they do not consider consuming animals wrong; (2) they consider consuming animals wrong, but not seriously wrong; (3) they say they consider consuming animals seriously wrong, but they are lying; (4) they consider it seriously wrong, but the motivation generated by this belief has to compete with other, opposing motivations; (5) they consider it seriously wrong and there are no opposing motivations, but they decide not to do what they feel motivated to do.

All this may cause some people to feel disappointed about the power of arguments to change people’s behavior. However, this is hasty. What we have seen above shows only that arguments are not magical tools that give us control over the decisions of those who will hear the arguments. As we have seen, a person’s behavior is the result of many factors and, however well someone argues, and even if the other person accepts the argument, we have no power to decide whether or not they will follow in practice what they have concluded. Only they can do that.

In view of this, some people might then think that it is better to abandon rational persuasion and adopt tactics of nonrational persuasion. But the point is this: any other form of persuasion has the same limits. Faced with tactics of nonrational persuasion, a person may simply pay no attention, or may say they agree and not act accordingly (again, there may be conflicting motivations, they may simply decide not to follow what they feel motivated to do, and so on). Indeed, tactics of nonrational persuasion seem to have even greater limits, since rational persuasion at least manages to explain the reasons for accepting or rejecting a given practice. This seems to show that rational persuasion, with all its limits, is still the best we have.

8. Normative Objections Disguised as Strategic Objections

8.1. Normative objections and strategic objections

Sometimes someone does not agree with a given goal. We will call this a normative objection. At other times, someone agrees with the goal but believes that a given strategy will not be efficient for achieving it. We will call this a strategic objection.

Sometimes people sincerely report whether their objection is normative or strategic. However, there are cases in which someone says their disagreement is strategic, but in fact does not agree with the proposed goal. In this text we will explore how this happens in debates on questions of animal ethics.

8.2. The claim that “this would be great, but it won’t work”

There are many cases in which someone states that they agree with a certain proposal but claims that defending it would be futile (that is, that it would have no effect) or even counterproductive (that is, that it would have the opposite of the intended effect).

Arguments of this kind frequently arise against any position that points out that we should be concerned with something that until then we had not seen as a problem. Below we will look at some examples.

8.3. Examples in questions of animal ethics

Below are examples of arguments of this kind in seven different contexts:

Example 1. Faced with the proposal to give moral consideration to animals, saying something like:

“I agree that we should consider animals. However, if it is already hard for people to consider humans, let alone other animals. So it is better to leave the defense of animals to future generations and for now defend only humans, since that is what will make it possible for people in the future to come to consider animals. Pointing out now that the reasons for considering humans imply considering animals will only make people find the very idea of moral consideration absurd and then refuse to consider even humans.”

Example 2: Faced with the proposal to fight speciesism, saying something like:

“I agree that we should reject speciesism. However, if it is already hard for people to reject racism and sexism, let alone speciesism. So it is better to leave the fight against speciesism to future generations and for now focus only on fighting racism and sexism, since that is what will make it possible for people in the future to reject speciesism. Pointing out at the present moment that rejecting racism and sexism implies rejecting speciesism will only make people reject neither racism nor sexism.”

Example 3: Faced with the proposal to advocate the abolition of animal exploitation, saying something like:

“I agree that animal exploitation should be abolished. However, if it is already hard for people to accept exploiting animals less, let alone accept abolishing exploitation. So it is better to leave the advocacy of abolition to future generations and for now focus only on reforms of animal exploitation, since that is what will make it possible for people in the future to accept abolishing it. Advocating abolition now will only make people reject even reducing the suffering of exploited animals.”

Example 4: Faced with the proposal to draw attention to the situation of invertebrates (since they are the vast majority of animals, both in the system of exploitation and in the wild), saying something like:

“I agree that we should consider invertebrates. However, if it is already hard for people to consider vertebrates, let alone invertebrates. So it is better to leave the defense of invertebrates to future generations and for now focus only on vertebrates, since that is what will make it possible for people in the future to consider invertebrates. Defending invertebrates now will only make people refuse to consider even vertebrates.”

Example 5: Faced with the proposal to help wild animals who are victims of natural processes saying something like:

“I agree with the proposal to help wild animals who are victims of natural processes. However, if it is already hard for people to accept being vegan, let alone accept caring about suffering and death that do not result from human practices. So it is better to leave this question to future generations and for now focus only on veganism, since that is what will make it possible for people in the future to accept the proposal to help wild animals. Pointing out now that considering animals implies, besides rejecting their exploitation, also helping wild animals will only make people fail to reject even exploitation.”

Example 6: Faced with the proposal that we should do something to prevent suffering from being multiplied to astronomical levels in the future, saying something like:

“I agree with concern for the long-term future. However, if it is already hard for people to care about the present or the short term, let alone the long term. So it is better to leave the advocacy of concern for the long term to future generations and for now focus only on the present or the short term, since that is what will make it possible for people in the future to accept concern for the long term. Pointing out now that considering the sentient beings of the present or the near future implies considering the sentient beings of the distant future will only make people refuse to consider even the sentient beings of the present.

Example 7: Faced with the proposal that, if nonorganic sentient beings come to exist in the future, they should receive as much consideration as any other sentient being, saying something like:

“I agree with consideration for nonorganic sentient beings. However, if it is already hard for people to accept considering animals, let alone accept considering nonorganic sentient beings. So it is better to leave the defense of all sentient beings, organic and nonorganic, to future generations and for now focus only on animals, since that is what will make it possible for people in the future to accept considering nonorganic sentient beings, should they come to exist. Pointing out now that considering animals implies considering nonorganic sentient beings, should they come to exist, will only make people refuse to consider even animals.

The examples above are just a few samples of this type of argument. As should now be clear, they all follow the same pattern (which we will detail in section 8.7), and this pattern appears in many other contexts. However, the examples above are sufficient for what this text aims to discuss.

8.4. One possibility: the real motivation is not the one stated

Something common to all the examples above is that the objections are presented as strategic objections. That is, the person raising the objection emphasizes that they agree with the proposed goal, but claims that defending it (or at least defending it now) will be futile or even counterproductive.

It is possible that, in several of the cases in which the above claims are made, the reservation really is strategic. However, there is at least one other possibility: the person does not in fact agree with the proposed goal, but says they are against defending it for strategic reasons.

In short, it may be that, although what is said is “don’t do this because it won’t work,” the real fear is exactly the opposite: “don’t do this because it might work, and I don’t want that result.” That is, although what is said is “there’s no point in defending this because no one will accept it,” it may be that the real fear is that people will accept what is being proposed. In these cases, what is sought is to get the other person to give up defending an idea one disagrees with, while pretending to agree with it.

This does not mean that it is necessarily done deliberately. It may be deliberate in some cases, and done unconsciously in others. But, whether conscious or unconscious, it is a normative objection disguised as a strategic objection.

8.5. Is it possible to detect a disguised normative objection?

Is there a way of knowing when someone presents a strategic objection to disguise the fact that their disagreement is normative? One possible test would be to ask: “if you found out that you are mistaken, and that defending the idea in question now is the best way to achieve it and to achieve the other goals we want, would you still be against defending it?” If in that case the person is still against it, then their objection is normative.

However, this test will not succeed if the person who disguises their normative objection as a strategic objection does so deliberately and realizes that we are trying to find out whether their reservation really is strategic, as they say. If they realize we are testing them, they may lie, claiming that, if defending the idea in question now were a good strategy, they would readily agree to defend it.

However, this test will work if the aim is to find this out about ourselves. As we will see in more detail in section 8.7, a normative objection is sometimes disguised as a strategic objection unconsciously. So it is always possible for someone to ask themselves: “if it were proven that defending the idea in question now is a good strategy for achieving what it proposes, would I still be against it?” If so, the disagreement is normative.

8.6. Why does this happen?

If someone disagrees with a certain goal, why do they not simply say that their disagreement is normative, instead of saying that their objection is strategic when that is not the case? There are several reasons why this may happen. Below are four examples.

A first possibility is that the person does this so that it does not become explicit that they have no good arguments for rejecting the proposed goal.

A second possibility is that the person thinks the disguise will make it easier to convince the other person. For example, someone may think that the other person will not listen to those who disagree with their goal, but will listen to those who accept the goal but think that defending it now will be futile or counterproductive.

A third possibility is that someone realizes that the idea in question is becoming increasingly accepted, and that disagreeing with it could be frowned upon. Let us take an example involving the moral consideration of nonhuman animals. In previous decades, objections to such consideration used to be explicitly normative: it was argued that we have no obligations toward animals, that humans should receive privileged treatment, that animal exploitation is justified, and so on. However, over the years an increasing number of people have come to reject speciesism. Thus, if someone realizes that defending speciesism may “not look good,” this may lead them to say that their disagreement is strategic (to disguise the fact that the objection is normative). The same holds for the contexts of the other examples we have seen.

Finally, a fourth possibility is the desire to avoid cognitive dissonance, that is, the discomfort that results from holding beliefs that conflict with one another or from having attitudes that conflict with our beliefs. For example, someone may believe that the proposal in question has good reasons in its favor, but it runs counter to beliefs and attitudes they have cultivated for many years. So they start claiming that defending the proposal in question will not work, so that they can keep holding the beliefs and attitudes they held before and thus escape cognitive dissonance. A good example is when it is claimed that helping wild animals would only make everything even worse, despite good intentions, without investigating whether this would really happen.

When those claims we saw in section 8.3 are made, their proponents rarely investigate whether or not what they claim would be very likely to happen. If there is no such investigation, then the claim is most likely made only to avoid cognitive dissonance, and not because the person really has good data to claim that what they allege would in fact happen. We will say more about this below.

8.7. A common pattern in objections of this kind

In the previous section we talked about possible motivations behind the claims we saw in section 8.3. Does the person really disagree for strategic reasons, or are they disguising their normative disagreement? If the latter, do they do so deliberately or unconsciously? Whether deliberately or unconsciously, why do they do it?

All this is interesting from a psychological point of view. However, to assess whether or not the claims in question are plausible, this investigation into the real motivation behind the claims is not necessary. In this and the next two sections we will discuss the plausibility of the claims.

To begin with, it is important to note that there is a common pattern in all of those claims:

(1) That no one will accept what is being proposed until another attitude is accepted.

(2) That getting people to accept this other attitude is so crucial for paving the way for the acceptance of what is being proposed that we should focus exclusively on this other attitude and leave the defense of what we want to propose to the next generations.

(3) That defending the proposal in question now will make people not accept other positions that we want them to accept.

Below we will discuss who bears the burden of proof with regard to these claims.

8.8. Who bears the burden of proof?

The proponents of those claims often assume that those who disagree with them have to prove that they could not be true. That is, they assume that the mere fact that it is not impossible for these things to happen shifts the burden of proof to the other side. But that is not how it works. The burden of proof lies entirely with those who make such claims, to show that these things would in fact happen (or, at least, that they would be highly likely to occur).

This is so for a simple reason: the burden of proof always lies with whoever makes a claim that is not obvious. For example, if I claim that people whose names begin with the letter L have a predisposition to like songs that begin in the key of C minor, it is up to me to prove that this is true (and not up to whoever doubts it to prove that it is false).

To better understand why the burden of proof lies with those who make such claims, consider the following example.

Example 8: Faced with the proposal that we combat racism and sexism, someone says something like:

“I agree that we should reject racism and sexism. However, if it is already hard for people to consider individuals of their own race and their own gender, let alone reject racism and sexism. So it is better to leave the fight against racism and sexism to future generations and for now focus only on fighting for people to respect individuals of their own race and their own gender, since that is what will make it possible for people in the future to reject racism and sexism. Pointing out now that what really explains why we should respect individuals of our own race and our own gender implies rejecting racism and sexism will only make people fail to respect even individuals of their own race and their own gender.”

Faced with a position of this kind, it would be very clear that claims are being made that are, at the very least, highly controversial (and, in this case, the possibility that a disagreement that is actually normative is being disguised as a strategic disagreement would probably be readily noticed). Note that it is not impossible for such claims to be true. But, since such claims are not at all obvious (indeed, they are highly controversial), it is up to their proponents to prove that they are true (or, at least, that they have a very high probability of occurring).

But that is not what usually happens in the case of the claims we saw earlier. Usually their proponents either assume that it is the other side that has to prove them false, or else they try to “meet” the burden of proof by saying things like “it is obvious that all this would happen” or “I know of cases in which this happened.” None of this meets the burden of proof. First, because saying “it is obvious that all this would happen” is not offering any reason at all for us to think that it would happen. Second, because pointing to cases where it happened does not show that it would happen in most cases, or even that it would happen frequently.

It is not easy to meet the burden of proof with regard to the claims we saw in section 8.3. First, because each of them involves not just one controversial claim, but three. Second, because if one of the three is not proven, the argument is already greatly weakened, even if the other two were proven.

Moreover, there are several reasons to doubt such claims. In the next section we will look at each of these reasons separately.

8.9. Reasons for rejecting the claims

We saw in the previous section that the burden of proof lies with those who make those claims. In this section we will see that, in addition, reasons can be offered for doubting the claims in question. We will also see that, with regard to some of those claims, even if they were true, they would not support the conclusion their proponents are aiming for.

Consider the claim that no one will accept what is being proposed until another attitude is accepted. Suppose this were the case. The fact is that, since there are already people who accept the other attitude, whoever makes the claim would have to admit that these people could accept what is being proposed. For example, one of the claims is that, to accept helping wild animals, someone first has to be vegan. Since there are people who are already vegan, whoever makes this claim would have to admit that it is worth talking about helping wild animals with these people. The same holds for any of the claims in the other examples.

Moreover, there are cases that show that accepting the other attitude is not necessary for accepting what is being proposed. Let us again take as an example the proposal to help wild animals. In fact, several of its proponents report that it is easier for people to accept it than to accept veganism. This is because this proposal demands less of each of us individually than veganism does, since usually those who would do the helping would be the professionals of the aid programs (what each of us would have to do is support such programs), whereas veganism involves each of us changing the way we eat and dress, for example. This shows that it is false that, to accept the proposal to help wild animals, someone first has to be vegan. In any of the other examples, pointing to the case of people who accept what is being proposed but do not accept the other attitude demonstrates that accepting this other attitude is not necessary for accepting what is being proposed.

And even if accepting the other attitude were necessary for accepting what we are proposing, this does not necessarily imply that we should stop defending what we are proposing and leave that task to future generations. For example, it could be that defending both ideas simultaneously now is the best way to achieve what we aim for.

Finally, there are also reasons to doubt the claim that defending the proposals in question now will make people not accept other positions that we want them to accept. There are at least two other possibilities. First, it may be that what is being proposed has no influence at all on getting people to accept or reject these other positions. Second, there is also the possibility that what is being proposed actually helps people understand why they should accept these other positions and would thus help people accept these other positions.

For example, if we explain to someone that the sentient beings of the future matter because they too would be capable of being harmed and benefited, since they would be capable of suffering and enjoyment, it is easy to explain why moral consideration for animals (nonhuman and human) rests on the same pillars. Similarly, if we explain to someone that speciesism is unjust because it violates the principle of equal consideration, it becomes easy to explain that we should reject racism and sexism for the same reason. If we explain that we should be concerned with the situation of wild animals because they are sentient beings and natural processes harm them, it becomes easy to see that we should also be concerned with the human practices that harm sentient beings, whether domesticated or wild, and so on.

As we saw in the previous section, the burden of proof lies with those who make those claims. However, as we have seen in this section, we also have reasons, in addition, to doubt those claims.

9. Focusing on Veganism versus Focusing on Reducing Consumption

9.1. Avoiding biases when assessing strategies

If what we aim for is to benefit animals in the best way possible, then we need to resist the temptation to reject or approve a certain strategy in advance, based on our intuitions (that is, our initial responses), before properly understanding what its possible positive and negative effects are.

Confirmation bias inclines us to notice what confirms what we already thought and to neglect what goes against our prior beliefs. This bias influences our attitudes in general, including when we assess activism strategies.

Another related bias is the take-the-best heuristic, a mental shortcut we use when choosing between alternatives, so as to decide quickly without needing to know all the information about each alternative. When we use this heuristic, instead of considering all the reasons why we might choose one alternative over another, we pick one reason and base our decision exclusively on it.

Let us look at an example. People generally consider that pointing out a single benefit of the strategy they intuitively sympathize with is already enough to prove that it is a good strategy. Similarly, they consider that pointing out a single negative effect of the strategy they intuitively dislike is already enough to prove that it is not a good strategy.

This way of thinking keeps us from making good decisions. For example, a strategy that has positive effects may have other, greater negative effects, resulting in a negative net balance overall. Similarly, it is possible that a strategy that has negative effects also has other, greater positive effects that give it a positive net balance. And even the fact that a strategy has a positive net balance does not show that there is no better strategy that could be tried in its place. A further complication is that sometimes one strategy carries fewer risks than another, but also has fewer positive effects. There are a series of difficulties we need to face if our goal is to help efficiently.

Analyzing the potential effects of each strategy is not an easy task. That is precisely why we should not rush to reject or embrace a strategy before investigating its likely effects.

9.2. Understanding when the disagreement is about strategies and when it is about goals

Sometimes disagreements that are strategic (that is, about the most efficient means of achieving the same goal) are mistakenly understood as if they were disagreements about the goals themselves, giving the impression that the degree of disagreement is greater than it really is. This makes it impossible to adopt mutual commitments that might have been possible had it been perceived that the disagreement is strategic.

Consider, for example, the following question: is it better to focus on trying to get people to adopt veganism or to get them to reduce their consumption of animal products?

This debate is often understood in the following terms: “advocates who focus on veganism believe that animal exploitation is unjust and aim to abolish it; advocates who focus on promoting reduced consumption, by contrast, believe that the problem is excessive consumption of animals and that, once it is reduced, there is nothing wrong with animal exploitation.”

This may be the case for many advocates, but it is certainly not the case for all of them. For example, there are advocates who focus on reduction but have the same goal as the advocates who focus on veganism: they aim for the abolition of the use of animals. However, they believe that, to achieve this goal, trying to convince people to reduce their consumption of animals is more efficient than trying to convince them to become vegan. Therefore, their disagreement is not about the goal: it is about which strategy is best for achieving that goal.

This does not mean that focusing on reduction is necessarily a better strategy than focusing on veganism, or vice versa. Next, we will look at some possible positive and negative effects of each of these strategies. The important point to note now is that disagreement about strategies does not necessarily indicate disagreement about goals. Realizing this (and also that the efficiency of the different strategies is, at least to some degree, uncertain) opens space for mutual understanding, avoiding the thought that people who follow strategies different from ours are bad or ignorant people.

As said before, examining each strategy carefully before approving or rejecting it is what is expected of those who aim for the best for animals. That is what we will try to do below.

9.3. The reasoning behind the focus on reduction

The main argument in favor of focusing on reduction is the following. Even if adopting veganism is an obligation in terms of justice toward animals, given the speciesist mentality of most people, if we ask them to do what is right, most people may find the required standard too high (although it really is not), and then simply continue to consume animals exactly as much as they did before. On the other hand, if we ask people only to reduce their consumption of animals, even though this is not what is truly just toward animals, since the demand is much smaller, many more people may come on board.

In short, the main argument in favor of focusing on reduction is this: by focusing on veganism, we may manage to convince a much smaller number of people and, although each vegan person prevents the deaths of many more animals than each person who merely reduces consumption, a much larger number of people doing less may, in the end, represent a much greater reduction in the number of animals killed than a much smaller number of people doing a lot.

Those who adopt this strategy may recognize that veganism is the ideal. However, they could argue that, given how humans are, if demanding the ideal greatly increases the risk of not achieving even the minimum, it is better to secure the minimum, even if this means calling for something that is not the ideal.

Of course, there are also serious arguments for adopting a focus on veganism (which we will see in section 9.5). Below are listed some arguments in favor of each of these approaches, which are a summary of the discussion contained in this list.

9.4. Arguments in favor of focusing on reduction

1) It is possible that many more people doing much less has a greater impact than many fewer people doing much more.

2) Asking people to reduce is less demanding and may therefore be more easily accepted.

3) It may be that, for people to call for the abolition of animal exploitation, it is enough for them to make a minimal change in their consumption.

4) If item 3 is correct, then focusing on reduction may generate broader support among the population for the cause of abolishing animal exploitation.

5) Given how hard it is to understand the difference between strategic disagreements and disagreements about goals, the focus on reduction, by providing an explanation of this, may contribute more to an activism that is sensitive to nuance and complexity.

6) Reduction does not carry the same stigma associated with veganism. Therefore, it may be more easily accepted.

7) The focus on reduction provides the opportunity to explain that the various animal products have different impacts on the suffering and number of deaths of animals. For example, it provides the opportunity to explain that the consumption of shrimp and insects causes many more deaths than the consumption of other animal products.

8) Even if what someone intends is to get people to become vegan, advocating reduced consumption may be a good “foot-in-the-door” strategy. This type of strategy consists of starting by proposing something less demanding, in order to try to make what one really aims for more easily accepted later, in stages. For example, if A asks for 5 dollars and B agrees to donate once, this increases the likelihood that B will agree to donate another 5 dollars later, more so than if A had initially asked for 10 dollars.

9.5. Arguments in favor of focusing on veganism

There are also arguments holding that focusing on veganism has better results. Below we will look at the main ones.

1) It emphasizes more strongly that consideration for animals is a serious matter and that animal exploitation is unjust.

2) Each person who adopts veganism causes a greater reduction in the number of animals exploited.

3) There is research suggesting that, on average, bigger goals produce bigger changes than more moderate goals.

4) Popularizing veganism right now, and also reducing the stigma associated with it, is important if the goal is the large-scale adoption of veganism later on.

5) Calling for reduced consumption may imply to the public that animal exploitation does not need to be abolished. So it is doubtful that, for the public to accept calling for abolition, it is enough for them to reduce their consumption.

6) Vegans seem to have more potential to become activists than those who merely reduce their consumption.

7) Asking people to reduce consumption may, paradoxically, increase the suffering and deaths of animals. This would happen if people misunderstood the message and, instead of consuming nothing of animal origin a few times a week, avoided beef but consumed more poultry, fish, or crustaceans, or avoided meat but consumed more eggs and milk, and so on. For this risk to be avoided, the message in favor of reduction has to be very clear on this point.

8) It is also possible that a smaller number of vegans has a greater impact than a larger number of people who merely reduce consumption. This is especially true if adopting veganism increases the chances of someone becoming an activist. In short, the result of each strategy will depend on these two factors: (1) how much larger or smaller the number of people reached by each strategy will be; and (2) how much benefit to animals each of these people would produce.

9) Veganism necessarily has a focus on consideration for animals. Reducing consumption, by contrast, can be done for environmentalist and anthropocentric reasons (although it can be done out of consideration for animals as well). There is a consensus among researchers that focusing on animals is not only more efficient at benefiting animals, but also that the use of environmentalist and anthropocentric arguments may be counterproductive, as we discussed in detail in Chapter 4.

10) Even if what someone intends is to advocate reduced consumption, advocating veganism may be a good “door-in-the-face” strategy. This type of strategy consists of first proposing something more demanding, so that what one really aims for will be more easily accepted later. For example, if A asks for fifty dollars and B refuses, and A then asks “what if it were just 5 dollars, would you donate?”, the probability that B will donate is greater than if A had started by asking for the 5 dollars, which is what A really wants.

9.6. Conclusion and some additional questions

Above, some arguments in favor of each type of focus were listed. However, there are also at least two other possibilities. One is to argue that there may be a better impact if different people advocate different focuses, instead of all focusing on the same strategy (or that we should try this at least as long as we do not have more precise data on the results of these different focuses). Yet another option would be for each person to try out the different focuses over the same period of time and then try to compare the efficiency of both. It is important to note that everything discussed here concerns changes in individual attitudes. Another parallel and important discussion is whether we should focus on changes in individual attitudes or on institutional changes.

The aim of this chapter, more than investigating which of these strategies is more efficient, was to show that, at least in this case, the disagreement among advocates is not necessarily about the goal. It seems to be much more about which strategy is best for achieving a shared goal, which is the end of animal exploitation. If there were a difference in goals, there would still be no reason at all for conflict and hostility, but rather for an honest and respectful debate about the goals. Now, if the goal is the same, conflict and hostility make even less sense. There are, instead, many reasons for us to carry out together — respectfully and honestly — a thoughtful and thorough examination of the pros and cons of each strategy.

10. Why the Term Welfarism Is Highly Ambiguous

10.1. Introduction

The term welfarism is highly ambiguous, since it is used to refer to positions that differ greatly from one another and that concern different debates. As we will see below, the term has at least seven meanings. This ambiguity often gives rise to the mistaken belief that accepting/rejecting a given position called welfarist means having to accept/reject other positions that go by the same name. As we will see, there is no such implication, since these positions concern different matters.

Below, I will explain the various positions that are usually called welfarist in different questions, and I will suggest substitute terms to avoid confusion.

10.2. Several positions called welfarist

The adjective welfarist is usually used to refer to the following positions:

(1) The position that holds that, as long as animal exploitation is regulated so that the animals do not suffer (or suffer less, depending on the variant), it becomes just.

Suggested substitute: RMJ position (in the sense of "regulating makes it just").

The main criticisms of this position are that it: (1) fails to take into account the harm of death for animals; (2) violates the principle of equal consideration; and (3) fails the impartiality test.

(2) The position that holds that, even if animal exploitation is regulated so that the animals do not suffer, it remains unjust and should be abolished, but that we should regulate it because doing so will gradually help abolish it.

Suggested substitute: RHA position (in the sense of "regulating helps abolish").

(3) The position that holds that, even if animal exploitation is regulated so that the animals do not suffer, it remains unjust and should be abolished, and that regulating it will not necessarily help gradually abolish it, but that we should try to regulate it because doing so will reduce the suffering of the exploited animals.

Suggested substitute: RRS position (in the sense of "regulating reduces suffering").

(4) Any and every position that aims to improve the well-being of animals, including animals that are not exploited by humans. For example, the proposal to help wild animals that are victims of natural processes is sometimes called welfarist in this sense, because its goal is concern for the animals' own good (rather than environmentalist values, centered on nonsentient entities), that is, because it is centered on beings that have well-being rather than on nonsentient entities. Work to protect abandoned animals is also sometimes called this.

Suggested substitute: Proposals aimed at the good of animals

(5) Positions that hold that what has value in itself is well-being (that is, the way sentient beings are affected positively or negatively), and not the way nonsentient entities (such as species, ecosystems, and nonsentient living organisms) are affected. In other words, in this sense the term refers to sentience-centered positions.

The main argument for the sentience criterion is the argument from relevance.

Suggested substitute: Sentience-centered positions

(6) Positions that hold that, in order to judge whether a situation involving several sentient beings has become worse/better in some respect, some sentient being must have had their well-being worsened/improved.

This is a debate that takes place in normative ethics, for example, between prioritarian positions and egalitarian positions. For example, let us compare situation S1, where A=+15, B=+14, with S2, where A=+14, B=+14. According to prioritarianism, S2 is not better in any respect, since there is no one who is better off compared to S1 (in fact, there is only someone who is worse off). Therefore, prioritarianism would be welfarist in this sense of the term. Egalitarians, by contrast, would say that S2 is better in at least one respect: in it, the total value is better distributed among individuals, even though S1 may be better all things considered (that is, taking into account everything that matters). This other text discusses this question in more detail.

Suggested substitute: Positions centered on changes in levels of well-being

(7) Theories about what the well-being of sentient beings consists of (which are called theories of well-being). There are several theories of this kind. However, all of them concern every circumstance in which a sentient being would be benefited or harmed. Thus, both a view that holds that the only form of harm is suffering and a view that holds that sentient beings can also be harmed in other ways (for example, by death, by being deprived of other positive events, by the frustration of desires, by being deprived of objective goods, etc.) are based on some theory of what their well-being consists of (that is, a theory about what harms or benefits individuals).

Suggested substitute: Theories of benefit/harm.

10.3. Conclusion

As should now be clear, since each of these terms concerns a different debate, accepting/rejecting any one of these positions does not necessarily imply accepting/rejecting any of the others that are referred to by the same name.

11. The Debate on Regulating Animal Exploitation

11.1. Introduction

There are people who hold that, as long as animal exploitation is regulated so that the animals do not suffer (or so that they suffer less, depending on the variant), there is nothing wrong with it, even if the animals are killed.

There are at least two good reasons to reject this position. The first is that animals are also harmed by death, regardless of suffering. The second is that it is speciesist, since it sees animals as mere resources for humans, violating the principle of equal consideration and the principle of impartiality.

However, among people who recognize that animal exploitation should be abolished, there are at least two other debates that revolve around regulating animal exploitation.

  • The first debate concerns whether regulating it could help gradually abolish it and, if so, whether animal advocates should advocate such regulations.
  • The second debate, in turn, concerns whether regulating it could reduce the suffering of the exploited animals (regardless of whether or not it helps abolish the exploitation) and, if so, whether advocates should advocate such regulations.

Below, we will look separately at the main arguments under discussion in the two debates45.

11.2. The debate over the causal relationship between regulation and abolition

As we have seen, the first debate involves two questions:

(1) Could regulating animal exploitation help gradually abolish it?

(2) If so, should animal advocates advocate such regulations?

We will now address each of these questions separately.

11.2.1. Could regulating animal exploitation help abolish it?

Those who hold that regulating animal exploitation could help gradually abolish it have two main arguments.

The first is that increasingly demanding regulations could make it increasingly difficult to exploit animals, and this would gradually lead to abolition, since the exploiters would see that the exploitation is not cost-effective.

The second is that, since the regulations are centered on concern for the animals' suffering, this could lead the public to increasingly recognize that animals matter in themselves, at least to some extent (or even to a great extent), which could lead the public gradually to support even the abolition of the exploitation.

The main argument of those who hold that regulating does not help gradually abolish exploitation, on the other hand, is that regulating could increase consumption, since it could make consumers feel more comfortable with their consumption because they think the animals' well-being is guaranteed. Proponents of this position generally argue that focusing on reforms can reinforce the notion that animals are resources for us to use.

11.2.2. If regulating helps abolish, should we invest in regulations?

One might think that, if it is shown that regulations gradually lead to abolition, then animal advocates should invest in regulations. However, we need to investigate whether this is the most efficient way to achieve abolition or to help animals in general. If it is, then animal advocates should certainly invest their resources in it. On the other hand, if there are one or more other, more efficient forms of activism, that is where they should invest their resources.

"More efficient" can mean several things. For example, it can mean that, with the same resources, a certain strategy reaches the intended goal sooner. Or it can mean that a certain strategy reaches the intended goal (regardless of when) while spending fewer resources. Or, again, it can mean that a certain strategy makes it harder, once the goal has been reached, to reverse it. There are several possibilities.

Accordingly, someone could argue that, even if regulations gradually lead to abolition, using the same resources to bring about changes in attitudes (for example, spreading the antispeciesist view), and/or focusing on technological changes (for example, investing in cultivated meat) and/or on behavioral changes (for example, promoting veganism or reduced consumption) could be more efficient for achieving abolition.

Thus, what is crucial for assessing this point is to compare the regulation-focused strategy with other possible strategies (and those other strategies with one another) and see which one (or ones) has the greatest potential for efficiency (bearing in mind, as we have seen, that the concept of efficiency has several aspects).

For example, it could be argued that investing the same resources in spreading an antispeciesist mindset would contribute greatly to people ceasing to consume animals, and that this would reduce the number of exploited animals more quickly than investing those resources in more regulations (even if regulations gradually led to a reduction in the number of exploited animals).

The same could be said when comparing regulations with cultivated meat technology. If cultivated meat technology arrives and becomes cheaper to produce than conventional meat, the exploiters themselves will have an interest in switching to cultivated meat. Moreover, unlike regulations, investment in cultivated meat does not carry the risk of increasing the consumption of conventional meat and, consequently, does not carry the risk of increasing the number of exploited animals (in fact, it would considerably reduce that number).

It could also be argued that, even if regulations helped gradually abolish exploitation, if people's mindset in general does not change (and they do not reject speciesism), they will probably continue to see animals as resources, and then abolition would be easily reversible once achieved. Accordingly, it could be said that the strategy of combating speciesism would be more efficient in terms of ensuring that abolition, once achieved, would not be reversed.

Moreover, it could be pointed out that the strategy of spreading an antispeciesist view has a reach that goes far beyond exploited animals, since rejecting speciesism also implies considering the animals that are victims of natural processes, who, as we saw in section 3.4, are vastly more numerous than exploited animals.

At present, there are no studies thoroughly testing the degree of efficiency of each strategy in these or other respects. The question of efficiency in activism has barely begun to be discussed. Therefore, more studies comparing the efficiency of each strategy are needed. This does not mean, however, that we should blindly trust such studies once they come to exist. Whatever a study argues in its conclusion, it is always important to evaluate its methodology because, for example, researchers may be biased depending on the activist strategy they themselves prefer.

Another important point is that, given the uncertainty about the degree of efficiency of each strategy, it is important to compensate for neglect. That is, the less a strategy has been tried so far, or the fewer people already work on it, the greater the potential for us to make a bigger positive difference if we invest in it. Investment (in terms of resources and number of people) in the strategy of regulating exploitation has been much greater over the years46 than investment in other strategies, such as antispeciesist education, spreading veganism and reduced consumption, investing in the development of cultivated meat, etc. Thus, given the uncertainty, there are reasons to invest more in these other strategies than in regulations.

11.3. The debate over the causal relationship between regulating and reducing suffering

The second debate also involves two equivalent questions:

(1) Does regulating animal exploitation reduce the suffering of the exploited animals?

(2) If so, should animal advocates advocate such regulations?

We will now address each of these questions separately.

11.3.1. Does regulating exploitation reduce the animals' suffering?
