Volume IX

Ethics and the Future

This book presents the debate on ethical questions concerning the long-term future, especially risks of future suffering: what they are, how to identify them, and how to prevent them.

Original text by Luciano Carlos Cunha, translated into English · ISBN 978-65-01-55743-4 · 1st edition, July 2025.

1. Future Risks for Sentient Beings: An Introduction

1.1. The past, the present, and the future

The emergence of factory farming in the 1930s and its subsequent large-scale application resulted in an enormous multiplication of two things: (1) the number of animals killed and subjected to living a life of suffering; (2) the levels of suffering for each animal. In short, factory farming multiplied the harms humans cause to other animals on a scale never seen before.

At the beginning of the twentieth century, animal advocates probably would not have imagined that factory farming would emerge just a few decades later. However, at that time there were already clues that the technology then emerging would result in factory farming.

Now consider two thought experiments1.

(1) You, going from the present to the past

Imagine that you could go back in time and warn those people that something terrible was about to emerge. Perhaps there would be time to prevent factory farming from emerging (or at least to reduce its negative impact). Of course, it might be too late to try anything. But imagine that your time machine allowed you to go back to well before the beginning of the twentieth century. It seems that the earlier you managed to go back, the greater your chances of preventing the catastrophe (or at least of minimizing its negative impact), since the people you influenced would have more time to try.

(2) You, coming from the future to the present

Now imagine that you are once again a time traveler, but this time from the future. Imagine that you have come from the year 4025 to warn the people of the present that things are about to emerge

in the future so terrible that they would make even factory farming look like "a tiny grain of sand" by comparison. As in the previous example, there is a reason for you to come back to the present moment. At first you tried going back to times closer to 4025, but you saw that your efforts would be futile: it was necessary to go back to earlier times to allow enough time to prevent the catastrophes. For this reason, you ended up in the present time.

What these thought experiments aim to ask is: with regard to the bad things that could emerge for sentient beings2 in the future, are we now perhaps in the same position that animal advocates were in before the emergence of factory farming? As we will see below, this is what the concept of s-risks is about: suffering on a gigantic scale that could arise in the future, and what to do to prevent it.

1.2. What are s-risks?

At present, a very large number of nonhuman animals suffer intensely, and in many cases in ways that did not exist in the past. Likewise, in the future new ways of harming sentient beings on a massive scale may emerge, on a scale vastly greater than anything that has existed so far.

One concept used to address this problem is that of risks of future suffering (usually abbreviated as s-risks). This concept concerns the possibility that suffering will be massively increased in the future3, and it can be defined as follows:

  • S-risks: risks that events will occur in the future that result in suffering of gigantic magnitude4, exceeding the suffering that has existed on Earth so far.

The concept of s-risks is centered on suffering, but there could be an analogous concept to address all the forms of harm that animals could endure, and not only suffering

(such as, for example, the harm of death). In that case, there could be a concept such as h-risks (risks of future harm). However, in this book we will speak of s-risks because that is the concept that has been widely used in the debate on these questions, even though, technically speaking, h-risks would be a more appropriate term, since it is more comprehensive.

1.3. Differences between s-risks and x-risks

S-risks are a different concept from x-risks (existential risks). Both s-risks and x-risks are about the long term and astronomical impacts. But whereas x-risks are about risks of the annihilation of humanity (or at least of a drastic reduction in its potential), s-risks are about scenarios involving astronomical suffering (and it is therefore a concept that necessarily takes into account all sentient beings).

Certain s-risks may also be x-risks, but there are s-risks that are not x-risks. For example, there are forms of suffering inflicted on nonhuman sentient beings that do not harm humans, and that may even promote certain human interests (the consumption of animals is an example).

1.4. Measuring the seriousness of an s-risk

Every s-risk concerns risks of suffering of astronomical magnitude, but each s-risk has a different degree of seriousness. This is because not only does the severity of each s-risk vary (for example, the number of victims who would potentially be affected and how much each one would suffer), but the probability of each s-risk materializing also varies.

Thus, one way to measure the seriousness of an s-risk is to multiply how bad the outcome would be by its probability of occurring (this would reveal its expected disvalue, or ED)5.

This calculation reveals something important about s-risks. Since s-risks are, by definition, many orders of magnitude greater than current suffering (even compared with animal exploitation combined with the suffering of animals in the wild), the ED of each s-risk is enormous, even when the probability of its occurring is small.

1.5. S-risks and new technologies

One factor that can give rise to s-risks is the emergence of new technologies. This risk is great especially if the technology would benefit those who hold it and they have no moral consideration for the beings negatively affected by it. If humanity has advanced technology but moral progress does not occur in parallel, there is a great risk that this will result in suffering of unprecedented magnitude.

As we have seen, one past example of how the emergence of a technology massively multiplied the suffering and deaths of sentient beings was the advent of factory farming (which, in turn, was a result of industrialization). Another example was the development of new weapons technologies.

If human extinction or a collapse of civilization does not occur, technology will probably continue to advance, perhaps making it possible to colonize planets and even billions of galaxies. Thus, technologies with a vastly greater impact may emerge in the future, which also increases the chances that their negative impact will be vastly greater.

For scenarios of astronomical suffering to occur, it is not necessary for the agents to intend to harm the victims: it is enough that they do not care (or care very little) about them, as happens with the act of consuming animal products, for example. New technologies, together with indifference, are already enough to considerably increase the probability that suffering of colossal size will be caused.

Moreover, it may also happen that the agents intend to use the technology to harm the victims. Or, again, suffering on a massive scale may arise accidentally. It is also possible that agents allow or promote the victims' suffering of natural harms when they could have prevented it. In short, there are many ways in which an s-risk could arise. We will see more about this below.

1.6. Classification of s-risks according to how they arise

S-risks can be classified according to various parameters. In this section, we will see how they can be classified according to the way they arise, following the classification given by Baumann (2022, p.13-9). In the next section, we will look at other parameters.

1.6.1. Incidental s-risks

These occur when ways of achieving a certain goal generate a great deal of suffering, but without the suffering being sought for its own sake. The agents may simply be indifferent, or may even prefer an alternative without suffering, but not be willing to pay the costs.

Some examples:

  • Suffering as an effect of high productivity. A present-day example is factory farming. In the future, similar scenarios may occur, but on a much larger scale.
  • Suffering for the sake of gaining information. A present-day example is animal experimentation. An example in the future would be the creation of virtual simulations with digital sentient beings to gain knowledge about how sentient beings behave.
  • Suffering for entertainment. Just as there are bullfights today, new kinds of sentient beings may be created in the future for similar forms of entertainment.
1.6.2. Agential s-risks

These occur when the agent aims to cause the harm. Let us look at some examples:

  • Sadists. Future technologies may multiply their potential to cause harm.
  • Feelings of hatred. A tribal "us vs. them" mentality can result in hatred against those who belong to a certain ethnicity, religion, political ideology, etc.
  • Extreme punishments. Past examples are the forms of punishment that were applied precisely because they caused extreme suffering.

A key factor in the increase of agential s-risks is the presence of malevolent traits (narcissism, psychopathy, Machiavellianism, and sadism) in powerful individuals6.

1.6.3. Natural s-risks

These arise without the action of agents. For example, independently of human action, natural processes already harm animals to an extremely high degree, tending to maximize the number of sentient beings who are born to have lives full of suffering7. For every animal who manages to survive, literally thousands or even millions are born only to experience suffering and die prematurely. The norm in the wild is for them to be victims of malnutrition, hunger, and thirst, disease, physical injuries, psychological stress, hostile weather events, natural disasters, and interspecific, intraspecific, and sexual conflicts.

These animals are the vast majority of sentient beings on Earth. For example, if we compare the populations of animals exploited by humans and of animals in the wild and draw an analogy with the span of one year, the former would represent only 14 seconds of the year8. All the rest (364 days, 23 hours, 59 minutes, and 46 seconds) would be animals in the wild. Natural s-risks are the risks that suffering resulting from natural causes will expand on an astronomical scale.

This suffering is a result of the way natural selection works. For example, the trait of maximizing the number of offspring offers a great advantage in transmitting genetic information: with such gigantic broods (with thousands or even millions of offspring, depending on the species), it is highly likely that at least one or two will survive and reproduce, passing this trait on. However, in stable populations, on average only one offspring survives per adult9 (that is, two per brood). All the rest are born almost solely to experience the suffering associated with death.

If this maximization of suffering is a result of natural selection, then, if there are other

planets where sentient life has developed, it is likely that this has also happened there and continues to happen.

There is also a risk that humans will in the future expand this suffering (for example, by spreading life beyond Earth). Although this would already be an incidental s-risk, it would also, indirectly, be a natural s-risk.

1.7. Other classifications

S-risks can be classified according to various other parameters, and not only according to the way they arise. Below are some other possible classifications10:

  • Known and unknown s-risks. These depend on whether or not we are currently able to imagine them (for example, in the Middle Ages no one imagined that the atomic bomb would come about).

Unknown s-risks can also be subclassified according to the way they arise:

  • Incidental: when unknown mechanisms will lead to incidental s-risks.
  • Agential: agents may come to have reasons in the future to cause harm that we do not yet know about.
  • Natural: the universe may already contain much more suffering than we think.

Other parameters according to which s-risks can be classified are:

  • According to the type of sentient being affected. For example, whether or not it is human, whether or not it is organic, etc.
  • Whether or not they can be influenced. That is, whether or not it is possible to do something to prevent or minimize them. Here, however, it is important to distinguish between: (1) scenarios that, given the laws of physics, it is impossible to influence and (2) scenarios that cannot currently be influenced but may become open to influence in the future.

There may be many other parameters according to which s-risks can be classified. The list above should not be seen as complete.

Below we will look at some concrete examples of s-risks.

1.8. Some examples of s-risks

In the debate about the future, there is a concern with trying to estimate what the main s-risks are and how to prevent them (or at least how to make them occur to a lesser extent). Let us look below at three possible scenarios of massive suffering in the future and the risk factors that could give rise to them. The risk factors will be discussed in more detail in Chapter 8. In Chapter 9 we will look at some strategies for preventing them.

Important: since it is difficult to estimate the probability of the future turning out one way or another, the following examples are well-informed guesses, but they are not necessarily the s-risks most likely to occur. Moreover, all of these examples may still be a small fraction of s-risks, compared with the s-risks still unknown.

S-risks can arise from a wide range of scenarios. Therefore, we must be careful with the availability heuristic, which is the bias that leads us to think that the cases we remember most easily are necessarily the most representative. This bias can lead us to think, mistakenly, that the s-risks we remember most easily will necessarily be the most likely.

With this in mind, here are some examples.

1.8.1. An increase in animal exploitation

There are at least three ways in which the suffering caused by animal exploitation could come to be massively increased:

  • Expanding it in scale (that is, affecting a greater number of sentient beings).
  • Making it qualitatively worse (that is, increasing the harms suffered by each animal).
  • Creating new ways in which it can happen.

One example of an s-risk of this kind that has materialized is the use of insects for consumption, which emerged at the end of the twentieth century and has been expanding in several countries11. Since these animals are very small, producing an equivalent amount of meat requires a vastly greater number of individuals to suffer and die12. Moreover, invertebrates are typically disregarded even more than other nonhuman animals. This degree of disregard magnifies the negative effect on each invertebrate. For example, the space allotted to insects on farms is extremely small, even smaller, in proportion to their size, than that given to other animals13.

1.8.2. The expansion of wild animal suffering

An increase in the suffering of wild animals may occur owing to an increase in the number of animals on Earth (as with rewilding14 practices, which aim to return ecosystems to their state prior to human presence) or owing to the intentional or accidental spread of life beyond it (as in panspermia15 and terraforming16).

These practices may be good from an environmentalist point of view or an anthropocentric one, but they are very negative for the animals affected. As we have seen, natural processes tend to maximize the number of animals who live lives full of suffering and die prematurely. This happens on a gigantic scale, much larger even than that of animal exploitation17, and it happens to a greater extent the greater the amount of plant biomass available, since this implies an increase in the number of reproductions, which, in turn, is directly linked to the maximization of suffering18. Given the prevalence of the environmentalist view and the disregard for the good of animals, the expansion of natural territory and of life are usually seen as entirely positive. For the animals affected by such practices, however, their effects are predominantly negative19.

1.8.3. The creation of new forms of sentience

The creation of new forms of sentience may also give rise to vast amounts of suffering, especially if there is a high probability that these beings will not receive moral consideration. Examples of risks of this kind are the creation of genetically modified animals and, especially, the creation of nonbiological forms of sentience20.

The possibility of nonbiological sentience exists because perhaps sentience appears whenever any physical structure is organized in such a way as to provide the conditions for it to appear, regardless of whether or not the structure is organic. One way to understand this possibility is through the following thought experiment.

Let us imagine that our neurons were gradually replaced by nonorganic neurons. If our sentience did not fade as the neurons were replaced, and if we remained sentient after all the neurons had been replaced, this would suggest that it is possible for nonorganic beings to be sentient in the future, should they come to have a structure organized so as to perform the same functions as a brain.

This possibility is an s-risk because, if these beings come to exist, there is a high probability that they will not receive moral consideration because they are not organic, and will then be harmed in all sorts of ways, just as nonhuman animals are today. The very mistaken idea held by many animal activists, that animals should be respected because they are animals or because they are living beings (and not because they are sentient), is a factor that has the potential to result in disregard for nonorganic sentient beings.

In the future, nonorganic sentience could arise not only through digital modifications of biological bodies, but also, for example, in sentient simulations within a computer program. Such beings, although sentient, might have no faces and might neither move nor scream. So it might be hard to feel empathy for them21. If such beings come to exist, humans will probably not care about them, just as happens with animals (or perhaps it will be even worse, since animals are already very similar to humans and yet,

even so, most humans do not care much about them). It may also happen that a digital entity is already sentient at a certain point without our noticing (and that we then cause it suffering without realizing it).

If nonorganic sentience is possible, enormous numbers of digital sentient beings may come to exist in the future, since creating them may involve far lower costs than creating biological sentient beings. Just as anyone can copy computer programs at will today, it is possible that in the future anyone will be able to create digital sentient beings.

Thus, the potential for vast numbers of digital sentient beings, together with a lack of consideration, poses a serious s-risk (exactly as happens in animal agriculture, all the more so since both are combined with economic incentives).

For this reason, it is important to combat not only speciesism, but also substratism. Just as speciesism is discrimination based on the species to which someone belongs, substratism is discrimination based on the type of substrate that makes up a being's body (for example, whether it is organic or nonorganic). Just as anthropocentrism is a form of speciesism (which discriminates against those who do not belong to the human species), carbonism is a form of substratism (which discriminates against those who are not organic).

Substratism, just like speciesism, can produce suffering in astronomical amounts in the future. That is why it is important to emphasize that animals should be considered because they are sentient (and not because they are animals or because they are living beings), and that this implies considering nonorganic sentient beings, should they come to exist.

1.9. Conclusion

The risks that the scenarios mentioned above will materialize are not trivial. In fact, they are very great, since it is easy to ignore such problems and, moreover, they are not being discussed. For this reason, it is extremely necessary to begin a broad debate on s-risks.

2. Temporal Impartiality: What It Is and Why It Matters

2.1. Introduction

The way our decisions may affect the sentient beings who will live in the distant future is still a greatly neglected question, though it has begun to receive attention22.

Below, we will look at one of the central reasons this question has been neglected (the presence of temporal bias) and at the reasons for adopting an approach centered on temporal impartiality23. We will also see that, even if someone rejects temporal impartiality, this is not enough to justify dismissing a strong concern with how our decisions will affect future sentient beings.

2.2. Temporal bias

Cognitive biases are systematic patterns of flawed reasoning, or mental shortcuts that cloud our judgment. One of the factors that leads people to neglect the impact of their decisions on future beings is temporal bias, which consists in the tendency to give less importance to an event depending on how far from the present it lies.

To understand why this tendency is a bias, we need only remember that the moment that is now the present was once the future, and that the coming future moments will also come to pass, just as this moment did. An example of temporal bias would be to think that, 10 years ago, we should not have cared about ensuring that the moment we are living now would not be bad for us, merely because at that time it was far off in time.

How hard we should strive to bring about or avoid a certain event ought to depend on how good or bad it is, not on how near to or far from the present it is. Thus, rejecting temporal bias means accepting that no moment in time, in itself, has a higher or lower status (what matters is how good or bad the event would be). This can be better understood through the idea of temporal impartiality, which is an implication

of the more general idea of impartiality. We will look at these concepts below.

2.3. Impartiality

  • Impartiality: the unbiased consideration of those affected by our decisions.

Impartiality24 implies that harms and benefits of equal magnitude must be given the same weight, regardless of arbitrary factors such as the race, gender, or species of those affected by the decision, or any other factor that is the result of the natural lottery.

It also implies that someone is unfairly disfavored not only when they are disregarded entirely, but also when, on the basis of arbitrary factors, their good is given less weight.

As we will see below, temporal impartiality is one specific application of this general idea of impartiality.

2.4. Temporal impartiality

To understand the idea of temporal25 impartiality, it helps to compare it with the idea of spatial impartiality.

We saw above that impartiality implies rejecting arbitrary distinctions, such as giving different degrees of moral consideration on the basis of the species, race, or gender of those affected by the decision. Another example of an arbitrary distinction would be to give different degrees of moral consideration depending on where someone happens to be. Thus, impartiality implies spatial impartiality:

  • Spatial impartiality: the unbiased consideration of those affected by our decisions, regardless of where they are located.

One implication of spatial impartiality is that there is no justification for giving less weight to the good of a sentient being just because that being is far away from us.

Note that spatial impartiality is not an idea distinct from impartiality in general: it is merely an implication of it. However, impartiality also implies the same with respect to time:

  • Temporal impartiality: the unbiased consideration of those affected by our decisions, regardless of the time in which they exist.

Thus, one implication of temporal impartiality is that there is no justification for giving less weight to the good of a sentient being just because that being will exist in the future (whether near or distant). The important practical conclusion is this: according to temporal impartiality, the fact that a harm will occur in the distant future does not weaken the reasons for preventing it.

Most people who aim to reduce suffering in the world think of the individuals alive today (one of the reasons for this, besides temporal bias, is that it is hard to empathize with individuals who will exist in the distant future). However, if what we have seen makes sense, giving someone less consideration depending on the time in which they will exist is analogous to discriminating against them on the basis of where they live, their species, skin color, gender, and so on.

This, in short, is the central idea of temporal impartiality.

2.5. The objection that future beings are merely potential beings

One objection to temporal impartiality holds that future individuals are, for now, mere possibilities that may never come to exist, unlike individuals who already exist. According to this objection, for this reason future individuals should either not count morally or be given less weight.

One response to this objection is to point out that our decisions can cause such possibilities to become real individuals in the future, and can also make their lives more positive or more negative. For example, even those who hold that there is no duty to bring new sentient beings into existence to have positive lives can recognize that there is a duty not to bring new sentient beings into existence to have negative lives. They can also recognize that, if a being will necessarily exist in the future regardless of what we decide, we should decide now in a way that avoids harming it and seeks to benefit it. These points will be discussed in more detail in the next chapter.

Thus, there are at least two ways in which our decisions can affect future beings:

  • Our decision may determine whether or not a future sentient being comes to exist, and whether it is born into a context in which it will probably have a predominantly negative or positive life.
  • Our decision may not determine whether or not a future sentient being comes to exist, but may determine the number of negative or positive events it will have in its life.

A good part of animal advocacy is already about future beings. For example, veganism is mostly about trying to prevent more animals from being born to lead lives full of suffering, not about animals who already exist. This is also the goal of sterilization programs, whether for wild or domesticated animals. Regulations that try to make exploited animals suffer less, in turn, are about ensuring that beings who will necessarily come to exist suffer less during their lives. Finally, spreading a view that gives consideration to all sentient beings aims mainly at increasing, from then on, the likelihood that future sentient beings will have lives with more positive events and fewer negative ones. Of course, part of animal advocacy is about helping animals who already exist. Examples include programs for vaccinating animals and treating diseases, helping animals in fires and other natural disasters, caring for orphaned animals, rescuing trapped animals, and programs for meeting animals' basic needs. However, as we have seen, a good part of animal advocacy already stems from recognizing that future beings deserve consideration.

One way to see that it is arbitrary to give less weight to someone's good depending on how far into the future they will exist is to imagine what we would think if generations before ours had believed there was nothing wrong with actions that would harm us enormously, simply because at the time we did not yet exist.

The veil of ignorance thought experiment can also help ground the idea of temporal impartiality26. Imagine that we had to decide which principles of justice people should follow, but without knowing in which era we would be born (knowing only that we would have to be born in some era). Under such conditions, it seems we would argue for giving equal consideration to all individuals who might be affected by agents' decisions, no matter in which era they would exist.

2.6. Does rejecting temporal impartiality justify disregarding future beings?

What we have seen above suggests that there are strong reasons to accept temporal impartiality and to give equal consideration to the beings who will exist in the future.

However, let us imagine that there were a justification for giving greater weight to the good of the sentient beings who exist now. Well, this would not show that there is a justification for disregarding future beings: there would only be a justification for giving them less weight.

And even if that were the case, we should still give enormous importance to the long-term future, to the point of prioritizing it over the present and the short-term future. This may sound strange at first. Below is an explanation of why this implication follows.

The future may last for many eons, and therefore the number of sentient beings who may exist over the course of the future would also be immense. The point is this: that number would be so immense that, even if we gave less and less weight to each sentient being depending on how far into the future it will exist, we would still have to conclude in favor of prioritizing concern for the long-term future, given the total number of individuals affected. This is one of the central arguments for a focus on the long term, which we will examine in Chapter 4.

2.7. Conclusion

If what we have seen above makes sense, then we must draw two important conclusions, if our goal is to make the world contain less suffering:

(1) We need to consider all sentient beings (including those of the distant future). (2) We need to give great weight to the long-term future.

Two factors have contributed greatly to the neglect of this important question. One of them, as we have seen, is temporal bias. The other is speciesism. The combination of these two factors contributes to the following result, which is a double neglect:

(1) Because of speciesism, when concern for the long-term future does appear, usually only future humans are taken into account.

(2) Because of temporal bias, those who already accept considering all sentient beings (for example, animal advocates) have usually disregarded future sentient beings.

If our goal is for there to be less suffering in the world, we need to reject this double neglect. Concern for the long term needs to reject speciesism and consider all sentient beings, and concern for sentient beings needs to reject temporal bias and take the long-term future into account27.

3. The Objection That Future Beings Are Merely Potential Beings

3.1. The objection that we should care only about beings who already exist

We saw in the previous chapter that one of the most common objections to concern for the long-term future is based on the idea that future sentient beings are merely potential beings, that is, beings who do not yet exist and who may perhaps never come to exist. According to this objection, for this reason we should care only about beings who already exist.

Now consider the following causes:

  • Spreading veganism.
  • Pursuing regulations to make exploited animals suffer less.
  • Protecting abandoned animals.
  • Working to reduce the suffering of wild animals.

According to the objection, fighting for these causes makes sense because "they are about helping those who already exist." By contrast, the objection maintains, concern for the long-term future makes no sense, because it concerns beings who may never even come to exist.

This objection is sometimes raised especially in connection with concern about the possibility that nonorganic sentient beings may emerge in the future. According to the objection, we should not worry about this because it is something that may never even happen. Organic sentient beings, on the other hand, the objection concludes, already exist, and so we should care about them.

Is this a plausible objection? That is what we will discuss in this chapter.

3.2. Should we care only about sentient beings who already exist?

A first way to challenge this objection is to question the assumption that we should care only about the sentient beings who have existed up to now. For example, it could be pointed out that, if the reason for caring about already existing sentient beings is the possibility that our decisions may affect them positively or negatively, then we have the same reason to care about sentient beings who do not yet exist but who may come to exist (since our decisions can also affect them positively or negatively).

It could be objected that, if no one has a duty to bring new sentient beings into existence, but we do have a duty not to kill those who already exist, this is because we have duties only toward individuals (and not toward future possibilities of individuals). Thus, the objection concludes, we have no obligations regarding how our decisions affect future beings.

However, someone could agree that we have no obligations toward future possibilities of individuals and still disagree that we have no obligations regarding how our decisions affect future beings.

First, someone could hold that we have a duty to make the history of the world from now on contain as many sentient beings with positive lives as possible. This duty would not be a duty toward this or that future possibility of a sentient being, but rather an impersonal duty to bring about the best consequences28.

Second, and more importantly, even if someone denies the duty to bring new sentient beings into existence, we could still have at least two kinds of duties toward future beings:

  • Not to bring new sentient beings into existence to live lives full of suffering.
  • If a future sentient being will necessarily exist, to try to make its life contain less suffering than it otherwise would.

Both duties could be recognized even by those who reject a duty to make future possibilities of sentient beings come to be realized29. And, contrary to what might seem at first, as will be explained in the next section, these two duties are

the central focus of veganism, of attempts to make exploited animals suffer less, of the protection of abandoned animals, and also of the cause that aims to reduce the suffering of wild animals.

3.3. The struggle for animals is usually already a struggle for possible future beings

We saw that the objection under discussion assumes that causes such as veganism, attempts to make exploited animals suffer less, the protection of abandoned animals, and the cause that aims to reduce the suffering of wild animals make sense because "they are about sentient beings who already exist." Meanwhile, the objection maintains, concern for the long-term future makes no sense because "it is about beings who do not yet exist (and who may never come to exist)."

However, this is mistaken. Each of those causes is also mostly about consideration for future beings. We will look at this point for each of them below:

The central goal of veganism is not to help animals who already exist, but rather to reduce the number of animals who would be born to lead lives full of suffering and to be killed. Veganism is therefore a recognition of the duty not to bring new sentient beings into existence to live lives full of suffering.

Now consider attempts to regulate animal exploitation so that animals suffer less. For the sake of argument, let us set aside the discussion of whether these regulations really reduce the suffering of such animals. Suppose they do. Even if that is the case, by the time a regulation comes into force, the animals who will benefit from it are generally not those who had already been born when the regulation was proposed. Of course, there may be some exceptions, as in the case of cows and sows who are exploited for several years. However, the vast majority of animals are killed within days or, at most, months. Thus, activists who pursue such regulations are recognizing a duty, if a sentient being will exist in the future, to try to make its life contain less suffering than it otherwise would.

Let us now consider the case of protecting abandoned animals, such as dogs and cats. Again, some actions may be aimed at benefiting animals who already exist, as in the case of providing food, shelter, medical treatment, vaccination, or responsible adoption. However, one of the main focuses of advocacy in this area is precisely sterilization, aimed at preventing more animals from being born into such situations. This focus is, again, a recognition of the duty to prevent the birth of new sentient beings who would have lives full of suffering.

The same holds for the cause that aims to reduce the suffering of wild animals30. Again, in this case too, various actions aim to help animals who already exist, such as vaccinating animals and treating diseases, helping animals in fires and other natural disasters, caring for orphaned animals, rescuing trapped animals, and programs for meeting animals' basic needs. However, the vast majority of wild animals' suffering and premature deaths results from their enormous reproductive rates31. Most species of animals in the wild reproduce in broods containing anywhere from thousands to many millions of offspring. For example, a single clutch of a common frog contains around 25,000 offspring32; that of octopuses, hundreds of thousands33; those of salmon, cod, and tuna, millions34; and that of the ocean sunfish reaches 300 million35. Terrestrial invertebrates can also lay hundreds, thousands, or even millions of eggs at a time36. In periods of roughly stable population, the average number of survivors from each brood is only two offspring (that is, one descendant per parent). All the rest are usually born only to experience the suffering of dying, without any positive experience. For this reason, the main focus of the proposal to reduce the suffering and premature deaths of wild animals is also to make fewer individuals be born into such conditions. It is, therefore, also a recognition of the duty to prevent new sentient beings from coming into existence to have lives full of suffering.

Thus, in all these struggles, the main focus is either to try to make beings who will exist in the future suffer less, or to try to prevent new sentient beings from coming to

exist to have lives full of suffering. In short, the animal cause is usually already about future beings. If so, then it makes no sense to claim that we should not care about the long-term future just because such concern would be about beings who do not yet exist and who may never come to exist. In concern for the long-term future, the goal is likewise to try to make beings who will exist in the future suffer less and to try to prevent new beings from coming to exist to have lives full of suffering (and, additionally, depending on the strand, to bring new beings into existence to have positive lives). This holds whether we are talking about possible future organic or nonorganic sentient beings.

4. What Reasons Are There to Focus on the Long Term?

4.1. What is longtermism?

The word longtermism37 is used to express different ideas, depending on the author. Sometimes it is used to refer to a goal. At other times, it is used to refer to a practical focus for trying to achieve that goal38. Below, two kinds of goals (one longtermist and one short-termist) and two practical focuses (one longtermist and one short-termist) are compared.

  • Longtermist goal: aims to have the best possible impact on history from now until the end of time. This goal necessarily implies giving equal weight to every moment in time (that is, it implies temporal impartiality).

However, two people who agree on the longtermist goal may disagree about what we should focus on in practice to best achieve it. Thus, there are at least two kinds of practical focus for achieving the longtermist goal:

  • Longtermist practical focus: to have the best possible impact on history from now until the end of time, we should focus on the impact our decisions will have on the long-term future.
  • Short-termist practical focus: to have the best possible impact on history from now until the end of time, we should focus on the impact our decisions will have at the present moment or in the near future.

Now consider the short-termist goal:

  • Short-termist goal: aims to have the best possible impact on the present or the near future. This goal will give less weight to (or even entirely neglect) the distant future (that is, it rejects temporal impartiality).

Since the short-termist goal does not seek to have an impact on the long-term future, there is only one kind of practical focus for achieving it:

  • Short-termist practical focus: to have the best possible impact on the present or the near future, we should focus on the impact our decisions will have at the present moment or in the near future.

We thus have the following possibilities:

  • Longtermist goal with a longtermist practical focus
  • Longtermist goal with a short-termist practical focus
  • Short-termist goal with a short-termist practical focus

4.2. What will we see in this chapter?

In section 4.3 we will look at the central reason for adopting a longtermist goal. In section 4.4 we will look at arguments for adopting a longtermist practical focus. In section 4.5 we will look at the main objections to the longtermist practical focus and how these objections can be answered.

4.3. Why adopt a longtermist goal?

The central reason for adopting a longtermist goal is this: if what matters to us is the good of all the beings we may affect, the question we ask will not be "how can we have the best impact on the present world or the near future?" but rather "how can we have the best impact on history from now on?". A more detailed defense of this idea can be found in Chapter 2.

4.4. Reasons for a longtermist practical focus

As we have seen, the practical focus on the long term holds that, to have the best impact on history from now on, we should focus on the long-term consequences of our decisions.

The main reason for the practical focus on the long term is that, unless there is a mass extinction of sentient life, it is very likely that there will be far more sentient beings in the distant future than in the present or the near future, both diachronically and synchronically:

  • Diachronically because the future may be immensely long. The individuals alive now or in the near future are very few compared with those who will live in the coming centuries, millennia, eons, and so on.
  • Synchronically because the population of sentient beings at each moment may increase. For example, space colonization could multiply them by many orders of magnitude39.

In short, depending on how we decide now, we will positively or negatively affect a gigantic number of beings who will exist over the course of the future.

Let us consider an analogy to better understand the practical focus on the long term. Imagine that someone has to choose between avoiding a certain suffering now or avoiding a certain suffering twenty years from now. Imagine, however, that the suffering that would occur twenty years from now would be much more intense and prolonged. If the person chooses to avoid the suffering of the present moment, they will make their life contain more suffering than if they had chosen the other option.

Analogously, if what we aim for is the best history of the world from now on for all sentient beings, we need to give equal weight to every moment. However, since the long-term future will contain far more sentient beings than the present moment or the short-term future, we have strong reasons to prioritize how our decisions affect the long-term future — this is the basic idea of the practical focus on the long term.

Interestingly, even if less and less weight were given to the good of each sentient being depending on how far into the future it will live, the number of sentient beings who may exist in the long-term future is so vast that we would still have to conclude in favor of prioritizing them, if our goal is the best complete history of the world. Thus, even those who reject temporal impartiality but still give some consideration to future beings would have to prioritize them.

Of course, how long the future will contain sentient beings and what the population of sentient beings will be at each moment is highly uncertain. But future beings vastly outnumber present ones in expectation (that is, multiplying their number by their probability of coming to exist), and this is enough for us to have strong reasons to care about them. This problem of uncertainty will be discussed below in section 4.5.3.

4.5. The debate over the focus on the long term

Below, some of the most common objections to the practical focus on the long term will be discussed40:

4.5.1. Is it better to leave future problems to future generations?

One objection to the practical focus on the long term holds that future generations will be better placed to solve future problems: they will know which s-risks41 (that is, risks of suffering on a gigantic scale) are most serious and which strategies are best for preventing them. For the same reason, the objection concludes, we have an advantage in terms of knowledge if we focus on the present.

One possible response to this objection is to note that it is not guaranteed that future generations will know how to solve such problems. For example, if we leave it to future generations to investigate these problems, it may be too late to prevent the worst scenarios42. In

short, this response holds that the sooner we begin working on these problems, the sooner solutions to them will emerge, and that this will make history better from then on.

Moreover, even if future generations are better placed to solve such problems, this does not mean they will want to do so (since this will depend on how much consideration they give to sentient beings). So we should try to bring about both the capacity and the will to prevent suffering in the future.

It is sometimes claimed that the future will be better anyway thanks to moral progress and that, therefore, we need not worry. However, this is not guaranteed, since it depends crucially on what we do now to spread consideration for all sentient beings and on what continues to be done over time.

4.5.2. Does focusing on the present have more influence?

Someone could accept that the good of future sentient beings counts equally but reject the practical focus on the long term because they believe we live in a crucial era for determining everything that will happen from now on. For example, certain events that will probably occur in the twenty-first century (such as the emergence of superintelligent, autonomous artificial intelligences) could have a disproportionate influence from then on. On this basis, it could be argued that, to have the best impact on the history of the world from now on, we should focus on the present (or, at least, on the near future).

One possible response here is to point out that we do not know how much influence each of these possible events will have on history from then on. For example, we do not know whether these will be the crucial events, whether others still unknown will be, or whether change will be gradual, with no crucial events. If we focus on particular events and they turn out not to have much influence on the future, we will have wasted our efforts43. Thus, it seems better to focus on investigating how our decisions can influence the future positively regardless of what happens. This can be done, for example, by investigating risk factors for s-risks and by planning broad strategies for preventing them.

4.5.3. The objection that our degree of certainty about the present is greater

Another objection to the practical focus on the long term points out that the longer the time frame, the harder it is to predict the probability that an event will occur. For this reason, the objection holds, we should focus on the short term, since in that case our degree of certainty is greater.

However, the degree of certainty should not by itself determine how much we ought to focus on a scenario. Another crucial factor is the magnitude of the scenario (that is, how good or bad it is). Depending on how bad a scenario is, it may still be worth prioritizing its prevention, even if we are more uncertain about whether or not it will occur. One way of taking both magnitude and degree of uncertainty into account is to multiply one factor by the other, and the result is called expected value (or expected disvalue, if the result is negative44).

Let us look at an example. Imagine that we have to choose between preventing a negative event that could occur in the near future and preventing a negative event that could occur in the distant future. Imagine that we are able to estimate how negative each event would probably be, and that the near-future event would be -100 and the distant-future event would be -1000. However, imagine that the probability of the near-future event occurring is 80% and that, owing to uncertainty about the future, the probability of the distant-future event occurring is only 10%.

The expected disvalue of the near-future event would be -100 x 0.8 = -80. The expected disvalue of the distant-future event, on the other hand, would be -1000 x 0.1 = -100. Thus, according to the expected disvalue calculation, we would still have reason to prioritize preventing the distant-future event, even though the probability of its occurring is lower.

In short, what this response points out is that the magnitude of the long-term future is so vast that, even if there is great uncertainty about the future, it would still be worth prioritizing trying to influence it.

At this point it could be objected that the expected disvalue calculation could lead us to prioritize preventing scenarios that would be disastrous if they occurred, but whose probability of occurring is extremely remote.

There are at least two possible responses to this objection. The first is to acknowledge that it points to a problem with the formula for calculating expected disvalue, but to argue that the formula can be adapted to correct this problem. For example, instead of the factors magnitude of the harm and probability of occurrence having the same weight in the multiplication, the probability factor could be given greater weight.

The second response points out that there are strategies that tend to influence the future positively without requiring us to estimate the probability of the future turning out this way or that. Longtermist strategies fall into two broad groups: targeted and broad. Targeted strategies focus on preventing specific catastrophic scenarios. Broad strategies, by contrast, are designed to influence the future positively regardless of which scenarios occur. Thus, the objection in question could make sense only with respect to targeted strategies, but would not affect broad strategies.

One example of a broad strategy is to identify risk factors for s-risks and try to prevent them. We will see more about this below.

4.5.4. The objection that the future is so uncertain that we have no way of deciding

A similar objection holds that the long-term future is so uncertain that we have not the slightest idea how our present decisions will affect it. For example, our influence will be diluted by the decisions of the many future agents45. The longer the future, the more is at stake, but also the smaller our influence. Thus, the objection concludes, the fact that the future is long is not enough to support the conclusion that we should focus on the long term.

However, there are things we can do now that tend to influence the long-term future positively even if we are highly uncertain about the future. For example, we can identify risk factors46 for s-risks and try to

do things that reduce these risk factors. Risk factors are not themselves s-risks, but they greatly increase the probability that s-risks will come about.

The concept of risk factors is already widely used in medicine. For example, smoking, eating poorly, and not exercising are not, in themselves, diseases, but they greatly increase the probability of various diseases, even though they do not necessarily entail them. To know that it is good to avoid these risk factors, we do not need to know what each individual's health trajectory will be. Similarly, we can try to identify risk factors for s-risks and try to identify the actions that would help avoid them.

Some of the risk factors for s-risks are:

  • Disregard for nonhuman sentient beings.
  • Disregard for possible future nonbiological sentient beings47.
  • Demand for products and services whose production harms sentient beings.
  • The prevalence of environmentalist values instead of concern for sentient beings.
  • Human expansion and increasing technological power.
  • Technological progress being much faster than moral progress48.

Each of these risk factors will be addressed in more detail in Chapter 8.

4.5.5. The objection that focusing on the long term would mean neglecting the present

Another common objection to the practical focus on the long term is to point out that it seems to imply neglecting present or near-future suffering, since this is vastly smaller in magnitude than possible long-term suffering.

One possible response here is to point out that, once again, there are actions we can take that tend to influence the whole of history from now on positively (for example, promoting the moral consideration of all sentient beings), and that, therefore, there is not necessarily a dilemma between addressing the long-term future and addressing the present.

At first glance, this may sound contradictory. Someone might ask, for example: "But aren't you defending the practical focus on the long term, then?". The answer is that some of the most promising strategies for the practical focus on the long term (such as advocating the moral consideration of all sentient beings) also help improve the short term.

4.6. Conclusion

We have seen that the practical focus on the long term is one possible answer to the question "how can we have the best impact on the history of the world from now on?". We have also addressed some objections to this focus and the responses that have been given to them.

There seem to be good reasons in favor of the practical focus on the long term. However, another important conclusion here is that even those who reject this focus (and choose to give priority, for example, to the present or the near future) still have strong reasons to accept the longtermist goal, even if they do not accept the longtermist practical focus.

5. Should We Focus on Preventing S-Risks or X-Risks?

5.1. S-risks and x-risks

As we saw in Chapter 1, risks of future suffering, or s-risks, are the risks that events will occur in the future resulting in suffering on a gigantic scale, exceeding all the suffering that has existed on Earth so far49. Examples include the potential of future technology to vastly increase animal exploitation and the harms animals suffer as a result of natural processes50, and to create new kinds of sentient beings, for example, in digital media51.

Existential risks, in turn, also known as x-risks, are the risks of the annihilation of humanity (or, at least, of a collapse of civilization). Examples include global warming, nuclear weapons, pandemics, and so on.

To have the best impact on history from now on, should we focus on trying to prevent s-risks or x-risks? That is what we will discuss in this chapter.

5.2. Discussing a speciesist attempt to defend the focus on x-risks

One way to defend the focus on x-risks is to argue that humans matter much more. However, there are two problems with this argument.

The first is that there seems to be no way to justify giving greater weight to humans. From an unbiased point of view, equal amounts of harm and benefit matter equally, regardless of factors that depend on luck, such as the species to which someone belongs.

The second problem is that, even if much less weight were given to

nonhuman sentient beings, the number of beings potentially affected by s-risks is so astronomically greater that we would still have to conclude in favor of investing more resources in preventing s-risks than x-risks.

5.3. The claim that humanity is essential for preventing suffering

It is sometimes argued that we should prioritize preventing x-risks not because humans matter more, but because doing so would be necessary to prevent s-risks. In the absence of agents with technology at their disposal, there will be no one to reduce the suffering in the world. On this basis, it could be said that, as long as there are x-risks, we should not worry about s-risks. In short, what this argument holds is that the most important thing is to prevent s-risks, but that, to do so, we need to focus on preventing x-risks and forget about s-risks for the time being.

The strength of this argument depends on how positive or negative humanity's impact on history will be from now on. In the best scenario, humanity would continue to exist and try to prevent suffering. But another possibility is that it continues to exist and does not care about reducing the suffering that would already exist naturally or, worse still, produces much more suffering than would already exist naturally. Let us compare three possible scenarios:

(1) Humanity continues and there is less suffering than if it went extinct. (2) Humanity goes extinct. (3) Humanity continues and there is more suffering than if it went extinct.

It seems that 1 is the best of the three scenarios, and that 3 is worse than 2. The idea underlying the focus on preventing s-risks is that it is more important to avoid the worst scenario of all (in this case, scenario 3). Moreover, a strategy that is essential for avoiding the worst scenario (scenario 3) is also essential for trying to achieve the best scenario (scenario 1): spreading, as efficiently as possible, consideration for all sentient beings. This is crucial to ensure that, if humanity continues to exist, it will try to prevent suffering rather than increase it.

5.4. The claim that we will obtain more resources if we prioritize humans

It is sometimes argued that, since people are speciesist, organizations whose goal is to benefit all sentient beings would gain more supporters and resources if they focused on human causes instead of on concern for all sentient beings. In short, what this argument means is that our goal should be to prevent harm to all sentient beings but that, curiously, the most efficient way to achieve this goal is to focus on humans.

A central problem with this argument is that it seems to overlook the fact that one of the main reasons why an astronomical amount of suffering is taking place, and why there is a great risk that it will be vastly multiplied in the future, is precisely the predominance of an anthropocentric view.

This is a very strong reason to prioritize advocating moral consideration for all sentient beings, and as soon as possible, since the non-acceptance of this idea is one of the main obstacles to the goal of preventing massive suffering in the world, both present and future suffering. For example, imagine that consideration for all sentient beings had begun to spread on a large scale two thousand years ago. There would probably be much less suffering than there is today.

If we advocate prioritizing humans, besides failing to spread consideration for all sentient beings, this will probably have the effect of reinforcing speciesism (or, at least, by not questioning it, of delaying changes in speciesist attitudes) and of being an obstacle to preventing the suffering that would occur from now on.

In short, it seems that the sooner (and the more widely) consideration for sentient beings is spread, the better the history of the world from now on is likely to be. One of the advantages of this strategy is that, if carried out carefully so as not to provoke rejection, it tends to influence the future positively, regardless of what might happen.

5.5. Reasons to focus more on s-risks

Some reasons to focus more on preventing s-risks than x-risks are:

(1) Severity. Risks of future suffering have the potential to have an astronomically greater impact than existential risks, both in terms of severity (since they represent the possibility of extreme suffering throughout the entire lives of future sentient beings) and in terms of scope (since they would affect all sentient beings in the universe from now until the end of time).

(2) Expected impact. The probability of s-risks is not lower than that of x-risks.

(3) Tractability. There is also much that could be done to try to minimize s-risks.

(4) Degree of neglect: There are already many more people trying to prevent x-risks than s-risks.

Therefore, all the priority criteria point toward giving great importance to risks of future suffering.

However, it is also important to remember that the focus on s-risks or x-risks may be a matter of degree. That is, one goal does not necessarily exclude the other. Thus, believing that preventing x-risks is more important does not justify thinking that preventing s-risks is not very important. Likewise, if someone prioritizes s-risks, this does not mean they think preventing x-risks is not very important, and so on.
