Volume XI

How Do the Various Ethical Theories Approach the Animal Question?

Exploring the Relationship Between Normative Ethics and Applied Ethics

This book presents an introduction to the main theories of value and normative ethics and to how they apply to our decisions that affect nonhuman animals.

Original text by Luciano Carlos Cunha, translated into English · ISBN 978-65-01-72085-2 · 1st edition, September 2025.

1. An Introduction to the Central Distinctions in Value Theory

1.1. Theories of value and theories of right action

Consider two kinds of question:

  • How should we assess which situations are good/bad, better/worse?
  • How should we assess which action is right?

Questions of the first kind are the object of study of value theory1. Those of the second kind are the object of study of ethics (more specifically, of normative ethics)2.

Theories of value do not study how people assess which situations are good/bad, better/worse, but rather how to assess them correctly. In the same way, theories of normative ethics do not study what people judge the right action to be, but rather how to judge it correctly. They are therefore essentially normative fields, and not psychological descriptions of what people think about these matters.

In ordinary language, when people speak of someone's values, what they usually mean are the principles that person follows when acting. However, as we have seen, although they are related (since the main function of judgments about value is to guide practice), the domains of value and of right action are two distinct domains of thought.

Whenever we make assessments of the kind good/bad, worse/better, we are in the domain of value. When we think about what we ought or ought not to do (and about what it makes no difference whether we do or not), we are in the domain of right action (that is, of ethics). Note that the term action is used broadly here, since it applies to the assessment of both acts and omissions. The debate in ethics therefore actually concerns the right decision. However, since the term action is already widely used in this field, we will keep it here. We must remember, though, that it also includes the assessment of omissions.

Normative ethics is a different field from that of normative theories of rational decision3. Although both fields are about what the right decision is, and both are normative, normative theories of rational decision aim to investigate how to choose the best means of achieving a given end (especially under conditions of uncertainty). In theories of normative ethics, by contrast, what is at issue in the first place is which ends we ought to adopt.

As we will see in Chapter 5, some theories of normative ethics determine the right action entirely on the basis of assessments of which situations are good/bad, better/worse, while others introduce further factors that function as constraints on the pursuit of the best situation.

In this chapter, however, we will speak only of the central distinctions in value theory.

1.2. Theories of value and the terminology used

The domain of evaluative judgments (that is, judgments about good/bad, better/worse) is very broad. Such judgments can be applied to situations, intentions, instruments (“is this a good hammer?”), etc., without necessarily being about right action. For reasons that will become clearer in later chapters, we will focus here on assessing the value of situations.

It is important to note that two kinds of terminology are used in this discussion, but they mean the same thing:

Terminology 1Terminology 2Meaning
X has valueX has positive valueX is good
X has disvalueX has negative valueX is bad
X is neutral in terms of valueX has neutral valueX is neither good nor bad

The fact that there are two terminological systems for saying the same thing can cause confusion. For this reason, we will try here to avoid both terminologies, and will speak only of good/bad/neutral and of better/worse.

1.3. Intrinsic value and instrumental value

A central distinction in value theory is between good/bad intrinsically and good/bad instrumentally4. When we say that something is intrinsically good, we are saying that it is already good without needing to lead to some other good thing. Similarly, if we say that something is intrinsically bad, we are saying that it is itself already bad without needing to lead to some other bad thing. On the other hand, when we say that something is good or bad instrumentally, we are saying that it leads to other good or bad things. Below we will look at some examples of both categories.

Suffering seems to be the most obvious example of something intrinsically bad. That is, suffering is already something negative in itself: it does not need to lead to anything else negative in order to be negative. Happiness, on the other hand, seems to be the kind of thing that is already positive in itself: it does not need to lead to anything else positive in order to be positive.

There are other things, however, whose value or disvalue depends solely on their leading to other good or bad things. For example, crossing the street does not seem to be good or bad in itself. It may be good if it leads us to find, on the other side of the street, something that benefits us; but it may be bad if we are hit by a car while crossing, for example.

In the vast majority of cases, however, a thing will be both intrinsically good or bad and instrumentally good or bad. Let us look at the possible combinations and an example of each:

(1) Something intrinsically good and also instrumentally good. Suppose we watch a movie we really like and this gives us a pleasant experience. This experience, being positive, seems to be already good in itself. Suppose also that the pleasure we feel watching the movie energizes us to the point that we manage to finish a task we had been

putting off. In this case, the pleasure was also instrumentally good, since it also led to something else good (assuming, of course, that the task in question produced something good).

(2) Something intrinsically good and instrumentally bad. Suppose we eat some very tasty food and, as a result, take immense pleasure in savoring it. The pleasure we feel seems to be already good in itself. Suppose, however, that this pleasure is so intense that it makes us overindulge, to the point that we get sick afterward. In this case, the pleasure, despite being intrinsically positive, was instrumentally negative (that is, it was good and led to something else bad).

(3) Something intrinsically bad and also instrumentally bad. Suppose I sprained my ankle and this caused me intense pain. Moreover, because I am in a lot of pain, I am out of the race I wanted to take part in. In this case, the pain I felt was both bad in itself (since pain is always a negative experience) and bad instrumentally (since it also prevented me from taking part in the race).

(4) Something intrinsically bad and instrumentally good. Suppose I touch a fire with my hand and the pain I feel makes me automatically pull my hand away. This pain was bad in itself: given the kind of experience it is, pain is always experienced as something negative. In this case, however, the pain was good instrumentally, since it prevented me from keeping my hand in the fire and burning myself even more5.

The distinction between good/bad intrinsically and good/bad instrumentally thus reminds us that:

(1) Something's being intrinsically good does not imply that it is necessarily instrumentally good. (2) Something's being intrinsically bad does not imply that it is necessarily instrumentally bad. (3) Something's being instrumentally good does not imply that it is necessarily intrinsically good. (4) Something's being instrumentally bad does not imply that it is necessarily intrinsically bad.

1.4. Modes of better/worse assessment: better/worse than and the best/worst of all

In the previous section we spoke of assessments of the good/bad kind. In this section we will speak of assessments of the better/worse kind. These assessments have two modes:

(1) Better/worse than (the comparative mode: better/worse than). (2) Best/worst of all (the superlative mode: the best/worst).

To understand this distinction, consider the following example. Imagine situations A, B, and C. Suppose that, from best to worst, we have: A > B > C. In this case, B is better than C, but it is not the best of the three. Likewise, B is worse than A, but it is not the worst of the three. Now, taking all three situations into account, A is the best and C is the worst.

Important: a situation's being better than another (or even being the best of all those being compared) does not guarantee that it is positive. Similarly, a situation's being worse than another (or even being the worst of all those being compared) does not guarantee that it is negative. Let us look at an example.

Suppose the value of the three situations above could be measured. A positive sign indicates that the situation is good, and a negative sign that it is bad. The numbers indicate how good/bad the situation is. Suppose we had: A=+3 > B=+2 > C=+1. Situation B's being worse than situation A does not imply that B is a negative situation (as we can see, it is positive). Not even situation C's being the worst of the three implies that it is negative.

Now imagine another case, in which A=-1 > B=-2 > C=-3. Situation B's being better than situation C does not imply that it is positive. Moreover, situation A's being the best of the three does not imply that it is positive either.

In short: while the concepts of good/bad tell us whether a situation is positive or negative, the concepts of better/worse (whether better/worse than or best/worst of all) do not give us that information.

1.5. Value: in a certain respect or all things considered?

Assessments of the good/bad and better/worse kind (“than” and “of all”) can refer to a situation as a whole (that is, all things considered) or only in a certain respect. Assessing the value of a situation all things considered is a matter of finding out whether, taking into account all the good and bad aspects of the situation, it is more positive or more negative, and how much more positive or negative it is. In section 1.5.1 we will see how this distinction operates in assessments of the good/bad kind. In section 1.5.2 we will see how it operates in assessments of the better/worse kind (whether “than” or “of all”):

1.5.1. Good/bad in a certain respect or all things considered?

Suppose I have a toothache and go to the dentist, who needs to perform a painful procedure on me to make the pain go away. I decide to undergo the procedure, which is carried out successfully. In this situation there are both bad aspects and good aspects. The bad aspect is that the procedure is painful. The good aspect is that the toothache goes away.

Now, when we assess the value of the situation all things considered, we have to weigh whether the good aspects outweigh the bad ones or vice versa. If I decided to undergo the procedure, it is very likely because I concluded that, although the treatment is painful, the harm it prevents is greater than the harm it causes. That is, this situation, despite having negative and positive aspects, is more positive than negative all things considered. My assessment would be the opposite if I realized that the pain the procedure causes is greater than the pain it would relieve/prevent.

Above we saw an example with the aspects causing pain vs. relieving pain. However, the distinction between good/bad in a certain respect vs. all things considered could apply to any other aspects we were taking into account (we will return to this topic in the following chapters).

1.5.2. Better/worse in a certain respect or all things considered?

Let us now see how the distinction in a certain respect vs. all things considered operates in assessments of the better/worse kind. Let us first take an example with the assessment “better/worse than.” Consider the following two situations:

SituationNumber of victimsSuffering per victimAggregate suffering
S1100-10-10 x 100 = -1000
S250-20-20 x 50 = -1000

Comparing these two situations, S1 is better in a certain respect: in it each victim suffers less. But S2 is better in another respect: in it there are fewer victims. From the standpoint of aggregate suffering (which involves multiplying the number of victims by the suffering of each victim), however, both are equally bad.

Now suppose we have to choose S1 or S2. To make that choice, we need to assess which of the two is better all things considered (it is not enough to assess only which is better in this or that respect). We will return to this question in section 1.6, when we discuss the question of commensurability.

Above we saw an example with the aspects number of victims vs. suffering per victim. However, the distinction between better/worse in a certain respect and better/worse all things considered could apply to any other aspects we were taking into account. We will return to this point in subsequent chapters.

1.5.3. Why is the distinction in a certain respect vs. all things considered important?

The distinction between the value of a situation in a certain respect and all things considered is important in reminding us of the following:

(1) If a situation is positive/negative or better/worse in a certain respect, this does not necessarily imply that it is positive/negative or better/worse all things considered. For example, a situation's being better in a certain respect does not necessarily imply that it is better all things considered (since it may have other, predominant negative aspects).

These possibilities are set out in the following table:

A situation's being... Does not necessarily imply that it is...
Positive in a certain respectPositive all things considered
Negative in a certain respectNegative all things considered
Better in a certain respectBetter all things considered
Worse in a certain respectWorse all things considered

(2) If a situation is positive/negative or better/worse all things considered, this does not necessarily imply that it lacks negative/positive or worse/better aspects in certain respects. For example, a situation's being better all things considered does not necessarily imply that there is no respect in which it is worse.

These possibilities are set out in the following table:

A situation's being... Does not necessarily imply that it lacks...
Positive all things consideredPositive in every respect
Negative all things consideredNegative in every respect
Better all things consideredBetter in every respect
Worse all things consideredWorse in every respect

1.6. How can we assess how good or bad a situation is all things considered?

As we saw in the previous section, a situation can be good/better in one respect and bad/worse in another. How, then, can we assess how good or bad a situation is all things considered6? This question is so much more complex that it will be the topic of the whole of Chapter 7. For now, we will look briefly at some possibilities. In Chapter 7 these possibilities will be explained in more detail and will also be compared in terms of their advantages and disadvantages.

As we will see in subsequent chapters, it will be necessary to make this kind of assessment whether we are examining the situation of each individual (which we will address in Chapter 2) or situations involving several individuals (which we will address in Chapter 3).

That said, some possible approaches to assessing how good/bad a situation is all things considered are:

1.6.1. Total incommensurability

This involves recognizing that there are several aspects that are good/bad in themselves, but holding that it makes no sense to compare them (or even to multiply or add them). According to this approach, the only circumstances in which it is possible to say, among several options, which is better all things considered are those in which there is one option that is better in every respect. In circumstances in which each option is better in some respect, this approach will say that it is not possible to say which of them is better all things considered.

1.6.2. Monism (general)

According to monist approaches, there is only one aspect that is good/bad in itself. All the others are seen as good/bad only instrumentally, depending on whether they increase or decrease what is seen as good/bad in itself. Thus, in monist approaches, how good/bad a situation is all things considered is determined solely by how good/bad it is in terms of a single aspect (namely, the one seen as having value/disvalue in itself). Although they share this common structure, the various monist approaches differ from one another according to which aspect is seen as good/bad in itself.

1.6.3. Aggregative monism (a specific application of general monism)

A common form of monism consists in determining how good/bad a situation is all things considered by aggregating what is seen as good/bad in itself. For example, suppose that what is bad in itself is suffering. Imagine that in situation S1 we have 20 victims, each with suffering of -5. In situation S2, by contrast, we have 10 victims, each with suffering of -10. According to this approach, the total disvalue of S1 is -100 (since it is - 5x20). The total disvalue of S2 is also -100 (since it is -10x10). That is, in this approach, neither the number of victims nor the severity of each victim's situation is seen as bad in itself (but rather only as bad instrumentally, insofar as they contribute to the total aggregate being negative). Thus, according to this approach, S1 and S2 are equally bad (the fact that S1 has more victims, and that in S2 each victim is suffering more, is not seen as relevant in itself).

1.6.4. Equal-weight pluralism

In this approach two or more aspects are recognized as good/bad in themselves, and how good/bad the situation is all things considered is determined either by multiplying these aspects (the multiplicative approach) or by adding them (the additive approach). What is characteristic of this approach is that each aspect is seen as equally important (hence they are multiplied or added, but both have the same weight). Note that, in a multiplicative variant of this approach, the result will be identical to the result obtained by an aggregative monist approach, which we saw in the previous section. Only the justification will be different: aggregative monism sees only one thing as good/bad in itself, while multiplicative equal-weight pluralism sees more than one thing as good/bad in itself. An additive variant, on the other hand, can generate results different from those generated by aggregative monism.

1.6.5. Pluralism with an absolute trump

In this approach two or more aspects are recognized as good/bad in themselves, but a hierarchy is constructed in which one factor is an absolute trump over those that come after it in the hierarchy. According to this approach, no increase in the secondary aspects, however large, can tip the balance to make the situation better all things considered if it represents a decrease in the main aspect, however small. That is, in this approach how good/bad a situation is all things considered is determined almost exclusively by the trump aspect (the secondary aspects serve only as a tiebreaker).

1.6.6. Pluralism with a trump up to a certain point

In this approach two or more aspects are recognized as good/bad in themselves; a hierarchy is constructed in which one factor is a trump over those that come after it in the hierarchy, but this trump is not absolute. Beyond a certain point (called the cutoff point or threshold), the hierarchy is reversed. Hence the name “pluralism with a trump up to a certain point.” For example, imagine that an approach of this kind holds that both the severity of each victim's situation and the number of victims are bad in themselves, and also holds that, when two situations are compared, the one in which the victims are in the worst condition is the worse situation all things considered, unless the other situation has at least ten times as many victims. In this case, the approach sees the severity of each victim's condition as a nonabsolute trump (since, depending on the number of victims, the priority is reversed).

1.6.7. Pluralism with fixed-weight aspects (without trumps)

In this approach two or more aspects are seen as good/bad in themselves, and they have different weights in calculating how good/bad the situation is all things considered – but without using the idea of trumps. The reasoning here is similar to what we saw in section 1.6.4 (equal-weight pluralism), except that here the weight of each factor is different. For example, suppose that factor A has twice the weight of factor B. In this case, the total value/disvalue of the situation will be determined by (2x.A) + (1x.B), if an additive method is used, or by (2x.A) x (1x.B), if a multiplicative method is used. The difference from the use of trumps is that here the influence of the factors is continuous and linear (with the use of trumps, it is discontinuous and nonlinear).

1.6.8. Pluralism with variable-weight aspects (without trumps)

In this approach two or more aspects are seen as good/bad in themselves, but there is no fixed weight between them: their weight is variable, decreasing proportionally as they are “filled” (which is why this approach is also called pluralism with diminishing returns). This approach is different from pluralism with a trump up to a certain point. Although they are similar in that, in both approaches, one factor can come to be more important than the other beyond a certain level (both are nonlinear), here the relationship is continuous, with each factor's importance gradually decreasing with each new unit filled (with a trump up to a certain point, the relationship is discontinuous, since the trump is reversed abruptly if a cutoff line is crossed).

1.6.9. Maximin/leximin priorities

In this method the idea is always to prioritize the worst individual case, then the second-worst case, then the third, and so on. This method resembles the idea of trumps, but whereas trumps are used to rank different aspects, in this method the aim is to rank the priority of individuals within one and the same aspect.

However, this method is also used to compare situations involving several individuals. For example, let us compare the following situations, where the letters represent individuals and the negative numbers their level of suffering (the larger the number, the more suffering).

Situation Individuals S1 A = -50 B = -30 S2 C = -49 D = -40 S3 E = -49 F = -39

According to this method, situation S1 would receive priority, since it is the one with the individual in the worst condition of all (A = -50). This is where maximin comes in, which prescribes maximizing the minimum level (and is, so to speak, the trump criterion). Now, imagine that we had to compare S2 and S3 to say which of them is more urgent. In this case, maximin does not help, since the victims in the worst condition in each of these situations are in an equally bad condition (C = -49, E = -49). In this case, leximin comes in as a tiebreaker, prescribing that we prioritize the second-worst case. Here, situation S2 would be considered the priority, since the second-worst case of all is D = -40.

1.6.10. Sufficiency

In this method an aspect matters in itself until it reaches a certain level of fulfillment established as sufficient. After that it ceases to count. If in an approach of this kind there are two or more aspects seen as good/bad in themselves, it may adopt any of the previous methods to commensurate them. However, what is distinctive about this kind of approach is that there comes a point at which the aspect is already sufficiently filled, and it then ceases to matter in itself.

1.6.11. Hybrid approaches

These combine one or more of the previous approaches. For example, they may use trumps (absolute or up to a certain point) up to a cutoff line and from there on use a continuous relationship (with fixed weight or variable weight).

1.6.12. Partial indeterminacy

This method holds that, in some cases, it is possible to assess which situations are better/worse all things considered, but that in other cases there is no correct answer (and so, in those cases, it would be as in the approach that defends incommensurability).

1.6.13. Probabilistic aggregation based on uncertainty

In this method several different approaches (or even all of those we have seen) are weighed on the basis of uncertainty about which of them is correct. In this method, one assesses how good/bad the situation would be all things considered according to each method taken into account, and multiplies each result by the degree to which one believes each method is correct. Then everything is added up, and one obtains the probabilistic aggregation based on uncertainty. In short, in this method a probabilistic mixture of several approaches is made, weighting how much one believes each of them is correct and aggregating these results.

1.7. Conclusion

In this chapter we have seen the main distinctions and inquiries in the field of value theory. From the next chapter on, we will apply this analysis to more specific questions. In the next chapter we will see how all of this appears in theories of well-being.

2. An Introduction to Theories of Well-Being

2.1. What do theories of well-being aim to investigate?

Theories of well-being investigate what is good/bad, better/worse for individuals7. That is, they concern assessing whether an individual is faring well or badly, better or worse, and to what extent.

Note that the term well-being, as it is used in this debate, is much broader than the way the term is used in ordinary language. In this debate, the term concerns any and every circumstance in which an individual could be harmed or benefited. In ordinary language, the term well-being is used in a more specific sense, which concerns how good or bad someone feels. In the philosophical context the term includes this sense, but is not limited to it. For example, the harm of death is also discussed by theories of well-being, but it is usually understood as a harm that depends on how much it deprives the individual of positive things, and not on how good or bad they are feeling8. The harm of death is part of the discussion of well-being because it concerns what would harm or benefit an individual. Likewise, it may sound strange to frame the following question within the discussion of well-being: “is someone harmed if their preferences are not satisfied after they die?” (since the individual will already be dead). But it is important to remember: theories of well-being concern everything that could harm/benefit someone. It is in this broad sense that we will use the term in this work.

What theories of well-being aim to discover, first of all, is: which things are good/bad in themselves for individuals, and not merely good/bad instrumentally (that is, as a means)? This is so for obvious reasons: to know whether something is good or bad as a means, we first need to know whether the other things it produces/prevents are good or bad in themselves. That is, inquiry into which things are good/bad instrumentally only makes sense if we first know which things are good/bad in themselves.

There are three main aspects under discussion in the debate about which things are good/bad in themselves with regard to the well-being of individuals: experiences, preferences, and objective goods. Below

we will look at each of these aspects separately and then at the debate between the theories based on them. The debate revolves around which of these aspects matter in themselves for assessing well-being and, if more than one does, whether they can be commensurated, and how.

Whichever of these aspects a theory claims to be important in themselves for well-being, there are two general ways in which an individual can be benefited and two general ways in which an individual can be harmed, as set out in the following table.

An individual is benefited by the... An individual is harmed by the...
Presence of whatever is positivePresence of whatever is negative
Absence of whatever is negativeAbsence of whatever is positive

Of course, the different theories disagree about which aspects are positive/negative for individuals. We will look at this debate from the next section on.

2.2. Aspects in assessing the well-being of individuals

2.2.1. Experiences

The most obvious aspect through which an individual can be affected for better or worse is through their experiences (that is, their mental states). In this sense, it is widely recognized that positive experiences (also referred to by the terms happiness, pleasure, enjoyment, etc.) are something good in themselves and/or that negative experiences (also referred to by the terms pain and suffering) are something bad in themselves.

With regard to this aspect, then, there are two basic ways in which someone can be harmed: when they have a negative experience (that is, when they suffer) and when they are prevented from having a positive experience (as when they die, for example). Similarly, there would be two basic ways in which someone can be benefited: when they have a positive experience (that is, when they feel pleasure) or when they are prevented from having a negative experience (when a pain is relieved or prevented, for example).

It is important to note that claiming that negative experiences are bad in themselves and that positive experiences are good in themselves is not to deny that negative experiences are sometimes good instrumentally (when they avoid something negative or lead to something positive) and that positive experiences are sometimes negative instrumentally (when they lead to something negative or prevent something positive). We have already seen examples of this in section 1.3 of the previous chapter.

Some views also hold that neutral experiences (that is, experiences that are felt neither as positive nor as negative) are also good in themselves. For example, some views hold that, if having neutral experiences is better than having no experience at all, then this is because neutral experiences are good in themselves (for example, it could be argued that being conscious is something good in itself)9. Another example is the views holding that the state of tranquility that accompanies neutral experiences is something good in itself10.

2.2.2. Preferences (desires)

Some views hold that another way in which individuals can be affected for better or worse is through the satisfaction or frustration of their preferences (understood as mental states in the form of desires). These views hold that the satisfaction of preferences is something good in itself (that is, regardless of whether satisfying them leads to positive experiences or avoids negative experiences) and/or that the frustration of preferences is something bad in itself (that is, that frustrating them is something bad, regardless of whether or not this results in negative experiences, and of whether or not it results in deprivation of positive experiences).

Views of this kind differ from one another according to the kinds of desires whose satisfaction they consider good in itself and/or whose frustration they consider bad in itself. Some hold that these are the actual desires individuals have. Others hold that they are ideal desires (that is, the desires individuals would have if they were rational and had access to the information relevant to their well-being).

2.2.3. Objective goods

Some views hold that certain things are objective goods, in the sense of being something good in itself, regardless of whether or not they generate positive experiences or accord with the preferences of whoever would have them. These views consider the presence of these things as something good in itself, and their absence as something bad in itself.

For example, some authors hold that true friendship, although it is preferred by most people and although it usually provides positive experiences, is good in itself (that is, it would be good even if no one preferred it and even if it did not provide positive experiences)11.

Other items frequently listed as objective goods are knowledge and the development of one's talents. Each view of this kind draws up lists with different items.

2.3. Monist and pluralist theories of well-being

Depending on whether they assume that one or more of the three aspects above are relevant in themselves for determining well-being, theories can be classified as monist or pluralist.

The three best-known categories of theories of well-being are: experientialist12 theories, preference-satisfaction13 theories (also known as desire-based theories), and objective list theories14. We will look at each of these categories below.

2.3.1. Experientialist theories

The label experientialist is given to any theory of well-being that claims that experiences are the only aspect through which an individual is harmed or benefited. They are therefore monist theories.

A very well-known experientialist theory is hedonism, which claims that what is good in itself is positive experiences, and what is bad in itself is negative experiences. For hedonism, the value of everything else is only instrumental to these things.

It is important to note that, in ordinary language, the word hedonist means something quite different from what this theory proposes. In ordinary language, a hedonist is someone who pursues momentary pleasures without worrying about their long-term well-being. The hedonist theory, by contrast, would say that such an individual is not acting rationally to maximize their well-being, since such behavior will probably cause their life to contain more negative experiences and/or fewer positive experiences.

Hedonism is not the only example of an experientialist theory. Another example is theories that hold that neutral experiences are something good in themselves, as is the case with tranquilism15. Some of these theories claim that neutral experiences are the only thing good in itself. Others claim that both positive and neutral experiences are good in themselves. In any case, they are all monist theories because they hold that only the aspect of experiences is relevant in itself for well-being.

2.3.2. Preference-satisfaction theories

For preference-satisfaction theories (also known as desire-based theories), what is good in itself is the satisfaction of desires, and what is bad in itself is the frustration of desires. The value of everything else is only instrumental to these things. As we saw earlier, these theories differ from one another according to the kinds of desires whose satisfaction they consider good in itself: the desires individuals actually have, or the desires they would have if they were rational and had access to the information relevant to their well-being. However, all of them hold that the only aspect relevant in itself for well-being is desires. They are therefore also monist theories.

2.3.3. Comparing experientialism and preferentialism

Let us compare these two categories of theories. Experientialist theories will maintain that satisfying desires is usually something good, but because doing so usually leads to positive experiences or avoids negative experiences. Similarly, preference-satisfaction theories will maintain that it is usually something good to promote positive experiences and

avoid negative experiences, but only because doing so coincides with what individuals desire.

However, these things do not always coincide. For example, someone may have a desire for something that will cause them suffering, or may not have a desire for something that would make them happy. In section 2.4 we will see examples of situations of this kind.

2.3.4. Negative versions of experientialist and preference-satisfaction theories

Experientialist and preference-satisfaction theories also have negative versions. According to the negative version of experientialism, negative experiences are bad in themselves, but positive experiences are not good in themselves. According to this version, what is good for individuals is only the absence of suffering. This view is slightly different from experientialist views that hold that neutral states have value in themselves. Negative versions of experientialism hold only that the absence of suffering is something good in itself (and not that neutral states are good in themselves). Thus, between having no experience at all and having neutral states, experientialist views that value neutral states in themselves would say that it is better to have neutral states, whereas negative versions of experientialism would say that it makes no difference, since in both cases there is an absence of suffering.

Similarly, according to the negative version of preferentialism, having frustrated desires is bad in itself, but having satisfied desires is not good in itself. According to this version, the satisfaction of desires is good only because it does not involve their frustration, but the best thing for the individual would be to have no desires, so as not to run the risk of not fulfilling them. It is important to note that, being a form of preferentialism, this version holds that having frustrated desires is something bad in itself, and not because it may cause suffering.

Everything we have seen so far consists of examples of monist theories of well-being, since they hold that there is only one aspect with value/disvalue in itself.

2.3.5. Objective list theories

Objective list theories hold that there are objective goods (which we saw in section 2.2.3), and they can be monist or pluralist. They will be monist when they draw up lists with a single item. Usually, however, they are pluralist, and claim that there are several items that have value in themselves independently (these items make up the various lists of the various objective list theories).

2.3.6. Other possible pluralist theories

It is important to remember that other kinds of pluralist views are also possible, combining some or even all of the aspects we saw earlier. One example would be to claim that both experiences (positive and/or neutral) and satisfied preferences are something good in themselves. Another example would be to claim that experiences (positive and/or neutral) and also certain objective list items are good in themselves. Or that satisfied preferences and also certain objective list items are good in themselves. Or else that experiences (positive and/or neutral), satisfied preferences, and objective list items are all good in themselves. There are many possibilities, set out in the following table:

PossibilitiesExperiencesPreferencesObjective goods
MonistX
X
X
Pluralist with two aspectsXX
XX
XX
Pluralist with three aspectsXXX

In the debate on theories of well-being, most of the theories discussed are monist, and many of the criticisms that one monist school makes of another concern precisely the fact that one group of theories fails to take into account what the other group considers important. One way to avoid this problem is to adopt a pluralist theory. Of course, pluralist theories also face problems that do not arise for monist theories. One example is the greater difficulty of finding an adequate method for commensurating the different aspects. That is, a defender of monism could claim that its great advantage is its greater simplicity of application. A defender of pluralism, however, could claim that it is better to have greater difficulty of application than to fail to take into account all the factors that may be relevant in themselves.

2.4. Examples illustrating the differences between the approaches

Below we will look at examples that illustrate how the various theories of well-being would apply to particular situations. These examples are useful not only for seeing where these theories converge and where they diverge. They also help us reflect on: (1) whether an aspect is good/bad in itself, or good/bad only as a means, and (2) if it is good/bad in itself, what its weight should be relative to other aspects.

2.4.1. The case of the harmful preference

Suppose a child has a desire whose fulfillment will be harmful to her (it will result in her later suffering or even her death). Imagine, for example, that she wants to put a plastic bag over her head, covering her whole face, because she does not know that it will suffocate her.

Experientialist theories would say that, if this child's preference is fulfilled, she is not benefited in any respect, since such fulfillment will result in negative experiences and possibly in the deprivation of positive experiences (for example, if she dies).

As for preference-satisfaction theories, at first glance one might think they would have to say that the child in question is benefited if her preference is fulfilled, even if she suffers afterward (and even if she dies). However, a preferentialist could claim that, if the child has this preference satisfied, she will be benefited in a certain respect (she had one preference satisfied) but that, all things considered, she will be harmed much more than benefited, precisely because fulfilling her preference in this case either results in the frustration of other, more important preferences she has (such as not suffering) or even prevents the fulfillment of any other preference she might have (if she dies).

There is a preference-satisfaction theory that would maintain that this child would not be benefited in any respect if this preference were fulfilled. This variant claims that the preferences that matter for well-being are not those we actually have, but those we would have if the information relevant to our well-being were available to us. However, even with the information available, we may still have preferences that are irrational (because we have drawn mistaken inferences, for example). Therefore, this position holds that the preferences that matter for well-being are not those we actually have, but those we would have if we were rational and had available the information relevant to our well-being16.

Another possible approach is to maintain a pluralist perspective, according to which both positive experiences are considered good in themselves (and negative experiences bad in themselves) and the satisfaction of preferences is considered good in itself (and the frustration of preferences bad in itself). In this case, this pluralist view could even claim that the child in question was benefited in one respect (she had a preference satisfied) but that, all things considered, she was harmed much more (since she then had negative experiences or was prevented from having positive experiences, and also had other preferences she held frustrated, or the preferences she would have had if she were rational and had the relevant information available). This pluralist position, if it also included items from an objective list, could say that such a child would be harmed in this further respect as well, if fulfilling this desire prevented her from enjoying any of those items.

2.4.2. The case of the dying person's preference

Suppose someone is on the verge of death and has a last wish. Common wishes of this kind are, for example, wanting one's body to be cremated rather than buried, or vice versa. Imagine the following example: someone wishes that, after their death, their body be buried next to their parents' bodies.

According to views that say that only experiences are directly relevant to well-being, such an individual will not be benefited if this wish is satisfied, nor harmed if it is not. Since it is a wish that can only be fulfilled after they die, its fulfillment will not increase this individual's positive experiences, nor reduce their

negative experiences, nor will its frustration cause them any negative experience or prevent any positive experience (assuming here that there is no life after death17).

Views that hold that the satisfaction of preferences is something good in itself, by contrast, will say that the individual in question will be benefited in a certain respect if the wish in question is satisfied, and harmed if it is not, even though the individual no longer exists. For example, they could say that some preferences are future-oriented, and that the holder of these preferences is benefited if they are satisfied, even if he or she has already died when this happens. This applies both to views that hold that preferences are all that matters (as in preferentialism, which is a monist approach) and to those that hold that preferences also matter (as in pluralist views).

2.4.3. The case of the painful truth that someone does not want to know

Suppose a person finds out that someone they cared about very much has died. Imagine that this person suffers intensely on finding out the truth, and also wished they had not found it out.

Experience-centered theories and preference-centered theories (and also theories that combine both) would say that this person was not benefited in any respect by finding out the truth, since they only suffered on finding it out, and also wished they had not found it out.

Now, imagine that an objective list theory maintains that knowing the truth is good in itself. This theory would say that, in this case, the person was benefited in a certain respect: they found out the truth.

At first glance, we might think that such an objective list theory would necessarily have to claim that, all things considered, this person was benefited more than harmed by finding out the truth. However, this will be so only if the theory in question claims that the only thing that has value in itself is truth (or that knowing the truth is always more important than avoiding negative experiences or avoiding frustrating preferences).

However, imagine that the theory in question recognized that, in addition to finding out the truth, having positive experiences and having preferences satisfied are also good things in themselves. In this case, the theory would say that, although this person was harmed in two respects (they had a negative experience and had a frustrated preference), they were benefited in at least one respect: they found out the truth (which, in this theory, is seen as something good in itself).

Of course, in this case, whether finding out the truth was better or worse all things considered will depend on how the weight of the value of preferences, experiences, and objective list items is compared (and on whether this is possible). We have already briefly discussed how to commensurate different aspects in section 1.6, and we will return to this topic in Chapter 7.

2.4.4. The case of the unconscious violation

Imagine that someone is violated while completely unconscious. Because they are completely unconscious, this person had no negative experience while being violated. Imagine also that the fact of being violated will not prevent them from enjoying any positive experience, nor will it bring them negative experiences later. When they wake up, they will not even know they were violated. Of course, in real life, it is possible that, even while unconscious, going through something like this leaves trauma at a subconscious level. But, for the sake of argument, imagine that no trauma of this kind occurs in our example.

According to views that value in themselves only having positive experiences and avoiding negative experiences, such an individual was not harmed in any respect. In defense of such a view, its proponents could offer the following counterexample: imagine that aliens with super-advanced technology have been doing exactly this to us for many years every time we go to sleep. If none of this has harmed us so far, the proponents of this counterexample would say, it is because there is no way to harm someone without giving them negative experiences or preventing them from having positive experiences18.

Now, according to preference-centered views, the answer may vary. Those centered on the preferences the individual actually has would say that, if someone prefers that this not happen to them, then they will be harmed if it happens, even if it does not affect their experiences. However, they will also have to say that someone who has not yet formed a preference not to be violated while unconscious (for example, a small child) would not be harmed if this happened. On the other hand, those centered on the preferences someone would have if they had the relevant information and were rational could say that such an individual was harmed regardless of whether or not they had already formed a preference about this, since they would probably form a preference not to be violated if they knew what was going to happen to them.

Finally, as for views centered on objective items, the answer will depend on which items they value in themselves. If they value, for example, the autonomous decisions someone would make about what will happen to their own body, they would probably say that such an individual was harmed by not being able to choose in this case. However, they would have to say that individuals incapable of making autonomous decisions would not be harmed if this happened.

2.4.5. The case of the happiness machine

One of the thought experiments most often used against the idea that only experiences matter in themselves for well-being is known as the case of the happiness machine19. Below we will reconstruct the example and then discuss it.

The example consists in thinking that, if all that matters is having positive experiences and/or avoiding negative experiences, then we would be benefited if we could live in a world that gave us only wonderful experiences but was entirely virtual, as in the movie The Matrix. For example, you eat your favorite dessert and it tastes delicious, more delicious than in the real world, but the dessert in question is virtual.

The aim of this example is to suggest that, if we would not want to live in such a machine (that is, if we would prefer to live in a nonvirtual world, even with fewer positive experiences), then it is because we think it matters not only that the experiences be

positive, but that the stimulus giving rise to them be real. Below is a summary of the debate about this thought experiment.

A first way of responding to this thought experiment is simply to hold that we would be benefited if we had to live in such a machine. A counterexample that could be given in this sense is the following: imagine we find out that, from the time we were born until now, we have already been in such a machine. Everything we have experienced so far has been virtual. Imagine also that we find a way to leave this virtual reality and go to actual reality, but that actual reality will be much worse for us than our current virtual life: we will have only excruciating suffering. This suggests that, from our point of view, virtual reality is better.

One possible response to this counterexample is to hold that it shows only that it is more important to avoid negative experiences and seek positive experiences, but that it does not show that this is all that matters. In this sense, it could be argued that, if we could compare two realities, one virtual and the other actual, both equal in terms of positive and negative experiences, and it were better for us to choose actual reality, then it seems that experiences are not all that matters.

Again, one response to this second example is to say that, in this case, it makes no difference. Another counterexample that could be given in this sense is to think of the following: imagine your favorite dessert. Suppose you found out that the last time you ate it, it was virtual. The question is: from the point of view of your experience, does this make any difference? Was the experience any less good because of it? Was the dessert any less tasty because of it? It seems not.

One possible response to this counterexample consists in first acknowledging that the value of some things (many things, perhaps) seems to lie solely in the kind of experience they provide, but then arguing that this does not apply to all things. It may make no difference to know whether the dessert we eat is virtual or not, as long as it provides the same pleasure. However, suppose we found out that all the individuals we love are in fact not sentient: they are merely virtual simulations of the real individuals. Imagine that we also found out that the real individuals are in another reality, and that we can move there if we want. However, if we move, the price to pay for being with the real beings we love is having fewer positive experiences than we would have in the virtual world.

If we decide that it is better to have fewer positive experiences in order to be able to interact with the real individuals we love, rather than with simulations, then we not only value such interactions in themselves, but also value them to a greater degree than having the maximum of positive experiences. Of course, this does not mean that we will always value such interactions to a greater degree than experiences. For example, if the choice were between remaining in the virtual world and keeping positive experiences, or meeting the real beings we love but at the cost of having to suffer excruciating torments for a long period of time, we would then have doubts about what is better for us20.

This was a brief summary of the debate about the example of the experience machine. This and the other examples we have seen above should not give the impression that the various approaches to well-being will always disagree. Below we will look at several points of convergence.

2.5. To what extent do these approaches diverge/converge?

What has been shown above may give the impression that the different approaches to well-being diverge fundamentally in every respect. However, this impression is mistaken: the degree of convergence is much greater than is usually imagined.

We have seen that most of the disagreements arise between views that see only one of the three aspects (experiences, preferences, and objective items) as relevant in itself for well-being. However, as we have seen, it is not necessary to adopt a view of this kind. It is also possible to consider several of these factors relevant in themselves. For example, even those who value

the satisfaction of desires or objective goods in themselves also usually recognize that suffering is bad in itself and that happiness is good in itself.

This is no accident. The fact that suffering is, in itself, a negative experience shows that suffering is bad in itself. Similarly, the fact that happiness is, in itself, a positive experience shows that it is good in itself21. This is something very strong in terms of proof22. For example, it is stronger than any proof we could give concerning descriptions of facts about the external world. We cannot prove that we are not mistaken in our belief that the external world actually exists (since, if it is a virtual simulation, we will have exactly the same experiences). By contrast, we cannot be mistaken when we say that suffering is already something negative in itself and that happiness is already something positive in itself, since in this case it is the very fact of experiencing them in this way that makes such experiences, respectively, negative or positive.

One criticism of this reasoning is to point out that it implies that the happiness a torturer feels when torturing his victims is something good in itself. Here, however, it is important to remember that we are talking about theories of well-being, and not theories of right action. All that theories of well-being would say is that the torturer in question was benefited by feeling such happiness (and that, obviously, his victims were harmed by being tortured). Such theories would not say that it is right for the torturer to do this, since they are not theories of right action: something's being good in itself for someone's well-being is not the same as its being an action that is right in itself.

Thus, although it is an open debate whether there are other things besides negative experiences that are relevant in themselves for well-being, such experiences are certainly relevant to well-being. Derek Parfit, a proponent of an objective list theory, puts the matter as follows:

On all theories, happiness and pleasure are at least part of what makes our lives go better for us, and misery and pain are at least part of what makes our lives go worse. These claims would be made by any plausible Objective List Theory. And they are

implied by all versions of the Desire-Fulfilment Theory. On all theories, the Hedonistic Theory is at least part of the truth23.

Thus, at least on this point the various approaches to well-being can converge. Moreover, in most cases what prevents suffering and provides positive experiences accords with what someone prefers, and also helps to attain the things usually regarded as objective goods. Of course, as we have seen, these factors sometimes conflict. However, it seems that in most cases they converge.

Discussions of theories of well-being (or of any other philosophical topic) tend to focus on the disagreements between the various approaches. Noticing these disagreements is important for evaluating them. However, focusing on disagreements can also obscure the degree of convergence. We may think there is no degree of convergence at all even when there may be quite a large degree of convergence, as seems to be the case among the various approaches to well-being.

2.6. The minimum degree of convergence and its implications for the well-being of animals

If every plausible theory of well-being must recognize the disvalue of suffering and the value of positive experiences, then all of them must recognize that nonhuman animals are greatly harmed in the circumstances in which they normally find themselves.

Whether they are born into animal exploitation or born in the wild, the norm is for their lives to be full of suffering and for them to die prematurely. Suffering is, in itself, a negative experience. Premature death prevents the individual from enjoying positive experiences (and the more premature it is, the less the individual has enjoyed so far and the more they would have had ahead of them to enjoy). Each of these animals usually has a life in which suffering (generally extreme) vastly outweighs positive experiences.

Therefore, whichever theory of well-being we judge to be the most adequate, we must recognize that animals are greatly harmed by finding themselves in such situations.

  12. Of course, as we have seen, some variants of these theories could also include the harm of being prevented from having neutral experiences. But let us then imagine that in our example no neutral experiences were prevented either. ↩
  13. This example is presented by Nozick (1974, p. 42-45). ↩
  14. Note that this is a debate about what is better for individuals, and not necessarily about what the right action is. For example, someone could maintain that it is better for the individuals to remain in virtual reality (if the price to pay for being in actual reality near the real beings they love were having excruciating torments), but that, even so, the right action is to go to actual reality to be near those real beings. This could be grounded in different ways. For example, it could be argued that the torment that loved ones in actual reality would suffer from the absence of the individuals now in virtual reality would be greater than the torment the latter would suffer by going to actual reality (this would be an example of how consequentialist ethical theories would reason). Another way of trying to ground it would be to say that, regardless of who would suffer the greater torment, there would be a duty to go to actual reality because of a rule of fidelity or gratitude toward one's real loved ones (this would be an example of how deontological ethical theories would reason). Theories of right action will be addressed from chapter 5 on. ↩
