3. Assessing How Good/Bad a Situation Containing Several Individuals Is

3.1. Introduction

We saw in Chapter 2 that each theory of well-being differs from the others according to which aspects it claims are good/bad in themselves for individuals, and how these aspects are to be weighed against one another. In what follows, we will not assume any specific theory of well-being. For simplicity, we will speak only of the well-being of individuals.

Most situations involve not just a single individual but several. Thus, we need not only a theory of what constitutes the well-being of individuals (that is, a theory of individual well-being), but also a theory for assessing how good/bad a situation involving several individuals is (which, for short, we will call here collective well-being).

We will see in this chapter that the same kind of disagreement that arises among theories of well-being (“which aspects are good/bad in themselves?” and “what weight should each of these aspects have?”) appears in the assessment of collective well-being.

3.2. Aspects in assessing a situation with several individuals

There are several possible aspects on the basis of which we could assess how good/bad a situation involving several individuals is. Below is a table with a brief explanation of the main aspects. They do not exhaust the possible aspects that could be used to make this assessment. They are, however, the aspects that predominate most in debates on the subject24:

Important: what follows are aspects, not theories. Theories incorporate one or more of these aspects to make the overall assessment. Thus, in the following table, it is important to note that the situation need not be assessed all things considered on the basis of a single aspect. It is possible to combine two or more of the aspects (or even all of them).

Aspect Explanation
Aggregate sum of well-being A situation is better the greater the aggregate sum of well-being. For example, imagine that in a situation we have individuals A, B, C, and D with the following levels of well-being: A=+16, B=+4, C=-8, D=-10. The positive total is +20 and the negative total is -18. The aggregate sum of well-being in this situation is +2.
Total aggregate suffering A situation is better the smaller the aggregate sum of suffering (regardless of what is positive in it).
Average A situation is better the greater the total aggregate sum of well-being divided by the number of individuals.
Minimum level A situation is better the higher the minimum level of well-being (that is, the better the situation of those who are worst off).
Maximum level A situation is better the higher the maximum level of well-being (that is, the better the situation of those who are best off).
Distributive equality A situation is better the more evenly the aggregate sum of well-being is distributed among individuals.
Number of individuals with positive well-beingA situation is better the greater the number of individuals with positive well-being.
Number of individuals with sufficient well-beingA situation is better the greater the number of individuals with sufficiently satisfactory levels of well-being.
Aggregate sum combined with each individual's level of well-beingA situation is better the greater the aggregate sum of well-being, but an additional unit of well-being has more value the worse off the individual whose well-being would be increased (this is known as the prioritarian conception of value).
DesertA situation is better the more the individuals in it receive benefits and harms according to what they deserve.
Kinds of actions A situation is better the greater the amount of certain kinds of actions present in it*.
Kinds of relationships A situation is better the greater the amount of certain kinds of relationships present in it**.

*The actions considered valuable vary according to each perspective, but common examples are respecting rights, telling the truth, and keeping promises.

**The relationships considered valuable vary according to each perspective, but common examples are relationships of friendship and mutual solidarity.

3.3. Monist and pluralist theories

In the previous section we saw several aspects that are frequently used to assess how good or bad a situation involving several individuals is. The various theories may see one or more of these aspects as valuable in themselves. If they see only one aspect as valuable in itself, and all the others are seen as having only instrumental value, they are monist. If they see more than one aspect as valuable in itself, they are pluralist.

Let us look at an example of this difference with the value of distributive equality (understood here as the distribution of total well-being among the individuals present in the situation). One view could maintain that distributive equality has value in itself. Other views could maintain that its value is merely instrumental. Even among the latter views, there may be disagreement about what its value is instrumental to. For example, one view could maintain that a more equitable distribution of value (that is, giving more to those who have less) has instrumental value for improving the situation of those who are worse off (and that this, indeed, is what has value in itself). Another view could maintain that reducing inequality is important only because it has instrumental value for maximizing the aggregate sum of well-being. This is so because the same amount of a given resource generally produces greater increases in well-being if it is given to someone who is worse off, and is therefore more efficient for maximizing the aggregate sum of well-being25.

This does not happen only with distributive equality. Any of the aspects can be seen as having value in itself or only instrumental value. For example, some people hold that treating individuals as they deserve is good only instrumentally: because it motivates individuals to refrain from causing harm to

others. Other people hold that treating individuals as they deserve, besides having instrumental value, is also something good in itself. This debate (whether something has value in itself or merely instrumental value) can arise with any other aspect.

3.4. When the aspects conflict

Sometimes the different aspects conflict. Below are some examples with the aspects aggregate sum of well-being and distributive equality (the reasoning, however, would apply equally to any other combination of aspects). Consider the following two situations, with individuals A and B.

SituationWell-being of AWell-being of BTotal sum
S1+20+10+30
S2+15+15+30

Suppose that neither of them did anything to deserve being better or worse off. If we consider S2 better than S1, it is because we consider that distribution has a value that is not merely instrumental to maximizing the sum, given that in both situations the total sum is the same. If we saw only the sum as having value in itself, we would say that S1 and S2 are equally good. Now consider situation S3, below.

SituationWell-being of AWell-being of BTotal sum
S3+15+14+29

Whoever claims that, all things considered, S3 is better than S1 is thereby claiming that distribution should sometimes carry more weight than the sum in assessing the value of the situation all things considered. However, contrary to what may initially appear, this does not mean that, in assessing things this way, we necessarily regard equality of distribution as something good in itself. That is possible, but it is also possible for us to hold that it is good because it improves the situation of those who are worse off (or for both reasons). There is, however, an aspect in which S1 is better than S3 (even if it is not better all things considered): in S1 the total sum of well-being is greater.

Saying that S3 is better all things considered than S1 does not commit us to maintaining that equality of distribution should always carry more weight than the total sum26. For example, let us now consider S4, below.

SituationWell-being of AWell-being of BTotal sum
S4+14+14+28

Although S3 contains a little inequality, it seems better, all things considered, than S4. We could maintain that this is so because, even though both aspects (total sum and distribution) have value in themselves, the maximization of the sum should sometimes carry more weight than equality of distribution in determining the value of the situation all things considered (in this case, we would say that S3 is better all things considered, and that S4 is better only in a certain respect: in it, the total value is better distributed). Or else we could hold that the value of equality of distribution is merely instrumental to improving the situation of those who are worse off. In this case, we would say that S3 is better all things considered because in S4 there is no one who is better off than in S3 (but we would also say that S4 is not better than S3 in any respect).

These examples show the following: (1) Maintaining that a certain aspect has value in itself does not commit us to maintaining that it is the only aspect that has value in itself (nor that it is necessarily the most important aspect). (2) Maintaining that a certain aspect should carry more weight than others under certain conditions does not commit us to maintaining that it should carry more weight under any and all conditions (that is, as we saw in section 1.6, the weight of the different factors can be variable, and, even when it is not, there may be compensations in the other aspects that tip the balance the other way).

In Chapter 6 we will return to this topic and see how the various aspects in assessing how good/bad a situation involving several individuals is appear in various theories of normative ethics.

Author’s notes

  1. For an introduction to each of these aspects, see Kagan (1998, p. 25-59). ↩
  2. This is called the principle of diminishing marginal utility. We will return to discuss it in section 6.8.2. ↩
  3. On this question, see Temkin (2000) and Horta (2010a). ↩

4. Value Judgments, Descriptions of Facts, Objectivity, and Subjectivity

4.1. The idea that value judgments are subjective

We saw in Chapter 1 that value judgments are any judgments of the good/bad, better/worse type. Such judgments are different from judgments concerning reasons to act in one way or another. Judgments about reasons for action include, for example, judgments about the best means to achieve an end (something discussed in theories of rational decision) and about which ends are justifiable (something discussed in the field of normative ethics). Value judgments are discussed in the field known as value theory.

Of course, the main function of a value judgment is usually to guide practice, since if we conclude that something is good or better, this seems to give us a reason to pursue it (and, likewise, if we conclude that it is bad or worse, this seems to give us a reason to avoid it). Nevertheless, these are different domains of thought (even though they interact with each other). That being so, it is important to note that everything that will be said in this chapter concerns value judgments only (the connection between what we have seen so far, and what we will see in the present chapter, and judgments about reasons for action will be addressed from the next chapter onward).

A very common idea is that “facts are objective, values are subjective.” Usually, what is meant by this is that it is possible to establish whether a description of facts is true or false, whereas no such thing is possible for value judgments. But is this idea plausible? That is what we will discuss next.

4.2. Two senses of the term “subjective”

Suppose we asked someone: “Why do you believe that facts are objective and values are subjective?” One possible answer would be to say that facts, by their very nature, are objective because they are located in the external world, the physical world, whereas values, by their very nature, are subjective because they are mental states.

If that is the answer, then the term “subjective” is being used, without anyone noticing, in two distinct senses. It is being used both to refer to “mental states” and to refer to “that which cannot be established as true or false.” However, if something is subjective in the first sense, it will not necessarily be so in the second. We can see this even in the case of descriptions of facts, since they describe not only phenomena in the external world but also mental events. For example, if I ask “Is João feeling pain?”, there is a correct answer to this question: it is “yes” if João really is feeling pain, and “no” if he is not. This alone shows that we cannot infer, from the fact that a question concerns a mental event, that there is necessarily no correct answer to it.

Thus, it is false both that descriptions of facts are limited to describing events in the external world (since they may involve describing mental events) and that, because a statement concerns a mental event, there is no way to assess it as true or false.

4.3. The activities of describing and evaluating

It might be objected that, in the example above, there is a correct answer to the question precisely because the answer involves describing mental states, not evaluating them. According to this objection, whether or not a question has a correct answer has nothing to do with whether it concerns a physical or a mental event, but rather with whether it involves the activity of describing or of evaluating.

On this objection's view, descriptions of facts (whether of external events or of mental events) can be assessed as true or false. Value judgments (that is, judgments about what is good/bad, better/worse), by contrast, cannot be assessed as true or false.

4.4. How can a value judgment be confirmed?

In the face of the objection above, we must ask again: “Why is it assumed that value judgments have no correct answer?” To this it might be replied that, in the case of descriptions, there is an event in the world (external or mental) that we can use to confirm whether or not the description is true. In the case of value judgments, by contrast, there is nothing of the sort.

In response, however, it could be argued that the objectivity of value judgments works in a different way: confirming that a value judgment is right or wrong does not come from checking whether there are certain facts in the world that correspond to the judgment, but (at least in some cases) from direct experience of what is being assessed as good or bad, better or worse. We will see more about this below.

Let us take an example with the most evident case of all, the case of suffering. By suffering, we mean here any and every negative experience, from the simplest to the most complex, from the mildest to the most excruciating, whether it arises from a physical or a psychological stimulus. Imagine someone says: “suffering is intrinsically negative.” This is clearly a value judgment. In making this judgment, we are not merely describing that whoever suffers is harmed by suffering. Rather, we are evaluating suffering negatively.

What is meant by intrinsically negative is that suffering is negative in itself: it is already bad on its own and does not need to lead to something else that is bad in order to be bad. This judgment also implies holding that suffering, when it has value, can only have instrumental value, that is, when it leads to something good or prevents something bad. This happens, for example, when the pain we feel on touching a fire makes us pull away, and this prevents us from being burned even more, or prevents us from dying. In that case, the suffering had instrumental value. For this very reason, the case of masochists does not show that suffering is not negative in itself: in fact, such a case confirms that suffering can only have instrumental value (since, in the case of these people, the suffering leads to pleasure).

So what really proves that suffering is intrinsically negative? It is the impossibility of experiencing it in any other way than as something negative. Everyone who experiences suffering experiences it as negative. If it is not negative, it is not suffering. What more could be done to establish the value judgment “suffering is intrinsically negative”? Since everyone who experiences suffering experiences it as negative in itself, and since it is impossible to experience it as something positive in itself, this value judgment is necessarily correct. If someone says that suffering is not intrinsically negative, their value judgment is incorrect, since suffering is negative in itself.

Everything said so far about the disvalue of negative experiences can be said, analogously, about the value of positive experiences. That is, everyone who experiences pleasure or happiness experiences these things as positive in themselves. Again, positive experiences can only be negative instrumentally. That is, they can only be negative if they lead to negative things or prevent positive things. This happens, for example, when, because some food is very tasty, we overeat and get sick afterward (and then we will suffer) or die (and then we will be prevented from enjoying positive states).

4.5. The example of aliens who have so far had only neutral experiences

We have direct access to suffering and pleasure. That is why we know which of them is negative in itself and which is positive in itself. This is so obvious to us that it does not even cross our minds that such direct experience is a proof regarding value judgments. If we did not have such experiences, all we could ask for by way of proof regarding value judgments would be to be able to have them. Below is an example to illustrate this point.

Suppose there were an alien species whose members were sentient, but in whose world there was nothing that caused them suffering or pleasure. Because of this, these aliens' experiences so far have all been neutral: neither positive nor negative. Keep in mind, however, that they are capable of negative and positive experiences: it is just that they have never encountered anything that caused them such experiences. Of course, because of natural selection and the survival value of positive and negative experiences, such a species probably does not exist in the real universe. Remember, though, that this is merely a thought experiment meant to support the claim that the objectivity of value judgments comes about through direct experience.

Now imagine that these aliens have heard that on Earth sentient beings experience suffering and pleasure. But because these aliens have never had these experiences, they have no idea what they are like. They have heard that Earthlings say that one of them is negative (suffering) and the other is positive (pleasure). But the aliens in question do not know what this means because, having never experienced anything positive or negative, they have not formed the concept of value. What could we do to prove to these aliens that it is suffering that is negative and pleasure that is positive (and not the other way around), and to explain what is meant by the concepts of negative and positive? Why, make them experience each of these things. That is why experiencing suffering as negative and pleasure as positive is the proof that suffering is negative and that pleasure is positive.

4.6. Things that cannot be explained except in terms of their value/disvalue

A further proof is that, unlike other things, it is not possible to explain what suffering and pleasure are without citing, as their main features, that they are, respectively, negative and positive. Compare this with other things. For example, some people argue that species or ecosystems have value in themselves. The reason it makes sense to maintain that such a claim is debatable (though not necessarily false) is that we can explain completely what a species or an ecosystem is without having to mention that they are “positive in themselves.” This, as we have seen, is not the case with the claim that suffering is negative in itself and with the claim that pleasure is positive in itself.

4.7. The confusion between the domains of value and ethics

It might be objected that, if pleasure is good in itself, then the pleasure a torturer feels in torturing his victims is good in itself. But, the objection would continue, it is absurd to say that this is good, since it is a very wrong action.

On this point, it is important to note that nothing said above concerns what the right action is (but rather how individuals are affected positively or negatively). We can, without contradiction, hold that pleasure is always intrinsically positive and also hold that a torturer's action is unjustifiable. The main reason for condemning such an action is precisely the harm caused to the victim (which we can recognize only if we recognize that suffering is negative in itself). Thus, when we say that suffering is bad in itself and that pleasure is good in itself, all this implies with regard to the case of torture is that we must recognize that the torturer was benefited by the pleasure he felt and that the victim was harmed by the suffering she felt. None of this implies approving of the torturer's action. In fact, it gives us excellent reasons to condemn such an action strongly, since the victim is harmed more if the torture is carried out than the torturer is harmed if the torture is not carried out.

4.8. Comparing the degree of certainty for value judgments and descriptions of facts

Sometimes the degree of certainty we can have in value judgments is greater than in many questions that involve describing facts. For example, the question “How many planets are there in the universe?” concerns describing facts, but it is very difficult to be certain of its answer. “Does the external world really exist, or is it a virtual simulation?” is another example. Now let us compare this with the value judgment “suffering is negative in itself.” In this case, since we are directly experiencing the object of our judgment, and our judgment concerns that very experience (and not objects in the external world), there is no way we can be mistaken in our judgment.

It is impossible for suffering to be a positive experience while we are all mistaken in experiencing it as negative: it is negative precisely because we experience it as negative (being experienced as negative is what makes something suffering). The same holds for the judgment that pleasure is positive.

Thus, if there is at least one thing that objectively has disvalue in itself (negative experiences) and one thing that objectively has value in itself (positive experiences), the thesis that “value judgments cannot be established as true or false” is completely mistaken.

In fact, everyone who knows (that is, has already experienced) suffering and happiness knows how easy this is to understand. That being so, it is strange, to say the least, how widespread the idea is that value judgments cannot be established as true or false.

4.9. The confusion between all and some

Another possibility for what may be meant by “value judgments are not true or false” is that “not all value judgments can be established as true or false.” But that is a different question (and, even with respect to that other question, it is not obvious that the claim is correct). When someone asserts that “value judgments cannot be established as true or false,” it is understood that they are speaking of any and every value judgment. And, to show that this thesis is false, it is enough to show a single case of a value judgment that can be established as true or false (which is what we did with the case of negative and positive experiences).

4.10. Conclusion

If there is at least one intrinsically negative thing (suffering) and/or at least one intrinsically positive thing (pleasure), and it is impossible for us to be mistaken about this verdict, then the claim that no value judgment can be assessed objectively is false.

Important: as we have seen, what we have discussed here concerns the objectivity of value judgments (that is, about good/bad, better/worse), and not of judgments about what we ought to do. For example, someone can, without contradiction, recognize that suffering is negative in itself and at the same time hold that they have no reasons to avoid suffering. However, although this is not contradictory in logical terms, that does not mean it is a plausible position. For example, if the main function of value judgments is to guide practice, then if something is negative, this is already a reason (conclusive or not, depending on the reasons on the other side) for us to try to avoid it. This relationship between value judgments and judgments about the right action will begin to be explored in the next chapter.

5. Categories of Normative Ethical Theories

5.1. Normative ethics and its categories

Theories of normative ethics27 investigate how we ought to act and why: which goals to pursue; which rules to follow; which character traits to cultivate; whether or not there are optional actions (that is, actions that should be neither required nor forbidden); whether or not there are actions that are praiseworthy but not obligatory, among other questions. In short, these theories do not describe how people act. Instead, they prescribe how they ought to act.

Although they too concern decisions that are open to rational assessment, normative ethical theories have an object of study that is different from the one studied by normative theories of rational decision28. In the latter, the focus is on the means we should adopt to achieve a given end (that is, instrumental reason). What is at issue in normative ethics, by contrast, is the ends themselves. Of course, if we think we should pursue a certain end (for example, reducing the suffering in the world), we will need to investigate the best means of achieving it. That is, these domains of thought are related but distinct, even though both are normative (since they concern what we ought to do).

There are three main categories of normative ethical theories: consequentialism, deontology, and character-centered ethics. Within each of these categories there are many normative ethical theories. Below we will look at each of these categories. In Chapter 6 we will explore the main theories individually.

5.2. Consequentialism

5.2.1. What unites the various consequentialist theories?

There are many consequentialist theories, and they differ from one another in many ways29. Which conditions must be met for a theory to count as consequentialist is a matter of controversy.

Horta, O’Brien, and Teran (2022) point out that all definitions of consequentialism accept the following condition:

(1) Outcome dependence: whether something (be it actions, decisions, rules, character traits, or anything else or any combination of things) is right or wrong (and to what extent) depends entirely on the outcomes that may occur.

However, there are other, additional conditions about which there is no consensus as to whether or not they are necessary for a theory to be consequentialist. They are listed below:

(2) Value dependence: whether something is right or wrong, and to what extent, depends entirely on how good/bad the outcomes that may occur are.

(3) Maximization: whether something is right or wrong, and to what extent, depends entirely on whether certain things are (or could be) maximized.

(4) Agent neutrality: what makes something right or wrong, and to what extent, is entirely independent of the point of view of any particular agent.

In this work we adopt a definition that incorporates all four features.

5.2.2. How does each consequentialist theory assess consequences?

The different consequentialist theories disagree with one another about how to assess “better consequences.” They can disagree at two levels:

(1) How to assess how well or badly off each individual is (that is, regarding individual well-being)

(2) How to assess how good or bad a situation involving several individuals is (that is, regarding collective well-being).

As we saw in previous chapters, there are many aspects that may be considered in each of these assessments. Below is a summary of some of the main ones.

Aspects in assessing the well-being of each individualAspects in assessing how good/bad a situation with several individuals is
Experiences Preferences Objective goodsAggregate total sum Aggregate negative total Average (sum/number of individuals) Minimum level of well-being Maximum level of well-being Number of individuals with positive well-being Number of individuals with sufficient well-being Total sum with greater weight given to improvements for the worse off Level of inequality Types of actions Types of relationships Desert

The various consequentialist theories may disagree:

(1) About which of these factors they consider important in themselves for such assessments.

(2) About how much weight each of these factors should have in such assessments.

There are many possible combinations, both in terms of which of these factors to adopt/exclude and in terms of the relative weight of the factors adopted. This is one of the reasons why there are countless possible consequentialist theories.

5.2.3. An example: act consequentialism

The different consequentialist theories also disagree about what the focus of moral reasoning should be: acts, rules, character traits, or something else. In this section we will look at an example with consequentialism centered on acts. In section 2.4 we will see examples of the other types.

Although they differ in how they assess how good or bad a situation is, what unites all forms of act consequentialism is that, in all of them, it is impossible for an action to be right and yet produce a worse outcome than another available option.

Important: act-consequentialist theories prescribe that we choose the option that has the best consequences among all the available options. Thus, for an action to be right on these theories, it is not enough to show that it has better outcomes than another (or than others): it must be shown that it is the one with the best outcomes among all the available options (that is, that it is the best of all). This is because of the maximization feature: consequentialist views aim to increase as much as possible whatever they consider valuable (and to minimize as much as possible whatever they consider disvaluable).

For these theories, in cases where more than one option results equally in the best consequences, it is morally optional to choose any one of the best options. However, any option that is suboptimal (that is, that is not among the best of all the available options) will be considered wrong, even if its consequences have a positive balance.

5.2.4. Consequentialism: objective, subjective, or prospective?

One possible objection to consequentialism in general is that we can never know what the right action is, since we will never be certain what the consequences of each option will be. One response to this objection is to hold that the right option really is the one that in fact results in the best consequences, but that, given our limited knowledge, we should choose the one we believe results in the best consequences.

On this question, we can distinguish three types of approach30:

(1) Objective consequentialism: the right action is to choose the option that results in the best consequences. For example, if A is the option that produces the best outcomes, the right action is to choose A, even if the agent has reasons to believe that another option would produce the best outcomes.

(2) Subjective consequentialism: the right action is the one that, given the evidence and knowledge available to the agent at the time of the decision, it is rational to believe is the option that will bring about the best consequences.

(3) Prospective consequentialism: the right action is to choose the option with the best expected consequences, calculated in probabilistic terms (and not merely in terms of subjective belief).

5.2.5. Is consequentialism the same as utilitarianism?

Utilitarianism31 is the oldest and best-known consequentialist theory. For this reason, it is not uncommon for utilitarianism to be confused with consequentialism as a whole. However, consequentialism is the category, and utilitarianism is one member of that category. There are many other consequentialist theories.

Another mistaken belief is that there are only two consequentialist theories: utilitarianism (which, as we will see in more detail in Chapter 6, gives equal consideration to everyone affected by the decision—that is, it is an impartial theory) and egoism (which, as the name itself says, places the agent above others). According to this belief, utilitarianism would then be the only impartial consequentialist theory. This too is mistaken. There are many other consequentialist theories (or theories that also have consequentialist versions) that are impartial, such as prioritarianism32, egalitarianism33, and sufficientarianism34.

Indeed, impartiality is such a central feature of consequentialism that some authors argue that, for a theory to be consequentialist, it must be impartial. According to these authors, theories such as egoism would be teleological (since they pursue a goal), but would not be consequentialist35.

Let us now talk about utilitarianism. The different variants of utilitarianism differ from one another in many respects. For example: (1) with respect to the factors they consider relevant to individuals' well-being; (2) as to whether they focus on acts, rules, character traits, or something else; (3) with respect to the weight they give to avoiding what is negative versus promoting what is positive. There are many variants of utilitarianism.

What all variants of utilitarianism have in common is that they assess how good/bad a situation containing several individuals is solely on the basis of the aggregate sum of well-being (whether the total sum, as in the classical version, or only the sum of the negative part, as in negative utilitarianism, or the average, as in average utilitarianism). In any form of utilitarianism, all other aspects are seen as only instrumentally relevant (depending on whether they increase or decrease the aggregate sum).

Because utilitarianism is often confused with consequentialism as a whole, it is not uncommon to believe that consequentialism cannot regard other aspects (such as equality in the distribution of well-being, desert, justice, rights, etc.) as having value in themselves, let alone as carrying more weight than the aggregate sum of well-being. It is not uncommon to believe that this is possible only for non-consequentialist theories.

As we have seen, this confuses one member with the whole category. Consequentialism includes utilitarianism, but it is much broader, since it includes many other variants that assess “better/worse consequences” on the basis of aspects that utilitarianism does not take directly into account. For example, egalitarianism is a theory that has consequentialist versions. Egalitarianism assesses how good/bad a situation containing several individuals is on the basis of two aspects: maximization of the sum and distribution of the total sum among individuals (and it holds that, at times, distribution should carry more weight than maximization of the sum). Another example is prioritarianism, which also seeks to maximize the aggregate total sum, but for which an additional unit of well-being has greater value the worse off the one who would receive it is. The differences between these theories (and several others) and utilitarianism will be detailed in Chapter 6.

There are many other types of consequentialist theories since, as we have seen, there are many aspects that can be considered when assessing how good/bad a situation is, and also different weights that can be assigned to each of these aspects. Each change in one of these things (the number of aspects regarded as having value in themselves, and the relative weight of each aspect) gives rise to another consequentialist theory. That is why it is sometimes said that there are as many consequentialist theories as there are consequentialists.

5.2.6. Should the focus be acts, rules, both, or something else?

A criticism commonly made of act consequentialism is that it is very difficult to estimate how the consequences of each act will unfold. The longer the time frame, the harder it is to predict the probability that the outcome of our decisions will be this or that (since this involves many factors we have no knowledge of, including other individuals' reactions to our decision). Moreover, we do not have time to make this calculation for every act.

One way to defend act consequentialism against this criticism is to argue that the best we can do is to try as hard as we can to estimate the probabilities of the consequences of each available course of action, and that, even if this is a rough approximation, it is still better than not trying to make such estimates. It is true that we do not have time to do this for every decision (and trying to do so would not have good consequences). However, it is something we can try to do with our most crucial decisions.

Another way to try to get around that criticism is to abandon act consequentialism and adopt some rule-consequentialist36 theory. These theories hold that, instead of investigating which courses of action have the best consequences in each act, we should consider which general rules have the best consequences if followed by everyone.

Thus, according to rule-consequentialist theories, it is possible for an action to be the right one while another course of action has better consequences, since what matters for rule consequentialism are the consequences of the general adoption of a rule, and not the consequences of each act.

For example, suppose that, on a given occasion, causing suffering to 10 innocents is the only way to prevent twice as much suffering to another 10 innocents. According to an act-consequentialist theory, however bad this may be, we should cause the suffering to the innocents, since it is the only way to prevent an evil twice as great. According to a rule-consequentialist theory, by contrast, what we would have to do is consider whether the rule “never cause suffering to innocents” has better or worse consequences if followed by everyone. If it does, then rule utilitarianism would condemn causing suffering to innocents, even if, on this particular occasion, the consequences of following this rule are worse.

One criticism of rule consequentialism is that it implies obeying rules even when complying with them results in worse consequences on a given occasion. What this criticism points out is that rule consequentialism is, then, not a genuine form of consequentialism, since the history of the world resulting from its adoption would not have the best possible consequences.

One way to try to get around the difficulties of act and rule consequentialism is to adopt two-level consequentialism37, which applies the rule version in some contexts and the act version in others. According to this approach, in everyday life, when we do not have time to reflect deeply, we should apply the rules that seem to have good consequences in general (this is called the intuitive level of moral reasoning); on the other hand, when we have time to reflect deeply, we should apply act consequentialism and, if necessary, violate the rules that we realize do not, on a given occasion, lead to the best consequences (this is called the critical level of moral reasoning).

The discussion about whether consequentialist theories should focus on acts, rules, or both is a discussion about what the focal point of moral reasoning should be. There are other possible focal points besides acts and rules. For example, there are character-centered consequentialist theories38. For these theories, the most important thing is to assess which character traits, if cultivated, would result in the best consequences (and not which acts or rules would bring about the best consequences).

Rule-consequentialist theories should not be confused with deontological theories (which also focus on rules). Likewise, character-centered consequentialist theories should not be confused with virtue ethics and the ethics of care (which are also character-centered). We will look at deontological theories in section 5.3 and at virtue ethics and the ethics of care in section 5.4.

5.3. Deontology

5.3.1. Deontological constraints: what they are, and examples

In contrast to consequentialist theories, there are deontological39 theories. What all deontological theories have in common is the view that the course of action or the rule we should adopt does not always coincide with what results in the best consequences (however we happen to be measuring “best consequences”).

Deontological theories work with the notion of restrictions (in English, constraints) on the pursuit of the best consequences. These constraints may be prohibitions or requirements. Deontological theories hold that we should not violate these constraints, even if, by respecting them, the outcome is worse than the one that would result from violating them.

Each deontological theory sets out a different set of constraints. Among the most common constraints are: do not violate rights; do not harm innocents; act in accordance with what each person deserves; do not lie; keep promises; fulfill special obligations (for example, toward loved ones, or professional obligations); fulfill obligations to oneself, among others.

Some deontological theories hold that we bear greater responsibility for acts than for omissions. Others hold that, for us to have an obligation to avoid an act with negative consequences, we must intend those consequences. Still others hold that, if a demand is beyond a certain threshold of difficulty, fulfilling it is optional (that is, not required), but doing so may be praiseworthy (these are called supererogatory

acts). Others, in turn, hold that certain acts are optional even if they are not difficult to perform, and so on. There are many variants of deontological theories.

In short, what characterizes all deontological theories is that they introduce factors (whether to determine the right action or to determine which rules we should follow) that have nothing to do with assessing how good or bad the outcome of the decision is.

5.3.2. Deontological constraints: relative to the agent and to the time of the decision

Deontological constraints refer to the agent and to the moment at which he or she makes the decision. That is, they do not depend on how the decision will influence other agents' decisions, nor on how it will influence the agent's own future decisions. This does not mean that deontologists are unconcerned with pursuing the best consequences. It means that this concern holds only if it does not violate a given constraint.

Below we will look at some examples to understand the difference between deontological and consequentialist approaches (whether act consequentialist or rule consequentialist).

Differences from act consequentialism

Suppose we have to choose among courses of action C1, C2, and C3, and that C3 has the best outcomes. An act consequentialist will say that the right action is to adopt C3. A deontologist will say that the right action is to adopt C3, provided there are no constraints relative to the agent and to the time of the decision that would be violated by adopting C3.

For example, under normal conditions, both consequentialists and deontologists hold that we should not cause suffering to innocents. But let us imagine the following dilemma: either we cause suffering to an innocent, or that innocent will suffer twice as much at the hands of other agents (and there is no other way to prevent the greater suffering).

The consequentialist will say that, in this situation, bad as it is, we should cause the suffering to the innocent, since if we do not, the consequences will be even worse. Now, suppose a deontological theory for which not causing suffering to innocents is an agent-relative constraint. This theory will say that we should not cause suffering to the innocent, even if this results in more suffering for that innocent at the hands of other agents.

The same would happen if the dilemma were the following: if we do not cause a certain amount of suffering to innocents today, we ourselves will have to cause twice as much suffering to innocents tomorrow. Again, consequentialists would say that the right thing is to cause the suffering to the innocents today (given that this, bad as it is, has less bad outcomes than twice as much suffering for innocents tomorrow). Now let us imagine a deontological theory in which not causing suffering to innocents is a time-relative constraint (relative to the time of the decision). This theory will hold that we should not cause suffering to the innocents today, even if this results in our having to cause twice as much suffering to innocents tomorrow.

Differences from rule consequentialism

As we have seen, deontological theories are also centered on following rules. However, unlike rule consequentialism, deontological theories adopt these rules not because they are believed to result in the best consequences if followed by everyone, but for other reasons (for example, because they pass some test of universalizability or impartiality).

Some authors argue that rule consequentialism is basically a prescription to act, in practice, as a deontologist would act, but with a consequentialist grounding40. However, what a deontologist and a rule consequentialist would do in practice does not always coincide. For example, deontological theories prescribe following certain rules even if the universal adoption of those rules does not result in the best consequences (something a rule consequentialist would never prescribe).

5.3.3. Deontological constraints: absolute or limited

Deontological constraints can be seen as absolute, or as applying only up to a certain point. For example, a deontologist who sees the constraint “do not cause suffering to innocents” as absolute would claim that we should not cause suffering to one innocent today, even if this means that the suffering of all other innocents is maximized throughout history for all eternity.

On the other hand, if he or she saw this constraint as moderate, he or she could admit that, depending on how bad the consequences of complying with a given constraint are, it would be right to violate it. For example, one could argue that we should not cause suffering to one innocent today even if this means the suffering of two or even ten innocents tomorrow, but that there would be a number of innocents beyond which the right thing would be to violate the constraint. This holds for any other constraint (do not lie, keep promises, etc.): all of them can be seen either as absolute or as holding only up to a certain point.

5.3.4. Is consequentialism centered on outcomes and deontology on actions?

It is sometimes said that the difference between consequentialism and deontology is that the former is centered on outcomes and the latter on actions. However, this is mistaken, because a given consequentialist theory may hold that what is valuable in itself is certain actions (for example, keeping promises or respecting rights) and not their effects. Recall that in section 5.2.2, in the table listing the different aspects that could be adopted by different consequentialist theories to assess how good/bad a situation is, one of the aspects is “types of actions.”

For this reason, there can be a consequentialist theory that prescribes that the right action is to pursue a world in which there are as many actions of this type as possible. These same elements (respecting rights, keeping promises, telling the truth, etc.) usually appear in deontological theories, but as constraints relative to the agent and to the time of the decision, and not necessarily as aspects for assessing how good or bad the situation is.

Let us look at an example to illustrate the difference between a consequentialist theory that valued the action of keeping promises as something good in itself (and not because doing so contributes to something else, such as making people happy) and a deontological theory in which keeping promises was a constraint relative to the agent and to the time of his or her decision.

Imagine the following situation: if we keep a certain promise, this will influence other agents to break many promises, and will also prevent us from keeping many other promises we have made. A consequentialist theory that sought to maximize the number of promises kept would say that the right thing to do, in this case, is not to keep the promise in question. A deontological theory in which keeping promises is a constraint relative to the agent and to the time of his or her decision, by contrast, would say that, even so, the right action is to keep the promise in this case. Again, an absolutist deontologist would say that this constraint must not be violated, no matter how many promises go unkept as a result of respecting it. A moderate deontologist, on the other hand, could admit that there is a certain number of promises beyond which the constraint would have to be suspended.

The same holds for rights. Although most theories of rights are deontological, there are two ways in which a consequentialist theory could incorporate respect for moral rights41: (1) either as something instrumentally good (since it would lead to other things the theory considers good in themselves, such as preventing harms and providing benefits to individuals); (2) or as something good in itself. The difference from deontological theories would be that such consequentialist theories would seek to maximize the number of rights respected, whereas, in deontological theories, respect for rights would appear as a constraint relative to the agent and to the time of the decision (absolute or moderate, depending on the variant).

In short, the main difference between consequentialism and deontology is that deontological theories give priority to what the agent himself or herself will do (compared with how other agents will be influenced to act because of the decision) and to the moment at which the decision takes place (compared with the agent's own future decisions). Consequentialist theories, on the other hand, give equal importance to what the agent or other agents will do, and also equal importance to decisions at the present moment and at the various future moments, since what matters for these theories is the resulting world, and not factors related to the agent.

5.4. Character-centered ethics

A third category of normative ethics is character-centered ethics. The central question for these theories is not “What is the right action?” but “Which character traits should we cultivate?” For these theories, in deciding how to live, we should consider not what would make the world a better place (as in consequentialism) or which norms we should obey (as in deontology), but what kind of moral agents we want to be. Character-centered ethics holds that ethics is more about the kind of person we should be than about what we should do. These theories set out models of the character traits a good person would have, and then argue that, if we cultivate these traits, we will know what to do in practice. Thus, in assessing how to act, according to character-centered ethics, we should ask: “What would a good moral agent do in such a situation?”

Two examples of character-centered ethics are virtue ethics42 and the ethics of care43. In virtue ethics the aim is to cultivate character traits that make someone virtuous. Each virtue theory draws up lists of different virtues to be cultivated (for example: justice, generosity, compassion, rationality, impartiality, prudence, temperance, etc.). These theories are different from character-centered consequentialism, discussed in section 5.2.6. The main difference is this: for character-centered consequentialism, certain virtues should be cultivated because they result in better consequences; for virtue ethics, by contrast, the virtues should be valued in themselves.

The ethics of care, in turn, as its very name suggests, holds that the main character trait we should cultivate is the disposition to care for individuals who depend on us, especially those who are most vulnerable.

Character-centered ethics (whether virtue ethics or the ethics of care) usually emphasizes that these traits need to be exercised until they become a kind of second nature. That is, it emphasizes that it is not enough to read and study about these traits; one must train their

exercise in daily practice and reflect on which character trait or traits apply in each context (which is called practical wisdom).

5.5. The focal point

We saw above that, despite their many practical disagreements, the different schools of normative ethics often agree about what to do in practice, though for different reasons. Kagan (1998, ch. 6, 7) frames this distinction in terms of agreement at the factoral level and disagreement at the foundational level. The factoral level concerns what to do in practice (for example, which factors are relevant to the right decision—hence the term factoral). The foundational level, in turn, concerns why those factors are relevant (for example, whether they are relevant in themselves or only indirectly relevant—that is, a difference in the foundations, hence the term foundational). Kagan (1998) frames the difference at the foundational level in terms of what the focal point of each of the three major schools of ethical theory is: consequences, rules, or character traits. The following table summarizes these distinctions in terms of focal point and what they imply at the factoral level for each of the three schools.

School Consequentialism Deontology Character-centered
Focal point ConsequencesRulesCharacter traits
Why pursue certain consequences? Because this should be the focal point. Because it accords with certain rulesBecause it is what a good agent would do
Why follow certain rules? Because it would result in good consequencesBecause this should be the focal point Because it is what a good agent would do
Why cultivate certain character traits? Because it would result in good consequencesBecause it would help in following certain rulesBecause this should be the focal point

5.6. To what extent do these theories converge/diverge?

Above we saw the basic differences between consequentialist, deontological, and character-centered theories. The debate among these theories usually centers on the points on which they disagree. Doing so is important for assessing the different foundations and the different practical implications of these theories. However, what often goes unnoticed is that there is also a great degree of convergence among these theories, despite their differences.

That is, there are many things on which these theories could agree, albeit on different grounds. One of these things is the equal consideration of all sentient beings. This is so for two reasons. First, there are arguments for the equal consideration of all sentient beings whose acceptance does not require committing oneself to a specific normative theory, or even to a specific school of normative theory. Second, there are specific arguments, coming from the vast majority of contemporary normative ethical theories (whatever school they belong to), for giving equal consideration to all sentient beings. We will look at these two points in more detail in the next chapter.

6. To What Extent Do Ethical Theories Agree About What We Owe Animals?

6.1. Introduction

Discussions in normative ethics usually emphasize the disagreements among the various approaches, especially among consequentialist, deontological, and character-centered theories. Paying attention to these disagreements is important for assessing the different foundations and practical implications of these theories. However, there are also points of convergence. Below we will see that one possible point of convergence is the equal consideration of all sentient beings, that is, of all beings capable of having experiences, regardless of species, degree of cognitive capacities, etc. This is so for two reasons, explained below.

(1) There are general arguments for equal consideration that do not depend on the prior adoption of any specific ethical theory/school. If these arguments are sound, every ethical theory must incorporate the equal consideration of all sentient beings.

(2) There are specific arguments, coming from the most varied contemporary ethical theories, in support of the equal consideration of all sentient beings. Some of these theories necessarily imply equal consideration, and those that do not are nonetheless compatible with equal consideration.

In section 6.2, we will look at the main arguments that have been used to defend the prevailing position, which gives little or even no moral consideration to nonhuman animals. In section 6.3 we will look at the main argument for the view that the good of any and every sentient being matters in itself. In section 6.4 we will look at the basis on which the idea that every sentient being should receive equal consideration is founded. Having seen these general arguments, which do not depend on the prior adoption of a specific normative theory, the following sections present the main theories of contemporary normative ethics and examine their implications for the moral consideration of nonhuman animals. At the end, we will look at practical implications specifically regarding the situation of exploited animals and of those living in the wild.

6.2. Arguments that attempt to justify disregard for animals

Animals are exploited for the most diverse purposes: food, as test models, clothing, etc. This use causes death and suffering to a gigantic number of animals. Despite this, it is a widely accepted practice. Moreover, animals are also harmed by natural processes, such as malnutrition, hunger, thirst, disease, weather events, natural disasters, etc. The standard view is that we should not help them. However, if the victims, whether of exploitation or of natural processes, were human, the standard view would be the opposite. Can this disparity be justified?

Among the most common claims made in an attempt to justify the standard view are44:

(1) “Only humans matter morally45.”

(2) “Animals were not made in the image and likeness of a creator46.”

(3) “Animals do not have (nor have the potential for) certain capacities47 (such as reason, language, freedom, moral agency, a sense of justice, autonomy, culture, the ability to claim rights, etc.) or certain relationships with us48 (affective relationships, relationships of mutual solidarity, political relationships, etc.).”

(4) “Animals do not belong to the same species as the individuals who have those capacities or relationships49.”

(5) “Disregarding animals is a natural or traditional attitude50.”

Below we will look at an argument that points out a problem common to all of these attempts to justify the standard position.

6.3. The argument from relevance

The argument from relevance51 starts from the trivial premise that, for a criterion to be justified, it must be relevant to what is at stake. For example, what is relevant in assessing a candidate for a medical team is their medical skills, whether they are punctual, whether they treat patients well, etc. By contrast, in assessing whom to attend to in an emergency, what is relevant is knowing who is injured, who is seriously ill, who is at risk of dying, etc.

Now imagine if it were required that, to be accepted to work on a medical team, one had to be ill, and that, to be seen by a doctor, one also had to be a doctor. This would be applying criteria that are relevant in one context to another in which they are not. The argument from relevance points out that the defenses of disregard for animals commit a similar confusion. This will be explained in more detail below.

What is at stake in questions of moral consideration is knowing how our decisions would positively or negatively affect those they reach. Giving moral consideration to someone means avoiding harming them and seeking to benefit them. If so, then the appropriate criterion for knowing whom to give moral consideration to is knowing who can be harmed and benefited.

The species to which someone belongs; whether or not they were created in the image of a deity; whether or not they have certain capacities or relationships (or the potential for them); whether or not a behavior is natural, etc.—none of this determines who can be harmed or benefited. Therefore, these are not relevant characteristics for knowing whom to give moral consideration to.

It is the possession of sentience (that is, the capacity to have experiences) that determines who can be harmed or benefited. This is so for two reasons:

(1) It is sentience that makes there be someone, an individual inhabiting a body, and not merely a living, “empty” body. It is what separates a human, a dog, a fish, a shrimp, and a bee, on the one hand, from a plant, a bacterium, and a fungus, on the other.

(2) It is what makes individuals capable of experiences (which may be positive, neutral, or negative), of desires (which may be satisfied or frustrated), and of enjoying items on a list of objective goods. Therefore, whatever theory of well-being one holds, one must recognize that sentience is what makes there be well-being at all—that is, it is what makes it possible for someone to be harmed or benefited.

Disregard for animals is commonly defended by claiming that we have duties only toward those capable of recognizing duties52; that we should protect with principles of justice only those who have a sense of justice53; and that only those who understand what rights are should have rights54. This is a confusion analogous to thinking that, for someone to be entitled to be seen by a doctor, they must also be a doctor. These capacities are relevant for knowing whom to hold responsible, but not for knowing whom to consider morally. This is already recognized in the case of babies and of humans with cognitive impairments: we recognize that we should consider them morally, even though they are incapable of being held responsible. However, this also implies that every sentient being, regardless of species, should receive direct moral consideration—that is, their good matters in itself.

6.4. Some consideration or equal consideration?

A common view is that we should give some consideration to animals, but less than we should give to humans. There is, however, a principle, called the principle of equal consideration55, which shows that this attitude is biased.

Equal consideration is already implied by the argument from relevance, which we saw in the previous section. If we have reasons to consider someone because that someone can be harmed and benefited, then the strength of these reasons must depend on the magnitude of the harms and benefits —and not on the species to which they belong.

In an unbiased approach, harms and benefits of similar magnitude receive the same weight, and greater harms and benefits receive greater weight. This suggests that not

only is there no justification for excluding animals from the sphere of moral consideration: there is also no justification for assigning less weight to their good.

It might be objected that there must be something wrong with the idea that the strength of the reasons to avoid harming and to seek to benefit should depend solely on the magnitude of the harms and benefits. According to this objection, if whoever suffers the greater harm has, for some reason, done something to deserve the harm they suffer, then we should not prioritize eliminating that harm (indeed, we should not even eliminate it, since it is deserved).

The reply to this objection involves pointing to three things:

The first is that the idea of desert can easily be incorporated into the principle of equal consideration. For example, the principle can be adapted to something like: “prioritize avoiding the greater harm, unless the potential victim of the greater harm has done something to deserve the harm they would suffer” and “prioritize promoting the greater benefit, unless the potential recipient of the greater benefit has done something not to deserve the benefit they would enjoy.”

The second is that the idea of desert actually depends on equal consideration to make sense. This is because, for someone to deserve the harm they suffer (and not to deserve the benefit they enjoy), they must first have acted unjustly toward someone—that is, they must first have violated the principle of equal consideration.

Finally, the third is that including the notion of desert in moral reasoning could never justify diminishing the strength of the reasons to avoid harming and to help nonhuman animals. This is because, for someone to deserve the harm they suffer, they must be a morally responsible agent. Since nonhuman animals do not have cognitive capacities above the level at which it makes sense to hold someone responsible, it makes no sense to say that they deserve the harms they suffer, whatever these may be.

In light of this, it might be objected that, for the same reason, only beings with cognitive capacities above a certain level can deserve benefits, and that this would justify prioritizing normal adult humans.

A first problem with this objection is that it could not prioritize benefiting all normal adult humans, but only those who had done something to deserve some extra benefit (and, even with respect to these individuals, prioritizing them would not be justified in any and every situation, but only in those in which they had done something to deserve some extra benefit—once they had received the extra benefit in question, their priority would be canceled until they again did something to deserve another extra benefit).

The second (and greater) problem is the following. It makes sense to say, of two individuals who have cognitive capacities above a certain level, that it is justified to give an extra benefit to one and not to the other, because one did something to deserve the extra benefit and the other could have done so but chose not to. However, it makes no sense to say, comparing an individual who has cognitive capacities above a certain level with another who does not, that it is justified to give an extra benefit to one and not to the other because the former did something to deserve the extra benefit, given that the latter does not have that capacity. For example, if we have two normal adult humans who could have cooperated in a situation, but one of them chose not to (and could have done so without sacrificing anything of greater importance), it makes sense to say that only the one who cooperated deserves a certain benefit. However, it makes no sense to say the same if we are comparing a normal adult human with, for example, a baby. The baby should receive all the benefits it needs without having to do anything to deserve them (since it does not have that capacity). But the same holds for nonhuman animals.

Thus, the notion of desert, although it can be incorporated as an addendum to the principle of equal consideration, would not justify giving less weight to the good of nonhuman animals, since the species to which someone belongs, like different degrees of cognitive capacities, are the results of the natural lottery, and not of merit or demerit.

Accepting the principle of equal consideration does not commit us to a specific ethical theory/school56. This is because this principle does not prescribe what the right action is (that is done by the substantive principles of each ethical theory, which we will see in the following sections). The principle of equal consideration only prescribes that, whatever substantive principle we adopt, there is no justification for applying it in a biased way—that is, there is no

justification for giving different weight to the good of individuals on account of arbitrary factors such as their species, their race, their gender, etc.

6.5. The moral consideration of sentient beings from the standpoint of various ethical theories

The full moral consideration of all sentient beings has been defended from the standpoint of the most varied theories of normative ethics57. In the following sections, we will look briefly at each of these theories, and then see how they would have to be applied with regard to the moral consideration of nonhuman animals.

In all the examples we will see, the letters represent individuals, and the numbers represent their respective levels of well-being. We will not assume here any specific view as to which aspects are relevant for assessing individuals' well-being (whether positive/negative experiences, satisfied/frustrated preferences, items on an objective list, etc.). We will leave this open and speak only of individuals' well-being, since the whole discussion here holds equally whatever factors we believe are relevant for assessing well-being.

6.6. Utilitarianism

The goal of utilitarianism58, in its classical version, is to maximize the aggregate total sum of the well-being of the individuals affected by the decision. Let us look at an example:

SituationABCDNegative totalPositive totalOverall total
S1-8+9-12+3-20+12-8
S2-2+3-10+5-12+8-4

If our only options are S1 or S2, utilitarianism will prescribe choosing S2, since it has the greatest overall total balance (that is, the positive total minus the negative total).

6.7. Number of beings with positive well-being, and average utilitarianism

Another possibility is to claim that the number of individuals with positive well-being is something valuable in itself (and not merely indirectly, in relation to the goal of maximizing the total balance). Below is an example to illustrate how this view would determine the right action, and also to illustrate the difference between it and average utilitarianism. Average utilitarianism is a variant of utilitarianism that prescribes that we choose not the situation with the greatest total sum, but the one with the highest average (that is, the total sum divided by the number of individuals):

SituationABCDNegative totalPositive totalOverall totalAverage
S1+10 -1-2-3-6+10+4+1
S2+8+2 -3-3-6+10+4+1

For utilitarianism, whether classical or average, both situations are equally good, since the total sum is the same (+4), and so is the average (+1). However, it could be said that S2 is better in at least one respect: in it, there are two individuals with positive well-being, whereas in S1 there is only one. Now consider the following situations:

SituationABCDNegative totalPositive totalOverall totalAverage
S1+10 -1-2-3-6+10+4+1
S3+7+2 -3-3-6+9+3+0.75

Classical and average utilitarians will say that S1 is better than S3, since in it both the total sum and the average are greater. By contrast, someone who holds that the more individuals with positive well-being the better will say that S3 is better in this respect, even though the total sum and the average are lower, since in it there are two individuals with positive well-being, whereas in S1 there is only one. Whether they will consider S3 better all things considered will depend on how much weight they assign to the aspect “number of individuals with positive well-being” compared with the aspects “total sum” and “average.” But they will consider it better at least in one respect.

6.8. Maximin

Maximin is directly concerned with individuals' levels of well-being (regardless of what the sum, the average, or the number of individuals with positive well-being is). It prescribes choosing the course of action in which the minimum level of well-being is highest (hence the name maximin, which comes from maximizing the minimum59). Let us look at an example:

Situation ABCDNegative totalPositive totalOverall totalAveragePositive lives
S1-1-6+10+4+1+2
S2-2-6+10+4+1+2

In this example, classical and average utilitarians, and even those concerned with the number of individuals with positive well-being, would have to say that both situations are equally good. However, proponents of maximin would say that S2 is better, since in it whoever is in the worst condition (C=-4) is better off than whoever is in the worst condition in S1 (C=-5).

Again, as happens in conflicts between any other aspects, in situations that are better with respect to the minimum level but worse in other respects, the situation will or will not be considered better all things considered depending on the weight given to maximin compared with the other aspects.

6.9. Prioritarianism

6.9.1. What characterizes prioritarianism?

Prioritarianism60 has differences from and similarities with maximin, utilitarianism, and egalitarianism (the last of which we will see in section 6.10). Let us begin by comparing it with maximin. Consider the following two situations:

SituationAB
S1-48-49
S2-50-30

According to maximin, S1 is better, because in it whoever is worst off (B=-49) is better off than whoever is worst off in S2 (B=-50). That is, S1 has the highest minimum level of well-being. However, one objection to the conclusion that S1 is therefore better all things considered is that, although in S2 the minimum level of well-being is lower, there is a considerable improvement in the well-being of one of the individuals. In S1 we have two individuals suffering greatly, and in S2 at least the suffering of one of them is considerably less than it would be in S1.

One way of trying to ground the claim that S2 is better is by appealing to the utilitarian principle: in S1 the aggregate total is -97, whereas in S2 it is -80. However, another way is to appeal to the prioritarian principle. Prioritarianism, like utilitarianism, also seeks to maximize the aggregate total balance. However, unlike utilitarianism, in which each additional unit of well-being has the same value regardless of how well or badly off the one who would receive that additional unit was, in prioritarianism each additional unit of well-being has greater value the worse off the one who would receive it is.

Thus, unlike maximin, which is concerned only with maximizing the minimum level, prioritarianism is also concerned with the amount of benefit that can be produced by each course of action. And, unlike utilitarianism, which is concerned only with maximizing the total benefit, for prioritarianism it matters whose well-being would be improved (the worse off someone is, the more value there is in improving that someone's well-being).

To better understand this difference from utilitarianism, we will now compare the prioritarian principle with the principle of diminishing marginal utility, found in utilitarianism.

6.9.2. Differences from the principle of diminishing marginal utility

The prescriptions of utilitarianism, in a wide range of cases (but not in all), coincide with favoring those who are in the worst situation. However, this happens in utilitarianism not because it values benefiting those in the worst condition in itself, but because doing so is usually more efficient for maximizing the total balance, owing to the principle of diminishing marginal utility, explained below.

The principle of diminishing marginal utility states that the smaller the amount of a certain resource someone has, the more well-being an additional unit of that resource generates for that someone. For example, if someone has only one kilo of rice, giving that person an additional kilo will make a greater positive difference to them than if we gave the kilo to another person who already has ten kilos of rice. Thus, what this principle says is that resources have diminishing marginal utility.

For example, suppose that initially we have A=+10; B=+1 (total = +11), and that we have a resource that, if given to A, will increase A's well-being by two points (A=+12, B=+1, total = +13), and that, if given to B, will increase B's well-being by four points, since B is in a worse situation (A=+10, B=+5, total = +15). Thus, utilitarianism would prescribe giving the resource to B because the outcome will then have a greater aggregate total balance.

This is different from having improving the situation of the worst off as a goal. If, in another situation, giving the resource to someone who is already better off is more efficient for maximizing the total sum, utilitarianism will prescribe favoring whoever is already better off. Let us look at an example.

Let us imagine the same situation: A=+10; B=+1 (total = +11). Suppose this time that A, even though already better off than B, would still have their well-being increased by more points if they received the resource in question. Imagine, for example, that A is a peanut fan and that B likes peanuts, but not as much as A, and that if we give a bag of peanuts to A their well-being will increase by three points (A=+13, B=+1, total = +14), and that if we give the bag of peanuts to B their well-being will increase by two points (A=+10, B=+3, total = +13). In this case, utilitarianism would prescribe favoring whoever is already better off, since this would be more efficient for maximizing the total sum.

In short, according to the principle of diminishing marginal utility, an additional unit of a resource is more efficient for maximizing the aggregate total if it is given to whoever has less of that resource. According to prioritarianism, by contrast, an additional unit of well-being has more value the lower the level of well-being of whoever would receive that additional unit. Parfit (1995, p. 105) sums up the difference this way: “just as resources have diminishing marginal utility, so utility has diminishing marginal value.” Let us look at an example:

SituationABTotal:
Initial situation+20-10+10
S1+25-10+15
S2+20-5+15

Let us imagine that, from the initial situation, we can increase the well-being of one of the two individuals by +5. In S1 we increase by +5 the well-being of A, who is already at +20. In S2 we increase by +5 the well-being of B, who is at -10. According to utilitarianism, both situations are equally good, since the total is the same (+15). Prioritarianism, in turn, would say that S2 is better, since in it the benefit of +5 goes to whoever is worse off. That is, prioritarians would say that increasing by +5 the well-being of B, who is in a worse situation, has more value than increasing by +5 the well-being of A, who is already better off.

6.9.3. Objections to prioritarianism

One possible objection to prioritarianism is to point out that, depending on how much greater the benefit that could be given to someone already much better off were, it would still have to prioritize benefiting the one already much better off, even while giving greater weight to units of benefit in proportion to how badly off someone is. A theory that apparently does not have this implication is egalitarianism. Below we will see the differences and similarities between prioritarianism and egalitarianism, as well as the debate surrounding egalitarianism.

6.10. Egalitarianism

6.10.1. What characterizes egalitarianism?

Consider the following situations:

SituationABTotalInequality
S1+25-10+15-35
S2+20-5+15-25
