5. Differences Between Environmentalism and Consideration for Animals

The term “environmentalism” is applied to views that are very different from one another. Sometimes it is used to refer to positions that aim to preserve the environment as a resource for humans or for animals of other species. At other times it is used to refer to positions holding that certain nonsentient entities (such as ecosystems and species, for example) have value in themselves, and not as a resource. In what follows, we will use the term “environmentalism” in this second sense, since it is these perspectives18 that are usually confused with the defense of animals, and the aim of this section is to make their differences explicit19. Much of the confusion arises from failing to see what the ultimate goals of each of these views are (that is, which things are valued in themselves) and which things are valued only as a means to achieve these goals. The following table sets out the ultimate goals of each of these positions:

Position The environment should be maintained...
AnthropocentricIn the configuration that is best for humans
Sentience-centeredIn the configuration that is best for sentient beings in general
EnvironmentalistIn certain configurations*, even if this is worse for sentient beings in general

*Each variant of environmentalism values different configurations20. Examples of criteria used are: the degree of complexity, rarity, the time it took to form, how little it has been modified by human actions, and its degree of aesthetic properties.

Most programs and legislation concerning wild animals have environmentalist goals. This is due in part to the predominance of the idea that animals do not matter individually (only ecosystems and species do). In these programs, animals will be harmed or benefited depending on what is most efficient for achieving environmentalist goals21. However, environmentalist programs are commonly misunderstood as aiming to benefit sentient beings. The following tables clarify the main confusions about this question.

Mistaken common belief What each position actually aims at
Environmentalism and animal advocacy both aim at the good of animals, but disagree about the means to achieve this goal: environmentalism agrees with killing a minority to save the majority, and animal advocacy disagrees. When environmentalist programs kill animals, they do so because this is the only way to save many animals from then on (that is their goal). (V, ch. 2 and 8).Environmentalism and animal advocacy have different goals. Animal advocacy values in itself the well-being of sentient beings. Environmentalism values in themselves nonsentient entities, such as ecosystems or species. The goal of environmentalism is to keep ecosystems in certain configurations it values, even if this is not what is best for their inhabitants. The goal of environmentalist programs is not to save sentient beings (whether the majority or the minority). Among animal advocates, on the other hand, there are both those who defend killing a minority if that is the only way to save a majority and those who reject this position.
Animal advocacy is centered on individuals, and environmentalism is centered on the “whole” (such as species and ecosystems). This means that environmentalism prioritizes saving the majority of sentient beings, even if this requires killing a minority (since it prioritizes the whole), and animal advocacy opposes this (since it prioritizes the individual). (V, ch. 2 and 8).Consideration for individuals does not necessarily imply prioritizing one individual over many. It means only that the focus of moral consideration is sentient beings (that is, individuals), and not nonsentient entities. This is compatible both with positions that prioritize saving the majority and with those that prioritize the minority under certain conditions (for example, because they are in a worse situation). Likewise, consideration for the “whole,” as found in environmentalism, is not consideration for the majority (or for any individual). It is consideration for the species as an abstract entity (and not for its members) and for ecosystems (and not for their inhabitants).
Animal advocacy defends helping wild animals without worrying about the consequences, and environmentalism prescribes not helping them for fear that doing so could cause even more suffering. (V, ch. 4).The difference between these positions has nothing to do with one of them considering the long term and the other not. Both can consider the long term. What distinguishes them is their goals. Claiming that a certain form of help should not be carried out because it could cause more suffering in the long term is a concern for sentient beings (and is therefore not an environmentalist concern).
Despite their differences, environmentalism and animal advocacy converge in practice, since animals need the environment, and environmentalism aims to preserve it. (V, ch. 3).This will happen in some cases, but not in others. It is possible to preserve the environment in the most diverse configurations. The configurations sought by environmentalism often do not coincide with the one that is best (or even good) for animals.
The greater the degree of ecological balance and biodiversity, the better for animals. That is why environmentalists aim at these things: because their goal is the good of animals. (V, ch. 5).Environmentalism does not value ecological balance and biodiversity out of concern for the good of animals. It values these things in themselves, or as a means of keeping ecosystems in certain configurations (which are what it values in themselves). Moreover, a greater degree of balance and/or biodiversity often does not coincide with what is best (or even minimally good) for animals. These concepts are based, respectively, on variation in population size over time and on the diversity of species. This does not indicate that the well-being of animals in these situations is necessarily positive.
Environmentalism is scientifically informed by ecology, whereas animal advocacy is anti-scientific. (V, ch. 6, VII, ch. 19).In fact, any normative view needs to be scientifically well informed since, otherwise, it will not achieve the goals it pursues. Ecology is a science that describes how interactions in ecosystems take place. This knowledge can be used in an attempt to pursue environmentalist goals, but it can also be used in an attempt to benefit sentient beings.
If it is shown that ecosystems and species have value in themselves, then it is justified to kill animals to preserve species and ecosystems, and it is also wrong to help animals when they are victims of natural processes. (V, ch. 10).No, because to support such conclusions it would be necessary not only to show that such nonsentient entities have value in themselves, but also that their preservation is more important than preventing the suffering and death of sentient beings. Moreover, there are reasons to prioritize sentient beings, since no nonsentient entity is capable of suffering or of being prevented by death from enjoying things – very serious harms.

6. The Situation of Wild Animals and the Proposal to Help Them

As we saw in the previous section, most programs dealing with wild animals are driven by environmentalist ideals. In these programs animals are not valued in themselves, but only as a means to preserve species and ecosystems. In recent decades, however, several authors22 have argued that programs dealing with wild animals should have as their goal the good of the animals themselves, seeking to prevent and minimize their suffering and deaths.

Since the emergence of animal ethics, whether with respect to domesticated or wild animals, the focus has generally been on animals harmed by human practices. However, a growing number of authors23 have drawn attention to the way animals are harmed by natural processes, especially animals living in the wild, and have proposed researching ways to reduce these harms. The central argument of this proposal is that, if we really care about animals, we will not limit our concern to harms caused by humans, since for the animals it makes no difference whether what harms them is a human or, say, hunger or disease. In more detail, the central argument is as follows24: if what gives us reasons to avoid harms is the fact that they are something negative, and if what gives us reasons to pursue benefits is the fact that they are something positive, then the strength of these reasons depends on the magnitude of the harms and benefits at stake, and not on whether their origin is anthropogenic or natural. In other words, we have reasons to give priority to avoiding the greater harm and to pursuing the greater benefit, regardless of whether they originate in human practices or in natural processes. Thus, the situation of wild animals who are victims of natural processes is just as important as it would be if these were equivalent anthropogenic harms.

In this section and the next two we will look at the debate on the proposal to reduce the suffering and deaths of wild animals25. In this section we will discuss the objections26 claiming that there is no need to help them, and the answers that have been given to these objections.

Objection How the objection has been answered
There is no need to help animals in the wild: it is enough to stop harming them, since, if we let nature take its course, animals will generally have predominantly positive lives. (VII, ch. 3).Animals in the wild are greatly harmed by natural processes. Malnutrition, hunger, thirst, disease, physical injuries, psychological stress, hostile weather events, natural disasters, and various kinds of conflict between animals are the norm in nature. In addition, the vast majority of animal species reproduce by maximizing offspring (in broods ranging from thousands to many millions, depending on the species). In periods of approximately stable population, it can be deduced that, on average, in each generation a single offspring per adult survives (that is, only two per brood). All the rest of the brood are generally born only to experience extreme suffering and die very 27 prematurely. Because of these factors, the number of animals who suffer and die as a result of natural processes is so enormous that it makes even the numbers of animal exploitation look small by comparison28.
Many eggs are destroyed before they develop into sentient beings. Thus, few animals are harmed. (VII, ch. 3).Even if this happened to the vast majority of eggs, there would still be an enormous number of individuals born to live a life in which suffering greatly predominates. For example, even if 90% of the 2 million eggs laid by a cod were destroyed before developing into sentient beings, the remaining 10% would still be 200,000 individuals.
Most animals die very young, and at that stage they are still barely capable of suffering. Therefore, they are only slightly harmed by what happens to them. (VII, ch. 3).There is no evidence that, because they are very young, they are barely capable of suffering. On the contrary, given that most of these animals are precocial, it is quite likely that their capacity to feel is very acute at this stage, since otherwise 29 such species would probably no longer exist. And even if they were barely capable of suffering, this does not mean they were only slightly unfortunate, since premature death aggravates the harm of death (they lived short lives full of suffering).

  8. On sentience in juvenile animals, see Animal Ethics (2022). ↩

7. The Debate on the Proposal to Help Wild Animals (Part 1)

In this section we will continue to address the most common objections to the proposal to help wild animals and how these objections have been answered.

Objection How the objection has been answered
We should not minimize natural harms because this question lies outside the scope of ethics, since neither natural processes nor animals are accountable. (VII, ch. 2, 15, 16).It is contradictory to claim that the question of natural harms lies outside the scope of ethics and then say that we should not minimize these harms. Moreover, the fact that natural processes and animals are not accountable is irrelevant, since the ones who have to decide are we, not they. When humans are the victims in similar situations, no one says that we should not rescue the victims just because natural processes and animals are not accountable.
Intervening in nature (that is, in natural territory and in natural processes) is always wrong, since it is an arrogant attitude. It amounts to “playing God.” (VII, ch. 6).There are many interventions in nature that are accepted by almost everyone. For example, those made to benefit humans (medicine, agriculture, the construction of housing, schools, hospitals, libraries, etc.) and to achieve environmentalist goals (interventions to preserve rare species, to keep ecosystems in a certain configuration, etc.). If any of these interventions is justifiable, then it makes no sense to say that it is wrong to help wild animals just because it would involve intervening in nature.
It is wrong to influence the fate of these animals. (VII, ch. 6).We will be influencing the fate of these animals either way, whether we decide to help or decide not to help.
The proposal is anthropocentric, since it comes from humans. (VII, ch. 7).The fact that a proposal is anthropogenic (that is, comes from humans) does not mean that it is anthropocentric (that is, that its goal is centered on benefiting humans). The proposal in question aims to benefit animals. Therefore, it is not anthropocentric.
The less human influence, the better for animals. (VII, ch. 8)Not necessarily. It would have to be assessed, case by case, whether acting or refraining from acting has the best results for animals. There is no basis for saying that refraining is always better.
We should reduce human influence on the world, even in situations in which reducing it would be worse for animals. (VII, ch. 8).It is contradictory to say that we should reduce human influence because it harms animals, and then say that we should reduce it even when doing so is worse for animals. To support such a thesis, what would have to be shown is that human influence is wrong in itself, entirely independently of how animals are affected. However, the objection in question already assumes that this thesis is correct, instead of demonstrating it.
From our human perspective, we cannot know what is best for animals. Hence, what is best for animals is to let nature take its course. (VII, ch. 7).It is contradictory to say, first, that we cannot know what is best for animals, and then say that we know that what is best for them is to let nature take its course. Moreover, in the situations in which the proposal to help wild animals aims to intervene, we do know what is best for the animals. It would be absurd to say that perhaps what is best for animals would be to have their bodies burned, to die of starvation or disease, to be born only to suffer, etc.
Helping would violate the animals' freedom. (VII, ch. 10).On the contrary. Helping is the only way to ensure that they can exercise their freedom, since to do so they need to be alive and free from extreme suffering. It could be objected that the proposal sometimes requires interfering with their freedom (for example, to vaccinate them). But if the degree of freedom depends on how far someone can do what they want, restricting their freedom at a certain moment may be necessary to ensure that they can continue to exercise it.
Helping them may make them dependent on human care. Hence, we should not help them. (VII, ch. 11).This objection does not apply to most interventions, since they aim to reduce the number of births, nor to the proposal to stop practices that make natural processes maximize suffering and deaths. Even interventions that help animals already born do not make them lose the abilities they already have, nor prevent them from acquiring them. It is not helping that would make animals unable to exercise the ability to seek food, or to acquire it, since they would die. Even if helping made animals dependent on human care, this would still be better for the animals than suffering more and dying soon.
The proposal to help them is paternalistic. Hence, we should not help them. (VII, ch. 12).If an action is paternalistic when it aims to benefit the one affected but goes against what they prefer, then helping animals in the wild would be paternalistic only if they preferred not to be helped in situations of starvation, disease, accidents, fires, floods, etc. But this is not the case. Of course, animals sometimes flee from attempts to help them. But this does not show that they prefer not to be helped (they flee because they do not understand that someone is there to help). And even if there were some animal who preferred to remain in a situation in which its suffering would increase, it would very probably not be in an epistemic position favorable to seeing what is best for its well-being in the long term. Therefore, even if helping it were paternalistic, it would be the justified kind of paternalism.
We should not help them, since suffering has instrumental value (that is, it helps the individual avoid what would harm them). (VII, ch. 13).In the case of the vast majority of animals who suffer in the wild because of natural processes, suffering, rather than helping them promote their well-being, only harms them (since they experience extreme suffering from birth until a very premature death caused by that suffering). Moreover, where suffering did help animals achieve something positive, there are reasons to research how to enable them to reach that positive state without having to suffer for it (that is why we prefer to receive anesthesia before surgery).
The proposal sees humans as something separate from nature. (VII, ch. 14).On the contrary. It is the idea that humans should not intervene in natural territory that seems to see humans as something separate from nature. If we see humans as part of the natural world, then outcomes influenced by human practices do not cease to be (nor are they any less) natural.
Nature is neither good nor bad. Natural processes are not accountable agents. Therefore, we have no reasons to help. (VII, ch. 2, 15, 16).It is true that natural processes are not accountable agents. But this does not mean that we have no reasons to prevent and minimize the negative effects resulting from natural processes (this is already widely accepted when humans are the victims of natural processes). Moral responsibility falls on us, in having to decide whether or not to help.
Nature is indifferent to the suffering of animals. Ecosystems arise, endure, and disappear with complete indifference to the suffering and death of animals. (VII, ch. 2, 15, 16).Yes, but that does not justify our being indifferent as well. Ecosystems also arise, endure, and disappear with complete indifference to human suffering, but that does not justify our being indifferent to suffering. The objection in question assumes that the way natural phenomena happen should be a model for what we ought to do. In doing so, it makes an unjustified leap from describing how things are to prescribing how they ought (morally) to be.
We should respect the nature of wild animals, and this requires leaving them to their own fate. (VII, ch. 17).We have to ask: why should we respect someone's nature? If the answer is “because doing so would benefit them,” then it is false that respecting the nature of wild animals requires leaving them to their own fate, since this would probably harm them. If, on the other hand, the answer is “just because, even when it would harm them,” then no reason is being given to explain why respecting someone's nature would be more important than avoiding harming them.
Intervening in conflicts between animals could make the situation even worse (for example, intervening in predation could cause a population explosion of prey). (VII, ch. 18, 31).In any case where intervening has a good probability of making the situation even worse because of knock-on consequences, the proposal to help wild animals would prescribe not intervening. However, this does not mean that intervening will always have worse consequences. For example, by reducing primary productivity, the tendency is for populations in general to decrease, since it is a “bottom-up” kind of intervention in the food chain.
The proposal would entail intervening in conflicts between animals, and this is wrong even when doing so improves the situation. (VII, ch. 18, 31).This objection assumes that the right action sometimes has worse consequences than other available courses of action. However, this thesis would have to be demonstrated, and the objection already assumes it to be correct in advance. Moreover, when humans are the victims of animals, this thesis is not defended. When humans are the victims, it is held that it is always right to help, regardless of the consequences. When animals are the victims, it is held that it is always wrong to help, even if the consequences of not helping are worse. This is speciesism.
This is a question for ecology to answer, not ethics. If we apply what ecology says, we will value species, ecosystems, and natural balance, and not this pursuit of avoiding the suffering and deaths of sentient beings. (VII, ch. 19).Describing what happens in natural ecosystems is a task for ecology. However, which goals we ought to pursue (for example, whether the good of sentient beings or environmentalist values) is a question for the field of ethics. No descriptive science has the answer to this question. Animal advocates do not reject knowledge in ecology (indeed, they depend on it in order to help wild animals safely). But ecology would never prescribe that we should value species, ecosystems, biodiversity, or anything else, since it only describes – like any science, it is not about which goals we ought to aim at. Those who oppose helping wild animals and claim that they are “just applying what ecology says” are disguising an environmentalist moral position as a morally neutral description.
What matters is ecosystems and species, not animals. So, if all this suffering and death neither drives species extinct nor threatens ecosystems, we need not worry. (VII, ch. 20).If the question of moral consideration exists because our decisions can benefit or harm those affected by them, then for someone to be morally considerable it is sufficient that they can be harmed/benefited. Every sentient being, because it is capable of experiencing certain states as positive and others as negative, can be harmed/benefited. If so, then each sentient being matters in its own right. The thesis that each sentient being matters in its own right is much less controversial than the thesis that species and ecosystems matter in themselves.
Even if animals matter, helping would conflict with environmentalist goals (such as keeping the ecosystem in certain configurations), and this makes helping wrong. (VII, ch. 20).In the vast majority of cases there would be no conflict of goals, since programs to help wild animals would not alter the properties of ecosystems that environmentalism values: they would only mean less suffering for the inhabitants of these ecosystems. There are even several programs that would achieve both goals. For 30 example, vaccinating bees prevents an enormous number of animals from suffering from disease and also helps in the conservation of species.
But there are clearly cases in which helping would conflict with environmentalist goals. For example, environmentalists may want to keep only the native vegetation of a place, but it may be that introducing non-native vegetation would reduce the total suffering of the animals living there. In those cases, wouldn't it be wrong to help? (VII, ch. 20).A conflict by itself is insufficient to support the conclusion that we should not help. It would have to be shown: (1) that we should abide by environmentalist goals, and (2) that these goals are more important than the basic interests of animals (such as not suffering and not dying). Even if point 1 were demonstrated, reasons could be raised for rejecting point 2. For example, it could be said that only sentient beings are harmed by suffering and death, and that these harms are particularly serious. Thus, whenever there was a conflict, there would be reasons to prioritize the basic interests of sentient beings. Environmentalists already accept this in the human case: they defend limiting the non-basic interests of humans (aesthetic, economic, recreational, etc.) to achieve their goals, but they do not hold that this justifies causing suffering and death to humans, or failing to help them when they are victims of natural processes.

Author’s notes

  1. On vaccinating bees, see Raukko (2018). ↩

8. The Debate on the Proposal to Help Wild Animals (Part 2)

In this section we will look at the last part of the most common objections to the proposal to reduce the suffering and deaths of wild animals that originate in natural processes, and the answers that have been given to them. We will now discuss objections that deny that we are morally responsible for doing something, or that question the practicality of such a proposal.

Objection How the objection has been answered

It is wrong to help, since humanity is morally responsible only for human practices (VII, ch. 21). Even if this were the case, it would mean only that there is no duty to help (and not that it is wrong to help). Helping could still be morally permissible, or even praiseworthy. Moreover, it could be said that we are morally responsible for a decision whenever it is decisive for the outcomes being one way or another, and this is not limited to human practices. For example, if doctors have an obligation to treat victims of naturally caused diseases, then it is false that we are morally responsible only for human practices.

We have no close relationship with these animals. Therefore, humanity has no obligation to allocate resources to help them. (VII, ch. 21)The absence of a close relationship is insufficient to show that humanity has no obligation to allocate resources to help them, since our decision to help or not to help, even from a distance, directly influences their situation (the same happens with human victims of natural disasters in distant places, for example). We also have no close relationship with exploited animals, but this does not mean that we cease to have an obligation not to harm them, since our decision at a distance affects them directly. Yet the same is true of animals living in the wild.
There is a general duty to help, but not this cause in particular. (VII, ch. 21)We will reject this position if we accept that we should prioritize causes in proportion to the number of victims, the total amount of suffering, and the degree to which the cause is neglected. By these criteria, the cause that aims to reduce the suffering of wild animals should receive a great deal of attention.
The proposal is too demanding. (VII, ch. 21)Such a proposal would demand very little of each person, since the interventions would be carried out by professionals who already work in this field (such as biologists and ethologists). Each person would merely have the duty to draw attention to the importance of this question and to call for resources to be devoted to addressing it. Life-science professionals, in turn, would continue to do their work as usual, with the difference that their research would now be guided by a direct concern for the good of the animals.
Helping domesticated animals is the priority, since we owe them a historical debt because of domestication. Therefore, we should not help wild animals. (VII, ch. 22).Even if helping domesticated animals were the priority, this would not support denying the duty to help wild animals (much less prohibiting helping them). Moreover, if priority depends on how serious the victims' situation is and on the number of victims, this does not necessarily coincide with the criterion of historical debt. Each wild animal also experiences extreme suffering, and they are vastly more numerous than domesticated animals. Finally, it could also be argued that we owe a historical debt to wild animals, since the benefits we enjoy arose from interventions in nature, and we have left wild animals subject to natural processes.
This proposal should be rejected because it would involve sterilization, and animals have a right not to suffer interference with their own bodies against their will. (VII, ch. 29).Three answers. (1) There are ways to minimize natural harms that do not involve sterilization: vaccinating, treating diseases, providing water, food, shelter, rescue in natural disasters, not recreating the conditions for maximizing births, etc. (2) Respecting the alleged right not to be sterilized would result in much more suffering and death than not respecting it (since it would entail the maximization of beings who would be born only to suffer and die prematurely), and it would thus violate the physical integrity and the lives of (many) third parties. (3) The sterilization of animals such as dogs and cats (who have on average 4 or 5 offspring per litter) is widely accepted by animal advocates. In the case of wild animals who have thousands or millions of offspring per brood, we have much stronger reasons to justify sterilization.
There is nothing that can be done to help. (VII, ch. 26).Animals are already being helped with vaccination and treatment of diseases, in fires and other natural disasters, with assistance to orphaned animals, the rescue of trapped animals, and programs to meet animals' basic needs31.
There is nothing that can be done on a large scale (VII, ch. 18, 24, 31, 36, 37).Many things could be done on a large scale. For example, it could be studied which elements in the environment tend to reduce primary productivity (and, consequently, total suffering). In addition, the human practices that contribute to natural processes maximizing the number of births (and, consequently, suffering) could be avoided. This alone would enormously reduce the number of animals who would be born only to suffer.
There is no way to help them all. Hence, we should not help any. (VII, ch. 25).Yes, it is true that there is no way to help them all. But for each animal helped, the help makes all the difference. There is also no way to help all domesticated animals, or all humans, but that does not imply that we should not help them. Something like this is said only in the case of helping nonhuman animals because of the prevalence of speciesism. None of us would refuse to be helped just because it is not possible to help everyone in need. Therefore, such a position violates impartiality.
We should first solve the problems that humans cause animals. If we cannot even solve the problems that humans cause animals, how much less can we solve the harms caused by natural processes. (VII, ch. 25).If our goal is to help as efficiently as possible, we should not base ourselves on the origin of the harm (whether or not it is caused by humans), but on the amount of benefit that could be produced with each strategy. It is not necessary to solve all (or even any) of the problems caused by humans in order to do something for animals who are victims of natural processes. Helping animals who are victims of natural processes is not necessarily harder than helping animals who are victims of human practices. In fact, in some cases it may be easier, since there may be less resistance. What we should do is investigate where our resources, if applied, would produce the greater good (for example, would help more victims, or would help those in the worst situation, etc.), and not investigate whether the harm originated in human practices or in natural processes.
The problem has so many victims that, even if we managed to help on a large scale, it would still be a small percentage of the problem (VII, ch. 25).The percentage does not matter; what matters is the actual amount of benefit we could produce. For example, suppose that with the same resource we can either help 90% of the animals in problem A or help to the same extent 0.1% of the animals in problem B (who are all in a situation as bad as that of the animals in problem A). If we are guided by the percentage, we will help the 90%. But suppose problem A involves a trillion animals and problem B a quadrillion. The point is: 90% of a trillion is 900 billion, whereas 0.1% of a quadrillion is a trillion. Solving 0.1% of problem B means helping 100 billion more animals with the same resource.
It is hard to predict long-term consequences. Helping could make things even worse. Better not to try to help. (VII, ch. 24).If it is hard to predict long-term consequences, then we cannot know for certain that not helping has the best consequences. What we would have to do is research ever more thoroughly how interactions in ecosystems take place (among animals and between them and their surroundings). By doing so, our knowledge of the probability of long-term knock-on consequences would keep increasing, which would make it possible to plan ever safer and more efficient programs of help.
Nature already balances itself, and this coincides with what is best for animals. Better not to intervene. (VII, ch. 24).In fact, populations naturally fluctuate enormously, almost always irregularly. Moreover, a situation can be stable and yet terribly bad for the animals affected. For example, situations in which, over generations, an average of only two offspring per brood survive are balanced in this sense, but, given the enormous size of the broods, it is also a scenario in which suffering and premature deaths are maximized.
But if there were less balance, there would be even more suffering (VII, ch. 24).Not necessarily. Everything depends on how the degree of balance or imbalance would influence other factors that directly affect animals (such as the number of births and in which species, the availability of food and shelter, the amount of disease and conflict, etc.). Thus, if the goal is what is best for animals, we should investigate these factors directly, and not the degree of balance. Moreover, since ecosystems tend to settle into balance at high levels of plant and animal productivity, disturbances probably tend to reduce, rather than increase, suffering.
We should not help these animals because doing so would prevent the best-adapted genes from prevailing. (VII, ch. 23).The traits most efficient at passing genes on do not necessarily benefit their bearers or their offspring. For example, the trait of maximizing the number of offspring is very efficient at maximizing genetic transmission, but being born a member of a species that reproduces in this way means having one's chances of survival drastically reduced. Moreover, the amount of natural suffering and death is so enormous that, even if helping animals meant that members of future generations would not have the best-adapted genes possible, this would still probably have a far less negative balance than letting nature take its course. Furthermore, various forms of intervention would not prevent the best-adapted genes from prevailing, as is the case with sterilization and with research into which kinds of elements in the environment result in fewer births in species whose members commonly have negative lives. Finally, if what the objection proposes were acceptable, all of us should be left to our own fate so that only the best-adapted humans would pass their genes on.
This proposal cannot be scientifically well informed. (VII, ch. 19, 27).Data from the science of ecology have been used predominantly to achieve anthropocentric and environmentalist goals, but they could also be used to guide programs aimed at preventing animal suffering. Moreover, as the field of welfare biology32 developed (which would study animals in their environments from the standpoint of what affects them positively or negatively, and not as components of ecosystems or specimens of species), there would be more and more data that could scientifically inform programs of help.
We are in no position to know when a life is or is not worth living. We may think a life is not worth living and be mistaken. Hence, it is better not to intervene. (VII, ch. 32).Imagine we were offered the chance to be reborn to live a life full of extreme suffering. If we could not judge that such a life is not worth living, we would be unsure whether or not it was worth accepting the offer. The situation of the vast majority of animals in the wild is of this kind. In response, it could be objected that, even if someone's life has been dreadful up to a certain point, it is still possible to improve it. This is true, but then it is a reason to try to help wild animals. Moreover, the goal of improving the lives of beings who already exist does not imply rejecting the goal of preventing new births. This is because the greater the number of births, the harder it is to improve the life of each of the individuals born.
If the lives of wild animals are full of suffering, helping them would merely prolong their agony. Better not to intervene. (VII, ch. 33).The fact that their lives are full of suffering is due to their being in an environment where the conditions for surviving for long are completely unfavorable. If we create conditions for them to survive longer, the chances that they will have a meaningful life increase. Prolonging their lives results in something worse (than their dying) only if we do nothing to prevent other forms of suffering to which they will be subject. Moreover, what causes them suffering generally also causes their death. If we offer treatment for such ills, we will be prolonging their lives, but also increasing their levels of well-being. In addition, it is also false that all interventions prolong animals' lives: many merely prevent new births.
This proposal should be rejected because it would entail prohibiting the treatment of parasitism (since doing so would kill many to save just one). (VII, ch. 30).When the parasites are not sentient and the host is, even if treating the parasitism results in more deaths, the resulting situation is better, since death is not a harm for such parasites. In the case of sentient parasites, it would have to be assessed whether their lives would be minimally meaningful. If they would not (and it is not possible to make them so), then death is not a greater harm for them than remaining alive. Even if in a given case the parasites would be more harmed by dying, and the right decision is not to treat the host, there could still be no objection whatsoever to preventing future cases of parasitism (for example, through sterilization), since failing to produce new beings is not the equivalent of killing beings who already exist. Moreover, not treating parasitism would probably result in a greater number of deaths and more suffering over time. Almost all parasites reproduce by maximizing the number of offspring. If they are sentient, the result is also the maximization of deaths and suffering for the members of those species themselves. Not treating the host will result in the parasites continuing to reproduce and infect new victims. This gives us reasons not only to treat victims of parasitism who are already infected, but above all to prevent parasitism in general. Thus, it is false that the proposal to prevent natural harms would prohibit treating cases of parasitism.
The situation may have a positive balance: the pleasure of the few animals who live long may outweigh the combined suffering of the vast majority. (VII, ch. 34).Suppose the total balance were positive. The reasons to reduce suffering do not diminish because of this. For example, the reasons to help humans starving in poor countries do not weaken just because there are affluent humans in rich countries. Moreover, even those who believe that all that matters is the total balance have reasons to prioritize eliminating suffering, since an extra unit of resources produces greater increases in well-being the worse the situation of whoever would receive it. Thus, prioritizing improving the situation of those in a negative situation is more efficient for increasing the total balance.
The debate on the expansion of nature
The proposal that aims to prevent the suffering of wild animals arising from natural causes implies that expanding natural territory (forests, for example) is something negative. That is why it is absurd. We should expand natural territory because sentient beings need it as a resource. (VII, ch. 37).Concern for sentient beings (of the current and/or future generations) would not approve of expansion, since the number of beings who would be born only to suffer would always be much greater than the number of those alive now or of those who would be born to have positive lives and would need the environment as a resource. The only way to defend expansion is from a view according to which a world history with a greater amount of suffering and premature deaths of sentient beings is better. But this is very hard to defend. It could be objected that expanding natural territory may be necessary to prevent the extinction of humans, who are the only ones who can prevent natural harms. This is an important concern, but it is also possible that the human presence will come to have a negative balance in the future. For example, if humanity develops space colonization in the future, it would recreate in many other places the natural processes that result in the maximization of suffering and deaths. Therefore, it is uncertain whether the human presence will have a positive or negative balance over the course of history. Moreover, even if we should prevent human extinction, this does not necessarily imply expanding natural territory, since there are ways to prevent climate change without creating new environments such as forests. One example is pursuing energy efficiency and renewable energy. In short, the cases in which expansion could be justified are those in which all the other options would result in something even worse. If such cases exist at all, they are a small fraction of the practices of expanding natural territory.
Simulation of the debate on the destruction of nature
Does the proposal to reduce the suffering of wild animals imply altruistic killing? That is, does it imply destroying natural habitats (for example, through urbanization)? (VII, ch. 36).There is disagreement among proponents of reducing wild animal suffering about whether or not there is such an implication. Below is a simulated debate summarizing the main arguments on each side.
Against destruction For destruction
By destroying nature (for example, through urbanization), we will harm many animals. The ideal would be to reduce births, and to carry out vaccinations, treatment of diseases, etc.Waiting for nonlethal solutions (which may take a long time, or may never come about) would entail the death and suffering of many more animals than altruistic killing.
Advocating altruistic killing would make people think that consideration for animals is absurd. The effect of this would be worse than the effect of waiting for nonlethal solutions, since it would lead humans to increase the harms they cause animals.Even if advocating altruistic killing influenced humans to increase the harms they cause animals, the destruction of habitats would prevent much more suffering and death than the sum of all the harms that humans cause.
So far, the harms that humans cause are smaller than natural harms, but this may change in the future if humans expand natural territory on Earth or beyond it. If altruistic killing contributes to wild animal suffering being neglected even more, and this results in the expansion of nature, then altruistic killing would be worse than waiting for nonlethal solutions.This shows only that we should not advocate altruistic killing, but not that it should not be carried out (for example, urbanization could continue). Moreover, if the greater risk is that humans will expand natural territory, then this risk is greater if we hold that it is always wrong to destroy natural territory. Altruistic killing makes it very clear that expanding natural territory is not something good.
If humanity already tends to expand urbanization, there is no need to advocate altruistic killing and, since advocating it also carries risks, it is better not to advocate it.Perhaps, but we could still encourage research into which land uses are most likely to have a positive balance for animals. We could encourage these changes and also changes in consumption practices, as is done with regard to animal exploitation.
The idea behind altruistic killing is so far removed from common sense that it would hardly be accepted (it would only create rejection of the proposal to reduce the suffering of wild animals). That is why the risk of advocating it is so high. Thus, it is better to maintain an absolute rule against the destruction of natural habitats.If we explain to the public that fewer habitats mean less suffering and death, this may reduce enthusiasm for conservationist policies and for policies expanding natural territory. Suspending such policies involves no expense and requires no activity at all, so it may be easier for the public to accept this than interventions to reduce suffering.
Proponents of destruction may be optimistically biased regarding the probabilities of the consequences of altruistic killing. They may be biased in this way because killing offers a quick solution. This may lead them to neglect the possible negative consequences arising from how it will influence the decisions of future agents.An aversion to violent interventions may lead us to assess the probabilities of consequences in a biased way. Moreover, the harms in the case of altruistic killing would occur through action, and in the case of waiting for nonlethal solutions they would occur through omission (but they could be much greater). Thus, we should be suspicious of the preference for waiting for nonlethal solutions.

In chapters 6, 7, and 8 we have seen, in very summarized form, a general overview of the debate on the ethical implications of the harms animals suffer as a result of natural processes. As you will have noticed, it is a debate full of nuances, with questions that greatly challenge the common perception of this subject. That is why it is well worth thinking about these questions calmly and with an open mind before rejecting or accepting a given position. As mentioned, Volume VII of this collection discusses each of these topics in detail, and contains many other pointers to materials that expand the discussion even further.

Author’s notes

  1. For a list of programs of help already being carried out, see Animal Ethics (2023 [2020], p. 69-97). ↩
  2. On welfare biology, see Faria and Horta (2020) and Soryl et. al. (2021). ↩

9. What Criteria Should We Use to Help Efficiently?

Suppose our goal is to make the world a less bad place, and that we want to do so as efficiently as possible. What criteria can we use to select: (1) which causes to prioritize, (2) which problems to prioritize within these causes, and (3) to choose strategies? Below is a list of criteria that have been proposed33.

Criteria Explanation
Severity of the situation. (VIII, ch. 1.2).It is usually measured by taking into account both of the following factors: (1) The number of victims (2) How bad each victim's situation is
When one problem has more victims, but in another the victims are in a worse situation, how should we proceed? (VIII, ch. 1.2; XI, ch. 1.6 and 7).One possibility is to ask: (1) How much worse does the minority's situation need to be for them to have priority? (2) How much larger does the number of victims who are not in the worst situation need to be for them to have priority? However, there are several other possibilities, which are addressed in: VIII, ch. 1.2; XI, ch. 1.6, 7.
Tractability of the problem. (VIII, ch. 1.3).Example. Problem A: 900,000 victims. Problem B: 500,000 victims. The victims of A and B are in equally bad situations. By the severity of the situation, we should prioritize A. But suppose that, with the resources we have, we can either help 400,000 victims of A or help to the same extent 450,000 victims of B. Thus, although A is a worse situation, it is B that presents the worse situation that can be improved.
Degree of neglect. (VIII, ch. 1.7).The greater the number of people already involved in trying to solve a problem, the greater the probability that the problem will be minimized without our help. And the more neglected a cause, the more difference each additional person makes, since there are still many easy opportunities to make a significant difference that have not yet been tried.
Size of the benefit to be brought about. (VIII, ch. 1.4).Imagine that problem A has 100 victims with suffering of -50 and problem B has 90 victims with suffering of -40. That is, A is more serious. Both problems are equally neglected, and it is possible to help all the victims of one or the other. However, imagine that, with the same amount of resources, we can either move all the victims of A from -50 to -49 (a very slight relief), or move all the victims of B from -40 to -10 (considerable relief). By prioritizing B we would bring about a greater good with the same amount of resources.
Is the size of the benefit always the most important factor? (VIII, ch. 1.4).Suppose that, in the example above, the decision were between either moving the 100 victims of A from -50 to -30 (total benefit = 2,000, 20 per victim) or moving the 90 victims of B from -40 to -10 (total benefit = 2,700, 30 per victim). In this case, some people would say that we should choose the first option (since the benefit goes to the victims in the worst situation and benefits a larger number of victims), even though with the second option we would produce a greater benefit (for each victim and in total).
How do we know when the size of the benefit weighs more and when the severity of the situation weighs more? (VIII, ch. 1.2; XI, ch. 1.6 and 7).There are several possibilities. For example: (1) establishing that one of the aspects is a trump (absolute or up to a certain point); (2) a continuous relationship: there are no trumps, and each aspect has either a fixed weight (equal or different) or a variable weight in the overall calculation; (3) combining approaches 1 and 2: using trumps (absolute or up to a certain point) up to a cutoff line and from there on using a continuous relationship (with fixed or variable weight). An example of a continuous approach (without trumps), with each aspect having variable weight, is the approach with diminishing returns, in which the weight of each aspect decreases proportionally as it is filled. One possibility along these lines would be to seek to maximize benefits, but to establish that a unit of benefit has more value the more serious the problem toward which that benefit would be directed.
Why is it crucial to try to estimate long-term effects? (VIII, ch. 1.5)When two strategies are compared, it is possible that one brings about more benefits initially, but that, taking into account the complete history (and therefore the long-term effects), it is the other that will bring about a greater total benefit. It is also possible that a strategy brings about great benefits in the short term but has negative effects in the long term, and may even have a negative total balance.
Why prioritize strategies that tackle the causes (and not only the symptoms)? (VIII, ch. 1.5 and 1.6)For example, if we compare a strategy that helps many animals if they are caught in a fire with another that prevents fires, the second probably has the better impact over time. That is why fighting speciesism has great potential for positive impact over time, since it directly tackles one of the main causes of the problems affecting animals (since speciesism leads people to attach little importance to the situation of animals, whether exploited or wild).

10. Which Problems Affect the Largest Numbers of Animals?

Below, we will look at the problems that affect the largest numbers of animals34

10.1. Exploited animals

Animal advocates, wishing to show how large the number of animals killed for consumption is, often say that around 80 billion animals are killed worldwide each year. However, this figure refers only to mammals and birds. The total number of animals killed is vastly larger. Below are some data on annual deaths of exploited animals at the global level.

Type of exploited animal Animals killed worldwide per year
Mammals and birds35Around 80 billion
Factory-farmed fishBetween 51 and 167 billion36.
Fish caught directly at seaBetween 787 billion and 2.3 trillion37.
Aquatic animals used as feed for fish farmed for consumption38Between 462 billion and 1.1 trillion.
Factory-farmed crustaceansBetween 255 and 604 billion39.
Silkworms for silk production40Between 420 billion and 1 trillion
Insects killed for consumption41Between 2 and 3.2 trillion
Cochineal insects in the production of carmine dyeBetween 4.6 and 21 trillion42.
Shrimp caught directly at seaAround 25 trillion43

The sum of these numbers suggests that somewhere between 34 and 54 trillion animals are killed annually at the global level. This means that the 80 billion usually mentioned by activists represent only somewhere between 0.1% and 0.2% of the animals killed in exploitation.

10.2. Animals in the wild

There are no statistics on the number of animals in the wild who die each year as a result of natural processes. But to get an idea of the difference in proportion, we can make a comparison with the populations at a given moment.

  • The total population of sentient animals in the wild at a given moment would be, according to certain estimates, between 1 and 10 quintillion individuals44.
  • Let us compare this, for example, with the world population at a given moment of animals bred as stock to be exploited (a total population of 434 billion):
  • Terrestrial vertebrates: 24 billion45.
  • Fish: 180 billion46.
  • Shrimp: 230 billion47.
  • Total: 434 billion.

How much larger is 1 to 10 quintillion compared to 434 billion? These numbers are so enormous that it is hard to visualize the difference. So, to understand it, it is useful to make an analogy with the span of a year. The combined populations of animals bred to be exploited would represent at most 14 seconds of the year. All the rest of the year (364 days, 23 hours, 59 minutes, and 46 seconds) would be the animals in the wild. This gives us a rough sense of how large the number of animals in the wild is. As we have seen, the vast majority of these animals have lives in which suffering greatly predominates.

10.3. The future

These numbers, both of animals harmed by human practices and of those harmed by natural processes, may become astronomically larger in the future. That is why, in recent years, the debate on the importance of how our decisions affect the long-term future has been growing, as we will see in the next chapter.

11. Key Concepts in the Debate on the Importance of the Future

11.1. What are s-risks?

Today, an enormous number of animals suffer intensely, and in many cases in ways that did not exist in the past. Likewise, in the future new ways of harming sentient beings on a massive scale may arise, on a scale astronomically larger than that of the suffering existing today. A key concept in this debate is that of s-risks48:

  • S-risks: risks that events will occur in the future resulting in suffering of enormous magnitude, exceeding all the suffering that has existed on Earth so far49.

11.2. Differences between s-risks and x-risks

X-risks are about risks of the annihilation of humanity. S-risks are about scenarios with astronomical suffering. There are s-risks that are not x-risks, since there are forms of suffering inflicted on nonhuman sentient beings that do not threaten humanity50.

11.3. How do we measure the seriousness of an s-risk?

The seriousness of an s-risk is measured by multiplying how bad the scenario would be by its probability of occurring (the result is its expected disvalue, or ED)51.

The following table shows some examples of s-risks.

11.4. Examples of s-risks

Examples of s-risks
Example Explanation
An increase in animal exploitation (IX, ch. 1.8.1).Examples: (1) Expanding it in scale (that is, affecting a larger number of sentient beings). (2) Making it qualitatively worse (that is, increasing the harms suffered by each animal). (3) Creating new ways in which it can take place.
An expansion of wild animal suffering (IX, ch. 1.8.2).This may occur because of an increase in the number of animals on Earth or because of the intentional or accidental spread of life beyond it52.
The creation of new forms of sentience (IX, ch. 1.8.3).One example would be the creation of nonbiological forms of sentience. Such beings, although sentient, might not have faces, nor move or scream. So it may be hard to feel empathy for them. It may also happen that a digital entity is sentient and we do not notice. Enormous numbers of these beings may come to exist in the future, since creating them for certain purposes could involve lower costs than creating biological sentient beings.

11.5. The concepts of speciesism and substratism

Just as speciesism is discrimination based on the species to which someone belongs, substratism is discrimination based on the kind of substrate that makes up a being's body (for example, whether it is organic or non-organic). Just as anthropocentrism is a form of speciesism (against those who do not belong to the human species), carbonism is a form of substratism (against those who are not organic). Substratism, just like speciesism, may produce suffering in astronomical quantities in the future53. That is why it is important to emphasize that animals should be considered because they are sentient (and not because they are animals or because they are living beings), and that this implies considering other, non-organic sentient beings, should they come to exist.

11.6. Classification of s-risks

S-risks can be classified in terms of various aspects54. Here are some examples:

Classification of s-risks according to how they arise55
Type They occur... Examples
IncidentalWhen ways of achieving a certain goal generate a great deal of suffering, but without the suffering being sought for its own sake. The agents may even prefer an alternative without suffering, but not be willing to pay the costs.Suffering as an effect of high productivity (as in factory farming) or of obtaining information (as in animal experimentation).
Agential When the agent wishes to cause the harm as an end.Sadistic agents, or harm as an effect of feelings of hatred between groups.
Natural They arise without the action of agents.Suffering resulting from the way natural processes take place.
Examples of other classifications of s-risks56
Classification Explanation
Known and unknownThis depends on whether or not we can imagine them today (just as people in the Middle Ages would not have imagined that the atomic bomb would appear, for example).
Unknown s-risks according to how they arise
IncidentalWhen unknown mechanisms will lead to incidental s-risks.
AgentialAgents may in the future come to have reasons to cause harm that we do not yet know about.
NaturalThe universe may already contain much more suffering than we imagine.

12. Identifying Risk Factors for S-Risks

One of the objections to concern with s-risks is the difficulty of estimating the long-term consequences of our decisions. One answer to this objection is to point to the possibility of investigating risk factors, which are not themselves s-risks but greatly increase their likelihood or severity57. The concept of a risk factor is already widely used in medicine. For example, eating poorly and not exercising are not, in themselves, diseases, but they greatly increase the probability of various diseases, even if they do not necessarily entail them. To know that it is good to avoid these risk factors, it is not necessary to know what each individual's health trajectory will be. Similarly, even if it is hard to estimate what the long-term future will be like, we can try to identify risk factors for s-risks and the actions that would help avoid them.

Some risk factors for s-risks

  • Disregard for nonhuman sentient beings.
  • Disregard for nonbiological sentient beings.
  • Demand for products and services whose production harms sentient beings.
  • Human expansion and increased technological power.
  • Technological progress is much faster than moral progress.

Below are other examples and an explanation of why they are risk factors:

Factor Why it is a risk factor
Advanced technology (IX, ch. 8.2.)Many s-risks are possible only because of new technologies. Examples: (1) Creating digital sentient beings could result in enormous amounts of suffering because of disregard for nonbiological sentient beings. (2) Space colonization could vastly multiply the population of sentient beings, who would be subject to the decisions of agents and to natural processes. There are between 100 and 400 billion stars in our galaxy, and between 100 and 200 billion galaxies in the universe. Without space colonization, suffering would remain limited to that on Earth (which is already enormous, but tiny compared to what could arise).
Aversion to technology (IX, ch. 8.3).Technology also offers opportunities to reduce suffering. If technological progress were halted, this would prevent the emergence of s-risks caused by humans, but not natural s-risks (and it would also mean there was no technology to prevent these other s-risks).
Lack of efforts to reduce s-risks (IX, ch. 8.5).We can prevent s-risks only if enough people care about it. Perhaps an enormous number of people is not necessary. Even if this number is not very large, these people can seek compromises with people who have other focuses (but who are not opposed to preventing s-risks), and try to get people who have more resources, power, or influence to want to prevent s-risks.
Ineffective efforts to reduce s-risks. (IX, ch. 8.6).Wanting to reduce s-risks is not enough. The efforts need to be well planned. Some risks related to these possibilities are: (1) If the cause of reducing s-risks becomes associated with highly controversial ideas, this may generate strong rejection. (2) It is possible that the relevant decision-makers want to prevent s-risks, but political institutions are ineffective or there are cooperation problems. (3) Decision-makers may fail to notice certain s-risks in their early stages and, by the time they do, it may already be too late.
Polarization, conflict, and hostility (IX, ch. 8.7 and 11).Large-scale polarization leaves little room for reflection (on s-risks or anything else) and for mutual compromise. It also has the potential to result in conflicts and even wars, which increases the chances of agential s-risks.
Lack of security against malevolent agents (IX, ch. 8.8).Malevolent individuals pose serious risks when they reach positions of power, which is not uncommon, since they have a strong desire for power and their personality gives them advantages in this pursuit. These risks increase if such agents have access to advanced technology. There are possible future scenarios in which ways of containing these agents (such as laws and moral norms) could be ineffective or insufficient (for example, in a future with powerful autonomous AIs and/or with space colonization).

As in the medical context, these catastrophes are more likely to occur if several risk factors coincide. Likewise, the chances of preventing them increase if several forms of prevention coincide. We will discuss the forms of prevention below.

13. Longtermist Strategies: Broad and Targeted

If our goal is for our decisions to have the best impact for all sentient beings, we need to take their long-term impact into account58. In this regard, there are two main groups of longtermist strategies: broad and targeted.

Strategy Broad Targeted
What it consists of Trying to have the best possible impact across a wide variety of scenarios.Trying to have the best possible impact in specific scenarios.
Advantage They will have a positive impact in a great many scenarios, perhaps in almost all of them.They can have a very large impact if the scenario they address occurs.
Disadvantage This impact is smaller than that of targeted strategies when the scenario for which those are designed occurs.They may have a very small or even no impact if other scenarios occur.

The following tables show some examples of broad and targeted strategies:

Examples of broad strategies
TypeExample
Increasing consideration for sentient beings. (IX, ch. 9.3.1).
• Advocating the moral consideration of all sentient beings (focusing on the most neglected, such as aquatic animals and invertebrates, and new forms of sentience that may arise in the future).
• Addressing all causes of harm to sentient beings (whether those caused by their exploitation, those due to their situation in the wild as a result of natural processes, or others that may come to exist in the future).
• Promoting institutional changes that reinforce the changes in attitude achieved and make future regressions harder.
Increasing our capacity for action in the future (IX, ch. 9.3.2).
• Spreading concern for the long-term future and for s-risks (this will lead more people to work on these topics).
• Trying to increase the resources of people interested in preventing future suffering.
• Increasing our knowledge about the long term. This will allow us to: (1) better understand how to plan strategies; (2) identify strategies not yet considered; and (3) clarify which of the available strategies have the greatest potential.
Examples of targeted strategies
TypeExample
Focus on avoiding animal exploitation (IX, ch. 9.4.1).
• Preventing new forms of animal exploitation (for example, by banning new forms of exploiting invertebrates for consumption).
• Developing proteins and materials of non-animal origin to replace those of animal origin.
• Trying to prevent artificial intelligence from being used to improve the efficiency of animal exploitation.
Focus on avoiding the suffering of wild animals (IX, ch. 9.4.2).
• Creating and consolidating the field of welfare biology59.
• Establishing regulations for space exploration so as to avoid the intentional or accidental spread of life beyond planet Earth (even nonsentient life, since over a long time it could evolve and give rise to sentient beings).
Focus on consideration for new forms of sentience (IX, ch. 9.4.3).
• Trying to prevent the engineering of new forms of sentience, both biological and nonbiological.
• Trying to secure legal rights for nonbiological sentient entities.
• Pursuing a non-anthropocentric alignment of artificial intelligence (that is, ensuring that artificial intelligence does not have anthropocentric values).

Precautions when choosing longtermist strategies

We have seen some examples of strategies for preventing long-term suffering. Below are some precautions we should take when choosing them60:

Risk Precaution
Underestimating the complexity of the questionGiven the uncertainty about the future, remember that there is probably no single, conclusive answer. We should always remain open to revising our beliefs about which strategies are best, and be prepared to change strategy if necessary.
Cognitive biases may lead us to trust certain approaches too much and to dismiss others prematurely. We tend to neglect the possible negative effects of the approaches we initially sympathize with and the possible positive effects of the approaches we initially do not sympathize with.Remember that we may be biased in our assessments, cultivate epistemic humility, and always seek new information.
Certain approaches carry a high risk of leading people who have other priorities to reject reducing s-risksIt is better to advocate goals that can be accepted by a wide range of perspectives.

We will see more about this last point in the next section.

14. Changing Public Debate and Political Institutions

In what follows, the term politics will be used in a broad sense, encompassing both institutions and public debate. Dysfunctional politics can encourage polarization, hinder efforts to reduce s-risks, increase the risk of malevolent agents coming to power, and, at the extreme, can even prevent discussion of any ethical question at all61.

Thus, trying to improve politics (both in terms of institutions and in terms of the level of public debate) is crucial for avoiding s-risks. Below are some strategies to this end.

Strategies for improving public debate and institutions
Strategy Explanation
Thinking in terms of nuance – and not in terms of “0 or 1,” “us vs. them,” etc. (IX, ch. 11.3, 11.4)If we try to think in terms of the positive and negative points of each perspective, and think in terms of degrees of confidence rather than rigid certainties, we can avoid a “0 or 1,” “us and them” kind of mindset. Tribalism creates an appearance of great disagreement even when disagreement is limited. Reducing tribalism opens the door to cooperation and mutual compromise.
Discussing the argument, whoever made it. That is, avoiding the ad hominem and appeal to authority fallacies. (IX, ch. 11.4).The general tendency is that, if the person who made the argument belongs to “our side” or to the group we want to defend, their argument is accepted even if they are wrong, and if they belong to the “other side,” it is rejected even if the argument is sound and points to a serious problem with our view. This tendency has prevented serious debate on any question, even in academic circles. One way to avoid this tendency is to discuss arguments without knowing who their proponents are (or, if this is not possible, to try to imagine what we would think if we did not know).
Intellectual honesty (IX, ch. 11.4).Discussing arguments in a serious and intellectually honest way, without distorting the position and arguments of those who disagree, and recognizing that we may be mistaken about many things.
Adopting an inclusive approach. (VIII, ch. 5; IX, ch. 11.5).This consists in emphasizing that the goals we want to achieve can be accepted even if people disagree with us on other points. This reduces polarization (since it shows that, despite disagreements, there can be common goals). Goals such as consideration for all sentient beings, the prevention of s-risks and of wild animal suffering, and the rejection of speciesism and substratism can be accepted without our having to accept a specific view, whether in ethics or in politics. Emphasizing this increases the potential for these goals to be accepted by people holding the most varied ethical and political positions. Another example: improving political culture and institutions is good not only for reducing s-risks, but for several other goals (which increases the likelihood of cooperation).
Protecting democracy. (IX, ch. 11.6).Democracy prevents any single individual from gaining too much power, and so reduces the influence of malevolent agents. In terms of s-risks, it is more important to avoid institutional catastrophes than to try to achieve the best possible institutions. For example, in terms of s-risks, the difference between a democracy and a totalitarian regime is much greater than that between a functioning democracy and a flawed democracy. Modern liberal democracies offer protection for human rights and civil liberties, such as freedom of expression, which are a precondition for raising ethical concerns.
Political representation of all sentient beings. (IX, ch. 11.6).Trying to establish representatives for sentient beings who cannot represent themselves (such as nonhuman animals and future sentient beings, whether future animals or possible sentient beings in digital media).
Why even a small improvement would make a big difference. (IX, ch. 11.7).The current situation (of institutions and of public debate) is so bad that even a marginal improvement would be very beneficial. It is realistic to hope that we will be less biased and tribal, that institutions will work better, and that we will rely more on considered values and evidence, even if we cannot change most of the picture. Modest, continuous improvements can, after a long enough time, make a big difference.

Author’s notes

  1. For a detailed discussion of this topic, see Baumann (2022, p. 65-76) and Vinding (2022). ↩

15. Debates on Activism Strategies

Another topic whose discussion has grown considerably in recent years is the efficiency of different kinds of strategies in animal advocacy62. The following table illustrates some debates about the degree of efficiency of different activism strategies. Important: this debate is not necessarily about “this strategy or that one?” It may be about how much to focus on one or the other. A further discussion is whether it would be better for everyone to focus on certain strategies (and whether or not always to focus on the same one), or to have different people focusing on different strategies, and to compensate according to how little a strategy has been tried.

Some debates on various activism strategies
What is at issue Main argument of the conflicting positions
Should we focus on advocating veganism or reduced consumption? (VIII, ch. 9).For a focus on reduction. It may be easier to get many more people to reduce their consumption than to accept becoming vegan. Many more people doing less may have a better impact for animals than a few people doing a lot.For a focus on veganism. Advocating reduction may give the impression that animal exploitation is acceptable. Even if fewer people adopt veganism than reduction, the total impact may be better for animals if these people are more engaged in activism.
Should we advocate the reform of animal exploitation so that animals suffer less, or only its abolition? (VIII, ch. 10,11)For reform. Regulating animal exploitation may reduce the suffering of exploited animals and may help to abolish it gradually, since it may make the public increasingly concerned about what happens to animals.Against reform. Since animals are items of property, laws requiring that they suffer less will hardly have any effect if they reduce profits. The public may mistakenly think that the animals are suffering less, and this may increase demand and thus increase the number of animals exploited
In activism against the consumption of animals, should we focus on the harm to animals, or should we also talk about environmental impacts and health risks (that is, indirect arguments)? (VIII, ch. 4).For indirect arguments. For the animals, the motive does not matter; what matters is that people stop exploiting them. Moreover, many people defend animal exploitation not because they believe it is just, but because they like the taste of animal-based food. Thus, if they give up consuming animals, for whatever reason, it will be easier for them later to take a stand against animal exploitation.Against indirect arguments. Different motives have different consequences for animals. Indirect arguments may reinforce the idea that the harm to animals is not enough to make animal exploitation unjust. Moreover, appealing to anthropocentric and environmentalist arguments may reinforce these views and make it harder for people to care about other, even greater harms to animals (as in the case of animals in the wild and s-risks63).
When talking about sentient beings, should we talk only about nonhumans, or about human problems as well? (VIII, ch., 4,6,8)For a broad focus. Addressing human problems may lead other social movements to be more accepting of the animal advocacy movement, as they come to see that there are common goals (consideration for all sentient beings).For a focus on animals. The vast majority of people already focus on human problems and neglect the situation of animals. That is why there are reasons to emphasize the situation of animals, since the resources for the animal cause are much more limited and it is much more neglected.
Focus on social change or technological change? (VIII, ch. 7, 12, IX, ch. 9).For technological change. Certain technologies may make the use of animals obsolete (for example, cultivated meat), and this may benefit animals even if people do not consider them.For social change. What will determine whether technology is used to cause suffering or to prevent it are the values people hold.
Focus on the general population or on people with influence and power?For a focus on people with influence and power. A smaller number of such people may have a greater impact than a majority.For a focus on the general population. Most changes will need the support of a large number of people (whether social or institutional changes).
Focus on changes in behavior or in attitude? For behavioral change. Practical changes are more engaging. They can also break down resistance to changes in attitude.For attitude change. It is hard for people to change their behavior toward animals if they do not change what they think about them.
How confrontational/ accommodating should the approach be? For confrontational action. Confrontational action draws attention to the problem.Against confrontational action. Confrontational action may generate rejection.
Focus on social changes or on institutional changes? For a focus on institutional changes. Most social movements that have grown (such as environmentalism, for example) did so by pursuing institutional changes. Moreover, for an institutional change to take effect, fewer people need to be convinced than for a social change to take effect. Finally, focusing on institutional changes emphasizes that this is not a matter of “personal choice,” but that there should be laws requiring everyone to respect animals.For a focus on social changes. Since animals are property under the law, it is hard to achieve an institutional change that actually protects them. What would have to be done is to remove them from the category of items of property. But for this to happen, many people need to call for such a change. Thus, social change is necessary for institutional change. Moreover, for institutional changes to actually be complied with, a change is needed in the way people regard animals.

  1. For a detailed summary of these and other debates, see Reese (2019). ↩
  2. One study suggests that people who stop consuming animal products for environmentalist reasons become more resistant to the proposal to help animals in the wild. See Greig (2017). ↩

16. Evaluating Different Strategies

Are there metacriteria that could be used to evaluate different strategies64? On the basis of the theoretical grounding we saw in chapter 9, we can derive some metacriteria. For example, we can always ask, for each strategy:

  • Does it tackle the cause of the problem or only its symptoms?
  • What is its potential to prevent the risk of setbacks?
  • How much/how little has it already been tried?
  • If it has already been tried, what is its implementation track record?
  • How many animals would it potentially benefit?
  • How much would each affected animal benefit?
  • What is its potential to facilitate later changes?
  • How great is the risk of negative knock-on effects?
  • What is its cost/benefit ratio?
  • Does it run the risk of producing low gains or even none?
  • How large is the positive balance that can be expected over time.
  • Potential for acceptance/rejection.
  • What is its degree of alignment/conflict with other goals?
  • Ease/difficulty of implementation
  • What is the degree of expectation regarding its success?
  • Does its success depend on other strategies being carried out?

Some challenges for further developments would be the following:

(1) It would have to be investigated whether all the parameters above should be included or not, and whether there are other important parameters that should be added to the list above.

(2) It would have to be investigated whether it is possible to offer an overall result, in terms of how much more/less promising one strategy is relative to another, taking all the parameters into account together, or whether such an assessment is possible only with respect to each

parameter separately, it not being possible to commensurate them.

(3) If the aim is to produce an overall comparison commensurating the various parameters, it would have to be investigated whether all the parameters should have the same weight, or whether there are some that should weigh more than others (and, if so, what their relative weight should be). It would also have to be investigated whether this weight would be fixed or variable and, if variable, how it should vary65.

(4) Investigating the possibility of obtaining objective data on how each type of strategy scores on each parameter.

  2. These questions were addressed in detail in Volume XI, ch. 1.6 and 7. ↩

17. Conclusion

In this material we have tried to present a general overview of the main questions discussed in the field of animal ethics. Obviously, for reasons of space, many important questions have been left out. We believe, however, that the material offers a good introductory foundation for those who later wish to go deeper and to have solid grounding for better understanding these and other questions.
